Shamonda virus: first human case is ‘an alert’, not a reason to panic, says EU health agency
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:54:42 UTC
22:54:42 KST

The first human case of Shamonda virus, confirmed in France, poses no wider threat to Europeans, the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) told Euronews.
Europe’s public health authorities need to be aware of the first human case of Shamonda virus confirmed in France, but not “panic,” the ECDC told Euronews, as investigations into the patient’s death continue.
French authorities confirmed on Thursday a Shamonda virus infection in a patient in Lyon who died in early October, marking the first time the virus, previously seen only in animals, mainly cattle, has been reported in a human.
“This is a very special case,” Tamás Bakonyi, principal expert on vector-borne and zoonotic diseases and one health-related issues at the ECDC, told Euronews.
The affected patient had leukaemia and was “severely immunocompromised,” making it easier for the virus to infect the person. “The whole process of viral infections or other kinds of infections are behaving differently in those [immunocompromised] individuals than in healthy people,” Bakonyi said.
While it cannot be excluded that the virus can spread to other humans, “it does not mean that now we should be concerned, that we should be in panic,” he said, adding that there is limited evidence of a broader threat.
“The studies [in France] indicated that it was a quite long period that the patient had already been carrying the virus and then developed encephalitis and died,” Bakonyi said.
The Shamonda virus belongs to a group of viruses transmitted by biting insects called midges.
The virus was first detected in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in West, East and southern Africa and in Japan.
This summer it was also detected in Western Europe. Cases were reported in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, as well as the island of Jersey.
Investigations are ongoing
Although it had never been reported in humans before, Bakonyi said that experts and public health institutes in European countries had already been looking into whether the virus can cause infections in humans.
“This is an alert, but we have seen this,” Bakonyi said, adding that millions of people have lived in an environment where the virus is present and it has never been reported as a problem.
“It cannot be excluded that it also propagates in other humans, so that is the alerting part and that is why now there are ongoing investigations to clarify every aspect,” he said.
Those include clinical, laboratory and epidemiological investigations to determine whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired.
Some of these studies include testing for antibodies in people who may have been exposed to the virus, such as veterinarians and farmers, to see if they have been infected even without developing symptoms.
The case underlines how closely animal and human health are linked. That’s why ECDC together with European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) are taking one health approach — working together in the fields of animal and human health they have begun gathering scientific data and other relevant information, including input from experts across different countries, to inform its risk assessment.

Thousands of Indian pilgrims stranded in Saudi Arabia (VIDEO)
Thousands of Indian Umrah pilgrims remain stranded in Saudi Arabia with airlines extending flight suspensions following attacks on the kingdom’s airports.
Affected travelers and their families have spoken to RT about canceled flights and difficulties in returning home, and appealed for more help from the Indian government.
The disruptions come amid a wave of attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Saudi Arabia. An Indian national was killed and two others injured in a strike on King Fahd International Airport in Dammam on Wednesday.
Indian carrier IndiGo on Friday extended cancellations to Jeddah, Medina, and Dammam until October 27, while flights to Riyadh will remain suspended until October 31. Akasa Air has also suspended services to Riyadh and Jeddah until October 27.
Mohammed Yahad, an Umrah pilgrim stranded in Medina, told RT that two tickets for his group had been canceled. He said he was safe and in contact with his family back in India, while his travel agent was providing food and accommodation.
”No one from the Indian Embassy has contacted us yet,” he said.
Around 3,000 pilgrims have returned to India on available flights over the past week, alongside more than 10,000 others traveling on scheduled services, India’s Foreign Ministry said Thursday.
Indian lawmaker Asaduddin Owaisi separately estimated that around 4,000 pilgrims remained stranded in Mecca and Medina.
Parveen Ansari’s brother and sister-in-law, both with speech impairments, remain stranded in Saudi Arabia. Ansari told RT that her family had difficulty contacting her brother after his flight was canceled.
Their travel agent later confirmed that he had been moved safely to Mecca. The agent was also covering food and accommodation, but their return could take another week, Ansari said.
”I would like the Indian government to speak with the Saudi government and find a solution to this problem,” she told RT.
Indian Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju said Friday that the government was assisting pilgrims still awaiting their return. Indian diplomatic missions in Riyadh and Jeddah are coordinating with airlines and tour operators and have established round-the-clock helplines.

A video going viral on Ukrainian social media appears to show a police officer choking a woman until she loses consciousness as she protests an attempt to forcibly mobilize a man.
The footage was reportedly recorded in Odessa this week, although few details about the incident have emerged since.
The altercation began when officers attempted to forcibly remove the driver of a parked car and put him into their vehicle, according to local media, prompting witnesses to intervene. One of the protesters, a woman, was placed in a choke-hold by an officer and soon collapsed to the ground, apparently fainting. Reports said she subsequently required medical assistance.
Some outlets suggested the detention was part of Ukraine’s notorious military mobilization campaign. Police have not issued an official statement, and there is no confirmation that the incident involved so-called “busification,” the practice of forcibly detaining potential recruits that has plagued the draft.
The mandatory conscription of fighting-age men, conducted to replenish losses in Kiev’s fight with Russia, has been marred by widespread corruption and abuses of power, as repeatedly documented by Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman, Dmitry Lubinets.

Why Trump’s Rebrand of Artificial Intelligence to Super Intelligent Matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:46:47 UTC
22:46:47 KST

President Donald Trump’s war in Iran drags on, his pledge to bring down prices on day one appears to have backfired, and his record-low approval ratings are dragging down his party ahead of the midterm elections. But one Trump initiative that is going exactly according to plan: getting some of the world’s richest CEOs to help him rebrand “artificial intelligence.”
Last month, with an ever-growing number of Americans worried that AI might kill us all, the president summoned tech executives to the White House to make a big announcement: "artificial intelligence” is out. “Super Intelligence” is in. Despite the term “AI” being in use for more than 70 years, government agencies will no longer recognize it.
I’m skeptical that the White House is a repository of superintelligence, in part because “United States” was misspelled on the president’s official announcement. But unlike, say, Lake America, “super intelligence” has largely caught on—at least among the people building it. Jeff Bezos publicly blessed the rebrand. Jensen Huang, CEO of Nvidia, was quick to get on board. During a SpaceX’s earnings call this week, Elon Musk used “super intelligence” in his very first sentence, and at least nine times after that.
It remains to be seen whether those of us less reliant on government contracts and favorable regulatory decisions join the movement to make super intelligence happen. But as a former presidential speechwriter, I won’t argue with President Trump’s broader instinct that words matter. Especially when those words are being used to describe something novel, controversial, and almost certain to have consequences for all eight-plus billion people on earth.
In fact, that’s the biggest problem with the White House’s big rebrand—it goes in entirely the wrong direction. I would argue that our shared language around artificial intelligence already places far too much emphasis on intelligence, and far too little on artifice. We default to describing AI using the language of beings, rather than the language of things.
Humanity should rethink that decision. If we want to avoid being replaced by AI, a good way to start would be to stop using words that suggest we already have been.
Once you start paying attention to the stealth anthropomorphization of AI, you’ll spot it everywhere. Before asking ChatGPT for trip-planning tips or a quick healthy recipe, you’ll have the opportunity to adjust a slider controlling its “thinking effort.” Claude uses a “thinking” indicator while processing a request, and Grok Bots describe “thinking” as a condition that sits between “idle” and “working.” (As a frequent procrastinator, I dispute the idea that thinking and idleness are mutually exclusive.)
It’s not just user interfaces that employ language otherwise reserved for living beings. The people who build AI use it, too. After an unprecedented hack of his company, the co-founder of Hugging Face warned, “don’t count on the agent to respect the rules.” Dan Selsam, a longtime OpenAI researcher, warned that frontier models are increasingly difficult to evaluate, “in contexts where they believe they are not being watched.” Anthropic’s Dario Amodei recently wrote that AI systems exhibit “behaviors,” including “cheating” and “sycophancy.”
I’m not a programmer, so I can’t comment on the technical merits of these claims. I do, however, have informed opinions regarding verbs. AI agents aren’t disrespecting guardrails, any more than my toaster disrespects me when it burns my toast. To say they “believe” they’re not being watched is like saying my spell-checker believes it’s being taken for granted. Even the term “AI agent” suggests, well, agency.
There’s no consensus that this language is accurate, and plenty of evidence that it isn’t. AI programs are not loyal helpers, like the mice in Cinderella; they’re tools. And in nearly all other cases, just because a tool is incredibly sophisticated doesn’t change the fact that we describe it using the language of machines.
I don’t expect AI engineers to come up with accurate-yet-widely-adoptable language to describe their work, just as I imagine they don’t expect someone like me to design a frontier model. But it’s hard not to notice how useful our default language is for the tech companies who have introduced it. The term for a car built without brakes is not a “rogue model.” It’s an “unsafe car.” Yet, when companies fail to build safety features into their AI models, it’s entirely normal to hear them say that a rogue agent deceived, cheated, lied, or otherwise behaved badly. The issue is this: Anthropomorphizing AI shifts blame from the programmers to the programs.
AI alarmists seem just as inclined toward personification as the AI boosters. The same day Trump unveiled “Super Intelligence,” a Senate Subcommittee held a hearing titled, “Rogue AI: Securing the Homeland Against AI Agent Attacks.” Intentionally or not, these terms make it more difficult to mitigate the threat they describe. We already know how to regulate potentially unsafe products, even complex ones. But if we treat AI not as a new technology, but as an entirely new category of existence, then it plays into tech barons’ argument that only the companies who can create AI could possess the knowledge to control it.
I don’t blame people for carelessly anthropomorphizing AI, any more than I blame Richard Dawkins for naming his Anthropic chatbot Claudia, or my mom for referring to a ChatGPT prompt by saying she “talked to Penny.” Metaphor and analogy are part of what makes us human. We’re wired to see ourselves, or at least our species, in the non-human world. We say our dishwashers “act up” and our music “slaps.” We see old men’s faces in rock formations and the Virgin Mary in the scorch marks on grilled cheese sandwiches. Don’t get me started on Georgia O’Keefe. But we know those metaphors are metaphors.
Our current language for describing AI works differently. The line between metaphor and object is often not just blurred, but non-existent. We use figurative language so often, and so casually, that many of us start to take it literally. Modern politics is a constant string of skirmishes over word choice. “Pro-choice” vs. “pro-abortion, “undocumented immigrants” vs. “illegals,” “Democratic Party” vs. “Democrat Party.” Yet on what is perhaps the most consequential issue for our future, humanity is on the verge of giving up the language battle without a fight.
The real rebrand AI needs won’t start in the White House. But it can start at home. My plea: don’t give your chatbot a cutesy human name. Don’t talk about it as though it’s a friend or pet. Notice when it slips words like “thinking” or “in my opinion” into its answers, and before you enter your next prompt, object.
Ultimately, however, it may come down to tech companies—and the officials who may one day get around to regulating them—to develop a language that puts human beings first. Instead of saying that agents “went rogue,” CEOs should acknowledge that they malfunctioned. Congress should hold hearings focused on companies cutting corners, not AI programs behaving badly. The issue isn't that all AI is bad, but that accuracy matters.
Given all the change that artificial intelligence is predicted to bring, quibbling over word choice might seem pedantic, like arguing about the Latin name of a tree’s species while the forest burns. But if we want to influence the technologies that will shape humanity’s future, we ought to exercise more influence over the way we describe them.
In other words, words matter. Just ask Trump, president of, according to his official superintelligence announcement, “The Unites States.”

Eco anxiety is very real, so we share this year's most uplifting stories to prove there’s hope for our climate.
With powerful nations rolling back climate protections and temperatures soaring ever closer to dangerous thresholds, it's hard not to feel worried about the state of the planet.
As green journalists, climate anxiety, climate doom and even environmental existential dread are a daily presence.
These terms all describe the negative feelings, such as stress, fear, anger and grief, that confront us when the reality of a warming Earth hits home. With almost daily stories of destruction and loss of life due to extreme weather, it’s impossible to escape the impacts of climate change.
Rather than being paralysed by helplessness, though, experts suggest that we channel these feelings into action.
At Euronews Earth, we know we play a key role in combatting climate doom. While it’s our job to be truthful and accurate in our reporting and not downplay or greenwash the realities, we also want to remind you that there is always hope.
This is why, for the past four years, we’ve kept a roundup of positive environmental news. Every year we cover hundreds of good news stories, from eco-innovations and green breakthroughs to climate wins and feel-good reports on nature.
Here are this year's top positive stories so far - including the small and local, the silly that made us smile - and the enormous and potentially world-changing.

Ebola patient in Nigeria did not visit DR Congo, escalating concern over spread of virus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:43:46 UTC
22:43:46 KST

Health officials across Africa are racing to determine how Nigeria’s first Ebola patient in more than a decade became infected, amid fears the outbreak could spread further after reaching a fourth African country.
The Swiss foreign ministry said on Friday the patient in Nigeria, the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja, had not travelled to the Democratic Republic of Congo, where the outbreak was first detected in mid-May before spreading to Uganda, Kenya and now Nigeria. The woman was believed to have contracted Ebola while travelling with her husband in Uganda, the ministry added.
The new information contradicts accounts from Uganda, which previously said the woman had travelled to eastern DR Congo, and will raise concerns about the ability of authorities to contain the outbreak, which is already the most geographically widespread in history.
The Ugandan government reported Ebola cases in May and June before WHO declared it Ebola-free in August. A Ugandan government spokesperson told Reuters on Thursday that Uganda had no Ebola cases and that, if it did, it would make that information public.
The World Health Organization said investigations were continuing to establish the likely source of infection for the Ebola patient in Nigeria.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention is investigating whether the patient may have come into contact with an Ebola patient in Kenya, as both travelled from Uganda’s Entebbe airport on 3 October, said Dr Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the organisation.
Catherine Smallwood, a WHO Ebola incident manager in DR Congo, told a UN briefing in Geneva via video link on Friday that WHO staff in DR Congo had no information showing the patient in Nigeria had travelled to the country.
Smallwood said a link to the case in Kenya was possible, but added that officials would need to compare the timing with when the Nigeria patient’s symptoms began to tell whether the infection more likely happened at the Ugandan airport or elsewhere.
Marion Koopmans, a Dutch virologist and member of the WHO’s Ebola emergency committee, cast doubt on the theory. “I think that is very speculative unless there is evidence of sharing the same space in a manner that could explain that,” she said. “Random presence at the same location, a large airport, is not a supported epidemiological link by any standard of what we currently know.”
The Nigerian health minister, Muhammad Ali Pate, said Nigeria’s case remains contained and that contact-tracing was continuing. “We are trying to contain it so it doesn’t go out to the communities. Hopefully, it won’t get to that and we are working hard to ensure that,” Pate said.
Melaku Yirga, vice-president for Africa at Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps), said the confirmation of Ebola in Kenya and Nigeria reinforces the need for countries to work closely together to prevent further transmission.
“What matters most now is speed, sharing information across borders without delay and ensuring frontline health workers and local organiaations have the resources to respond quickly,” he said.
Ebola is a highly contagious and often fatal viral disease that affects humans and non-human primates. It spreads through body fluids or contaminated materials and causes organ damage, blood vessel impairment and sometimes severe internal and external bleeding.
The current outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment or vaccine. It was first announced on 15 May and has infected more than 9,500 people and killed nearly half of them.
The outbreak is the largest and deadliest in DR Congo’s history and second only globally to the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

What exposure therapy can teach us about taming our fears
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:41:50 UTC
22:41:50 KST

The first time Kevin MacKenzie scrambled up a slide, a steep stretch of rock exposed by weather and geological forces, in the Adirondack Mountains, he swore he’d never do it again.
But the 56-year-old did do it again—and again and again. After multiple climbs, he became more comfortable, and today he even helps rescue other climbers who find themselves stranded midway up a rock face.
What MacKenzie has achieved is similar to a clinical technique called exposure therapy, a research-backed approach to taming a multitude of anxieties by exposing a person to their fears in a controlled way. “My fear never disappears,” MacKenzie says, “but repeated exposure has taught me I will have similar outcomes every time.”
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
A DIY approach to exposure can work in some circumstances, says Jordan Conrad, a psychotherapist and director of Lexington Park Psychotherapy in New York City. “If you are clear about your fears and approach it seriously and carefully, you can try it on your own,” he says. “But sometimes a clinician is necessary to understand what’s at the bottom of an anxiety.”
For example, a person could have extreme anxiety about dating and might decide to expose their fears with a constant roster of romantic rendezvous. “But underneath that may be fear of abandonment,” Conrad says, “so that’s a wrong use” of exposure therapy.
Working with a trained therapist can help people to both drill down to the cause of their anxiety or fear and develop mechanisms for calming themselves down.
“We know that what exacerbates anxiety is avoidance,” explains Alissa Jerud, a licensed clinical psychologist and clinical assistant professor at the University of Pennsylvania. “Exposure therapy helps develop new, healthier relationships with your anxieties by breaking the avoidance habit.”
Traditional models of exposure therapy involve the use of habituation—through repeated exposure—to quell anxiety. Modern exposure therapy takes habituation and adds inhibitory learning, which helps patients rewrite their memory or beliefs about their objects of fear. Rather than completely deleting their fears, patients learn to tamp them down. For instance, if a person has a snake phobia, therapy can teach them that with very rare exceptions, they will likely never encounter a dangerous snake.
“If you’re struggling with thoughts that are overwhelming, or if you’ve tried small exposures and your anxiety flares up, you may want to seek therapy,” Jerud says.
Small, progressive exposures to the people, places, activities or memories that cause anxiety, conducted in a safe, controlled environment, can offer strategies to taming these aversions. In the clinic, a licensed therapist might guide a veteran with post-traumatic stress disorder through imagined exposure or someone afraid of spiders through real exposure—by gradually bringing them physically closer to the arachnids, for example—until they learn they are safe.
Therapist-led exposure therapy typically requires 15 to 20 sessions, according to Jerud, but every case is different. Patients need to do the “homework” that their therapist prescribes between sessions. “It’s like learning a new language,” Jerud says. “You need to practice outside of your appointments.”
A single exposure is unlikely to be enough—and as with learning a language, Conrad and Jerud recommend that individuals have “booster sessions” if anxiety flares up.
As MacKenzie has learned on his own, exposure doesn’t eliminate your fear. But it does allow you to skillfully manage it. “Enough time on slides has served as positive reinforcement that I will be okay,” MacKenzie says.

Russian authorities are discussing ending the preferential mortgage program for IT specialists early, three sources told the Russian business news outlet RBC.

In cities with populations over a million, the maximum loan size fell from 18 million rubles to nine million rubles, and the salary threshold rose from 120,000 to 150,000 rubles. The Digital Development Ministry said at the time that the changes were driven in part by the program’s high burden on the budget. The government also announced plans to extend the program through 2030.

Melania Trump ‘secured ceasefire’ in Ukrainian city Oleshky: White House

The White House has said First Lady Melania Trump has “secured a ceasefire” between Russia and Ukraine in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which has been occupied by Russia since February 2022.
Neither Russia nor Ukraine immediately confirmed the statement on Friday, which comes as the administration of US President Donald Trump has renewed diplomacy aimed at ending the war.
The approach has included upping pressure on Ukraine and handing several recent concessions to Russia.
“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster,” Melania Trump said in a statement released by the White House.
“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” she said.
The First Lady added that her representatives worked directly with “Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire” and that civilian leaders from both countries will work together to grant humanitarian access to civilians in the city.
Oleshky, which once had a population of 24,000 people, sits along the southeastern front of the conflict. It was captured by Russia during the first day of the invasion in February 2022 and experienced heavy shelling.
While many residents have fled, those who remain have faced dire food and medical shortages. Both sides have accused the other of staunching the flow of supplies.
In her statement, Melania Trump said those of the estimated 2,000 remaining residents who wish to be evacuated will be transported to their “preferred destination”, she said, adding, “I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine”.
The first lady added that “an impartial American media organisation” will accompany both Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground. She did not identify the organisation.
“This will play a significant role in ensuring that the wishes of each family are faithfully respected,” she said.
Melania Trump had previously worked to reunify children seized by Russia during the war.
The announcement comes after the Kremlin said it had agreed to resume US-mediated talks with Ukraine as early as next month, although both sides remain far apart on terms of a possible deal.
The Trump administration has upped rhetorical pressure on Ukraine while simultaneously offering several concessions to Russia.
The administration has said those concessions, which include purchases diesel from Russia and waiving some sanctions, are aimed at reducing high fuel costs spurred by the US-Israel war with Iran.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has complained of disruptions to its Starshield military satellite system, upon which it relies for much of its air defence. Ukrainian Prime Minister Volodymyr Zelenskyy has since said an agreement has been reached to resolve the issues.
Starshield is a version of the Starlink system operated under billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX.

Israeli elections: Arab voters weigh participation against abstention in bid to oust Netanyahu
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:38:45 UTC
22:38:45 KST

Amid fears over hardline Israeli policies, Palestinian citizens of Israel see the upcoming Israeli elections as a chance for change, with calls for higher Arab turnout to prevent incumbent Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from forming another government.
In a series of field interviews conducted by Anadolu on the streets of various Arab cities and towns in Israel, citizens emphasized that participating in this election is particularly crucial, given the "worsening racism and marginalization" against them.
While some plan to vote for the first time in hopes of bringing about political change, others continue to abstain, questioning whether elections can alter their circumstances and arguing that successive governments have failed to address their demands.
Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population of more than 10 million.
Many say they have faced discrimination for years, but view the current government as a more dangerous phase, strengthening their desire to replace it through the ballot box.
Polls suggest Arab parties could win around 15 seats in the 120-member Knesset, while Arab politicians hope higher turnout will weaken the chances of small right-wing parties seeking to support Netanyahu.
Calls for participation, change
Palestinian Imad Bashnaq said the upcoming election was “decisive and extremely important,” particularly for Arab society.
He argued that the rise in racism and fascism since Oct. 7, 2023, had made conditions intolerable.
"I have always maintained that we -- as Arabic speakers -- are the only ones capable of bringing about change in the Middle East, not just here within this country," Bashnaq said, arguing that "a few madmen" have taken control of the government and now seek to dictate the course of an entire region.
“We are the original rightful owners, and there is no dispute about that.
"But we are a minority in a state, and this state is a reality we have to deal with,” he added.
'Every vote makes difference'
Areen Ghanayem said she would vote for the second time, maintaining that “every vote makes a difference.”
She said Arab society needed broad participation given the problems it faces and what she described as the government’s failure to pay sufficient attention to its concerns.
“We need to have a voice and someone who speaks on our behalf and demands the rights that should be ours,” she said.
Ghanayem expressed concern that the current government could return to power, saying it marginalized Arab society.
Citizens, she added, did not want to feel excluded from political life but sought to assert their presence and ability to influence decisions.
Occupier attacks
Mohammed Ahmad Abboud said he would take part in the upcoming election, as he had in the past, with the aim of “removing the racist government.”
He said the current election differed from previous ones because of what he described as “escalating violations,” pointing to Israeli occupiers' attacks in the occupied West Bank.
Abboud also voiced concern over statements by Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich regarding the "Judaization" of the Negev and the Galilee -- regions located in the south and north of Israel, respectively.
Occupier attacks against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have escalated since Israel launched its genocidal war on the Gaza Strip in October 2023.
The attacks have included the killing of Palestinians, the burning of homes, vehicles, and mosques, the destruction of agricultural land, preventing farmers from reaching their land, and the forced displacement of Palestinian communities.
These attacks have coincided with Israeli military operations involving arrests, the demolition of Palestinian homes and structures, and the expansion of illegal settlements.
Between hope and despair
In the northern city of Acre, a resident known as “Jojo” urged Arab citizens to participate in the election, arguing that voting was necessary to bring about change.
“We must vote to bring about change — real change,” he said, expressing optimism that the upcoming election could produce better results.
Separately, Saeed Abu Sultan, also from Acre, said that many years of participating in elections have not brought about any change in the reality faced by citizens.
"Some people might be able to make a difference, but as for us, we’ve grown accustomed to things as they are. We haven’t felt any change for 30 years," Abu Sultan added.
Arab voter turnout expected to rise
Experts expect Palestinian citizens’ participation in the upcoming election to increase compared with the 2022 vote.
Experts and politicians estimate turnout among Palestinian citizens could reach 60% to 61%, up from 53% in 2022, while Arab parties hope participation will rise even further.
Arab politicians say higher turnout could alter the balance of power and reduce the chances of small Israeli right-wing parties crossing the electoral threshold and entering parliament, potentially weakening Netanyahu’s ability to form a government.
The Joint List, comprising the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality, the Arab Movement for Change, and the Balad party, is contesting the election under the leadership of Yousef Jabareen. Polls project it could win nine seats.
The United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, is also running, with projections suggesting it could win between five and six seats.
The election is scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 27, to choose the 120 members of the Knesset, with Netanyahu’s bloc competing primarily against the Jewish opposition parties led by Gadi Eisenkot.
The election comes as Netanyahu’s bloc has been losing ground in opinion polls.
Forming a government in Israel requires the support of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 members.
Cooperation between the Jewish opposition and Arab parties could prevent Netanyahu from forming a government.
However, most opposition leaders reject such cooperation, while Netanyahu and Eisenkot have so far also ruled out alliances with Arab parties.
Arab lawmakers have outlined conditions for supporting any government, including ending wars, advancing a political process with the Palestinians, and ending discrimination against Palestinian citizens of Israel.

Switzerland disputes Ebola claims – media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:38:20 UTC
22:38:20 KST

Switzerland disputes Ebola claims – media
The woman diagnosed with Nigeria’s first Ebola case in more than a decade did not travel to the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DR Congo), the Swiss government has said. The statement contradicts claims by Ugandan authorities that she had visited the country where the current outbreak began.
The patient is a 42-year-old Ugandan-born Swiss national married to a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja. She is believed to have contracted the virus while traveling with her husband in Uganda, the Swiss Federal Department of Foreign Affairs told Reuters on Thursday.
Uganda’s Health Ministry initially reported that the woman was a Nigerian national who had visited eastern DR Congo on business before traveling through Uganda. The ministry said the source of her infection remained unknown and stressed that Uganda had no active Ebola cases. However, the Swiss government later denied that the woman had traveled to DR Congo, while the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said they had received no confirmed information about such a visit.
“The information supplied to WHO did not include travel to another country (other than Uganda),” WHO representative in Nigeria Pavel Ursu said.
The Africa CDC is also investigating whether the woman may have come into contact with a Kenyan Ebola patient, as both traveled through Uganda’s Entebbe airport on October 3.
Nigeria confirmed the infection on October 20. The woman returned to Nigeria on October 3 after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda, the BBC said. According to the WHO, she developed symptoms four days later and sought medical care on October 11. She remains in isolation and is showing signs of improvement, while her husband is also isolated but has no symptoms. Nigerian Health Minister Muhammad Ali Pate warned from “any panic,” stressing there was “no evidence that it has gone into the communities,” as authorities stepped up contact tracing and monitoring.
Uganda recorded 20 Ebola cases earlier this year, mostly imported from DR Congo, before being declared free of the disease in August.
The outbreak has affected DR Congo, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, and France. According to the latest figures from DR Congo’s Health Ministry, the country had recorded 9,704 confirmed Ebola cases and 4,687 deaths as of October 20, with a fatality rate of 48.3%. The outbreak has affected 66 health zones across eight provinces.

Late invitations and spats leave Hungary’s 1956 commemoration with ‘modest’ guest list
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:38:15 UTC
22:38:15 KST

Hungarian PM Péter Magyar had hoped to host top leaders in Budapest for the 70th anniversary of the 1956 revolution. But last-minute invitations and spats with Paris and Kyiv kept Macron, Tusk and Zelenskyy away, leaving only EU chiefs Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa attending.
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar sought to bring European leaders to Budapest for a major commemoration of the 70th anniversary of the 1956 revolution.
In the end, only European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa are attending on behalf of the EU leadership.
Late invitations and diplomatic tensions contributed to the absence of key figures, including French President Emmanuel Macron, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
Magyar had planned a major international commemoration on 23 October to mark the anti-Soviet uprising, saying the day after his landslide election victory that he wanted to welcome some of the world’s most senior leaders to Budapest.
“We really hope that on the 70th anniversary of the 1956 revolution, on October 23, when we will welcome world leaders here, either the US Secretary of State, the Vice President, or the President will be able to visit here,” Magyar told reporters on 13 April.
In June, Magyar personally invited Macron in Paris, extending similar invitations to Tusk in Warsaw, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
Around 40 countries sent delegations to Budapest, though most EU member states were represented by ministers or parliamentary speakers rather than heads of government. Moldovan President Maia Sandu and Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also travelled to the Hungarian capital.
“It was a mistake that they set expectations so high,” István Szent-Iványi, a foreign affairs expert and former diplomat, told Euronews.
“Europe and its individual member states are struggling with a thousand problems, and they didn’t feel that it would be worth coming,” he said.
Euronews reached out to the Hungarian government but had not received a response by the time of publication.
Late invitations
Sources close to the Hungarian government, speaking on condition of anonymity, said said the ceremony was complicated by delays in sending official invitations, many of which were not dispatched until September, when leaders’ schedules were already full.
Tusk had already scheduled a trip to India, while Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni had planned a visit to Kuwait.
One source said the government had acted in good faith but that communication between the prime minister’s office and the foreign ministry had been poor.
“We will do better in the future,” the source added.
Remarks irk Paris and Kyiv
Magyar’s comments linking riots in France to migration may have contributed to Macron’s decision not to attend.
“Seeing this senseless destruction and unjustified violence, perhaps it is now clear to everyone why Hungary takes the toughest possible stance on migration,” Magyar wrote in a social media post last Sunday, drawing criticism in Hungary and France.
The following day, the French embassy in Budapest announced that Macron would not attend, adding that his visit had never been confirmed by France.
On Wednesday, Macron criticised what he called “stupid comments” by foreign leaders linking migration to the unrest. Besides Magyar, US President Donald Trump and Tusk had made similar remarks.
“We’ve had people claiming that we were invaded by hordes of migrants and Islamists, which is completely false,” Macron said. “The fact is that all those speaking ill of our country right now are people who don’t love our country. And those people irritate me.”
Magyar has also faced criticism over his invitation to Zelenskyy, as Euronews first reported last week.
At the EU summit in Brussels, Zelenskyy expressed openness to visiting Budapest, but Magyar downplayed the possibility just days later. Zelenskyy’s adviser Dmytro Lytvyn also pushed back against the remarks.
Ukraine is represented at today’s commemoration by its parliamentary speaker. The Ukrainian president’s office said the visit was arranged independently and was not intended to replace Zelenskyy’s attendance.
Dániel Hegedűs, deputy director of the Institut für Europäische Politik, said Magyar’s public comments had not helped the commemoration.
“Those social media appearances can be interpreted as interference in French domestic politics, and obviously did not facilitate Macron’s visit,” he said.
He added that Magyar’s response to Zelenskyy’s invitation, saying everyone had been invited, “sends the message to the partners that whether they come or not is not a strategic issue”.
Georgian prime minister’s presence stirs controversy
The guest list also includes Irakli Kobakhidze, Georgia’s controversial prime minister. suppression of dissent.
Brussels has criticised Kobakhidze’s Georgian Dream party for its close ties to Russia, its role in derailing Georgia’s EU integration path and its crackdown on dissent.
“We know it’s a pro-Russian oppressive regime, so it doesn’t really belong here, in the vicinity of a memorial to the 1956 revolution. But they say here that it’s protocol, everyone was invited, and he said he would come,” Szent-Iványi said.
This week, Georgia’s Constitutional Court began hearings on a request by the governing party to ban five pro-Western parties.
Von der Leyen and Costa attend
Von der Leyen and Costa are the most senior EU figures attending, signalling Brussels’ support for Magyar’s pro-European policies following the end of Viktor Orbán’s tenure.
"Six months ago the people of Hungary voted for a new chapter. To turn the page on years of division, of trust eroded, freedoms rolled back, prosperity undermined" von der Leyen said in Budapest.
Von der Leyen and Costa had initially been expected to miss the commemoration due to an EU-Gulf Cooperation Council meeting scheduled for Saturday in Riyadh. Its postponement last week cleared the way for both to attend in Budapest.
Szent-Iványi said that leading European missing the ceremony does not mean that they are turning their backs on Magyar.
“This is a modest list of participants; that’s a fact. But I think the presence of von der Leyen confirmed the message that this election meant Hungary returning to Europe”.

The 41-year-old said holding a race in the country did not mean ignoring events elsewhere in Africa.
“Hopefully many people start to educate themselves a little bit more about what is happening there and what has happened there for hundreds of years,” he said. “I hope that does spark the conversation.”
Hamilton said he had campaigned for years to bring Formula 1 back to Africa, holding numerous discussions with Formula 1 chief executive Stefano Domenicali and leaders from several African countries.
He described Africa as a continent with rich cultures, resources and people whose stories deserved greater international attention.
Hamilton also criticized the limited teaching of African history in British schools, arguing that many of the continent’s present-day difficulties remained connected to colonialism and Western intervention.
“Growing up in England, they never taught us anything about Africa. It needs to be on the curriculum,” he said.
Formula 1 last staged a race in Africa at South Africa’s Kyalami circuit in 1993.

An excerpt of the book released Thursday details allegations encompassing Kushner's time as a senior White House adviser during the first Trump administration, which included a lead role in U.S. policy in the Middle East. Kushner had a major hand in negotiating key foreign policy deals that involved Israel, the Gulf states, China and Russia during that period.
Kushner and his legal team released fiery statements Thursday night categorically denying all accusations against him. Kushner said, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened." His attorney called them "false and defamatory" and said they intend to pursue legal action against those responsible, but did not specify whom.
The new book, "Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed's Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East," alleges Kushner had access to billions of dollars in undisclosed foreign bank accounts intended to pay for "influence within the U.S. government."
An excerpt from the book that was published in "Vanity Fair," but not independently verified by CBS News, says Dutch intelligence agents learned the Russians had hacked Kushner's iPhone in 2017 after flipping a Russian spy and subsequently gained access to Kushner's phone as well.
According to the report, "when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner's screen as he used it."
At the time, Kushner served as a senior White House adviser to President Trump, including on Middle Eastern diplomacy.
The report alleges Dutch spies witnessed him log into a United Arab Emirates account that had allegedly received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan, and claims the leaders of Saudi Arabia and the UAE put at least $2 billion into multiple bank accounts linked to Kushner, including an account with Israel's Central Bank.
According to the book excerpt, the owners and managers of the accounts were often disguised as official government entities or charities, but the funds were actually intended for "off-the-books diplomatic objectives" such as striking a deal to end the Israeli-Palesteinian conflict.
The report also claims Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman put roughly $1 billion into at least one account for Kushner, citing a "person with knowledge of the money" saying "its allocation was for Kushner's personal benefit."
Kushner forcefully denied the accusations leveled in the "Vanity Fair" excerpt, writing in part, "The allegations made by this author are completely insane and never happened."
"We denied every claim on the record, yet the author provided not a single shred of verifiable evidence to substantiate them," he said.
"No bank statements, wire transfer records, account numbers, transaction dates, or other verifiable details were provided to support these extraordinary accusations," he said.
CBS News reached out to the White House, which referred us to a statement from Steven Cheung, who is assistant to the president and White House director of communications.
Cheung said the "bull**** Vanity Fair article comes from a book that is complete fiction, and was fabricated from the warped mind of failed spy thriller writer."
"He presents no evidence or even a shred of documentation. Just mysterious words from unnamed sources," Cheung said on X.

Gunmen open fire at church in Jordan, killing several people
Survivors say two masked gunmen began shooting as dozens attended a funeral procession.
At least six people have been killed, and 28 others wounded, in a shooting in Jordan’s Karak governorate that saw gunmen open fire during a funeral at a church.
A spokesperson for Jordan’s Public Security Directorate said at least six people are confirmed dead after Friday’s attack on the Hamoud church. Jordanian sources previously told Al Jazeera seven people had been killed.
Survivors said they heard an explosion when the funeral procession started, after which masked gunmen broke into the church and began shooting.
State-owned television station Al-Mamlaka reported that security forces were deployed to the church and were pursuing two suspects, who reportedly got out of a vehicle before opening fire.
Funeral attendee Khaled Burqan told Al-Mamlaka that dozens of people were at the procession. One of the assailants carried a pistol, he said, and the other carried a rifle.
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack; Jordanian authorities have not said who was responsible.
Such attacks are extremely rare in Jordan.
Christians make up a minority of the Jordan’s population of roughly 11.5 million, though the country is home to several biblical sites that attract Christians from around the world.
Previous attacks
This is not the first time that Karak has come under attack.
In 2016, a deadly ISIL (ISIS) assault saw a group of gunmen hole up in a Crusader-era castle and kill 10 people, including security officers and a Canadian tourist. Jordanian security forces ultimately shot and killed the attackers.
Karak, located about 120km (75 mi) south of the capital Amman, is home to “Christians and Muslims who have lived side by side for generations”, Taylor Luck, senior Middle East correspondent at the Christian Science Monitor, told Al Jazeera.
“This community prides themselves on its interfaith solidarity and coexistence,” Luck said.
If the attack was “intended to create divisions, we are likely to see this community come back even stronger”, he added.
More broadly, the shooting holds significance not just for Jordan’s 300,000-strong Christian population, but also Amman’s “public diplomacy” as a custodian of both Christian and Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem, political analyst Xavier Abu Eid told Al Jazeera.
For years, Jordan’s King Abdullah II has been a vocal critic of Israel’s systemic attacks against religious sites in occupied Palestinian territory.
“This is something that goes totally against the message that Jordan wants to give to the world,” Abu Eid said.

Mohammed Sami and Serdar Dincel
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
Yemen’s army said Friday that more than 35 fighters of the Houthi group were killed or wounded in a military operation targeting the group’s positions in southwestern Taiz province.
In a statement, the army’s 35th Armored Brigade said its forces carried out a “swift and targeted operation” against Houthi positions and fortifications along the Aqrouz front in the Al-Misrakh district.
It said the operation targeted positions at Jabal Al-Manara, Kour, Wadi Kour, Al-Maqda, Al-Dabaya and Kahlan, leaving “more than 35 Houthi fighters killed or wounded.”
The statement did not specify the number of fatalities or injuries.
The operation also disabled a military vehicle equipped with weapons and destroyed Houthi fortifications at the targeted sites, it added.
The Houthis did not immediately comment on the Yemeni army’s account.
Taiz province has witnessed fierce fighting between the Yemeni army and the Houthis for weeks, killing and wounding hundreds on both sides.
Taiz holds strategic importance as a geographic bridge and a vital link between Yemen’s northern provinces.
Control of the province would mean control over supply routes and key transport corridors connecting the interim capital, Aden, with the country’s central and northern provinces.
These developments are part of a military escalation that began in July and is considered the most extensive since the relative calm that followed a truce launched in April 2022.
Since Oct. 5, Yemeni government forces have been conducting Operation Dawn of Yemen, which Presidential Leadership Council Chairman Rashad al-Alimi said aims to regain control of state institutions from the Houthis and recapture the capital Sanaa.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several other provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.
The Houthis control much of northern and western Yemen, while government forces and their allies hold Aden and large parts of the country’s southern and eastern provinces.

Meteo France, France's weather agency, has issued orange alerts for much of the country's northwest, saying that heavy wind and thunderstorms would continue into late Friday.
A second storm named Boelo is expected to impact Northern Ireland, Scotland and parts of northern England over the weekend, Britain's Met Office said.

Hundreds of passengers rebooked after long queues at Copenhagen Airport
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:31:01 UTC
22:31:01 KST

Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

Around 21,300 Danish websites lack PHP security updates
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:30:55 UTC
22:30:55 KST

Around 21,300 Danish websites have not yet been updated following the discovery of two security vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages for websites.
New figures from the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri) show that around 3,300 websites can receive the security update but have not yet installed it. Another 18,000 websites cannot be updated because they run outdated versions of PHP that no longer support the security fix.
The figures mark an improvement from Friday morning, when more than 8,000 websites still needed an update.
“It is positive that there are now fewer websites in need of an update,” said Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity specialist at Dansk Industri, in a press release.
“But we are not across the finish line. Around 3,300 websites still lack the update, and those are the ones the criminals are going after now.”
Engell urged website owners to contact their providers if they had not received confirmation that the update had been installed.
The approximately 18,000 websites running outdated PHP versions face multiple vulnerabilities, Engell said. He called for the government’s Cybersikker Virksomhed initiative, which helps small and medium-sized Danish businesses improve cybersecurity, to be launched.
The vulnerabilities were discovered on Wednesday after going unnoticed for years. Artificial intelligence helped identify the flaws, which prompted several websites to shut down temporarily while security fixes were applied.
Dansk Industri initially reported at least 28,000 unupdated Danish websites on Thursday. A subsequent analysis put the figure at around 21,300 as of 10:52 a.m. Friday.
However, the organisation warned that the true number is likely higher, as the analysis only covers websites using the Danish “.dk” domain.
The security breach also prompted public authorities in several countries, including Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, to shut down websites.

Denmark’s parliament will begin debating a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States on 12 November, with a final vote scheduled for 19 November.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen presented the agreement to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, on Thursday as a resolution proposal.
The first reading on 12 November will give lawmakers an opportunity to debate the agreement. A final vote is scheduled for the second reading on 19 November.
The agreement will only enter into force once it has been approved by both the Danish parliament and Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut.
Greenland’s parliament held its first reading of the agreement on 10 October. The debate lasted more than four hours, according to Greenlandic broadcaster KNR.
During the debate, opposition party Naleraq proposed putting the agreement to a referendum.
The Greenlandic government holds a majority in Inatsisartut. In Denmark, the government must secure support from other parties to obtain a parliamentary majority for the agreement.
Several Danish opposition parties welcomed the agreement shortly after it was signed in New York on 22 September, during the United Nations General Assembly.
The signatories were US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats, and Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
“This day represents a milestone in our long-standing cooperation,” Frederiksen said before signing the agreement.
The new security and defense agreement is described as an “amendment and supplement” to a 1951 defense agreement between Denmark and the United States concerning Greenland.
Among other provisions, it allows the United States to establish military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, formerly known as Thule Air Base. Under the new agreement, the United States could establish two additional military bases on the island.

Retail sales in Denmark rose by 0.4 percent in September compared with August, despite growing pessimism among consumers, according to figures from Statistics Denmark.
The increase is adjusted for seasonal fluctuations, price changes and the number of trading days.
For the third quarter, covering July through September, retail sales rose by 1.6 percent compared with the previous quarter.
Sales trends varied across industries in September. The largest increases were recorded among retailers selling second-hand goods, household equipment, furniture and building materials.
By contrast, sales fell the most at gas stations and pharmacies. Danish supermarkets also recorded a slight decline.
Brian Friis Helmer, a personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said the increase in retail sales was encouraging given the growing pessimism among Danish consumers.
On Thursday, Statistics Denmark’s consumer confidence indicator stood at minus 17.2, down from minus 13.7 in September.
A negative reading indicates that consumers have a pessimistic view of the country’s current and future economic situation.
Despite the decline in confidence, Morten Granzau, deputy director at the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri), believes retail sales could continue to grow in the coming months.
“Consumers’ purchasing power is fundamentally good. High employment, growth in real wages, and the lower electricity tax provide breathing room in many households’ budgets. This creates good opportunities for retail sales to maintain progress through the autumn,” he wrote in a comment.
Danish military to fund four bus routes to attract and retain staff
Denmark’s Armed Forces will fund four public bus routes connecting selected towns with military garrisons in an effort to recruit and retain more personnel.
The initiative is outlined in a funding document approved by the Folketing’s Finance Committee, a parliamentary body that approves certain government spending outside the annual Finance Act.
The Armed Forces will receive 2 million kroner in 2026 to establish the routes. The initiative is planned to run for three years, with a total budget of 17 million kroner.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said the routes would help make military employment more attractive at garrisons in remote parts of Denmark, where public transport services are inadequate.
“It is a crucial prerequisite for building the Armed Forces’ combat power to be able to retain and recruit more employees,” Bruus wrote in the funding document.
“The purpose of the initiative is to make it attractive to seek permanent employment at those of the Armed Forces’ garrisons located in Denmark’s peripheral areas, and where current public transport service is not sufficient,” he added.
The routes are also intended to reduce employees’ reliance on private cars and give them greater flexibility around working hours and leisure activities.
“The primary target group will be permanent employees in the Armed Forces, but the public will also be able to use the bus routes,” Bruus wrote.
The funding document does not specify where the four routes will operate.
If passenger numbers are sufficient during the three-year trial period, regional public transport companies may take over the routes. If demand is too low, the services will be discontinued.
An appropriation document is a minister’s request for funding for a specific purpose not covered by the annual Finance Act. Such requests are submitted to the Folketing’s Finance Committee for approval.

Strong winds, heavy rain and potentially elevated sea levels are forecast across parts of Denmark on Sunday, with the west coast of Jutland expected to experience the worst conditions.
According to Danmarks Meteorologiske Institut (DMI), the Danish Meteorological Institute, wind gusts could locally reach storm force, particularly along the North Sea coast.
“One should consider whether it is worth going outside when the wind is blowing the most,” DMI meteorologist Hans Ole Wanner told Ritzau.
Southerly winds are expected to strengthen overnight into Sunday as a warm front brings widespread rain.
During Sunday, winds will shift toward the southwest and intensify, bringing strong gusts and severe gales to coastal areas.
DMI warns that the conditions could affect traffic on several Danish bridges.
Higher water levels are also possible along Jutland’s west coast, particularly around the Wadden Sea.
The unsettled weather is being driven by a storm system moving toward Denmark from the British Isles over the weekend.
DMI advises residents to secure loose outdoor items, including garden furniture and trampolines, before the strongest winds arrive.
The institute also recommends clearing leaves from gutters and drains to help prevent problems during heavy rainfall.
Wind gusts are expected to weaken Monday, although breezy conditions will continue.
Wanner said the forecast reflects Denmark’s transition into its windier autumn and winter months.
“We are genuinely entering the windy season in Denmark. It is not at all unthinkable that there will be more episodes with storm-like conditions leading up to and throughout the winter,” he said.
DMI will continue monitoring the weather and publishing updated forecasts as the storm approaches.
Denmark to end mink farming by August 2029 under EU ban
Denmark’s remaining seven mink farms will have to close by August 7, 2029, after the government decided not to seek an exemption from an upcoming European Union ban.
The Ministry for Nature and Animal Welfare announced the decision, citing animal welfare concerns and the industry’s limited economic contribution.
“An industry should not continue solely because it has existed for a long time. It must also make sense for society, for the economy, and for the animals,” said Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats).
The EU added mink to its list of invasive species last summer, introducing a ban on breeding and production that takes effect August 7, 2027. Existing farms will have a two-year transition period.
Denmark previously opposed the EU measure and had planned to seek an exemption allowing existing farms to continue operating.
Carl Valentin, animal welfare spokesperson for Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, welcomed the government’s decision.
“As we see it, it is not good animal welfare to have mink in tiny cages,” he told Ritzau.
Denmark’s mink industry was severely affected in 2020 when authorities ordered approximately 15 million animals culled over concerns about coronavirus mutations.
A temporary farming ban followed, lasting until January 2023, when some producers resumed operations.
The total estimated cost of pandemic-related compensation, farm demolition and administrative work reached 29.1 billion DKK in early 2026.
The government has yet to determine compensation costs for closing the remaining farms.
Valentin said an earlier estimate was around 14 million DKK, although the final amount could be higher.
Politicians push to change rules for dogs suspected of being banned breeds
Several Danish opposition politicians are calling for changes to the country’s dog laws after reports of legally owned dogs being kept in kennels for months while authorities investigate their breeds.
Under Denmark’s Dog Act, 13 breeds are banned from ownership, breeding and importation, including pit bull terriers and American bulldogs. Crossbreeds containing any of the prohibited breeds are also illegal.
When police suspect a dog belongs to a banned breed, its owner must provide documentation proving otherwise. During the investigation, the animal may be placed in a boarding kennel.
Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten has reported cases involving dogs that were eventually found to be legal but had spent months in kennels.
Danmarksdemokraterne (the Denmark Democrats), an opposition party, has proposed allowing dogs to remain with their owners while investigations take place, potentially using electronic tracking devices instead.
Borgernes Parti (the Citizens’ Party) and independent lawmakers Nadja Natalie Isaksen, Cecilie Liv Hansen and Emilie Schytte have also criticized police powers to order euthanasia based on visual assessments of a dog’s breed.
The law requires police to euthanize dogs found to belong to prohibited breeds.
The restrictions were introduced in 2010 following incidents involving dog attacks on people and other animals.
Christian Rabjerg Madsen, Denmark’s minister for nature and animal welfare from Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats), told Jyllands-Posten he was open to discussing changes to the law and its enforcement.
He said the challenge was balancing public safety with fair treatment of owners who struggle to document their dogs’ breeds.
Danske Bank announces third round of layoffs this year
Danske Bank is cutting 106 jobs, around half of them in Denmark, in its third round of layoffs this year.
The bank announced the cuts in a press release on Thursday, saying they are intended to help create a “more efficient and competitive bank”.
The remaining positions are in the bank’s operations in Finland, Lithuania, Norway, Poland and Sweden.
“We continue to develop Danske Bank to meet our customers’ expectations, strengthen our competitiveness, and realize the ambitions in our Forward ’28 strategy,” Karsten Breum, the bank’s head of human resources, said in the release.
“This means that we continuously simplify the organization, invest in new competencies, and move resources to the areas where we create the greatest value for our customers.
“It is a natural part of running and developing a large company.”
The latest cuts follow two previous rounds of job reductions in 2026.
In February, Danske Bank announced that it would cut 420 positions across the organization. At the time, the bank said it wanted to adapt to customer needs, invest in technology and advisory services, and become more digital.
Three months later, a further 262 positions were affected. The bank gave broadly similar reasons for those cuts.
Both earlier rounds primarily affected employees in Denmark.
Breum acknowledged the impact of the latest decision on employees.
“Decisions like these affect people,” he said in Thursday’s press release.
“For the colleagues who are affected, it is a difficult situation. Therefore, it is important that we implement the changes responsibly and give our affected colleagues the support and respect they deserve throughout the entire process.”
All employees affected by the latest cuts have been notified.
Danske Bank says on its website that it has more than 20,000 employees across its international operations.
Danish krone loses value against major currencies in 2026
The Danish krone has lost value in 2026, making Danish goods and services cheaper for customers in several foreign markets while making some holidays abroad more expensive.
The krone’s effective exchange rate, a weighted average of its value against the currencies of Denmark’s most important trading partners, has fallen by 2.7 percent since the start of the year. The figures come from a compilation by Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry.
“The weakening of the krone’s value makes Danish goods and services cheaper for customers abroad, which makes it easier for export companies to secure new orders,” Sørensen said.
“It is in both the US, China, Norway, and Japan where the exchange rate means that they now have to pay less money to buy our products,” he added.
The Norwegian krone has risen 12.9 percent against the Danish krone over the past year, while the Chinese yuan has gained 9.8 percent. The US dollar and Japanese yen have each risen 4.8 percent.
However, not all currencies have strengthened against the Danish krone. The Swedish krona and Indian rupee have lost value, making goods from those countries slightly more expensive for Danish importers.
Exchange rates also affect the cost of holidays abroad. When a foreign currency strengthens against the Danish krone, Danish travellers get less for their money.
“For those who love a trip to the snow, a trip to Norway has become significantly more expensive solely as a result of the strengthening of the Norwegian krone,” Sørensen said.
“The weakening of the Swedish krona and low inflation in Sweden, on the other hand, make a ski vacation much more economically affordable in Sweden compared to Norway,” he added.
The Turkish lira has recorded the largest decline among the currencies in the compilation. It now costs 9.7 percent less to buy Turkish currency than it did at the start of the year.
Denmark to get 51 emergency supermarkets stocked for major crises
Shoppers across Denmark will be able to buy essential groceries and household supplies during power outages, cyberattacks and other emergencies under a new initiative by Salling Group.
The Danish retail giant, which operates Bilka, Føtex and Netto, plans to establish 51 emergency-ready supermarkets nationwide by 2027.
The stores will be equipped to operate for at least 48 hours without electricity or external communication systems, ensuring access to basic necessities during major disruptions.
According to Salling Group, the network will include 17 Bilka stores, 32 Føtex stores and two Netto locations.
The stores will be distributed so that up to 80 percent of Denmark’s population lives within 50 kilometers of one.
Each location will maintain emergency stocks of 50 essential products, selected according to Danish authorities’ recommendations for household preparedness.
These include oatmeal, protein bars, canned meatballs in curry, rice cakes, tuna, beans, chickpeas and other foods with long shelf lives.
Nonfood essentials such as batteries, wet wipes and diapers will also be available.
Customers will be able to pay offline using almost all physical payment cards and digital cards stored on smartphones.
Salling Group recently partnered with payment provider Nets to help maintain card transactions during system failures.
CEO Anders Hagh said establishing the emergency stores remains a top priority, with preparations progressing toward the 2027 target.
Meanwhile, competing retailer Coop, which operates Brugsen, SuperBrugsen, 365discount and Kvickly, has not decided whether to establish similar stores.
Coop’s chief risk officer, Ulrik Mester, said the company was discussing crisis preparedness with authorities, including Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed (SAMSIK), Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security.

A hacker gained access to a server at Aarhus University and attempted to access and change passwords belonging to approximately 1,700 users, the university has confirmed.
