Aula reopens as Danish authorities restore websites following security scare
Aula, Denmark’s widely used school communication platform, reopened Thursday morning after being taken offline Wednesday afternoon because of a global cybersecurity vulnerability.
Aalborg Municipality confirmed the reopening in a press release, saying the necessary security measures had been implemented.
The platform connects schools, daycare facilities and families across Denmark. It has approximately two million active users, with more than 600,000 logging in on a typical weekday.
The disruption followed the discovery of security flaws in PHP, a programming language widely used to operate websites, online shops and digital services.
The vulnerabilities left websites worldwide potentially exposed to cyberattacks, prompting authorities and public institutions in several countries to temporarily shut down services as a precaution.
In Denmark, affected websites included those belonging to Copenhagen Municipality, Danmarks Meteorologiske Institut (DMI), the Danish Meteorological Institute, and Vejdirektoratet, the Danish Road Directorate.
All affected Danish websites have since reopened.
Minister for Societal Security and Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen of Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, stressed Wednesday that the incident was not a cyberattack.
Speaking to TV 2, she explained that the vulnerabilities could nevertheless have serious consequences if left unaddressed.
The situation also prompted Denmark’s National Operational Staff, known as NOST, to activate its lowest crisis preparedness level, according to TV 2.
NOST brings together several public authorities to coordinate responses to major emergencies and crises.
The activation, known as information readiness, is the lowest of three preparedness levels and allows authorities to share information and coordinate their response to developing threats.
The measure was introduced Wednesday evening as authorities monitored the global security situation.
Security flaw in widely used software forces Danish websites offline
Several Danish public websites were shut down Wednesday after security vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language used by websites and online services worldwide.
Minister for Societal Security and Preparedness Lisbeth Bech-Nielsen described the situation as a “global incident” but stressed that it was not a cyberattack.
Speaking to TV 2, she warned that websites could face serious risks unless their operators installed the necessary security updates.
“It can potentially be really serious if system owners do not get a security update done. If that is not possible right here and now, then one must consider going offline,” she said.
The vulnerabilities affect PHP, which powers many websites, online shops and digital portals.
According to Reuters, PHP’s developers identified the flaws Tuesday but released an update to fix them Wednesday at 1:45 p.m.
Bech-Nielsen told Denmark’s public broadcaster, DR, that websites without the update could be exposed to attacks.
“It is in a way positive that we have found these vulnerabilities. But because it is publicly known, there are some who will exploit it,” she said.
Authorities and public institutions in several countries temporarily shut down websites as a precaution.
In Denmark, affected services included websites belonging to Copenhagen Municipality, the Danish Road Directorate and the Danish Meteorological Institute, known as DMI.
Kombit, an organization that manages shared IT solutions for Danish municipalities, also confirmed that Aula, the digital communication platform used by schools and parents, had been taken offline.
The ministry said authorities were closely monitoring developments but did not clarify whether further political action would be necessary.
Fake meat ban email tricks 1,200 Danish regional employees in phishing test
A warning about meat disappearing from workplace canteens prompted 1,200 employees in Denmark’s Capital Region to click a suspicious link in an internal cybersecurity test.
The exercise, reported by TV 2 Kosmopol, was designed to assess how well employees recognize phishing attempts, in which scammers impersonate trusted organizations to trick people into clicking links or sharing information.
Of the 13,000 employees who received the fake email, approximately 9 percent clicked the link.
The message claimed that meatballs and roast beef would be removed from workplace canteens and that some would switch to entirely vegan menus, excluding meat, dairy and eggs.
Employees were invited to click a link to find out how the changes would affect their local canteen.
However, the sender’s email address contained a small but important difference: it ended in “reqionh.dk” rather than the Capital Region’s actual domain, “regionh.dk”.
Anna Aaskilde Laursen, the region’s head of security, explained that the email deliberately targeted something employees cared about.
She told TV 2 Kosmopol that emotionally charged messages can prompt people to react without thinking, making it important to pause before clicking.
Laursen confirmed that the 1,200 employees who clicked the link would face no consequences.
Instead, the region intends to use the results to improve its preparedness for genuine cyberattacks.
Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security warns that phishing emails can be difficult to recognize because criminals often imitate official logos and use convincing language.
The agency recommends checking senders’ email addresses carefully and, when uncertain, contacting the supposed sender by telephone to verify whether a message is genuine.
Danish bishops consider moving Great Prayer Day to autumn when holiday returns
Great Prayer Day could return to Denmark’s calendar in a different season, with most bishops of the Church of Denmark open to moving the public holiday from spring to autumn.
The discussion follows the government’s announcement that Store Bededag, or Great Prayer Day, will be reinstated as a public holiday in 2030, according to Kristeligt Dagblad.
The holiday was abolished by the previous Social Democrat, Venstre and Moderates coalition government, with the change taking effect in 2024.
The Ministry of Ecclesiastical Affairs has confirmed that the Church of Denmark will be involved in the reinstatement process. A bill is expected in spring 2027.
Thomas Reinholdt Rasmussen, bishop of Aalborg, suggested that late October might be a suitable alternative.
“Liturgically, it does not really fit into the period from Easter to Pentecost, so perhaps it would be good to place it at the end of October,” he told Kristeligt Dagblad.
Marianne Gaarden, bishop of Lolland-Falster, also expressed openness to changing the date, noting that spring already has several public holidays.
“I like the idea of a prayer day where the focus is on spiritual reflection, and that focus must be preserved. But of course it is possible to consider that it can be moved,” she said.
Bishops in Funen, Aarhus and Viborg are similarly open to discussions, while Helsingør’s bishop, Peter Birch, has not taken a position.
However, the bishops of Ribe and Roskilde favor restoring the holiday to its original spring date.
The bishop of Copenhagen has not commented, while Haderslev’s bishop, Marianne Christiansen, will wait until the government presents its proposal.
Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey
Queen Mary to attend COP31 climate summit in Turkey with Danish minister
Denmark’s Queen Mary will travel to Antalya, Turkey, from November 8 to 10 to participate in the United Nations climate summit COP31, the Danish Royal House has announced.
She will be accompanied by Climate, Energy and Utilities Minister Samira Nawa of Radikale Venstre, the Social Liberal Party.
Turkey is co-hosting this year’s summit with Australia, which is responsible for leading the negotiations.
The annual UN climate conferences bring countries together to discuss international efforts to address climate change and reach agreements on reducing its impact.
During her visit, Queen Mary will meet representatives of Danish companies showcasing environmentally friendly technologies and solutions at the Danish pavilion.
She will also focus on the challenges facing Pacific island nations, including Vanuatu and Fiji, which are particularly vulnerable to rising sea levels and other consequences of climate change.
Another part of her program involves meeting young delegates from around the world to hear about their experiences with climate change and efforts to support the green transition.
Queen Mary also attended last year’s UN climate summit in Brazil, where her program included visits to a cocoa production facility and a research institute working on sustainability.
Her upcoming visit follows a new report from the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), published Wednesday, warning that global warming will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels.
The report attributes this to decades of insufficient climate action.
Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, countries committed to keeping global warming well below 2 degrees Celsius compared with temperatures between 1850 and 1900, while pursuing efforts to limit the increase to 1.5 degrees.

New partnership aims to connect lonely patients with social activities through their GPs
A new partnership in Denmark aims to help people experiencing loneliness and social isolation access community activities through referrals from their general practitioners.
Many people visit their doctors because they feel lonely, but their needs cannot always be addressed through medical treatment, said David Vincent Nielsen, a loneliness consultant at Ældre Sagen, a Danish association for older people, and chairman of Folkebevægelsen mod Ensomhed, a national movement against loneliness.
“There are a lot of people who seek out the healthcare and care system because they experience loneliness and social isolation.
“Most often, they cannot get help from the healthcare system because they need companionship and social relationships,” he said.
Under the proposed system, a doctor could issue a social referral for a patient. A professional or volunteer would then contact the patient and help identify activities and community groups suited to their needs.
The professional, known as a bridge-builder, would discuss the patient’s situation and help them find relevant offers from local organizations and municipalities.
These could include knitting groups, card game clubs or local exercise groups. Patients could also be encouraged to become volunteers themselves.
Nielsen said many people experiencing loneliness face barriers that make it difficult for them to seek out social activities and build relationships on their own.
For social referrals to become a regular part of Denmark’s health care system, however, the public sector would need to fund the service, he said.
“In 2017, the University of Southern Denmark calculated that loneliness cost 5.5 billion kroner, but since then, the prevalence of loneliness has increased by 42 percent, so around 10 billion kroner would be a qualified estimate today,” Nielsen said.
He argued that social referrals could also help reduce health care costs by addressing loneliness before people repeatedly seek medical assistance.
“But social referrals will not necessarily be an expense. Right now, there are at least 500,000 extra visits to general practice each year that are due to loneliness and paid for by the regions,” he said.
Pilot projects are already underway, Nielsen said. The new partnership aims to bring the existing efforts together into a coordinated model that could eventually be introduced nationwide.
The World Health Organization recognizes social referrals as a way to connect people with nonmedical support. According to the organization, one in five doctor visits is prompted by problems that cannot be resolved through clinical treatment.
The United Kingdom was the first country to incorporate social referrals into its health care policy. The WHO says there are now 3,300 active bridge-builders in the country.
The Danish partnership brings together Ældre Sagen, the Danish Red Cross, Social Sundhed, DGI, Sund By Netværket, Not a Box, and Frivilligcentre og Selvhjælp Danmark, an organization representing volunteer centers and self-help initiatives in Denmark.

The Danish labor market added 3,600 wage earners in August, according to a report published Wednesday morning by Danmarks Statistik, the national statistical authority of Denmark.
The increase follows a July that showed signs of a small slowdown.
The new numbers support the view held by financial group Nykredit that the Danish job market remains active.
Palle Sørensen, who serves as chief economist at Nykredit, noted that the trend is clear over a longer period.
“It is completely clear when you look at the development over a slightly longer horizon. In the past 12 months alone, there have been 29,638 more wage earners,” Sørensen said in a written comment.
He added that the job market matches the general economy.

“An important explanation is that more foreign employees have arrived, at the same time as more seniors are staying longer in the labor market,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said in a written comment.
He explained that these groups have helped employers find staff.
“This has made it possible for employment to continue to rise without companies having a correspondingly harder time finding employees,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said.
Neither Nykredit nor 3F expects the Danish labor market to slow down in the near future.
Sørensen said that recent experience shows that later retirement and foreign workers make the size of the total workforce more flexible.
“This is somewhat of an innovation compared to previously, where employment growth was often assumed to be temporary,” Sørensen said.
Energinet to prioritize addressing public service queries as power grid capacity runs short
Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

Share of 21-year-olds living at home in Denmark nearly doubles since 2011
More young adults in Denmark are choosing to stay in their family homes, with the share of 21-year-olds living with their parents rising from 32 percent in 2011 to 57 percent in 2025.
The figures come from Statistics Denmark and are highlighted in a new study by Realdania, a Danish philanthropic association focused on the built environment.
Henrik Mahncke, Realdania’s head of analysis, says high housing prices could partly explain the trend. Another possible reason is that many young people enjoy living with their parents.
However, where young people grow up also influences when they move out.
In Albertslund, a municipality near Copenhagen, 61 percent of 21-year-olds still live at home. On the island of Læsø, the figure is just 14 percent.
According to Statistics Denmark, distance to educational institutions is an important factor. Young people who live farther from places of study are more likely to move out.
Cultural background also plays a role, with young people from non-Western backgrounds generally staying at home longer.
Housing availability and prices may also influence their decisions.
Mette Mechlenborg, a senior researcher at Aalborg University who studies housing, points to another explanation: the design of modern family homes.
Many young people grow up in spacious houses with separate areas for parents and children, giving them greater privacy and independence.
This can make staying at home more attractive than moving into a small, expensive room.
Realdania’s study also found no overall difference in quality of life between young adults living with their parents and those who have moved out.

The changes were part of the government’s proposed 2027 budget and were expected to save 200 million DKK in 2028, 500 million DKK in 2029 and 800 million DKK in 2030.

“On the contrary. The fact that I called the colleagues from the other parties together today was precisely an expression of the fact that I actually wanted to discuss it with them, and that I respect that the agreement we have with each other gives all of them a veto right against changes in this area,” she added.
Dropping the proposal leaves a gap in the government’s budget plans.
Halsboe-Jørgensen said spending priorities would need to change but did not specify where the missing funds would come from.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard will now have to address the shortfall during negotiations on the 2027 Finance Act.

The European Commission has made security the main focus of its new Arctic strategy as Russia and China expand their activity in the region.
The approach marks a significant shift from the European Union’s 2021 strategy, which concentrated primarily on international cooperation, climate and environmental protection.
“As Russia and China increase their presence and ambitions, the Arctic has become a frontline in the global power competition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
The Commission fears the Arctic could become a major source of conflict with Russia after the war in Ukraine ends.
The strategy proposes expanding Europe’s icebreaker capacity and strengthening protection of northern maritime borders and critical undersea infrastructure.
The EU’s 27 countries collectively have about 10 icebreakers, compared with an estimated 40 operated by Russia.
The Commission also proposes creating a maritime security center to monitor activity in the Arctic.
A separate Arctic cable center would monitor, protect and repair undersea cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic. It could later track ships belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which transports sanctioned oil and gas.
Western intelligence services also suspect that Russia has used shadow fleet vessels in hybrid attacks.
The strategy contains no spending figures and must now be discussed with EU governments.
Kallas said Arctic security was a European concern because Denmark, Sweden and Finland are Arctic countries and more than 500,000 EU citizens live in the region.
Record trout catch in Varde River follows restoration efforts
Anglers caught a record 1,400 large trout in Denmark’s Varde River during 2025, according to science news outlet Videnskab.dk.
Researchers have also found trout fry at more locations in the river system than at any point during the past 40 years.
“It is good to see that efforts to remove obstacles to fish movement are beginning to work in Varde Å,” said Bjarke Ibsen Dehli, a fish conservation adviser at DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources.
However, he said Denmark remained far behind in restoring healthy, natural river systems.
Rivers have historically been straightened, widened and deepened to drain surrounding farmland. Stones and gravel were removed, despite fish such as trout and salmon relying on gravel for spawning.
Aquatic plants have also been removed, reducing places where fish can hide.
Sluices, dams, water mills, fish farms, bridges and pipes can block migrating fish. Fish gathered near such barriers may become easier prey for cormorants, herons, otters and seals.
DTU Aqua’s latest survey found healthy trout populations along 14 percent of the examined stretches of the Varde River system. That was up from five percent in 2016.
Associations can apply for funding to restore local waterways, including grants from DTU Aqua for spawning gravel and shelter stones.
Dehli encouraged residents to join local organizations working to improve rivers and streams.

Chief of Defence hosts tenth Dragon Group meeting in London
The Chief of Defence Staff, Air Chief Marshal Sir Richard Knighton, hosted the tenth Dragon Group meeting this week at Trinity House in London.
The UK was proud to host the 10th Dragon Group at Trinity House, welcoming friends and partners from across the Gulf and Middle East.
Named after its first meeting aboard HMS Dragon in 2018, the Dragon Group regularly brings together Defence Chiefs to exchange perspectives on the security challenges facing the region and wider world.
At a time of heightened regional instability, maintaining open and candid dialogue between trusted partners is more important than ever. The meeting provided an opportunity to discuss shared challenges, learn from recent experience and consider how we can deepen cooperation in support of regional security and stability. Discussions covered a range of global and regional issues, including the impact of Houthi escalation against Saudi Arabia, conflict between US and Iran, while reinforcing the importance of the longstanding defence relationships between the UK and our partners across the region.
Members include: Bahrain, Egypt, Iraq, Jordan, Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Lebanon, Oman, Qatar, UAE, and a representative from the GCC.

Jacob Harris receives three-year bankruptcy ban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:30:50 UTC
22:30:50 KST

Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

EXPLAINER – What to know about Serbia’s parliamentary elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:27:19 UTC
22:27:19 KST

- Around 6.45M voters registered for the snap election, according to the Republic Electoral Commission
- Parties differ over EU membership, relations with Russia and Kosovo, and Serbia’s political direction
Serbian voters will elect a new parliament on Sunday, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), a student-backed list and several opposition coalitions competing for seats.
Around 6.5 million voters are registered to elect 250 members of the National Assembly. The results will determine the distribution of parliamentary seats and which party or coalition can secure the support needed to form the next government.
The election campaign has also been marked by diplomatic tensions. Serbia has sent a protest note to Croatia over alleged interference in its domestic political affairs and election campaign, local media reported Wednesday.
The snap parliamentary election comes amid months of student-led protests and President Aleksandar Vucic’s resignation.
Vucic stepped down in late September ahead of the vote and announced his intention to seek the premiership as the SNS candidate. Having served two presidential terms, he is constitutionally barred from seeking a third.
His resignation has also triggered the process for an early presidential election, which, under Serbian law, must be held within three months.
Who are the main contenders and what are their agendas
The ruling camp, the Serbian Progressive Party, is represented by the electoral list “Aleksandar Vucic – United Serbia.” Vucic, who resigned as president in September, is seeking to return to government as prime minister.
The SNS has been the dominant force in Serbian governing coalitions since 2012. Its campaign emphasizes political stability, infrastructure development, economic growth and continued investment.
The ruling camp presents its record in government as a reason for voters to support it, highlighting economic measures and development projects.
The Student List – Students Win emerged from the protest movement that followed the November 2024 collapse of a railway station canopy in Novi Sad, which killed 16 people.
Its campaign focuses on accountability, the rule of law and reforms intended to strengthen public institutions. Protesters have demanded investigations into the disaster, the publication of relevant documents and accountability for those responsible.
The Socialist Party of Serbia (SPS), led by Ivica Dacic, has participated in successive governments, including coalitions with the SNS.
The party presents itself as a force for stability and emphasizes social protections, workers’ rights and the role of the state in economic policy.
Dacic has opposed recognizing Kosovo’s independence, imposing sanctions on Russia and joining NATO.
The European Serbia coalition, associated with opposition figures Marinika Tepic and Zdravko Ponos, advocates Serbia’s membership in the European Union.
The coalition identifies the rule of law, independent courts, and anti-corruption measures as central priorities.
The coalition has also pledged not to support a government led by the SNS or its partners, presenting the election as an opportunity to change the country’s political direction.
The Authentic Right bloc, led by Milos Jovanovic, represents a nationalist and conservative alternative.
The bloc supports cooperation with the EU but opposes full membership, arguing that Serbia should retain its political sovereignty and that accession conditions should be subject to public debate. Jovanovic has called for a referendum on EU membership.
How does the election work?
Serbia elects 250 members of the National Assembly through proportional representation. Voters choose electoral lists, and seats are allocated according to the votes received.
Most lists must win at least 3% of valid votes to qualify for seats, while lists representing national minorities are exempt from the threshold.
A party or coalition needs at least 126 seats to command a majority in parliament. If no political bloc secures a majority, parties must negotiate to form a governing coalition.
The Republic Electoral Commission has reported 6,450,523 registered voters and 8,392 polling stations. Voting arrangements also include stations abroad and in prisons.
Polling stations are scheduled to open at 7 am and close at 8 pm local time.
A further 60 polling stations have been designated in four Serbian municipalities for voters registered in Kosovo according to the Republic Electoral Commission.
The election is parliamentary, not presidential. The formation of parliament will determine which party or coalition can form the next government.
What are the main foreign policy issues?
Serbia is a candidate for European Union membership but maintains political and economic relations with Russia and China.
Belgrade has not joined Western sanctions against Moscow over the war in Ukraine. Relations with Russia remain an important domestic political issue, particularly for parties opposing sanctions and closer alignment with NATO.
Kosovo is another central issue. Serbia does not recognize Kosovo’s 2008 declaration of independence, and relations between Belgrade and Pristina remain a challenge for regional diplomacy and Serbia’s European integration process.
The parties differ over how closely Serbia should align with the EU, whether it should impose sanctions on Russia and how it should approach NATO.
European Serbia advocates EU membership, while the SPS opposes sanctions on Russia and NATO accession. Authentic Right opposes full EU membership.
What happens after the vote?
The election will determine which parties can form a government and whether the SNS-led governing camp retains power.
The student-backed list’s performance will indicate whether they can translate public mobilization into parliamentary representation. Smaller parties and minority representatives could also become important in coalition negotiations if the leading contenders fail to secure a majority.
The next government will face pressure to address demands for accountability and institutional reform while managing economic priorities, relations with the EU and Russia, and the unresolved issue of Kosovo.
The result will also shape Serbia’s domestic political balance and its approach to regional and international relations.

Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered the army to prepare for a “very extensive” operation in the occupied West Bank after two Israeli soldiers and two Palestinians were killed in an exchange of fire near a checkpoint in Hebron.
Netanyahu said the military would go house to house and demolish homes in an operation on a scale unseen in the occupied West Bank for decades, after the Israeli military said it had thwarted a “terror attack” by two armed Palestinians on Friday, amid heightened tensions before next week’s election.
According to the Israel Defense Forces, the two assailants opened fire on soldiers at a temporary checkpoint outside Hebron after failing to reach a nearby highway, where the Israeli military believes they had intended to attack civilians. According to a preliminary military investigation, the ensuing gunfight lasted more than 20 minutes, leaving five Israelis wounded, two of whom later succumbed to their injuries.
An AFP photographer who was en route to another assignment and witnessed the gun battle saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces.
Netanyahu’s office later said it had instructed security forces to immediately cordon off Hebron and prepare for a full closure of the West Bank starting on Friday.
After the shooting, the Israeli prime minister held an emergency meeting of his security cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies. He said Hamas was “planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians”.
During a visit to Hebron after the attack, Netanyahu later said Israeli forces would enter the neighbourhood of the attackers and displace its residents. He said the military would apply a model previously used in refugee camps in the northern West Bank.
A large-scale military operation named the “Iron Wall” launched in January 2025, forcibly displaced tens of thousands of people across several refugee camps, according to the UN rights office.
“We will evacuate the residents, we will go from house to house, we will also seize the weapons there, and all the terrorist infrastructure will be dealt with and destroyed,” Netanyahu said, according to his office.
Closures of the West Bank are becoming more common. Friday’s lockdown was the fourth time in the past month that Israel had imposed restrictions across the territory, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads, which will remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area.
Bezalel Smotrich, the far-right Israeli finance minister who also holds a position within the defence ministry, called for a military campaign in the West Bank “exactly like in Gaza”.
 
He said: “There is no other option but a comprehensive military campaign to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, collect weapons and eliminate terrorists. Exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon.”
Smotrich added: “In the next government this will be one of the first measures that we must demand and apply.”
Human rights groups warned that Netanyahu and his government could use the attack on Israeli soldiers to justify tougher measures against Palestinians and bolster their security credentials before the election.
“Every day in the West Bank is a dramatic day for the Palestinians,” Yariv Oppenheimer, the former director of Peace Now told Al Jazeera. “The Israeli army is getting into the Palestinian cities, the settlers are attacking Palestinians, and the situation is impossible.
“There will be house demolitions. We will see [a] curfew. We will see more soldiers … making arrests, and definitely we might see the settlers trying to target Palestinians in revenge for this attack, and trying to take advantage of this situation in order to escalate the situation even more.”
Voters go to the polls on Tuesday in an election that will help to determine whether Netanyahu secures another term as prime minister. The vote comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.
Israeli settlers are increasingly taking over Palestinian properties, and authorities have stepped up demolitions of homes lacking building permits, displacing families.
The campaign has intensified since the war in Gaza started in October 2023 amid accelerating land seizures and settlement expansion across the occupied West Bank. More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed there by Israeli forces or settlers, whose violence has surged during the annual olive harvest.
On 16 October settlers attacked Palestinian villages, burning cars and trees and injuring a Washington Post photographer. The next day they attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinian olive pickers, injuring three people and damaging a diplomatic vehicle.

Hundreds to defy Palestine Action ban in protest at US embassy in London
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:25:58 UTC
22:25:58 KST

Hundreds to defy Palestine Action ban in protest at US embassy in London
Campaigners plan Halloween mass action days before the UK Supreme Court hears a challenge to the group’s ‘terrorist’ proscription.
More than 400 people are expected to gather outside the United States embassy in London on October 31 in the latest act of mass defiance against the British government’s ban on the Palestine Action group.
Protesters plan to hold placards reading: “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action,” and campaign group Defend Our Juries said a parallel action will take place outside the US consulate in Edinburgh, Scotland.
More than 3,850 people have been arrested for publicly backing Palestine Action since the United Kingdom’s government proscribed it as a “terrorist” organisation in July 2025, Defend Our Juries said.
The timing of the demonstrations is calculated. In June, the Court of Appeal sided with the government and overturned a High Court ruling that had found the proscription unlawful.
On November 4 and 5, the UK Supreme Court will hear an appeal by Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori.
‘Arrested again and again’
Among those Al Jazeera spoke to at the group’s previous action outside Westminster Magistrates’ Court was Teresa, a former teacher-turned-activist who has been arrested multiple times for protesting against the proscription.
“It’s a badge of honour, to be able to do this for Gaza” she told Al Jazeera.
She is not alone. Those arrested at recent actions include Massive Attack’s Rob del Naja, 94-year-old human rights barrister Margaret Owen, former government adviser Jonathan Porritt and the Reverend Sue Parfitt.
Why the US embassy?
Organisers want to raise the possibility that the UK move to ban Palestine Action came under pressure from US President Donald Trump.
The proscription followed an incident in which activists spray-painted Trump’s Turnberry golf course in Scotland. The US president labelled the action “terrorism” on his Truth Social platform and praised then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s response.
During the legal challenge, it emerged that Trump and Starmer had spoken by phone twice about Palestine Action in March 2025. Starmer had requested updates from Police Scotland on the arrests and briefed Trump on developments.
The US president’s son Eric Trump also met Scottish First Minister John Swinney before the ban was announced, and documents released under the Freedom of Information Act showed the Turnberry protest was discussed.
The Halloween protests will also come three days after a hearing in the trial of the Turnberry protesters at the High Court in Glasgow. Prosecutors are now seeking to have the seven defendants sentenced as “terrorists”, a move critics called “completely disproportionate”.
The same week that the prosecutors made that call, Washington designated Palestine Action a “terrorist organisation”.
Defend Our Juries said the resulting sanctions have blocked Ammori from crowdfunding for her Supreme Court challenge.
Growing opposition
This week, actors Paul Mescal, Jessie Buckley and Susan Sarandon along with broadcaster Gary Lineker signed a letter published on the cover of the New Statesman magazine urging Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government to drop the “draconian” legislation.
Campaigners said the ban on the group has also in effect halted UK sales of books by the Irish novelist Sally Rooney, a Palestine Action supporter.
However, when author Sarah Helm, wife of National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell, publicly declared her support for Palestine Action, the Metropolitan Police took no action. Defend Our Juries said that exposes a ban that cannot be enforced evenly.
Shami Chakrabarti, a senior figure in the ruling Labour Party, has urged the home secretary to lift the ban.
Speaking to the LBC radio station, the former shadow attorney general said it “makes a mockery” of counterterrorism law and the power to proscribe should be exceptional and kept under constant review.
“I’d better be careful what I say, or I’ll be arrested,” she added.
The government’s case
The government argued that Palestine Action’s campaign of break-ins and criminal damage at defence sites, including those linked to Israeli arms maker Elbit Systems, meets the legal threshold for proscription. The Court of Appeal described it as a covert organisation operating through secret cells.
Defend Our Juries insisted its own protests are entirely peaceful.
“This mass defiance and the mass arrests expected to follow will lay bare the fundamental rights to free expression at stake in the Supreme Court hearing just days later,” a spokesperson said.

1,000 Patriot missiles arrive too late for this winter, so Ukraine asked the Ramstein arms coalition to open its warehouses
The ministry's readout says Ukraine has Patriot missiles under contract. It also says Kyiv asks partners to transfer interceptors from their stocks in exchange for future deliveries allocated to Ukraine.
Khmara made the same request at the Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting on 8 September. He said then that Ukraine was contracting about 1,000 Patriot missiles with partners' help and an EU loan, but they would arrive only in the coming years, LB reported. He asked allies for missiles from their stocks now, in exchange for future upgraded missiles under Ukraine's contracts.

Zelenskyy spoke to journalists before meeting Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo, Ukrinform reported. He said the Americans had reduced supplies and Russia would step up ballistic attacks.
"Europeans can provide the missiles only when the American side approves it," Zelenskyy said.
He said the US had sent most of its interceptors to the Middle East.
On 19 October, Zelenskyy told US senators that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth was not signing off on Patriot deliveries allies had already paid for. Axios obtained the call transcript from Ukrainian officials. A US government official told the Kyiv Independent that Ukrainian officials' claims that Hegseth was holding up the missiles were "not true."
Washington says nothing has changed. "We have our own needs, too," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on 20 October, but there is "nothing being deliberately denied to Ukraine." Hegseth told reporters in Eau Claire, Wisconsin, that the US had not changed its posture toward Ukraine, "but certainly with things like interceptors, we want to make sure our guys have the most possible as well."

Kazakhstan and Czech Republic expand agricultural cooperation
Kazakhstan and the Czech Republic intend to broaden trade and economic cooperation in the agro-industrial sector, develop livestock breeding, and introduce modern agricultural technologies, Qazinform News Agency reports, citing Kazakh Agriculture Ministry.
Over the first eight months of 2026, bilateral trade in agricultural products between the two countries increased by 31%.
During a meeting, Kazakh Vice Minister of Agriculture Yermek Kenzhekhanuly and Czech Deputy Minister of Agriculture Jaroslava Špalková discussed prospects for increasing mutual agricultural exports, expanding cooperation in livestock and crop production, and strengthening collaboration in veterinary and phytosanitary safety.
“We highly value the steady development of Kazakh-Czech relations in agriculture. Expanding cooperation with Czechia is one of the most promising avenues for strengthening the position of Kazakhstan’s agricultural products in the European market. To realize the existing potential, it is important to develop direct business contacts, broaden the range of exported products, and ensure compliance with European quality and safety standards,” the vice minister said.
For her part, Jaroslava Špalková outlined key priorities for the development of Czech agriculture. Among them, she highlighted cooperation in pedigree livestock breeding, aquaculture, and organic agricultural production.
The Kazakh side emphasized the importance of diversifying the trade structure, increasing supply volumes, and expanding the range of products of mutual interest.
Promising areas of cooperation also include supplies of pedigree cattle and genetic material from high-value breeding bulls, improvements in breeding programs, the development of artificial insemination technologies, and the exchange of expertise in herd reproduction.
Plant quarantine and protection issues, as well as the digitalization and automation of related processes, also featured prominently on the agenda.
The parties discussed opportunities for sharing experience and technological solutions to enhance phytosanitary control of agricultural products and improve the efficiency of related procedures.
Following the meeting, both sides reaffirmed their commitment to further developing cooperation in the agro-industrial sector. The implementation of the agreed initiatives is expected to strengthen Kazakhstan-Czech trade and economic ties, expand business contacts, and foster long-term partnership in agriculture.
To note, Kazakhstan, Mongolia also expand cooperation in energy, agriculture and mining.

CineCrossroads: What to watch this weekend - “Clayface,” “The Mask,” and “Megamind”

CineCrossroads: What to watch this weekend - “Clayface,” “The Mask,” and “Megamind”
The weekend is approaching, bringing three stories about characters whose transformations force them to question who they really are. In this edition of CineCrossroads, a disfigured actor undergoes a terrifying experiment, a timid bank clerk discovers a mask that unleashes his wildest impulses, and a famous supervillain finds himself searching for a new purpose. Qazinform News Agency correspondent wishes you an enjoyable viewing.
Movie of the Week: Clayface (2026)
Behind every face is a story, but Matt Hagen is about to lose both.
Directed by James Watkins, Clayface presents the origin of one of the most unusual villains from Batman’s rogues gallery. Tom Rhys Harries stars as Hagen, a rising actor whose promising career is destroyed after a violent attack leaves him severely disfigured.
Desperate to recover his appearance and return to the screen, Hagen turns to scientist Caitlyn Corr, played by Naomi Ackie, and agrees to undergo an experimental treatment. The procedure initially appears successful, but its effects soon transform his body into an unstable, clay-like form capable of assuming other identities.
Rather than following the structure of a conventional superhero film, Clayface combines psychological thriller, tragedy and body horror. Hagen’s transformation gives him extraordinary abilities, but it also weakens his grip on reality and drives him towards revenge.
Written by Mike Flanagan and Hossein Amini, the film also stars Max Minghella, Eddie Marsan and David Dencik. Released in cinemas on October 23, Clayface explores identity, ambition and the dangerous pursuit of physical perfection.
Classic Pick: The Mask (1994)
What if putting on a new face allowed you to become everything you were too afraid to be?
Directed by Chuck Russell, The Mask stars Jim Carrey as Stanley Ipkiss, a shy and frequently overlooked bank clerk whose life changes when he discovers a mysterious wooden mask. After placing it over his face, Stanley transforms into a green-faced figure with extraordinary powers, unstoppable confidence and the energy of a living cartoon.
The mask gives Stanley the courage to pursue singer Tina Carlyle, played by Cameron Diaz, but it also attracts the attention of dangerous criminals. As his second identity becomes increasingly difficult to control, Stanley must decide whether real confidence can exist without magic.
Combining comedy, romance and inventive visual effects, The Mask became one of the defining films of Carrey’s career. Like Clayface, it explores physical transformation and hidden identity, but approaches those ideas with color, humor and playful chaos.
Family Pick: Megamind (2010)
What happens when a villain finally wins?
Directed by Tom McGrath, Megamind follows a blue-skinned alien who has spent his life trying to defeat Metro Man, the celebrated protector of Metro City. When Megamind unexpectedly succeeds, he discovers that ruling the city is far less satisfying than fighting for it.
Without a hero to oppose him, Megamind creates a new one. However, the experiment quickly goes wrong, forcing the self-proclaimed villain to decide whether he is capable of becoming the person he always believed he could never be.
Featuring the voices of Will Ferrell, Tina Fey, Brad Pitt and Jonah Hill, Megamind combines superhero action with comedy and family adventure. Like Clayface, it explores how public labels can shape a person’s identity, while suggesting that individuals are not permanently defined by the roles assigned to them.

FACTBOX: Bank of Russia holds key rate at 14%
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:19:51 UTC
22:19:51 KST

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia has decided to maintain its key rate at 14% per annum, stating that current price pressures remain elevated, according to the regulator's press release.
TASS has compiled the key details of the decision.
Regulator’s press release
- The Bank of Russia's Board of Directors has decided to maintain the key rate at 14% per annum.
- The economy as a whole is growing at a moderate pace in the second half of 2026.
- Current price pressures remain elevated, and inflation expectations remain high.
- According to the Bank of Russia's assessment, underlying price growth is not slowing and remains within the 5-6% range on an annualized basis, primarily due to the impact of temporary capacity constraints in certain industries.
- This requires restrained growth in aggregate demand to resume a decline in underlying inflation, the Central Bank emphasized.
- The Bank of Russia noted that it will make further decisions on the key rate depending on inflation dynamics and inflation expectations, as well as an assessment of risks from domestic and external conditions.
- In Q3 2026, seasonally adjusted price growth averaged 8% on an annualized basis, up from 4.8% in Q2 2026.
- The corresponding core inflation rate increased to 6.2%, up from 4.5% in the previous quarter.
- Price dynamics continued to be influenced by volatile items, primarily motor fuel, the regulator noted.
- Annual inflation stood at 6.8% as of October 19 and is projected to settle within the 7.1-7.6% range by year-end.
- High inflation expectations are hindering a slowdown in inflation.
- Despite a slight decline in household and business expectations in October, overall, they have remained near their highest levels in two years in recent months, the Central Bank emphasized.
- The expectations of financial market participants and analysts have increased.
- According to high-frequency data, the economy is growing at a moderate pace in the second half of 2026.
- Business sentiment improved slightly in October following the low levels of previous months.
- Consumer demand growth is slowing but remains elevated, the Central Bank pointed out.
- Investment activity continues to recover compared to levels at the beginning of the year.
- Tensions in the labor market are gradually easing.
- According to surveys, the supply of workers at enterprises continues to improve, but the situation remains uneven across industries, the Central Bank noted.
- Wage growth is slowing and gradually converging with productivity growth.
- However, the gap in their dynamics remains significant, the regulator emphasized.
- At the same time, companies plan more moderate wage indexations in 2027 compared to 2026.
- Unemployment remains near historical lows.
- Lending activity was elevated on average in Q3 2026, driven primarily by the corporate segment.
- The retail loan portfolio grew moderately, the regulator noted.
- Households' propensity to save has declined somewhat but remains high.
- The Bank of Russia is proceeding from the announced fiscal policy parameters.
- Over the medium term, this will contribute to a slowdown in inflation.
- If fiscal policy parameters change, monetary policy may need to be adjusted, the regulator pointed out.
Ruble reaction
The ruble slowed its gains on the Moscow Exchange following the Bank of Russia's decision to maintain the key rate at 14% per annum, trading data showed.
Prior to the announcement, the yuan was trading at 12.037 rubles, down 12.8 kopecks, according to data as of 1:25 p.m. Moscow time.
By 1:30 p.m. Moscow time, the yuan paired its losses to 11.45 kopecks, trading at 12.05 rubles.
MOEX reaction
The MOEX Index turned lower following the central bank's decision to hold the key rate at 14% per annum, trading data showed.
As of 1:25 p.m. Moscow time, ahead of the rate announcement, the MOEX Index was up 0.22% at 2,434.74 points.
The RTS Index stood at 945.44 points, up 0.22%.
By 1:30 p.m. Moscow time, the MOEX Index reversed its gains to trade down 0.45% at 2,418.68 points.
The RTS Index also slid 0.45% to 939.21 points.

UNDP urges faster green investment as Istanbul hosts pre-COP31 summit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:19:19 UTC
22:19:19 KST

A senior UN Development Programme official has called for faster action to turn available capital and technology into green investments, as Istanbul hosts an investment summit ahead of COP31.
Speaking at the summit on Friday, UNDP Deputy Assistant Administrator Nick Rene Hartmann said the challenge was connecting financial resources with viable climate and development projects.
“We do not lack the capital,” he said. “Time is not our friend.”
Jointly organised by the Turkish Presidency’s Investment and Finance Office and the International Investors Association, the summit brought together government officials, international organisations and global companies at Ziraat Bank’s headquarters in the Istanbul Financial Centre.
Discussions focused on mobilising international investment in clean energy, sustainable industry, infrastructure and the circular economy ahead of the UN climate conference, which Türkiye is set to host in Antalya in November.
Hartmann estimated the value of the global financial system at $305 trillion, comparing it with an annual financing gap of $4.3 trillion for achieving the Sustainable Development Goals in developing countries, roughly 1.4 percent of that total.
Yet clean energy projects in developing countries can face financing costs up to seven times those in advanced economies, he said.
Since 2010, solar energy costs have fallen by 90 percent and battery storage costs by 93 percent, he added, stressing the need for effective regulation, reliable infrastructure and risk sharing to translate those gains into investment.
Turning climate commitments into projects
Hartmann welcomed Türkiye’s ambition to make COP31 an “implementation COP”, saying investment must advance at speed and scale.
The Climate Bridge initiative, to be presented at COP31, aims to turn climate commitments into investment opportunities, with initial demonstration projects envisaged in Ethiopia, Fiji, Indonesia, Pakistan and Uzbekistan.
The approach would combine concessional finance, grants, guarantees, risk-sharing instruments and private capital, he said.
UNDP has identified 700 sustainable development investment opportunities across 50 countries, Hartmann said. Since 2022, it has supported initiatives helping align more than $920 billion in public and private financing with the Sustainable Development Goals.
Strengthening Turkish suppliers
In Türkiye, UNDP and the Industry and Technology Ministry have developed a resource efficiency programme backed by $5 million in EU support, Hartmann said.
The programme aims to prepare investment-ready projects and strengthen Turkish suppliers’ competitiveness as low-carbon partners for international investors and European buyers.
Hartmann urged investors to look beyond projects already close to securing financing, invest in skills and local suppliers, and incorporate sustainability from the outset.
“Sustainability should therefore not be treated simply as a compliance cost,” he said. “It is an increasing source of economic value and an investment worth making.”

Trump ordered to testify in $10bn BBC lawsuit discovery: What happens now?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:17:46 UTC
22:17:46 KST

Trump ordered to testify in $10bn BBC lawsuit discovery: What happens now?
Trump could face sanctions, including dismissal of his lawsuit, if he fails to cooperate with questioning.
United States President Donald Trump must answer questions under oath in the discovery stage of his $10bn lawsuit against the BBC, a federal judge has ruled, warning that failure to cooperate could lead to the dismissal of his case.
The dispute centres on a BBC documentary which combined separate excerpts from a speech he gave before the January 6, 2021 attack on the US Capitol.
The broadcaster has apologised for the edit but denies that Trump has grounds for a defamation claim. Here is what the ruling means and how the case reached this point.
What has the judge ordered?
Trump has been ordered to make himself available for questioning by the BBC’s lawyers by December 11, unless the judge overseeing the case extends the time frame for gathering evidence. That process is currently scheduled to end on December 18.
The ruling comes after the president’s legal team sought to postpone questioning until January. Judge Enjolique Lett also rejected his lawyers’ attempt to prevent the session from being filmed. Access to the recording will initially be restricted to lawyers involved in the case.
Separately, she gave Trump’s side 30 days to hand over relevant documents requested by the BBC.
What is a deposition?
A deposition is a formal interview under oath, usually conducted outside the courtroom before a trial. Lawyers question a witness and the answers are recorded in a transcript. The testimony can later be used in court, including to challenge a witness whose account changes.
It forms part of “discovery” – the stage of a US civil lawsuit in which both sides are given time to obtain relevant evidence through examining documents, submitting written questions and taking witness testimony. The process allows each side to examine the other’s claims and prepare its case.
Trump’s deposition is expected to last up to seven hours.
Why is Trump suing the BBC?
Trump filed his lawsuit against the British broadcaster in federal court in Florida on December 15, 2025, over a Panorama documentary which was broadcast shortly before the 2024 US presidential election.
His complaint seeks at least $5bn for alleged defamation and another $5bn for alleged violations of Florida’s Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act. He alleges that the programme damaged his reputation and business interests by falsely portraying him as directly encouraging violence at the Capitol.
The BBC, which has apologised for the way the programme was edited, however, disputes those allegations and has sought to have the case dismissed. It also challenges the Florida court’s jurisdiction, arguing that the documentary was produced in London and was never broadcast in the US.
Trump’s lawyers contend that viewers in Florida could have accessed the programme through BritBox or by using a virtual private network (VPN), which can disguise a user’s location. The BBC says the documentary was not available on BritBox International or its international website.
How was Trump’s speech edited?
The documentary combined remarks from separate sections of Trump’s January 6 speech into what appeared to be a continuous statement: “We’re going to walk down to the Capitol and I’ll be there with you… And we fight. We fight like hell and if you don’t fight like hell, you’re not going to have a country anymore.”
Two quotes that make up the excerpt used by the BBC were delivered roughly 54 minutes apart. The programme also left out his appeal for supporters to “peacefully and patriotically make your voices heard”, Trump’s lawyers say.
The BBC acknowledged that the edit created the mistaken impression that Trump had made a direct call for violent action. It apologised, while rejecting his demand for compensation and denying a legal basis for the defamation claim.
The controversy was followed by the resignations of BBC director-general Tim Davie and its news chief, Deborah Turness.
Trump has also suggested, without evidence, that artificial intelligence was used to put words into his speech.
Why has the deposition been delayed?
Trump had agreed to be questioned on October 16, but his lawyers cancelled that date, citing a matter of national importance.
Trump’s lawyers subsequently proposed dates between January 11 and 22 of next year.
At Thursday’s hearing, BBC lawyer Charles Tobin said Trump had instead been campaigning in Georgia and asked the court to compel Trump to attend the deposition sooner, arguing that waiting until January would push the questioning beyond the existing deadline for gathering evidence.
Lett upheld the BBC’s complaint that Trump’s team had been too slow to hand over internal documents. Charles Tobin, on behalf of the BBC, told the Miami court: “We still have a completely lopsided [situation] here on discovery. They have produced absolutely nothing of any substance”.
What happens if Trump does not comply?
Lett warned that failure to cooperate could lead to sanctions, including dismissal of the lawsuit altogether. That would mean Trump’s own attempt to recover damages could end because he would have failed to fulfil his obligations as the person bringing the case.
Under federal civil procedure rules, discovery sanctions can also include ordering a party to pay legal expenses caused by noncompliance, preventing it from introducing certain evidence or striking out parts of its case. These are possible penalties, rather than sanctions already imposed on Trump.

Russia drops cluster bombs on Ukraine as Kyiv consolidates front line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:17:18 UTC
22:17:18 KST

Russia drops cluster bombs on Ukraine as Kyiv consolidates front line
Russia’s territorial gains this year are effectively nil as it heads into trilateral talks with Ukraine, US.
Ukraine said it recaptured more of its territory than Russia had managed to seize this year, despite restrictions on US satellite services critical to its defence.
Russia responded by hitting dozens of Ukraine’s energy facilities and using cluster bombs in attacks that harmed civilians.
“Our soldiers have liberated more territory since the beginning of autumn than the Russians have managed to capture,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a public address.
Ukrainian General Staff spokesman Andriy Kovalev denied Russian claims to have seized 1,800 sq km (700 square miles) of Ukrainian territory during the autumn.
The Institute for the Study of War, a Washington-based think tank that uses geolocated open-source information to assess territorial movements, said Ukraine had made a net gain of 241 sq km (93 square miles) since September 1, effectively eliminating any Russian territorial gains this year.
Russia’s casualties suggest the effectiveness of its forces is in decline.
Russian losses – meaning those killed or severely wounded – hovered around 30,000 a month from January to May, but steadily increased over the summer. According to Ukrainian estimates, Russia lost 46,230 soldiers in September, its highest monthly losses of the year, and 37,000 so far in October.
October 21 marked its highest daily losses of the entire war, at 2,250, said Robert Brovdi, the commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces of Ukraine, as his unit’s kill rate had climbed to a new record.
Overall, Ukraine estimated there were more than 350,000 Russian dead and wounded since the beginning of the year.
Many of Ukraine’s territorial gains were made by Operation Vivaldi, a Ukrainian counteroffensive that stopped a Russian pincer movement to recapture the remaining one-fifth of Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region – roughly 5,500 sq km (2,000 square miles).
General Andriy Biletskyi, who led Ukraine’s Third Army Corps to victory in that campaign, said he had eliminated a Russian bridgehead on the western bank of the Zherebets river, and crossed over to the east bank, shortening his own front line and concentrating artillery and unmanned aerial firepower, stabilising its defence.
The defeat of the pincer, said Biletskyi, had left Russia with the unsavoury option of a frontal assault on the “fortress belt” of heavily defended cities of Kramatorsk, Sloviansk and Druzhivka.
Russia had “temporarily abandoned this plan, although it plans to resume it,” Biletskyi told the Ukrainian news outlet Suspilne. Russian military expert Andrey Marochko told Russia’s state news agency TASS that Ukraine was reinforcing the fortress cities.
Russia has responded to its sagging military fortunes by increasing the ferocity of its attacks on civilians.
On October 22, it flew three ballistic missiles with cluster warheads into Kyiv, Zelenskyy said.
“This warhead detonates above the ground and is specifically designed to inflict maximum damage on people and equipment within an area of 400 by 400 metres,” said Ukrainian Defence Ministry senior adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov. “45 submunitions explode in the air.”
One of the warheads struck an area between the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra cathedral and a monastery.
“There was not even theoretically any military object nearby,” said Zelenskyy. “It is a deliberate choice of weapons, a deliberate choice of the area.”
Russia’s Defence Ministry claimed it had targeted an assembly building for the FP-5 long-range drones and FP-9 missiles Ukraine has been using against it, as well as other drone manufacturing sites.
More than anything else, though, Russia has relentlessly targeted Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, despite United States President Donald Trump declaring an energy ceasefire for both sides on October 11.
Since then, there had been more than 170 strikes on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, Zelenskyy said.
“Russia is not achieving any significant results on the front lines. Therefore, it is directing all its aggression and hatred towards terrorising civilian infrastructure: electricity, heating, and now, water. The goal is clear – to exhaust the people,” Prime Minister Serhiy Khoretskyi told the BBC.
Since he assumed office on July 16, he said, Russia had attacked Ukraine’s energy infrastructure 2,147 times.
Ukraine has been hampered in its defence by the US, which on October 8 was understood to have stopped providing early warning of incoming ballistic missiles for the second time this year.
Zelenskyy said that early warning had been restored on October 20, but three other US actions detrimental to Ukraine’s defence had not been reversed.
One was Trump’s waiver of oil export sanctions on Russia to lower the price of diesel, which he formalised with an executive order on October 16. Putin said on October 21 that Russia’s first shipment of 40,000 tonnes of diesel to the US would depart within two or three days.
Another issue was that the US has not released Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, which are its most effective defence against ballistic missiles, despite having previously supplied a dozen a month, and despite the fact that Europe has paid for them.
But the biggest problem was that Ukraine’s ability to fly its drones at more than 150kmh (100mph) using the Starshield satellite navigation system remained suspended.
Ukraine has said it cannot intercept fast-moving jet-powered drones at such speeds, and its attacks on Russian logistics, as well as the resupply of its own front lines by drone, are also rendered more vulnerable.
Starshield was created as a military application of Starlink, owned by Elon Musk, and he and the White House traded blame for making the decision to restrict it throughout the week. Trump said on October 22 that Starlink and Starshield services were about to be restored.
After initially observing Trump’s energy ceasefire, Ukraine resumed targeting Russian energy infrastructure, as part of an economic strategy to starve the Russian war machine of export revenue.
On October 18, it struck the St Petersburg oil terminal, Russia’s biggest offloading terminal for oil exports. It also hit a data centre serving Russian social media platform Vkontakte, disrupting services.
Other facilities were likely targeted. Russia’s Defence Ministry said it had downed 1,015 Ukrainian drones over various regions that night.
The US appeared to leverage its waiver of diesel sanctions and the suspension of Starshield services to push for a trilateral meeting among the US, Russia and Ukraine.
US envoy Steve Witkoff met with Zelenskyy in Oslo on October 20, and followed up with a meeting with Putin in St Petersburg the following day.
Putin aide Yuri Ushakov told the media that Russia had agreed “in principle” to meet on November 10. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the planned meeting would be held in Abu Dhabi.

Ukrainian media identifies Russian officers responsible for blockade, starvation of occupied Oleshky
An investigation by Ukrainian media outlet Slidstvo.info published on Oct. 23 has uncovered the identities of Russian officers involved in the blockade of the city of Oleshky in Kherson Oblast.
The Russian-occupied city, located just across the Dnipro River from Kherson, has been effectively blockaded by Russian forces in the area, who prevent humanitarian aid from entering. Civilians attempting to flee via the only roads in and out of the city are frequently targeted by drones.
Building on a previous investigation published in late September that identified the commanders of the Russian 126th Coast Guard Brigade of the Black Sea Fleet and the 331st Guards Airborne Regiment as operating in the area, Slidstvo.info established the presence of the 217th Guards Airborne Regiment and its commander, Georgy Yanchev.
According to the Oct. 23 investigation, the 217th Regiment previously took part in the Battle of Kyiv at the outset of Russia's full-scale invasion and later fought in Chasiv Yar, one of the main hotspots of fighting in Donetsk Oblast.
Yanchev, who has served in the Russian military since 1993 and holds the rank of colonel, has three children who live in the central Russian city of Samara.
Oleshky has been under Russian occupation since the early days of the full-scale invasion. Residents face severe shortages of food, water, and electricity, while mined roads, constant drone attacks, and interrogations by Russian troops at checkpoints make safe evacuation virtually impossible.
As the humanitarian crisis in the city has grown increasingly severe this autumn, international pressure to provide assistance to the remaining residents trapped inside has mounted.
On Oct. 16, Pope Leo XIV expressed concern over the worsening situation in Oleshky during a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The pope called for a local ceasefire to allow humanitarian aid deliveries and the safe evacuation of civilians from the front-line city, where around 2,000 residents remain trapped amid severe shortages of food and medicine.
Ukraine and Russia are nearing an agreement on the final details of civilian evacuation from Oleshky and nearby settlements, Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 18.
In the meantime, Ukrainian soldiers fighting on the western bank of the Dnipro have made repeated deliveries of food aid to the area by drone.

Wholesale revenue also hit a monthly record in September, reaching NT$1.94 trillion, up 52% year over year and marking the sector’s 20th consecutive month of growth. The ministry attributed the increase mainly to strong demand for AI-related products.
The ministry forecasts wholesale revenue of NT$1.85 trillion to NT$1.91 trillion in October, up 48.7% to 53.3% from a year earlier. Chen said wholesale revenue typically peaks in September and December, and is expected to ease slightly from September’s record level.
