====================================================================================================

France's bond drama takes centre stage ahead of ECB rate decision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:14:55 UTC
22:14:55 KST

The European Central Bank is expected to hold rates next week as France's bond sell-off tightens borrowing conditions across the eurozone, while ECB President Christine Lagarde has made clear that the first steps to tackle French debt woes must come from Paris, not Frankfurt.
When the European Central Bank (ECB) meets next Thursday, it is widely expected to leave interest rates unchanged, partly because rising government bond yields are already pushing up borrowing costs across the eurozone.
ECB President Christine Lagarde has played down hopes of a rescue, saying the solution to France's debt problems lies at home.
The yield on France's 10-year government bond traded above 5% on Friday after rising to that level on Wednesday for the first time since 2002. The gap with German 10-year bonds, the eurozone's safest debt, was above 170 basis points.
Meanwhile, the 30-year yield was at 5.5%, and the gap with German 30-year bonds was even wider at 184 basis points.
On Thursday, the cost of France's five-year credit default swaps, contracts that insure investors against a government default, also climbed above 100 basis points for the first time since October 2012, when the eurozone was going through its sovereign debt crisis.
Lawmakers remain split over next year's budget, which includes €43 billion in spending cuts and additional revenue measures that the government has no majority to push through.
Ratings agency Moody's, which rates France Aa3, its fourth-highest grade, with a negative outlook, delivers its verdict on Friday evening, and a downgrade is widely expected. A one-notch cut to A1 would put France's rating at the equivalent level to those assigned by S&P and Fitch.
Civil unrest is adding to investors' concerns.
More protests are expected this weekend, and Paris police prefect Patrice Faure has advised business owners in a letter to hire private security.
French trade unions, unanimously disappointed after meeting Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu on Wednesday, have called for a large mobilisation on 5 November.
Sophie Binet, head of the CGT, one of France's biggest unions, urged workers to "generalise the strike".
Bonds doing the ECB's job
The case for another rate hike is still there.
The ECB has raised rates twice this year, lifting its deposit rate to 2.5%, and eurozone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September, driven by energy prices.
Yet German yields have climbed so much since September that their effect on growth and inflation roughly matches a 25 basis point hike, Carsten Brzeski, global head of macro at Dutch bank ING, estimated in an investor note on Thursday.
"For France, it’s closer to a 50 basis point hike," Brzeski wrote, adding that "the bond market has taken over the ECB's job".
Brzeski expects the ECB to wait for new staff forecasts in December before deciding on its next hike.
ECB President Christine Lagarde told the European Parliament on 28 September that long-term rates "have risen notably, which will slow growth".
Could the ECB intervene?
ECB officials have played down the possibility of intervening to lower France's borrowing costs, but have stopped short of ruling it out.
The central bank bought government bonds during the eurozone debt crisis to stabilise markets and ensure its rate decisions continued to feed through to the economy.
Speaking on the sidelines of the annual meetings of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank in Bangkok last week, Lagarde said that "there are particular circumstances that lead to some countries being more affected, France being a case in point."
"The primary and first solution lies at home in France. And it has to do with fiscal policies," the ECB president added.
Banque de France governor Emmanuel Moulin went further last Friday, saying the conditions for ECB intervention were not met at that time because there was no financial fragmentation in the eurozone.
However, both officials spoke before France’s 10-year borrowing costs rose above 5%.
If the ECB decides to intervene in the French bond market, one option could be the Transmission Protection Instrument (TPI), which was created in 2022 and has never been used.
The TPI lets the ECB buy the debt of countries whose borrowing costs climb in ways it judges unjustified by their economic fundamentals and threaten the transmission of monetary policy across the eurozone.
For a country to be eligible, it needs to meet several criteria, including following EU fiscal rules and keeping its debt on a sustainable path.
France is nursing a debt-to-GDP ratio of 119.1%, and the current budget negotiations offer little prospect of a quick reduction in the deficit, which is necessary to put the debt on a sustainable path.
Meanwhile, the government expects its debt-servicing costs to rise by more than €10 billion in 2027 compared with this year.
"The bar for activating the ECB's bond-buying programme remains high," Brzeski wrote in a separate investor note last week.
He added that, for France, that would at least mean passing its full budget. Acting too early could be "interpreted as monetary financing of the debt of a country unwilling to follow the rules," he warned.
The ECB's other emergency tool, Outright Monetary Transactions (OMT), was created in 2012 at the height of the eurozone debt crisis to allow unlimited purchases of a struggling country's short-term bonds.
However, it is only available to governments that first sign up to a bailout programme from the eurozone's rescue fund, the European Stability Mechanism.
Instead, Brzeski expects the ECB to quietly pause the reduction of its bond holdings, reinvesting maturing debt flexibly as it did during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Should turmoil spread to other eurozone bond markets, Brzeski sees TPI as a last resort. If France continued to fall short of EU fiscal rules, "the ECB might even consider purchasing bonds from almost all eurozone countries, except for France," he said.
For now, Brzeski sees next week’s rate meeting as "uneventful on action but clearly not on words".

PRETORIA, South Africa, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- A briefing reception held in Pretoria, South Africa's administrative capital, has highlighted growing opportunities for South African businesses to expand exports to China under China's zero-tariff treatment for African countries with which it has diplomatic ties since May 1.
The reception, hosted by the Chinese Embassy in South Africa and co-hosted by the South African Department of Trade, Industry and Competition and the South African Revenue Service (SARS) on Thursday, brought together about 400 government officials, business leaders, exporters and entrepreneurs to discuss the implementation of the policy and opportunities arising from improved access to the Chinese market.
Chinese Ambassador to South Africa Wu Peng said the policy is bringing businesses and consumers in the two countries closer together and has already generated positive momentum in bilateral economic and trade cooperation.
Citing SARS figures, the ambassador said that bilateral trade between China and South Africa reached nearly 15 billion U.S. dollars from May to August, up nearly 24 percent year on year, as South African exports to China rose nearly 25 percent to 5.3 billion dollars and imports from China increased 23 percent to 9.47 billion dollars.
South Africa's agricultural exports to China reached nearly 500 million dollars during the period, up more than 35 percent year on year, while non-mineral exports grew 21.8 percent, he added.
"Zero tariffs significantly reduce the cost of trade between South Africa and China," Wu said, adding that the measure could strengthen the competitiveness of companies operating in South Africa and encourage investment and production.
South Africa is China's largest trading partner in Africa, while China has remained South Africa's largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, with bilateral trade reaching 53.58 billion dollars in 2025.
South African Trade, Industry and Competition Minister Parks Tau said the government is working to ensure that the tariff measure translates into more exports, investment and jobs rather than simply increased trade volumes.
Noting that South African products meeting the applicable rules of origin can benefit from the preferential treatment when entering the Chinese market, Tau said SARS has issued 25,975 certificates of origin between June 1 and Aug. 31, while customs declarations increased 199 percent year on year.
The minister said the two countries are negotiating an early harvest arrangement through the Southern African Customs Union, following the signing of a framework agreement on economic partnership for shared development in February.
"Let us move from interest to deals, and from deals to prosperity," Tau said. ■

Xinhua Headlines: FAO honors highlight China's efforts to strengthen global food security
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
21:14:08 CST
22:14:08 KST

* The recent FAO honors awarded to Chinese desertification control pioneer Yin Yuzhen and a Chinese research institute highlighted China's broader efforts to strengthen global food security through ecological restoration, technological innovation and international cooperation.
* Jordan's Princess Basma bint Ali described Yin's decades-long efforts as "the other face of innovation." She stressed that addressing hunger, climate shocks and inequality required sustained attention and action.
* Beyond ecological restoration, technological innovation offers another way to strengthen food security, helping countries boost agricultural production, address environmental risks and build more resilient food systems.
* In an interview with Xinhua, FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero noted that China had been preparing for natural and geopolitical risks by diversifying imports, keeping its market open and improving stock management.
ROME, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- As Chinese desertification control pioneer Yin Yuzhen was honored at the headquarters of the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO) in Rome, her longtime American friend Ronald Sakolsky looked on, his eyes filled with tears.
"Yin deserves everything that she gets. She is the heroine," said Sakolsky, a retired teacher who helped fund her tree-planting efforts more than two decades ago.
At the Oct. 15 ceremony, Yin was named among the FAO's 100 Women Heroes in Agrifood Systems and Rural Development, an initiative marking the International Year of the Woman Farmer 2026.
A day later, a Chinese research institute received an FAO award for its crop-monitoring technology.
Together, the honors highlighted China's broader efforts to strengthen global food security through ecological restoration, technological innovation and international cooperation.
FROM SHIFTING SANDS TO A GREEN LANDSCAPE
The story of Yin and Sakolsky began in 1999, when Sakolsky was teaching in central China's Henan Province. After seeing a TV report about Yin's efforts to hold back the encroaching sands in north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, he raised 5,000 U.S. dollars to support her afforestation endeavor.
After losing touch for years, the two reunited in Inner Mongolia in August 2026. By then, the seedlings supported by Sakolsky's donation had grown into more than 50,000 trees.
Since planting her first tree in 1986, Yin has helped green over 70,000 mu (around 4,667 hectares) of sandy land, an area roughly the size of 6,500 standard soccer pitches. Today, the area supports a greater variety of crops and plants, including cherries and roses, creating new opportunities for agricultural production and income growth.
"I have spent more than 40 years transforming this desert, and now all kinds of food can grow here," Yin told Xinhua.
Yin's efforts reflect China's broader push to combat desertification, a major part of which is the Three-North Shelterbelt Forest Program, launched in 1978 to restore degraded land and strengthen ecological security in northern China.
For Yin, combating desertification is also essential to agricultural production. "If we cannot control the sand, how can we grow good crops when sandstorms come? How can we improve the soil?" she said.
At the World Food Day ceremony in Rome on Oct. 16, Jordan's Princess Basma bint Ali described Yin's decades-long efforts as "the other face of innovation." She stressed that addressing hunger, climate shocks and inequality required sustained attention and action.
"It must be the steady kind that plants, tends and finally harvests the gains. As did Yin Yuzhen," the princess said.
INNOVATION FOR GLOBAL FOOD SECURITY
Beyond ecological restoration, technological innovation offers another way to strengthen food security, helping countries boost agricultural production, address environmental risks and build more resilient food systems.
On Oct. 16, the Aerospace Information Research Institute of the Chinese Academy of Sciences received the 2026 FAO Achievement Award for its CropWatch, a cloud-based crop-monitoring platform.
Developed by a team led by researcher Wu Bingfang, the platform combines satellite observations with climate and agricultural data to monitor crop conditions, assess production prospects and identify risks such as drought and abnormal rainfall.
Through its open cloud service, CropWatch allows users to conduct their own crop assessments without investing heavily in local computing infrastructure.
According to the research team, the platform has helped more than 40 countries and regions monitor crop conditions, and its bulletins have served users in 173 countries and regions.
CropWatch has also been integrated into the FAO's Hand-in-Hand Geospatial Platform and the Group on Earth Observations Knowledge Hub. It serves as an important channel and an independent source of timely crop monitoring information for users worldwide.
Wu told Xinhua after receiving the award that the recognition affirmed the team's more than three decades of dedication.
"This is not the end, but a milestone on a new journey ahead," he said.
SHARING CHINESE EXPERIENCE FOR FOOD SECURITY
China's contribution extends beyond domestic production to international agricultural cooperation.
In addition to feeding its own population of more than 1.4 billion, China has also provided assistance to countries in need, contributing to global food security.
Zhang Lubiao, China's permanent representative to the FAO, said China would deepen cooperation with the FAO in hybrid rice, water-saving irrigation, digital agriculture and climate-adaptive technologies, among other areas.
Such cooperation is already yielding tangible results in various countries.
Nosipho Jezile, South Africa's permanent representative to the UN food and agriculture agencies, said China's South-South cooperation projects with the FAO had supported rice cultivation, aquaculture, irrigation infrastructure, mechanization and agricultural innovation in African countries.
"These projects have brought tangible increases in output and created employment opportunities," she said.
Food security depends on more than agricultural production. Keeping food affordable and ensuring a stable supply of fertilizers and other agricultural inputs are also essential, particularly amid economic and geopolitical uncertainties.
In an interview with Xinhua, FAO Chief Economist Maximo Torero said rising prices, rather than immediate food shortages, posed the biggest risk to global food security at present.
Torero noted that China had been preparing for natural and geopolitical risks by diversifying imports, keeping its market open and improving stock management.
China's urea exports were also helping bring down prices, he said, urging major producers and importers not to distort markets or restrict exports of agricultural inputs. ■

SYDNEY, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Chinese basketball star Yang Shuyu battled foul trouble while the Sydney Flames continued their unbeaten start to the WNBL season with an 82-70 victory over the UC Capitals on Friday.

Guidance: Ex-Gratia Medical Payments reviews
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:11:48 BST
22:11:48 KST

Ex-Gratia Medical Payments reviews
Guidance for former locally employed staff who were injured in the course of their service.
Documents
Details
Overview
The UK government initiated the Ex-Gratia Medical Payments (EGMP) policy to provide support to former locally-employed staff in Afghanistan who were injured as a result of their employment with the Ministry of Defence (MOD) between 2001 and 2021. The EGMP scheme was closed to new applications in 2021.
The EGMP Review was initiated in June 2020 to enable reviews of payments under the EGMP.
The EGMP Review was closed to new applications on 23 July 2026. Those who have already applied will also no longer be able to provide further evidence on their applications.
All valid applications received before the scheme closed will be processed.
No new applications are being accepted.
This publication explains the eligibility criteria for the EGMP Review.
Background
Between 2001 and 2021, local staff in Afghanistan who worked with the UK government played an important part in our joint efforts towards the shared goal of a more secure, stable and prosperous Afghanistan.
Extremely brave people worked alongside our soldiers on patrol, and in some cases suffered profoundly life-changing injuries as a result of enemy action. The government committed to awarding appropriate payments for these people through the EGMP.
In 2020, the MOD initiated a process for reviewing the EGMP cases relating to individuals who wish to have their cases re-assessed. Its intent was to enable those whose condition has deteriorated beyond their original prognosis, or those who have developed a late-onset condition, to receive a fair full and final payment without prejudice.
Eligibility Criteria
To be eligible for the EGMP Review, the applicant must satisfy all of the following criteria:
- The injury must have occurred during MOD employment and have been recorded by the Department at the time;
AND
2. There must be sufficient evidence that the condition has deteriorated beyond what was assessed as the projected recovery at the time, or that a new condition has arisen as a result of the original injury;
- For EGMP Review applications received prior to 23 April 2026, these must have been reported to us within 3 years of formal diagnosis of the deterioration or new condition (as opposed to 3 years of the date of initial award payment for applications submitted on or after 23 April 2026). Consideration will also be given to cases where eligibility to the EGMP was previously considered but a payment was not awarded, where evidence supports this;
- For EGMP Review applications received after 23 April 2026 these must have been reported to us within 3 years of the initial EGMP award unless the condition could clearly not have been known to the individual within that timescale;
AND
3. The deterioration or new condition must be a significant permanent physical or mental impairment or disability, including any serious scarring or disfigurement.
These payments are not intended to provide compensation for those injuries where the individual is expected to make a complete recovery or where they may be left with some permanent or long-lasting impairment of a less serious nature, for example limited in either the degree of pain or loss of faculty.
Making a claim
The EGMP Review was closed to new applications on 23 July 2026. Claims received after 23 July 2026 will not be accepted.
Claims were required to be submitted before 23 July 2026 must have submitted a completed Ex-Gratia Medical Review Claim Form to DARR-Medical-Casework@mod.gov.uk, along with photocopies of two forms of identification: either a passport or a driving license, and a utility bill showing the claimant’s current address dated within the previous three months. Claims submitted without all required documents and/or after 23 July 2026 will be considered as invalid without a right to appeal.
Appealing the review decision
In the event you are not satisfied with the outcome of your application to the EGMP Review, you can appeal the decision within 28 days of being sent the outcome letter. You can appeal the review decision by submitting a completed EGMP Review Appeal form to DARR-Medical-Casework@mod.gov.uk. The appeal form will be published before substantive decisions are issued.
Eligibility to appeal
Individuals who did not submit a valid application before the closure of the scheme (23 July 2026) are not eligible to submit an appeal, as a substantive action was not taken.
Applicants who have submitted a valid claim and received an EGMP Review decision letter may submit one appeal against that decision, including where they have been found ineligible under any element of the eligibility criteria.
Applicants may submit one appeal in relation to their EGMP review application. The appeal must include all injuries that the applicant wishes to have reconsidered.
Separate appeals for individual injuries will not be accepted.
Receiving your decision
A decision on your EGMP application, either initially or following the appeal, will be communicated to you electronically from DARR-Medical-Casework@mod.gov.uk.
Receiving your payment
If a review payment is awarded to you, this will be on a full and final settlement basis without prejudice. You will be asked to sign your understanding of this before the payment can be made. You will also be asked to provide your bank details. Upon receipt of these, the payment will be made as soon as practically possible. If you accept the payment following the award at initial decision, you then have no right of appeal.
If you accept a payment for an injury that has been awarded at the initial decision stage, you will lose your right to appeal that injury. However, if you claimed other injuries that were either not awarded or were found not to meet the eligibility criteria, you may still submit an appeal in relation to those injuries.
Related information
- Afghanistan Locally Employed Staff Ex-Gratia Scheme
- Supporting UK locally employed staff in Afghanistan
MOD collects, holds and uses personal data for the reasons provided in the MOD Privacy Notice and allowed under UK data protection law. To learn more, please see the MOD privacy notice - GOV.UK.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine hits Russian data centres in blow to Moscow's AI capabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:07:54 UTC
22:07:54 KST

Drones hit three Yandex facilities, a Sber centre and a VKontakte server farm across five Russian regions, causing persistent failures in payments, navigation and cloud services. Experts say restoring the infrastructure could take months or years.
Ukrainian drones struck five data centres belonging to Russia's largest technology companies in October, causing widespread failures in cloud services, payment systems and navigation apps nationwide.
The Ukrainian armed forces hit three Yandex facilities: in Sasovo in the Ryazan region on 7 October, in Kaluga on 9 October, and in Vladimir on 11 October.
On 14 October a Sber data centre in Balakovo in the Saratov region was struck, and on 18 October a VKontakte data centre in the Leningrad region near St Petersburg came under attack.
Yandex, Sber and VKontakte together run much of Russia's consumer internet infrastructure, from taxi apps and card payment processing to cloud storage and messaging.
None of the companies has disclosed the scale of the damage. Russians have reported persistent difficulties paying for goods, ordering taxis, using navigation services and accessing cloud storage.
Experts say restoring the infrastructure could take months or years, and the strikes have set back Russia's artificial intelligence development, Mikhail Klimarev, head of the Internet Protection Society, told AP.
Russia continues to target Ukraine's IT sector
The attacks come as Russia has itself been systematically targeting Ukrainian data centres this autumn.
On 19 October a Russian strike completely destroyed one of the largest facilities of the Ukrainian operator Datagroup in Kyiv, which was declared beyond repair.
The following day a Russian attack damaged Kyiv's GigaCenter. Russia hit several other Ukrainian data centres in September and October.
An earlier Russian strike on a Kyiv data centre in July disrupted internet access, mobile communications and television across the city.
Moscow has targeted Ukraine's IT systems since day one of Russia's full-scale invasion: cruise missiles struck a government server facility on 24 February 2022, and a Russian missile hit the National Data Backup Centre in central Kyiv on 1 March.
Ukraine has since moved most of its data to servers in European countries, limiting the impact of subsequent attacks.
Russian data centres are more vulnerable than Ukrainian ones, analysts say. Under legislation designed to create a so-called "sovereign internet," Russia requires companies to store all data on servers inside the country. That concentration makes the facilities easier to target.
"Russia's problem is that it has to provide air defence over a vast territory, and it does not have enough resources for that," said Nick Reiners, senior geo-technology analyst at Eurasia Group.
"Since all the infrastructure and all the data are located inside Russia, it is relatively easier to disable them." Why air defence systems were not protecting Russian data centres, or failed to do so, has not been explained.
Sensitive to fire
Analysts describe the facilities as soft targets: vast halls filled with servers, power equipment and cooling systems where even a small explosive charge can cause serious damage.
Satellite imagery of the struck Yandex facilities shows fires that may have destroyed microchips and other fragile components.
"After such a strike it is hard to expect anything to have survived: data-centre equipment is fragile, demanding and expensive. Soot from fires is extremely harmful to electronics," Klimarev told AP.
The damage to Yandex is particularly significant for Russia's AI ambitions. The company's three supercomputers, used to develop AI models, rank among the world's top 500. The most powerful, housed in the Sasovo facility, once ranked 19th globally but has since fallen below the top 100.
"Ukrainian drone strikes will probably delay the development of Russian artificial intelligence even further," Connor Martin of the Council on Foreign Relations said. Before the strikes, Russia was already several years behind the US and China.
Restoring the hardware will be complicated by Western sanctions and the global chip shortage. Yandex's supercomputers run on Nvidia A100 processors, which Russia cannot legally import.
Klimarev said the strikes may carry an unintended consequence for Russian internet policy.
"Paradoxically, the attacks on data centres have saved the Russian internet from isolation, because companies will now be forced to move their computing resources, most likely to Europe," he said.
"It is quite likely that many Russian companies are now studying the European market in search of opportunities to rent computing capacity," Klimarev said. He added that Russian authorities might ease their attempts to tighten internet controls to limit the economic damage.
Infrastructure for malign purposes
Moscow has for years actively used its IT sector for spying on its users, as well as conduct malign hybrid operations elsewhere.
Under Russia’s SORM legislation, all domestic internet companies including Yandex, VKontakte and Sber are legally required to install FSB backdoors giving the security services access to user data and communications.
These data centres are integrated into Russia’s surveillance apparatus, not purely commercial infrastructure.
VKontakte specifically has been extensively used for state-sponsored propaganda and recruitment. Ukraine banned it in 2017 partly on those grounds.
The Kremlin has demonstrably used AI tools in its disinformation operations, such as rewriting real news articles with pro-Kremlin slants and fabricated claims, publishing them across dozens of sites designed to mimic legitimate international outlets, including Euronews.
It has also used AI-generated video and audio to fabricate statements attributed to Western officials. AI-cloned voices impersonating European politicians have also circulated, though some were detected before they spread widely.
More recently, it has flooded the internet with repetitive pro-Kremlin content to skew what AI chatbots retrieve and eventually how they are trained. NewsGuard stress tests found chatbots repeated false claims in roughly a third of responses when prompted adversarially.
Researchers at the Carnegie Endowment have however stated that training-data poisoning is slow, heavily filtered and increasingly countered by behavioural rules built into newer models.
EU sanctions prohibit the supply of IT services, software and cloud capacity to Russian companies.
Firms seeking to circumvent the restrictions have used intermediaries, anonymous hosting providers or foreign corporate structures. Brussels has been tightening enforcement of those rules.

Putin’s key remarks on peace talks and Europe’s ‘schizophrenia’ (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:07:00 UTC
22:07:00 KST

Putin’s key remarks on peace talks and Europe’s ‘schizophrenia’ (VIDEO)
Russia remains ready to negotiate a lasting settlement in Ukraine but will achieve its objectives regardless, Russian President Vladimir Putin told journalist Pavel Zarubin on Thursday. He also outright rejected “schizophrenic” claims in Western media that Moscow could be seeking a war with Europe.
Putin’s comments followed nearly three hours of talks with US envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Witkoff brought new peace talk proposals following his own discussions with Vladimir Zelensky, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s Chief of Staff Bjoern Siebert, and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store in Oslo.
The new diplomatic engagement comes after Putin’s October 9 agreement with US President Donald Trump on Russian diesel supplies, whereby Washington eased fuel export restrictions while engaging with Moscow on broader economic cooperation.
Lasting peace, rather than a temporary pause
Putin confirmed Russia’s readiness to resume trilateral contacts with the US and Ukraine, focusing on security arrangements for both countries after a final settlement. The goal is to achieve definitive peace agreements, rather than “a suspension of hostilities for some short period,” he stressed.
The Russian leader also stated that he agrees with Witkoff’s argument that such discussions would also need to address Europe’s wider security architecture.
Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov previously suggested the talks could resume around mid-November, potentially in Abu Dhabi.
Putin said an agreement was possible, but insisted that “all the goals of the special military operation will be achieved” one way or another.
Europe’s ‘political schizophrenia’
European claims that Russia poses a military threat and preparations for confrontation amount to “political schizophrenia,” Putin said, arguing that European populations do not want war with Russia and explicitly rejected suggestions that Moscow is preparing to attack them.
“We do not want, we are not preparing for any war with Europe,” he said.
Putin described inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia as unrealistic, expressing hope that its opponents would recognize that peaceful relations better serve their own populations.
‘Historic Russia’ and the territorial question
Asked about Zelensky’s recent comments to Fox News that he would be willing to give up 25% of his territories in order to freeze the conflict on the current battle lines, Putin rejected the premise.
“It is not their territory, it is the territory of historic Russia,” he said, citing residents’ votes for independence and subsequently for reunification with the Russian Federation.
He acknowledged that the issue remained disputed, but argued that describing these developments as Ukraine losing territory was inappropriate.
Fighting ‘to the last Ukrainian’
Putin called it “incomprehensible” that Kiev expects that “the entire world should pay them, fight for them, supply them with weapons, ammunition, equipment,” and stressed that Russia has no desire to fight Ukraine.
“If Ukraine’s current leadership wants to wage war, let them fight. But why do they think everyone should pay for it and supply them with weapons?” Putin questioned.
He noted that much of this desire for war can be attributed to foreign countries that want to fight against Russia in order to weaken it and have promised support to Kiev.
However, Putin stressed that these foreign entities are prepared to fight until “the last Ukrainian” and questioned whether Ukraine’s leadership similarly treats its citizens as expendable cannon fodder.
Putin accused Ukrainian authorities of rounding up men “like stray dogs” and forcibly sending them to the front, undermining motivation. He also argued that nationalist groups that carry out this so-called “busification” do not always bear the frontline burden themselves.
He recalled that, according to official figures, there have been half a million deserters in Ukraine and over 300,000 criminal cases opened, adding that the actual numbers could be significantly higher.
Shared history and missed opportunities
Putin said Moscow had sought a negotiated resolution with Kiev since 2014, including through the Minsk agreements intended to settle the Donbass conflict. He blamed Ukrainian authorities for repeatedly rejecting opportunities to reach an agreement before Russia’s military operation began in 2022.
He described Ukrainians as a people closely related to Russians, pointing to genetic research that has shown they are “one people.” However, he acknowledged that some wished to identify differently and said Russia accepted that reality.
“We are ready even now to negotiate and seek solutions to this difficult, complicated situation,” Putin said. “Everything can be agreed upon.”

Proposal. New national roadmap requires Estonian Convention on the Future
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:07:00 UTC
22:07:00 KST

Proposal. New national roadmap requires Estonian Convention on the Future
Estonia needs a new mechanism for making long-term strategic decisions that brings together experts, politicians and citizens while remaining above day-to-day party politics, Erik Terk, Mati Heidmets and Marju Lauristin write.
The world finds itself in rough seas where many of the old rules and assumptions no longer apply. The power struggle between major powers and the redistribution of positions in the global market are dangerously rocking the boats of small countries, but they may also open up new windows of opportunity.
We must place Estonia within the broader picture of a changing world to ensure both our resilience against threats and our capacity for development. We need both the ability to adapt quickly and the capacity to make strategic changes that require sustained action over a longer period.
Unfortunately, we are witnessing trends in the opposite direction.
For example, efforts to reform the energy, education and healthcare systems are becoming bogged down in a deadlock of conflicting initiatives. Strengthening defense capabilities, ensuring the sustainability of the Estonian language and culture and achieving economic success all require a long-term vision, consistent action and shared determination.
Without these, development becomes erratic. Today we rush in one direction, tomorrow in another. Eventually, we may even lose sight of what kind of society we want to be once we have somehow managed to struggle through the waves of crises.
Successful governance of Estonia requires a different mechanism for shaping the future than the current practice of short-term political agreements can provide.
While firmly defending the values of democratic governance, we must acknowledge that the traditional forms of representative democracy inherited from the last century have become trapped in partisan conflicts that prevent them from effectively managing today's rapid and complex changes.
Building resilience for the future requires a broader societal platform that would both strengthen the intellectual capacity for planning long-term development and help ensure the quality and consistent implementation of strategic decisions that shape the country's future, regardless of the turbulence of day-to-day political confrontations.
To achieve this, we must find a way to bring together all the knowledge and goodwill available in Estonia when preparing decisions that will shape long-term development. This means involving as many leading researchers from different fields as possible, experts with significant international experience, political leaders from different party backgrounds, experienced and critically minded entrepreneurs and specialists who stay out of party politics and active ordinary citizens with extensive practical experience.
Borrowing the name of the Convention on the Future of Europe, which met some years ago, we have called our proposed mechanism the Estonian Convention on the Future. It would be a body that convenes periodically to review and refine the country's course of development and examine possible solutions to emerging issues of central importance.
The convention would not relieve elected representatives of their responsibility for political choices. Rather, it would serve as an additional or supporting mechanism for parliament, providing a stronger scientific and societal foundation for policymaking. As a body that we could reasonably expect to act in Estonia's overall interests, it would operate at some distance from day-to-day political life and competition between parties.
The convention would not make final decisions. Its task would be to carry out essential preparatory work for strategic choices, bringing together knowledge, experience and different perspectives from across society, examining alternatives and formulating possible options and proposals. Ideally, the convention could develop a comprehensive vision of development that takes into account the key dimensions of Estonia's future: social well-being, economic competitiveness, national security, environmental protection, demographic sustainability and the vitality of Estonian-language cultural life.
The central principle behind the convention's structure would be to bring together two distinct levels of participation: experts and the public.
On one side would be what we might call a chamber of experts, to which Estonia's knowledge-based umbrella organizations, such as universities, the Estonian Academy of Sciences and professional associations, would delegate representatives. All political parties represented in parliament would also be able to appoint representatives. The chamber of experts would operate through a series of sessions held over a designated period.
On the other side, the convention would include a chamber operating as a citizens' assembly, giving citizens interested in solving problems the opportunity to contribute their ideas and proposals to the formulation of strategic decisions through an online discussion platform.
The online citizens' assembly could be formed through both voluntary registration by individuals wishing to participate, with the necessary personal information provided and the application of representative sampling principles.
Both chambers of the convention would need to be supported by a team of specialists responsible for organizing expert sessions, managing the online citizens' assembly platform and ensuring the flow of information between the two levels.
Artificial intelligence could be used to quickly summarize and compare expert opinions and citizens' proposals, formulate recommendations based on them and put those recommendations to a vote. It could also be used to analyze background materials and datasets relating to the issues under discussion and visualize possible solutions.
In this way, the convention could become a genuine forum for collective deliberation, helping to build societal consensus on strategic issues important to Estonia's future. It would also enable both lawmakers and the government to base their plans for reforms with long-term consequences on a diverse range of thoroughly examined, publicly debated and interconnected perspectives.
--
Editor: Marcus Turovski

PHP: what it is and why everyone is fixing it now
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:05:21 UTC
22:05:21 KST

For more than a decade, serious flaws went unnoticed in a technology that underpins a vast portion of the internet—and it took artificial intelligence to uncover them, reports the BBC.
The vulnerabilities were discovered in PHP, a programming language that has been widely used globally for website development since the early 2000s. Following the public disclosure of this information on the 21st of October, governments and cybersecurity agencies have been working to mitigate the potential fallout, urging users to install emergency updates or even consider temporarily taking their websites offline.
Wiz—one of the companies whose researchers contributed to the project that led to the discovery—described the vulnerability as the most severe ever identified by artificial intelligence.
Most people have likely never heard of PHP, even though they encounter it every single day. PHP (Hypertext Preprocessor) is an open-source, back-end programming language that operates on a web server. It was developed in the early 1990s to help create dynamic websites and is still used on a large number of platforms, including Wikipedia, online stores, and WordPress (which serves as the foundation for many websites). When a user visits a site, PHP code gathers data and effectively transforms it into a viewable page. Furthermore, PHP is used to build various tools for creating or accelerating web applications; popular content management systems and frameworks include Laravel, Symfony, and Drupal.

Lithuania’s Environmental Protection Agency has approved an environmental impact assessment for a planned ammunition factory being built by the German defence group Rheinmetall and its local partners in Radviliskis district, concluding that the project will have no significant environmental impact.
The agency said Friday that the project complies with environmental, public health, cultural heritage, fire safety and civil safety requirements.
The factory is being developed by Rheinmetall Defence Lietuva, a joint venture involving Rheinmetall and state-owned investment company Epso-G Invest.
Buildings and structures will cover 3.5 hectares of the 340-hectare site, according to the agency. The planned facilities include thermal processing, artillery shell filling, assembly and packaging, component manufacturing, production and storage buildings, ammunition bunkers, an administrative building and auxiliary structures.
Mindaugas Keizeris, head of the state-owned Epso-G group, previously said that establishing the production lines was the project’s priority.
The factory is expected to produce up to 75,000 155 mm artillery shells annually.
Epso-G, through its subsidiary Epso-G Invest, holds a 48% stake in Rheinmetall Defence Lietuva. Rheinmetall owns 51%, while the remaining 1% belongs to Lithuania’s Giraitė Armament Plant.
Construction officially began in early November 2025.
Rheinmetall also plans to build a competence centre for artillery shell propellant charges in Lithuania, with an estimated value of about 400 million euros.

Apprentices BAE and Babcock cannot take offered elsewhere
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:00:57 BST
22:00:57 KST

Strong apprenticeship applicants who cannot be offered a place by BAE Systems or Babcock will be put in front of smaller firms in the same communities under a scheme launched at Barrow-in-Furness, with pilots covering the North West and Devonport, according to The 5% Club.
The Apprenticeship Talent Bridge was opened by Pat McFadden, the Work and Pensions Secretary, at an event bringing together defence employers, local businesses and government. Babcock supports the South West pilot covering Devonport and BAE Systems supports the North West pilot covering Barrow-in-Furness and the Preston area. Apprentices will be matched to smaller companies from April 2027, with sign-up opening this month.
The charity said major defence employers attract large numbers of applicants for their apprenticeship programmes but cannot offer a place to every strong candidate, while other employers in the same communities struggle to attract the people and skills they need. Research published by Make UK in March found half of manufacturers identify skills shortages as their biggest barrier to growth.
Mark Cameron, chief executive of The 5% Club, said: “Talent shouldn’t be lost because opportunity can’t be seen. Major employers have more talented apprenticeship applicants than they can employ, while other businesses are struggling to find the people they need.
“The Apprenticeship Talent Bridge connects the two. It is a simple idea, but one that could keep more talent in the sector, open up opportunities young people may never have known existed, and help employers access the skills they need to grow.”
Tania Gandamihardja, group human resources director at BAE Systems, set out the scale of the company’s intake and the competition for places: “Over the last decade, we’ve recruited more than 9,000 apprentices across the UK and know first-hand the value that apprenticeships bring to individuals, businesses and the wider industrial base. They’re one of the best routes into a skilled and rewarding career, but that also makes them highly sought-after.
“By connecting applicants with fantastic opportunities elsewhere in the sector and with our supply chain SMEs, we can help more young people take that first step, while also supporting businesses across the North West to access the talent and skills they need to grow.”
Debbie Joce, skills director at Babcock, said: “Apprenticeships are vital to the future workforce and the long-term success of the defence industry. At Babcock, we recognise the role we play in creating these opportunities, not just within our own organisation but across the communities where we live and work.
“The Apprenticeship Talent Bridge is a great way of industry working together with government to open doors and create opportunities across the wider employer and supply chain community. By helping more people access high-value, skilled careers, we can make the most of the talent coming through and help ensure that talented people aren’t lost.”
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, said: “Every young person who shows the talent and drive to succeed in defence deserves a route into the industry. Initiatives like this make that happen, with industry working together to build skills, create jobs, and strengthen our defence industrial base for the long term.”
McFadden said: “This partnership will open doors for young people to exciting careers in the defence industry and help businesses boost their talent pipeline. More opportunities for our young people seeking a career in defence will help to boost our engineering and manufacturing skills base and ensure they benefit as we deliver record increases in defence spending.”
The two pilot areas are the obvious places to start, because Barrow builds the submarines and Devonport refits them, and both have supply chains full of firms competing for the same machinists, electrical technicians and welders as the yard down the road. A candidate good enough to reach the final stages at BAE Systems is more than good enough for a tier two supplier, and until now that candidate simply disappeared.
Participation is voluntary and applicant data is shared only with consent, with employers keeping their own selection processes. The initiative is funded by Ufi VocTech Trust and the ERA Foundation with in-kind investment from the charity, and draws on insight from Airbus Defence and Space.
It builds on a commitment in the Defence Industrial Strategy to develop a clearing-style approach for defence apprenticeship and graduate applicants. The Defence Youth Participation and Employment Pledge set a wider no wrong door approach, an ambition to increase opportunities for under twenty fives by a quarter to more than forty thousand a year by the end of this Parliament, and support for at least fourteen thousand people annually through apprenticeships across defence and its supply chain by 2035.

People who believe conspiracy theories overestimate how many others agree, new research finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:00:32 UTC
22:00:32 KST

Reading a conspiracy theory does more than just introduce a suspicious narrative; it also inflates a person’s estimate of how many other people believe the claim is true. According to new research published in the European Journal of Social Psychology, this exaggerated sense of public agreement may help explain why people come to accept conspiracy theories after encountering them. In one of the experiments, showing people concrete statistical data about how few others actually endorsed these claims reduced their own belief in them.
Conspiracy theories are explanations for events that assume multiple actors are secretly working together to achieve a harmful or unlawful goal. When people feel uncertain about how to interpret events, they often look to others for cues on what to think or do. Psychologists refer to these cues as descriptive norms, which are perceptions of how common a particular belief or behavior is within a group. Relying on descriptive norms is a form of social proof, where people assume that if many others hold a view, that view is likely valid.
Although conspiracy theories frequently draw massive attention online, actual believers usually represent a minority of the broader public. Still, those who endorse these narratives often assume their views are widely shared. For example, a 2021 study of British participants found that people consistently overestimated how much their peers believed in conspiracy theories, and that thinking peers endorsed these ideas strongly predicted a person’s own belief. Similarly, a 2023 study in Turkey indicated that people who believed local conspiracy theories overestimated how many ordinary citizens and experts agreed with them.
Correcting these misperceptions can alter how people think. In a 2021 experiment with British parents, showing participants that most other parents rejected anti-vaccine conspiracy theories reduced their own endorsement of those claims. Building on this foundation, the new research was led by Jan-Willem van Prooijen, head of the Social Psychology section at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, senior researcher at the Netherlands Institute for the Study of Crime and Law Enforcement, and endowed professor of radicalization, extremism, and conspiracy thinking at Maastricht University.
He and his colleagues wanted to test whether simply encountering a conspiracy theory inflates perceived descriptive norms, and whether providing hard data on public skepticism can reduce belief in a wide variety of general conspiracy theories.
“People often encounter conspiracy theories, for instance online,” van Prooijen told PsyPost. “One problem is that extreme voices that spread conspiracy theories (e.g., online influencers) sometimes get excessive exposure. That might raise the impression that these conspiracy theories are more widely believed than is actually the case. We wanted to examine these dynamics in our research: Do conspiracy beliefs depend on how normative people think they are, and can we use these insights to develop an intervention?”
To investigate these questions, the researchers conducted six online studies totaling 2,906 participants from the United States and the United Kingdom. All six studies were preregistered, meaning the researchers publicly recorded their hypotheses and analysis plans before collecting data.
In the first pair of studies, the researchers examined the relationship between personal conspiracy beliefs and perceived norms using 300 American participants in Study 1a and 299 British participants in Study 1b. Participants rated how plausible they found 10 popular conspiracy claims, such as the idea that the 9/11 terrorist attacks were an inside job by the U.S. government, on a scale from 0 to 100, and then used the same scale to estimate the average plausibility rating given by the other participants in the study.
In both countries, the actual average belief in these 10 theories was relatively low, sitting at 33.09 out of 100 in the American sample and 34.16 in the British sample. However, participants estimated the group average to be higher, guessing 39.85 in the United States and 42.30 in the United Kingdom. Those who strongly endorsed the conspiracy theories themselves were much more likely to think other participants believed them too, with strong correlations of 0.65 in the U.S. sample and 0.71 in the U.K. sample, and their estimates of the group average were less accurate than the estimates of skeptics.
The researchers also tested whether conspiracy believers saw themselves as standing out from the crowd, given that past research has linked conspiracy belief to a desire to feel unique. By comparing each person’s own rating to their estimate of the group rating, the team found that stronger believers saw the gap between their own views and the group’s as no larger than skeptics did.
These initial findings align with research covered by PsyPost in 2025, which found that individuals who are overconfident in their thinking abilities tend to hold stronger conspiracy beliefs and vastly overestimate how many others agree with them.
Because the first two studies only looked at correlations, the researchers next tested whether reading a conspiracy theory directly causes people to think the idea is popular. They recruited 505 American participants for Study 2a and 501 British participants for Study 2b. In each study, half of the participants were randomly assigned to read an anonymous blog post claiming that pharmaceutical companies secretly suppress medical cures to boost their profits, while the other half read a blog post arguing that pharmaceutical companies do not hide cures.
After reading and summarizing the text, participants rated their own belief in four statements about pharmaceutical conspiracies on a 0 to 100 scale, and estimated how the other participants in the study rated them. In the American sample, reading the conspiratorial blog post raised personal belief to an average of 61.78, compared to 49.46 among those who read the non-conspiratorial text. It also pushed estimates of other people’s belief up to 62.64, compared to 51.00 in the control group.
The British sample in Study 2b showed the same pattern. Personal belief averaged 59.78 after reading the conspiracy post versus 41.99 in the control group, while estimates of others’ beliefs rose to 60.28 compared to 46.41 in the control condition. Statistical mediation analyses were consistent with the idea that the increase in personal belief ran through this heightened sense that others believed the claim. But the reverse pattern, in which people’s newly strengthened beliefs shaped their guesses about others, also fit the data, so these analyses cannot establish which came first.
“One reason why people believe conspiracy theories is because they assume many others believe them as well,” van Prooijen explained. “Conspiracy beliefs thus spread via social influence processes. Understanding these processes can help design effective interventions to reduce conspiracy beliefs.”
To test whether changing perceived norms can directly alter conspiracy beliefs, the researchers manipulated the norm information given to participants in Studies 3 and 4. In Study 3, 501 American participants were presented with six popular conspiracy theories, such as the claim that the government uses subliminal messages on television. Half were told that “especially many” previous participants found the statements plausible, while the other half were told that “only a few” found them plausible.
This vague wording did not produce a statistically significant difference between the two groups. Participants told that many others believed the claims scored an average of 44.48 out of 100 on personal belief, compared to 41.65 among those told that few others believed them. The authors noted that words like “many” and “few” are open to personal interpretation; for instance, learning that even 10 percent of the public believes an extreme claim might still register as a large number to some people. Because this study did not measure whether participants’ sense of the norm actually shifted, the authors acknowledge another possibility: that people do not take their cues from norm information at all, and that the link seen in earlier studies reflects people projecting their own beliefs onto others.
In Study 4, the team tested whether providing specific, factual statistics would be more effective. They recruited 800 American participants and showed them eight conspiracy theories from the first study. Half of the participants saw a bar chart for each theory displaying the actual distribution of ratings from Study 1a, along with the median score and a note explaining that most participants did not find the statement plausible at all. The other half saw the conspiracy statements without any statistical data.
Providing concrete data shifted how participants viewed both the public consensus and the theories themselves. Those who saw the charts estimated the previous group’s average belief at 20.95 out of 100, compared to 38.34 among those who received no data. In turn, personal endorsement of the conspiracy theories dropped to an average of 24.06 in the group that saw the factual charts, compared to 33.70 in the control group.
“We have done two studies testing the intervention, but it only worked if we gave people factual statistical information of how few people believed a conspiracy theory,” van Prooijen noted. “If we provided more abstract information, only stating that ‘few people’ believe the theory without providing concrete numbers, the intervention did not work. It remains speculative why that is the case, but it is nevertheless informative for future interventions based on this research.”
“The practical significance is that these insights quite directly suggest an intervention to reduce conspiracy beliefs,” van Prooijen said. “We have tested the effects of exposing people to factual statistical information of how widespread belief in a particular conspiracy theory is. Such information often clarifies to people that a conspiracy theory actually is not widely endorsed at all, which decreases the likelihood that people will believe the theory themselves.”
As with all research, there are some caveats to consider when interpreting these results. Participants in brief online experiments may partly respond the way they think researchers expect, which the authors note could mean these effects are smaller in everyday life, and the “others” in these studies were fellow online participants rather than the broader population. In addition, social media algorithms and online communities can surround users with like-minded believers, creating environments where conspiracy theories genuinely are the local norm.
“It is important to keep in mind that in everyday life, these processes are likely to be more complicated,” van Prooijen said. “For instance, we examined the effects of exposing people to conspiracy theories on their perceptions of how normative belief in these theories is. But in real life, people to some extent also choose what information they wish to be exposed to. People may for instance actively search the Internet looking for conspiracy theories, and be motivated to think belief in these theories is widely shared.”
The authors also point out that factual norm interventions could backfire if applied to the rare conspiracy theories that actually are endorsed by a majority of the public, such as theories surrounding the assassination of John F. Kennedy. Future studies could examine how these social processes operate in real-world online networks and in more collectivistic cultures, where pressure to conform to group norms may be even stronger.
“An important caveat is that the intervention that we tested might only work in communities where a particular conspiracy theory is indeed not so widespread,” van Prooijen added. “Some conspiracy theories ARE widespread, for instance in the general population (e.g., about the Kennedy assassination), or in specific groups (e.g., online anti-vaccination groups). These are complications that need to be investigated further, and are important to take into account before putting these insights into practice.”
“We were excited to see that our findings almost naturally suggested an intervention, which indeed had the anticipated effects,” he continued. “At the same time, the intervention was successful in only one experiment. We need more testing to assess the effectiveness of this approach. One possible goal is to examine these issues in a longitudinal design: What is the long-term effectiveness of an intervention based on information about descriptive norms?”
The study, “Everyone Knows It’s a Hoax: The Role of Perceived Descriptive Norms in Conspiracy Beliefs,” was authored by Jan-Willem van Prooijen, Paul K. Bergmann, Vladimira Čavojová, and Jakub Šrol.

The Real Child Protection Cases That Loosely Inspired Fjord
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:00:03 UTC
22:00:03 KST

From the Palme d’Or-winning abortion drama 4 Months, Three Weeks, and Two Days (2007), to the institutional corruption-themed Graduation (2016) and beyond, Romanian auteur Cristian Mungiu’s body of work has always concerned itself with the human cost of systemic oppression and bureaucratic faultlines. With the searing legal and familial drama Fjord, which earned Mungiu his second Palme at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival in May, the filmmaker once again brings his signature sense of slow-burning tension to the clash between individual and societal codes of morality. Except this time, he shrewdly flips the script. With the story of a religious immigrant family of seven facing an uphill battle against Norway’s child protection services (known as Barnevernet), Fjord dares to imagine a scenario where well-intentioned progressive values can backfire as severely as rigidly conservative ones if they disregard basic human principles like empathy, compassion, and respect.
Written by Mungiu, Fjord follows Mihai and Lisbet Gheorghiu, a Romanian engineer and Norwegian nurse played by Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, respectively. Set in their modest ways, the couple tries to settle into their lives in Norway, having moved there after the death of Mihai’s parents to be closer to Lisbet’s family. Raising their five children with a conservative ethos, they don’t quite mesh with the liberal community that surrounds them. But their eager kids still build close friendships with the children of their progressive neighbors, Mats and Mia Halberg, a development that further underscores the two families’—and consequently, the two belief systems’—political and practical differences.
Tensions rise in town when the kids’ school raises child-abuse allegations against the Gheorghius after teachers notice some mysterious bruising on one of their kids. While the film never spells out their precise origins, Barnevernet steps in at once, separating their five kids (including a baby, still breastfeeding) from Mihai and Lisbet, placing them in foster care after the couple admits to some physical discipline that would be considered mild in Mihai’s culture, but is against the law in Norway. Claiming that they are being harshly discriminated against due to their religion and conservative beliefs, the couple asks help from Mia, an attorney, to represent their case in the Norwegian court.
The real court case that loosely inspired Fjord
Joining TIME on Zoom recently, Mungiu emphasizes that “the film is fictional. It’s not a reenactment associated with any one particular case.” Still, there were a number of real-life court cases that intrigued him as a storyteller with a journalism background. Chief among them was that of the Bodnariu family, who occupied international headlines for several months after they were separated from their five children in November 2015. Pentecostal parents Ruth and Marius were accused of domestic violence, with worldwide protests criticizing what dissenters called harsh and hasty steps taken by Norwegian social workers without proper evidence. In Romania, one of the indirect results of the wildly popular case went as far as a constitutional referendum in 2018 that aimed to alter the definition of a traditional family and prevent same-sex marriages. (The referendum eventually failed due to low turnout.)
“So you couldn’t avoid the Bodnariu case,” recalls Mungiu. He followed the story as it remained in the papers, and during that time and the years that followed, Mungiu began to notice other cases that displayed a similar pattern. “Whenever there was this encounter between, let's say, families coming to Scandinavia from more conservative parts of the world, there was a cultural clash.” What eventually convinced him to pursue the topic through a film was a recent-enough realization that the world somehow became more illiberal than it used to be. “I thought that through this story, I could talk about the [confrontational] state of the world today. People are not listening to the other group. I hope that the world can be a bit more rational than this.”
Upon deciding to write Fjord, Mungiu read everything he could online, moving to Norway for several extended periods to investigate the country’s child-protection laws and relevant cases on the ground. His process involved talking to several families involved with child protection cases and their relatives, as well as journalists who covered cases like the Bodnarius’, court interpreters, police officers, NGO representatives, and various different religious groups. “Finally, I talked to Barnevernet about these cases in general,” he adds. “They were willing to also give details about how things have changed.”
One key tool Mungiu didn’t have access to was the recording and transcription of the Bodnariu trial, which is among the reasons why Fjord had to be largely fictional. “Norwegian authorities said only the family could have access to the recording if they came over. But the family knew that they couldn’t come over. Because if they did, they could be arrested,” he explains. “The family was trying to get their justice in the European Court of Justice, but they first had to utilize all the legal procedures [in Norway]. And because they left Norway before having a final decision about their proceedings, they couldn't get a positive answer from the European Court of Justice.”
The audience is on trial too
To accentuate the connection between Fjord’s searching themes and lean visuals, Mungiu purposefully embraced long shots and continuous takes beginning during the scripting phase, in order to fully immerse the audience in the conflicting world of the characters in a neutral fashion. Indicating that he avoids many of the mainstream filmmaking methods that he finds manipulative, “I don't use anything [distracting] within the scene,” Mungiu says. “I don't use coverage. I don't use music. I don't have funny angles. The camera doesn't move unless it follows a movement in the shot. I try to do this in a sober way, just with the actors and their emotions. I think it's a respectful way of telling the audience, ‘You are adults like we are, you are as smart as I am, so feel free to see [for yourself] what's more important in this shot, or who the main character is.’”
Similarly, he carefully scouted locations in sync with his ideas around isolation and lack of communication. “It was important for us to set this story in a small community, with two houses at the end of this fjord in a lovely but somehow curled world,” he explains. “It’s very majestic, and [it’s a location where] people will have to talk to one another eventually because there's nobody else around.”
He remembers an anecdote about the real inhabitants of the two houses he uses in the film for the Gheorghius and Halbergs, who were in fact not communicating with one another. That all changed shortly after the production convinced one of them to allow the film crew to shoot in his house. Mungiu recalls the homeowner saying, “I will let you, but my neighbor is very grumpy. He hasn’t talked to me in the 10 years that we have been neighbors, so you are going to have problems with him." But when the crew contacted the owner of the other house, they found that he was quite open-minded. “We asked him, ‘Do you have a conflict with your neighbor?’ He said, ‘No, but none of us have started a conversation, so I let him enjoy his privacy.’ At the end, they were communicating normally, and we had a very good relationship with both of them.”
Can a person ever really be fully objective?
No matter how neutral Mungiu tried to stay throughout his research process, there were some moments that made him face his own biases. “I went [to Norway] with this idea that I will meet a society that is not at all religious. This is the idea that we project onto the Protestant north.” As such, he was surprised to notice deeply rooted religious leanings there, especially among older people with a connection to the Norwegian church. He also learned about the younger population’s attraction to new neo-cult movements. “I watched at least a couple of documentaries about this phenomenon. People are really worried that the younger generations are [drawn to] these new cults. So I noticed that the people there are just as inclined to have religious beliefs as any other.”
With this discovery, Mungiu eventually eliminated various scenes in Fjord which would have insinuated that Norwegian people saw the world in a more rational way only because they weren’t religious. “Making decisions on rational grounds is of course a very good thing to do,” Mungiu explains. “But [there is also] this need of belonging to something bigger than just [rationality] that we all feel. Some people still long for the discomfort that there's something bigger than them. And as long as this belief places them on the right side of the world through [tolerance] and [inclusivity], I think we should be tolerant to it.”
“You shouldn't answer radicalization with radicalization”
His time in Norway also led Mungiu to learn more about the Sami people. “I didn’t know much about them before, but the Sami population sets a good [historical] example about how bigger communities and countries were not acting in an ethical way towards minorities. You can see this in the U.S. as well, [in the way] Native Americans were treated,” he adds. “And I think that we should learn from this [that] maybe this ‘we want to civilize you’ idea is not the most ethical one,” he reflects, clarifying that while everyone should obey the laws and respect the culture of the country they live in, real integration cannot happen by enforcing one’s own values onto others. “That won't change [the way] someone thinks. You will just frustrate them, [reinforcing] that there is a hypocrisy in the world.”
Mungiu cautions against the ongoing ideological war that he says is moving in the wrong direction across the globe. “I don't want to be preachy, but hopefully there's something that stays with you after you watch a film like Fjord,” he reflects. “I took the risk of talking about things that people need to listen to even if they’re not nice. Don't kill the messenger. It's time to start to have a dialogue and this is what cinema can do.”

E9X: The battery-powered plane with 90 passengers on board and a range of 1,000 kilometres
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Flying without kerosene is no longer just a dream, with pilots being trained to fly electric planes in the Netherlands. Before long, these battery-powered planes could be carrying 90 passengers and flying distances of up to 1,000 kilometres.
Johannes, Peter and Floris are thrilled. The pilots are carrying out the first test flights for the scaled E9X demonstrator. It’s a world premiere — and if all goes to plan, their electric model plane could soon become a big passenger aircraft.
After a soft landing, the aircraft is still in one piece — and now the real adventure can begin: analysing the flight data in the Elysian Aircraft laboratory, which sits beside Amsterdam’s Schiphol Airport.
Over the next two decades, the global number of air passengers could double. This is bad news for the global climate, so the young Dutch start-up Elysian is working on a solution.
The world’s first battery-powered passenger aircraft
Daniel Jacobson is one of the founders of Elysian Aircraft. With ten million euros in start-up capital, his team now aims to develop one of the world’s first big, battery-powered passenger aircrafts.
“The design pretty much stands”, Jacobson tells Euronews in his workshop. “There will be 6 engines. And we have folding wingtips, so that we fit into the current gates’ infrastructure of the airports, because the wings are very large. We are talking about more than 50 metres.”
Battery-packed wings
Jacobson shows Euronews the first full-scale model of the innovative wing. The battery packs are integrated into the wing’s structure. To give a better idea of the scale, there are roughly 40 battery packs across the entire wing, each pack weighing around 1000 kg.
“Yes, we are an obese plane”, the Elysian manager admits. Yet he smiles confidently: “We are always on a diet, trying to reduce weight. How can you use different materials, how can you combine things, how you do thermo-management. And it’s also IP (intellectual property) that we are generating here.” There are no further details — it’s top secret at this stage.
Battery-wings — a revolutionary idea, and the key to success. The co-founder and co-CEO of Elysian Aircraft sounds rather proud: “There was really this consensus in the academic world and in the industry that flying electrically with a large aircraft would never be possible. We have disproven that with our research on our design.”
Reducing global aerospace emissions
But what are the benefits? “By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometres and eventually 1000 kilometres you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights”, Jacobson says. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20%.”
The E9X is due to be operational by 2034. Europe is doing rather well in the race for the future of aviation, Jacobson believes. “But comparing it to the US or even China, we should fund start-ups and innovation much more aggressively when we want to keep our advantage”, the top manager urges with regard to the EU.
Pilots prepare for electric take-off
We stop at the small regional airport of Teuge. Here, flying on electricity is already a reality. The E-Flight Academy trains pilots from several airlines in an environmentally friendly way at a low altitude.
Co-founder Merlijn van Vliet takes Euronews on a ride in a small 2-seater: “In this aircraft we have two batteries with 11 kilowatt-hours each. So, in total we have 22 kilowatt-hours on board. We can fly 45 to 50 minutes with them and still have ten minutes of reserve capacity.”
We follow the banks of a river through green meadows where Dutch cows are grazing. “We are now flying towards the old city centre of Deventer. They don’t hear us. So, we can fly wherever we want and they don’t hear us on the ground”, Merlijn beams.
What is his vision for the future? “In ten years, this will grow big and we will fly electric with 40 or 60 passengers — or even more.”
Charging infrastructure
Jurjen de Jong has made a lot of money from charging stations for electric cars and is one of Europe’s pioneers in the field. He is now investing his profits into the development of a European charging infrastructure for electric aircraft.
“We will expand from the Netherlands to the Nordic States, to France, to Germany and Switzerland”, the co-founder of NRG2fly tells Euronews. “And then we will have a fully-fledged network of low-emission, low-noise electric mobility and that is really what we’re going for”.
Airports are surrounded by huge car parks. Solar panels, tens of thousands of electric cars and stationary energy storage systems could be connected to form a network — “the inter-net of energy”, as Jurjen calls it.
Teuge airport is testing the scaled concept. “We have 500 solar panels on the rooftop”, Jurjen explains, “their energy is stored in a battery. So basically, we have a whole energy hub which is providing energy instead of taking energy from the grid.”
NRG2fly co-founder Jurjen de Jong has a broader vision too: “My dream is to have all regional electric planes powered by the sun. And then we can leave a better world for me, my children and everybody.”
