Electric stoves could help people with asthma breathe easier
Swapping polluting gas stoves for electric ones reduced asthma symptoms, a study finds
Biomedical Writer
For people with asthma, switching from a gas stove to an electric one might be a breath of fresh air. The combustion that creates the flame of a gas stove or oven releases pollutants, including nitrogen dioxide, which can trigger asthma symptoms. After a research-backed electric stove replacement, people reported more symptom relief than is often achieved with asthma medications.
“We were really surprised at how large the benefit was,” says Ashwini Sehgal, a clinician who studies community health at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland. With funding from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency during the Biden administration, Sehgal and colleagues spearheaded a project to install electric stoves in Cleveland households that had at least one person with asthma.
Eighty-five participants who had poorly controlled asthma were given a questionnaire a few months after the switch. They reported symptom improvement that was roughly two to three times as large as what’s typical with medication. Those with the worst symptoms saw the biggest improvement. Participants also reported fewer emergency room or hospital visits and said they missed work or school less often.
One 38-year-old woman told Sehgal’s team that whenever she cooked on her gas stove, she felt like her throat was closing. But the sensation disappeared after she switched to electric. Another participant, a 36-year-old man, found it difficult to walk uphill and play with his kids. With the stove swap, “he described how much better he felt as ‘magical,’ ” Sehgal says.
While heating, steaming or frying on a gas stovetop, nearby NO2 levels can skyrocket, reaching hundreds of parts per billion. That’s much higher than the EPA’s one-hour outdoor air quality standard of 100 parts per billion. NO2 exposure is linked to increased asthma symptoms. For example, research in children has found the pollutant can boost wheezing, coughing and asthma attacks.
The project was initially funded to follow 1,200 households for 12 months. But the Trump administration terminated the EPA’s Community Change Grants early, which drastically reduced the number of study participants. Yet even with this small group, the symptom improvement was significant.
The decision to replace a gas stove “depends on how much you are struggling with your own illness,” says environmental epidemiologist Carrie Breton of WashU Bursky School of Public Health in St. Louis. As a trial run, Sehgal suggests using an electric hot plate and a toaster oven to see if keeping the gas stove off helps improve symptoms.
If a stove swap isn’t in the budget, reducing NO2 exposure is still worthwhile, says pulmonologist Laura Paulin of Dartmouth Health. She recommends using kitchen ventilation, either via an exhaust hood that vents to the outside or an open window. A HEPA filter with a carbon insert can trap NO2 to decrease airborne concentrations. And try to keep children with asthma out of the kitchen when the stove is on, Paulin says. “It is a daunting task to replace a stove, but it doesn’t have to be an all-or-nothing thing.”
For researchers, the next step would be to measure lung function before and after a stove switch, Breton says. It would also be helpful to account for more factors, such as seasonal effects. “Many things can trigger people’s asthma,” Paulin says. Researchers could do a randomized trial in which some people get the electric stove right away while others wait for six months, Sehgal says, to allow time for comparison.
If electric stoves continue to be linked with fewer trips to the emergency room, fewer hospitalizations and better symptom control than medication can provide, “health insurance companies should consider paying for or subsidizing” stove swaps, Sehgal says. “If it truly works this well,” Breton says, “it’s got a bigger bang for your buck.”

Syria's Suweida: Analysts warn of Israeli agenda behind unrest
Unknown

2026-10-23

Breadcrumb
'Israeli agenda' behind National Guard moves in Suweida, analysts warn
The activities of the "National Guard" militia in Syria's southern province Suweida, led by Druze spiritual leader Sheikh Hikmat al-Hijri, are increasingly coinciding with violations committed by Israeli forces occupying southern Syria and moves by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to win over Palestinian Druze voters ahead of the upcoming elections.
Militia members recently threatened to attack Umm Walad, a town in eastern rural Daraa near the administrative boundary between Daraa and Quneitra governorates, according to video recordings. The threats came as the militia carried out a drone attack early on Wednesday targeting a government-affiliated internal security checkpoint near Tal Hadid, west of Suweida.
Wael Alwan, a researcher at the Jusoor Centre, said military operations by the National Guard and affiliated armed groups in Suweida were expected.
Speaking to The New Arab, Alwan said the activities would serve Netanyahu's aim to secure votes from Druze communities in the occupied Palestinian territories. They also provided him with an opportunity to demonstrate his alleged commitment to protecting Syria's Druze, as he claims to be doing within Israel, while supporting and arming them.
Alwan said these actions by militias in the governorate, as well as calls for Israeli intervention, were primarily political and media-driven and were part of their continuing attempts to create unrest and block efforts to resolve the situation in Suweida.
Israeli arms openly supplied in Suweida
Israeli arms supplies to militias opposed to the Syrian government are no longer being concealed, according to Charles Lister, director of the Syria programme at the Middle East Institute.
On 19 October, Lister wrote on X that National Guard members had obtained US-made M16 and AR-15 rifles, suggesting Israel had supplied them.
Rashid Hourani, a researcher specialising in security and military affairs, told The New Arab that the National Guard's escalation was linked to efforts on the ground to return the Suweida issue to square one.
These efforts had intensified followed the militia's takeover of Waqm willage in western rural Suweida on 8 October, he said—with the group seeking to expand its areas of control in the province while the Syrian government worked to restore stability and facilitate residents’ return.
Hourani also linked the developments to continuing Israeli military operations on the "Sufa 53" road project, which aims to extend a route through western rural Daraa to the Jordanian border.
He said these activities were an attempt to undermine efforts by Jordan, the US, Turkey and Saudi Arabia to reach a solution to the Suweida crisis, particularly the implementation of the Syrian-Jordanian-US roadmap.
Hourani said the National Guard had recently received weapons and ammunition from Israel, transported by military helicopters. Israeli reconnaissance aircraft had also increased their aerial coverage of the militia, particularly over areas controlled by the Syrian government.
Israeli reconnaissance flights had also covered Daraa governorate and the skies over Damascus and its countryside, he added.
Hourani said Israel's movements and support for the National Guard were part of its efforts to impose a new reality on the ground that will strengthen its hand in negotiations with the Syrian government.
Damascus, meanwhile, was relying on diplomacy and US pressure to curb Israeli violations and intervention in Syria.
He said Israel's main current objective was establishing a security buffer zone along the Syrian side of the occupied Golan Heights.
US concern over renewed escalation
The Suweida crisis returned to the forefront after al-Hijri declared on 25 August that the Unitarian Druze, were "an inseparable part of the State of Israel".
The remarks prompted objections from Druze figures and religious authorities in Syria, Lebanon and the occupied territories, and saw an increased crackdown within Suweida against voices opposing al-Hijri.
Tom Barrack, the US special envoy to Syria, expressed Washington's concern over renewed escalation in Suweida in September, when armed militias also intensified their military activities, calling on all sides to exercise restraint.
Barrack called for Suweida's reintegration in accordance with the roadmap agreed by the US, Jordan and Syria approximately a year earlier.
He urged dialogue, understanding and cooperation between the Druze, tribal communities and neighbouring countries, warning that the alternative to dialogue was not victory but another round of mourning.
He said he had signed a tripartite peace roadmap for the governorate a year earlier with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani and Jordanian Foreign Minister Ayman Safadi, the aim of which was to reintegrate Suweida into Syria in a dignified manner, while guaranteeing full citizenship rights and ensuring that all obligations were met.
Journalist Samer al-Miqdad told The New Arab that the danger posed by the National Guard's military movements extended beyond changes in territorial control or the spread of fighting into rural Daraa. The greater risk was a return to widespread chaos across southern Syria and the reignition of the crisis.
"People in eastern rural Daraa fear the consequences of this militia's military operations," he said. "We had reached an acceptable level of calm and de-escalation, but the militia is trying to undermine it."
He added that the group continued to marginalise opponents in Suweida who called for a resolution, even if that meant using force and repression. Any further escalation would directly harm residents, he warned, and an extension of the fighting into Daraa would be disastrous, given the militia members' threats.
The roadmap for resolving the Suweida crisis was signed on 17 September 2025, following meetings in Amman in July and August that year between the Syrian government, Jordan and the US.
It affirmed that any solution must preserve Syria's territorial unity and that Suweida's affairs could not be addressed outside the Syrian national framework. The roadmap called for the withdrawal of security forces, the establishment of local administration with security and administrative arrangements, the delivery of humanitarian aid, the release of abductees and the return of displaced residents.
It also called for an end to foreign interference alongside regional security understandings, and an investigation into the deadly events in Suweida in July 2025, when clashes erupted between Druze gunmen on one side and government forces and Bedouin fighters on the other.

Greece joins push to ban social media for minors
A growing number of countries are tightening rules governing children’s online activity amid fears of addiction.
The Greek parliament has passed a law banning the use of social media by people under the age of 15.
Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis’s party, New Democracy, used its majority to pass the bill on Friday. None of the other political parties backed the bill in a heated debate that started on Thursday, despite the fact that a growing group of countries worldwide have introduced restrictions on minors.
Greece’s new laws will come into effect on January 1 2027. It will require age verification on social networks and impose harsh penalties should companies fail to comply.
Mitsotakis previously announced plans for the ban in April, taking to TikTok, one of the most popular social networks with young people in Greece, to explain the “difficult but necessary” measure that his government planned to take.
The opposition socialist PASOK party abstained from the vote, after seeking an alternative bill that would have banned social media for under-13s and parental controls for 13- and 14-year-olds.
The ban brings Greece into line with about 20 countries that now restrict access to social media apps for young people. Australia, France, Brazil, Indonesia, Austria, Denmark, and the UK are among those that have either introduced or plan similar restrictions.
Critics say social networks use addictive algorithms to glue kids to their screens, and warn excessive scrolling can damage their mental health.
Bans have also faced pushback though, with questions about their enforcement and how effective they really are.

Where Intuitions Conflict
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:54:48 UTC
21:54:48 KST

If you ask a group of people a philosophical question or present them with a challenging thought experiment, it’s often the case that they will express very different views about it. We quite naturally interpret this as different people having different intuitions. But is that what’s going on?
In “Conflicting Intuitions,” published earlier this year, Joshua Knobe (Yale) takes up this question. Having imagined posing a question about free will to a group of students who express disagreement over its answer, he writes:
[I]t might be that some people have compatibilist intuitions, while others have incompatibilist intuitions, and similarly for each of the other traditional questions of philosophy. Then the puzzlement we feel regarding these questions might be explained in terms of the conflict between the intuitions of different people.
But that’s not the only possible explanation:
I will argue that experimental research has been providing evidence for a very different hypothesis. On this hypothesis, the difficulty is in large part a matter of individual people having conflicting intuitions. Thus, when a person encounters a thought experiment designed to get at one of the traditional questions of philosophy, she will often have an intuition pulling her in one direction but also an intuition pulling her in the exact opposite direction. This might seem like an obvious hypothesis, and perhaps it is. Still, I think that its implications haven’t been fully appreciated. If true, it would have important implications both empirically and philosophically.
On the empirical side:
The conflicting intuitions hypothesis has important implications when it comes to what exactly our theories about people’s intuition are supposed to explain…
If we assume that the difference in responses is due to different people having different intuitions, we would naturally assume that the theory should explain why different people have different intuitions regarding this case. So we might think that our theory of the underlying cognitive processes should explain why [some] have one intuition and the other[s] have the opposite intuition.
However, if we conclude that the difference in responses is due to each individual person having conflicting intuitions, there is an important sense in which there is more that needs explaining. An adequate theory would not merely have to explain why half of the participants have the intuition that it is a case of causation; it would have to explain why those people are conflicted…
There are various issues on the philosophical side. Here’s one, mentioned after the discussion of some empirical work on cases about which respondents say that apparently conflicting intuitions are both correct:
Independent of anything that could be settled through further empirical work on ordinary intuitions, we need to know whether there is some way of working out a philosophical theory that makes sense of what people seem to be saying in these cases. For example, within the philosophy of law, we can ask whether there is any way of developing a theory on which it can be right to say something like: there is a sense in which this action clearly violates the law, but there is a deeper sense in which it does not violate the law. Similarly, within the work on personal identity, we can ask whether there is any way of developing a theory on which it can be right to say: there is a sense in which this person is clearly Phineas, but there is also a deeper sense in which he is not truly Phineas.
Here again, I suspect we will arrive at different answers for different philosophical issues. For some, we may find that it is possible to develop such a theory, and philosophical work along these lines might lead to important new insights. For others, we will presumably arrive at the opposite conclusion. We will find that there is simply no possible way for both intuitions to be true.
Additionally, “we would need a clear answer to the… question as to how conflicting intuitions can have a larger philosophical significance even when we recognize that there is no possible way that both intuitions can be true.”
The whole article is here. Discussion welcome.

Uninvited guest: How a GRU spy connected to state hackers broke into the African Union’s diplomatic residence in Ethiopia
Unknown

After the death-by-plane crash of Wagner Group founder Yevgeny Prigozhin in August 2023, the Kremlin’s influence operations in Africa have undergone a transformation. In addition to the Africa Corps — a state-run armed formation made up mostly of former Wagner fighters — Russia’s military intelligence agency (GRU) is also active on the ground. However, fresh revelations about a GRU break-in at an African Union facility in Addis Ababa threaten to tarnish relations between the Kremlin and the continent. The news couldn’t come at a worse time for Moscow, which is set to host the third ever Russia-Africa Summit on October 28-29.
On April 28, 2025, Mahamoud Ali Youssouf, the Chairman of the African Union Commission, arrived at a house in the upscale neighborhood of Bole Atlas in Addis Ababa, where the union’s secretariat is headquartered. The property is the official residence of Selma Haddadi, the Deputy Chairperson of the Commission, which is the executive arm of the supranational body representing all 55 African countries. But on that afternoon, it was in use by Youssouf and his family, who were then still recent transplants to the Ethiopian capital after arriving days earlier from Djibouti, Youssouf’s native country, where up until the previous month he’d served as its foreign minister.
At 3:32 p.m., a vehicle with diplomatic license plates pulled into the parking area outside the main compound of Africa House. Out of it stepped a white man of medium build with short hair, dressed in a button-down shirt and tie. He waited until a car transporting Youssouf’s university-aged daughter entered the premises via an opened security gate and then snuck in on foot before the gate closed behind him. The intruder entered the residence and proceeded directly to the bedroom where Youssouf was staying, remaining inside the building for 4 minutes and 24 seconds. At some point, the unknown intruder ran into the daughter (The Insider is withholding her name) inside the house. A stationed private security detail met the man as he exited the residence at 3:37. They tried to question him, but the detail worried he might have been a VIP who’d gotten lost or entered without the proper checks. Amid the confusion, the intruder drove off at 3:38.
The exterior moments of this brief and seemingly uneventful trespass were captured on CCTV images, which The Insider has exclusively obtained. Facial recognition software confirms that the break-in artist was Major Aleksandr Dubikov, the assistant to Nikita Zayats, Russia’s military attaché in Ethiopia.
The footage of the break-in is available in our video below.
Zayats was reportedly expelled from Portugal in 2022 over alleged links to the GRU, Russia’s military intelligence agency. As it happens, Dubikov, a 36-year-old Moscow resident, is also a GRU officer, meaning his illicit entry into a diplomatic residence in Addis Ababa was almost certainly an intelligence operation.
The Insider is publicly revealing his identity as the break-in artist for the first time. It is unclear if the African Union or the Ethiopian government knew of Dubikov's role in this incident, or his work for the GRU.
Records show that he was registered to a well-known dormitory of the GRU Academy at 52 Narodnogo Opolcheniya Street in Moscow. On his VK profile, last updated in May 2008, Dubikov says that he is a student of the Peter the Great Military Academy of the Strategic Missile Forces, a premier defense institution now based in Balashikha, Moscow region, where he studied computer science and information technologies in control systems. “Like everyone else,” he writes, “I study — but in my own way, combining usefulness with pleasure… Just a cadet.”
He described himself as “[v]ery kind and cuddly. I’m a well-rounded person interested in many things,” and was a fan of Rihanna, Chris Brown, the Mafia and Max Payne video games.
An Insider analysis of Dubikov’s phone data found several numbers belonging to GRU officers. His second-most frequently called number belongs to 37-year-old Vladislav Popov, a known GRU hacker linked to “Sandworm,” or GRU’s Unit 74455, responsible for launching a series of destructive and costly cyberattacks — including one in 2017 shutting down operations by Danish shipping company Maersk and U.S. pharmaceutical giant Merck, and mission-critical hospital computers in Pennsylvania. NotPetya, malware developed and deployed by “Sandworm” that initially infected Ukrainian computer systems, caused more than an estimated $10 billion in damages globally.
Following the 2025 incident in Addis Ababa, a source familiar with the matter told The Insider on the condition of anonymity that the African Union’s Security Directorate had strengthened security measures around Africa House. However, the breach raises concerns that Dubikov may have tried to steal files, data, or electronic devices belonging to Youssouf, or to install surveillance equipment to gather information about the chairman. Dubikov’s closeness to Popov and Sandworm only adds to that suspicion.
The breach raises concerns that Dubikov may have tried to steal files, data, or electronic devices belonging to Youssouf
According to flight records, Dubikov is still in the country—which means that either the Ethiopian authorities failed to identify him prior to this report, or they simply chose to ignore the scandal. The latter cannot be ruled out; judging by the frequent travel of GRU operatives — as analyzed by The Insider — Ethiopia has become a key hub for Russian intelligence activity in recent years.
“Ethiopia has long been an important operating base for Russian intelligence in East Africa,” according to Philip Obaji, a Nigerian Russia expert and investigative journalist who has extensively reported on Russia’s covert operations in Africa. “Senior GRU officials Anton Papshev and Yury Mikheyev, who play key roles in coordinating Russian intelligence activities across the continent, were based there for years.”
A spokesperson for Youssouf did not respond to a request for comment.
The disclosure of a Russian spy’s break-in of a diplomatic compound in East Africa comes at an awkward moment. On October 28-29, the third Russia-Africa summit is set to take place in Moscow, with Yuri Ushakov, Vladimir Putin’s adviser, heading its organizing committee. The second summit, held in 2023, aimed to “bolster comprehensive ties between the Russian Federation and African states, while establishing fresh frameworks for bilateral and multilateral collaboration,” according to its official website.
The co-chairs for the upcoming summit will be Vladimir Putin and Évariste Ndayishimiye, the Burundi president who this year holds the African Union’s rotating chairmanship.
“While Russia continues to establish relations with many African Union member states, the GRU break-in reveals its twofold game,” a Western security official told The Insider. “While it officially engages in cooperation with African Union members, it does not hesitate to use manipulation and lies to achieve its aims.”
Russia’s role in Africa is both expansive and fraught. Much of its military presence was established by the Wagner Group, formerly headed by catering magnate-cum-mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin, who died in a plane bombing in August 2023, two months after attempting an abortive mutiny against the Russian government. From 2017 until its demise, Wagner acted as a plausibly deniable arm of the Kremlin in multiple African theatres — Mali, Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic. The mercenaries have acted as bodyguards and protection squads to help coup-proof regimes (they were the praetorian guard for CAR President Faustin-Archange Touadéra for over half a decade) and as combat forces to wage war against jihadist and rebel groups.
From 2017 until its demise, Wagner acted as a plausibly deniable arm of the Kremlin in multiple African theatres — Mali, Libya, Sudan and the Central African Republic
Wagner’s political technologists have also overseen information operations similar to the troll farm campaigns Prigozhin’s employees ran out of St. Petersburg to interfere in Western elections. Using the front organization AFRIC, they imported European neo-Nazis and white supremacists to act as ”election monitors” in several African countries, though their real purpose was to act as agents of influence to promote certain candidates and drum up anti-Western sentiment. (That white racists were at times pushing a pan-Africanist agenda at the expense of the bitter legacies of British and French colonialism was an irony Prigozhin may have relished privately.) Quite often, in fact, Wagner armed and funded opposing sides or a multiplicity of political actors vying for control of the same government — especially in Libya, where it worked on behalf of Saif al-Islam Gaddafi, the son of slain dictator Col. Muammar Gaddafi, and also of Gen. Khalifa Haftar, a Libyan warlord once beholden to the CIA.
“Russia’s broader approach in Africa is highly opportunistic,” Obaji told The Insider. “It deals with sitting governments while quietly maintaining relationships with opposition figures working against them. Rather than showing consistent loyalty to any one side, Moscow runs a dual-track strategy designed to protect and advance its own interests no matter which way the political winds blow.”
Wagner has enriched itself by extracting natural resources where it operated, running gold and diamond mines. In late 2021, Wagner usurped the French military in Mali at the invitation of the country’s ruling junta to defend the Bamako regime against Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin, the al-Qaeda affiliate, and Tuareg rebels. Both groups routed Wagner in Tinzaouatène, Mali, in 2024, precipitating the group’s withdrawal in 2025.
The UN Panel of Experts for Mali stated in an August 2023 report that Wagner, which was credibly accused of gross human rights abuses such as torture, beheadings, and summary executions, has hardly been a successful counterterrorist force in the country, allowing the ISIS franchise in Mali to nearly double its territorial control in under a year. Wagner has, however, tried to pass off its atrocities as the work of the French military, including the on-camera burial of bodies in a mass grave near a Malian military base Wagner was using in April 2022.
Wagner has hardly been a successful counterterrorist force in Mali, allowing the ISIS franchise to nearly double its territorial control in under a year
Since Prigozhin’s death, Wagner’s operations have largely been incorporated into Africa Corps, a Russian state-run expeditionary force headed by Gen. Andrey Averyanov, now the deputy director of the GRU but formerly the founding commander of Unit 29155, the service’s black ops team responsible for poisoning the Skripals in Salisbury, staging a failed coup in Montenegro, and blowing up a series of weapons and ammunition storage facilities across NATO territory, where materiel destined for Georgia, Ukraine and Syrian rebels were being stockpiled. Averyanov, in fact, took Prigozhin’s place at a roundtable discussion on the last day of the second Russia-Africa summit in St. Petersburg in July 2023. Seventy to eighty percent of Africa Corps’ forces are ex-Wagner mercenaries, according to an investigation by Reuters.
Moscow’s hard power projection in Africa, meanwhile, competes with soft power initiatives that are often masquerades for intelligence operations. Rossotrudnichestvo, the Foreign Ministry’s cultural arm, which doubles as a conspicuous clearinghouse for the SVR, has plans to open new “Russian Houses,” or educational and cultural centers, in Egypt , Zambia, Tanzania, South Africa, and Ethiopia. In 2025, Russia granted 5,000 state-funded places at Russian universities to African students, mainly from Sudan, Guinea, Ghana, and Chad.

As President Paul Biya returns to Cameroon, can he still rule?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:52:28 UTC
21:52:28 KST

As President Paul Biya returns to Cameroon, can he still rule?
Cameroonians are wondering who Biya will appoint as vice president and possible successor.
Cameroonian President Paul Biya, 93, is once again the subject of death rumours.
Africa’s longest-serving president, known for his long stays away from the Central African nation he governs, only recently returned home from one of his longest stints abroad. His long absence renewed speculation about his health amid unconfirmed reports that he had been hospitalised or had even died.
Despite Biya returning to the country in late August after more than two months abroad, some are unsatisfied.
Biya’s most recent “vacation” also got Cameroonians talking about what a post-Biya future could look like as his likely successors jostle for dominance – and whether he can rule at all given the uncertainty over his health.
Cameroonians hope a government reshuffle will be announced soon. Although the president was re-elected for an eighth term in disputed elections in October last year, he has not announced a new government since.
Many are also hopeful that a vice president, preferably one who stays in the country, will finally be appointed. Here’s what we know:
Who is Biya?
Biya has ruled Cameroon since 1982 under the Cameroon People’s Democratic Party (RDPC). That’s significantly longer than any of Cameroon’s under-30s, who make up 70 percent of the nation’s 30 million population, have been alive.
He is Africa’s oldest leader and among the world’s longest ruling leaders.
Under his rule, attacks by the armed group Boko Haram have continued in the country’s north while separatists are active in the west. Despite the nation’s oil wealth, the economy has largely stagnated.
Analysts said Biya, often called “the absentee president”, largely delegates governance to his cabinet. Opposition leaders have accused him of running Cameroon on “autopilot”.
The president is believed to spend extensive periods at the InterContinental Hotel in Switzerland. By 2018, he had spent a total of four and a half years on private visits abroad, according to an analysis from the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project. His wife, Chantal Biya, is known for her flamboyant style.
Biya’s latest re-election triggered mass protests, which were violently suppressed by security forces. Rights groups said at least 48 people were killed.
Opposition leader Issa Tchiroma Bakary, who claimed victory, was forced into exile in The Gambia.
Tchiroma was formerly part of Biya’s government, holding several ministerial positions over 16 years. He also served as government spokesperson during the years the government fought Boko Haram, and he defended the army when it stood accused of killing civilians. He was once regarded as a member of Biya’s “old guard” but has campaigned on a promise of “change”.
How long was Biya away from Cameroon this time?
Biya arrived in Cameroon on August 20 after 74 days away – one of his longest absences. In 2024, he was absent for 42 days.
The president had been in Geneva for what his office called a “short private stay” since June 7. According to local media, he was joined by family members and some of his close aides.
As speculation grew about his health during his absence, officials denied reports that Biya had been hospitalised at a clinic in Geneva.
Upon their return, Biya and his wife were welcomed by a huge crowd of party supporters. There were fleeting images of the president as he waved from the presidential limousine and shook hands with Prime Minister Joseph Ngute. But many Cameroonians were not satisfied with so little video to indicate the state of the president’s health.
What has happened since Biya’s return?
Not much has happened since the president returned, which has frustrated some people. Since his re-election, he has not announced a new cabinet or a vice president.
While he was away, his office issued several decrees: A presidential act promoted five colonels and another reorganised transfers within the military. But things have since quieted.
Now, Cameroonians are joking online that the president is merely on a visit and will soon return to his residence in Switzerland.
One person posted a playful headline on social media, saying: “Cameroonian President Paul Biya, aged 93, is expected to visit Cameroon next week for a two-week working visit, before returning to Geneva, Switzerland, where he resides.”
Will there be a cabinet reshuffle – and can he still rule?
While he was absent, Cameroon’s ruling party dismissed voters’ concerns and insisted there was no constitutional or political vacuum. However, now that Biya is back, it’s unclear what he plans to do next.
Jason Healy, a sub-Saharan African country risk analyst, told Al Jazeera previously that delaying ministerial appointments could be a strategic move that allows Biya to maintain control over any political changes.
But experts have warned that the prolonged political stagnation is affecting investor confidence in the country.
Cameroonians are now highly curious about who might take over from the president if he is unable to continue as his long stay abroad intensified a power struggle among his would-be successors in the ruling party.
Biya has never identified or groomed a likely successor, adding to the uncertainty.
Now, all eyes are on who might be appointed as vice president. The post was abolished in 1972, but in April, the parliament surprisingly re-established it.
Under the new law, the president can select and dismiss the vice president. The appointee would serve out the remainder of the president’s seven-year term if he is unable to.
Some see the law as an attempt by Biya to select a possible successor although opposition parties have criticised it as undemocratic, saying it essentially blocks elections.
With no vice president, Senate President Aboubakary Abdoulaye would be next in line to lead until elections could be held. Analysts, however, pointed to the country’s secretary-general, Ferdinand Ngoh-Ngoh, believed to be the “de facto president”, as the possible vice president-in-waiting.
There is also Biya’s son, Franck Biya, who would likely enjoy support from his father’s strong base in southern and central Cameroon. But he lacks political experience.

Austria foreign ministry expels four Russian diplomats from Vienna over suspected espionage
Unknown

2026-10-23

21:51:34 KST

Austria's foreign ministry said on Friday it was expelling four Vienna-based Russian diplomats over "activities incompatible with their diplomatic status," a term usually used for spying.
"Based on findings by the Austrian security authorities, the Austrian foreign ministry has taken measures against four Russian diplomats in Vienna," it said in a statement, adding that they had been declared personae non gratae and ordered to leave the country.
Three of them worked at Russia's embassy to Austria and one at the Russian delegation to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) on military security and arms control, the ministry said.
Russia will respond to the expulsions, Russian news agencies cited a foreign ministry official as saying soon after Friday's announcement, without elaborating.
The move brings to 18 the number of Russian diplomats Austria has expelled since 2020. While Austria is a neutral country, politically its governments have sided with Ukraine since Russia launched its all-out invasion in 2022.
While Austria does not usually comment on the specifics of such expulsions, during the last round in May, when it expelled three Russian diplomats, it said it was because of an "antenna forest" on the roofs of Russian diplomatic buildings that could be used for spying.
Vienna is major diplomatic center for OSCE, UN organizations
Vienna is a major diplomatic center, hosting the OSCE and United Nations organizations such as the International Atomic Energy Agency.
Larger countries like Russia and the United States often have separate ambassadors to Austria, the OSCE, and UN organizations, each running an embassy or mission.
Vienna, which was divided into Allied sectors after World War Two, has long had a reputation as a den of spies. The large diplomatic presence offers the opportunity to station intelligence agents there under cover of diplomatic immunity.

Russian Diesel Tanker Heads to New York After Trump-Putin Deal

Representatives of Ukraine, Russia and the US held three rounds of negotiations earlier this year: two in Abu Dhabi in January and February, followed by talks in Geneva in February. Those meetings did not produce an agreement to end the war.
Moscow emphasizes postwar security
Ushakov said Moscow wanted the next round to focus on security arrangements for Russia and Ukraine after the war.
Kyiv has backed renewed negotiations while also calling for a ceasefire, an end to attacks on energy infrastructure and humanitarian measures. No shared agenda for the proposed Abu Dhabi meeting has been announced.
Ukraine is also seeking enforceable guarantees against another Russian attack. As Kyiv Post reported, Zelensky has outlined US commitments modeled on NATO’s Article 5 and backed by Congress, alongside NATO membership and a European-led Coalition of the Willing.
He has described those arrangements as complementary, rather than competing alternatives. No final agreement on the guarantees has been announced.
The proposed November meeting would bring negotiating teams back together; it would not itself constitute a leaders’ summit or confirmation that the parties are ready to sign a settlement.

The 2026/2027 Grand Prix series begins in France on October 23. Ukraine will be represented by the junior pair Hanna Herrera and Ivan Khobta.
On October 23, the Grand Prix series in figure skating for the 2026/2027 season will begin in the French city of Angers. Over three days, the world's leading athletes will compete in four disciplines. Ukraine will be represented at the first event by the junior world championship bronze medalists Hanna Herrera and Ivan Khobta. UNN explains the tournament format, the main favorites, and the broadcast schedule.
How the Grand Prix series works and where the events will take place
The International Skating Union (ISU) Grand Prix series consists of six events held in different countries. Athletes compete in men's and women's singles, pairs, and ice dance. Based on their performances, figure skaters receive ranking points. The six best competitors or teams in each discipline qualify for the final. An athlete may compete in a maximum of two events.
The following competitions are currently scheduled for the 2026/2027 season:
-  October 23-25: France, Angers; 
-  October 30 - November 1: Canada, Kelowna; 
-  November 6-8: China, Shenzhen; 
-  November 13-15: United States, Everett; 
-  November 20-22: Finland, Helsinki; 
-  November 27-29: Japan, Tokyo. 
The series final is scheduled for December 10-13 in Chongqing, China.
Grand Prix de France in Angers: competitors and favorites
The first event will take place at the Angers IceParc arena. Among the main contenders for victory in the men's event are 2026 Olympic champion Mikhail Shaidorov of Kazakhstan and two-time European champion Adam Siao Him Fa of France. They will be challenged by Japan's Kao Miura and Sota Yamamoto.
In the women's event, particular attention is focused on Belgium's Nina Pinzarrone, the 2026 world championship bronze medalist, Japan's Ami Nakai, and Georgia's Anastasiia Gubanova.
Among the favorites in the pairs event are Georgia's Anastasiia Metelkina and Luka Berulava, while in ice dance the favorites are the French duo of Laurence Fournier Beaudry and Guillaume Cizeron, the 2026 Olympic champions.
Will Ukrainian figure skaters compete?
Ukraine will be represented at the competition by the pairs team of Hanna Herrera and Ivan Khobta. In March 2026, they won bronze medals at the junior world championships, earning 160.15 points for their two programs combined. The skaters have been competing together since 2025, so their participation in Angers will be an important test at the senior level. Their opponents will include experienced medalists from international championships.
Other Ukrainians are expected to compete at subsequent events in the series, including Kyrylo Marsak, the pairs team of Sofiia Holichenko and Artem Darenskyi, and the ice dance duo of Iryna Pidhaina and Artem Koval.
Competition schedule and where to watch
The Grand Prix de France broadcasts in Ukraine will be provided by Suspilne Sport. The performances can be watched on the television channel, the website, and local Suspilne broadcasting channels.

====================================================================================================

Yle price comparison: Finland's food prices lower than Sweden, Estonia
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:48:12 EEST
21:48:12 KST

The same product, the same retail chain and possibly even the same manufacturer.
But the price can vary considerably depending on whether you buy the item in Helsinki, Athens or Stockholm.
Yle compared the price of the same basket of groceries in Lidl stores in Finland, Sweden, Estonia, Poland, Germany, Spain and Greece.
Lidl was chosen for the comparison because it is the only grocery chain with stores both in Finland and in other European countries. Thirty staples were included in the shopping basket.
Finland has long been known as an expensive country in comparisons, but the old perceptions are becoming outdated. Tallinn, for example, once a go-to for cheap shopping, has closed the price gap and is now more expensive than Helsinki.
Food in Finland still costs more than the European average, but the gap has narrowed in recent years. In this comparison, the grocery basket cost roughly the same in Helsinki, Stockholm and Tallinn.
Inflation main driver
Differences in the grocery basket prices are explained by taxation, wage levels and transport costs, as well as competition between shops and consumer habits.
But the biggest factor behind the differences is food inflation in recent years. Prices have risen in Finland too, but elsewhere inflation has galloped ahead faster. In Estonia, for example, food prices climbed faster than anywhere else in the eurozone in 2022, by more than 19 percent.
Finland's food prices were lower last year than in Estonia and in the other Nordic countries, according to Eurostat.
Price differences between Finland and Estonia are explained by wages and taxes, among other things.
Retail workers in Finland earn more than their Estonian counterparts, which pushes up costs.
In Estonia, meanwhile, the value-added tax on food is 24 percent, compared with 13.5 percent in Finland. This raises prices in Estonia relative to Finland and partly explains why a grocery basket in Tallinn has crept up to Helsinki's level, both in Yle's comparison and in Eurostat's figures.
Pricey vegetables, cheap coffee
Finns' preference for domestic products shows up especially in meat. Lidl in Finland sells plenty of Finnish meat because consumers want it.
"Estonian consumers favor imported products more than Finns do. That means meat can be brought in from Poland, for example, where production costs are lower," said Bate Ismail, an economist at the Finnish Food and Drink Industries' Federation.
Vegetables in Finland are up to a fifth more expensive than the EU average. Transport costs are among the factors behind this. When it comes to domestic production, heating and lighting greenhouses drive up costs.
The flip side is coffee, which is cheaper in Finland. Cheap coffee is an important way for shops to lure customers, as are cheese and sweets.
The same phenomenon shows up in olive oil, which is cheaper in southern countries than in the north. In Greece and Spain, olive oil is a so-called loss leader.
In Finland, Lidl keeps a particularly close eye on S Group pricing. If shoppers pay more for comparable products in rival Finnish stores, Lidl has no need to cut its prices to the level of other countries.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the suspected attacker had been "apprehended and placed in police custody".

Rabeh said the shooter had hit a health centre, a petrol station and several vehicles during the spree.
The suspected attacker was then arrested at the nearby town of Coignières, local media report.

PNAT said their investigation also includes "possession of a Category A weapon" - which includes military-grade weapons or weapons capable of firing in bursts.

Brazil's tense presidential run-off campaign feels like a psychological thriller
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:45:49 UTC
21:45:49 KST

Brazil's tense presidential run-off campaign feels like a psychological thriller
Insults traded on social media and a combative debate have intensified the pressure ahead of a fiercely contested presidential run-off on Sunday, with only a few points separating leftist pro-union President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and far-right challenger Flavio Bolsonaro, the son of former president and Trump ally Jair Bolsonaro.
With music blaring, parade floats and glitter in the colours of the Brazilian flag, several hundred supporters rallied in street-carnival style on Wednesday in the working-class neighbourhood of Bangu, in western Rio, to support right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro.
In the heart of the Vidigal favela some 40 kilometres (25 miles) away, a few dozen members of President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's Workers’ Party were rallying the troops by handing out flyers to the last undecided voters.
But in both Bangu and Vidigal, the festive spirit is gone.
Both camps mobilise their 'armies'
Since the extremely close first-round results were announced on October 4, war has been declared between the two candidates. The self-proclaimed “Commander-in-Chief of the President”, MP André Janones of Minas Gerais, has created “Lula’s army” – a WhatsApp channel that garnered more than 8 million followers in just a few days. The channel aims to mobilise activists and anti-Bolsonaristas by issuing them challenges on social media or in the streets.
Surprised at not having won the first round, Lula has handed over control of his campaign to the younger generation of elected party officials. These digital soldiers have re-energised his campaign, which was criticised for its inertia before the first round. But it may be too little, too late. “This is the least-organised campaign I have taken part in since 1989, and we reap what we sow,” the president admitted in a meeting with allied lawmakers.
The octogenarian president has recently begun filming himself, always accompanied by activists under 30. The goal is to win over young non-voters, some 6.9 million Brazilians – only a fraction of those would have been enough to tip the election. For Josue Medeiros, coordinator of the Political and Electoral Observatory at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, this digital awakening could make the difference. “The number of undecided voters has risen, to between 7 and 14%, and that is a good sign for whoever came second in the first round, because these are people who are wavering and could change their vote. It means this digital mobilisation is working; it creates doubt and reduces the sense that President Lula was being rejected, which was very strong before the first round.”
The Bolsonarist camp, for its part, is not sitting on its hands. Facing Lula’s army, Flavio has unleashed his own “troops”, led by young MP Nikolas Ferreira, who can activate his 25 million followers on demand. Their specialty? Using AI-generated content to disparage left-wing rallies.
The digital battle has also moved into the courts. Accused of favouring the right-wing candidate, Lula’s camp denounced Meta for “algorithmic manipulation” in Bolsonaro's favour and asked the Superior Electoral Court to annul the challenger's candidacy. Bolsonaro, in turn, accused the incumbent of “abuse of power” for flooding WhatsApp with content praising his government’s record. Under pressure from the high court, which threatened the company with a fine of around R$500,000 (€88,500) per day, Meta now says it has put measures in place to guarantee equal treatment of both candidates.
Polls tighten
Having come out ahead in the first round with about 47% of the vote against 45% for Lula, Bolsonaro seemed to have the momentum: an October 9 AtlasIntel poll credited him with 52.8% of the vote to Lula's 47.2%. Ten days later, the same firm had him at only 51.1% against 48.9% for the incumbent president while other pollsters (Datafolha, Quaest, CNT/MDA) showed a gap of just one or two points between the candidates. In the meantime, Lula won a major victory in Congress: a vote to end the six-day work week. The overwhelming approval of this measure by the Senate (75 votes to 1) made this labour-law reform a strategic victory as the run-off approached. Initially opposed to the measure, the Bolsonarist camp ended up voting in favour. The left now warns that Bolsonaro will reverse the law if elected, given that he has been a staunch ally of business owners and agribusiness, which fiercely opposed the law. “It is important to remember that our opponents decided yesterday to vote for this measure. But let’s stay vigilant! They voted for it out of electoral opportunism,” Lula said in a video posted on his Instagram account.
An anxiety-provoking debate
Amid repeated charges of opportunism and lying, the tone of the run-off had turned tense even before reaching a fever pitch in the first debate between the two candidates on October 18. The face-off was highly anticipated, particularly after Lula refused to debate his opponent ahead of the first round.
A contentious debate of nearly two hours live on the Band channel held the attention of some 158 million Brazilian voters. But little detail emerged on the candidates' respective platforms regarding security, health or the economy – instead there was an avalanche of insults and jabs, often referencing the allegations of corruption tainting both parties.
The debate was meant to convince the 33 million abstainers to vote on October 25. But according to Joao Ferres, political scientist at the University of Rio de Janeiro, “debates are watched less and less by Brazilians and do not influence voting intentions much. This confrontation mostly hurt Flavio Bolsonaro, who came across as aggressive; Brazilian voters don’t like that kind of behaviour.”
The electric atmosphere sent deputy Andre Janones to intensive care shortly after the debate with severe cardiac arrhythmia triggered by stress and fatigue. He was not the only one to have suffered aftereffects, with some viewers reporting symptoms of "political anxiety" including cold sweats, panic attacks, irritability or insomnia.
A few days after the debate, Bolsonaro relented and agreed, with conditions, to accept Lula's challenge to make their banking, tax and phone records public.
Verdict at the ballot box
Progressive independent media outlet Brasil fora da Caverna recommended voting early on Instagram: “Go vote before noon on Sunday, October 25, because afterward we don’t know what might happen.”
Lula’s supporters are also urging voters to go to the polls as early as possible: “In case of transport problems, a change of polling station, queues or any other unforeseen event, you will still have time to find a solution and exercise your right to vote,” his team posted on Instagram.
In an election that is widely expected to be decided by just a few points, every vote is going to count.

Belgium boosts heating-oil aid for vulnerable households as energy prices rise
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:44:14 UTC
21:44:14 KST

Belgium is stepping up targeted aid to shield vulnerable households from soaring energy costs, but the limited support may fall short as prices rise.
Belgium will set aside €15 million to increase heating-oil subsidies for vulnerable households this winter as rising fuel prices squeeze household budgets.
The temporary measure will cover heating-oil deliveries made between 1 December 2026 and 28 February 2027, Federal Energy Minister Mathieu Bihet announced on Friday.
The existing allowance will rise progressively with prices, from a maximum of €0.20 per litre to €0.50 when heating oil reaches €1.775 per litre or more.
The move comes amid persistent disruption in the Middle East, which has fuelled energy-market volatility. Brent crude was trading at $114 a barrel on Friday, up from $70 before the US-Israeli war with Iran.
The additional support is targeted at eligible households facing higher heating costs, rather than consumers as a whole.
"Heating one's home should never become a luxury. When the price of heating oil rises sharply, it is the most vulnerable households that feel the impact most severely," Bihet said.
"We are temporarily increasing support to help them get through the winter with greater peace of mind and protect their purchasing power."
Although heating oil is being phased out, it remains an important source of residential heating in some EU countries, including Cyprus and Ireland. In Belgium, it accounts for around 35% of residential space heating, second only to natural gas.
Consumption is particularly high in rural areas and older buildings, especially in Wallonia, where nearly half of households rely on heating oil because they lack access to the gas grid.
Across the EU, heating oil accounts for about 14% of residential space-heating energy, with roughly one in six heating systems running on oil, according to Odyssee-Mure, a tool supporting the evaluation of energy-efficiency policies.
At the current Belgian price of €1.62 per litre, a delivery of 1,500 litres costs €2,430. The existing maximum subsidy of €300 covers only a fraction of the bill.
Under the reinforced scheme, the allowance would rise to €487, bringing the household's net cost down to €1,943.
The support is limited to households meeting the existing eligibility criteria for the Social Heating Fund; it is not available to everyone who uses heating oil.
Federal Energy Minister Mathieu Bihet advised applicants to check their eligibility and the application procedure with their local public social welfare centre, known as the CPAS in French or OCMW in Dutch.
The government has allocated €7.5 million to the Social Heating Fund to finance the increased heating allowance, with a further €7.5 million earmarked for the Gas and Electricity Fund. Support under the latter scheme is also distributed through public social welfare centres, subject to eligibility criteria.
The measures offer short-term relief but are limited by their budget and eligibility requirements, leaving many households facing higher energy bills without additional support.
Bihet said the increase was intended to protect the purchasing power of families most exposed to rising heating costs.
The government has not said whether further measures will be introduced if prices rise beyond the levels covered by the scheme.

Font size
The relic of St John of Rila’s right hand, kept on the Greek island of Tinos, is a little-known link between Bulgaria and Greece, says forum coordinator Gencho Banev.
An academic forum taking place in Athens from 22 to 25 October marks the 1,150th anniversary of the birth of St John of Rila the Wonderworker, celebrated this year.
Historians and Slavic scholars from the universities of Thessaloniki and Athens, alongside representatives of Bulgaria’s academic community, have been invited to take part in “Days of St John of Rila in Athens – Spiritual Heritage Beyond Borders”. The initiative has also attracted interest from Greek students and dozens of families whose children attend Bulgarian Sunday schools in Greece.
The forum explores the saint’s spiritual legacy across several disciplines, showing how it brings cultures together. The earliest accounts of his life in Bulgarian and Greek bear witness to this, as does his image on Bulgaria’s one-euro coin today — a symbol of a shared European spiritual tradition. The academic round table in Athens will explore questions of theology, hagiology, history, literature and contemporary social developments.
PHOTO graecobulgarica.gr
The second part of the forum focuses on the Bulgarian diaspora, good practices from Bulgarian Sunday schools abroad and educational projects aimed at building a network of cooperation beyond Bulgaria’s borders. The programme is headed by a simple message from the life of St John of Rila: “Have peace among yourselves.”
That message, passed down a millennium ago, seems to shine through the children’s drawings dedicated to the patron saint of all Bulgarians. The exhibition, which accompanies the academic programme, features work by pupils at Bulgarian schools in Greece, Bulgaria, Spain, Germany, Italy, the United Kingdom and elsewhere.
“This is an encounter between Bulgaria’s spiritual heritage and the world of children’s imagination,” says Maya Lungolova, chair of the board of the Ivan Seliminski Centre.
Maya Lungolova

When I say ‘our children’, I mean all of them, both in Bulgaria and abroad. They simply exceeded our expectations. They did not just depict the saint’s daily life and his likeness, but told little stories, taking us back to the legends of the little shepherd of the Rila Mountains and his meeting with Tsar Peter. All this can be seen in the drawings. The drawing competition is not about competing with one another; the best drawings are simply selected for the exhibition.
“The Bulgarian church in Athens, which bears the saint’s name, is the focal point of the anniversary celebrations, bringing together Bulgarian scholars, students and Sunday school teachers in the Greek capital. A representative of the Bulgarian Orthodox Church, sent by the Holy Synod in Sofia, will also take part in the service.”

PHOTO BTA
“Bulgaria and Greece are linked through the memory of St John of Rila in a very unusual way that few people know about. The saint’s right hand is in Greece, on the island of Tinos. We visited the monastery where the relic is kept and spoke to the people there. That was how the idea of bringing the celebrations together in Athens came about. And so our celebration of the Bulgarian saint begins right beneath the Acropolis, where the club hosting the exhibition of children’s drawings is located.
“The celebrations are on a larger scale, with many students from different countries taking part in translating literary works. There is considerable interest. Distinguished lecturers and researchers from the universities of Athens and Thessaloniki are coming especially for the event. One of the speakers will present his research into the relic of the saint’s right hand and how it came to Greece. Scholars believe it reached the Aegean islands in the late 18th century and came to Tinos in the early 20th century. The saint is deeply revered in Greece as well as in Bulgaria. In the early 20th century, a prominent Greek writer composed a liturgical service in his honour. The text explicitly identifies the relic as the hand of St John of Rila, from the Rila Mountains in Bulgaria,” says Gencho Banev.
Ceremony welcoming the remains of Tsar Samuel to Bulgaria (3 October 2026).
PHOTO BGNES
History shows how closely connected we are here in the Balkans. One example is the return from Greece of the remains of the medieval Bulgarian Tsar Samuel and their ceremonial interment in St Sophia Church, an act affirming the good-neighbourly relations between the two countries. Scholars attending the Bulgarian-Greek academic forum in Athens say there is much more of interest concerning the written records and relics of the Rila hermit that has yet to be substantiated through research and published.

Air raid alerts close all Moscow airports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:42:47 UTC
21:42:47 KST

Air raid alerts close all Moscow airports
All four of Moscow’s international airports have suspended flights amid a drone attack threat, with passengers being evacuated from Sheremetyevo terminals following an air raid alert.
Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo, and Zhukovsky airports have halted all arrivals and departures, Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency has announced.
Sheremetyevo airport has confirmed that an evacuation is underway, with staff assisting passengers in reaching shelters, including escorting people off aircraft. Access to secure departure areas across all terminals has been temporarily restricted.
The shutdown affects all four international airports serving the Russian capital, which together handle roughly 200,000 passengers and more than 1,000 aircraft arrivals and departures on a typical day.
Sheremetyevo, located northwest of Moscow, is Russia’s busiest airport and the main hub for Aeroflot. It handles around 111,000 passengers daily, serving destinations across the country as well as in Asia, the Middle East, and other regions.
Domodedovo, southeast of the capital, handles approximately 39,000 passengers daily, while Vnukovo, southwest of Moscow, serves around 49,000. Both operate domestic and international services, including flights to Türkiye, Central Asia, and the Middle East.
Zhukovsky, the smallest of the four airports, is located southeast of Moscow near the city of the same name. It handles approximately 4,000 passengers daily, primarily on routes connecting Russia with neighboring countries and other international destinations.
The airports have urged passengers to follow official announcements and check flight information directly with their airlines, as schedules remain subject to change.
Moscow’s three largest airports – Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, and Vnukovo – handled a combined 40.4 million passengers in the first seven months of 2026, down 3.5% from the same period last year, according to Rosaviatsia figures analyzed by Interfax. Domodedovo recorded the steepest decline, with passenger traffic falling 13.2% to 6.9 million. Vnukovo saw a 1.4% drop to just over 9 million passengers, while Sheremetyevo, the capital’s busiest airport, reported a 1% decline to 24.5 million.
Russian air defenses shot down 155 Ukrainian drones over Moscow and the surrounding region overnight, according to Russian authorities. Earlier on Friday, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin reported that 19 of the UAVs had been intercepted on approach to the capital.
Moscow-bound flights have been diverted to other airports, including Pulkovo in St. Petersburg, which confirmed it was receiving aircraft originally destined for the Russian capital.

Japan-Russia ties erode as journalist sits in Moscow jail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:42:00 UTC
21:42:00 KST

Japan-Russia ties erode as journalist sits in Moscow jail
October 23, 2026
Japanese Foreign Ministry officials were in Moscow this week in an attempt to contact a journalist arrested in Russia's far east on spying claims.
Journalist Yuki Imai was arrested on October 14 by Russia's FSB security service in the city of Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk on Sakhalin Island. Televised footage of the arrest showed FSB officers barging into his hotel room as he slept.
The correspondent for the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper was accused of attempting to obtain information on soldiers in the region, which is near the Kiril islands, a geopolitical sore spot in Russia-Japan relations.
Russian authorities quickly transferred him to Lefortovo Prison in Moscow, where a court ordered him to be held in pre-trial detention until at least December 12. If convicted, 34-year-old Imai faces up to 20 years in jail, according to the International Federation of Journalists, which has called for his immediate release.
Officials of the Japanese embassy in Moscow have been refused access to Imai. In Tokyo, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has condemned the arrest and dismissed the claim that Imai was a spy.
Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev said Imai had been caught "red-handed," Russia's TASS news agency reported. He has claimed that Japanese intelligence agencies use Japanese journalists to collect classified information with the goal of "undermining Russia's security and defense capability."
Russia accuses journalists of being 'spies'
Yoji Gomi, a veteran journalist and author who has reported from across Asia, told DW Japanese journalists may occasionally meet with diplomats in the course of their work and "share thoughts and impressions." However, he rejects the idea that reporters are paid spies.
"One-party nations often see foreign correspondents as spies because that is exactly what they use their journalists for," he said.
"I can completely see how the Russians decided that Imai was a spy, as it is how they operate, plus he was in a sensitive part of Russia where there are lots of North Korean laborers that they want to keep quiet," Gomi added.
Stephen Nagy, a professor of international relations at Tokyo's International Christian University, said that Russia may see Imai as a bargaining chip it can use to exchange for its nationals detained overseas.
However, Nagy doubts Japan will give in to pressure.
"They are going to resist because it means that Russia, or any other country, can then just seize a Japanese national, put them on trial for espionage and demand the release of one of their people," he told DW.
"It would set a dangerous precedent," he added.
The arrest comes after a member of a Russia-linked hacking group "Qilin" was arrested in Japan and extradited to Germany to face charges in connection with a 2024 cyberattack on a logistics center.
The last time a journalist was arrested in Russia was in 2019 for "attempting to obtain classified information about Russia's military potential in the Far East," Russia's Interfax news agency reported. However, in this case, the journalist was quickly released.
Imai's case is perhaps the most serious since 2023, when Wall Street Journal reporter Evan Gershkovich was arrested in Russia and sentenced to 16 years in a penal colony before being released in a prisoner exchange with Western countries in 2024.
Strained Japan-Russia ties
Imai's arrest is the latest in a series of incidents that have sent bilateral relations into a tailspin.
Nagy said Imai's seizure is designed to put pressure on Tokyo. He added this is part of a coordinated approach with China to isolate Japan at a time when the US is preoccupied with domestic issues and the conflict in the Middle East.
"Moscow and Beijing are coordinating to create the image that Japan is not a reformed member of the international community but still the military state of the 1930s and that it poses a threat to stability in the Indo-Pacific region," Nagy said.
"This is all designed to smear Japan's efforts to lead diplomacy in the region at a time when the US is perhaps distracted," he told DW. "And it does not even matter much that it is not true; they will just continue to repeat the claim to discredit and weaken Tokyo."
Decades-long row over disputed islands
Tadashi Anno, a professor of politics at Tokyo's Sophia University, believes Japan had been working hard to maintain a stable relationship with Moscow, even after Tokyo joined international condemnation of the invasion of Ukraine.
Anno said Moscow's timing on turning up the heat on Tokyo is puzzling.
"Japan condemned the invasion of Ukraine in 2022 because it was a fundamental violation of international law, but Russia is only now pushing back hard," he told DW.
At the center of deteriorating ties is a territorial dispute about a chain of islands off the far north of Japan that were seized by Soviet forces after Japan's surrender in World War II.
Known as the Northern Territories in Japan and the Southern Kurils by Russia, there have been hopes in the past in Tokyo that a concerted diplomatic effort could be sufficient to convince Russia to return them to Japanese sovereignty.
That campaign has faltered in the last couple of years, however, and was further dented when Japan announced in the spring that it would be joining the NATO initiative to provide non-lethal assistance to Kyiv.
In August, President Vladimir Putin visited the disputed islands, only the second Russian leader to do so. Earlier this month, a delegation of Chinese businesspeople was welcomed on one of the islands and talks are under way on the possibility of economic cooperation.

Ukraine Loads Up F-16 Vulcans With 50,000 Danish Rounds for Russian Drone Intercepts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
12:40:08 UTC
21:40:08 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Loads Up F-16 Vulcans With 50,000 Danish Rounds for Russian Drone Intercepts
Denmark has supplied Ukraine with more than 50,000 rounds of 20mm ammunition for the cannons aboard its F-16 fighters, giving Ukrainian pilots a far cheaper way to destroy Russian drones than using scarce air-to-air missiles, Ukraine’s Defense Ministry reported on October 23.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukrainian pilots are already using the ammunition during interception missions against both jet-powered and propeller-driven Russian strike UAVs.
The cannon option is particularly valuable against drones because it allows F-16s to engage relatively inexpensive targets without expending guided air-to-air missiles that can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars or more and are needed for higher-priority threats.
The F-16’s primary gun is the M61A1 Vulcan, a six-barrel 20mm rotary cannon capable of firing at rates of up to 6,000 rounds per minute.
The weapon uses 20×102mm ammunition, including armor-piercing incendiary and high-explosive rounds. Its effective range against aerial targets is roughly 1,000 to 1,500 meters, requiring pilots to close much nearer to a drone than when engaging it with a missile.
That makes cannon interceptions more demanding, but also far more economical when conditions allow them.
Previously, a Ukrainian Mirage 2000-5F scored a first, shooting down a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile not with an air-to-air missile, but with bursts from its built-in 30mm cannons.

Ukrainian Drones targeted infrastructure facilities across several Russian regions overnight on Oct. 22-23, with fires reported near the Baltimor military airfield in Voronezh.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Fire reported near military airfield in Voronezh
A fire broke out near the Baltimor military airfield in Voronezh following the overnight attack, according to an analysis by the Russian outlet Astra.
An OSINT analyst examined footage provided by eyewitnesses and determined that the fire had occurred in the vicinity of the airfield, with flames and smoke visible.
Voronezh Region Governor Alexander Gusev said dry grass had caught fire due to falling debris.
“Air defense forces on duty detected and destroyed several jet-powered aerial targets in the sky over Voronezh. According to preliminary data, there are no casualties. The fall of debris from the intercepted targets ignited dry grass in the suburbs; the fire has since been extinguished,” he wrote on his Telegram channel.
He added that outbuildings in a garden cooperative (SNT) and several passenger cars sustained damage.
Gusev had earlier warned of a potential missile threat in the region. In the early hours of Oct. 23, he also reported that drone debris had damaged the facade of an apartment building and a passenger car in Voronezh.
US Reportedly Plans to ‘Offer’ Ukraine EU Membership for Dropping NATO Bid
Meanwhile, the Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ reported that, according to preliminary information, the former Voronezh Military Aviation Engineering University and an adjacent military aircraft parking area had been
The university specialized in training military aviation engineers, technicians, and aircraft maintenance specialists. In 2012, it was incorporated into the Zhukovsky and Gagarin Air Force Academy.
“The extent of the damage and potential losses of aviation equipment are currently unknown. We are awaiting confirmation of the results,” the report stated.
According to open-source data, the 47th Guards Bomber Aviation Regiment is stationed at the Baltimor airfield. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine on Feb. 24, 2022, the Russian Aerospace Forces have regularly used the airfield to launch airstrikes against Ukrainian territory.
A fire near the Baltimor airfield was previously reported on Sept. 2. Before that, the airfield had been targeted in an attack on May 27.
Chemical plant in Perm Krai reportedly hit
Monitoring channels reported that the Azot plant in the city of Berezniki, Perm Krai, had been struck. The facility is owned by Uralchem, a company belonging to billionaire Dmitry Mazepin.
Both Astra and Exilenova+ confirmed the reported strike through its own analysis. According to the outlet’s OSINT assessment, smoke was rising from the plant’s premises.
The facility is located nearly 2,000 kilometers (1,243 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
Perm Krai Governor Dmitry Makhonin said on Telegram that air defense forces and mobile fire groups had repelled a drone attack on Friday.
“Twenty drones were shot down in the skies over Perm Krai. Emergency services are working at the sites where the debris fell... An industrial facility sustained minor damage. There are no casualties. Emergency services are on-site,” he wrote.
Makhonin did not identify the industrial facility that had been damaged. He added that the response to the attack had also resulted in minor damage to the windows of two apartments in residential buildings in Berezniki and Solikamsk.
The Azot plant manufactures various chemical products, including nitric acid, ammonium nitrate, and potassium nitrate, which are used, among other things, in the production of gunpowder and explosives.
It is also the only plant in Russia that produces sodium nitrate and crystalline sodium nitrite. Azot was previously targeted in an attack on Sept. 11.
Tax service data center reportedly damaged in Nizhny Novgorod region
In the city of Gorodets in Nizhny Novgorod region, Ukrainian channels and Astra’s OSINT analysis reported damage to a data center belonging to Russia’s Federal Tax Service.
The facility serves as a backup data center for the tax authority and has been operating since 2015. It was officially opened on Dec. 7, 2015, in a ceremony attended by then-Prime Minister Dmitry Medvedev, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov, and Mikhail Mishustin, who headed the Federal Tax Service at the time and is now Russia’s prime minister.
United Russia, the country’s ruling party, said at the time that the Gorodets facility was part of a three-center system designated as Data Center No. 1. The system also includes the Federal Data Center in Dubna, Moscow region, and Data Center No. 2 in the settlement of Yerzovka in the Volgograd region.
The facilities were designed to back one another up in the event of a failure, helping ensure the “continuity of service provision.”
“Data Center No. 2 provides partial replication of the most critical services in the event of an emergency,” United Russia added.
The centers can store not only tax information but also data from the Unified State Register of Legal Entities (EGRUL), population records – including civil registry (ZAGS) data – cadastral records, and other information.
Municipal authorities in Gorodets and the surrounding district introduced several restrictions following the attack, according to the news outlet NN.ru.
Schools and colleges switched to remote learning, public events were canceled, and traffic across the dam of the Gorky Reservoir was suspended.
Regional Governor Gleb Nikitin acknowledged damage following a drone attack, including damage to “one piece of infrastructure.” He also said three people had been injured “as a result of falling debris.”
Following the reported attack on the Gorodets data center, Mikhail Klimarev, executive director of the Internet Protection Society, suggested on the radio station Echo of Moscow that the consequences could “collapse the entire tax system” and create serious problems for many Russians, who might have to prove their ownership of apartments and land plots.
Russia reports 443 drones downed
On the morning of Oct. 23, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported that air defenses had shot down 443 drones over the country. Nizhny Novgorod region and Perm Krai were among the regions listed as having been targeted.
The Ukrainian side has not yet commented on any involvement in the reported attacks.

Russia raises inflation forecast for 2026
The Central Bank of Russia has kept its interest rate at 14% and increased its inflation forecast for 2026 to 7.1-7.6%.
Source: press release from the Bank of Russia
Details: As of 19 October, annual inflation in Russia stood at 6.8%, meaning it is expected to rise by the end of the year.
The press release notes that the acceleration in inflation is primarily driven by motor fuel prices.
Overall, in the third quarter of 2026, current seasonally adjusted price growth averaged 8.0% in annualised terms, up from 4.8% in the second quarter of 2026.
The corresponding core inflation indicator rose to 6.2%, up from 4.5% in the second quarter.
Russia expects the inflation rate to stand at 4% in 2027.
Background: In July, the Central Bank of Russia's inflation forecast for 2026 was raised from 4.5-5.5% to 6.0-7.0%. The Russians also revised their GDP growth forecast for 2026 from 0.5-1.5% to 0-1%.

He added that preparing a development project of this scale would take at least three to five years.
According to the company's CEO, the existing Skonto Stadium will remain available for football for the next five years.
Vähi said he had informed key officials involved in the development of Latvia's new national stadium about this commitment, including the president of the Latvian Football Federation (LFF), the chair of Riga City Council's Urban Development Committee and the city's chief architect.
"I am confident that these five years will give them sufficient time to find a solution for developing the new national stadium," Vähi said.
Skonto Stadium is currently owned by SIA Adventika Group.
As previously reported by LETA, the Latvian Football Federation signed a letter of intent with Adventika Group in early 2026 concerning the acquisition of Skonto Stadium for the national football stadium project.
The proposal involved reconstructing the existing stadium while making use of its current infrastructure.
The national stadium project was intended to be developed in cooperation with the Latvian government, Riga City Council and international football organisations, including the Union of European Football Associations (UEFA) and the International Federation of Association Football (FIFA).
