US-Iran war, then and now: How the landscape has changed since February
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:43:53 UTC
20:43:53 KST

US-Iran war, then and now: How the landscape has changed since February
The positions of Washington and Tehran have changed dramatically since US-Israeli strikes began the war, analysts say.
Iran says seven oil tankers have caught fire or sustained damage in and around the Strait of Hormuz as its Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) warns that renewed US attacks could trigger a wider response and the world braces for the possibility of renewed hostilities.
Although analysts consider a US attack before the November 3 midterm elections unlikely, sabre-rattling on both sides has raised fears that escalating rhetoric could give way to renewed attacks with control of the Strait of Hormuz and Iranian nuclear facilities at the heart of the conflict.
But the critical Gulf waterway, through which one-fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies were shipped before the war, was not even an issue before the United States and Israel first launched strikes on Iran on February 28. Furthermore, talks over Iran’s nuclear programme were under way at the time.
As the US wrestles with depleted defensive weapons stocks and a global energy crisis mounts, how does the land lie now before potential renewed strikes and how does it differ from February before any of this began?
Here is what we know:
How has the geography of the war changed?
Unlike in February before the war began, the US and Iran would be fighting it out on several different fronts if attacks resume.
Iran’s regional allies and Lebanon
While the objective of US-Israeli strikes on Iran was initially to topple its leadership, another aim was to weaken Iran’s regional allies, including Hamas and Hezbollah. Announcing the offensive, Trump pledged to prevent Tehran-backed groups from attacking US forces and destabilising the region.
While the offensive failed to force a change in Iran’s government, Hamas has been severely weakened as Israel continues to attack Gaza – with more than 1,400 Palestinians killed since a US-backed “ceasefire” was announced in October last year.
Hezbollah’s retaliation against targets in northern Israel after the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei in the first US-Israeli air strikes brought Lebanon into the war in early March.
Israel launched a bombing campaign against sites in southern Lebanon and the suburbs of Beirut it considers Hezbollah strongholds and, at one point, occupied about one-fifth of the country, displacing more than one million people. It still occupies significant land on Lebanon’s southern border.
Waterways, energy facilities now battlegrounds
The biggest geographical change, however, has been the emergence of the Gulf’s waterways and energy infrastructure as key targets. Iranian attacks on US military assets and civilian infrastructure have exposed Gulf countries to the consequences of a war they had hoped to avoid.
Urban Coningham, a research fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, told Al Jazeera: “US-Iran negotiations had previously centred on Iran’s regional allies and nuclear programme. The Strait of Hormuz and attacks on the Gulf have now become central points of contention.”
While the Gulf has experienced attacks before, Coningham said the scale and “velocity” of recent Iranian strikes, including on oil and gas infrastructure, have marked a significant shift.
The Strait of Hormuz between Iran and Oman, which had been freely open to international shipping before the war, now gives Tehran a means of imposing costs far beyond its borders. Iran continues to threaten and attack shipping there while the US maintains its own blockade of Iranian ports. Traffic has been severely disrupted and supplies of oil and gas have been sharply reduced.
In March, CNN reported that the Pentagon and US National Security Council had significantly underestimated Iran’s willingness to restrict passage through the strait and the consequences of that. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth rejected the reporting, insisting the military had planned for that possibility.
Renewed fighting in Yemen
Renewed fighting between the forces of the Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government of Yemen and the Iran-backed Houthis has added another front to the regional crisis. Yemen’s war has expanded to Saudi Arabia as Houthi missile and drone attacks target Saudi airports and oil infrastructure.
This front has brought another trade chokepoint into sharper focus – Bab al-Mandeb, the strait that links the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden. Houthi threats against Saudi-linked shipping there could compound transportation disruptions in Hormuz, undermine efforts to move Gulf exports through alternative routes and place additional pressure on the US.
How have the political stakes changed?
The two countries’ leaders face different constraints. Iran’s rulers remain concerned about unrest and their own survival but do not face the same electoral reckoning as Trump’s Republican Party, which faces midterm elections in less than two weeks.
In Iran
Before the February strikes, Iran’s government faced deep public anger after its deadly crackdown in January on nationwide protests against high inflation and the plummeting value of Iran’s currency. US-Israeli attacks subsequently killed Khamenei, who had ruled since 1989, and security chief Ali Larijani. But they did not topple the Islamic Republic.
Khamenei’s son Mojtaba succeeded him. His elevation and the influence of the IRGC has reinforced the position of hardliners within the government.
Coningham cautioned that the absence of demonstrations during a war should not be interpreted as support for the government.
“While the conflict had produced a rallying effect around resistance to foreign attacks, that did not mean Iran had emerged stronger,” he said.
In the US
Meanwhile, Trump faces much tougher political pressure before any renewed strikes. His approval rating has fallen from 40 percent in a Reuters/Ipsos poll reported days before the war began to just 31 percent in a survey released on Monday – the lowest recorded by the pollster across either of Trump’s presidential terms – amid frustration over high petrol prices and the deep unpopularity of the war on Iran among Americans.
How has the economic balance changed?
In Iran
Iran’s economy was already struggling before the war, weighed down by sanctions and assets frozen abroad. The conflict has deepened those pressures as the US combines military force, more sanctions and a naval blockade to squeeze the country further.
In April, Iran’s government estimated the direct and indirect damage from US-Israeli attacks at $270bn. The pressure intensified in late August when Washington launched Operation Economic Outcast, seeking to isolate Iran from international trade by imposing penalties on those doing business with it.
Official figures showed Iran’s gross domestic product contracted by 10.1 percent year-on-year from March 21 to June 20. Energy exports have been severely curtailed by the US blockade while the rial has plunged in value.
In the US
The US has also incurred substantial costs. In September, the Congressional Budget Office estimated that the conflict had cost the Department of Defense $38bn as of August 1. It said continued operations were expected to cost about $2bn to $3bn a month, depending on the intensity of fighting.
As a result of the additional costs of the war, US government debt surpassed a record $40 trillion in August – two years before it had been expected to reach that level.
How has the military balance changed?
For the US
While the US has demonstrated its ability to strike deep inside Iran, that destructive capacity has not brought down Iran’s political system nor has it finished off Tehran’s ability to retaliate with strikes on US assets and energy infrastructure in neighbouring countries.
Coningham said the difficulty for Washington is “translating military superiority into strategic results”. He also described recent troop redeployments as possible military posturing, but he added that the deployments do represent a shift from earlier efforts to reduce the US military footprint in parts of the region.
US media reports suggested there is now a severe shortage of weapons in the US arsenal in the Middle East as expensive defensive missiles have been depleted against a bombardment of cheap Iranian drones.
Fox News reported that the USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit were expected to reach the Middle East by the end of November, bringing about 10,000 military personnel. The deployment would expand Trump’s military options as he weighs further action.
For Iran
Coningham said, for Iran, the conflict fits a longstanding narrative of resistance against what its leadership portrayed as US and Israeli colonialism and imperialism.
Since February 28, the IRGC has demonstrated its skill at “asymmetric warfare” as it has held off expensive US military might with cheap, mass-produced drones.
Furthermore, its use of “decentralised structures” has allowed it to continue operating despite disrupted communications and the loss of senior decision-makers, Coningham said.
US strikes have severely damaged Iran’s navy and increased its reliance on smaller vessels, including speedboats used in recent attacks in the Strait of Hormuz. On that front, geography is on Iran’s side as it can fire at ships in the Strait of Hormuz from ground positions along its coast. It can also place sea mines in the strait using rockets to drop them.
These are tactics the US had not necessarily expected to contend with when it initiated the strikes on Iran but will certainly face now.
How has global trade changed?
A mounting global energy crisis was not on the cards in February, but it is certainly looming now.
Disruptions to Gulf energy supplies caused by the war and fears of further escalation have pushed oil prices sharply higher. Brent crude, the global benchmark for oil prices, settled at $72.48 a barrel on February 27, the day before the war began.
It hit $126.41 on April 30, its highest level in four years. By early trading on Friday, it stood at $114.47.
But the crisis extends beyond crude oil. Damage and disruptions to fuel production in the Middle East alongside sanctions on Russian supplies have tightened diesel markets while the global supply of liquefied natural gas has also been heavily affected. The International Energy Agency warned in October that supply constraints could persist well into 2027.
Diesel, which has doubled in price in the US, is a big problem for Trump because farmers and businesses in the US, key voting blocs for him, rely on it for production and transport.
Alternative ports, pipelines and ship-to-ship transfers have helped Gulf producers restore exports but at higher logistical costs and with continuing exposure to attacks.
Re-establishing shipping through vital waterways in the Middle East, therefore, has now become a primary objective in the war.

Russia and Ukraine hold latest POW swap
Russia and Ukraine have exchanged 270 prisoners of war each, the Defense Ministry in Moscow announced on Friday. The returning Russian servicemen are currently in Belarus, where they are receiving assistance before being transported home for treatment and rehabilitation.
Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova is working with the freed servicemen in the neighboring country, according to the ministry. The troops will receive medical and psychological assistance before being transferred to Russian Defense Ministry facilities for further treatment and rehabilitation.
Prisoner exchanges between Moscow and Kiev are generally conducted on an equal basis, unlike the repatriation of fallen soldiers, which has frequently involved Russia handing over significantly more bodies than it receives.
The latest exchange follows previous humanitarian arrangements between the two sides despite the continuing hostilities. On Thursday, Russia handed over the remains of 252 Ukrainian soldiers killed in the conflict and received the bodies of 25 Russian troops in return.
Such disparities are typical of repatriations, unlike prisoner-of-war swaps, which are generally conducted on an equal basis. Pro-Kiev commentators have long argued that the imbalance does not reflect the actual ratio of battlefield casualties, as advancing Russian forces are better positioned to recover the bodies of fallen Ukrainian soldiers. However, Thursday’s exchange, which followed Kiev’s claims of a major offensive near the city of Liman, showed no significant change in the proportion.

Serbia: Hope, tension and apprehension as voters prepare to elect new parliament
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:43:00 UTC
20:43:00 KST

Hope, tension and apprehension as Serbia approaches crucial election
October 23, 2026
A sense of hope swept through Belgrade on Thursday evening as thousands gathered for the final rally of the Student List, the group of candidates put forward by the student movement that has been protesting against the government for almost exactly two years.
The Student List is calling for an end to the current regime in Serbia via the ballot box in Sunday's parliamentary election.
Many of those who attended the rally had spent days walking to the Serbian capital from all four corners of the country, turning the campaign finale into a display of solidarity and peaceful determination.
"We have walked across Serbia from one end to the other, visited villages and neighborhoods, looked you in the eye and realized that we can count on you," biology student Arsa Stojanovic told the crowd.
"People, it smells like freedom," added Aleksandar Cupic, professor of transport and traffic engineering, and a candidate on the Student List.
Students emerge as agents of change
After 24 months of protests sparked by the collapse of a concrete canopy at Novi Sad railway station, which killed 16 people in November 2024, Serbia is heading into an election unlike any other in the 14 years since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) first came to power.
For the first time in years, the ruling party faces a serious political challenge, which this time comes from a student movement that has channeled widespread public discontent into an electoral campaign.
"These are the first elections since [Aleksandar] Vucic came to power in 2012 that are competitive and whose outcome is uncertain," political scientist Dusan Spasojevic told DW. "The student movement has generated hope among citizens and substantial support. Polls suggest that they could even win more than 40% of the vote."
The Student List has framed the election as a chance to confront corruption and demand accountability for a disaster that became a symbol of institutional failure.
In doing so, the students have sought to put aside the ideological, social and foreign-policy divisions that have long shaped Serbian politics.
SNS presents itself as a guarantor of continuity
Just a few kilometers away, also in Belgrade, the ruling SNS held its own final rally.
The message here was familiar: A vote for the SNS means stability, continuity and further prosperity, while a change of government would risk plunging the country into chaos.
The party framed the election as a battle for Serbia's future and sovereignty, accusing its opponents of serving foreign interests.
"They tried to destroy our country on foreign orders, and that is why this is the hardest battle," former President Aleksandar Vucic told his supporters. "They attacked us with billions of euros, and we defended ourselves with integrity, our program, love for our homeland and Serbia's achievements."
Rising tension
The campaign has increasingly been overshadowed by violence, reflecting a society in which political opponents are often portrayed not simply as rivals, but as enemies.
By the final week of the campaign, CRTA, an independent election-monitoring organization, had recorded 116 incidents involving physical violence or verbal threats. The incidents included physical confrontations, attacks on campaigners and attempts to seize campaign banners.
CRTA also reported that opposition activists, particularly those linked to the Student List, were also subjected to surveillance and police questioning. In some cases, the organization said, police were slow to protect opposition candidates and supporters.
Allegations of links to criminal networks
In the final runup to the election, there have also been a series of investigative reports examining alleged links between people connected to the ruling SNS and criminal networks.
Published by independent media in the days before the election, the reports have brought renewed attention to questions of corruption, political influence and accountability — issues at the heart of the student movement's challenge to the government.
But Spasojevic is skeptical that the revelations will make a significant difference to the election outcome.
He argues that those who trust investigative media are likely to have already made up their minds, while voters who rely on pro-government outlets may never even see these reports.
Concerns about irregularities
There are also serious concerns about the fairness of the election process.
CRTA told DW that the election campaign has not been either free or fair from day one, citing "a narrowing of freedoms and deepening inequality" among candidates and voters.
Its report found a pronounced imbalance in media coverage: Almost three-quarters of airtime devoted to political players on national television has featured government representatives, while more than 80% of coverage on the Student List has been negative.
Ahead of the vote, the Balkan Investigative Reporting Network (BIRN) published the testimony of a former member of the SNS, who described how public-sector employees were pressured to deliver votes for the party.
DW has also learned from sources who want to remain anonymous that voters have been offered between €30 and €150 to vote for the SNS, with holiday packages reportedly offered to entire families if they pledge all their votes to the ruling party.
What could come after the election?
Many fear a period of turbulence, uncertainty and political crisis after the vote, with election night itself a particular source of anxiety.
For weeks, the authorities have warned that students, allegedly with the help of foreign intelligence services, are preparing violence in the streets. In the final days of the campaign, several people were arrested on what the prosecution has said was the suspicion of plotting disturbances on election night.
The best-case scenario, says Dusan Spasojevic, would be a decisive victory for one of the two opposing camps, leaving little room for the other to challenge the result.
"But polls suggest that the margin will be narrow, and we will probably enter some kind of post-election crisis," he said, adding that a narrow victory for the ruling party would almost certainly be contested, given longstanding concerns about the fairness of the electoral process and allegations that some votes may have been obtained illegally.
The EU's reaction could be crucial
Whatever happens, the European Union's response could be crucial.
"I think the international response will be crucial in preventing major incidents and a further escalation of the crisis. It is the only thing that can persuade the authorities to accept defeat and refrain from an overly heavy-handed response to any protests or incidents," he told DW.
An EU Commission spokesperson acknowledged to DW that key recommendations on improving Serbia's electoral framework remain unimplemented and also stressed that democracy and the rule of law are key to the accession process. Serbia has been an EU candidate country since 2012.
Back in Belgrade, the students ended their rally with a kolo, a traditional Serbian circle dance, projecting confidence in their chances at the ballot box.
But the path to victory could prove difficult. The movement has vowed to defend every vote — setting the stage for a potentially tense election night if the results are disputed.

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Britain is the leader of the Western world in prolonging the Ukrainian conflict; London is not interested in normalizing relations with Russia, the director of the North Atlantic Department of the Russian Foreign Ministry, Alexander Gusarov, said in an interview with the International Affairs Journal.
"The facts are stubborn, and they speak directly to the opposite, that it is London today that is one of the leaders of the Western collective advocating the escalation and prolongation of the Ukrainian conflict," Gusarov said. "All this convinces us that London at this stage is not interested in normalizing relations. This does not mean that we are forgetting important memorable pages of our history, including the history of the military alliance of our countries in countering fascism and Nazism. We remember the Arctic convoys, but for us the national security of our country is absolutely imperative, and we will never allow any threats to come from Britain or any other country."
Gusarov sees no reason to believe that with the formation of a new government in London there will be at least some progress for the better in bilateral relations.
"This would require London’s decisive break with the foreign policy guidelines that they, London, have been nurturing over the past years," he noted. "In the meantime, there is only one goal, this is inflicting a strategic defeat on Russia, and by someone else, in this case, by Ukrainian hands. London has been working towards this goal for a long time, generating anti-Russian provocations, replicating anti-Russian sanctions, expelling our diplomats, encouraging this, the implementation of the same similar goals of their European allies. At the same time, as we see, the degradation of the socio-economic situation in Britain itself, as well as the consequences of this disastrous line for the level of tension throughout Europe, is not taken into account."
"In this regard, we are forced to be extremely skeptical about the narratives that are periodically voiced by representatives of the British establishment, and, in particular, the Foreign Office, regarding the alleged absence of hostile plans towards Russia," Gusarov said.

The investigation centers on more than half a million euros awarded to two consultants ahead of the 2024 European election.
The European Parliament, which finances European political parties, refused to reimburse the contracts in full after deeming the costs excessive.
Advertisement
It covered only the initial €110,000 payments, leaving the EPP to pay roughly €350,000 itself, according to Germany’s Süddeutsche Zeitung, Dutch investigative outlet Follow the Money and Greece’s Inside Story.
The consultants were hired to work on the party’s communications ahead of the election campaign. However, former EPP employees told reporters at the outlets that their fees were disproportionate to the work they delivered. The consultants disputed that assessment and said they had subsequently reimbursed part of the money.
The EPPO neither confirmed nor denied the investigation, saying it could not comment in case it jeopardized any ongoing proceedings or their outcome.
A spokesperson for the EPP said: “We have not been formally notified regarding this matter. The EPP fully respects the independence and mandate of the relevant authorities and remains committed to providing them complete transparency and full cooperation, should it be requested.”

Oil has hit its highest level in more than five months as fears of fresh escalation in the Middle East conflict grip the energy markets.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil, rose by 1% on Friday morning to above $115 a barrel – its highest level since May.
The increase came after Tehran said it would attack oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities in the Gulf region if a new US-Israeli offensive was launched against Iran.
Richard Hunter, of the broker Interactive Investor, said: “Widespread reports that the US is considering renewed military strikes on Iran after the midterm elections rather than pursuing a diplomatic route was enough for the price to pop, after what many had considered would be a brief conflict is now in its eighth month.”
Oil had traded at about $72 a barrel back in February, before the Iran war began, but soared to $126 a barrel by the end of April.
Tensions in the region have been rising this week and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps claimed to have struck four commercial ships in the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday. The US state department ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia, which has faced continued attacks from Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Susannah Streeter, the chief investment strategist at the broker Wealth Club, said fears were rising that American and Israeli forces would be ordered to launch strikes on Iran’s energy infrastructure after the US elections on 3 November.
She added: “At the same time, the attacks on Saudi Arabia’s facilities by Houthi rebels have intensified this week, and for ships attempting to cross the strait of Hormuz, it’s still a dangerous journey, with projectiles still being fired.”
Streeter said Ukraine’s bombardment of Russian diesel refineries was also adding to supply concerns.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Hualien District Court on Thursday ordered seven suspects in a bribery investigation involving solar farm projects in Hualien County’s Fenglin to be held incommunicado for two months to prevent collusion with other suspects or witnesses.
The court said Friday that evidence presented by prosecutors indicated the seven suspects may have been involved in breach of trust, bribery, money laundering, and other offenses, per UDN. It cited concerns that some suspects had not responded to prosecutors' summonses and that the statements given by the seven detained suspects differed from prosecution evidence and from each other's accounts.
Those detained include former Fenglin Township Mayor Hsiao Wen-lung (蕭文龍), former Hualien County Farmers' Association General Manager Kuan Chun-yen (官俊彥), HD Renewable Energy Group Chair Edward Hsieh (謝源一), General Manager Jason Chou (周仕昌), Deputy Manager Li Yung-ching (李永清), Senior Assistant Manager Hsieh Tzu-yen (謝紫燕), and former Feng Kuang Chu Neng Inc. General Manager Lin Chun-cheng (林俊呈), per Mirror Daily.
HD Renewable Energy reportedly began targeting Fenglin Township for solar farm development in 2019 because of its relatively flat terrain and sunny weather, per Liberty Times. After the Ministry of Economic Affairs authorized township offices to review small-scale solar farm projects, higher electricity purchase prices in eastern Taiwan attracted investors to the area.
However, HD Renewable Energy's proposed solar farm projects, covering more than 1,000 hectares, faced strong local opposition. Projects near Indigenous lands on occasion required the company to obtain consent from local tribes in addition to addressing broader community resistance, per Tai Sounds.
To overcome these obstacles, HD Renewable Energy allegedly paid kickbacks of approximately NT$30 million (US$920,000) to Hsiao and NT$10 million to Kuan. Opposition nevertheless persisted, and the company eventually decided to withdraw from the projects.
The Investigation Bureau deployed 11 units across Taiwan on Wednesday to conduct simultaneous searches at 55 locations. HD Renewable Energy executives were allegedly attempting to flee, while investigators seized the suspects and the company's financial records.
Hualien County Government commented on the case Thursday, saying that, apart from a solar farm project approved under acting county magistrate Tsai Pi-chung (蔡碧仲) in 2018, it had not approved any new projects since then, per CNews.
HD Renewable Energy was previously implicated in a scandal involving a feeder-line application and former Green Energy Industry Promotion Center Deputy CEO Luke Cheng (鄭亦麟), per Storm Media. Hsiao is running for Fenglin Township mayor as a KMT candidate in the November election, per PTS.

Ukrainian Drone Attack Hits Perm Region Chemical Plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:34:50 UTC
20:34:50 KST

A Ukrainian drone strike damaged an industrial plant in the Ural Mountains region of Perm, Governor Dmitry Makhonin said Friday.
Makhonin said air defense systems intercepted 20 drones over the Perm region overnight, with falling debris shattering windows in residential buildings in the city of Berezniki and the nearby town of Solikamsk.
“An industrial facility also sustained minor damage,” he wrote on Telegram without identifying the site.
The exiled news outlet Astra used eyewitness footage of rising smoke from the purported area of the attack to identify the targeted facility as the Azot chemical plant in Berezniki. Azot is part of Uralchem, a corporation controlled by billionaire Dmitry Mazepin.
The facility is Russia’s sole producer of higher aliphatic amines, sodium nitrate and crystalline sodium nitrite, and manufactures ammonium nitrate, liquid ammonia, urea, nitric acid and nitrite-nitrate salts.
Ammonium nitrate is widely used as fertilizer and is also a component in explosives.
The Azot plant, which employs around 2,500 people and is located more than 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from the border with Ukraine, was previously targeted in Ukrainian drone attacks in September 2026 and October 2025.
Russian civil aviation authorities issued airspace restrictions during the air raid alert in the Perm region on Friday.
The Defense Ministry said it intercepted 443 Ukrainian drones across Russia and annexed Crimea between Thursday night and Friday morning.

Kyrgyzstan to reduce energy deficiency through new hydropower and thermal power projects
Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov outlined measures to address the country’s energy deficit during a national meeting on strategic socio-economic development, a Qazinform News Agency correspondent in Bishkek reports.
Efforts will focus on two main areas. The first includes modernizing power grids and energy infrastructure, expanding generating capacity, and developing renewable energy sources. Thousands of homes without power as Storm Austen hits south-west England
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:32:25 UTC
20:32:25 KST

Thousands of homes are without power and schools have been closed as the first named storm of the year hit UK shores.
Storm Austen brought severe conditions to parts of the south-west, with a gust of 76mph recorded at St Mary’s airport on the Isles of Scilly on Friday morning. Just before 11am, more than 16,000 homes in the south-west were without power, according to National Grid.
Dozens of schools across Cornwall were forced to open late, while others did not open at all.
Images showed part of Brighton’s West Pier falling into the sea after it was battered by wind and waves. The pier, first opened in 1866, has grown increasingly derelict since it closed to the public in 1975, with storms and fires destroying much of what remained. English Heritage has previously declared the structure beyond repair.
National Rail reported severe disruption across the rail network with cancellations across England, Wales and Scotland.
Forecasters have put an additional amber weather warning for wind in place from Saturday into Sunday as the second named storm of the year, Boelo, heads in.
Speaking to reporters on Friday, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, said: “We potentially are facing a winter of greater flooding, so it’s about recognising all of those risks and taking action.”
A government campaign aimed at urging people to stock supplies of food and essentials in case of multi-day emergencies made headlines overnight. Burnham was asked if the government was playing catchup with civil preparedness as he attended a summit organised to learn from the summer’s record wildfires.
He answered: “No. We are having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we’re living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.
“We’re in a situation today where the UK is facing storms, and obviously we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now. It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments [and] we are having that conversation about resilience. That’s why we’re holding this summit today, it’s why we’re putting the guidance out to the public.”
National Grid said engineers had restored power to more than 12,000 properties affected by Storm Austen by 8am on Friday.
A Met Office amber warning for wind covering Cornwall, Devon and the Isles of Scilly was issued on Wednesday, taking effect on Friday from 1am until 10am.
The Met Office has now issued a 24-hour amber warning for wind from Storm Boelo from 9pm on Saturday, covering Scotland, the north coast of Northern Ireland, and Cumbria and Northumberland in the north of England.
The forecaster said gusts of up to 80mph could hit exposed coastal areas, with winds of 60-70mph widespread elsewhere, and it warned of danger to life from flying debris.
It said there was also a “good chance” of power cuts, damage to buildings, trees being uprooted and rail and flight cancellations.
The Republic of Ireland’s weather agency, Met Éireann, issued six warnings of varying severity for Saturday, mostly affecting counties along the west coast.

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China on Friday called on the United States to immediately stop its erroneous practice of taking discriminatory and restrictive measures against Chinese research institutions, saying that China would take necessary steps to safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of Chinese research institutions, according to the Ministry of Commerce.
The remarks came in response to a media query about research security mitigation results announced by the U.S. Department of Defense on Oct. 19 (U.S. Eastern Time). The announcement said the universities concerned had fully mitigated identified relationships with foreign entities of concern on the 1286 list, which includes many Chinese research institutions.
China has consistently opposed the U.S. practice of overstretching the concept of national security, politicizing, weaponizing and instrumentalizing scientific exchanges and cooperation, and making groundless accusations that stigmatize Chinese research institutions, a ministry spokesperson said.
Such actions essentially coerce U.S. research institutions into "taking sides" and deliberately undermine normal scientific cooperation between China and the United States, the spokesperson noted, adding that such actions would only backfire on the United States itself, undermining its own scientific and technological progress and innovation.
Strengthening scientific research cooperation between China and the United States serves the common interests of both sides, while imposing restrictions and pursuing "decoupling" would only harm both sides, the spokesperson said.
China urged the United States to respect facts and act in line with the general principles and prevailing trend of global scientific and technological exchanges and cooperation, said the spokesperson. ■

====================================================================================================

Interview: Unlocking opportunities through Australia-China economic, trade ties: peak Aussie industry body chief
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:31:34 CST
20:31:34 KST

by Qi Zijian, Zhang Shuhui, Liu Xiaoyu
SYDNEY, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Australia and China can unlock new opportunities by combining their expertise, technology and investment to develop better products, cultivate new skills and build stronger businesses, said the chair of a peak Australian industry body.
Vaughn Barber, chair of the China-Australia Chamber of Commerce (AustCham China), told Xinhua in a recent interview that the two sides can achieve more by working together, describing this approach as "joint capability."
AustCham China, established in 1994, is the peak industry body representing Australian businesses in China to advance the Australia-China commercial relationship.
EXPLORING NEW OPPORTUNITIES
"China's significance now includes its ability to turn technology into products, manufacture competitively and deploy at scale, as we see in batteries, electric vehicles and clean-energy equipment," said Barber.
Business exchanges have highlighted the scope for closer cooperation between Chinese and Australian companies.
Barber recently led an Australian business delegation to a meeting in Shenzhen, south China, where participating companies discussed electricity, chips, data centers and commercial AI applications.
"What struck me was how the technology, infrastructure and commercial applications were being developed together," he said.
As Australia is trying to lift productivity and make the energy transition affordable, the country should enhance its understanding of China's relevant capabilities, he said.
"So we can assess where it could help solve those problems," added Barber.
Barber cited Australia's Woodside Energy's Scarborough floating production unit (FPU) as "a concrete example." Its hull and topsides were built in China for an Australian energy project.
"It shows how Australian resource development can draw on Chinese industrial capability," he said.
After a 4,000-plus nautical mile journey from China, the Scarborough Energy Project's FPU, involving four shipyards in China, arrived in Australia in January 2026.
The project will bring thousands of job opportunities and significant economic benefits for Western Australia.
CLOSER COOPERATION
"Australia and China are often described as complementary economies," Barber said. "Each has strengths that meet the other's needs."
"We can build on that by combining our expertise, technology and investment to develop better products, new skills and stronger businesses," he said.
Housing is an area where the two countries can translate their complementary strengths into practical cooperation.
In this area, Chinese manufacturing can be combined with Australian design, construction expertise and standards to improve the delivery of housing projects.
CHINESE INVESTMENT IN AUSTRALIA
Barber stressed Chinese investment can help Australia improve productivity, add value to its resources and build industrial capability.
Barber noted that these objectives align with the Australian government's broader manufacturing and economic agenda, describing it as a commercially viable partnership that helps the investor grow while building Australian capability.
Looking ahead, Barber expected the two countries to build on the foundation, broaden the opportunity and build capability together.
"Success means more competitive businesses, quality jobs and lasting benefits for communities in both countries," he said. ■

China issues guidelines to promote employment amid AI advances
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:31:33 CST
20:31:33 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China has rolled out guidelines on adapting to advances in artificial intelligence (AI) to promote employment-friendly development, aiming to harness the technology to create jobs, improve employment quality and stimulate entrepreneurship while mitigating job displacement caused by AI applications.
The guidelines, issued by the General Office of the State Council, set out 18 tasks in six areas, including boosting AI's job-creation potential, making AI adoption more employment-friendly, improving workers' digital skills, enhancing employment services, strengthening labor and social security protections, and monitoring and addressing employment risks.
The guidelines call for expanding employment opportunities in emerging fields, helping micro, small and medium-sized enterprises stabilize and expand employment, fostering new forms of employment and entrepreneurship in the AI sector, and developing new AI-related occupations.
The guidelines urge efforts to tap AI's job-creation potential in traditional sectors, mitigate job displacement caused by AI applications, and establish a mechanism to assess employment risks associated with AI adoption.
The guidelines emphasize improving the framework for protecting workers' rights in human-machine collaboration, strengthening social security for people in flexible employment and those in new forms of employment, and refining income distribution mechanisms to adapt to advances in AI. ■

====================================================================================================

Economic Watch: China's green finance helps drive global low-carbon transition
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:31:25 CST
20:31:25 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's integration of digital technologies with green finance is opening up new opportunities for global cooperation on the low-carbon transition, participants said at the Annual Conference of Financial Street Forum 2026 in Beijing.
Under the theme "Building an Open, Collaborative and Inclusive Ecosystem for Global Financial Development," the four-day event concluded on Thursday. It brought together participants from both home and abroad, online and offline, to discuss financial development and cooperation in the face of global economic challenges.
"Over the past few years, we've seen China's green finance market grow several-fold," said Ma Jun, president of the Institute of Finance and Sustainability in Beijing. "The integration of digital and green finance has created many growth opportunities and helped boost cross-border investment."
The growth has won international recognition. "China has improved air quality by developing a circular economy and building an environmentally friendly society," said Yaseen Anwar, former governor of the State Bank of Pakistan, at a parallel forum.
He added that the country's installed wind and solar power capacity continues to grow, while green products such as new energy vehicles (NEVs) are leading globally.
Data released by the Ministry of Ecology and Environment shows that the country's installed capacity of renewable energy power generation reached 2.455 billion kilowatts in the first half of this year, accounting for 60.7 percent of its total installed power generation capacity. China has ranked first worldwide in both the production and sales of NEVs for 11 consecutive years.
In recent years, China has offered broad opportunities for global green investment and low-carbon transition by applying technologies such as big data, blockchain and AI to improve green finance governance, upgrade industrial structures and enhance the ecological environment.
The Bank of China has issued green bonds under the Belt and Road Initiative to support major green projects such as large-scale photovoltaic power stations in partner countries. These projects are expected to provide local communities with long-term, stable supplies of clean renewable energy.
The carbon market is an important policy tool for addressing climate change through market mechanisms and for accelerating the comprehensive green transformation of economic and social development.
The cumulative trading volume of carbon emission allowances in China's national carbon market has exceeded 1 billion tonnes, according to data from the Ministry of Ecology and Environment. China's experience in developing its carbon market also offers lessons that other countries can learn from.
"China's carbon emission commitments and the development of its carbon market have made a tremendous contribution to global climate action," said Charles Bowman, co-chair of the UK-China Green Finance Taskforce. "Green finance cooperation between China and the United Kingdom has promoted economic transformation, biodiversity conservation and sustainable development in both countries," he added.
Such cooperation is also extending to Belt and Road partners. Many of them are actively implementing green and sustainable policies while mobilizing capital. "China tailored services for different regions, including promoting the application of green finance instruments and market development, conducting in-depth research on green policies, and advancing carbon market mechanisms," said Cheng Lin, head of the Secretariat Beijing Office for the Green Investment Principles for the Belt and Road.
Experts noted at the conference that as digital and intelligent technologies have profoundly reshaped the financial sector in recent years, empowering green finance with such technologies is a key pathway toward global sustainable development.
"Digital and intelligent technologies can provide important support for green finance by overcoming bottlenecks in data collection, analysis, risk monitoring and assessment," said Zhang Bei, deputy head of the research bureau of the People's Bank of China.
As extreme weather events become more frequent, technologies such as geographic information systems, satellite remote sensing and large language models can help assess more accurately how different regions and population groups are coping with climate change, identify priorities for adaptation and guide funding toward areas with the greatest needs, Zhang said.
The expanding role of digital technology in China's green finance is poised to benefit more global partners in their sustainable development efforts.
Mari Elka Pangestu, vice chair of Indonesia's National Economic Council, said China is a leader in clean technologies. She expressed hope for deepening cooperation with Chinese partners beyond capital investment by establishing more joint ventures, increasing local production and enhancing technology transfer.
China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for expanding green financial products and services and encouraging greater investment in green and low-carbon development. ■

====================================================================================================

China's fiscal revenue sees steady growth in Jan.-Sept.
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
19:31:23 CST
20:31:23 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's fiscal revenue grew steadily in the first three quarters of 2026, with general public budget revenue reaching about 17.23 trillion yuan (about 2.56 trillion U.S. dollars) during the period, latest official data showed.
The figure marked a 5.1 percent year-on-year growth, with the growth rate 0.4 percentage points higher than that in the first half of the year, according to data released Friday by the Ministry of Finance.
Tax revenue in the first three quarters totaled about 14.07 trillion yuan, up 6.1 percent year on year, with the growth rate also 0.8 percentage points higher than that in the first half of the year.
Among specific revenue items, value-added tax came in at about 5.54 trillion yuan, up 6 percent year on year, and corporate income tax totaled about 3.48 trillion yuan, up 7.1 percent.
In contrast, deed tax and land appreciation tax posted declines in revenues.
In terms of fiscal expenditure, general public budget spending in the first three quarters amounted to about 21.02 trillion yuan, up 1 percent year on year, the data showed.
During the period, China's healthcare expenditure reached 1.69 trillion yuan, up 7.7 percent year on year, while spending on social security and employment totaled 3.67 trillion yuan, up 5.2 percent. These marked the two largest increases among major expenditure categories, underscoring the country's ongoing policy support for improving people's livelihoods.
Fiscal expenditure on education also rose 1.1 percent to 3.2 trillion yuan.
The generally stable macroeconomic performance secured fiscal revenue and expenditure. In the first three quarters of 2026, China's GDP grew 4.6 percent year on year, highlighting the resilience of the world's second-largest economy.
The Ministry of Finance said in a policy implementation report released earlier this month that it will vigorously and effectively implement a more proactive fiscal policy by accelerating fund disbursement and speeding up government bond issuance, to expand domestic demand and advance technological and industrial innovation. ■

Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 Review: The Littlest Smartphone That Could
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:30:00 UTC
20:30:00 KST

Compact and lightweight. Top-notch performance. Solid main camera. Handy AI features.
TIRED
Price bump over last year. No telephoto camera. Cover screen is more useful but still limited.
If you crave a compact phone that doesn’t feel like a brick in your pocket and slips easily into a small bag, the flip style is for you. Samsung’s eighth-generation clamshell is seriously refined, and as svelte and slick as it comes. It may not offer a tablet-sized screen or the fashionable new passport shape, but it is arguably the most practical type of folding phone.
Like almost every other phone this year, the Z Flip8 offers tiny improvements over its predecessor and costs $100 more. If you’re wondering whether it’s worth updating from last year’s Z Flip7, it’s not. The Flip8 is a teeny bit lighter and slimmer with a newer processor, and that’s about it. But if you’re looking to dip a toe in folding-phone waters or just want something small, the Z Flip8 should be in the conversation.
Slimmer and More Foldable
Photograph: Simon Hill
Everyone is excited about the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8’s sexy new form factor, but Samsung continues to iterate on the flip phone format for folks who prize compact devices. The Z Flip8 shaves off 0.02 inches (0.55 millimeters) and a third of an ounce (8 grams) compared to its predecessor, making it the slimmest and lightest option in this category. The improved hinge makes the crease slightly less noticeable and a little easier to open. I still found it a bit tricky to open one-handed, but you get the knack after a while. The new hinge is also supposed to be more durable.
The Flip8 has an IP48 rating, so you don’t need to worry about dropping it in the bath, but tiny dust and dirt particles (less than 1 millimeter) can still cause damage. It comes in pink, like my review unit, as well as graphite, cream, and mint. It still has a physical SIM slot, and the power button has a fingerprint sensor in it that works pretty well.
The screens are the same as last year's. It has a sharp 4.1-inch AMOLED display on the outside with a 60- or 120-Hz refresh rate. Open it up to reveal the 6.9-inch main display, also AMOLED but with a variable refresh rate (1 to 120 Hz) that’s better for battery life. Both screens are reasonably bright (2,600 nits peak), and I never struggled to read the screen outdoors.
Powerful Performer
Photograph: Simon Hill
Flip phones used to get palmed off with lesser processors, but the Z Flip8 boasts the Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 for Galaxy (the same cutting-edge chip that's in its two bigger siblings). It has 12 GB of RAM and 256 GB of storage. You can jump to 512 GB for an extra $200, but there’s no option to increase the RAM.
I encountered no stutters or lag and found performance to be generally excellent, whether jumping in and out of apps, firing up the camera, or gaming. The Z Flip8 can get warm, and this may throttle the processor somewhat if you’re playing a demanding game for a while (more than an hour). This is mostly down to the compact design.
The stereo speakers are better than I expected. They get quite loud without distortion, and they’ll serve you just fine for watching videos. Call quality is also solid, and slamming it shut to end a call never gets tired. I also like opening it to answer calls, but you must enable this in the Phone app settings under Flip options. Connectivity includes 5G (no mmWave), Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 5.4, but there’s no ultra-wideband (UWB) for more precise positioning. The Fold8 models have Bluetooth 6 and UWB.
While it’s very capable, the Z Flip8 is only average when it comes to battery life, another drawback of its size. Samsung put in a 4,300-mAh silicon-carbon battery that’s good enough for casual use. If you’re on your phone a lot, you’ll want a power bank handy. Charging speeds are disappointing at 25 watts wired and 15 watts wireless, and I’m annoyed by Samsung’s refusal to implement the magnetic feature of Qi2.
Snap Shot
If you’re a keen photographer, you can get many better camera systems in a range of Android phones for the same money or less. That said, the main 50-megapixel shooter is perfectly good in many situations, and most folks will be happy with the photos it captures. Some noise creeps in when it’s dark. The 12-megapixel ultrawide is useful when you want to cram a lot in or take a group selfie, but it’s a definite step down in quality. Sadly, there’s no telephoto lens, but you can emulate 2X zoom without losing detail by cropping, and it offers passable results in good lighting up to 10X.
Photograph: Simon Hill
Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8, main camera.
I don’t see much reason to use the 10-megapixel punch-hole selfie camera outside of video calls, since you can flip it to get a cover-screen preview and use the main camera for selfies (a big benefit of this design). I also love Samsung’s Horizon Lock, which lets you shoot video with a steady horizontal plane no matter how you turn or move the phone.
Another new AI feature from Samsung is My FanCam, which lets you pick a subject to focus on in group videos and reframes them as though your chosen subject is the star. Handy for school plays or soccer games, if you remember to use it. (You can also apply it to old videos.) Speaking of AI, Samsung offers Now Brief to float up calendar events, reminders, and useful info like local weather, and Now Nudge to suggest adding dates to your calendar from messages, sharing locations or photos, and auto-filling forms.
Compact Competition
The cover screen, or FlexWindow, has been a weakness for Samsung’s Flip line, and it’s still limited in the Flip8. On the plus side, you can use more apps with the cover screen, including most of Samsung’s apps (Health, Calendar, Browser), YouTube, Netflix, Google Maps, and Messages. But if you want other third-party apps, you still have to install Good Lock, then the MultiStar plug-in, and select the apps you want to use. It’s stupidly convoluted, and I don’t understand why it isn't preinstalled, especially since Samsung has virtually all its other apps on there, along with a few third-party apps I never asked for (Facebook, Spotify, and Instagram). This is admittedly a bugbear of mine, but it's disgraceful that Samsung is including bloatware on a phone this expensive.
Photograph: Simon Hill
I like that you can have YouTube on the cover screen, as you can prop it up and there’s a little toggle at the bottom to switch between full screen, above the camera lenses, or standard vertical format for scrolling. You’ll mostly use the inner screen, but I have sometimes used the Flip8 this way to prop up a video I’m half-watching on my desk, and it’s a nice option to have.
There’s only really one competitor for Samsung if you’re set on a flip phone, and that’s Motorola's Razr line. You can step down to a less powerful but much cheaper Razr at $800, or spend a little more to snag the superior Razr Ultra. The latter has a better camera, more RAM and storage, and charges much faster, but it costs $1,500. The awkward middle child, the Razr+ at $1,100, is a tougher sell (it has an older processor and shorter software support). You might consider last year’s Z Flip7 if you can find it discounted.
Sadly, this might be your last chance to get a Samsung flip phone. Persistent rumors suggest Samsung will sunset this form factor as the Fold8 takes off and goes head-to-head with the iPhone Duo, though Samsung hasn't officially confirmed it. If you do pull the trigger on the Flip8, you get an excellent seven years of platform and security software updates, potentially taking you all the way to 2033. Who knows, maybe small phones will be back in fashion by then.
Simon Hill is a senior writer for WIRED and has been testing and writing about technology for around 20 years. You can find his previous work at Business Insider, Reviewed, TechRadar, Android Authority, USA Today, Digital Trends, and many other places. "We received a report of a shooting attack targeting a military force on Route 35, with casualties. Security forces from the area rushed to the scene, including me," he told ynet. Watch footage from his helmet camera:
"In the morning, residents are traveling along the road, including buses taking students to schools in Kiryat Arba. I arrived at the scene about 15 minutes after the incident began. When I got there, I joined the fighting. Two terrorists were firing from higher ground, and we exchanged fire for about 20 minutes until a force commanded by the deputy battalion commander responsible for the area killed the terrorists.
Describing the scene, Botavia said, "The terrorists arrived in a 'mashtuba' (an illegally operated, deregistered) vehicle with a yellow Israeli license plate. The soldiers at the scene prevented the attack from spreading to the main road and endangering passersby. That prevented a much greater disaster."
He praised the security forces, saying, "The army works hard every night, carrying out numerous operations to maintain residents' security and protect roads and communities. We must remain vigilant."
Since Friday morning, troops from the IDF's Duvdevan undercover unit, Paratroopers Brigade and Search and Rescue Brigade, along with Border Police forces in the West Bank, have been conducting offensive counterterrorism operations in Hebron and surrounding villages. The forces are also preparing to expand their operations.
So far, a full lockdown has been imposed on the cities of Hebron and Halhul, dozens of roadblocks have been set up across the area and the IDF's elite Maglan unit has been deployed to the Judea Regional Brigade to reinforce counterterrorism and defensive operations. In addition, work has begun to clear and demolish all illegal infrastructure at the site of the attack.
Police said a situation assessment had been completed under the leadership of Judea and Samaria District Commander Maj. Gen. Moshe Pinchi. Pinchi assigned the investigation to the district's Central Investigations Unit minority affairs division, which will also assist the Shin Bet security agency in investigating the attack.
He also ordered investigators to focus on the use of a "mashtuba" vehicle, an Arabic term referring to a vehicle that has been taken off the road, for example because it was stolen or had become too old for legal use, but continues to be driven illegally.
The attackers used such a vehicle, which had been taken off the road but bore an Israeli license plate.
"This is a phenomenon that must be eradicated," Pinchi said.
District police forces will step up enforcement on roads, including inspections of vehicles and suspects and the seizure of "mashtuba" vehicles.

One in six Swiss spend more than a third of income on housing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:29:00 UTC
20:29:00 KST

One in six Swiss spends more than a third of income on housing
A significant proportion of the Swiss population finds it difficult to spend less than a third of gross household income on accommodation.
According to a representative survey commissioned by the online comparison service Comparis, 16% of those surveyed (i.e. one in six) spend more than this threshold on their home.
The situation is particularly difficult for tenants: 22% exceed the limit, compared with 7% of homeowners. Unsurprisingly, the low-income households struggle the most. Amongst those with a gross monthly income of up to CHF4,000, 36% spend more than a third of their income on housing.
“The so-called ‘one-third rule’ is not a law of nature, but it is an important warning indicator,” comments Harry Büsser, a property expert at Comparis, quoted in a press release. Those who consistently exceed this threshold risk having to cut back on other essential expenses, including healthcare and pensions, or finding themselves in difficulty when faced with unexpected outgoings.
More
Housing shortages – what works and what doesn’t
The problem also affects homeowners, despite the checks carried out by banks before granting a mortgage. Financial institutions assess the affordability of the mortgage by generally applying a theoretical interest rate of 5%, which is higher than current market rates. However, the assessment carried out at the time of purchase does not guarantee that the burden will remain sustainable in subsequent years. A loss of income, a divorce, a reduction in working hours or retirement can significantly alter a household’s finances. This is why, according to Comparis, it is important to consider not only the ability to meet housing costs under current conditions, but also the ability to cope with financial changes and unforeseen events.
“When it comes to monthly housing costs, owning a property often seems more affordable than renting: however, people often forget that a considerable portion of their equity is tied up in the house or flat,” emphasises Büsser. “This money cannot be invested to generate a return. Furthermore, there are maintenance costs, renovations and major repairs to factor in. Home ownership may be attractive in the long term, but it is not automatically more cost-effective,” concludes the specialist.

French associations challenge Macron's call to ban non-union protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:28:18 UTC
20:28:18 KST

French associations have filed an urgent legal appeal against President Emmanuel Macron’s call to ban demonstrations not organised by trade unions ahead of nationwide protests planned for Saturday, October 24.
The Association for the Defence of Constitutional Freedoms (Adelico) and the Magistrates’ Union filed an application with the Council of State, France’s highest administrative court, broadcaster Franceinfo reported on Thursday.
The associations asked the court to suspend Macron’s decision and any instructions issued to enforce it. They argued that the president had no legal authority to establish a policy of banning demonstrations.
Jean-Baptiste Soufron, a lawyer representing Adelico, described the announcement as an “abuse of power”, according to the appeal.
The associations also challenged what they said was a distinction between trade unions and other citizens, arguing that unions do not have a monopoly on organising demonstrations and that the right to protest belongs to everyone.
The Council of State has 48 hours to rule on the appeal.
Security tightened ahead of protests
Macron announced on Thursday that demonstrations not organised by trade unions would be banned in the coming days, particularly on Saturday, “wherever possible”.
Prefects were instructed to examine union requests and propose alternative routes to protect city centres.
Government spokesperson Maud Bregeon said restrictions on non-union demonstrations would be decided on a case-by-case basis.
Several local authorities have already imposed restrictions. According to Franceinfo, authorities in Paris approved only one of two routes requested for Saturday, while all gatherings were banned in Lyon and parts of Nice city centre.
The prefecture of Bouches-du-Rhone also banned demonstrations across the department, including in Marseille, on Saturday, even those concerning issues other than purchasing power.
In Lille, authorities announced a ban on all demonstrations and gatherings in the city centre.
Around 70,000 security personnel expected
Meanwhile, BFMTV reporte on Friday that police academy trainees nearing the end of their training will be deployed as reinforcements during Saturday’s demonstrations.
The trainees will guard buildings and perform administrative duties at police stations, allowing experienced officers to focus on more sensitive operations.
They will not be deployed for crowd control or public order duties, which are prohibited under a 2022 law. Several dozen trainees have volunteered, according to the broadcaster.
The government plans to deploy around 70,000 security personnel mobilised during protests on October 17, which resulted in damage to businesses and public buildings.
Jean-Didier Berger, minister delegate to the Interior Ministry, said security deployments on Saturday would be 20 percent higher than on October 17. Sentinelle military personnel, specialist units GIGN and RAID, and riot police are also expected to be deployed.
Authorities have introduced additional restrictions across the Paris metropolitan area, including bans on transporting fuel and flammable gases, carrying protective equipment within 100 metres of a school, and possessing fireworks mortars.
Paris police have also imposed a curfew for adults and minors around Place de la Republique and Les Halles, from 11 pm to 6 am, running from Thursday evening until Sunday.

Red Cat adds attack drone boat to U.S.-built USV lineup
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:27:55 UTC
20:27:55 KST

- Red Cat’s Blue Ops opened orders for its 18-foot B-18 attack and reconnaissance USV and its 39-foot B-39 vessel, already in low-rate production.
- The flagship B-26, formerly Variant 7, remains in full-rate production at Blue Ops’ plant in Valdosta, Georgia.
Red Cat Holdings’ maritime division, Blue Ops, has opened orders for two new uncrewed surface vessels, an 18-foot boat built for reconnaissance and one-way attack missions and a 39-foot vessel already in low-rate production, as part of a new B-Series lineup named after each boat’s length.
The company announced the family on Oct. 22, 2026. The B-18 has completed sea trials and is available for orders ahead of its original schedule, the B-39 is in low-rate production and also available for orders, and the flagship B-26, previously called Variant 7, is already in full-rate production. Blue Ops said the designations follow the traditional American approach of naming vessels by length in feet, which puts the three boats at roughly 5.5 meters, 7.9 meters and 11.9 meters.
The B-18 is the smallest and most aggressive of the three. Blue Ops said it is built around the internationally recognized form factor for one-way attack vessels, the explosive-laden drone boats designed to ram their targets, and that it was developed with U.S. Navy requirements in mind, including deployment from Littoral Combat Ships. Its listed missions are tactical reconnaissance, shipboard launch and recovery, and one-way attack, using a Modular Open Systems Approach architecture that lets operators swap in different payloads and equipment.
The company pitched the B-18 at a U.S. Navy that, in Blue Ops’ words, is reassessing its autonomous surface vessel requirements and looking at more capable, cost-effective options.
The B-39 is aimed at longer missions. It is built on an established commercial vessel platform with an existing manufacturing base, and Blue Ops said it offers more range, endurance and payload capacity than its smaller boats for persistent maritime surveillance, integrated defense systems and logistics, with room to add sensors, mission payloads and command-and-control systems.
“The Navy doesn’t need examples of what autonomous vessels might deliver years from now. It needs affordable, reliable systems that perform in real-world conditions and are available today,” said Barry Hinckley, president of Blue Ops. “That’s exactly what we’re building at Blue Ops. From one-way attack and tactical reconnaissance to maritime defense and logistics, our B-Series vessels are designed to meet immediate operational needs. Combined with Red Cat’s aerial assets, we’re delivering a complete family of systems that gives U.S. and allied forces the capabilities and flexibility to operate across air and sea.”
The B-26 is the most established boat in the family. As the Variant 7, it was described by Hinckley earlier this year as a 7.8-meter vessel with a stated range of 800 nautical miles (1,480 km) at 40 knots and a payload capacity of 1,800 pounds (816 kg), and Red Cat CEO Jeff Thompson said a base configuration costs about $700,000 before weapons or counter-drone payloads are added. The boat moved into full-rate production in May 2026, and Blue Ops has since added Kymeta multi-orbit satellite communications and a Volvo Penta diesel propulsion option.
Red Cat launched Blue Ops in August 2025, building its first prototypes with Hodgdon Shipbuilding in Maine before moving production to a 155,000-square-foot plant in Valdosta, Georgia, which marked its first year of operation in September. Red Cat told investors in March that it aims to build more than 100 USVs in 2026 at the Georgia site.
Blue Ops is now taking orders for both the B-18 and B-39, with the B-26 continuing in full-rate production in Valdosta.

The Kremlin said on Friday that the first tanker carrying Russian diesel fuel under a deal between Moscow and Washington had departed for its intended buyers.

Novak said the tanker would carry 40,000 tonnes of Russian diesel to the US, adding that further shipments would follow and that Russia would meet American demand within its available supply capacity.
Trump announces wider supply agreement
Earlier this month, US President Donald Trump announced a diesel supply agreement following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Under the arrangement, Moscow agreed to “immediately supply” more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets, according to Trump.
He said Russia would supply a further 500,000 tonnes in November, followed by 1 million tonnes “immediately thereafter”.
Trump added that another 3 million tonnes would be delivered “within a short period,” depending on the condition of Russian diesel refineries.
Putin said Russian diesel supplies to US and global markets would benefit the world economy.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticised the deal, warning that easing restrictions on Russian diesel exports could help finance Moscow’s war effort.

European, regional powers to discuss maritime security at Istanbul meeting: German FM
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:26:43 UTC
20:26:43 KST

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said on Friday that a first-of-its-kind meeting bringing together four European countries and four regional powers in Istanbul aims to explore ways to resolve stalled regional conflicts.
Speaking before his meetings in Istanbul, Wadephul stressed that the gathering would focus on safeguarding freedom of navigation in international waters, developments in the Black Sea, and other conflicts.
“At our first meeting in this format we Europeans and the four regional powers want to jointly explore how we can bring movement into the conflicts in the Strait of Hormuz, at Bab al Mandab and in the Black Sea,” he said.
The meeting is being held on the initiative of Germany and Türkiye, Wadephul noted, bringing together the foreign ministers of the E4 states — Germany, France, the UK and Italy — and the R4 partners Egypt, Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye.
“The eight of us are taking a stand together: We will not accept Iran and the Houthi militias holding global trade to ransom and maintaining their stranglehold on the world’s supply of energy and fertilisers,” the minister underlined.
“These indiscriminate attacks on free navigation and neighbouring countries must come to an end,” he insisted. “For the people in the region, those suffering from hunger or fearing that they are no longer safe even within their own homes, this persistent insecurity is unacceptable.”
Attacks on shipping routes are also felt in Europe, from prices at gas stations to supermarket shelves, he noted. Delays in fertiliser deliveries risk increasing the danger of famine in some regions, Wadephul warned.
Black Sea grain shipments under pressure
Wadephul also accused Russia of targeting free navigation in the Black Sea and of threatening global food security through attacks on grain shipments.
”By attacking grain shipments, Russia is knowingly risking food shortages in the Global South,” he said. “This hits the world’s poorest, whose survival depends heavily on wheat, as well as our partners, such as Türkiye, which is the largest processor of wheat for the global market.”
Attacks on civilian ships and port infrastructure since July 2026 have nearly halted Ukrainian grain exports via the Black Sea, which previously accounted for about 30 percent of global wheat trade, according to official figures.
Alternative routes can only partly make up the shortfall. Houthi attacks have intensified since July 2026. Bab al Mandab handles about 12 percent of world seaborne trade, while the Strait of Hormuz carries roughly one-fifth of global oil consumption.

Unknown Publisher

Three miners were killed and five injured, two of them seriously, in an explosion at a privately owned mine in northern Turkey.
The miner who had been trapped following an explosion at a coal mine in northwestern Turkey has also been confirmed dead, local authorities reported, bringing the death toll to three.
The explosion at the mine in the town of Gelik was caused by a "firedamp," or flammable gas, local authorities said.
Five others were injured, two of whom are in serious condition.
"Eight people were in the tunnel, seven were rescued. Unfortunately, two of our miners died after being taken to hospital," said Zonguldak governor Osman Hacibektasoglu.
A rescue operation had been underway to reach one person trapped in the mine, who has now been confirmed dead.
Two of the rescued miners suffered burns and were in serious condition. One of the critically injured miners had been transferred to Ankara and preparations are under way to transfer the second miner.
"One of the miners is still inside the mine. We have made contact with him and are trying to get him out," the governor added.
The blast occurred at around 10 in the morning. After an emergency call, teams from the Disaster and Emergency Management Authority (AFAD), as well as medical and fire crews, were dispatched to the site.
According to local newspaper Pusula, the explosion took place at a private mine owned by Demir Madencilik. An investigation has been opened to determine the exact cause of the blast.
Mine accidents are not uncommon in Turkey. Earlier this month, five people were killed in a coal mine collapse in Soma, Manisa in western Turkey.
The independent monitoring group, Worker Health and Work Safety Assembly, or ISIG, reported that 1,267 miners were killed in workplace accidents between 2013 and 2025, mostly from incidents of cave-ins and suffocation.

“The Japanese government denied me entry and held me in solitary confinement for 24 hours over a standup comedy show with 40 attendees,” Obeid wrote in a five-part thread on X.
Obeid said he arrived in Tokyo two days before the shows with two other comedians, who were allowed to enter. Immigration officials questioned him through an interpreter about his work, travel plans and activities in Japan.
He said authorities demanded an hour-by-hour itinerary and later told him he lacked the visa required to work as an entertainer.
Japanese authorities had not publicly commented on his account as of Friday, and his description of the detention conditions could not be independently verified.
He acknowledged responsibility
Obeid acknowledged some responsibility for the visa issue, saying he had been unable to secure the sponsorship required for the relevant visa because the venues were small.
He said nobody in Japan was paying him directly and tickets were sold through a US-based platform, leading him to believe he would be allowed entry based on advice and previous travel experience.
“And yeah, it’s on me for not seeing this coming,” he wrote.
Japanese immigration rules classify entertainment performances under the “Entertainer” residence status. Short-term visits for tourism or business cannot include paid activities, while the entertainer visa process generally requires a Certificate of Eligibility.
Obeid said officials offered him the option to appeal the refusal, but told him the process could take 72 hours, during which he would remain confined. He chose to leave instead.
He claimed he was kept alone for about 22 hours without food, a shower, his phone, laptop or reading and writing materials. Officials also searched his luggage for weapons and drugs, he said.
Obeid said authorities required him to return to the US on the airline he had arrived with, rejecting his request to continue his tour in Hong Kong or Taiwan.
Although he accepted that authorities had identified a visa violation, he questioned whether he had been singled out and cancelled his weekend shows, offering ticket holders refunds, admission to another performance or access to a future virtual show.
Obeid, who describes himself as Lebanese-Palestinian-Syrian-Italian-American, has appeared on Conan, America’s Got Talent and Netflix’s 100 Humans. His comedy also addresses Palestine and Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
