2026-10-23
12:00:27 BST
20:00:27 KST

Police Scotland, the Ministry of Defence and the Scottish Government should be brought together to protect defence industry staff after a run of attacks on manufacturing sites and on the private homes of workers, according to a letter sent to the Home Secretary by the Shadow Scotland Secretary.
Harriet Cross, the Conservative member for Gordon and Buchan, warned of a “dangerous escalation” in attacks on the Scottish defence sector, citing incidents at Leonardo UK in Edinburgh, Bruntons Aero Products in Musselburgh, Ultra I&C in Aberdeenshire and Kelvinside Electronics in Kilsyth, all of which she described as having links to Israel.
The pro-Palestinian group The List has claimed responsibility for vandalising the homes of two defence workers in Dunfermline and South Queensferry earlier this month, and has threatened to target more employees. Cross told the Home Secretary that the attacks form part of a wider rise in antisemitism across the United Kingdom, pointing out that the Community Security Trust recorded 1,926 antisemitic incidents in 2026, up 21 per cent on the previous year. She has asked ministers for an urgent meeting to discuss what can be done to protect the industry, its workforce and the wider Jewish community in Scotland.
Cross said: “These criminals have gone from attacking defence manufacturers to targeting innocent employees in their own homes.
“This is not peaceful protest. It is blatant criminality and intimidation, and those responsible must face the full weight of the law.
“These attacks cannot be viewed in isolation, nor as relating solely to the defence sector. They form part of a wider climate of a rising tide of antisemitism across the United Kingdom.
“The Home Secretary needs to work with Police Scotland, the Ministry of Defence and the SNP government to protect the defence industry, its employees and the wider Jewish community in Scotland.”
Scottish defence sites have been targeted repeatedly over the past two years, and a van was driven into the Leonardo plant in Edinburgh by activists who then damaged the building. Leonardo’s Edinburgh site produces targeting and laser systems, and employs around two thousand people in the city.

Venezuelans Take to the Streets to Demand Democracy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:00:24 UTC
20:00:24 KST

Thousands of protesters took to the streets in Venezuela on Thursday afternoon to demand presidential elections and call for the return of exiled Nobel Prize-winning opposition leader María Corina Machado.
In the capital, Caracas, protesters gathered in Plaza Venezuela and called for presidential elections to be scheduled as early as 2027, as well as the release of all political prisoners in the country.
“We will have presidential elections very soon with María Corina as president,” said former congressman Piero Maroun, who attended the protests, according to independent local news organization Efecto Cocuyo. The Machado-led activist group Vente Venezuela spearheaded the protests, which led to the closure of some streets in Caracas. Others also staged protests in the states of Nueva Esparta, Táchira, and Zulia.
The ruling party that acting President Delcy Rodríguez belongs to, the United Socialist Party of Venezuela, also staged a gathering near the opposition demonstrators in Caracas, though for a women’s march for Breast Cancer Awareness Month.
Protesting has become common for disgruntled Venezuelans since the forced end of Nicolás Maduro’s presidency. Maduro and his predecessor Hugo Chávez heavily cracked down on political dissent. But since Maduro’s removal in January by U.S. forces, protesters have taken to the streets “with increasing frequency,” according to the international civil society alliance CIVICUS, citing data from the Venezuelan Observatory of Social Conflict, which recorded 1,101 protests during just the month of September, or about 37 demonstrations per day. These protests, however, have not necessarily been large.
Until this week. The Thursday protests, which Reuters described as “the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years,” coincided with the third anniversary of the opposition’s presidential primary elections, in which Machado emerged victorious.
Machado is still the opposition’s most prominent figurehead in the transition toward a democratic government: in an AtlasIntel survey conducted for Bloomberg News, Machado received 52% support, compared with 19% for Rodríguez. But Machado has her work cut out for her.
The protests also happened as Rodríguez met with Dinorah Figuera, the opposition representative backed by the U.S. State Department in negotiations for a political transition, inside the Venezuelan presidential palace. The three rounds of U.S.-backed talks between the Venezuelan government and Figuera’s faction have yet to yield an agreement on elections.
In a statement reported by El País after the meeting, Rodríguez appeared to reference the opposition protests, saying in Spanish: “There are still very, very small groups that resist and believe that trying to set the country ablaze and block streets is the way for Venezuela to move forward. I recognize the good Venezuelans who, through this dialogue, are promoting necessary changes.”
Since arresting Maduro in an extraordinary military operation in January, the U.S. has been working with an interim government led by Rodríguez, Maduro’s former deputy. Rodríguez and U.S. President Donald Trump both have said elections will eventually be held in the country, though Trump told TIME in late September: “It’s so raw now, you know that I just think it’s too soon.”
Why has an election not yet been scheduled?
The post-Maduro government opened talks in August with the opposition faction led by Figuera, the president of Venezuela’s 2015 National Assembly, to help the country achieve a democratic transition. But the changes are expected to take time.
Domestic opposition and international observers have long slammed Maduro’s 2018 and 2024 re-elections for lacking transparency and fairness, disputing the results and arguing that Machado’s proxy, Edmundo González Urrutia, actually won in the latter. This raised questions about the independence of the Supreme Court and Venezuela’s National Electoral Council, which have been packed with loyalists of the regime.
For the transition, the establishment and the opposition are trying to iron out details of reforming the court and the council. Even if this happens, experts told Reuters that authorities will still need to update voter rolls and ensure that parties can reach a consensus on how subsequent elections would work.
The twin earthquakes that struck Venezuela in June and caused extensive damage also complicated efforts toward stability in the country.
But the U.S. has also set certain prerequisites that could affect how soon elections could happen. President Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio outlined that they seek stabilization, economic recovery, and national reconciliation in Venezuela, on top of a political transition. Axios reported that it’s a multi-step process: change the court makeup, reform the electoral commission, and then announce an election date. Rubio also announced other requirements, including a truly free press.
“What would threaten an enduring republic in Venezuela would be that someone is elected and they inherit a complete catastrophe, economic and social, and then the whole project is endangered because now anything can happen,” Rubio said on Sept. 23, following Trump’s meeting with Rodríguez in New York. “We want to do two things at the same time.”
Critics argue that the Trump Administration’s position sidelines the opposition faction led by Machado and instead prioritizes oil agreements and economic stabilization over Venezuela’s democratic transition. In August, Trump announced that Washington agreed to a deal with Caracas, saying it would give the U.S. majority control over more than 65 billion barrels or about a fifth of Venezuela’s oil reserves.
Dhayana Fernández-Matos, a professor of political science at the Federal University of Pelotas in Brazil, told Spain’s broadcaster RTVE last month that an election in Venezuela is not a priority for Trump, as his “primary interest lies in oil and the geopolitical power of controlling the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves.”
TIME’s September interview with Trump hinted at the U.S.’s potential financial bias for a delayed election: after saying that it would be too soon for Venezuela to hold an election, the President said, “A lot of money is being made by us, but a lot of money is also being made by Venezuela, and we have complete control of all of them.”

“AI psychosis” appears rare but real, and first-episode patients may be most vulnerable, study suggests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:00:23 UTC
20:00:23 KST

A review of electronic health records at a large medical center suggests that conversational artificial intelligence chatbots are associated with worsening psychotic symptoms in a small fraction of mental health patients. These interactions tend to validate preexisting delusions and appear to occur most frequently among patients experiencing their very first episode of psychosis. The findings were published in JAMA Psychiatry.
Psychosis is a psychiatric condition in which a person loses touch with reality, often experiencing hallucinations or delusions, which are firmly held false beliefs that persist despite contradictory evidence. These false beliefs frequently adapt to reflect the surrounding culture and the latest consumer gadgets. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2025 found that more than half of patients experiencing delusions incorporated modern technology, such as smartphones and social media algorithms, into their false beliefs.
Unlike passive technologies like television or radio, modern artificial intelligence chatbots actively converse with users in real time. Some researchers have used the term “AI psychosis” for cases in which chatbot interactions are linked to emerging or worsening psychotic symptoms. The author of a 2023 commentary argued that chatbot conversations feel so realistic that users can sense a real person on the other end while knowing there isn’t one, and that this tension might fuel delusions in people prone to psychosis.
Subsequent medical observations began to back up these early warnings. A 2025 study of psychiatric records in Denmark, first released as a preprint and since published in a peer-reviewed journal, identified 38 patients whose mental health appeared to suffer after using chatbots, most commonly through the worsening of their delusions. While early reports and the Danish data established that the phenomenon exists in clinical settings, researchers still lacked systematic data from the United States examining the specific traits of affected patients and the exact roles chatbots play in their illness.
To address this, Zachary Bergson and senior author Julia M. Sheffield, who leads the Sheffield Lab and is an associate professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Vanderbilt University Medical Center, along with their colleagues, conducted a systematic analysis of patient records at their institution. They aimed to estimate how often AI psychosis appears in a large American hospital system, identify the clinical characteristics of the affected individuals, and categorize how chatbot conversations interact with psychotic symptoms.
“The study was motivated by the lack of published data on the prevalence and characteristics of AI Psychosis,” Sheffield told PsyPost. “Many theoretical articles had been published, but very few empirical studies existed at the time we started. We wanted to understand simply: 1) at Vanderbilt, how prevalent is AI Psychosis? 2) what generally characterizes AI Psychosis cases in terms of demographics and psychiatric history, compared to other individuals with psychosis who have reference to AI in their medical record but did not develop AI Psychosis.”
The researchers searched an electronic health record database containing 578,058 medical progress notes from 215,712 unique patients who received behavioral health care between December 1, 2022, and April 15, 2026. They filtered these records for keywords related to artificial intelligence and narrowed the pool to patients who had a documented diagnosis of a psychotic disorder. Two raters manually reviewed the resulting notes to remove irrelevant matches, ultimately identifying 187 medical encounters across 73 unique patients.
The team divided these 73 patients into three distinct groups based on how they interacted with the technology, with raters agreeing on the group assignment 86.1% of the time. The first group, labeled “neutral interaction,” included 17 patients who used chatbots for everyday tasks unrelated to their mental illness, such as searching for cooking recipes. The second group, “AI-related psychotic content,” consisted of 28 patients who held delusions about artificial intelligence in general, but had no documented history of actually using a chatbot.
The third group, representing “AI psychosis,” included 28 patients whose medical notes documented chatbot use that appeared to worsen their psychotic symptoms. The researchers also checked each patient’s medical history to see if their hospital visit represented their very first psychotic episode, known clinically as an index episode.
For the 28 patients in the AI psychosis group, the authors further sorted the interactions into four theoretical categories describing how the software influenced the illness, reaching 83.3% agreement between raters. A “catalyst” interaction meant the chatbot triggered new psychotic symptoms in a previously healthy person. An “amplifier” meant the chatbot worsened existing symptoms by validating distorted ideas. A “coauthor” interaction involved the user and the machine building a harmful narrative together through back-and-forth dialogue, while an “object” interaction meant the chatbot itself became the target of the patient’s delusional beliefs.
The 28 patients identified with AI psychosis represented 0.013% of all patients receiving mental health care at the medical center during the study period. This group was predominantly male, at 67.9% (though the neutral group was even more heavily male, at 88.2%), and White, at 75.0%, with a median age of 27.5 years. Patients in the AI psychosis group were younger than those who merely held general delusions about artificial intelligence without using a chatbot, who had a median age of 36.5 years.
The authors note that this rate converges with figures from OpenAI, which has reported that about 0.07% of ChatGPT users active in a given week show possible signs of mental health emergencies related to psychosis or mania, though the two figures measure different populations.
“This is a relatively small percent, and is in line with what has been reported by the tech companies using in-house data that the public does not have access to,” Sheffield explained. “However, 28 people just within a single medical center is still a lot of patients and families that have been impacted, and if you scale this up to the number of people using generative AI, that is millions of people around the world. In addition, psychosis is a highly distressing and often debilitating experience, that can be difficult to recover from; so if AI is contributing to the experience or severity of psychosis, then it needs to be considered potentially harmful to mental health.”
When comparing clinical histories, the researchers found no statistically significant differences between the three groups regarding prior psychiatric hospitalizations, past use of psychiatric medications, outpatient treatment history, or past suicide attempts. However, a major difference emerged regarding the stage of the patients’ illness. About 60.7% of the patients in the AI psychosis group were experiencing their first episode of psychosis, compared to just 17.6% in the neutral interaction group and 28.5% in the AI-related content group.
In addition, patients in the AI psychosis group were more likely to be diagnosed with “unspecified psychosis” (a temporary or broad diagnosis often used when a patient’s exact condition is still being evaluated), at 28.6%, compared to 0% in the neutral group. Among the AI psychosis cases, OpenAI’s ChatGPT was the specific product named in 53.6% of the records. Notably, 85.7% of all AI psychosis interactions were recorded after May 2024, which coincided with the release of the GPT-4o model.
Looking at the four categories of chatbot interaction, the researchers found that the technology functioned as an “amplifier” in 64.3% of the AI psychosis cases. It served as the “object” of delusions in 21.4% of cases, and acted as a “catalyst” in 10.7% of cases. None of the cases fit the “coauthor” category, and one case could not be classified into any of the four types.
“Our finding that the majority of AI Psychosis cases were first episode patients confirmed our suspicions, but was still striking to see in the data,” Sheffield said. “In reading the notes from the medical record it was clear that those vulnerable to or in the midst of experiencing psychosis for the first time were turning to AI for answers, understanding or support and were instead having their delusional thought content confirmed or amplified.”
“AI Psychosis – the worsening of psychotic experiences (typically delusional beliefs) in the context of using generative chat-based AI – is a real clinical phenomenon that we observe in practice,” she added. “People are coming to behavioral health providers in the real world with these types of experiences.”
These findings align with a case report covered by PsyPost in late 2025, which detailed an individual patient rather than a retrospective cohort of electronic health records, and similarly found that conversational AI chatbots often amplify and validate psychotic delusions. The results are also consistent with the peer-reviewed version of the Danish records study described earlier, which was covered by PsyPost in early 2026 and documented how chatbot interactions were associated with exacerbated delusions, self-harm or suicidal ideation, and eating disorders among vulnerable psychiatric patients.
One outside expert said that as large language models (LLMs), the technology that powers conversational chatbots, become part of everyday life, their mental health risks and potential benefits both need study. “This study is one of the first to dive into texts from medical records to find suggestions for associations between use of LLMs and psychosis,” Iris Sommer, a professor and psychiatrist at the University Medical Center Groningen in the Netherlands and president of the Schizophrenia International Research Consortium, who was not involved in the study, told PsyPost. “This study found remarkably few cases of an association between LLM use and psychosis (only 0.013% of service users). With the steep increase in LLM use in recent years, this frequency can be expected to also go up.”
“While the potential for triggering or worsening psychosis is an important issue to investigate, there is also potential of a broadly available app, that can be used in many languages, free of charge, which may offer some benefits to those struggling with mental health issues who do not have access to any form of regular mental health care,” Sommer added. “Understanding in which circumstances and for which users LLM use can be harmful or helpful is a major challenge that mental health researchers are now facing.”
The concentration of cases after May 2024 coincides with the release of GPT-4o, a model OpenAI later acknowledged had at times been overly sycophantic, meaning it tended to flatter users and agree with them rather than push back. The authors caution that their design cannot show the model caused these cases, and the timing could also reflect the overall growth in chatbot use and in clinicians’ attention to it. Still, when a person in the early, confusing stages of psychosis shares a distorted belief with an overly agreeable chatbot, the software may validate the belief rather than challenge it.
At the same time, chatbot technology continues to evolve as developers adjust how their models handle sensitive topics. “The newer versions of commercially available LLMs are less likely to confirm irrational or unlikely beliefs than the initial (2022 and 2023) versions,” Sommer noted. “Newer versions have become trained to recognize signs of psychosis, depression or mania and now recommend seeking professional help (also providing local possibilities to find professional help) when such signs are detected.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. Because the study relied on existing medical notes, the prevalence rate of 0.013% only reflects cases where doctors happened to ask about or document technology use. Clinicians do not routinely screen patients for chatbot habits, meaning many interactions likely went unrecorded, and first-episode patients may also receive more thorough intake interviews that make chatbot use more likely to be noted.
The study’s observational design also means it cannot establish that chatbots directly cause psychosis in otherwise healthy people. In most cases, the medical notes described chatbots as appearing to amplify symptoms that were already developing, though three cases were classified as chatbot use preceding new symptoms in previously healthy people. Additionally, the data came from a single medical center in Tennessee, and the four-part classification system used to sort the interactions has not yet been formally validated for clinical use.
“We cannot say from this study if AI use causes psychosis or simply exacerbates it,” Sheffield noted. “This is similar to studies on substance use: for those vulnerable to psychosis, using cannabis or other substances may worsen psychosis symptoms but we frequently cannot say for certain that it caused them. However, the addition of a pervasive, always available, technology that interacts with mental health in a negative way is highly concerning and requires regulation.”
Sommer was more cautious about the “AI psychosis” label itself. “We should be rather careful with this very term, as causality is very difficult to establish, as the authors of this paper also emphasize,” she said. “LLM use may coincide with psychosis, but if it is the delusional way of thinking that has triggered LLM use or the other way around is rather difficult to disentangle retrospectively. Also, if LLM use worsens psychotic symptoms, or if LLM use increases as a result of more delusional thinking is also difficult to tease out.”
To better understand how these digital conversations unfold, the authors note that future research should track patients over time and directly analyze their actual chat logs, rather than relying solely on doctors’ summaries. In the meantime, the researchers suggest that mental health professionals consider routinely asking patients about their use of conversational artificial intelligence during psychiatric evaluations.
“I just attended the first annual AI Psychological Research Coalition (AIPRC) conference, which brought together academia, advocacy and policy to discuss AI regulation,” Sheffield said. “I hope my research can add to this conversation about what types of AI use are harmful for those at risk for psychosis. I also am very interested in understanding how delusional ideas are reinforced by chatbots, in order to reverse-engineer this process, with an eye towards treatment.”
Sommer agreed that examining the actual transcripts of these digital conversations is a necessary step forward. “An important next step would be to analyze the exact interactions between people with emerging psychotic symptoms and LLMs,” she said. “Such analyses should be undertaken open-minded, with a focus on both potentially harmful and helpful interactions.”
The study, “Characterizing Artificial Intelligence Psychosis in a Large Medical Setting,” was authored by Zachary Bergson, Sarah G. Vassall, Adam Wright, Allison B. McCoy, Katherine M. Schafer, Margaret C. Achee, and Julia M. Sheffield.

Split Tunneling Is Your VPN’s Best Feature. Here’s How to Make the Most of It
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

While you may well be familiar with virtual private network apps, you might not have come across one of the best features available inside these privacy protectors: a feature called split tunneling.
In simple terms, split tunneling lets you choose which apps or sites use the protection of a VPN and which don't. While VPNs are worth using for extra security and privacy online—foiling trackers, spoofing your location, and stopping your internet provider from seeing your browsing—they do by their nature come with some compromises in speed.
If, for example, you want to get the fastest possible speeds with your online games, you might want to leave your games outside of the VPN's remit. Likewise, since VPNs typically obfuscate your actual location, if you want to make sure you can always check movie showtimes in your local area, you can use split tunneling to keep those ticketing apps outside your VPN. Putting a VPN in place can also interfere with access to other devices on your local network, like smart home gadgets and printers.
For all these reasons, you might want the extra control that split tunneling gives you, and it's available in a lot of VPN packages. Here's what you need to know about it.
How VPN Split Tunneling Works
VPNs work by offering an encrypted bridge for data going to and coming from the web. This bridge means your internet provider, law enforcement agencies, and people connected to the same Wi-Fi can't see what you're doing online. Split tunneling lets you route some online traffic away from that bridge, without you having to constantly turn your VPN on and off.
App-based split tunneling is the most common type you'll come across, as it's the most straightforward and easiest to understand. Some of your apps use the VPN, and some don't. So maybe you want your banking app connected to a VPN for maximum protection, but you're less concerned about a weather app, and you don't want to see forecasts from whatever location the VPN is spoofing.
Depending on the VPN, you might also see URL-based split tunneling. This lets you set the rules based on domain names. It's the same idea as with apps: For websites that need fast internet access and where privacy is less important, there's no VPN. So you can keep the VPN turned on for a search engine page where you're typing information you want protected, but off for a local news site.
There are other types of VPN tunneling too, including route-based tunneling (based on specific IP addresses on the internet) and policy-based tunneling (essentially a set of overarching rules), but these are less common in consumer VPN software, and you're unlikely to come across them unless you're somehow managing other users.
It's not a complicated technology to understand, and it can be genuinely useful—but it's also a feature that users tend not to notice or think about when they're enabling and disabling VPNs on their devices.
How to Enable Split Tunneling
The exact steps needed to enable split tunneling will vary depending on the VPN software you're using, but they shouldn't be too difficult to find. Most, but not all, VPN programs now offer some kind of split tunneling feature. If you're using a popular app, then you should find the option somewhere, especially if you're on a paid tier.
To give you some idea how it works: In ProtonVPN for Windows, on the main console there's a split tunneling link on the right, together with other features like a kill switch and port forwarding. Click Split tunneling, and once it's enabled, you can start picking your apps. You can either select a list of apps to be included by the VPN (with everything else excluded) or a list of apps to be excluded (with everything else included).
For NordVPN on Windows, you can access the feature by clicking the cog icon in the bottom left of the main interface, then choosing Split tunneling and enabling the Split tunneling toggle switch. Again, you'll be able to choose which apps are included in the VPN protections and which ones aren't.
On mobile, it's a similar process: Delve into the settings for whatever VPN app you're using, wherever those settings might be. Note, though, that iPhones don't allow as much freedom for VPNs here as Android devices and desktop platforms: You'll typically be limited to selecting websites and IP addresses to exclude, rather than apps.
Most of the time, it's going to be a set-it-and-forget-it type routine, and you're not going to need to keep diving back into the options screen to change around the apps that have VPN access—though you can if you want. It means VPN peace of mind where you need it, without the inconvenience of having a VPN applied where it's not useful.

“Barcelona” - “Real” - preview of El Clásico at “Camp Nou”
Kyiv • UNN
On October 25, Barcelona and Real will play the first El Clásico of the season in La Liga. The Catalans are leading, but both teams have lost players.
On Sunday, October 25, "Barcelona" and "Real Madrid" will play the first El Clásico of the season in La Liga. The match will take place at Barça's home stadium, "Camp Nou." The Catalans enter this crucial clash as league leaders with a 100% record, although both teams have suffered significant personnel losses due to injuries and suspensions, UNN reports.
Details
The first match this season between "Barcelona" and "Real Madrid" will take place on Sunday, October 25, as part of La Liga. It will be played at "Camp Nou," where construction work is still ongoing.
This means that the stadium's capacity is limited to just over 60,000 seats, so buying tickets will be more difficult than in previous years. By the 2027/28 season, the stadium is expected to accommodate 105,000 spectators, once again making it the largest football stadium in Europe.
"El Clásico" is not just a football match. Every season in La Liga, "Barcelona" and "Real Madrid" become the main protagonists of one of the biggest sporting events in the world.
"El Clásico" is a match eagerly awaited by football fans around the world, and it is broadcast in more than 190 countries.
Head-to-head history
The first time "Barcelona" and "Real Madrid" met in an El Clásico in La Liga was on February 17, 1929. The match took place at the "Les Corts" stadium in the second round of the championship, and "Real Madrid" won 1–2 thanks to a brace from Morera.
Throughout the clubs' history, the teams have met 300 times. "Real Madrid" have won 110 matches, "Barcelona" have won 128, and 62 encounters have ended in a draw.
In La Liga alone, "Real Madrid" and "Barcelona" have met 192 times, with "Los Blancos" holding the advantage: 80 victories compared with 77 for Barça.
Last season, the teams met three times: twice in La Liga and once in the Spanish Super Cup.
In the first half of the Spanish championship, "Real Madrid" celebrated a 2–1 victory, while in the second half "Barcelona" won 2–0, allowing the "Blaugrana" to become champions ahead of schedule.
In January, "Barcelona" won the Spanish Super Cup by defeating Madrid's "Real Madrid" in the final. The match was marked by high scoring, a tense contest, and a sending-off in stoppage time.
Before the match
During the week, the teams played their Champions League matches, with "Barcelona" losing to "PSG" of Illia Zabarnyi (4–2), while "Real Madrid" thrashed "Leipzig" 4–1.
In this match, "Real Madrid" will be without Raúl Asencio and Rodrygo due to injuries, as well as Vinícius Júnior, who received a straight red card in the match against "Villarreal" and was subsequently handed a four-match suspension.
"Barcelona" will be without Roony Bardghji, Eric García, and Dani Olmo, who was injured in the match against "PSG."
Favorites and where to watch
Barcelona currently lead the standings, having won all nine of their league matches. "Los Blancos" are six points behind the Catalans.
The bookmakers consider "Barcelona" the favorite for this match, with odds of 1.61 on a win. A draw is priced at 5.66, while a Madrid victory is set at 3.80.
The match will be available live on the "Football 1" channel of the Megogo media service.

National event aims to raise public awareness of digital media

National event aims to raise public awareness of digital media
TEHRAN – Media and Information Literacy Week is being observed nationwide from October 24 to 30, with the aim of promoting media literacy and raising public awareness of how to engage with media and navigate the digital space.
Media literacy is the skill to distinguish misinformation from truth. It is the practice of taking in media messages and understanding what they are trying to convey via news, movies, and TV programs, analyzing the information, and making informed decisions. It is the ability to remain a critical, thoughtful, and responsible consumer of information.
Academic Center for Education, Culture, and Research (Jahad-e Daneshgahi), and other cultural and media organizations and institutions are observing the week with a wide range of programs to popularize media literacy and empower audiences to assess the information presented in media and social media, IRNA reported.
The inauguration ceremony of the week kicks off on Saturday, with the head of the National Cyberspace Center delivering a lecture. A media-parenting channel titled ‘Media compass’ on Shad messaging application will be unveiled during the ceremony.
A major conference on ‘media parenting’ is scheduled for Sunday in Alborz province.
National Cyberspace Center has organized a consultative meeting on the role of online platforms and media in enhancing media literacy on Monday, and an educational seminar is planned to be held at Farhangian University on Tuesday.
On Wednesday, the Association of Iran Media Literacy in cooperation with Yasan Academy, an educational academy that uses educational technologies and computational thinking to foster individual skills in children and adolescents, will host a webinar on artificial intelligence (AI) for teachers and media literacy educators.
‘Media literacy and informed citizen’ conference is planned to be held on Thursday and Friday.
Holding training courses for video game narrators by the Iran Computer Games Foundation, and media literacy educators by the Association of Iran Media Literacy and National Cyberspace Center, as well as unveiling ten books on media and information literacy are among other programs considered for the week.
Global Media and Information Literacy Week is marked from October 24 to 31. In 2026, the week is held under the theme ‘We All Play a Part – Media and Information Literacy for the People’, highlighting the power of individuals and communities to make informed decisions, think critically and participate meaningfully in an increasingly complex information landscape. This year, the campaign puts collective action at its heart, bringing together educators, journalists, young people, policymakers, digital creators, parents and civil society across the world.
Significance of media literacy in war
Information literacy and media literacy are among essential tools to confront the threats posed by foreign media’s psychological operations during wartime, and to ensure the coherence of society.
Media literacy is an expanded conceptualization of literacy that includes the ability to access and analyze media messages as well as create, reflect, and take action, using the power of information and communication to make a difference in the world.
According to Javad Taleschi, the head of the Iranian social work media, psychological operations of foreign media can have adverse effects on society. However, improving information literacy and media literacy in society, through holding educational workshops, creating content, strengthening the national media, and monitoring social media, will help boost social resistance against the threats to society.
Foreign media can carry out psychological operations in different ways, such as broadcasting fake news and rumors, with the aim of demoralizing people and making them feel extremely frightened.
Another way is to distort the facts and spread incomplete or false news to present an unreal image of the war; they may even fuel ethnic and civil conflicts to disunite society.
Another strategy is to weaken people’s trust in the government through unjustified criticism and by spoiling the image of governmental bodies.
Foreign media also attempt to promote foreign cultures and values to weaken the national identity of a country. However, media literacy helps people use critical thinking to evaluate information and news, identify the reliability of news sources, and decide if the information is real.
To be able to use media effectively and safely, media literacy skills have to be improved.
There are different ways to improve this skill among Iranian families. Media education is one of the best ways. The skill can be developed at schools through holding educational workshops for parents.
The national media needs to be strengthened as a powerful, people-centered medium to be able to function as a reliable source of news broadcasting. Families have to be encouraged to use reliable sources such as books, scientific articles, and specialized websites.

Worries about the cost of AI spending deepened after Meta Platforms outlined plans to raise capital expenditure, stoking fears that tech firms may borrow more to fund their expansion.
Climbing crude also weighed on gold by sharpening inflation fears and strengthening expectations that interest rates could stay high for longer. Higher rates typically dull the appeal of gold, which pays no interest, compared with assets that do.
Some support came from doubts over whether AI investment, a key driver of US economic growth, can be sustained. Those doubts led markets to scale back bets on further Federal Reserve rate hikes.
Oil and gas prices climb
Energy markets also moved higher on Friday. Brent crude hit a more than five-month high, gaining 1.14 percent to $114.47 a barrel, while European natural gas reached its highest level since December 2022, rising 1.37 percent to €91.28 ($102.40) per megawatt-hour.
Crude was lifted by escalating attacks on Saudi targets and reports that the US and Israel could renew strikes on Iran after next month's US midterm elections.
Yemen's Houthi militia claimed responsibility for recent attacks on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Yanbu, and reports suggested Iran's energy infrastructure could be among potential targets.
Despite regional tensions and threats to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Gulf crude exports have recovered to near prewar levels.
In Europe, gas climbed further as Middle Eastern liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipments stayed about 80 percent below year-earlier levels, sharpening competition between European and Asian buyers ahead of winter.
Gas storage stood at 74.62 percent of capacity on 22 October, the lowest for this time of year since records began in 2009. That leaves the region exposed to further supply disruptions and higher heating demand.

Rosoboronexport to unveil 'Anti-Drone Dome' UAV defense concept
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:57:47 UTC
19:57:47 KST

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russia’s state arms exporter Rosoboronexport (part of the Rostec State Corporation) will showcase for the first time its latest air defense system designed to protect the population, troops, and facilities from drones, called the Anti-Drone Dome, the company’s press service reported.
The Anti-Drone Dome is designed to shield the civilian population, as well as strategic and infrastructure facilities, bridges, buildings, fuel and energy complex enterprises, and troop deployment sites from unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) attacks. "Options are also available for protecting convoys and vehicles transporting VIPs or sensitive cargo," the press service stated. It said that the project will be presented at the third Russia-Africa Summit, which will be held at Moscow’s Gostiny Dvor fairground on October 28-29.
The project was developed by specialists from Rosoboronexport in collaboration with leading Russian manufacturers of counter-UAV systems and representatives of specialized law enforcement agencies. It draws on practical experience in countering UAVs gained during military and counterterrorism operations in recent years.
"Protecting critical infrastructure from unmanned aerial vehicles has today become the cornerstone of national and economic security, as well as the foundation for further technological development. The proper design and implementation of such a system makes a significant contribution to demonstrating the effectiveness of government and business operations, maintaining supply chains, and signaling to investors that their investments are secure. Rosoboronexport offers the implementation of reliable site-specific protection against UAVs, tailored to each specific partner and facility. All the equipment and solutions used in this system have proven their effectiveness in real conditions," said Rosoboronexport CEO Alexander Mikheyev, quoted by the press service.
It added that the project is a multi-layered system comprising airspace reconnaissance capabilities, firepower capabilities, and electronic countermeasures against UAVs, a geoinformation system based on an automated control system, as well as engineering (physical) protection measures.
Concept and solutions
The company said that during the third Russia-Africa Summit, Rosoboronexport will present the concept itself to its partners, along with solutions designed for the development of the Anti-Drone Dome. These include physical UAV destruction systems such as the Pantsir-SMD-E air defense missile system and the Pantsir-S1M air defense missile and gun system developed by the High Precision Systems Holding Company, the Verba man-portable air defense system (MANPADS) and the TKB-1167 air defense system, as well as the Citadel anti-aircraft artillery system with programmable-detonation ammunition, developed by Rostec.
The company is also showcasing the Silok, Repellent-Patrol, Sky-Hunter 4PC, and Radescan (in its anti-drone version) systems for detecting and electronically jamming the control and navigation channels of unmanned aerial vehicles.
The Anti-Drone Dome is a comprehensive system whose configuration and functionality are adapted to a specific customer, taking into account the characteristics of the protected facility.
All of its components are developed and manufactured at facilities in Russia.

Health Insurance Week to highlight 'health along path of life'
TEHRAN – Under the theme “Health Along the Path of Life,” National Health Insurance Week will be held from October 24 to 30, focusing on “Innovation and Transformation in the Basic Health Insurance System: Shifting from Treatment-Oriented to Health-Oriented Care.”
The themes for each day of the week are as follows:
 
* Saturday, October 24: National Consensus and Universal Health Insurance for Health Equity
 
* Sunday, October 25: From Government Support to Philanthropic Contributions: Ensuring Sustainable Support for Patients with Hard-to-Treat Diseases
 
* Monday, October 26: Data Mining and Smart Monitoring to Safeguard Resources and Ensure Families’ Financial Protection
 
* Tuesday, October 27: Smart Innovation, Transparency, and Easy Access to Services
 
* Wednesday, October 28: Health Literacy, Family Physicians, and Sustainable Prevention Through Public Participation
 
* Thursday, October 29: Joining Forces with the National Health Team for a Healthier Nation
 
* Friday, October 30: Supporting People from Healthy Childbearing to Healthy Aging
According to the health ministry, the Health Insurance Organization covers about two million patients with rare and hard-to-treat diseases.
All resident and non-resident foreign nationals with legal stay in Iran must have basic health insurance coverage under a new Cabinet of Ministers enactment.
To safeguard the patients’ health and lower financial burden on households, tens of specialized healthcare service packages have been defined for them, with some more being continuously developed.
The packages include diagnostic, therapeutic, pharmaceutical, rehabilitation, and dental services, whether in the form of outpatient or inpatient services, which are provided with minimal deductibles or free of charge.
In 2024, seven more anti-cancer drugs were added to the list of rare diseases fund, with health insurance covering 70 percent of the costs.
“Currently, with the inclusion of these seven drugs, a total of 90 anti-cancer drugs are covered by the rare and hard-to-treat diseases fund, and the health insurance is paying 70 to 95 percent of their costs,” IRIB quoted Kameli, an official with the health insurance organization, as saying.
The number of health centers that have concluded contracts with the Health Insurance Organization increased by seven percent in the past Iranian calendar year (ended on March 19) compared with the year before.
In 2025, more than 53,000 centers concluded contracts with health insurance organizations, IRNA quoted Keivan Tajbakhsh, an official with the Organization, as saying.
Health insurance contracts have been signed with government, non-government, private, and charity centers for services.
The centers include doctors’ offices, hospitals, pharmacies, rehabilitation centers, and all medical centers.
“We hope to witness an increase in the number of health centers that are parties to the contract with Health Insurance Organization as new forms of the contract, approved by the Supreme Council of Insurance, are announced,” Tajbakhsh said.
He stated that 13,931 pharmacies, 20,804 doctors’ offices, 2,049 clinics, 2,446 independent laboratories, and 4261 rehabilitation centers, both independent and affiliated with other organizations, have concluded contracts with the Health Insurance Organization.
Efforts to enhance intl. cooperation
In August, the head of the Iranian Health Insurance Organization, Mohammad-Mehdi Nasehi, and officials from the International Conference on Public Health (ICOPH) committee explored avenues to enhance collaborations.
The Conference chair, Hematram Yadav, and its convener, Isanka Gamage, held a meeting with Iranian officials to discuss ways to boost cooperation in the fields of health insurance research and the exchange of managerial expertise, Borna news agency reported.
The officials met on the sidelines of the 12th International Conference on Public Health (ICOPH) held from August 5th to 7th in Bali, Malaysia. An Iranian delegation led by Nasehi attended the conference.
Lauding Iran’s active participation, Yadav said enhancement of scientific cooperation with Iran would be a valuable opportunity for ICOPH members.
For his part, Nasehi voiced the country’s readiness for the promotion of scientific cooperation with ICOPH. Referring to the scientific and practical capabilities of Asian countries, he stated that fostering ties with universities, research institutes, and health organizations in the ICOPH member states could pave the way for broader scientific, research, and managerial cooperation in health and health insurance sectors.
In May, Iran and Tajikistan signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) in the health sector focusing on six parts, including medical education, research, healthcare, treatment, medicine, and health insurance.
According to Nasehi, the MOU was signed on the sidelines of the 18th session of the Joint Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technical, and Cultural Cooperation between the Republic of Tajikistan and the Islamic Republic of Iran which was held on May 26, in Dushanbe under the chairmanship of the co-chairs of the commission — Minister of Energy and Water Resources of the Republic of Tajikistan Daler Juma and Minister of Energy of the Islamic Republic of Iran Abbas Aliabadi, IRNA reported.
Fostering ties in the health sector, particularly health insurance, is a part of Iran’s six-point roadmap for water diplomacy.
Referring to Iran’s expertise in health insurance, the official said the country’s experiences in implementing health insurance, referral systems, and other fields of health will be shared with Tajikistan through consultation and implementation.
In December 2025, Nasehi and the Minister of Health and Social Protection of Tajikistan, Jamoliddin Abdullozoda, agreed to promote cooperation between the two countries in the field of medical health insurance.
During a meeting held in Tajikistan, the two sides discussed the potential for expanding ties by launching joint investments in the health sector, ihio.gov.ir reported.
For his part, Nasehi announced the organization’s readiness to share experiences with Tajikistan to help strengthen its insurance system.

“We have no intention to interfere with their democratic processes,” Carney said, adding that Canada was focused on strengthening its economy and expanding international partnerships.

Diplomats told to limit contact with candidates
The remarks came after Canada instructed its diplomats to avoid engaging with candidates in the upcoming US midterm elections, POLITICO reported on Thursday.
Global Affairs Canada issued the guidance on Tuesday, directing officials to limit public engagement and avoid being photographed with US lawmakers until November 3, the date of the midterm elections, according to the report.
“Government officials are always instructed to limit public events and stakeholder engagement during election periods in their host country,” a Global Affairs Canada spokesperson said.
The guidance reportedly applies to engagement with US lawmakers running in the elections but does not extend to American officials who are not candidates.
The directive came a day before the US Embassy in Ottawa circulated a fact sheet accusing several Canadian political leaders of interfering in American politics. Canadian officials have rejected the allegations.
Peter Navarro, a senior trade adviser to US President Donald Trump, said on Thursday that Canadians should stay out of US politics.
Dispute unfolds amid trade tensions
The row comes amid a broader trade conflict following Trump’s tariff measures against Canada.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford has also denied any intention to influence the US vote, saying his government remains focused on economic issues.
During the midterm elections, Americans will elect members of the House of Representatives and a portion of the Senate, determining which party controls Congress for the remainder of Trump’s term.

Free dental services offered during national oral health week
TEHRAN – The health ministry provided different dental services during the week-long national oral and dental health campaign, held from October 17 to 23 nationwide.
The campaign centered on training, self-care, prevention, and raising awareness about the importance of oral health. The health ministry, in cooperation with the Ministry of Education, conducted oral health education at schools to improve the knowledge of children and families about oral health.
Dental screening at schools focused on proper tooth brushing, applying fluoride varnish, promoting oral health habits, and referring those who need further treatment to medical centers.
With the help of student health ambassadors and healthcare providers at school, they would teach students about proper nutrition and how to brush and floss their teeth correctly.
“Apart from schools, dental services are being offered in rural and urban areas with a population of less than 20,000 individuals; pregnant mothers, mothers with children under two years old, and children aged under 14 are receiving free oral health packages and dental treatment,” IRNA quoted Zahra Qorbani, an official with the health ministry, as saying.
In other cities, dental services were also offered with health insurance covering 70 percent of the total costs. The dental services included tooth extraction, filling, scaling, and preventive care.
The official said that the health ministry programs are not limited to oral and dental health week; the health ministry is endeavouring to enhance both access to and the quality of services through upgrading equipment, supplying needed materials, and dispatching dentists to areas where there are not enough specialists.
Referring to the high costs of dental treatment, Qorbani highlighted that the main responsibility of the health ministry is to prevent diseases and reduce the need for costly medical care. To preserve natural teeth, promote oral health, and reduce the burden of costs, dental services need to target individuals at early ages of life while simultaneously increasing access to necessary treatments.
The week-long event was held under the theme ‘Don’t forget two times two, brushing your teeth for two minutes twice a day’, the health ministry’s website reported.
The health ministry also benefited from the capacity of dental offices, mass media, and social media to hold educational and preventive programs related to oral health for the promotion of self-care and enhancement of oral health literacy among the public.
In the past Iranian year, the program was held in some 34,000 schools, providing services to more than three million students across the country, Qorbani said in January.
World Oral Health Day (WOHD) is celebrated every year on March 20 to empower people with the tools and knowledge to prevent and control oral diseases, which affect nearly 3.5 billion people worldwide.
It encourages people to look after their oral health by adopting a good oral hygiene routine and managing risk factors.
Themed ‘A Happy Mouth Is… A Happy Life’, WOHD 2026 spotlighted oral health as the foundation of lifelong well-being — from a baby’s first teeth to maintaining a healthy smile in older age.

Romania blames Russia for drone that sinks cargo ship; 1 killed, 3 missing
BUCHAREST, Oct 23 - Romanian President Nicusor Dan accused Russia of escalating its attacks on NATO's eastern flank on Friday, after a drone strike sank a cargo ship off the Romanian Black Sea coast, killing at least one sailor with three still missing.
Video released by Romanian authorities showed only a small part of the hull of the capsized tanker still visible above the waves as it sank. Emergency vessels were searching the surrounding waters for survivors in choppy seas and high wind.
Romania's naval authority said the Comoros-flagged Khoryv, with a crew of 13 Ukrainian and Azeri sailors, had sent a distress signal 13 nautical miles off Romania's port of Constanta, just beyond Romanian territorial waters. Nine sailors were rescued from the water, three were missing and one body was recovered.
The past two weeks have seen a sudden surge in deadly attacks on commercial ships off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, with at least seven cargo ships hit and some 30 sailors reported dead or missing.
"It is part of Russia's escalation process in its war in Ukraine," President Dan told reporters, later saying the ship had been hit by a drone.
NATO said on Tuesday it would send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea. The alliance has not specified what capabilities would be sent. On Saturday, Romanian jets shot down two of the latest generation of Russian drones over Romanian territorial waters.
The vessels that have been struck lately have either been anchored near or headed towards the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube River to the Black Sea.
The canal has become the primary export route for Ukraine, one of the world's biggest grain and food oil exporters, which has relied on Danube River ports and Romanian territorial waters as Russia has attacked Ukraine's own Black Sea ports.
Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria have called on NATO to do more to protect commercial shipping in the Black Sea. REUTERS

10-year-old girl whose mother died abducted from Kostiantynivka and handed over to "uncle" in Russia
Russian forces deported 10-year-old Sofiia from Kostiantynivka after her mother was killed. The girl has now been placed in the care of an "uncle" whom she had never met before she was abducted. For a month, the Russian occupation authorities concealed the child's whereabouts before presenting a story about her "rescue".
Source: human rights activist Oleksandra Dvoretska
Details: Maria Lvova-Belova, Russia's Commissioner for Children's Rights, who has been accused of involvement in the mass deportation of Ukrainian children, had previously spoken about Sofiia's removal from Kostiantynivka.
Lvova-Belova claimed that Russian soldiers had found the girl alone in a basement in Kostiantynivka, "looked after" her for a month and later "evacuated her to a safe place".
Sofiia reportedly said that her mother had been killed, that she did not remember her father, and that her grandmother and grandfather had died from injuries sustained in a drone strike. However, the Russians blamed the attacks on Ukrainian forces.
"At the beginning of July, Maria Lvova-Belova announced Sofiia's 'rescue' as though it had just happened. Yet by that point, the child had already been deep in Russian-occupied territory for at least a month. They held back the story until a convenient moment for propaganda purposes, linked to Russian claims about the 'capture' of Kostiantynivka. And that is how we learnt about yet another child in Russian hands.
Instead of informing the Ukrainian side of Sofiia's whereabouts and arranging for her return to her relatives in Ukraine, the girl was placed in a residential institution and information about her was concealed," Dvoretska said.
Since then, the occupation authorities have forced the child to appear in various videos. In them, the girl can be seen thanking Russian soldiers and saying that her relatives had supposedly been killed by the Ukrainian military.
"We established all the circumstances back in the summer. Sofia has close relatives in Ukraine who were looking for her, waiting for her and asking for her to be returned. But the Russians kept the child in a residential institution for months, with no possibility of returning to them," Dvoretska wrote.
Lvova-Belova recently said that Sofiia was being placed in the care of an "uncle" who lives in Russia with his wife.
The Russian official claimed that the child herself had expressed a desire to live with her "uncle". Dvoretska, however, says Sofiia had not known that this "relative" existed before she was abducted.
A video was subsequently posted on Lvova-Belova's Telegram channel showing the "uncle" and his wife collecting Sofiia. In the footage, the girl is wearing a camouflage cap bearing the Russian flag and the word "Spets" [short for "specialist" or "special forces"]. The "guardian's" face is blurred.
"The Russians suddenly remembered the child's privacy. In the new video, they carefully blurred the face of the uncle to whom Sofiia is being handed over, as well as those of the other adults. But this was not done to protect the child. It was done to make it difficult to establish who these people are and exactly who the Ukrainian child has been handed over to.
"When they needed to film propaganda, no one cared about the privacy or safety of 10-year-old Sofia. She was simply needed as a tool for propaganda," Oleksandra Dvoretska said.
Background: A Ukrainian girl with a disability who had been abducted by Russian forces from a residential institution in Oleshky was previously reported missing in Russia.

UK makes quiet shift to prepare for supply chain shortages
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:48:00 UTC
19:48:00 KST

UK quietly warns citizens to stock up on emergency supplies
- The UK government told households to be ready for emergencies and keep three days of supplies, as it warns of weather, cyber and hostile threats.
- The guidance was quietly launched on Oct 22, with Paymaster General James Murray saying households and government both have a role in resilience.
- Ministers want to avoid panic buying, recalling Covid-19 shortages, while also preparing for supply chain disruption and bigger spending choices on defence and infrastructure.
AI generated
LONDON – Britain is trying to get its citizens to prepare for the worst – without descending into a panic.
The British government has quietly published guidance for households to “be ready” in the event of a national emergency.
The advice that they should have enough supplies to be self-sufficient for three days represents a subtle shift towards more urgent messaging amid growing concern about threats ranging from Russian hybrid attacks and AI-driven cyberwarfare to climate change.
The recommendations were slipped onto a government website on Oct 22, along with a written statement to Parliament by Security Minister Dan Jarvis.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting separately said he wanted people to be “alert, but not alarmed” in a 21st-century update to Britain’s wartime slogan: “Keep Calm and Carry On”.
The nature of the roll-out highlights the government’s concern about overdoing the worries, with memories of the empty supermarket shelves of the early days of the Covid-19 pandemic still fresh.
However, the UK faces an expanding list of threats, including droughts and flooding, and the head of MI5 said earlier in October that the security service devotes more resources to countering actions by hostile states, such as Russia and Iran, than during the Cold War.
The preparedness campaign had been planned for earlier in the year by former Prime Minister Keir Starmer.
However, his successor Andy Burnham delayed its launch due to concerns that it could be seen as an overly pessimistic start to his premiership, as reported by Bloomberg in August.
Burnham has spent his first four months in office trying to build optimism across the country. Policy announcements have focused more on feel-good steps such as bus fare caps and greater devolution than on thorny issues such as defence spending and the threats facing the UK.
But the decision to publish guidance on Oct 22, telling households to “take a few simple steps to stay prepared if everyday services are temporarily disrupted”, suggests the government is now seeking to build voter awareness of the difficult decisions facing John Healey in his Budget next week.
“Individual households can play their role in making sure that they’re more resilient, but government has a role in making sure we’ve got the right defences,” Treasury Minister James Murray told Sky on the morning of Oct 23.
“The big focus, rightly for many years and into the future, is on our military capability, our defensive capability.”
The online checklist advised Britons to stock up on three days’ supply of bottled water and non-perishable foods, as well as hand sanitiser, a torch and batteries, and a radio. It also advised them to keep cash at hand, copies of important documents, and blankets and warm clothing.
“The storms last winter and the wildfires this summer have shown how severe weather events can cause disruption to our everyday lives and impact the services we rely on, like phones, power, water and the internet,” Jarvis said in his statement.
They “are a reminder that we can all play our part to keep ourselves, our loved ones, and our communities safe in times of emergency”.
The move comes at a time when ministers are under pressure to take significant steps to modernise infrastructure and prepare for the future.
Hotter summers and plans for data centre construction are increasing demand for water, but the UK has not built a new reservoir since 1992, shortly after the privatisation of the water sector.
Britain has also been warned by its top defence experts that it needs to invest heavily in its military, as it is unprepared to defend itself in the event of a full-scale war.
Healey quit his job as defence secretary under Starmer in a row over military spending, and now as chancellor faces the conundrum of getting defence spending to 3.5% of GDP by 2035.
Jarvis said the move “brings the UK into line with many of our European peers who also have the three-day message at the heart of their campaign”.
No government ministers had been scheduled to speak on the launch of the resilience campaign this week.
Streeting only revealed the launch was imminent when asked by journalists about preparation for resilience when he appeared at the opening of a new weapons factory in the West Midlands on Oct 22.
He said the public needed to be prepared for supply chain disruption caused by “hostile state actors or terrorists”.
UK shoppers rushed to stockpile essentials in March 2020 as the Covid-19 pandemic stoked fears of lockdowns and shortages. Toilet paper, pasta and cleaning products vanished from shelves in many stores, forcing supermarkets to ramp up restocking efforts.
Tesco, Sainsbury’s, Asda and Morrisons joined the BRC that month in urging shoppers to buy only what they needed, warning that panic-buying risked leaving others without essentials.
Speaking in front of the House of Commons Public Accounts Committee last week, Jim Bligh, corporate affairs director of the British Retail Consortium, said he was concerned about being too alarmist.
“Panic-buying is quite easy to generate, particularly if you tell people to buy a particular type of product – they will go out to buy it,” he said.
“If the government were to say to you, ‘Go and buy x liters of water,’ would we run out of water? I do not know.” BLOOMBERG

Digested week: If you were under house arrest, would you be wishing for more books about soil?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

19:47:30 KST

Monday
“Who’s Nicole Kidman?” asked my 11-year-old. For God’s sake. “You know Nicole Kidman,” I said. “She’s in ...” I tried to think of a single thing she might have seen her in. “She’s that witch queen with the hair in Aquaman.” Blank stare. “She’s in … she’s an icon, she’s really famous. She used to be married to Tom Cruise.” A pause. “Oh for God’s sake, Tom Cruise, from Top Gun.” “Oh yes.” “She was the villain in Paddington!” Thank God.
Kidman had come to her attention, and that of every other 11-year-old girl in the land, via Adéla, the Slovakian singer whose song, Nicole Kidman, from her debut album, Prima, has caused a minor TikTok sensation and went to No 1 on Spotify earlier this month.
“Do you mean Adele?” I said, when we got to this part of what already seemed like a very long conversation. Excoriating, alright-grandma look. “It’s Adéla. With an ‘a’. She was in Dream Academy, she went out in the first round.” I knew what this meant and got briefly excited. “So she’s a Katseye reject!” More stern looks. “She’s in trouble for mocking Christians.” I gave up at this point.
The Nicole Kidman song, given a discreet nod by Madonna in a TikTok, was inspired by a corset Adéla wore to the Golden Globes and contains the lyrics: “Babygirl in control / I feel like Nicole,” and: “Every single night / I pray that my tits are sittin’ right / Moulin Rouge, my corset is so tight.” Hmm.
Kidman has graciously accepted the compliment and this week, when the song played at a runway show for Victoria’s Secret in LA, the actor, in the front row, laughed and put her head in her hands. I thought the whimsy of the song was quite clever, then made the mistake of watching the video and, after having a full Mary Whitehouse moment, am rehearsing remarks I intend casually to launch over dinner on the relationship between thongs and UTIs.
Tuesday
What do we think of King Charles sending Aung San Suu Kyi, the imprisoned Burmese leader, two books about soil? Suu Kyi, who is 81 and has been under house arrest at an undisclosed compound since her government was ousted by a military coup in Myanmar in 2021, was pictured receiving the books and smiling in a photo apparently staged by her captors.
It’s either a genius move on the part of the king – bringing to the gated leader visions of rolling English countryside and vistas she has, at present, zero chance of enjoying – or else, a little tactless. Soil to Table by gardeners Bridget Elworthy and Henrietta Courtauld, has been described as “a celebration of soil and its connection to the food we eat”. And the second title, Soil: The World at Our Feet, is a catalogue from an exhibition held in London last year.
Gift diplomacy is, of course, always tricky. You may recall the king’s father’s blunt knockback of a gift from a wellwisher during a walkabout with his wife in 2016. Offered a framed picture of Elizabeth II, the then Duke of Edinburgh snapped: “I don’t want that and neither does the queen. She knows what she looks like.” (The Lady Mayor of Windsor briskly stepped forward to accept the gift and smooth things over.)
Wednesday
Larry David’s new essay in Air Mail, the online newsletter, caused enough division this week to provoke coverage in the New York Times. “In our Socialist America,” David went after the Democrat Socialists of America (DSA), aping the style of Jonathan Swift’s A Modest Proposal to write: “Everyone will be so fulfilled spiritually and financially that the police department will be dramatically reduced to where an officer’s only job will be to adjudicate domestic disputes. Toward that end, stands will be set up at local farmers markets, where they will work to resolve marital issues in a folksy, farm-to-table manner. Fresh berries will be provided.”
It’s a weaker effort on David’s part than when he went after Bill Maher in the New York Times last year, savaging him in an essay entitled My Dinner with Adolf for approving remarks made after a meeting with Donald Trump. (“This private Hitler was a completely different animal. And oddly enough, this one seemed more authentic, like this was the real Hitler. The whole thing had my head spinning.”) Predictably, it’s David’s final section on the Middle East that has triggered a lot of take-the-phone-off-gramps fury from gen Z.
“We strongly believe in a two-state solution,” David writes in his mock manifesto. “To this end, we propose that Palestinians should be given all the land currently occupied by Israel and that Israel should be given Pitcairn Island in the South Pacific, where the weather is beautiful and grapefruits are aplenty.” Zohran Mamdani and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are great advocates for the DSA, but for a fuller picture it’s worth returning to DSA co-chair Megan Romer’s side-splitting efforts to explain her party’s policies to David Remnick, earlier this year. “Yeah. You know, again, I don’t have, like, a solid …”
Thursday
Andrew Scott is everywhere promoting Elsinore, his Oscar-bait movie about the Shakespearean actor Ian Charleson, who died of Aids in 1990, and which I can’t wait to see. (Even though, occasionally, I feel about Scott the way I have come to feel about Nicola Walker – that the acting tics are visible enough to pull me out of the performance.)
Elsewhere in gay content, it’s worth stopping by a much-overlooked and very good show, Fellow Travelers, currently airing on Channel 4, in which Matt Bomer and Jonathan Bailey’s characters fall in love in 1950s Washington, right in the middle of Senator Joe McCarthy’s various purges. Alongside the well-known anti-communist witch-hunt, McCarthy also went after gay and lesbian federal workers in what came to be called the Lavender Scare, ruining lives as he went. Bailey, who looks like a young Gregory Peck and as an actor just gets better and better, is heartbreaking in this show about an underdocumented episode of history. Highly recommended.
Friday
News this week of Andy Burnham’s appearance on Gogglebox raises the happy, theoretical spectre of what previous incumbents at No 10 might have looked like on equivalent shows. Thatcher on The Weakest Link? Churchill on Bake Off? One feels that Blair would have actively enjoyed scaling the bouncy houses on It’s A Knockout. Someone alert the AI!

Taiwan September unemployment falls to lowest level in 26 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:46:31 UTC
19:46:31 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) –The unemployment rate fell to 3.36% in September, the lowest level for the month in 26 years, the government said Friday.
The 0.05% drop compared to August was the result of recent graduates finding jobs, according to the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics. The September work participation rate of 59.59% was the highest in 34 years for September, per Liberty Times.
Women and middle-aged people had also returned to the workplace in higher proportions, the government said. The forecast for October is a continuing decline in the unemployment rate.
In September, 11.64 million people were employed, a decline of 15,000 from August, but an increase of 10,000 compared to September 2025. An estimated 405,000 people were out of work in September, a decline of 6,000 from the previous month, Liberty Times reported.
Looking at age groups, the highest jobless rate was for recent graduates and new jobseekers, registering 11.59% for the group from 15 to 24 years of age. The group from 25 to 29 experienced a jobless rate of 5.69%, while the rate fell to 3.4% for those aged 30 to 34.
