10:45:00 UTC
19:45:00 KST

Highly customizable, both physically and through software tweaks. Great to type on. Reliably responsive inputs. Excellent macro manager.
TIRED
No Hall effect keys. Inverted media wheel and some non-functioning LEDs. Plastic basin underside feels cheap.
Turtle Beach is no stranger to competitive-grade gaming keyboards. In recent years, it has focused on its mid- to high-tier Vulcan range, with the Vulcan II XP as its newest entry.
It has a lot going for it—Titan HS mechanical switches, easy modification and customization options, and a suite of pro-tier gaming features available through its support software. However, while it arrives as a full-size keyboard (NumPad included!), a series of trade-offs and compromises ultimately make it feel very middle-of-the-pack.
Measuring 462 x 153 x 32 millimeters, it looks undeniably sharp thanks to its low profile and floating-key approach, all sitting atop a premium brushed-aluminum top plate. Unfortunately, the first compromise is the disappointing underside: a cheap-feeling basic plastic shell basin. Thankfully, the legs feel sturdy when popped up, adding around 10 mm in height and a comfortable angle to the board.
I also like the included soft foam wrist rest, which snaps to the front underside and adds nice support when gaming or typing. It's not memory foam, though, so I fear it might lose some of that cushion over time. The Vulcan also has integrated media controls on the top right with back, play/pause, and forward buttons, plus a media wheel with a push-to-mute feature.
It’s a $150 wired-only device (Turtle Beach is launching a wireless version, the Vulcan II XP Air for an extra $50) that connects via a detachable 1.8-meter USB-C to USB-A cord. A physical connection means zero input latency, which competitive gamers will benefit from.
Swarm Mode
The corded approach does make the Vulcan II XP a breeze to set up. Plug it into a Windows PC, and that's it. But you’ll need Turtle Beach’s Swarm II app to get the most out of it, especially given that the default RGB lighting is a blinding rainbow cascade.
Swarm II brings out the best in this keyboard. Visually, it offers 10 built-in customizable light effects—you can adjust brightness, pattern speed, and colors for some templates. They're pretty gimmicky—especially the Snake one—but it makes for a fun showcase. What's cooler is that you can adjust every LED, perfect for the 11th “custom” slot where you can choose colors, speed, and one of six patterns. You can turn the LEDs off entirely, but only through the app.
Beyond the eye candy, Turtle Beach packs in an impressive slate of features. You can remap inputs down to the individual key and store those configurations as one of five onboard profiles—perfect if you want layouts tailored to specific games, or a more work-oriented profile.
Critical to the keyboard’s gaming credentials, it includes a macro manager that lets you create custom inputs and command combos, down to how many milliseconds of input it should take before activating a keypress. It supports dozens of popular games by default, from competitive favorites like Counter-Strike and Overwatch to single-player epics like Skyrim, which have popular modding scenes and can benefit from bespoke controls. It even has presets for office apps and Photoshop, adding to the Vulcan’s overall versatility. You can easily import new layouts, too.
Touch Typing
I’ve been testing the version with linear switches—Turtle Beach also offers a model with tactile switches, both available in black or white. If you’re new to mechanical keyboards, the main difference is that linear keys press all the way down smoothly, while tactile ones have a little “bump” of resistance as the internal switch activates, which you can feel as the keystroke registers. It’s ultimately personal preference.
For the most part, this is a joy to type on, with precise spacing between keys, and the keys themselves having a satisfying “clackiness” when fully pressed. The only small issue is that the factory-lubed linear keys are so smooth and silent until you get that clack as they hit the base, that it’s easy to accidentally long-press a key. Until you’re used to that, it can catch you off-guard—not an issue when typing, where the worst is an errant stretch of letters whennnnnnnn pausing to think mid-sentence, but it tripped me up a couple of times in games until I was used to it.
Unfortunately, unlike Turtle Beach’s earlier Vulcan II TKL Pro, the keys here aren’t Hall effect, but they are hot-swappable—another trade-off, exchanging long-term reliability and accuracy for the ability to replace or upgrade keys easily. The board supports three-pin or five-pin mechanical switch keys and makes swapping them easy. The flat keycaps also pop off without trouble, which makes cleaning simple. Turtle Beach claims the switches last 50 million keystrokes, which should be plenty, but only a third of the TKL Pro's 150 million.
In gaming, the Vulcan II XP offers a 1,000-Hz polling rate for a 1-millisecond response time, which is competition-grade but falls short of the higher-end 8,000-Hz keyboards on the market. Hopping back to Swarm II, you can activate its more advanced features, like Easy-Shift, allowing for key duplication—basically putting commonly used features within easier reach—and ReacTap, assigning two commands to the same key, useful for games that require very swift inputs. (This might be banned in some competitive scenes under automation rules, though.)
These features can be a little fiddly to set up and map, but with a little experimentation, you can build layouts and input fields that work exactly as you want or need. I tailored a bunch of controls for Borderlands 3 and was dropping Psychos like never before. A minor annoyance, though: Reverting a specific input while trying to create a custom setup would sometimes revert the entire profile, which meant I had to redo everything.
Back to the Drawing Board
While the Vulcan II XP offers great performance for the price, I do have concerns about the overall build quality. On the unit I received, the media wheel was inverted by default—turning it counter-clockwise toward the minus symbol turned the volume up. This was even after I updated the board’s firmware through the Swarm II app, and I had to remap the inputs for it to work as intended. It’s good that the Vulcan II XP’s customization is specific and nuanced enough to remap even the dial direction, but I shouldn’t have had to.
I also found that the LEDs below the “0” and “.” keys on the NumPad don’t seem to work properly, glowing a stubborn, glaring white no matter what color or pattern is assigned. I even tried turning off every other key’s light and manually assigning colors to just those—to no avail.
It’s another reason the board feels middle-of-the-road. Like the shiny metallic top plate hiding the cheaper plastic base, the Vulcan II XP dazzles at a glance, but the closer you look, the more flaws and small annoyances are revealed.
For the price, some of those annoyances are forgivable. For anyone who hasn't upgraded to a mechanical keyboard, this is a decent entry without breaking the bank, delivering a lovely typing experience backed up by enough pro-tier gaming features to feel like a real upgrade—but more demanding or professional players will want to aim higher.

Bank of Russia has decided to keep its key rate at 14%

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. The Bank of Russia has decided to keep its key rate at 14%, as current price pressure remains elevated, according to a press release from the regulator.
"On 23 October 2026, the Bank of Russia Board of Directors decided to keep the key rate at 14.00% per annum. The economy as a whole is growing at a moderate pace in 2026 H2. Current price pressures remain elevated. Inflation expectations stay high. According to the Bank of Russia’s estimates, underlying price growth has not yet decreased and remains in the range of 5-6% in annualized terms, primarily due to the impact of a temporary reduction in production capacities in certain sectors. This requires aggregate demand to grow moderately for underlying inflation to resume its decline," the regulator said.
The Bank of Russia notes that it will make further decisions on the key rate depending on the dynamics of inflation and inflation expectations, as well as the analysis of risks posed by domestic and external conditions. According to the Central Bank, the current seasonally adjusted price growth averaged 8.0% in annualized terms compared to 4.8% in 2026 Q2. The similar indicator of core inflation rose to 6.2% from 4.5% in 2026 Q2. Price dynamics were still affected by volatile components, primarily motor fuel. As of 19 October 2026, annual inflation stood at 6.8% and is expected to come in at 7.1-7.6% as of the end of 2026
"High inflation expectations impede a slowdown in inflation. Despite a slight decrease in the expectations of households and businesses in October, they have generally remained near two-year highs in recent months. Expectations of financial market participants and analysts have increased," the regulator added.
The Bank of Russia noted that according to high-frequency data, the economy is growing at a moderate pace in 2026 H2.
"Business sentiment improved somewhat in October compared to low levels of the previous months. Growth in consumer demand is slowing but remains elevated. Investment activity continues to recover compared to the levels of early 2026," the regulator said.

Eritrea detains Yemeni fishermen for forced labour
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:44:23 UTC
19:44:23 KST

Eritrea's Gulag: detention camps and forced labour for Yemeni fishermen
Driven by painful memories of his detention in an Eritrean prison, Yemeni fisherman Tareq al-Nahari instinctively raised his left hand to protect his head from a barrage of bullets fired by an Eritrean naval boat.The gunfire severed his ring and middle fingers, while one bullet pierced his skull.
Yet he survived, thanks to a medical miracle. However, the projectile that struck his temporal lobe erased his past, identity, and even his future, leaving him unable to form new memories, a condition known as anterograde amnesia.
Despite this, al-Nahari, who is in his forties, remains alive among his family, having escaped death. This is a better outcome than that suffered by his peers, including two fellow fishermen who were aboard the same boat and died in the same incident. One of them was his maternal cousin.
Yemeni fishermen face repeated acts of violence and successive crimes at the hands of Eritrean naval personnel, who intercept them and take them to a network of prisons and detention centres resembling Soviet Gulags.
Eritrean detention centres are no different. Abducted Yemenis are forced to perform arduous labour, including cutting roads through mountains, paving them and constructing military and civilian facilities, without pay or even adequate meals.
This is confirmed by the reports received by Majed Abdo, the sheikh of fishermen in Yemen's Hodeidah governorate. He holds his fellow countrymen responsible for what happens because they enter the territorial waters of a neighbouring sovereign state in their boats.
Amjad al-Omaisi, director-general of al-Khawkhah, a district in the Hodeidah governorate that faces Eritrea on Yemen's western coast, rejects this view. Former Eritrean Supreme Court judge Abdullah Khayyar shares al-Omaisi's assessment.
Life in the Gulag
Tens of thousands of people earn their living from fishing in villages and settlements along Yemen's western coast.
Salem Alyan, a member of the Fisheries Cooperative Union, which organises and oversees the sector, estimates that there are 100,000 traditional fishermen supporting around one million people. However, the sea has become an immediate source of danger amid Eritrean attacks, he told our Arabic-language sister publication, Al-Araby Al-Jadeed.
This is borne out by the account of Issam Mohammed al-Nahari, who is accompanying his brother Tareq, now suffering from memory loss, on a medical trip to Sanaa. He is one of over 20 fishermen we interviewed during this investigation.
Issam said that when the boat incident occurred on Sunday, 25 January 2026, 50 fishermen were aboard the wooden vessel with his brother.
They were taken to the port of Massawa in southern Eritrea, despite insisting that they had been attacked in Yemeni territorial waters.
They were imprisoned for periods ranging from two months to one year. Issam said his brother arrived at Hodeidah hospital alongside the bodies of the two fishermen killed in the incident.
Tareq remained in intensive care for two months before being discharged with memory loss. He could no longer recognise any of his family members apart from his four-year-old daughter, Aya.
Issam said similar incidents frequently occurred to his fellow fishermen, who faced crimes, abuses, and enslavement in detention centres in Asmara without those responsible being held accountable.
"We were tortured to coerce us into forced labour and deprived of food, except for one meal of poor-quality lentils," he said.
He recalled another experience in the summer of 2024, when he was arbitrarily detained by the Eritrean navy alongside his father, Mohammed al-Nahari, and others.
"Throughout the month, I was subjected to severe beatings in front of my father. In the end, I gave in and agreed to work breaking stones from a nearby mountain in the city of Assab, in southeastern Eritrea, so they could be transported and used to pave the roads," he said mournfully as he sat beside his brother Tareq.
He said he spent daylight hours working alongside 20 fellow fishermen under close surveillance by Eritrean naval soldiers armed with rifles and batons.
Medical reports obtained by Al-Araby Al-Jadeed indicate that Tareq al-Nahari is suffering from a concussion and has undergone two head surgeries.
His treatment has cost more than seven million Yemeni rials ($12,500), and he can no longer afford further medical expenses.
Some of his fellow fishermen were also detained in 2023 and forced into hard labour, breaking stones and building a school in Assab under the supervision of naval soldiers.
The soldiers repeatedly beat them whenever their performance declined because of the scorching heat.
They were fed only flour bran, normally used as animal feed, in addition to a meal of lentils.
As a result, Yemeni fishermen flee immediately whenever they sense an Eritrean naval boat approaching. This has led to repeated cases of drowning and injuries at sea.
The consequences of division and war
On 18 May 2023, Mwatana for Human Rights, a Yemeni non-governmental organisation, announced that Eritrean naval forces had detained 69 Yemeni fishermen in three incidents between 2019 and 2022. Minors were among those detained and subjected to forced labour.
Meanwhile, fishermen whose testimonies were documented by this investigation, said 184 of their colleagues had been detained between the beginning of 2023 and January 2026. Of these, 95 remain in captivity.
However, sources agree that the actual number is much higher and that no official body has documented the total number of fishermen detained over the past years.
This is due to the political and security crises that have gripped Yemen for more than a decade, with serious consequences for traditional fishing.
While politicians have been preoccupied with the war, attacks by the Eritrean navy have escalated amid the difficult economic conditions facing fishermen and their families.
Fishermen either lose their lives or have their equipment seized by Eritrean naval forces before being taken to detention centres in Marsa Fatima, Assab, Massawa, Dahlak and Tiro, as well as Terma Island in eastern Eritrea.
Accounts also indicate that some detainees are transferred to Lesser Assab and forced to work for Eritrean project contractors.
They work throughout the day and return to detention centres only in the evening. They are not repatriated to Yemen until the project is completed.
Their return takes place in stages, beginning with the injured, the sick, the elderly and younger detainees unable to endure the hardships of the work.
Among them is Abdul Salam Bishara, a fisherman from al-Khawkhah in the southern Hodeidah governorate. He suffered a slipped disc after being forced to break stones on a mountain near Assab in 2017.
He received no medical assistance before being deported to Yemen.
"They left me only because I was no longer able to work," he said.
He added that when Eritrean authorities decide to release detainees, another crime reportedly follows.
Large numbers of released fishermen are crammed into unseaworthy boats and sent towards the Yemeni coast without any consideration for their safety.
Between 50 and 60 fishermen are placed on a boat that would normally accommodate no more than 30 people.
Al-Omaisi, the director-general of the al-Khawkhah district, described this as one of the crimes against humanity committed by the Eritrean armed forces.
Speaking to Al-Araby Al-Jadeed, he said Yemeni human rights organisations should defend the rights of these victims and file lawsuits against the Eritrean regime in international courts.
Violations of international law
Mohammed Amin, a lawyer at the Court of Appeal in Hodeidah, said the arbitrary detention, torture, enforced disappearance and coercion of fishermen into working under threat constituted serious violations of international law.
These acts could amount to enslavement and crimes against humanity when committed on a widespread or systematic basis.
To secure justice for the victims, Amin told Al-Araby Al-Jadeed that each case should be documented separately through the testimonies of survivors and witnesses, medical reports, photographs and documents, while identifying the date and place of detention and the authorities, individuals or officials responsible.
"After gathering the evidence, human rights organisations and victims' lawyers can submit case files to the relevant international bodies or explore the possibility of prosecution before national or international courts with jurisdiction. This would help ensure investigations, accountability, compensation and reparations for the victims," he added.
This view is shared by Colonel Abdul Ghani Abu Halfah, who has been tasked by the Sanaa authorities with following up on the treatment of injured people in government hospitals, both military and civilian.
He cited the case of Tareq al-Nahari, who was transferred to the military hospital in Sanaa. Abu Halfah noted that he is facing extremely difficult financial circumstances after becoming unable to work.
Between August and September, during this two-month-long investigation, 26 fishermen, most of them from al-Khawkhah, managed to return to Yemen. Port Director-General Ghali Qashr, the head of the Red Sea Fisheries Authority, Wael Abdul Wadoud, and al-Khawkhah Director-General Amjad al-Omaisi received them.
During their meeting with the officials, the returning fishermen confirmed that they had been in Yemeni territorial waters aboard two traditional wooden boats known as jalbah vessels when Eritrean naval boats attacked them and took them at gunpoint to Eritrean prisons.
Held in a prison in Assab, they endured torture and starvation before being forced into hard labor.
The Eritrean forces had seized a tonne of fish they had caught before their arrest, in addition to looting their fishing equipment.
They also took one of the boats, removed its engine and replaced it with an old, dilapidated one. Upon their return, the fishermen were forced to sail the vessel back to Hodeidah's shores, said al-Omaisi.
Seizing fishermen's livelihoods
Yemeni fisherman Musad Yusuf Zakhm, from Al-Khawkhah, said he was detained in June 2023 for two months alongside nine other fishermen in a prison in Assab.
During their detention, they were forced to cut and pave a road with stones near the city port after their boats had been intercepted and confiscated. They were also tortured and transferred to Lesser Assab, where they spent about 15 days before being released and deported to the city of Mokha.
He added that he had previously been detained in another incident, when he was abducted to Dahlak Island in mid-2022 and held for two months alongside 15 fishermen.
Their fishing equipment and supplies, including nets, refrigerators, the boat engine and its contents, were confiscated. The value of the seized property amounted to $10,000.
In another case, a fisherman estimated his losses at 18 million rials ($33,000), according to documentation examined by Mwatana for Human Rights.
For fishermen, confiscation means more than simply losing property: their boat represents their livelihoods and the means to provide for their families.
A timid official response
According to an official memorandum (No. 355) sent by Hussein Hamed al-Attas, chairman of the General Authority for Red Sea Fisheries, to Hodeidah Governor Abdullah Abdu Ahmed Ateifi on 21 February 2026, at least 95 Yemeni fishermen remain detained in Eritrean prisons.
Al-Omaisi, the director-general of al-Khawkhah, confirmed that violations against fishermen "take place almost daily, without any genuine official action to compensate the victims or prosecute the Eritrean authorities in international courts".
However, al-Omaisi emphasised that these crimes have no time limit for prosecution.
According to lawyer Amin, since Yemeni fishermen conduct their work under the ruling issued by the International Court of Arbitration in The Hague in 1998-1999, which demarcated the maritime boundary between the two countries, the abductions, torture, and forced labour they face constitute violations requiring accountability.
He explained that "what is happening to these fishermen violates Eritrean law, as they are subjected to abuses, have everything they own confiscated and are forced to work. It also violates international human rights law, which prohibits subjecting anyone to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment, and to arbitrary arrest or detention without a legal charge or a fair trial."
If Yemeni fishermen commit an offence, the appropriate measures under Eritrean law would be to confiscate any fish they are carrying and return them to their country, according to former Eritrean Supreme Court Judge Abdullah Khayyar.
He pointed out that Eritrea has no clear laws and that, even where laws exist, they are not enforced.
"Military rule and its consequences dominate the functioning of state institutions. Everything that happens is dealt with [...] through administrative and military procedures that fall outside the law," he told Al-Araby Al-Jadeed.
In light of all this, the internationally recognised Yemeni government has limited its response to calling on Eritrea to release the fishermen held in its custody.
However, these appeals do not always receive a response, according to a source at the Ministry of Agriculture, Irrigation and Fisheries in Aden, who declined to be named because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
The source cited a request made by the government in June 2020 for the release of detained fishermen and confiscated equipment.19 fishermen were released, while another 100 remained in detention.
Their suffering continues, with no solution in sight. Yet, as Issam al-Nahari said, fishermen cannot abandon their only source of livelihood.
"Death while searching for food to feed your children is better than dying of hunger."

Cities end contracts with Go Church following shocking Pano report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:41:48 UTC
19:41:48 KST

Flemish politicians have spoken out and cities have ended their relationship with Go Church following a VRT investigation uncovering exploitation, manipulation and sexual assault of young people involved in the religious organisation
Officials in Leuven, Mechelen, Sint-Niklaas and Turnhout, among other Flemish cities, have ended their rental contracts and other agreements with the religious organisation Go Church following a scathing report by VRT investigative programme Pano in collaboration with daily newspaper De Morgen.
The programme, which can be seen on VRT Max, interviewed more than 30 of the church’s former followers and went undercover to discover that the church recruits mostly vulnerable young people – often minors – and then manipulates them into giving money, working for free and cutting ties with family and friends who might question the church.
Pano began an investigation following an appeal on TikTok by a schoolteacher who teaches religious studies. “I want to warn young people,” she told VRT. “Go Church is destroying children. They pressure them into going to the church, and they manipulate them. This should not be allowed.”
What is Go Church?
Go Church is part of the Lighthouse Group of Churches, an international network with more than 7,600 churches worldwide and millions of online followers. In Belgium, the movement previously operated under the names Pleasant Surprise Church International (PSCI) and Mustard Seed Chapel International (MSCI).
The group is led by Dag Heward-Mills, a Ghanaian bishop who is highly revered within the movement. Followers address him as “Daddy” or “Prophet.” Go Church recruits new members at busy spots, such as train stations, specifically targeting young people.
According to the organisation itself, Go Church is active in Antwerp, Boom, Bruges, Brussels, Duffel, Ghent, Leuven, Mechelen, Sint-Niklaas and Turnhout. Around 450 people attend its services every week.
Go Church recruits young people on the street at busy locations such as train stations. It offers a fun atmosphere and personal attention, which appeals to teenagers and 20-something who are seeking connection.
Church leadership build personal relationships with its young members, visiting their homes and inviting them to theirs. The 20-year-old “Anna” is a typical example of how the church uses its youthful membership. She and other members of the church would go to their pastor’s home on a daily basis to “cook for him, do the grocery shopping and take him to work.”
When I didn’t answer their messages for a few days, they showed up at my door at 23.00
At one point, Anna sought comfort and advice from the pastor, and he sexually assaulted her. “I don’t even know how long it lasted; my head was in shutdown,” she said. It began a months-long experience of sexual abuse. “At one point, it turned into rape. Sometimes he raped me multiple times a week.”
The pastor, who had come from the UK to help grow the church in Belgium, opened bank accounts for a few girls and coerced them to putting all their money in the accounts, with which he paid his own expenses. When he was eventually called back to the UK, their money disappeared with him.
Many young people report similar grooming by church leaders. They are asked to provide their phone numbers and addresses. “When I didn’t answer their messages for a few days, they showed up at my door at 23.00,” one young woman said.
The church also insisted on approving any marriages, and they were encourage to marry only within the church, being told that outsiders would lead them straight to hell. Women were told that they needed to do the cooking and the cleaning and could not refuse their husbands sex.
If members dared to try to speak out, the church convinced other members to harass them on social media. Former church members continue to suffer trauma, and religious experts say that Go Church meets the criteria to be considered a cult.
Lack of judicial follow-up
Belgium has an agency where cult activity can be reported (IACSSO), but, according to federal parliamentarian Stefaan Van Hecke (Groen), the information collected there has not been followed up by State Security for a few years now. “There used to be 15 people in the State Security department who followed up on this,” he said, “but now there is literally no one.”
According to Van Hecke, State Security sees the problem as “from another century”. But that’s not the case, he says. “It’s always been here, but we just don’t have a view on it anymore.” He does recommend reporting any criminal activity to the IACSSO and to the local police.
In the meantime, cities are shutting down all ties with Go Church. “They meet in a city-owned neighbourhood house under the name of an individual,” said Mechelen mayor Bart Somers (Voor Mechelen). “We have ended that contract. There was an immediate response from a lawyer, very aggressive, trying to intimidate us. But we’re having none of that.”

Duchess of Sussex ‘deeply distressed’ over child sexual abuse image claims against father

The Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving child sexual abuse images against her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, and revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018 by the Metropolitan police.
Meghan issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother Thomas Markle Jr alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.
In an interview with the Daily Mail, Markle Sr denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”.
It is understood that authorities in the UK previously told Meghan that allegations made about her father in a 2018 letter sent to Scotland Yard, and subsequently shared with her by the police, were being investigated.
Meghan was informed by the Met of the allegations in the summer shortly after her wedding, it is believed.

“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
The 2018 letter was understood to have been shared with Meghan by the royalty and specialist protection unit within the Met police.
Markle Sr has been estranged from the duchess since he failed to attend her wedding to Prince Harry on health grounds, and he has never met his grandchildren Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.
The Sun reported that Thomas Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.
Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.
The undersecretary for the Philippine justice department, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC “the matter is currently being investigated” by a human trafficking and child sexual exploitation taskforce in Cebu.
The Philippine interior secretary, Jonvic Remulla, separately told the BBC that national police had secured Markle Sr’s computer in order to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination. Remulla said it would take “one week to get the forensic [results]”.
Meghan’s father has vehemently denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail that the accusations were “sick lies”.
He told the newspaper that the computers had not been in his possession since he left Rosarito, Mexico, with his son in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.
Speaking from a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk with a prosthetic limb after his left leg was amputated because of a blood clot, he told the Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.
“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

EU envoy signals progress on visa-free travel

European Union Ambassador to Türkiye Aivo Orav addressed members of the press at the EU Delegation’s headquarters in Ankara. (AA Photo)
European Union Ambassador to Türkiye Aivo Orav said Turkish officials had received instructions at the highest level to resolve outstanding issues related to six criteria required for visa liberalization, expressing cautious optimism about progress on the long-standing issue.
Speaking at a press conference, Orav said visa-related difficulties, including lengthy waiting lists and problems securing appointments, had been raised in almost all his meetings in Türkiye. “These issues need to be addressed systematically,” he said, adding that EU member states were trying to assign more staff to their consular services to ease the pressure on visa applications.
Orav stressed that visa liberalization remained important for both sides and said his recent discussions with Turkish politicians and public administration officials had been encouraging. “In my meetings in Türkiye, they say they have received instructions at the highest level to resolve the problems related to these six criteria,” he said.
The six outstanding criteria concern anti-terrorism legislation, data protection, Europol cooperation, anti-corruption measures, judicial cooperation and the implementation of the EU-Türkiye readmission agreement.
Visa liberalization would allow Turkish citizens to travel to the Schengen area for short stays without obtaining a visa.
Orav also called for a forward-looking approach to EU-Türkiye relations, acknowledging the difficult history between the two sides while emphasizing their mutual interests. “Türkiye needs the EU, and the EU needs Türkiye,” he said, urging diplomats to help political leaders focus on future cooperation.
He said the EU was ready to move forward, pointing to an increase in high-level contacts over the previous six months. In June and July, two EU leaders visited Türkiye within a two-week period, while the bloc’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy visited twice. Four European Commission members also made visits, he added.
Orav said the frequency of these contacts demonstrated that both sides had the tools and mechanisms needed to advance their relationship.

Hijab ban in Azerbaijan raise fears over religious freedom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:39:35 UTC
19:39:35 KST

Breadcrumb
'I have a right to study': The Azerbaijani schoolgirls shut out of class over their hijabs
"I want to study. I have my hijab on, but they are not letting me study. I have a right to study," a distressed Azerbaijani schoolgirl was filmed saying in a video posted online, passionately advocating for her right to attend school like other children while wearing an Islamic headscarf.
Across Azerbaijan, pupils and teachers wearing hijabs have reportedly been denied entry to schools since new regulations were implemented earlier this month.
The restrictions have prompted emotional scenes captured in online footage, with schoolgirls seen in tears and students looking on in distress as a visibly veiled teacher was dismissed from school premises.
The decision, approved last month, has sparked outrage both domestically and internationally, with human rights groups such as Amnesty International describing the restrictions as discriminatory.
Speaking to The New Arab, Amnesty International’s Eastern Europe and Central Asia director, Marie Struthers, emphasised that excluding pupils and teachers who wear the hijab from schools "violates their rights to education, and the freedoms of religion and expression."
School exclusions
The restrictions have also sparked protests across Azerbaijan, with local reports documenting demonstrations against the headscarf rules, involving girls wearing Islamic headscarves and boys joining their classmates in solidarity.
On Monday, the Ministry of Internal Affairs said it had detained 37 people for disrupting public order during the protests.
Struthers also called for the release of those detained.
"The international community should call upon Azerbaijani authorities to: reverse these discriminatory restrictions and ensure that affected pupils and teachers can return to school; immediately and unconditionally release anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights; and respect the right to peaceful protest and all human rights," she said.
Struthers cited recent Amnesty reporting on the detention of Shahizyar Huseynova, the wife of Azerbaijani Muslim activist Aga Huseynov.
She was reportedly arrested last Wednesday after protesting outside a school in Baku, where their daughter had been refused entry the previous day.
"According to [Huseynov], she has been detained for four months, and the charges against her have not been provided."
Struthers also cited other reports the organisation received, including one about activist Matanat Turan (Mahmarzayeva), who is affiliated with the Azerbaijan People’s Front Party (APFP).
On Sunday, a court in the Azerbaijani city of Sumgayit reportedly imposed a two-month preventive measure on Turan after she protested against the headscarf restrictions in Khirdalan.
She added: "Ilkin Huseynov, an activist who had launched a free online platform connecting volunteer teachers with children excluded from school, including for wearing hijabs, went missing on 14 October after leaving his Baku home accompanied by unidentified people."
Growing protests amid a regional fallout
Smuthers’ urgent calls reflect concerns voiced across the country, as the controversial ban has escalated into a regional dispute, with ally Turkey declaring its firm opposition to Baku’s decision.
Oktay Saral, an adviser to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, criticised the restrictions on hijabs in Azerbaijani schools, prompting President Ilham Aliyev’s ruling party to accuse Turkish figures of interfering in Azerbaijan’s domestic affairs.
Ankara’s condemnation of the hijab ban has prompted a fierce backlash from the Azerbaijani government, which has barred 31 Turkish nationals from entering the country, including Fatih Erbakan, leader of Turkey’s New Welfare Party.
Caught in the middle of the public feud, however, are Azerbaijan’s women and girls, whose lives are being affected by the new school regulations in a country where 96 per cent of the population identifies as Muslim.
Rafig Shahbazov, a Georgia-based journalist covering developments in Azerbaijan, told TNA that there was currently “no publicly available comprehensive official figure showing how many students or teachers have been affected nationwide” by the restrictions.
He said there was also no comprehensive information on how many schools had implemented the rules, how many pupils had missed classes or whether the restrictions were being enforced consistently across the country.
However, Shahbazov stressed that continuing reports of hijab-wearing pupils and teachers being turned away from schools suggested that "the issue has not been confined to one school or a single district."
"The first protest videos I encountered came from Jalilabad, after which reports and footage emerged from Baku and surrounding villages, as well as Sumqayit and other locations," Shahbazov added.
"Baku’s School No. 69 and the school in Mollaoba village in Masalli district are among the locations mentioned in reporting and discussions surrounding the restrictions."
Shahbazov also noted that, based on publicly available evidence, students, teachers, and parents responded in various ways, including expressing solidarity with girls and women who wear the hijab.
"Some students have continued to attend school wearing hijabs despite the restrictions, while others have reportedly been prevented from entering classrooms," Shahbazov told The New Arab.
In some locations, male classmates have reportedly refused to attend lessons in solidarity with girls who were denied access.
Protesters have used slogans such as ‘Freedom for the hijab’ and ‘Let the girls go to school’, framing the issue as one of access to education as well as religious freedom.
"Parents have also challenged the restrictions. Some have protested outside schools after their daughters were reportedly refused entry," Shahbazov added.
"For many families, the central concern is not simply whether a particular item of clothing is permitted, but whether girls should have to choose between practising their faith and continuing their education. Teachers have expressed concern about the impact on their professional lives and personal religious choices."
Protests involving schoolchildren are unusual in Azerbaijan. The demonstrations have also prompted a social media campaign, with protest footage spreading online.
However, local users have since reported disruptions to access to Instagram and TikTok in the country, raising questions about the authorities’ response to the growing controversy.
Internet monitoring groups have also documented restrictions on access to the platforms, but Azerbaijani authorities have not explained the reported disruptions.
Legal questions
The growing controversy follows a series of legal changes, beginning with amendments to Azerbaijan’s general education law that reaffirmed the principle of secular education and required pupils and teachers to comply with school dress codes.
Subsequent regulations prohibited additional clothing deemed to disrupt the standard uniform or conflict with secular education.
Although the school rules do not explicitly mention the hijab, they have since been interpreted in ways that restrict the wearing of Islamic headscarves.
Emin Abbasov, an Azerbaijani human rights lawyer and chair of the Independent Lawyers Network (ILN), told The New Arab that the secularism requirement introduced under the new regulations "amounts to a ban on expressing religious belief through clothing in state schools."
He added: "Wearing religious clothing is a protected manifestation of belief which is a core part of freedom of religion both in national and international law. Restrictions must therefore have a sufficiently clear legal basis, pursue a legitimate aim and be necessary and proportionate. A general reference to secularism does not, by itself, establish that excluding pupils or teachers wearing a hijab meets these requirements."
Abbasov continued: "The vague requirement to dress ‘in accordance with secularism’ also raises questions about foreseeability and the scope for arbitrary enforcement and its impacts."
The ILN chief also cited reports by his organisation, which found that pupils and teachers wearing hijabs were reportedly denied entry to schools across Azerbaijan since October 12, sparking warnings that such restrictions raise serious concerns about freedom of religion, equality and access to education.
"The justifications appeared in state officials and pro-governmental media refer to social equality, secular education and protecting girls from religious coercion require careful scrutiny," Abbasov told The New Arab.
"However, protecting children from coercion is a legitimate concern, as is ensuring neutrality and secularity in education, but the authorities failed to demonstrate the problem of coercion and alternative — less intrusive measures such as education at schools on secularism, increased civil society role in promoting secularity, etc."
He added: "Excluding a girl from school because of her clothing risks punishing the very child the state claims to protect. It can interrupt her education, deepen isolation and undermine her future independence."
Abbasov argued that an outright ban "is a clear intervention in the right to believe of citizens," adding that it also infringes on the right to education and, for teachers, constitutes “a breach of employment rights."
The head of the ILN cited constitutional protections and international law safeguarding freedom of belief and the right to education.
He added that Azerbaijan’s government must, under both international law and the country’s constitution, adhere to key legal principles, including necessity and proportionality.
Rights at risk
In response to the backlash, Azerbaijani authorities have blamed Iranian influence for stirring division in the country — in addition to alleged Turkish influence.
More ethnic Azerbaijanis live in Iran than in Azerbaijan itself.
Azerbaijan’s State Service for Special Communications and Information Security alleged that a "foreign hacker group" had attacked more than 100 state websites on the night of 13 October.
Abbasov criticised the government’s "divisive narratives," describing the accusations of foreign influence involving Iran, Turkey and people of Arab backgrounds as "absolutely unacceptable and very harmful."
He warned that such rhetoric risked deepening isolation and perpetuating harm against the women and girls affected by the ban.
"From what we see from the protests, mostly by the secular parts of Azerbaijan, supporting religious people or the young girls and women wearing hijabs, it shows that society is not convinced that it faces any religious fundamentalism or any harm," Abbasov told The New Arab.
"The Azerbaijani government now wants to divide society between secular and religious people. And it needs somehow a foreign influence, a foreign enemy and new threats in society in order to govern or to continue governing Azeris with coercive and repressive methods that society does not want to continue."
He continued: "There are no threats; there is no reason to take any measure for protecting secularity in Azerbaijan."
The New Arab contacted Azerbaijan’s Ministry of Science and Education for comment but had not received a response by the time of publication.
However, Azerbaijani officials have continued to defend the ban in public statements.
MP Nigar Arpadarai alleged that children did not choose to wear the hijab themselves but were influenced by their families.
"A child has no freedom to choose a religion. This is a conscious prerogative of adults," she told the 1news.az website.
After decades of Soviet rule, Azerbaijan emerged as one of the most secular states in the Muslim world.
Under President Ilham Aliyev, the country has maintained a poor human rights record, with the government repeatedly targeting journalists, activists and independent politicians.
Human rights organisations have long accused Aliyev’s administration of intensifying its crackdown on freedom of speech.
Assiah Hamed is a staff writer at The New Arab

Kazakhstan approves 2026-29 plan to develop unmanned systems
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23

19:38:25 KST

Kazakhstan approves 2026-29 plan to develop unmanned systems
Kazakhstan has approved a comprehensive plan to develop unmanned systems between 2026 and 2029, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The relevant government resolution was signed by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov on October 13, 2026.
The plan aims to establish the legal framework, infrastructure and incentives needed to advance unmanned technologies across Kazakhstan, improve economic efficiency and strengthen the country’s export potential.
Under the plan, Kazakhstan intends to launch a unified digital platform for unmanned systems and introduce an Unmanned Aircraft System Traffic Management (UTM) system. It also provides for the establishment of at least two research and development (R&D) centers.
Workforce development is another key priority. The plan calls for training at least 1,000 specialists, including drone operators, design engineers, embedded software developers, UTM specialists, cybersecurity professionals and maintenance technicians.
Kazakhstan also plans to expand domestic production capabilities by developing the assembly, testing and servicing of unmanned systems. Additional measures will focus on manufacturing critical components, secure software and artificial intelligence models locally.
Unmanned technologies are expected to be introduced across agriculture, transportation and logistics, public services and industry.
The plan also seeks to establish a sustainable domestic market involving government agencies, businesses, universities, national companies and the Astana Hub autonomous cluster fund.
Implementation will be overseen by the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development. The responsible authorities will be required to report regularly on the progress of planned activities and the achievement of established targets.
Earlier, Qazinform reported the NVIDIA CEO hailed Kazakhstan’s ambitious push to build an AI economy.

Across China: Herder photographers document snow leopards and beyond in China's "water tower"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:36:38 CST
19:36:38 KST

XINING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- On a craggy rock in a grand canyon in northwest China's Qinghai Province, Sangdrup raises his camera, scanning the rugged cliffs for a glimpse of wildlife.
From the forests flanking the gorge, white-lipped deer, blue-eared pheasants and blue sheep emerge from time to time, becoming the subjects of Sangdrup's lens. The autumn air carries the scent of grass and trees, while the Lancang River rushes below.
The 32-year-old Tibetan is among a cohort of herders who have taken up cameras at the Sanjiangyuan National Park, serving as wildlife photographers, grassroots guardians and caretakers for injured animals.
Established five years ago as part of China's first batch of national parks, Sanjiangyuan is the largest and highest. Covering 190,700 square km in the heart of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, it guards the headwaters of the Yangtze, Yellow and Lancang rivers at an average elevation exceeding 4,700 meters.
On his daily patrols, Sangdrup has made a habit of photographing wild flowers and animals, both as a record of his rounds and as a precious gift for future generations.
What he wants to capture most is the snow leopard, dubbed "the king of snow mountains."
Born and raised on the grasslands, Sangdrup first heard about snow leopards from his family as a child.
"All I knew was that they were beautiful and mysterious, like a big cat, but none of my pals around had ever seen one," he recalled.
His first encounter came in 2018, when he was on patrol at dawn and a grayish-white animal darted across the slope in front of him. In that instant, Sangdrup realized it was a snow leopard. He froze, then fumbled for his phone and pressed the shutter.
"I felt nothing but sheer awe," he later recalled. "I was so thrilled that I forgot there could be danger."
Looking at the blurry figure on the small screen, Sangdrup felt both excitement and regret: the phone's low resolution had spoiled a rare close-range opportunity.
Soon after, he spent a substantial sum on his first professional camera. At first, he knew little about technique -- aperture, ISO, shutter speed -- and could only fumble his way through, as few people around him knew photography then.
"I was afraid of breaking the camera by messing with the settings, so I basically stuck to auto mode," he said. "But I just loved taking pictures."
On every patrol, he would head out with his camera and keep shooting until the battery died before going home.
With constant trial and error, his photos kept improving. White-lipped deer, leopards, vultures, golden eagles, and blue sheep began appearing frequently in his photographs, but snow leopards remained his main subject.
To capture better images, Sangdrup has come to know the snow leopard's habits well. "Blue sheep are their main prey. Where you see a large herd, a snow leopard won't be far away," he said, adding that the best months are January through May.
In Sanjiangyuan National Park, 20,800 herders have been hired as rangers. Together with professional rescue teams, they have found and helped rescue many wild animals in need, including two snow leopard cubs that were not suitable for release and have now become public favorites at the Xining Wildlife Zoo in Xining, the provincial capital, drawing tens of millions of views online.
The snow leopard is under first-class national protection in China and is listed as vulnerable by the International Union for Conservation of Nature.
China is home to about 60 percent of the world's snow leopard habitats. The Sanjiangyuan area is one of the areas with the highest snow leopard density in the country and the world.
According to survey results released in early 2025, the average snow leopard population density in the Sanjiangyuan area is about 0.9 individuals per 100 square km, with an estimated total population of around 1,002.
The herder photographers' images are no longer private keepsakes. In 2023, a documentary film "Snow Leopards and Friends," partly filmed by three local herders, won the Best Documentary award at the 36th China Golden Rooster Awards, one of the country's top film awards.
For 35 days, the team camped near a den, capturing rare close-up footage of a mother snow leopard nursing her cubs without disturbing them.
"We wanted the world to see the snow leopard in its most natural state," said Konchok Choephel, one of the filmmakers.
In 2021, China established its first national parks: the Sanjiangyuan National Park, the Giant Panda National Park, the Northeast China Tiger and Leopard National Park, the Hainan Tropical Rainforest National Park and the Wuyishan National Park.
The five national parks cover a total area of 230,000 square km and incorporate more than 120 nature reserves of various types and levels.
By implementing a series of measures such as habitat restoration, ecological corridor connectivity, and regulation of human activities, the five national parks have delivered notable ecological successes over the past five years.
For example, as "the water tower of China," Sanjiangyuan National Park has significantly enhanced its water conservation capacity, channeling an average of 80 billion cubic meters of high-quality water downstream annually. Degraded grasslands have turned green, rivers run clearer, and populations of Tibetan antelopes, also under China's first-class national protection, have rebounded from less than 20,000 to over 70,000.
As China marks the fifth anniversary of the national parks, a photography exhibition was held in Qinghai earlier this month, showcasing 100 images by ecological photographers and rangers. The photos depicted snow-capped peaks, rare wildlife and the harmonious coexistence of herders and nature in the province.
"We hope these images help more people understand the achievements of national park construction and encourage wider participation in protecting our shared home," said an official from the provincial forestry and grassland bureau. ■

7.0-magnitude Xizang quake an extensional fracture: expert
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:36:24 CST
19:36:24 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The 7.0-magnitude earthquake that struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Thursday was an extensional rupture, according to experts with the China Earthquake Networks Center (CENC).
The quake occurred at around 10:33 p.m., causing heavy casualties. Focal mechanism solutions show the event was basically consistent with regional tectonic characteristics.
"An extensional fracture, in simple terms, occurs when the crust is stretched horizontally and, under tension and gravity, faultage slides downward along existing faultage, forming fractures and rupture surfaces," said Han Yanyan, a senior engineer with the earthquake prediction department of the CENC.
The CENC explained that the collision between the Indian and Eurasian plates had caused the uplift of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, crustal shortening and thickening, and widespread plateau deformation. These processes are the main dynamic mechanism controlling tectonic deformation in the western part of the Chinese mainland.
The interior of the plateau is subjected to both north-south compression and east-west extension, and two typical fault systems, trending roughly north-south and east-west, have developed there.
"The epicenter is located within the Changtang block of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, about 2 km from the nearest fault, the Baqen-Riwoqe fault," Han said.
Under such intense crustal deformation, the Changtang block and its surrounding fault zones are particularly active. Since 1900, the block has experienced six earthquakes of magnitude 7 or above, including this one. The largest was a 7.5-magnitude earthquake in Shuanghu on Nov. 8, 1997.
"Therefore, this earthquake was an energy release of the Changtang block," Han said. ■

Thailand to mandate safety standards for EV batteries
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
18:36:22 CST
19:36:22 KST

BANGKOK, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Thailand plans to impose mandatory safety standards on electric vehicle (EV) batteries covering their manufacture, import and sale, the government said on Friday, as the country seeks to build confidence in its growing EV industry.
The standard applies to non-lead-acid rechargeable batteries in battery-electric passenger and goods vehicles with at least four wheels. It requires protection against overcharging, overheating, and short circuits, said deputy government spokesperson Lalida Periswiwatana.
Under a draft ministerial regulation, manufacturers and importers would need licenses under Thailand's Industrial Product Standards Act, while retailers would only sell products that are licensed and meet the standard.
The rules would take effect 180 days after publication in the official Royal Gazette. Businesses are advised to follow the progress of the regulation and prepare for product standards, testing, and licensing requirements, Lalida said in a statement.
Beyond pre-market safety controls, the Ministry of Industry has also been asked to study how to track batteries after their service life ends. Lalida said the work remains at the consideration stage and is not yet a take-back or mandatory recycling scheme.
The government wants Thailand's EV industry to grow with quality, not just by increasing production capacity or sales, she said, adding that this approach would build consumer confidence, strengthen the competitiveness of the Southeast Asian country's EV industry, and drive the economy alongside sustainable environmental care. ■

Streeting declines to discuss Faslane shelters
United Kingdom

19:30:29 KST

The Secretary of State for Defence has declined to discuss reported ballistic shelters at Faslane in open session, telling the Defence Committee there is a difference between what others report and what the department is willing to say.
Wes Streeting was giving evidence to the committee on the work of his department.
Michelle Scrogham, the Labour member for Barrow and Furness, raised air and missile defence, noting the committee had heard that covering what is needed would cost a billion pounds per city. She said: “I am interested to hear it reported that Faslane is getting ballistic shelters. Are you looking at rolling that out in other areas?”
Streeting said: “There is a danger of my being dragged into a level of operational security detail that I would not want to share in this format.”
Scrogham replied: “It is public knowledge. It is in the UK Defence Journal.”
Streeting said: “There is a difference between what others report and what we are willing to say. Given the spirit in which we engage with this Committee, first, I would always be happy to try to share with the Committee in a closed format as much as we can of that which we would not want to share in an open session. Given your constituency interest in this, I can reassure you that the security of our nuclear deterrent and the enterprise that underpins it is obviously of the highest importance to us. I would be very happy to make sure that we properly brief you as the Member of Parliament for Barrow.”
Faslane on the Clyde is the base for the Vanguard class ballistic missile submarines that carry the continuous at-sea deterrent, and for the Astute class attack submarines. Coulport, a few miles away, stores and loads the warheads. Barrow-in-Furness, which Scrogham represents, is where the submarines are built by BAE Systems.
Earlier in the same exchange Streeting addressed homeland air defence more generally, saying the government is putting £790 million into integrated air and missile defence to modernise older systems and that a layered approach is needed. He noted that Luke Pollard had described the idea of an iron dome for Britain as an iron sieve.
Ministers confirmed in Parliament this month that a future requirement for hardened aircraft shelters across Royal Air Force bases in the United Kingdom has been identified, and that hardened shelters may form part of future infrastructure considerations at RAF Akrotiri in Cyprus.
The Defence Committee reported this week that Russian submarine and sabotage forces in the High North pose direct risks to the North Atlantic and to Britain, including to the nuclear deterrent, and that failure to deter Russia from underwater threats puts subsea data cables and energy pipelines in British waters at particular risk.

TDM Neo Hybrid Headphones Review: Two-in-One Woes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Unveiled at CES 2026, the TDM Neo is a pair of on-ear headphones that transform into a Bluetooth speaker. It caught the imagination of the attending media, won a handful of awards, and inspired countless column inches.
Given the current state of the portable audio industry, it's easy to understand why. Most designs seem to revolve around incremental updates and new colorways rather than genuine technical innovation. Neo is an exciting alternative, and it’s little wonder the startup brand went on to smash its Kickstarter targets.
I’ve spent the past couple of weeks listening to the headphones and Bluetooth speaker, and have lost count of the number of times I’ve showed off the clever twist-and-fold mechanism to friends. But has TDM managed to produce a genuine tech twofer, or designed a novelty product that gives you the worst of both worlds?
Twist and Shout
The twist-and-fold mechanism on the Neo is clever and addictive. Rotate the ear cups around the cushioned but flexible headband, bring them together, and strong magnets snap everything firmly in place. Once connected, the headphone drivers disable, and the outward-facing Bluetooth speakers kick in. Twist them apart and you've got your headphones back.
It’s innovative, and the engineering is impressive. Once in speaker mode, the two rubber TDM logos sit closely together and form a protective base, while the asymmetrical twisted headband cocoons the ear cups together. It works well—it never once popped open accidentally. The action is smooth, the connection reassuringly solid, and switching between modes works exactly as intended.
The Neo has four 40-mm drivers—two for the headphones and two for the speakers. The outward-facing speakers are each rated at 5 watts (for a total of 10). Ten watts is not a lot for a modern Bluetooth speaker, but wattage doesn't automatically tell you how loud or good a speaker will sound, especially in the current age of digital signal processing. The highly regarded $55 JBL Go 5 has just 4.5 watts of output, for instance.

Loader Monteith expands red-brick bungalow within "remarkably compact footprint" near Manchester
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

Loader Monteith expands red-brick bungalow within “remarkably compact footprint” near Manchester
Scottish architecture studio Loader Monteith has transformed a two-bed, red-brick bungalow into a four-bedroom family home in Prestwich, UK.
Described by the studio as “squeezing a quart into a pint pot”, the project involved expanding and reorganising the 69-square-metre home in the town near Manchester to accommodate a growing family and improve connections to a rear garden.
Loader Monteith designed a rear brick extension that opens up the home’s living spaces to the garden, while a new upper floor has been nestled beneath a dormer roof.
“The challenge was to maximise the space without compromising on architectural ambition,” studio co-founder Matt Loader told Dezeen.
“We developed the design in response to the existing house and its local context, creating appropriately scaled additions that respect the surrounding architecture,” Loader added.
“This delivers four bedrooms and two bathrooms within a remarkably compact footprint.”
The extension was designed by Loader Monteith for clients Matt and Angie Maurer, who took on much of the project’s construction themselves.
“Taking on so much of the work ourselves meant we also had to find the right contractors and suppliers who understood our vision and cared about the details in the same way we did,” Matt Maurer told Dezeen.
“Both clients were keen to embrace an ambitious architectural solution,” Loader added.
The home’s front elevation is marked by a green-toned, copper entryway that contrasts with its red-brick walls and clay roof tiles.
This is complemented by the angular red-brick extension at the home’s rear, which is also framed by copper detailing and topped with a sedum roof.
“We began by analysing the local architecture of Prestwich, where red brick predominates,” Loader said.
“We used brick for the new extensions, incorporating decorative corbelling and folded details inspired by local architectural patterns.”
At the front of the home, the living spaces have been relocated to accommodate two street-facing bedrooms, including one ensuite, along with a study, utility room and toilet.
Behind this, the kitchen, living and dining spaces are organised as a trio of interconnected spaces within the rear extension.
Steps between the spaces lead down to the sunken dining and living area, which sit level with the garden and open onto it through sliding doors.
“The challenge was fitting so much accommodation into such a small house while making it feel generous and improving its connection to the garden,” Loader said.
At the centre of the plan, a skylit staircase leads up to the newly-added first floor, where the primary ensuite bedroom and an additional bedroom and bathroom are located.
A pared-back material palette is used throughout the home, including concrete floors and white walls set off by exposed timber joinery.
Other UK home extensions recently featured on Dezeen include the expansion of a Grade II-listed rectory in the Cotswolds by Prest Vale Architects and the renovation of a terraced home in London by Polysmiths using “light as the primary material”.
