Trump Invokes Defense Production Act to Boost Oil Production
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

President Donald Trump has invoked a Cold War-era law in an effort to boost oil production and lower energy prices.
In a presidential memorandum issued Thursday, Trump determined that petroleum production, refining, and related activities are essential to national defense under the 1950 Defense Production Act. The determination follows Trump’s declaration of a national energy emergency in January 2025.
“Ensuring resilient domestic petroleum production, refining, and logistics capacity is central to United States defense readiness,” the memo reads. “Without immediate Federal action, United States defense capabilities will remain vulnerable to disruption.”
The memo comes as the price of gas and diesel has soared across the country amid supply disruptions caused by the U.S. and Israel’s war against Iran. Brent crude futures rose 1.2% to $114.47 a barrel early Friday, extending gains after Thursday hit a five-month high. U.S. diesel pump prices averaged $6.32 a gallon, slightly higher than Thursday but below the September record, according to AAA. The high energy prices, and related inflation, have become a defining issue for voters in the coming midterm elections.
Here’s what to know.
What does the memo mean for energy production?
The memo means that energy production shortfalls are seen as a national defense risk.
The memo invokes Section 303 of the Defense Production Act, a law that allows the federal government to intervene in private industry for national defense. Section 303 allows the President to make purchases, purchase commitments, provide financial support and equipment, and expand production through other measures.
The memorandum also removes certain Section 303 requirements through an emergency waiver, including ordinary congressional notification and authorization constraints.
While the memo does not specify which projects could be funded, Vice President J.D. Vance said last week that the Administration would use the Defense Production Act to expand capacity at a Delek U.S. Holdings-owned refinery in Texas.
Without taking action, the memo said, U.S. industry would be unable to provide sufficient energy services in a “timely manner due to constrained financing, long lead times, permitting and infrastructure bottlenecks, and supply chain limitations.”
Has the Defense Production Act been invoked before?
Enacted during the Korean War, the Defense Production Act was first used to expand domestic industries in critical materials, such as aluminum and titanium, for national defense.
Section 303 of the act was also used during the pandemic to fund domestic production of medicines and vaccines. Former President Joe Biden also invoked the statute to support clean energy manufacturing and supply chains, including minerals used in electric vehicle batteries and the production of of energy-efficient heat pumps and insulation.
In April, more than a month after Iran began disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for U.S.-Israeli Feb. 28 strikes, Trump invoked the act to declare petroleum, natural gas, coal, electricity grid, and other energy infrastructure essential to national defense. Citing April’s natural gas determination, the Department of Energy on Monday committed up to $42 million to advance the proposed Constitution Pipeline linking Pennsylvania and New York. The department also announced up to $50 million last week for transmission upgrades in Virginia and West Virginia, citing April’s grid determination.
Last year, Trump signed legislation providing $1 billion for Defense Production Act activities, including energy projects deemed critical to national security.
Trump’s use of Section 303 of the act for fossil fuel projects has drawn criticisms from environmentalists, with the Center for Biological Diversity calling the April memoranda, which waived congressional notification, “unlawful.” Nevertheless, the statute expressly includes energy production and construction in its definition of national defense.
How else has Trump tried to lower energy prices?
The Trump Administration has pursued a number of other measures aimed at lowering energy prices since the Iran War began. Earlier this month, Trump signed an executive order temporarily expanding access to tax-exempt dyed diesel, which is typically reserved for off-road farm and construction vehicles. The Group of 7 countries, including the U.S., also agreed to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil reserves to the world over four months.
In August, the Administration extended the Jones Act waiver for another 90 days, allowing foreign-flagged ships to transport oil and certain other commodities between U.S. ports.
Trump also announced an agreement with Putin earlier this month to import diesel from Russia, alongside temporary sanctions relief. The deal has faced significant backlash from lawmakers.
For many of these measures, industry analysts and stakeholders have said the reduction in energy prices is likely to be limited and possibly short-lived. Analysts estimated that the Jones Act waiver was expected to reduce gasoline prices by only pennies per gallon. Capital Economics economist Hamad Hussain said the reserve release could lower diesel prices temporarily, but would not resolve the underlying supply crunch. And analysts warned that the dyed diesel measure would have a limited effect on most consumers since the tax-exempt fuel isn’t widely available at ordinary commercial pumps. A Council on Foreign Relations analysis also suggested that damaged Russian refining capacity may make a near-term effect of the Russia deal on diesel markets unlikely, although Trump said the agreement would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to U.S. and global markets immediately.
Meanwhile, oil exports from the Middle East topped prewar levels last week, marking a rebound in regional oil shipments despite continuing security risks. Ships sailing through the Strait of Hormuz, however, still face attacks from Iran, while the Bab el-Mandeb Strait near Yemen has been threatened by the Houthi rebels. Analysts previously told TIME in June that the risk of further attacks and damage to facilities could delay a full-scale recovery.
Thursday’s memorandum could support investment in fuel capacity, but it’s uncertain how quick or measurable an effect it will have on energy prices. Gas prices still depend heavily on globally traded crude, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration, although they can be influenced by domestic refining and distribution conditions. The U.S. was the largest crude producer globally last year, averaging 13.6 million barrels of crude a day.
Analysts warned, after the April memorandum, that federal support would not necessarily translate into immediate price relief.
“Until the pipes are in the ground and the fuel is flowing or transported, it may not be able to be called a true structural shift,” Cyrus Brooks, director of marketing at energy research firm RBAC, wrote in April.
Still, Brooks said of the April action that federal recognition of energy as important to national security could support important infrastructure investment, potentially relieving a bottleneck in domestic fuel production, refining or transportation.
“Energy security seems to be the brightest neon sign flashing,” he wrote. “Not because it’s everything, but because nothing works without it.”

A Dating App Is Offering ‘Chivalry Mode’ and ‘Marriage Timeline’ to Get Gen Z Married
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:15:00 UTC
19:15:00 KST

When Adreanna Pulliam signed up for the Christian dating app Upward over the summer, she was prepared to come across men who identified as hyperconservative.
So when she swiped on a guy’s profile that listed “a progressive donkey or a ‘Trump is King’ elephant” as his relationship deal-breaker, she was shocked. “I hadn’t expected to see a moderate libertarian” on the app, she says.
It only got more bizarre from there. There was the guy advertising his Snapchat with the username “Yaboi Blaze reallysexgod.” Another dater, for reasons she still can’t fathom, included a photo of him at a funeral, standing in front of a poster-size image of the deceased.
While Pulliam was apprehensive about the prospects, she wanted to see how different Upward, one of the lesser-known apps in Match Group’s sprawling portfolio of dating platforms, was from Hinge and Tinder. She hadn’t had much luck with either of them. Many of the profiles she encountered on Upward, she tells WIRED, were “MAGA types of men” who “fit more of that red-pill, trad wife, conservative values” category of dater.
A 25-year-old opera singer in Bloomington, Indiana, for whom marriage has always been “the end goal,” Pulliam is the kind of person Upward is trying to appeal to since relaunching last month.
The relaunch was redesigned around two key data points from Match Group’s 2026 Singles in America study: 72 percent of Gen Zs want to get married, and a quarter of singles aged 18 to 34 “identify with a combination of traditional values around family, faith, and community,” a news release about the survey noted.
The pivot away from an app exclusively for Christian daters was about opening up its doors for people “who share those same goals, but may not lead with a faith-first mindset,” says Lauren DeFord, director of brand marketing at Match, of the app’s new focus on Gen Z singles.
Upward’s expansion is representative of the ongoing change in the dating market. Dwindling engagement and the introduction of AI have pushed companies to reassess user growth. For some, that means abandoning their original mission.
Upward, which runs on a tiered subscription, works similarly to Tinder. You can swipe left or right on profiles, and users are encouraged to include a Faith Statement on their page, explaining what they value most about their relationship to God. Among its new features are Chivalry Mode, which, if you’re familiar with how Bumble used to operate, persuades men to message first, and Marriage Timeline, which lets daters share when they hope to get married with potential suitors.
But while a marriage-focused app like Upward may be tapping into a genuine desire for commitment, that doesn’t mean young people are returning to traditional relationship norms en masse, says Daniel Cox, author of Generation Uncoupled: America’s New Gender Divide and the Crisis of Human Connection. In fact, the opposite is happening.
In his book, Cox argues that Gen Z is entering adulthood with a less clear sense of their “relational priorities,” and a decline in social and civic life has given rise to a “hyperindividualistic culture” that doesn’t always prioritize things like marriage. As a result, fewer Gen Zs are coupling up today. An American Institute for Boys and Men survey found that 44 percent of Gen Z men have had no relationship experience at all during their teen years, double the rate for older men. “This movement makes it a lot harder to ... want to sacrifice and to be there for someone,” he says.
Upward’s relaunch framed the app as the “home of modern courtship,” including video testimonials of singles who’d found love on the app. But aesthetically, there wasn’t anything “modern” about its promotional rollout. In one video, newly married Zach donned a cowboy hat and blue jeans, doing all the things men should presumably do for their significant others: gift them flowers, carry her through a meadow, open the car door. A bold text overlay on the video read “chivalrymaxxing.” According to the company, branding was inspired by an “Americana” theme, and its “Wanted: For Life” campaign draws on Western-style imagery.
Cox, who is the director of the Survey Center on American Life, is convinced that the trad trend is “a reaction to the lack of cultural norms around courtship. People are wanting something over nothing,” he says, adding that daters are desperate for “a script” with direction and defined roles, given how nontraditional approaches to partnership, such as polyamory and relationship anarchy, are increasing among young people. “And something that’s nice about the trad script is it’s very clear. Though I don’t think it’s close to ideal for a lot of young people.”
A 2023 Pew Research survey found that only 23 percent of adults considered being married “extremely” or “very important” to living a fulfilling life, compared with 61 percent who said the same about having close friends. In the last 30 years, the percentage of high school seniors who said they were likely to marry someday had fallen from 80 percent in 1993 to 67 percent in 2023, according to Pew. The decline was driven mostly by changing views among young women who, despite the portion of married adults slightly increasing from 50 percent to 51 percent between 2019 to 2023, remain more likely than men to be unpartnered.
The trend is likely to continue in that direction. “There’s increasingly a belief among young women that marriage makes them less happy,” Cox says. “So it’s not only that they have less of a desire to get married. There’s a concern that if they get married, they won’t be as happy as if they are single. That seems like a view that is potentially not going to change.”
Upward, which declined to share information regarding the number of active users on the platform, is betting that it will.
When setting up her account, Pulliam was baffled to find out that Upward let users list their body type, ranging from “fit” and “curvy” to “chubby,” a feature typically reserved for hookup apps. She was also confused that Upward allows married people on the app. Some of the stranger options for relationship type included “it’s complicated” and “I’m not into labels.” “I’m not knocking open relationships or anything like that, but it was interesting to see such a progressive take from a more of a conservative demographic,” she says.
Tauti, a social work student who lives in California, lasted less than 48 hours on the app, disturbed by the overwhelming conservative majority looking for domesticated partners. Sometimes the hook with mission-specific apps like Upward is that the religious identity associated with the platform can create an assumption of compatibility before users have really gotten to know one another. “I did not know me being Christian and leaning liberal was a big ask,” she said on TikTok. “It’s turned me off from Christian dating altogether.”
Some users believe the recent pivot is diluting the experience for daters who joined seeking out people with purely Christian beliefs. “Why are you on there if you’re agnostic?” Heidi Marais, a teacher and single mom, asked on TikTok in September. “And Upward, why is it an option?”
DeFord, who maintains that Christian singles remain at the core of Upward’s mission despite describing the relaunch as a “brand shift,” pushes back against the assertion that the experience is worsening. “Those users can still interact and match with people who share the same denomination, the same religious views, the same cadence of how they like to practice.”
Since its debut in 2020, Upward has struggled with various hiccups that include everything from functionality issues to user perception. Many reviews in the Apple App Store complain of terrible user support, poor filtering features, and automatic bans, with one user calling the app “janky as hell.”
Cox notes there is ample reason to be wary of Match’s claim that a majority of Gen Z want to get married. Given that Gen Z is younger, it is likely that more people have never tied the knot. “So if they’re comparing Gen Z to millennials or Gen Xers in the survey, it could be that they have already been in relationships, maybe even divorced, so they are not as eager to get married again.” Match’s survey, which the company says is “demographically representative” of the US Census, sampled 5,000 US singles over the age of 18 who were not married, living with a partner, or in a committed relationship. In any case, Cox says, the “norm around what is the ideal age to get married” has vanished.
Pulliam still wants to get hitched but doesn’t consider it a priority right now. She attended a Christian college and recognizes the potential for Upward to be a hit “within communities of Christian private universities,” she says. “But I think the only way that the app works is for maybe someone who has a little bit more of a closed mind.”

Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:10:11 UTC
19:10:11 KST

Scientists discover a surprising double benefit of exercise for Parkinson’s
- Date:
- October 23, 2026
- Source:
- American Academy of Neurology
- Summary:
- A seven-year study found that people with Parkinson’s disease who were more physically active experienced slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement abilities. Those exercising more than eight hours per week showed almost no average cognitive decline, suggesting that staying active may offer important benefits as the disease progresses.
- Share:
People with Parkinson's disease who are more physically active may experience slower declines in memory, thinking, and movement, according to a new study published October 7, 2026, in Neurology, the official medical journal of the American Academy of Neurology.
The findings suggest that staying active could offer two important advantages for people living with Parkinson's. However, researchers emphasize that the study identified a connection between physical activity and slower symptom progression. It does not establish that exercise directly causes the disease to progress more slowly.
"Parkinson's disease is a brain disorder that causes movement and cognitive problems that gradually worsen leading to disability and a loss of independence," said study author Dong-Woo Ryu, MD, PhD, of the University of Cincinnati in Ohio. "Previous research has shown associations between physical activity and movement symptoms. Our study found physical activity may have dual benefits, with associations with slower declines in movement and cognition."
Tracking Exercise and Parkinson's Symptoms Over Seven Years
The research involved 294 adults with mild to moderate Parkinson's disease. Participants were 66 years old on average, and researchers monitored their health for up to seven years.
To understand their activity habits, participants completed questionnaires estimating how many hours each week they spent being physically active. The questions covered activities performed at work, around the home, and during hobbies or recreation.
Researchers classified activities by their intensity. Moderate activities included brisk walking, doubles tennis, leisurely swimming, and household tasks such as cleaning windows, vacuuming, or mowing the lawn. More demanding activities included running, cycling at higher speeds, participating in team sports, playing singles tennis, shoveling, and carrying heavy objects.
The team examined physical activity in three ways. First, they calculated the total time participants spent doing moderate or vigorous activities. Second, they estimated overall activity volume by combining duration with intensity, giving greater weight to strenuous exercise. Third, they separately measured the amount of time spent doing vigorous activities.
Based on total weekly activity time, participants were placed into three categories. Those in the least active group reported up to four hours per week, the moderately active group reported four to eight hours, and the most active group reported more than eight hours.
Each year, participants also completed assessments designed to track changes in thinking and memory, along with tests evaluating the severity of their Parkinson's symptoms.
More Activity Linked to Slower Memory Decline
One of the most striking differences emerged in cognitive performance. Researchers used a 30-point test of thinking and memory, with lower scores reflecting poorer cognitive function.
Among participants in the least active group, scores fell by an estimated average of 0.478 points each year. The moderately active group experienced a much smaller annual decline of 0.090 points.
For the most active participants, the estimated average yearly decrease was only 0.007 points, indicating that their cognitive scores remained nearly unchanged over time.
The researchers also examined changes in Parkinson's movement symptoms using an assessment scored from zero to 132. Higher numbers represented more severe symptoms, and participants began the study with an average score of 23.
In the least active group, symptom scores increased by an estimated 0.143 points annually, indicating a slight worsening. By contrast, scores decreased by 0.225 points per year in the moderately active group and by 0.783 points in the most active group.
Even after accounting for participants' age, sex, and how long they had been living with Parkinson's, the researchers found that the most active group experienced slower cognitive decline and less worsening of movement symptoms than the least active group.
The connection was not limited to one measure of exercise. Higher total activity time, greater overall activity volume, and more time spent exercising vigorously were each associated with slower deterioration in both thinking abilities and movement symptoms.
Why Consistent Physical Activity May Matter
The results suggest that remaining physically active over time could be especially important for people with Parkinson's disease. Researchers noted that even relatively small differences in the rate of decline might become more significant when they accumulate over several years.
"The possible benefits of physical activity for people with Parkinson's disease may depend on how long they stay active and whether they continue exercising over time," said Ryu. "While our study found small differences between activity levels, these differences may become more meaningful over time. Since participants generally had good thinking and memory skills at the start of the study, our results should be interpreted with caution and further studies are needed."
The researchers also identified an important limitation. Physical activity levels were based on participants' own reports rather than direct measurements, meaning some estimates may have been inaccurate.
Although the findings strengthen the evidence connecting physical activity with better long-term outcomes in Parkinson's disease, additional research will be needed to determine whether exercise itself can slow the progression of symptoms.
Funding for the study came from a grant provided by the Gardner Family Foundation and the Precision Medicine in Neurodegenerative Diseases Fund.
Story Source:
Materials provided by American Academy of Neurology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Dong-Woo Ryu, Kevin R. Duque, Luca Marsili, Jesus Abanto, Nathaly Chinchihualpa Paredes, Heba A. Deraz, Andrea Herrera Gorriti, Emily J. Hill, Abhimanyu Mahajan, Andrew Duker, Alberto J. Espay. Physical Activity and Motor and Cognitive Progression in Parkinson Disease. Neurology, 2026; 107 (9) DOI: 10.1212/WNL.0000000000218682

- The army said it “eliminated two terrorists” and launched raids and arrests in Hebron. Netanyahu praised the soldiers and vowed to “pursue Hamas terrorists” everywhere.
- Hamas praised the attack as a “heroic operation”, while tensions stay high in the West Bank. AFP says 1,113 Palestinians and 49 Israelis have been killed since October 2023.
AI generated
HEBRON, West Bank – Palestinian militants wounded five Israelis in an attack on Oct 23 before being killed in a prolonged shoot-out with soldiers, leading Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to order a lockdown in the occupied West Bank days before Israeli elections.
Netanyahu, facing a tight race for a new term in the election on Oct 27, said that Israeli troops prevented what could have been a major attack, with the two assailants allegedly carrying a large quantity of ammunition in their vehicle.
An AFP journalist who witnessed the gun battle saw two Palestinian men armed with a handgun and an automatic rifle exchanging fire with Israeli forces at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint near the Palestinian city of Hebron.
Israeli forces eventually shot and killed the attackers, with the AFP journalist seeing their two lifeless bodies on the ground next to a petrol station as troops patrolled all around.
The Israeli military said soldiers had rushed to the Judea Junction area after the early-morning shooting attack and “eliminated two terrorists”.
The attack wounded five people, two of whom were in a critical condition, said Magen David Adom, Israel’s emergency medical rescue service.
The service said all five were Israelis in their 20s, including one man in a “very serious condition” with gunshot wounds.
With the clock counting down to election day, Netanyahu called for all Likud party political meetings to be cancelled on Oct 23 due to the attack.
“I salute the courage of our soldiers who acted with determination and prevented what could have been a major attack,” Netanyahu said in a statement.
“I have instructed the IDF (army) and security forces to impose an immediate cordon on the city of Hebron and to prepare for a full lockdown of all of Judea and Samaria starting today,” Netanyahu said, using the biblical name for the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
He added that troops were “carrying out stepped-up operations to thwart terrorist activities and are conducting large-scale waves of arrests”.
The military said it had “launched offensive counter-terrorism operations in the Hebron area”, adding that troops were raiding homes of the suspects and others.
Hamas praises attack
Israeli National Security Minister and far-right firebrand Itamar Ben Gvir, who has been rising in the polls, called for the Ramallah-based Palestinian Authority to be dismantled because of the attack.
“The Palestinian Authority must be dismantled and demilitarised, and its terror infrastructure wiped out completely,” he said in a statement.
No evidence suggests that the Palestinian Authority, the Palestinian government in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, was connected to the Oct 23 attack.
Hamas, which is based in Gaza and carried out the Oct 7, 2023, attack – the deadliest in Israel’s history – hailed what it called an “exceptional heroic operation” near Hebron and mourned the two dead assailants, without claiming responsibility.
The attack is a “natural and legitimate response to the ongoing crimes and brutal attacks against our people”, Hamas, the rival of the Palestinian Authority’s ruling Fatah faction, said in a statement.
Netanyahu in his statement vowed to “pursue Hamas terrorists” everywhere, adding: “You have no place to hide.”
Gadi Eisenkot, the former army chief who is Netanyahu’s top rival in the election, praised the response by troops.
“Like all Israelis, I pray for the complete and quick recovery of the injured,” he said.
The incident comes as tensions soar in the West Bank, including over attacks by extremist Israeli settlers against Palestinian olive harvesters.
According to an AFP tally based on data from the Palestinian health ministry, Israeli forces or settlers have killed 1,113 Palestinians in the territory since the start of the Gaza war in October 2023.
Israeli figures show at least 49 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations during the same period. AFP

Russia develops advanced Titan robotic demining system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:09:44 UTC
19:09:44 KST

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russian specialists have created the Titan advanced robotic demining system, the system’s developer told TASS.
"To address the challenge of clearing mine and explosive obstacles using robotic systems amid the enemy’s widespread use of anti-personnel mines and improvised explosive devices in the special military operation zone, the latest robotic demining system, Titan, has been developed. The use of electric motors, a low-profile design, and all-round fragmentation protection against all known performed fragments of anti-personnel engineering munitions ensure stealth during missions and the necessary survivability. The system has increased blast resistance. According to our information, there are no counterparts with comparable quality of equipment and protection being used on either side of the line of contact," a company representative stated.
The system is designed to clear a continuous route through anti-personnel minefields by sweeping away the main types of anti-personnel mines. "The Titan enables the sweeping of mines equipped with pressure-action, pull-action, and break-wire target-sensors," he noted.
He specified that the system has successfully completed testing and is expected to be deployed in the special military operation zone. "Work is currently underway to improve the level of protection, add new controls, and refine the design of the sweeping equipment," he added.
The system’s total weight is 2.3 metric tons, and its payload capacity is one ton. "The Titan’s maximum speed with the sweeping equipment is seven km/h, and without it - 14 km/h. The system is capable of operating autonomously for at least 3.5 hours. The sweep width is two meters. If necessary, the Titan can be equipped with electronic warfare capabilities. The system’s control range depends on the type of communication used but is at least 500 meters," the developer added.

MOSCOW, October 23. /TASS/. Russia completely recognizes the importance of maintaining stable and predictable relations with the United States, a senior Russian Foreign Ministry official said on Friday.
"Russia’s approach to relations with the United States is well known, and it remains unchanged," Alexander Gusarov, director of the ministry’s department of North Atlantic, said in an interview with the International Affairs magazine.
"We fully recognize the indispensability of maintaining stable and predictable relations between Russia and the United States, which remain the main guarantors of international strategic stability," he noted.
In this regard, Gusarov pointed out that Moscow is "interested in working together with US colleagues to form precisely such relations that rest on equality, mutual respect, consideration of each other’s national interests and non-interference in internal affairs."

Russia rejects Netanyahu&#8217;s accusations of involvement in antisemitic online campaign
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:09:03 UTC
19:09:03 KST

Russia has rejected accusations by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu concerning Moscow’s alleged involvement in an antisemitic online campaign, Anadolu agency reported.
The Russian Foreign Ministry told state news agency Tass on Thursday that it was “perplexed” by the “entirely unsubstantiated accusations,” saying attempts to claim Moscow operated such a campaign appeared “particularly absurd.”
It said that this is so, “given a fact well known to – and repeatedly acknowledged in public by – the Israeli side, that thanks to the Russian leadership’s policy of strengthening interethnic peace and harmony, manifestations of antisemitism in our country are virtually non-existent.”
On Sunday, Israel’s i24 News reported that Netanyahu, in response to a question from the news channel, accused Russia of “aiding Iran and using artificial intelligence to operate antisemitic bot networks targeting Israel and Jews worldwide.”
READ: BDS co-founder dismisses as ’empty talk’ Adidas apology over Israeli soldier campaign
The ministry noted that it is regrettable Netanyahu’s remarks came on the 35th anniversary of the restoration of diplomatic ties between the two countries, and that it took note of his statements concerning Moscow’s alleged bot activities.
“Yet, as early as 2018, Russia proposed that Israel enter into a bilateral agreement on cooperation in the sphere of information security – a proposal to which no response was ever received,” the ministry said, noting this “could have prevented problems from arising out of thin air.”
It also described that it is “regrettable” Netanyahu chose to engage “in media-driven allegations” ahead of Israel’s legislative election scheduled for Tuesday rather than fostering dialogue between relevant experts on cybersecurity issues, noting this is not the first time Russia has “encountered such fakes.”
“There is a well-known Russian expression: ‘Shifting the blame from a sick head to a healthy one.’ Perhaps this is precisely such a case. It is clear that the world’s attitude toward Israel is determined solely by the course of action taken by its own authorities,” it added.

Danish parliament to debate Greenland-US defense agreement in November
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:07:29 UTC
19:07:29 KST

Denmark’s parliament will begin debating a new security and defense agreement between Denmark, Greenland and the United States on 12 November, with a final vote scheduled for 19 November.
Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen presented the agreement to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, on Thursday as a resolution proposal.
The first reading on 12 November will give lawmakers an opportunity to debate the agreement. A final vote is scheduled for the second reading on 19 November.
The agreement will only enter into force once it has been approved by both the Danish parliament and Greenland’s parliament, Inatsisartut.
Greenland’s parliament held its first reading of the agreement on 10 October. The debate lasted more than four hours, according to Greenlandic broadcaster KNR.
During the debate, opposition party Naleraq proposed putting the agreement to a referendum.
The Greenlandic government holds a majority in Inatsisartut. In Denmark, the government must secure support from other parties to obtain a parliamentary majority for the agreement.
Several Danish opposition parties welcomed the agreement shortly after it was signed in New York on 22 September, during the United Nations General Assembly.
The signatories were US President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats, and Greenland’s head of government, Jens-Frederik Nielsen.
“This day represents a milestone in our long-standing cooperation,” Frederiksen said before signing the agreement.
The new security and defense agreement is described as an “amendment and supplement” to a 1951 defense agreement between Denmark and the United States concerning Greenland.
Among other provisions, it allows the United States to establish military bases in Greenland.
The US currently operates Pituffik Space Base in northwestern Greenland, formerly known as Thule Air Base. Under the new agreement, the United States could establish two additional military bases on the island.
Hundreds of passengers rebooked after long queues at Copenhagen Airport
At least 352 passengers booked on SAS flights have been rebooked after long queues at security control at Copenhagen Airport caused them to miss their departures.
“We understand the frustration and inconvenience that the situation causes, and share our passengers’ frustration. We know that Copenhagen Airport is working hard to resolve the problem,” she said.
Rival airline Norwegian has also been affected. Country Manager Sara Neergaard told Danish broadcaster DR that 200 passengers missed their flights on Thursday, with a further 30 missing their departures on Friday.
“Unfortunately, we cannot do much other than ask people to arrive more than two hours early,” Neergaard told DR.
Norwegian has offered affected passengers the option of rebooking their flights.
Long queues were reported at Copenhagen Airport on Thursday evening and again on Friday morning. The Danish Transport Authority said on Thursday that an inspection had led the airport to introduce additional security measures temporarily.
SAS has advised passengers to arrive earlier than usual and allow extra time to pass through security.
Kaoukji said the situation appeared to have improved by midday Friday, but SAS was hoping the airport could maintain sufficient capacity as passenger traffic increased later in the afternoon.
Copenhagen Airport’s Head of Communications, Lise Agerley Kürstein, told TV 2 on Friday that the airport did not yet know how long the temporary measures would remain in place.
However, the airport hopes to have a solution in place at the beginning of next week.
Around 21,300 Danish websites lack PHP security updates
Around 21,300 Danish websites have not yet been updated following the discovery of two security vulnerabilities in PHP, one of the world’s most widely used programming languages for websites.
New figures from the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri) show that around 3,300 websites can receive the security update but have not yet installed it. Another 18,000 websites cannot be updated because they run outdated versions of PHP that no longer support the security fix.
The figures mark an improvement from Friday morning, when more than 8,000 websites still needed an update.
“It is positive that there are now fewer websites in need of an update,” said Jeppe Engell, a cybersecurity specialist at Dansk Industri, in a press release.
“But we are not across the finish line. Around 3,300 websites still lack the update, and those are the ones the criminals are going after now.”
Engell urged website owners to contact their providers if they had not received confirmation that the update had been installed.
The approximately 18,000 websites running outdated PHP versions face multiple vulnerabilities, Engell said. He called for the government’s Cybersikker Virksomhed initiative, which helps small and medium-sized Danish businesses improve cybersecurity, to be launched.
The vulnerabilities were discovered on Wednesday after going unnoticed for years. Artificial intelligence helped identify the flaws, which prompted several websites to shut down temporarily while security fixes were applied.
Dansk Industri initially reported at least 28,000 unupdated Danish websites on Thursday. A subsequent analysis put the figure at around 21,300 as of 10:52 a.m. Friday.
However, the organisation warned that the true number is likely higher, as the analysis only covers websites using the Danish “.dk” domain.
The security breach also prompted public authorities in several countries, including Norway, Finland, the Netherlands, France and Germany, to shut down websites.
Jacob Harris has been banned from managing or sitting on the board of a company for three years following a ruling by the probate court in Roskilde on Friday.
TV 2 reported the decision, citing trustee and bankruptcy lawyer Morten Bjerregaard.
The ban also means Harris, an independent member of the Danish parliament, cannot own a company unless he accepts personal liability.
The ruling concerns Harris’ activities in Krokodille ApS, a company for which his wife, Tetiana Harris Nielsen, served as director. The court declared the company bankrupt in the autumn of 2025.
According to TV 2, Harris’ wife has also received a three-year bankruptcy ban. The ruling was reportedly based on the couple’s conduct in the company, whose bookkeeping was deficient and entirely absent for 2025.
Krokodille ApS was founded in Hedehusene, west of Copenhagen, in December 2021 under the name Vostok Sokol ApS. A holding company owned by Tetiana Harris Nielsen is registered as its founder. The company changed its name in March 2022 and moved its registered address from the couple’s home to an address in Ringsted in October 2025, shortly before its bankruptcy.
Harris was elected to the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament, for Borgernes Parti in the March election but was expelled from the party days later. The party said he had “not provided truthful information to the party and, moreover, repeatedly acted contrary to the party’s values.”
Harris has also faced criticism over plans to meet Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, on 10 November.
Responding to the controversy, Harris wrote on Facebook: “Talking to a foreign ambassador is not treason.”

Netanyahu orders West Bank lockdown after shooting near Hebron
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has ordered an immediate closure of the city of Hebron and instructed the military to prepare to shut down the entire West Bank following a shooting that left at least five people injured.
Netanyahu announced the measures in a post on X, according to the French news agency AFP.
“I have ordered the IDF and the security forces to impose an immediate closure of the city of Hebron and to prepare a full shutdown of all of Judea and Samaria effective from today,” he wrote.
Judea and Samaria are the names Israel uses for the territory known internationally as the West Bank. It remains unclear what the planned shutdown will mean in practice.
Netanyahu said the military had begun “counter-terrorism operations” in the area, including searches of homes belonging to people suspected of involvement in terrorism.
“Soldiers are currently operating inside the homes of terrorists and other suspects,” AFP reported.
The announcement follows a shooting early Friday near Hebron, during which two Palestinian men were shot by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF). They are suspected of carrying out an attack that left at least five people injured.
The incident involved an exchange of fire between the two men and Israeli forces at the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint near Hebron. According to AFP, the Palestinians were armed with a pistol and an automatic rifle.
Netanyahu praised the military for preventing what he described as “a major terrorist attack” and vowed to pursue Hamas members.
“You have nowhere to hide,” he wrote.
Israel is due to hold parliamentary elections next week. Following the shooting, Netanyahu cancelled all political meetings.
Israel’s National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, also responded to the shooting by calling for the dissolution and demilitarization of the Palestinian Authority.
“We have to act before it is too late. The Palestinian Authority must be dissolved and demilitarized, and its terrorist infrastructure must be completely eradicated,” he said.
The Palestinian Authority administers parts of the West Bank and was established under the Oslo peace agreements. It is led by President Mahmoud Abbas, whose Fatah party is a rival of Hamas.
There is currently no indication that Palestinian Authority officials were involved in the shooting.
Hamas praised the attack but did not claim responsibility, according to AFP.
“The attack is a natural and legitimate response to the ongoing crimes and brutal attacks against our people,” the group said, describing it as “an exceptional heroic operation”.
Retail sales in Denmark rose by 0.4 percent in September compared with August, despite growing pessimism among consumers, according to figures from Statistics Denmark.
The increase is adjusted for seasonal fluctuations, price changes and the number of trading days.
For the third quarter, covering July through September, retail sales rose by 1.6 percent compared with the previous quarter.
Sales trends varied across industries in September. The largest increases were recorded among retailers selling second-hand goods, household equipment, furniture and building materials.
By contrast, sales fell the most at gas stations and pharmacies. Danish supermarkets also recorded a slight decline.
Brian Friis Helmer, a personal finance economist at AL Sydbank, said the increase in retail sales was encouraging given the growing pessimism among Danish consumers.
On Thursday, Statistics Denmark’s consumer confidence indicator stood at minus 17.2, down from minus 13.7 in September.
A negative reading indicates that consumers have a pessimistic view of the country’s current and future economic situation.
Despite the decline in confidence, Morten Granzau, deputy director at the Confederation of Danish Industry (Dansk Industri), believes retail sales could continue to grow in the coming months.
“Consumers’ purchasing power is fundamentally good. High employment, growth in real wages, and the lower electricity tax provide breathing room in many households’ budgets. This creates good opportunities for retail sales to maintain progress through the autumn,” he wrote in a comment.
Danish military to fund four bus routes to attract and retain staff
Denmark’s Armed Forces will fund four public bus routes connecting selected towns with military garrisons in an effort to recruit and retain more personnel.
The initiative is outlined in a funding document approved by the Folketing’s Finance Committee, a parliamentary body that approves certain government spending outside the annual Finance Act.
The Armed Forces will receive 2 million kroner in 2026 to establish the routes. The initiative is planned to run for three years, with a total budget of 17 million kroner.
Defence Minister Jeppe Bruus of the Social Democrats said the routes would help make military employment more attractive at garrisons in remote parts of Denmark, where public transport services are inadequate.
“It is a crucial prerequisite for building the Armed Forces’ combat power to be able to retain and recruit more employees,” Bruus wrote in the funding document.
“The purpose of the initiative is to make it attractive to seek permanent employment at those of the Armed Forces’ garrisons located in Denmark’s peripheral areas, and where current public transport service is not sufficient,” he added.
The routes are also intended to reduce employees’ reliance on private cars and give them greater flexibility around working hours and leisure activities.
“The primary target group will be permanent employees in the Armed Forces, but the public will also be able to use the bus routes,” Bruus wrote.
The funding document does not specify where the four routes will operate.
If passenger numbers are sufficient during the three-year trial period, regional public transport companies may take over the routes. If demand is too low, the services will be discontinued.
An appropriation document is a minister’s request for funding for a specific purpose not covered by the annual Finance Act. Such requests are submitted to the Folketing’s Finance Committee for approval.

Strong winds, heavy rain and potentially elevated sea levels are forecast across parts of Denmark on Sunday, with the west coast of Jutland expected to experience the worst conditions.
According to Danmarks Meteorologiske Institut (DMI), the Danish Meteorological Institute, wind gusts could locally reach storm force, particularly along the North Sea coast.
“One should consider whether it is worth going outside when the wind is blowing the most,” DMI meteorologist Hans Ole Wanner told Ritzau.
Southerly winds are expected to strengthen overnight into Sunday as a warm front brings widespread rain.
During Sunday, winds will shift toward the southwest and intensify, bringing strong gusts and severe gales to coastal areas.
DMI warns that the conditions could affect traffic on several Danish bridges.
Higher water levels are also possible along Jutland’s west coast, particularly around the Wadden Sea.
The unsettled weather is being driven by a storm system moving toward Denmark from the British Isles over the weekend.
DMI advises residents to secure loose outdoor items, including garden furniture and trampolines, before the strongest winds arrive.
The institute also recommends clearing leaves from gutters and drains to help prevent problems during heavy rainfall.
Wind gusts are expected to weaken Monday, although breezy conditions will continue.
Wanner said the forecast reflects Denmark’s transition into its windier autumn and winter months.
“We are genuinely entering the windy season in Denmark. It is not at all unthinkable that there will be more episodes with storm-like conditions leading up to and throughout the winter,” he said.
DMI will continue monitoring the weather and publishing updated forecasts as the storm approaches.
Denmark to end mink farming by August 2029 under EU ban
Denmark’s remaining seven mink farms will have to close by August 7, 2029, after the government decided not to seek an exemption from an upcoming European Union ban.
The Ministry for Nature and Animal Welfare announced the decision, citing animal welfare concerns and the industry’s limited economic contribution.
“An industry should not continue solely because it has existed for a long time. It must also make sense for society, for the economy, and for the animals,” said Nature and Animal Welfare Minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen of Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats).
The EU added mink to its list of invasive species last summer, introducing a ban on breeding and production that takes effect August 7, 2027. Existing farms will have a two-year transition period.
Denmark previously opposed the EU measure and had planned to seek an exemption allowing existing farms to continue operating.
Carl Valentin, animal welfare spokesperson for Socialistisk Folkeparti (SF), the Socialist People’s Party, welcomed the government’s decision.
“As we see it, it is not good animal welfare to have mink in tiny cages,” he told Ritzau.
Denmark’s mink industry was severely affected in 2020 when authorities ordered approximately 15 million animals culled over concerns about coronavirus mutations.
A temporary farming ban followed, lasting until January 2023, when some producers resumed operations.
The total estimated cost of pandemic-related compensation, farm demolition and administrative work reached 29.1 billion DKK in early 2026.
The government has yet to determine compensation costs for closing the remaining farms.
Valentin said an earlier estimate was around 14 million DKK, although the final amount could be higher.
Politicians push to change rules for dogs suspected of being banned breeds
Several Danish opposition politicians are calling for changes to the country’s dog laws after reports of legally owned dogs being kept in kennels for months while authorities investigate their breeds.
Under Denmark’s Dog Act, 13 breeds are banned from ownership, breeding and importation, including pit bull terriers and American bulldogs. Crossbreeds containing any of the prohibited breeds are also illegal.
When police suspect a dog belongs to a banned breed, its owner must provide documentation proving otherwise. During the investigation, the animal may be placed in a boarding kennel.
Danish newspaper Jyllands-Posten has reported cases involving dogs that were eventually found to be legal but had spent months in kennels.
Danmarksdemokraterne (the Denmark Democrats), an opposition party, has proposed allowing dogs to remain with their owners while investigations take place, potentially using electronic tracking devices instead.
Borgernes Parti (the Citizens’ Party) and independent lawmakers Nadja Natalie Isaksen, Cecilie Liv Hansen and Emilie Schytte have also criticized police powers to order euthanasia based on visual assessments of a dog’s breed.
The law requires police to euthanize dogs found to belong to prohibited breeds.
The restrictions were introduced in 2010 following incidents involving dog attacks on people and other animals.
Christian Rabjerg Madsen, Denmark’s minister for nature and animal welfare from Socialdemokratiet (the Social Democrats), told Jyllands-Posten he was open to discussing changes to the law and its enforcement.
He said the challenge was balancing public safety with fair treatment of owners who struggle to document their dogs’ breeds.
Danske Bank announces third round of layoffs this year
Danske Bank is cutting 106 jobs, around half of them in Denmark, in its third round of layoffs this year.
The bank announced the cuts in a press release on Thursday, saying they are intended to help create a “more efficient and competitive bank”.
The remaining positions are in the bank’s operations in Finland, Lithuania, Norway, Poland and Sweden.
“We continue to develop Danske Bank to meet our customers’ expectations, strengthen our competitiveness, and realize the ambitions in our Forward ’28 strategy,” Karsten Breum, the bank’s head of human resources, said in the release.
“This means that we continuously simplify the organization, invest in new competencies, and move resources to the areas where we create the greatest value for our customers.
“It is a natural part of running and developing a large company.”
The latest cuts follow two previous rounds of job reductions in 2026.
In February, Danske Bank announced that it would cut 420 positions across the organization. At the time, the bank said it wanted to adapt to customer needs, invest in technology and advisory services, and become more digital.
Three months later, a further 262 positions were affected. The bank gave broadly similar reasons for those cuts.
Both earlier rounds primarily affected employees in Denmark.
Breum acknowledged the impact of the latest decision on employees.
“Decisions like these affect people,” he said in Thursday’s press release.
“For the colleagues who are affected, it is a difficult situation. Therefore, it is important that we implement the changes responsibly and give our affected colleagues the support and respect they deserve throughout the entire process.”
All employees affected by the latest cuts have been notified.
Danske Bank says on its website that it has more than 20,000 employees across its international operations.
Danish krone loses value against major currencies in 2026
The Danish krone has lost value in 2026, making Danish goods and services cheaper for customers in several foreign markets while making some holidays abroad more expensive.
The krone’s effective exchange rate, a weighted average of its value against the currencies of Denmark’s most important trading partners, has fallen by 2.7 percent since the start of the year. The figures come from a compilation by Allan Sørensen, chief economist at Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry.
“The weakening of the krone’s value makes Danish goods and services cheaper for customers abroad, which makes it easier for export companies to secure new orders,” Sørensen said.
“It is in both the US, China, Norway, and Japan where the exchange rate means that they now have to pay less money to buy our products,” he added.
The Norwegian krone has risen 12.9 percent against the Danish krone over the past year, while the Chinese yuan has gained 9.8 percent. The US dollar and Japanese yen have each risen 4.8 percent.
However, not all currencies have strengthened against the Danish krone. The Swedish krona and Indian rupee have lost value, making goods from those countries slightly more expensive for Danish importers.
Exchange rates also affect the cost of holidays abroad. When a foreign currency strengthens against the Danish krone, Danish travellers get less for their money.
“For those who love a trip to the snow, a trip to Norway has become significantly more expensive solely as a result of the strengthening of the Norwegian krone,” Sørensen said.
“The weakening of the Swedish krona and low inflation in Sweden, on the other hand, make a ski vacation much more economically affordable in Sweden compared to Norway,” he added.
The Turkish lira has recorded the largest decline among the currencies in the compilation. It now costs 9.7 percent less to buy Turkish currency than it did at the start of the year.
Denmark to get 51 emergency supermarkets stocked for major crises
Shoppers across Denmark will be able to buy essential groceries and household supplies during power outages, cyberattacks and other emergencies under a new initiative by Salling Group.
The Danish retail giant, which operates Bilka, Føtex and Netto, plans to establish 51 emergency-ready supermarkets nationwide by 2027.
The stores will be equipped to operate for at least 48 hours without electricity or external communication systems, ensuring access to basic necessities during major disruptions.
According to Salling Group, the network will include 17 Bilka stores, 32 Føtex stores and two Netto locations.
The stores will be distributed so that up to 80 percent of Denmark’s population lives within 50 kilometers of one.
Each location will maintain emergency stocks of 50 essential products, selected according to Danish authorities’ recommendations for household preparedness.
These include oatmeal, protein bars, canned meatballs in curry, rice cakes, tuna, beans, chickpeas and other foods with long shelf lives.
Nonfood essentials such as batteries, wet wipes and diapers will also be available.
Customers will be able to pay offline using almost all physical payment cards and digital cards stored on smartphones.
Salling Group recently partnered with payment provider Nets to help maintain card transactions during system failures.
CEO Anders Hagh said establishing the emergency stores remains a top priority, with preparations progressing toward the 2027 target.
Meanwhile, competing retailer Coop, which operates Brugsen, SuperBrugsen, 365discount and Kvickly, has not decided whether to establish similar stores.
Coop’s chief risk officer, Ulrik Mester, said the company was discussing crisis preparedness with authorities, including Styrelsen for Samfundssikkerhed (SAMSIK), Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security.
Politicians across Danish political spectrum condemn MP’s meeting with Russian ambassador
Politicians from both left and right have criticized independent Danish MP Jacob Harris for planning to meet Russia’s ambassador to Denmark, Vladimir Barbin, on 10 November.
Venstre leader Troels Lund Poulsen, Denmark’s former defense minister, expressed strong opposition to the meeting in a post on X.
“I actually thought it was a bad joke when I read it,” he wrote, adding that “we must fight Putin. Not drink coffee with his ambassador”.
“It is completely, completely the wrong way to go, and it actually makes me furious. Fake meat ban email tricks 1,200 Danish regional employees in phishing test
A warning about meat disappearing from workplace canteens prompted 1,200 employees in Denmark’s Capital Region to click a suspicious link in an internal cybersecurity test.
The exercise, reported by TV 2 Kosmopol, was designed to assess how well employees recognize phishing attempts, in which scammers impersonate trusted organizations to trick people into clicking links or sharing information.
Of the 13,000 employees who received the fake email, approximately 9 percent clicked the link.
The message claimed that meatballs and roast beef would be removed from workplace canteens and that some would switch to entirely vegan menus, excluding meat, dairy and eggs.
Employees were invited to click a link to find out how the changes would affect their local canteen.
However, the sender’s email address contained a small but important difference: it ended in “reqionh.dk” rather than the Capital Region’s actual domain, “regionh.dk”.
Anna Aaskilde Laursen, the region’s head of security, explained that the email deliberately targeted something employees cared about.
She told TV 2 Kosmopol that emotionally charged messages can prompt people to react without thinking, making it important to pause before clicking.
Laursen confirmed that the 1,200 employees who clicked the link would face no consequences.
Instead, the region intends to use the results to improve its preparedness for genuine cyberattacks.
Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security warns that phishing emails can be difficult to recognize because criminals often imitate official logos and use convincing language.
The agency recommends checking senders’ email addresses carefully and, when uncertain, contacting the supposed sender by telephone to verify whether a message is genuine.

New partnership aims to connect lonely patients with social activities through their GPs
A new partnership in Denmark aims to help people experiencing loneliness and social isolation access community activities through referrals from their general practitioners.
Many people visit their doctors because they feel lonely, but their needs cannot always be addressed through medical treatment, said David Vincent Nielsen, a loneliness consultant at Ældre Sagen, a Danish association for older people, and chairman of Folkebevægelsen mod Ensomhed, a national movement against loneliness.
“There are a lot of people who seek out the healthcare and care system because they experience loneliness and social isolation.
“Most often, they cannot get help from the healthcare system because they need companionship and social relationships,” he said.
Under the proposed system, a doctor could issue a social referral for a patient. A professional or volunteer would then contact the patient and help identify activities and community groups suited to their needs.
The professional, known as a bridge-builder, would discuss the patient’s situation and help them find relevant offers from local organizations and municipalities.
These could include knitting groups, card game clubs or local exercise groups. Patients could also be encouraged to become volunteers themselves.
Nielsen said many people experiencing loneliness face barriers that make it difficult for them to seek out social activities and build relationships on their own.
For social referrals to become a regular part of Denmark’s health care system, however, the public sector would need to fund the service, he said.
“In 2017, the University of Southern Denmark calculated that loneliness cost 5.5 billion kroner, but since then, the prevalence of loneliness has increased by 42 percent, so around 10 billion kroner would be a qualified estimate today,” Nielsen said.
He argued that social referrals could also help reduce health care costs by addressing loneliness before people repeatedly seek medical assistance.
“But social referrals will not necessarily be an expense. Right now, there are at least 500,000 extra visits to general practice each year that are due to loneliness and paid for by the regions,” he said.
Pilot projects are already underway, Nielsen said. The new partnership aims to bring the existing efforts together into a coordinated model that could eventually be introduced nationwide.
The World Health Organization recognizes social referrals as a way to connect people with nonmedical support. According to the organization, one in five doctor visits is prompted by problems that cannot be resolved through clinical treatment.
The United Kingdom was the first country to incorporate social referrals into its health care policy. The WHO says there are now 3,300 active bridge-builders in the country.
The Danish partnership brings together Ældre Sagen, the Danish Red Cross, Social Sundhed, DGI, Sund By Netværket, Not a Box, and Frivilligcentre og Selvhjælp Danmark, an organization representing volunteer centers and self-help initiatives in Denmark.

The Danish labor market added 3,600 wage earners in August, according to a report published Wednesday morning by Danmarks Statistik, the national statistical authority of Denmark.
The increase follows a July that showed signs of a small slowdown.
The new numbers support the view held by financial group Nykredit that the Danish job market remains active.
Palle Sørensen, who serves as chief economist at Nykredit, noted that the trend is clear over a longer period.
“It is completely clear when you look at the development over a slightly longer horizon. In the past 12 months alone, there have been 29,638 more wage earners,” Sørensen said in a written comment.
He added that the job market matches the general economy.
“The development in the labor market matches well with the general economic development. Activity is increasing, and it is therefore not surprising that more people are entering employment,” Sørensen said.
There are multiple reasons for the increase in employed people.
One of the main reasons is foreign labor, according to Jesper Grunnet-Lauridsen. He works as chief analyst at 3F, Fagligt Fælles Forbund, which is the United Federation of Danish Workers and the largest trade union in Denmark.
“An important explanation is that more foreign employees have arrived, at the same time as more seniors are staying longer in the labor market,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said in a written comment.
He explained that these groups have helped employers find staff.
“This has made it possible for employment to continue to rise without companies having a correspondingly harder time finding employees,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said.
Neither Nykredit nor 3F expects the Danish labor market to slow down in the near future.
Sørensen said that recent experience shows that later retirement and foreign workers make the size of the total workforce more flexible.
“This is somewhat of an innovation compared to previously, where employment growth was often assumed to be temporary,” Sørensen said.
Energinet to prioritize addressing public service queries as power grid capacity runs short
Denmark’s power grid operator will answer hundreds of connection requests in November while big data centers face long delays.
Energinet, the Danish state-owned electricity transmission company, has now mapped out the capacity needs on the country’s strained electricity grid, the company said in a press release on Wednesday.
With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

The ruling was delivered Wednesday by Sø- og Handelsretten, the Danish Maritime and Commercial Court.
Nets had asked the court to set aside a decision made by the Competition Council. That decision concluded that Nets abused its dominant position in the market for payment solutions between the years 2012 and 2016.

Share of 21-year-olds living at home in Denmark nearly doubles since 2011
More young adults in Denmark are choosing to stay in their family homes, with the share of 21-year-olds living with their parents rising from 32 percent in 2011 to 57 percent in 2025.
The figures come from Statistics Denmark and are highlighted in a new study by Realdania, a Danish philanthropic association focused on the built environment.
Henrik Mahncke, Realdania’s head of analysis, says high housing prices could partly explain the trend. Another possible reason is that many young people enjoy living with their parents.
However, where young people grow up also influences when they move out.
In Albertslund, a municipality near Copenhagen, 61 percent of 21-year-olds still live at home. On the island of Læsø, the figure is just 14 percent.
According to Statistics Denmark, distance to educational institutions is an important factor. Young people who live farther from places of study are more likely to move out.
Cultural background also plays a role, with young people from non-Western backgrounds generally staying at home longer.
Housing availability and prices may also influence their decisions.
Mette Mechlenborg, a senior researcher at Aalborg University who studies housing, points to another explanation: the design of modern family homes.
Many young people grow up in spacious houses with separate areas for parents and children, giving them greater privacy and independence.
This can make staying at home more attractive than moving into a small, expensive room.
Realdania’s study also found no overall difference in quality of life between young adults living with their parents and those who have moved out.

Plans to tighten Denmark’s senior pension rules dropped after political opposition
The government has abandoned proposed changes to Denmark’s senior pension scheme after failing to secure support from parties behind the existing agreement.
Employment Minister Ane Halsboe-Jørgensen announced the decision Tuesday following a meeting with the parties involved.
The changes were part of the government’s proposed 2027 budget and were expected to save 200 million DKK in 2028, 500 million DKK in 2029 and 800 million DKK in 2030.
Under the proposal, applicants would have needed to prove that their ability to work was limited to 15 hours a week or less across all types of jobs, rather than just their most recent job.
This would have made qualifying for senior pension more difficult. In 2026, a single person receiving senior pension gets 22,053 DKK per month.
The scheme was introduced through a political agreement in 2019. Its signatories include the Danish People’s Party, the Social Democrats, the Socialist People’s Party, the Moderates and the Social Liberal Party.
Changes to the agreement require approval from all participating parties during the parliamentary term.
Several center-right parties opposed the proposal, while the Red-Green Alliance also rejected changes.
“We respect the agreements we have. It has not been my intention to terminate any agreement,” Halsboe-Jørgensen said.
“On the contrary. The fact that I called the colleagues from the other parties together today was precisely an expression of the fact that I actually wanted to discuss it with them, and that I respect that the agreement we have with each other gives all of them a veto right against changes in this area,” she added.
Dropping the proposal leaves a gap in the government’s budget plans.
Halsboe-Jørgensen said spending priorities would need to change but did not specify where the missing funds would come from.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard will now have to address the shortfall during negotiations on the 2027 Finance Act.

Venstre leader Troels Lund Poulsen said his party supports reducing corporate and intermediate taxes but wants cuts for everyone in employment.
Liberal Alliance leader Alex Vanopslagh said “completely ordinary Danes must get more out of going to work”.
Denmark Democrats leader Inger Støjberg called for tax changes that would help families facing higher fuel, energy and food prices.
The government may need support from the four center-right parties to pass its plan.
Its usual parliamentary allies, The Red-Green Alliance, a left-wing party, and The Alternative, a green progressive party, are not expected to support several of the proposed measures.

About 14,000 higher education students living with their parents would lose their entire state education grant under the government’s proposed 2027 budget.
Another 8,000 students in the same group would receive lower payments, Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates said in a parliamentary response.
Denmark’s state education grant is commonly known as SU.
An estimated 31,800 higher education students living at home received SU in 2025.
The government proposes ending payments for students whose parents have a combined annual income above 710,077 DKK. This corresponds to an average monthly income of 29,583 DKK for each parent in a two-parent household.
Payments would gradually decline for students whose parents earn between 419,589 and 710,077 DKK annually. The lowest monthly grant would be 500 DKK before disappearing entirely above the upper threshold.

Economic and Interior Affairs Minister Pia Olsen Dyhr will convene labor unions, employer organizations and other groups for talks on preventing work-related stress.
The first roundtable discussion will take place Friday following a new report from the Danish Economic Council’s independent economic advisers.
The report estimates that severe work-related stress reduces Denmark’s labor supply by between 16,000 and 39,000 people.
More than one in 10 people affected by severe stress do not return to employment, while more than one in three disability pension recipients receive the benefit after a stress reaction, according to the report.
“Stress makes us poorer,” Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party said. “This applies both to the individual person who becomes ill with stress and their family, but it also matters for our society.”

The European Commission has made security the main focus of its new Arctic strategy as Russia and China expand their activity in the region.
The approach marks a significant shift from the European Union’s 2021 strategy, which concentrated primarily on international cooperation, climate and environmental protection.
“As Russia and China increase their presence and ambitions, the Arctic has become a frontline in the global power competition,” EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said.
The Commission fears the Arctic could become a major source of conflict with Russia after the war in Ukraine ends.
The strategy proposes expanding Europe’s icebreaker capacity and strengthening protection of northern maritime borders and critical undersea infrastructure.
The EU’s 27 countries collectively have about 10 icebreakers, compared with an estimated 40 operated by Russia.
The Commission also proposes creating a maritime security center to monitor activity in the Arctic.
A separate Arctic cable center would monitor, protect and repair undersea cables in the North Atlantic and Arctic. It could later track ships belonging to Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which transports sanctioned oil and gas.
Western intelligence services also suspect that Russia has used shadow fleet vessels in hybrid attacks.
The strategy contains no spending figures and must now be discussed with EU governments.
Kallas said Arctic security was a European concern because Denmark, Sweden and Finland are Arctic countries and more than 500,000 EU citizens live in the region.
Record trout catch in Varde River follows restoration efforts
Anglers caught a record 1,400 large trout in Denmark’s Varde River during 2025, according to science news outlet Videnskab.dk.
Researchers have also found trout fry at more locations in the river system than at any point during the past 40 years.
“It is good to see that efforts to remove obstacles to fish movement are beginning to work in Varde Å,” said Bjarke Ibsen Dehli, a fish conservation adviser at DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources.
However, he said Denmark remained far behind in restoring healthy, natural river systems.
Rivers have historically been straightened, widened and deepened to drain surrounding farmland. Stones and gravel were removed, despite fish such as trout and salmon relying on gravel for spawning.
Aquatic plants have also been removed, reducing places where fish can hide.
Sluices, dams, water mills, fish farms, bridges and pipes can block migrating fish. Fish gathered near such barriers may become easier prey for cormorants, herons, otters and seals.
DTU Aqua’s latest survey found healthy trout populations along 14 percent of the examined stretches of the Varde River system. That was up from five percent in 2016.
Associations can apply for funding to restore local waterways, including grants from DTU Aqua for spawning gravel and shelter stones.
Dehli encouraged residents to join local organizations working to improve rivers and streams.

Denmark’s housing market is showing signs of slowing after a strong start to 2026, according to transaction figures from property portal Boligsiden.
