Fake meat ban email tricks 1,200 Danish regional employees in phishing test
A warning about meat disappearing from workplace canteens prompted 1,200 employees in Denmark’s Capital Region to click a suspicious link in an internal cybersecurity test.
The exercise, reported by TV 2 Kosmopol, was designed to assess how well employees recognize phishing attempts, in which scammers impersonate trusted organizations to trick people into clicking links or sharing information.
Of the 13,000 employees who received the fake email, approximately 9 percent clicked the link.
The message claimed that meatballs and roast beef would be removed from workplace canteens and that some would switch to entirely vegan menus, excluding meat, dairy and eggs.
Employees were invited to click a link to find out how the changes would affect their local canteen.
However, the sender’s email address contained a small but important difference: it ended in “reqionh.dk” rather than the Capital Region’s actual domain, “regionh.dk”.
Anna Aaskilde Laursen, the region’s head of security, explained that the email deliberately targeted something employees cared about.
She told TV 2 Kosmopol that emotionally charged messages can prompt people to react without thinking, making it important to pause before clicking.
Laursen confirmed that the 1,200 employees who clicked the link would face no consequences.
Instead, the region intends to use the results to improve its preparedness for genuine cyberattacks.
Denmark’s Agency for Societal Security warns that phishing emails can be difficult to recognize because criminals often imitate official logos and use convincing language.
The agency recommends checking senders’ email addresses carefully and, when uncertain, contacting the supposed sender by telephone to verify whether a message is genuine.

New partnership aims to connect lonely patients with social activities through their GPs
A new partnership in Denmark aims to help people experiencing loneliness and social isolation access community activities through referrals from their general practitioners.
Many people visit their doctors because they feel lonely, but their needs cannot always be addressed through medical treatment, said David Vincent Nielsen, a loneliness consultant at Ældre Sagen, a Danish association for older people, and chairman of Folkebevægelsen mod Ensomhed, a national movement against loneliness.
“There are a lot of people who seek out the healthcare and care system because they experience loneliness and social isolation.
“Most often, they cannot get help from the healthcare system because they need companionship and social relationships,” he said.
Under the proposed system, a doctor could issue a social referral for a patient. A professional or volunteer would then contact the patient and help identify activities and community groups suited to their needs.
The professional, known as a bridge-builder, would discuss the patient’s situation and help them find relevant offers from local organizations and municipalities.
These could include knitting groups, card game clubs or local exercise groups. Patients could also be encouraged to become volunteers themselves.
Nielsen said many people experiencing loneliness face barriers that make it difficult for them to seek out social activities and build relationships on their own.
For social referrals to become a regular part of Denmark’s health care system, however, the public sector would need to fund the service, he said.
“In 2017, the University of Southern Denmark calculated that loneliness cost 5.5 billion kroner, but since then, the prevalence of loneliness has increased by 42 percent, so around 10 billion kroner would be a qualified estimate today,” Nielsen said.
He argued that social referrals could also help reduce health care costs by addressing loneliness before people repeatedly seek medical assistance.
“But social referrals will not necessarily be an expense. Right now, there are at least 500,000 extra visits to general practice each year that are due to loneliness and paid for by the regions,” he said.
Pilot projects are already underway, Nielsen said. The new partnership aims to bring the existing efforts together into a coordinated model that could eventually be introduced nationwide.
The World Health Organization recognizes social referrals as a way to connect people with nonmedical support. According to the organization, one in five doctor visits is prompted by problems that cannot be resolved through clinical treatment.
The United Kingdom was the first country to incorporate social referrals into its health care policy. The WHO says there are now 3,300 active bridge-builders in the country.
The Danish partnership brings together Ældre Sagen, the Danish Red Cross, Social Sundhed, DGI, Sund By Netværket, Not a Box, and Frivilligcentre og Selvhjælp Danmark, an organization representing volunteer centers and self-help initiatives in Denmark.

The Danish labor market added 3,600 wage earners in August, according to a report published Wednesday morning by Danmarks Statistik, the national statistical authority of Denmark.
The increase follows a July that showed signs of a small slowdown.
The new numbers support the view held by financial group Nykredit that the Danish job market remains active.
Palle Sørensen, who serves as chief economist at Nykredit, noted that the trend is clear over a longer period.
“It is completely clear when you look at the development over a slightly longer horizon. In the past 12 months alone, there have been 29,638 more wage earners,” Sørensen said in a written comment.
He added that the job market matches the general economy.
“The development in the labor market matches well with the general economic development. Activity is increasing, and it is therefore not surprising that more people are entering employment,” Sørensen said.
There are multiple reasons for the increase in employed people.
One of the main reasons is foreign labor, according to Jesper Grunnet-Lauridsen. He works as chief analyst at 3F, Fagligt Fælles Forbund, which is the United Federation of Danish Workers and the largest trade union in Denmark.
“An important explanation is that more foreign employees have arrived, at the same time as more seniors are staying longer in the labor market,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said in a written comment.
He explained that these groups have helped employers find staff.
“This has made it possible for employment to continue to rise without companies having a correspondingly harder time finding employees,” Grunnet-Lauridsen said.
Neither Nykredit nor 3F expects the Danish labor market to slow down in the near future.
Sørensen said that recent experience shows that later retirement and foreign workers make the size of the total workforce more flexible.
“This is somewhat of an innovation compared to previously, where employment growth was often assumed to be temporary,” Sørensen said.

With this overview finished, the company will be able to answer applications from several hundred electricity consumers and power producers in November about whether they can connect to the grid.
“In a time of sharply rising demand for electricity, we unfortunately cannot give connection to everyone at the pace they desire,” said Soren Dupont Kristensen, the acting chief executive officer of Energinet.
“But there is room in the transmission grid to cover the electricity needs of ordinary households, smaller businesses, and critical societal functions such as healthcare, defense, and emergency preparedness, both now and in the years to come,” Kristensen said.
Customers will be sorted into four priority categories that were recently passed by a broad political majority as part of an emergency plan for the power network.
Projects placed in Category 1 and Category 2 will get their answers first. These two groups include critical public services, as well as green transition and electrification projects.
Category 3 includes energy storage systems, such as large battery facilities. Category 4 covers major electricity users, including data centers.
“We do not have all the results in place, but it looks difficult to give full grid access to projects in categories 3 and 4,” Kristensen said in Wednesday’s statement.
The political emergency plan was designed to let Energinet and local electricity companies choose who gets hooked up to the power lines. Under this plan, large data centers are pushed to the back of the line because the grid does not have room for huge new projects.
Energinet has faced heavy criticism for expanding the Danish electricity network too slowly. This criticism has come from several groups, including Rigsrevisionen, the National Audit Office of Denmark.
In March, the state company stopped connecting new projects. At that time, Energinet announced that no new connection contracts would be signed until the autumn.
In May, the company stated that very large connection projects could face waiting times of five to ten years. At that point, Energinet also admitted that demand for power had grown at an unexpectedly rapid speed.
Several business groups say it is good news that applicants will soon get answers, but they stress that Denmark still has a real shortage of space on its power grid.
This warning came from DI, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, which is the main employers’ and business association in Denmark; Dansk Erhverv, the Danish Chamber of Commerce, an employers’ organization representing businesses; and Green Power Denmark, the business and trade group for the green energy sector.
Ulrich Bang, the deputy director for climate, energy, environment, and building at Dansk Erhverv, said the likely lack of space for Category 3 and Category 4 projects shows how serious the situation is.
“Denmark cannot build the industries, business community, and jobs of the future in a waiting room,” Bang said.
“Therefore, action must be taken now, and we look forward to dialogue with authorities and grid companies on how room can be made for more on the electricity grid in the very short term,” Bang said.

Nets had asked the court to set aside a decision made by the Competition Council. That decision concluded that Nets abused its dominant position in the market for payment solutions between the years 2012 and 2016.
The case involves the company Teller, which was a subsidiary under Nets during that period. Teller offered what were described as exclusivity discounts to a number of large customers. Share of 21-year-olds living at home in Denmark nearly doubles since 2011
More young adults in Denmark are choosing to stay in their family homes, with the share of 21-year-olds living with their parents rising from 32 percent in 2011 to 57 percent in 2025.
The figures come from Statistics Denmark and are highlighted in a new study by Realdania, a Danish philanthropic association focused on the built environment.
Henrik Mahncke, Realdania’s head of analysis, says high housing prices could partly explain the trend. Another possible reason is that many young people enjoy living with their parents.
However, where young people grow up also influences when they move out.
In Albertslund, a municipality near Copenhagen, 61 percent of 21-year-olds still live at home. On the island of Læsø, the figure is just 14 percent.
According to Statistics Denmark, distance to educational institutions is an important factor. Young people who live farther from places of study are more likely to move out.
Cultural background also plays a role, with young people from non-Western backgrounds generally staying at home longer.
Housing availability and prices may also influence their decisions.
Mette Mechlenborg, a senior researcher at Aalborg University who studies housing, points to another explanation: the design of modern family homes.
Many young people grow up in spacious houses with separate areas for parents and children, giving them greater privacy and independence.
This can make staying at home more attractive than moving into a small, expensive room.
Realdania’s study also found no overall difference in quality of life between young adults living with their parents and those who have moved out.

Record trout catch in Varde River follows restoration efforts
Anglers caught a record 1,400 large trout in Denmark’s Varde River during 2025, according to science news outlet Videnskab.dk.
Researchers have also found trout fry at more locations in the river system than at any point during the past 40 years.
“It is good to see that efforts to remove obstacles to fish movement are beginning to work in Varde Å,” said Bjarke Ibsen Dehli, a fish conservation adviser at DTU Aqua, the National Institute of Aquatic Resources.
However, he said Denmark remained far behind in restoring healthy, natural river systems.
Rivers have historically been straightened, widened and deepened to drain surrounding farmland. Stones and gravel were removed, despite fish such as trout and salmon relying on gravel for spawning.
Aquatic plants have also been removed, reducing places where fish can hide.
Sluices, dams, water mills, fish farms, bridges and pipes can block migrating fish. Fish gathered near such barriers may become easier prey for cormorants, herons, otters and seals.
DTU Aqua’s latest survey found healthy trout populations along 14 percent of the examined stretches of the Varde River system. That was up from five percent in 2016.
Associations can apply for funding to restore local waterways, including grants from DTU Aqua for spawning gravel and shelter stones.
Dehli encouraged residents to join local organizations working to improve rivers and streams.

LSD pushes brain activity toward a more fractal, complex state, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:23 UTC
19:00:23 KST

A new neuroimaging study indicates that lysergic acid diethylamide, commonly known as LSD, alters human brain activity not just by weakening regular brain waves, but also by speeding them up and making neural signals more complex. The weakening of brain waves and the rise in signal complexity were most pronounced in regions tied to sensory processing, language, emotion, and mental imagery, while areas that control physical movement were largely spared. The findings, published in Communications Biology, also hint that listening to music may dampen rather than amplify these drug-induced changes, though that trend did not hold up after statistical correction.
LSD is a potent psychedelic drug that temporarily alters perception, mood, and the sense of self. Like other classic psychedelics, it works primarily by attaching to and activating serotonin 2A receptors on brain cells, though LSD also binds to dopamine receptors. Studying how this compound changes large-scale brain activity helps scientists understand the biological processes that generate conscious experience.
In human studies, researchers often use magnetoencephalography, or MEG, to track the fast-paced electrical activity of the brain. MEG is a non-invasive procedure where a participant sits with their head inside a helmet-like scanner containing sensitive magnetic detectors. As groups of neurons fire together, they produce tiny magnetic fields that the scanner records at a millisecond-by-millisecond scale.
This electrical activity consists of two main types of signals: rhythmic brain waves and background noise. Rhythmic waves, or neural oscillations, happen when thousands of brain cells fire in a synchronized beat, much like a choir singing a specific note. Two of the most common resting rhythms are alpha waves, which cycle at about 8 to 13 times per second (measured in hertz, or Hz) during relaxed wakefulness, and beta waves, which cycle faster at 15 to 30 Hz and relate to active thinking and alertness. These rhythms ride on top of non-rhythmic, background electrical activity that naturally loses strength at higher frequencies.
Previous psychedelic studies consistently showed that drugs like LSD and psilocybin cause a widespread drop in the strength of alpha and beta waves, a process called cortical desynchronization. Because traditional brain wave analyses measure activity within fixed frequency windows, they can confuse a change in wave speed with a loss of wave strength, or mistake shifts in the background noise for changes in actual rhythms. If an alpha wave speeds up against a background that naturally falls off at higher frequencies, it can look as though the wave lost strength when it actually just shifted to a faster tempo.
Beyond brain wave speed and strength, psychedelics also change the unpredictability and structure of brain signals over time. Scientists measure this using two mathematical tools: Lempel-Ziv complexity, which counts how many new and distinct patterns appear in a signal over time, and Higuchi fractal dimension, which measures how “rough” or self-similar a signal looks when zoomed in and out across different time scales. Higher scores on both metrics indicate richer, less predictable brain activity.
The physical and social environment also plays a major role in shaping a psychedelic experience, with music frequently used in both traditional rituals and modern psychedelic-assisted therapy. For example, a study covered by PsyPost in 2018 showed that LSD heightened brain responses to music across regions tied to auditory processing, emotion, and memory. The new research was led by first author Venkatesh Subramani, who holds a doctorate in neuroscience, and senior author Karim Jerbi, a full professor in the psychology department, both of the Cognitive and Computational Neuroscience Laboratory (CoCo Lab) at the Université de Montréal. The team aimed to separate true changes in brain wave strength from shifts in wave speed and background activity, while also testing how music interacts with these electrical signatures.
“A characteristic effect of classic psychedelics is the desynchronization of rhythmic brain activity (that is, reduced coordination of activity among neural populations) in the alpha (8-13 Hz) and beta (15-30 Hz) bands,” Subramani told PsyPost. “LSD, however, appears somewhat unique because it also speeds up these intrinsic oscillations, by up to 2 Hz for alpha and up to 5 Hz for beta. This acceleration creates an ambiguity: it is unclear whether LSD genuinely desynchronizes these rhythms, or whether the previously reported desynchronization is an artifact of shifts in the spectral peaks.”
To investigate these questions, the researchers analyzed existing MEG data originally collected from 17 healthy volunteers. The experiment used a within-subject, single-blind, placebo-controlled design with a counterbalanced session order, meaning each participant completed two separate scanning sessions spaced 14 days apart without being told which treatment they were receiving. In one session, participants received an intravenous injection of 75 micrograms of LSD, and in the other, they received an inactive saline placebo.
Roughly four hours after the injection, participants underwent MEG brain scans under two different conditions, each lasting seven minutes. In the first condition, they rested with their eyes closed in silence. In the second condition, they kept their eyes closed while listening to ambient music excerpts. The research team used anatomical MRI scans of each participant’s head to map the MEG signals onto 360 distinct regions across the outer surface of the brain.
The authors then used a specialized mathematical tool to separate the rhythmic brain waves from the non-rhythmic background activity in each brain region. Instead of measuring wave strength inside rigid frequency boxes, they tracked the exact peak frequency where each participant’s alpha and beta waves were strongest. They also calculated Lempel-Ziv complexity and Higuchi fractal dimension for each region, and trained machine learning algorithms to see which brain features best distinguished the LSD state from the placebo state.
When the researchers separated the rhythmic waves from the background noise and accounted for shifting frequencies, they found that LSD still caused a genuine drop in the strength of alpha and beta waves. Alpha wave weakening was most pronounced in the temporal lobes, while beta wave weakening occurred broadly across the brain’s surface. However, ignoring the shifting frequencies made the wave weakening look much more widespread than it actually was, confirming that standard methods can inflate the apparent spatial extent of the drug’s effect.
“This study clarifies the ambiguity,” Subramani explained. “It shows that the weakening of oscillations, the usual marker of desynchronization, is genuine even after accounting for the peak shifts, a potential confound.”
Separating the signals also clarified what was happening in the posterior cingulate cortex, a major hub for self-reflection and daydreaming. In standard analyses that mix all signals together, this hub showed large drops in brain wave power under LSD. Once the background noise was removed, those rhythmic differences vanished, indicating that LSD mainly altered the background electrical activity in this region rather than its synchronized waves.
Alongside weakening the waves, LSD systematically sped them up across large portions of the brain. On average, the peak frequency of alpha waves increased by about 2 Hz, while beta wave peaks shifted upward by roughly 5 Hz. Machine learning models trained solely on these frequency shifts were able to correctly identify whether a scan came from an LSD or placebo session with over 82 percent accuracy, where chance would be 50 percent.
The background electrical activity also flattened out across the brain, meaning there was less slow background activity relative to fast activity. At the same time, both Lempel-Ziv complexity and fractal dimension rose substantially, especially in the back of the brain where visual information is processed. Machine learning decoders using these complexity and fractal measures distinguished the LSD state from placebo with over 76 percent accuracy, compared to a 50 percent chance level.
“In plain terms, LSD makes the brain’s main rhythms faster and weaker, and makes its activity more complex,” Subramani noted.
These results align with research covered by PsyPost in 2024, which examined brain activity under microdoses using EEG rather than full psychedelic doses using MEG, and similarly found that LSD increases neural signal complexity. The broader shift away from slower rhythms is also in line with a study covered by PsyPost in March 2026, which examined scalp EEG activity following psilocybin rather than source-resolved MEG following LSD and found that the drug weakened slower theta and alpha waves while strengthening faster beta and gamma activity. That study measured the strength of different frequency bands rather than the speed of individual rhythms, however, and the authors of the new paper note that a clear speeding of alpha and beta peaks has not been consistently observed with psilocybin.
To understand how these electrical changes relate to everyday mental functions, the researchers compared their brain maps against a massive database of over 14,000 prior brain imaging studies. They found that LSD’s effects followed distinct functional hierarchies across different brain systems. Reductions in alpha and beta wave strength, background flattening, and complexity increases were strongest in networks tied to vision, hearing, language, emotion, and mental imagery, while the motor cortex, which controls physical movement, remained largely unaffected.
The weakening and speeding of brain waves did not always line up. The functional systems that showed the largest drop in alpha wave strength, such as auditory and language networks, showed only minimal alpha speeding, while motor and attention networks retained relatively more of their alpha strength but showed the largest increases in alpha speed. In the beta range, the pattern reversed, with the biggest speed-ups occurring where beta strength dropped the most. Because the two effects were not statistically linked across the brain, the authors suggest that wave weakening and wave acceleration may reflect separate processes happening at the same time.
When the researchers examined the effect of music, they did not find any results that survived strict statistical corrections for multiple comparisons across the whole brain. However, uncorrected trends pointed in the opposite direction of what the team initially expected. Instead of boosting the brain effects of LSD, listening to music tended to slightly calm them down, resulting in less background flattening and lower signal complexity compared to experiencing LSD in silence.
The authors suggested that music might act as an external attentional anchor. Building on a 2024 analysis of this same dataset that found psychedelic-induced signal complexity was highest with eyes closed and dropped when attention turned outward, they propose that resting in silence allows the mind to wander freely into unconstrained internal states, whereas focusing on an external structured sound may gently ground and stabilize the brain’s electrical activity.
“Music can be very emotionally powerful, and music and psychedelics have been used together in rituals across many cultures,” Subramani said. “We wanted to formally test how music modulates the way LSD affects the brain. We hypothesized that music potentiates the effect of the drug. Somewhat surprisingly, and albeit not statistically robust, we found the opposite trend: music appeared to reduce the drug effect, which could suggest that the stimulus acts as an anchor that keeps subjects from fully experiencing the psychedelic state.”
“As noted in the paper, this is only hypothesis-generating,” he added. “It calls for studies with more subjects and targeted experimental designs with better controls.” He cautioned that “the music result is exploratory and should not be over-interpreted.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these results. The study relied on a relatively small sample of 17 participants, which limits the statistical power needed to detect subtle interactions between the drug and external factors like music. In addition, the MEG scans were recorded about four hours after the LSD injection, roughly two and a half hours after the drug’s subjective effects had peaked. This timing gap may explain why the researchers found few strong links between the brain measurements and participants’ questionnaire ratings.
Looking at music over a single seven-minute average also treats a dynamic song as if it were a static event. Future studies with larger groups could track how brain waves respond to changing musical moments in real time, and use muscle sensors to help rule out muscle activity as a source of the fastest brain signals. Comparing LSD directly with other psychedelics using these same signal-separation methods will also help determine whether speeding up alpha and beta rhythms is a unique signature of LSD’s pharmacology.
The team is already extending their analytical approach to see how these faster brain wave frequencies might affect other common measures of brain communication, such as functional connectivity, which tracks how closely pairs of brain regions coordinate their activity over time.
“This study shows that LSD shifts the oscillatory peaks and that there is a genuine weakening of oscillations beyond these shifts,” Subramani said. “Power is one measure that could be confounded by peak shifts. Another is functional connectivity between pairs of brain regions. We have been actively working on this, and a preprint will be out shortly!”
The study, “LSD reconfigures cortical dynamics through faster brain rhythms and increased fractal dimension,” was authored by Venkatesh Subramani, Timothy Nest, Annalisa Pascarella, Jérémy Brunel, Yorguin José Mantilla Ramos, Yann Harel, Suresh Muthukumaraswamy, Robin Carhart-Harris, Giulia Lioi, Nicolas Farrugia, and Karim Jerbi.

NEW DELHI: Speculation over a possible reunion between the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and the Shiromani Akali Dal (SAD) gathered pace on Friday after SAD chief Sukhbir Singh Badal said his party was open to an alliance with parties that agree with its ideology and programmes, a day after Union home minister Amit Shah predicted an NDA government in Punjab in 2027.Badal, however, ruled out any understanding with the Congress and the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP), calling them the “two biggest enemies of Punjab”."During the SAD-BJP rule, peace prevailed in Punjab, and the state witnessed development, be it in infrastructure, industry, or the state becoming power surplus," Badal told reporters on Friday, according to PTI."Whether we form the government or not, we will continue to fight for the people of Punjab. There are many other parties besides these and those who agree with the Akali Dal's ideology and programmes; we are open (for a tie-up)," he said.The remarks came a day after Union minister Amit Shah said Punjab's people had decided that an NDA government would come to power in the state in the 2027 assembly elections.

Any formal announcement would have to come from BJP national president Nitin Nabin, the functionary said.
Why a SAD-BJP reunion matters
The SAD and BJP were long-time allies in Punjab before the regional party ended their 24-year-old alliance in September 2020 over the now-repealed farm laws. SAD MP Harsimrat Kaur Badal, Sukhbir Singh Badal's wife, had also served as a Cabinet minister in the Narendra Modi government before the split.The former allies contested elections together for years, but their political fortunes were limited in the 2022 Punjab assembly polls. The BJP won two seats, while the SAD secured three in the 117-member Assembly.In recent months, several Punjab BJP leaders had maintained that the party was preparing to contest all 117 assembly seats independently. Dhillon reiterated that position on Friday, even as Shah's remarks and Badal's openness to an alliance renewed questions about the parties' electoral plans.Badal made the comments after leading an SAD delegation to meet Punjab governor Gulab Chand Kataria on Friday. The delegation submitted a memorandum over the killing of anti-drug activist Parvinder Singh Jhota in Mansa and demanded, among other measures, the dismissal of Chief Minister Bhagwant Mann.
Badal accused the AAP government of mishandling Punjab's affairs and said the state's law and order situation had deteriorated. He also blamed the Congress and AAP governments for what he described as the worsening situation in the state.With the 2027 assembly elections approaching, the public statements have revived the possibility of a realignment between the former allies. However, neither party has announced a formal agreement, and the BJP's Punjab leadership continues to maintain that it is preparing to contest all 117 seats.

Governors Have an Opportunity to Give Civics Education a Badly Needed Boost
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:03 UTC
19:00:03 KST

Governors have no shortage of ideas about how to improve education. But before deciding what to change, they need an honest answer to a more basic question: How are our students doing?
That sounds simple. It isn’t.
We governed Tennessee at different times and from different political parties. But we learned the same lesson: you cannot improve what you are unwilling to measure honestly.
Governors will get the chance to see how students in their state are doing in a critical,often-overlooked subject: civics. But they have to sign up by the end of January to get state-level results on the National Assessment of Educational Progress civics assessment, also known as the Nation’s Report Card, or NAEP.
For newly elected governors, that will mean making a quick decision shortly after taking office. It shouldn’t be a hard one, though.
U.S. students get limited instruction, particularly in early grades, about how our government works, the rights and responsibilities of citizens, and how to apply civics knowledge beyond the classroom. Governors can help change that by prioritizing and measuring what students know and can do in civics.
What we know now is limited but concerning: only 1 in 5 eighth graders in U.S. schools reached the NAEP Proficient level on the most recent Nation's Report Card in civics, meaning the vast majority of students likely struggle to identify the separation of powers and checks and balances spelled out in the Constitution.
Unlike in subjects like reading and math, we don't have state-specific information about how our own students are doing compared to students in other states in civics. That puts leaders at a disadvantage when trying to improve schools and communities and help young people develop the civic knowledge and skills they need to excel academically, in the workforce, and in their communities.
But beginning in 2028, if they meet the January deadline, states can get state-specific results in eighth-grade civics rather than just national averages. Tennessee's academic progress over the past two decades serves as an example of why all states should capitalize on this opportunity. In 2007, Tennessee’s extremely low Nation's Report Card scores in reading and math, which contradicted our own state assessment results, served as a wake-up call. Our state got to work raising K-12 expectations, increasing the rigor of our end-of-year state tests, and improving classroom practices.
The strategy worked: Between 2011 and 2015, Tennessee became the fastest-improving state on NAEP. And progress continues. Recently, for the first time, the state ranked in the top quarter of states for reading and math achievement.
This is why we believe NAEP is a particularly valuable tool. It’s considered the gold standard in assessments and is the only common yardstick that measures student learning across the country. It lets us know whether students today are doing better or worse than kids in those same grades did two years or two decades ago and how students in our state are doing compared to other states.
We didn't always have the benefit of state-level NAEP results. NAEP didn’t produce any state-specific data at all until the 1980s, when Tennessee joined other southern states in a pilot program to determine whether valid state results could be obtained from NAEP data. That paved the way toward a federal requirement 25 years ago that results for all 50 states in 4th- and 8th-grade reading and math be reported publicly.
That was a win for states and kids. But today, we have to ask ourselves, what about those other essential things that children learn in school besides reading and math?
States now have an opportunity to answer that question in civics. We hope they'll take it. We know from experience how valuable it is to have an honest, independent measure of how students are doing. Good policy requires good information. And good leadership requires being willing to confront what that information tells us.

Foster + Partners designs pair of skyscrapers connected by garden bridges in Armenia

Unknown Publisher

Foster + Partners designs pair of skyscrapers connected by garden bridges in Armenia
A pair of skyscrapers joined by three bridge elements will form the centrepiece of World Trade Center Yerevan, a development by British studio Foster + Partners set to be built in Armenia.
Situated in the Armenian capital of Yerevan, one of the towers will house offices and the other will contain apartments and a hotel.
Foster + Partners plans to connect the skyscrapers with enclosed bridges that will provide amenities for occupants of both buildings, including landscaped terraces.
Wrapped in glazed facades, the pair of skyscrapers will have a concrete structural frame with steel bracing and a split core, catering for open, flexible interior spaces.
The towers will be angled to give views of notable landmarks, including the National Assembly of Armenia, the Armenian National Opera and Ballet Theatre, the Armenian Genocide Memorial and Mount Ararat.
The World Trade Center Yerevan development will also feature low-lying buildings at the base of the skyscrapers containing entertainment, hospitality and shopping spaces arranged around a public square.
“Our new development is in close dialogue with the country’s history and culture,” said Foster + Partners senior partner Niall Dempsey.
“The low-rise buildings seamlessly stitch into the wider urban fabric, while the towers are elevated above ground level, freeing up 50 per cent of the site and making an important contribution to the life of the city.”
The central green axis of the nearby park will be extended to form a route leading to a podium at the base of the skyscrapers.
Foster + Partners aims for the public spaces to reference the area’s architectural heritage in its design for World Trade Center Yerevan.
The development is set to be built in an area of Yerevan that was masterplanned in 1924 by Armenian architect Alexander Tamanian, who had ambitions to transform the Armenian capital into a garden city.
“Our scheme celebrates the outdoor life of the city by connecting the urban fabric with public spaces, ensuring our new interventions work in harmony with the historic grain,” said Foster + Partners partner Juan Frigerio.
“To the north of the towers, the events plaza responds to the significant St John the Baptist Church and its forecourt, creating a seamless connection between old and new.”
Other designs recently unveiled by Foster + Partners include its plans for the Two World Trade Center skyscraper in New York and a masterplan to transform the area surrounding an airport near Luanda, Angola.
The images are by Foster + Partners.

Many Latinos are over Trump. The shift is especially striking in Texas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:00 UTC

See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- President Trump’s approval rating among Latino registered voters has fallen to 24% from 38% at the start of his second term, polls show.
- Tejano singer Bobby Pulido is trying to flip a Texas congressional seat in a district Trump won by 18 points in 2024.
EDINBURG, Texas — Clad in pressed jeans and cowboy hats, dozens of riders on horseback and drivers in pickups kicked up dust along a dirt road in Edinburg, near the southern tip of Texas. They were there for a cabalgata, a traditional horse procession, with a political message: Send Tejano singer Bobby Pulido to Congress.
Some were lifelong Democrats. Others had voted for President Trump two years ago. But on this Saturday, they all rode for Pulido, a Democrat trying to flip a House seat Trump carried by 18 percentage points in 2024.
Among them was David Lopez, 54, astride his brown horse, Black Jack. He voted for Trump because he saw him as a good businessman. But now, Lopez says the president’s tariffs have hurt his truck and trailer repair shop in nearby McAllen, and business is down about 20% from last year.
“I am voting Democrats all the way. Trump is no longer doing a good job,” Lopez said. “We need to find a way to make it out of this together.”
Lopez is part of a shift rippling through Latino communities across the country. Two years after helping return Trump to the White House with a Republican-controlled Congress, Latino voters are souring on the party in power, fueled by frustration over rising costs and the administration’s aggressive approach to immigration enforcement.
In 2024, Trump won the support of 48% of Latino voters, expanding Republican gains with a group that has long leaned Democratic. Now, that support is cratering. The president’s approval rating among Latino registered voters has fallen to 24% from 38% at the start of his second term, polls show.
Among Latinos who voted for Trump, 65% say they plan to back Republicans on Nov. 3, while more than a third said they were ready to vote for a Democrat or were undecided, according to a Pew Research Center poll released this month.
More broadly, Latino voters favor Democrats in House races 51% to 24%, and those who sat out the 2024 election are leaning toward Democrats. Those shifts could help decide control of the House, in part because Republicans in Texas and Florida redrew their congressional maps betting that their 2024 gains among Latino voters would last through the midterms.
The race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton is hotly contested and enormously expensive, with total ad spending topping $500 million.
Nowhere is that test sharper than in the borderlands of the Rio Grande Valley, where voters say that Trump has failed to deliver on his economic promises and that his administration has gone too far on immigration enforcement, an issue they wanted addressed, but humanely.
In more than two dozen interviews in the Latino-majority region, voters say they are driven less by party loyalty and more by frustrations that they have been taken for granted, and want to elect politicians who take their votes seriously.
They say it has become harder to keep up with rising costs, including for the diesel that fuels their trucks and their weekly grocery runs. Builders say construction projects have ground to a halt as workers are detained or deported. And small-business owners say sales have dropped, either because customers are afraid to leave their homes or because tariffs have driven up their costs.
1. Sebastian Guevara, 65, poses for a photo at a political rally on Oct. 16, 2026, in Mercedes, Texas. “Trump forgot about Latinos as soon as he won,” he said. 2. Luis Sustaita, 49, a mariachi musician who had voted Republican in previous years, says he will be voting for Bobby Pulido.
Nidia Olivarez, 48, and her husband, Arnulfo, 55, voted for Trump in 2024 but have grown frustrated with how he has handled the economy and immigration raids in their community. This year, they’re backing Pulido over GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in Texas’ 15th Congressional District. But not because they’ve had a change of heart about the Democratic Party.
“We are only voting for Pulido, not other Democrats,” Olivarez said. The couple are still unsure whether they’ll support any Republicans.
For them, the vote is personal. They’ve long loved Pulido’s Tejano music and like that he’s a familiar figure in their community. They trust him, she said. They’re less sure about the Republicans at the top of the ticket: Ken Paxton, the Senate nominee running against Democrat James Talarico, and Gov. Greg Abbott, who is seeking reelection.
“We want to see who continues to show up in the area,” Olivarez said. “That matters to us.”
Latino voters in Texas are increasingly willing to consider candidate over party, said Brandon Rottinghaus, a professor of political science at the University of Houston.
“They are not just looking for what party to align with. They want to know that they can trust the person they’re voting for,” Rottinghaus said.
That dynamic will play a role in the competitive races for Texas’ 15th, 28th and 34th congressional districts and in the Senate seat, which has proved to be one of the most expensive and high-profile contests this year. In a sign of GOP concerns, Trump and Vice President JD Vance have repeatedly traveled to Texas this month to rally voters.
In recent weeks, Trump has brushed off polls that show him losing ground with Latino voters.
“I think we are doing great, I won Hispanics,” Trump told reporters on Monday. “I’ve done more than any other Republican in history, I got tremendous Hispanics.”
In early October, Trump was asked about Latino voters who say they feel betrayed by his administration’s immigration and economic policies. His message to them was that “we have to do what we have to do,” in reference to his immigration crackdown.
1. People dance during Bobby Pulido’s concert. 2. A man rides his horse before a parade in support of Bobby Pulido on Oct. 17, 2026, in Edinburg, Texas. 3. Bobby Pulido, in brown vest and white cowboy hat, upper left, takes a photo with rallygoers after speaking on Oct. 16, 2026, in Mercedes, Texas.
Gloria Rodriguez, a social worker in Edinburg, has seen the impact the immigration raids have had on children. Since Trump returned to the White House, she has helped coordinate services for hundreds of kids whose parents or caregivers have been detained or deported. She worries many of them will develop post-traumatic stress disorders.
“Everything they are doing with immigration is too much,” said Rodriguez, 50, who is voting for Democrats down the ballot. Her 15-year-old daughter, Angelina, says she told her mother to vote for Democrats, in part because she is scared her friends will be deported.
Luis Sustaita, 49, a mariachi who owns a music store that sells instruments to school districts, is voting Democrat this year because he says he is disheartened by the values of the modern-day Republican Party.
In the latest “The De Los Podcast” episode, Times columnist Gustavo Arellano talks with hosts Fidel Martinez and Suzy Exposito about how the Latino vote will influence the 2026 midterm elections.
“There are no old-school Republicans anymore. It is all MAGA,” said Sustaita, who lives in Weslaco. “They used to be about the people. Trump is all about himself and making himself rich.”
In South Texas, Republicans and Democrats alike are trying to court voters on a more personal level. It is about identity more than political affiliation in many ways.
In the majority-Latino 15th Congressional District, Pulido’s campaign slogan is “Not team red, not team blue — South Texas I am team you.” In an interview, Pulido added that his message to Latino voters is: “I hear you loud and clear, and I believe I share values with you.”
De La Cruz, a former insurance agent and a staunch Trump ally, said Latinos are “tired of being taken for granted” and said Pulido “has some nice records, but he’s a product of the same corrupt system that got rich and made us poorer.”
“I grew up in South Texas watching the compadre system steal from us while our families struggled to get by,” De La Cruz said in a statement. “You work hard and want a little more for your family and safe communities. I cut your taxes, protected Social Security and Medicare, stood with Border Patrol agents, and I’m fighting every day to bring down gas and grocery prices.”
Whether that message will resonate with voters will be seen on Nov. 3.
Tina Treviño, 61, said she hopes “la raza” — a term used in the Mexican American community that is widely understood as “the people” — will deliver political change to Texas. She says the system is not working for Latinos, and believes Democrats will be able to bring that change.
“It’s about Chicano power,” Treviño said. “We need that more than ever.”

Trump ramps up fraud investigations of immigrants as election approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

Trump ramps up fraud investigations of immigrants as election approaches
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- As the midterms approach, the Trump administration is expanding fraud investigations involving immigrants.
- Studies and state reviews find noncitizen voting is rare. California officials say many registrations flagged by federal authorities as possible fraud appear to belong to U.S.-born voters.
- Immigration attorneys say minor inconsistencies in applications are increasingly triggering fraud findings, the denial of benefits and deportation proceedings.
WASHINGTON — President Trump has alleged that elections, public benefit programs and federal grants to nonprofits are rife with fraud. Now, he is increasingly focusing on fraud in his effort to detain and deport more immigrants.
Recent, high-profile flash points include 28 lawful permanent residents accused this week of illegally voting in California and the federal investigation into Somali-born Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.).
The broader crusade takes many forms, including allegations of fraud in immigration applications, illegal voting by noncitizens and misuse of federal benefits by immigrants who don’t qualify.
“This administration has purposefully mischaracterized immigrants and asylum seekers as fraudsters,” said Royce Murray, a former senior official at the Department of Homeland Security under the Biden administration. That, she said, “serves a narrative that immigrants are not to be trusted and are here to take something rather than contribute, with an end goal of trying to make Americans less welcoming and more comfortable with a mass deportation agenda.”
On Tuesday, Trump and Vice President JD Vance announced a $25-million program under the Justice Department to encourage the public to report suspected fraud in the U.S. government.
 This administration has purposefully mischaracterized immigrants and asylum seekers as fraudsters
— Royce Murray, former Department of Homeland Security official
The White House said the first check, for $10,000, will go to right-wing influencer Nick Shirley, who posted a video last year alleging that Somali residents in Minnesota were running fake child-care centers to collect federal subsidies. Dozens of people were convicted in connection with a sprawling, $250-million children’s food assistance scheme that predated this administration, though more charges have been announced in recent months.
Also Tuesday, administration officials launched another nationwide anti-fraud crackdown, this time targeting immigrants who they allege have illegally collected SNAP benefits. Homeland Security highlighted the arrests of five people, calling them “the opening salvo in a sustained, large-scale ICE operation.”
“From day one of my administration, we’ve waged an unprecedented war on corruption and fraud, and will not let our country be looted and plundered by thieves and pirates and foreign fraudsters and basically scum,” Trump said during a news conference announcing the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program.
Earlier this year, the White House created a task force to eliminate fraud and the Department of Justice created a fraud enforcement division, in part, to target immigration-related offenses. Prosecutors have put aside thousands of other cases to zero in on immigration enforcement.
The focus on fraud has noticeably accelerated in the weeks leading up to the election.
Federal authorities charge 28 people in California with alleged illegal voter registration or voting, escalating the Trump administration’s fight with state election officials.
In California, some of the green card holders arrested this week over voter fraud said they didn’t remember registering to vote. The daughter of one defendant, Omar Muñoz, 72, of Belize, said she wondered whether her father had been confused with his U.S.-born son of the same name, who is a registered voter.
California officials pounced on the small number of people alleged to have cast illegal ballots. Illegal voting by immigrants “is so rare that the Trump admin is parading around town about .0001% of California voters,” Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office wrote on X.
In the last seven weeks alone, the State Department said, 112 noncitizens across 20 states have been charged with illegal voting and registration offenses. Overall, since Trump returned to the White House, 155 people have been charged with voting fraud-related offenses.
Mullin and Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche said earlier this month that Homeland Security agents had secured 10 convictions and detained 100 others for civil immigration violations since August.
During the Biden administration, voter fraud charges were brought in just 13 cases, Blanche added.
Studies and audits of state voter rolls have repeatedly found that voting by noncitizens is rare and hasn’t swayed any elections.
Last week, with mail-in voting already underway, the Justice Department sued California, asking a federal court to bar the state from counting the ballots of 20,000 voters who were flagged by federal officials as “likely noncitizens.” Los Angeles County officials reviewed a sample of 200 of those voter registrations and found that nearly 40% indicated they were born in the U.S.
That number of flagged ballots — 20,000 — is a substantial reduction from the 190,000 noncitizens the administration alleged were on state voter rolls earlier this year, though federal authorities this week said they had found a “separate batch of 17,000 voting records potentially tied to noncitizens.”
California leaders pointed to other states, such as Nevada, where similar accusations have proved meritless.
Murray, the former Homeland Security official, said she believes the administration is “trying to sow the seeds of doubt that the midterm outcomes will be trustworthy, so that if the Republican Party loses as badly as they’re predicted to, they can characterize it as due to fraud.”
Murray said the Trump administration has largely misconstrued what it means to commit fraud.
“Fraud is a very specific thing — it’s essentially lying,” she said. “Because you don’t get asylum does not mean you committed fraud, it just means you were ineligible.”
In September, a Homeland Security whistleblower told Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) that hundreds of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services employees had been tasked with quickly reviewing the voter information of thousands of people in search of suspected noncitizen voters, and were given a quota of investigating 40 subjects per day.
On Wednesday, a federal judge restricted Homeland Security agents from carrying out sweeping field operations aimed at rooting out voter fraud in nine states, including California.
It is against federal law for immigrants who are not naturalized citizens to vote or register to do so. Penalties can include fines, jail time and even deportation, though authorities rarely pursued that option.
Eric Balliet, a former special agent with Homeland Security Investigations, the criminal investigative arm of ICE, said he takes no issue with investigating fraud, but the timing of this operation and significant resources dedicated show it is “highly politically charged.”
Balliet worked for various administrations, including Trump’s first, before retiring in 2024. Homeland Security Investigations agents typically focused on transnational criminal investigations such as drug smuggling and human trafficking.

In one case that resulted in a denial based on fraud, she said, the allegation was simply that her client failed to disclose a two-week work assignment in another state.
“In the past, the worst that would happen is your citizenship application would be denied,” O’Neil said. “Now we have seen through several of my clients that, not only is the citizenship application denied, but they are placed into removal proceedings.”

Many Latinos are over Trump. The shift is especially striking in Texas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
10:00:00 UTC
19:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- President Trump’s approval rating among Latino registered voters has fallen to 24% from 38% at the start of his second term, polls show.
- Tejano singer Bobby Pulido is trying to flip a Texas congressional seat in a district Trump won by 18 points in 2024.
EDINBURG, Texas — Clad in pressed jeans and cowboy hats, dozens of riders on horseback and drivers in pickups kicked up dust along a dirt road in Edinburg, near the southern tip of Texas. They were there for a cabalgata, a traditional horse procession, with a political message: Send Tejano singer Bobby Pulido to Congress.
Some were lifelong Democrats. Others had voted for President Trump two years ago. But on this Saturday, they all rode for Pulido, a Democrat trying to flip a House seat Trump carried by 18 percentage points in 2024.
Among them was David Lopez, 54, astride his brown horse, Black Jack. He voted for Trump because he saw him as a good businessman. But now, Lopez says the president’s tariffs have hurt his truck and trailer repair shop in nearby McAllen, and business is down about 20% from last year.
“I am voting Democrats all the way. Trump is no longer doing a good job,” Lopez said. “We need to find a way to make it out of this together.”
Lopez is part of a shift rippling through Latino communities across the country. Two years after helping return Trump to the White House with a Republican-controlled Congress, Latino voters are souring on the party in power, fueled by frustration over rising costs and the administration’s aggressive approach to immigration enforcement.
In 2024, Trump won the support of 48% of Latino voters, expanding Republican gains with a group that has long leaned Democratic. Now, that support is cratering. The president’s approval rating among Latino registered voters has fallen to 24% from 38% at the start of his second term, polls show.
Among Latinos who voted for Trump, 65% say they plan to back Republicans on Nov. 3, while more than a third said they were ready to vote for a Democrat or were undecided, according to a Pew Research Center poll released this month.
More broadly, Latino voters favor Democrats in House races 51% to 24%, and those who sat out the 2024 election are leaning toward Democrats. Those shifts could help decide control of the House, in part because Republicans in Texas and Florida redrew their congressional maps betting that their 2024 gains among Latino voters would last through the midterms.
The race between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton is hotly contested and enormously expensive, with total ad spending topping $500 million.
Nowhere is that test sharper than in the borderlands of the Rio Grande Valley, where voters say that Trump has failed to deliver on his economic promises and that his administration has gone too far on immigration enforcement, an issue they wanted addressed, but humanely.
In more than two dozen interviews in the Latino-majority region, voters say they are driven less by party loyalty and more by frustrations that they have been taken for granted, and want to elect politicians who take their votes seriously.
They say it has become harder to keep up with rising costs, including for the diesel that fuels their trucks and their weekly grocery runs. Builders say construction projects have ground to a halt as workers are detained or deported. And small-business owners say sales have dropped, either because customers are afraid to leave their homes or because tariffs have driven up their costs.
1. Sebastian Guevara, 65, poses for a photo at a political rally on Oct. 16, 2026, in Mercedes, Texas. “Trump forgot about Latinos as soon as he won,” he said. 2. Luis Sustaita, 49, a mariachi musician who had voted Republican in previous years, says he will be voting for Bobby Pulido.
Nidia Olivarez, 48, and her husband, Arnulfo, 55, voted for Trump in 2024 but have grown frustrated with how he has handled the economy and immigration raids in their community. This year, they’re backing Pulido over GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz in Texas’ 15th Congressional District. But not because they’ve had a change of heart about the Democratic Party.
“We are only voting for Pulido, not other Democrats,” Olivarez said. The couple are still unsure whether they’ll support any Republicans.
For them, the vote is personal. They’ve long loved Pulido’s Tejano music and like that he’s a familiar figure in their community. They trust him, she said. They’re less sure about the Republicans at the top of the ticket: Ken Paxton, the Senate nominee running against Democrat James Talarico, and Gov. Greg Abbott, who is seeking reelection.
“We want to see who continues to show up in the area,” Olivarez said. “That matters to us.”
Latino voters in Texas are increasingly willing to consider candidate over party, said Brandon Rottinghaus, a professor of political science at the University of Houston.
“They are not just looking for what party to align with. They want to know that they can trust the person they’re voting for,” Rottinghaus said.
That dynamic will play a role in the competitive races for Texas’ 15th, 28th and 34th congressional districts and in the Senate seat, which has proved to be one of the most expensive and high-profile contests this year. In a sign of GOP concerns, Trump and Vice President JD Vance have repeatedly traveled to Texas this month to rally voters.
In recent weeks, Trump has brushed off polls that show him losing ground with Latino voters.
“I think we are doing great, I won Hispanics,” Trump told reporters on Monday. “I’ve done more than any other Republican in history, I got tremendous Hispanics.”
In early October, Trump was asked about Latino voters who say they feel betrayed by his administration’s immigration and economic policies. His message to them was that “we have to do what we have to do,” in reference to his immigration crackdown.
1. People dance during Bobby Pulido’s concert. 2. A man rides his horse before a parade in support of Bobby Pulido on Oct. 17, 2026, in Edinburg, Texas. 3. Bobby Pulido, in brown vest and white cowboy hat, upper left, takes a photo with rallygoers after speaking on Oct. 16, 2026, in Mercedes, Texas.
Gloria Rodriguez, a social worker in Edinburg, has seen the impact the immigration raids have had on children. Since Trump returned to the White House, she has helped coordinate services for hundreds of kids whose parents or caregivers have been detained or deported. She worries many of them will develop post-traumatic stress disorders.
“Everything they are doing with immigration is too much,” said Rodriguez, 50, who is voting for Democrats down the ballot. Her 15-year-old daughter, Angelina, says she told her mother to vote for Democrats, in part because she is scared her friends will be deported.
Luis Sustaita, 49, a mariachi who owns a music store that sells instruments to school districts, is voting Democrat this year because he says he is disheartened by the values of the modern-day Republican Party.
In the latest “The De Los Podcast” episode, Times columnist Gustavo Arellano talks with hosts Fidel Martinez and Suzy Exposito about how the Latino vote will influence the 2026 midterm elections.
“There are no old-school Republicans anymore. It is all MAGA,” said Sustaita, who lives in Weslaco. “They used to be about the people. Trump is all about himself and making himself rich.”
In South Texas, Republicans and Democrats alike are trying to court voters on a more personal level. It is about identity more than political affiliation in many ways.
In the majority-Latino 15th Congressional District, Pulido’s campaign slogan is “Not team red, not team blue — South Texas I am team you.” In an interview, Pulido added that his message to Latino voters is: “I hear you loud and clear, and I believe I share values with you.”
De La Cruz, a former insurance agent and a staunch Trump ally, said Latinos are “tired of being taken for granted” and said Pulido “has some nice records, but he’s a product of the same corrupt system that got rich and made us poorer.”
“I grew up in South Texas watching the compadre system steal from us while our families struggled to get by,” De La Cruz said in a statement. “You work hard and want a little more for your family and safe communities. I cut your taxes, protected Social Security and Medicare, stood with Border Patrol agents, and I’m fighting every day to bring down gas and grocery prices.”
Whether that message will resonate with voters will be seen on Nov. 3.
Tina Treviño, 61, said she hopes “la raza” — a term used in the Mexican American community that is widely understood as “the people” — will deliver political change to Texas. She says the system is not working for Latinos, and believes Democrats will be able to bring that change.
“It’s about Chicano power,” Treviño said. “We need that more than ever.”

Trump ramps up fraud investigations of immigrants as election approaches

Unknown Publisher

Trump ramps up fraud investigations of immigrants as election approaches
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- As the midterms approach, the Trump administration is expanding fraud investigations involving immigrants.
- Studies and state reviews find noncitizen voting is rare. California officials say many registrations flagged by federal authorities as possible fraud appear to belong to U.S.-born voters.
- Immigration attorneys say minor inconsistencies in applications are increasingly triggering fraud findings, the denial of benefits and deportation proceedings.
WASHINGTON — President Trump has alleged that elections, public benefit programs and federal grants to nonprofits are rife with fraud. Now, he is increasingly focusing on fraud in his effort to detain and deport more immigrants.
Recent, high-profile flash points include 28 lawful permanent residents accused this week of illegally voting in California and the federal investigation into Somali-born Rep. Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.).
The broader crusade takes many forms, including allegations of fraud in immigration applications, illegal voting by noncitizens and misuse of federal benefits by immigrants who don’t qualify.
“This administration has purposefully mischaracterized immigrants and asylum seekers as fraudsters,” said Royce Murray, a former senior official at the Department of Homeland Security under the Biden administration. That, she said, “serves a narrative that immigrants are not to be trusted and are here to take something rather than contribute, with an end goal of trying to make Americans less welcoming and more comfortable with a mass deportation agenda.”
On Tuesday, Trump and Vice President JD Vance announced a $25-million program under the Justice Department to encourage the public to report suspected fraud in the U.S. government.
 This administration has purposefully mischaracterized immigrants and asylum seekers as fraudsters
— Royce Murray, former Department of Homeland Security official
The White House said the first check, for $10,000, will go to right-wing influencer Nick Shirley, who posted a video last year alleging that Somali residents in Minnesota were running fake child-care centers to collect federal subsidies. Dozens of people were convicted in connection with a sprawling, $250-million children’s food assistance scheme that predated this administration, though more charges have been announced in recent months.
Also Tuesday, administration officials launched another nationwide anti-fraud crackdown, this time targeting immigrants who they allege have illegally collected SNAP benefits. Homeland Security highlighted the arrests of five people, calling them “the opening salvo in a sustained, large-scale ICE operation.”
“From day one of my administration, we’ve waged an unprecedented war on corruption and fraud, and will not let our country be looted and plundered by thieves and pirates and foreign fraudsters and basically scum,” Trump said during a news conference announcing the Fraud Whistleblower Incentive Program.
Earlier this year, the White House created a task force to eliminate fraud and the Department of Justice created a fraud enforcement division, in part, to target immigration-related offenses. Prosecutors have put aside thousands of other cases to zero in on immigration enforcement.
The focus on fraud has noticeably accelerated in the weeks leading up to the election.
Federal authorities charge 28 people in California with alleged illegal voter registration or voting, escalating the Trump administration’s fight with state election officials.
In California, some of the green card holders arrested this week over voter fraud said they didn’t remember registering to vote. The daughter of one defendant, Omar Muñoz, 72, of Belize, said she wondered whether her father had been confused with his U.S.-born son of the same name, who is a registered voter.
California officials pounced on the small number of people alleged to have cast illegal ballots. Illegal voting by immigrants “is so rare that the Trump admin is parading around town about .0001% of California voters,” Gov. Gavin Newsom’s office wrote on X.
In the last seven weeks alone, the State Department said, 112 noncitizens across 20 states have been charged with illegal voting and registration offenses. Overall, since Trump returned to the White House, 155 people have been charged with voting fraud-related offenses.
Mullin and Atty. Gen. Todd Blanche said earlier this month that Homeland Security agents had secured 10 convictions and detained 100 others for civil immigration violations since August.
During the Biden administration, voter fraud charges were brought in just 13 cases, Blanche added.
Studies and audits of state voter rolls have repeatedly found that voting by noncitizens is rare and hasn’t swayed any elections.
Last week, with mail-in voting already underway, the Justice Department sued California, asking a federal court to bar the state from counting the ballots of 20,000 voters who were flagged by federal officials as “likely noncitizens.” Los Angeles County officials reviewed a sample of 200 of those voter registrations and found that nearly 40% indicated they were born in the U.S.
That number of flagged ballots — 20,000 — is a substantial reduction from the 190,000 noncitizens the administration alleged were on state voter rolls earlier this year, though federal authorities this week said they had found a “separate batch of 17,000 voting records potentially tied to noncitizens.”
California leaders pointed to other states, such as Nevada, where similar accusations have proved meritless.
Murray, the former Homeland Security official, said she believes the administration is “trying to sow the seeds of doubt that the midterm outcomes will be trustworthy, so that if the Republican Party loses as badly as they’re predicted to, they can characterize it as due to fraud.”
Murray said the Trump administration has largely misconstrued what it means to commit fraud.
“Fraud is a very specific thing — it’s essentially lying,” she said. “Because you don’t get asylum does not mean you committed fraud, it just means you were ineligible.”
In September, a Homeland Security whistleblower told Sen. Alex Padilla (D-Calif.) that hundreds of U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services employees had been tasked with quickly reviewing the voter information of thousands of people in search of suspected noncitizen voters, and were given a quota of investigating 40 subjects per day.
On Wednesday, a federal judge restricted Homeland Security agents from carrying out sweeping field operations aimed at rooting out voter fraud in nine states, including California.
It is against federal law for immigrants who are not naturalized citizens to vote or register to do so. Penalties can include fines, jail time and even deportation, though authorities rarely pursued that option.
Eric Balliet, a former special agent with Homeland Security Investigations, the criminal investigative arm of ICE, said he takes no issue with investigating fraud, but the timing of this operation and significant resources dedicated show it is “highly politically charged.”

Earthquake kills 16, injures 76 in Tibet as rescue efforts continue
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
09:59:45 UTC
18:59:45 KST

A magnitude 7 earthquake in Tibet has killed at least 16 people and injured 76, with hundreds of homes destroyed as rescuers search remote, high-altitude communities for survivors amid freezing temperatures, dangerous aftershocks and rockslides.
Rescue teams have searched villages and damaged homes in China's Tibet region after a magnitude 7 earthquake killed at least 16 people, injured 76 and forced more than 12,000 residents to evacuate, state media and local officials said Friday.
The earthquake struck Nagqu, a sparsely populated city in northern Tibet about 4,800 meters (15,750 feet) above sea level, late Thursday. At least 339 homes collapsed, while other buildings developed cracks or began leaning, raising fears they could fall during aftershocks.
Authorities warned that the remote terrain, low temperatures and potential rockslides were complicating rescue operations. Intermittent snowfall is forecast over the next three days, adding to concerns for residents displaced by the disaster.
Nagqu's acting mayor, identified by his surname, Dunzhu, said rescuers had completed three rounds of searches by Friday afternoon, checking individual households and villages for survivors.
More than 5,000 people from three local counties were deployed to support the response. Authorities also sent more than 300 police officers, including traffic and community police, to assess damage, assist evacuations and help residents reach safer locations.
Emergency supplies arriving in the region included 2,000 prefabricated housing units, about 3,400 tents, 2,000 folding beds, flashlights and winter clothing.
More than 12,000 people had been safely relocated, according to the official Xinhua News Agency. Videos released by local media showed residents fleeing their homes and taking shelter outdoors or in parked cars as the earthquake shook buildings.
The U.S. Geological Survey said the earthquake occurred at 10:33 p.m. Thursday local time, with its epicenter 191 kilometers (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu and a depth of 18 kilometers (11 miles).
China's Earthquake Networks Center reported 413 aftershocks. The U.S. agency separately recorded at least seven aftershocks measuring between magnitude 4.3 and 5.2, each at a depth of about 10 kilometers (6 miles).
The tremors and resulting rockfalls disrupted transportation and communications. Local railway authorities halted trains passing through the affected region, while officials closed part of National Highway 317 to clear debris. Only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles were permitted through the restricted section.
Communication and power supplies were gradually being restored, local officials said.
Chinese President Xi Jinping called Friday for all-out rescue operations and medical assistance, underscoring the seriousness of the disaster.
The earthquake was China's strongest since a magnitude 7.1 tremor struck neighboring Qinghai province in January 2024, according to the report. A magnitude 7.1 earthquake hit Yushu in Qinghai in 2010, killing at least 2,698 people and leaving nearly 300 others missing.
