Standoff hits Sudanese consumers as Egypt halts cargo trucks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:11:19 UTC
17:11:19 KST

Breadcrumb
Border standoff hits Sudanese consumers as Egypt halts cargo trucks
Egyptian authorities have suspended cargo truck crossings into Sudan, triggering severe shortages and price hikes that ordinary Sudanese are struggling to absorb.
The decision followed the killing of two Egyptian truck drivers and the injury of a third on 12 October, when a 23-year-old Sudanese gunman opened fire on them in a popular market south of Khartoum.
The incident occurred only a day after scores of artisanal miners, including Sudanese nationals, were killed by Egyptian airstrikes in the border area between Egypt and Sudan.
According to the Egyptian army, the strikes were staged inside Egypt. However, unofficial Sudanese claims to the contrary have caused anger in different parts of Sudan.
Sudanese demonstrators took to the streets, particularly in Nyala—the capital of South Darfur State and a stronghold of the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces which battles the Sudanese Armed Forces for control over Sudan.
Activists also called for a boycott of Egyptian goods, planning to blockade the desert road linking Khartoum to border crossings to halt incoming freight.
Cairo framed the suspension as a protective measure to shield Egyptian drivers from targeted violence.
Regardless of Cairo's rationale, the move has dealt an immediate blow to Sudanese consumers, threatening to trigger widespread inflation at an already precarious moment.
A recent viral video captured a Sudanese shopkeeper gesturing to his fully stocked shelves. Most of the goods, he noted, were either imported directly from Egypt or relied on Egyptian raw materials.
"Do you know what the decision to suspend the entry of cargo trucks from Egypt into Sudan means?" the trader asks. "It means that the prices of all these products will shoot up in the coming days."
Lifeline severed
Egypt serves as a vital gateway for Sudan's access to global markets, particularly as international sanctions continue to cripple Sudanese businesses.
Sudan's civil war, which has been grinding on since April 2023, has also put the brakes on a sizeable portion of the country's industrial and agricultural production, making it more dependent on imports for the needs of its people.
In 2025, bilateral trade reached $1.19 billion, with Egyptian exports accounting for $933.3 million.
In the first half of this year, bilateral trade reached $759 million, up from $570 million in the corresponding period of the previous year, according to the Egyptian government. Egyptian exports amounted to $595 million, almost 40% up from the export figure recorded in the first half of 2025, the government says.
Trade between the two countries partly owes its activity to their ability to develop a barter-style system that helps them avoid stringent international sanctions on Sudanese businesses and foreign currency shortages on both sides, specialists said.
However, cutting off Egyptian goods leaves the war-ravaged nation deeply vulnerable, forcing consumers to endure sudden supply bottlenecks alongside skyrocketing prices, Sudanese specialists said.
"This suspension is having far-reaching economic and human consequences," Sudanese political analyst Osman al-Merghani said.
Speaking to The New Arab, he added that the market has been paralyzed in almost all Sudanese states due to the dramatic rise that happened in commodity prices.
"Some commodities, including sugar and rice, have also completely disappeared, which is causing a lot of suffering to ordinary consumers," al-Merghani said.
Online hostility vs. diplomatic containment
The current disruption to bilateral trade comes at a time when a social media war is raging on between the Egyptians and the Sudanese against the background of the 11 October strikes.
Sudanese nationals commenting on the incident slam Egypt for killing what they describe as "innocent" artisanal miners and allegedly infringing on Sudanese territories, throwing light on growing anti-Egypt sentiments in some parts of the southern neighbouring country.
Egyptian social media users counter by defending their national army, and accusing the Sudanese of mining for gold inside Egypt, hence stealing the country's mineral resources.
The surge in anti-Egyptian rhetoric has heightened anxiety among the estimated 1,000 Egyptian nationals still remaining in Sudan.
Before the war erupted in April 2023, between 10,000 and 15,000 Egyptians lived in Sudan, mostly those married to Sudanese, working in Sudan or investing in the country.
An Egyptian national has recently posted a video where he implored Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi to help him and others return safely to Egypt.
"The Sudanese are lying in wait for us on the road between Khartoum and the Egyptian border," the man said in the video which appeared on social media on October 14.
Most Egyptian nationals present in Sudan are reportedly concentrated in coastal areas under the control of the Sudanese Armed Force, especially Port Sudan where the Egyptian Consulate operates and business activities remain comparatively stable.
The governments of the two countries keep working, meanwhile, to contain fallout from the 11 October strikes.
On 16 October, Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and Sudanese Finance Minister Gibril Ibrahim rejected attempts to harm their countries' bilateral relations, noting that those relations are based on shared respect and good neighbourliness.
Meeting the Sudanese minister on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Washington DC, the Egyptian foreign minister reaffirmed Cairo's unwavering support for Sudan's unity and territorial integrity.
This meeting came four days after the foreign ministers of the two countries underscored the importance of respecting each other's country's sovereignty, territorial integrity and borders.
Analysts in Cairo view these diplomatic containment efforts as proof of the high strategic value both nations place on bilateral ties.
They call for managing those relations wisely, especially in the presence of persistent attempts by some parties to sabotage them.
"It is clear that some parties work to widen the gap between the two countries and cause a rupture in their relations," Egyptian political analyst Islam Mansi said.
"These parties do their best to incite the Sudanese people against Egypt, a country bound by historical ties and a shared destiny with Sudan," he told TNA.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Taiwan Institute of Economic Research said Friday that manufacturing and construction sentiment improved in September, while services sector sentiment declined for a third consecutive month.
TIER’s manufacturing business climate index rose 0.5 points from August to 101.39, while the construction index gained 2.81 points to 110.42, per UDN. The services index fell 3.15 points to 92.65. Among manufacturers, 26.8% rated business conditions as good, while 20.3% rated them as bad.
Manufacturing sentiment benefited from expanding global AI infrastructure and demand for smartphones, which boosted inventory-building, per CNA. These trends supported advanced semiconductor production, memory chips, and semiconductor packaging and testing. Higher oil prices also drove up plastic and rubber material costs.
However, manufacturers are more cautious about the next six months. The share expecting conditions to improve fell from 27.1% in August to 24% in September, while the share expecting them to worsen rose from 18% to 19.8%. The institute cited the Middle East conflict, high oil and raw material costs, and oversupply in traditional industries as key concerns.
Rising memory chip costs driven by AI demand could raise consumer electronics prices, weaken demand and reduce future orders, TIER explained. Meanwhile, new petrochemical capacity in China is adding pressure on traditional manufacturers already facing weak demand.
Services sentiment weakened despite stronger business for hotels and restaurants during major exhibitions, Mid-Autumn Festival celebrations, and travel. Restaurants reported lower revenue than in August, while banks faced lower investment returns amid rising US Treasury yields and reduced dividend income.
Construction sentiment improved on high-tech factory expansions, public infrastructure projects, and urban renewal. Property transactions across the six special municipalities rose 14.1% month over month in September, partly as delayed ownership transfers and new-home handovers were completed.
Looking ahead, TIER said department store anniversary sales, online shopping and the government’s universal cash payment could boost retail spending over the next six months. However, it said financial market volatility and uncertainty in overseas markets are expected to keep the services outlook cautious.

Taiwan's Nan Ya sees structural shift in PCB materials market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:09:48 UTC
17:09:48 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan's Nan Ya Plastics Corp. has observed a shift in the printed circuit board materials market, with supply shortages reshaping product demand and supplier selection, CTEE reported Thursday.
PCBs are boards that hold and connect electronic components in devices. Copper-clad laminates (CCLs) form the base of circuit boards, helping determine their signal transmission and heat resistance. Fiberglass cloth, made by weaving fine glass fibers, is a key material in CCLs that provides heat resistance and electrical insulation, according to Pocket Securities and Business Next.
The supply chain expects prices for both fiberglass cloth and CCL to rise 10-15% starting in November, although increases will vary by product specifications and suppliers. This reflects a broader market shift, Nan Ya said, as manufacturers focus on higher-end products while demand for standard-grade materials remains strong.
Nan Ya noted that the tight supply has also changed how customers choose suppliers. In the early stages of price increases, customers tended to favor suppliers offering a wide range of products and specifications. As shortages have worsened, however, access to materials and reliable delivery schedules have become more important than product variety.
On the pricing front, China-based CCL leader Kingboard Laminates Holdings Ltd. has raised prices 12 times this year. Meanwhile, prices for thinner 1080-grade E-glass fiberglass cloth have climbed about 300% from their lows to their peaks.
Thin fiberglass cloth is in particularly short supply, as limited capacity to install additional weaving machines makes it difficult to ramp up production in the short term.
However, new production capacity may not ease shortages of thin fiberglass cloth. China Jushi Co., a leading manufacturer, is expected to begin mass production at its new facilities next year, but the added capacity will mainly produce thicker grades rather than the thinner varieties facing the most severe shortages.
Supply chain estimates suggest the shortage may gradually ease from the second half of 2027 through 2028. The timing will depend on equipment deliveries, the commissioning of new capacity, and how quickly manufacturers can shift production between product grades.
However, rising demand for higher-end applications could keep supplies tight even as capacity expands. Higher material costs are also expected to be passed on to manufacturers downstream.

Taipei's Royal Joying Soiree unveils seasonal crab feast
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:09:29 UTC
17:09:29 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – Stepping into Taipei’s modern Chinese restaurant Royal Joying Soiree, diners are greeted by the rich, savory aromas of autumn.
Executive chef Li Kuan-yi (李冠儀) and dim sum chef Li Kuo-sheng (李國聖) have teamed up to debut an 11-dish seasonal crab menu blending Cantonese foundations with global and regional inspirations.
Among the standout dishes is the stir-fried mud crab with aged black vinegar. Inspired by Li Kuan-yi’s time working in Shanghai, where vinegar-simmered seafood is a staple, the dish features a measured touch of sugar and aged vinegar to create a caramelized glaze over the crab and vegetables.
Paired with crisp Japanese yam and purple sweet potato, it balances the rich crustacean meat.
Attention to detail drives the menu's soup selection. The lotus seed and intestine mud crab soup originally stemmed from a concept inspired by Shanghai’s traditional pork and bamboo shoot soup.
Due to seasonal availability constraints of authentic Jinhua ham and fresh bamboo shoots, the team instead adapted Taiwanese sishen soup. After simmering pork bone and lean meat for six hours to build a gelatinous base, they added daikon radish to draw out the crab's sweetness, incorporating handmade lotus seed intestines and Job's tears for a nourishing broth.
Another creation, the braised mud crab and ginger duck in clay pot, marries Taiwanese winter ginger duck tonic with traditional Fujianese dry-braising.
To keep the duck tender, the kitchen pressure-cooks ingredients on demand. Diners can enjoy the dry-braised dish before pouring in Wenchang chicken broth for a comforting second course.
Subtle touches elevate even the vegetable courses. To eliminate the raw, grassy taste of carrots in the golden pumpkin puree for the braised baby bok choy and sea cucumber, the kitchen slices and deep-fries the carrots first, locking in natural sweetness for a velvety finish.
On the dim sum front, chef Li Kuo-sheng navigates the technical hurdles of handling perishable, fresh crab meat without freezing.
The menu features steamed prawn dumplings with crab roe and mentaiko — combining tiger prawns, rich crab roe, and vegetarian shark’s fin — alongside crispy kataif-wrapped snow crab legs coated in a crab roe white sauce.
The autumn crab feast runs through Oct. 31. During the promotional period, orders of any mud crab dish include a complimentary nourishing soup, while red swimmer crab selections come with a complimentary serving of signature lava mushroom buns.

Shen calls for separating Taiwan stock trading from typhoon closures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:09:22 UTC
17:09:22 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — DPP Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen (沈伯洋) on Thursday called for discussions on separating stock market closures from local government decisions to suspend work and classes during typhoons.
CNA reported that Shen said the city's role as the main financial center makes typhoon closure decisions more complicated. He suggested reviewing whether financial institutions and stock trading should follow separate closure rules.
Local governments should explain the weather conditions and other factors behind their decisions to suspend work and classes, Shen said. He added that changing stock market closure rules would require cooperation between central and local authorities.
Currently, the stock market closes for the day if Taipei announces a full-day or morning work suspension before trading begins at 9 a.m. If the city announces an afternoon suspension after trading has begun, regular trading continues until 1:30 p.m., but trading scheduled after that time is canceled.
This means Taipei's decision to suspend work can halt stock trading nationwide, even if other cities remain open. However, closures in other cities do not automatically stop trading, although affected securities firms may need special arrangements to complete transactions.
KMT Spokesperson Liu Tsai-wei (柳采葳) questioned how financial workers would be protected if trading continued during severe weather. She said Shen had not explained how securities transactions and bank settlements would be handled, while financial market rules fall under the central authorities, per UDN.
Taipei Mayor Chiang Wan-an (蔣萬安) said the issue had been discussed before and could be reviewed with the central government. His campaign questioned why Shen, who is also a legislator, had not used his position to seek changes from financial regulators, per Nownews.
Taoyuan Mayor Chang San-cheng (張善政) said central authorities should assess whether online trading is widespread enough to support the change. New Taipei Mayor Hou Yu-ih (侯友宜) said public safety must remain the government's top priority during typhoons, per Taisounds.
The Financial Supervisory Commission said it was reviewing how other countries handle stock trading during severe weather. Securities and Futures Bureau Deputy Director-General Huang Chung-hao (黃仲豪) said the review included Japan and South Korea, but no decision had been made, per SETN.
Japan does not automatically suspend stock trading when a typhoon warning is issued. The Tokyo Stock Exchange considers the extent of damage, whether brokers can trade, and public safety before deciding whether to suspend trading.
Reuters reported that the Tokyo Stock Exchange suspended all stock trading on Oct. 1, 2020, after a hardware failure disrupted its trading system. The shutdown lasted the entire day, with trading resuming the following morning.
South Korea's stock market can remain open during typhoons, rather than automatically closing when severe weather strikes. Yonhap reported that the benchmark KOSPI index continued trading on Sept. 6, 2022, when Typhoon Hinnamnor struck the country.
However, trading can still be suspended when technical problems disrupt market operations. Yonhap reported that a system error halted all KOSPI stock trading for seven minutes, from 11:37 a.m. to 11:44 a.m., on March 18, 2025, marking the first such market-wide technical suspension since 2005.

Members of the execution team tasked with putting Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike to death repeatedly questioned whether they had damaged her veins while attempting to establish an intravenous (IV) line, according to a detailed account by her lawyer.
The team used about 10 needles and spent nearly 50 minutes trying to establish a working line before proceeding with the lethal injection on September 30, attorney Randy Spivey said in a court filing cited by The Guardian.
Team members expressed concern that Pike’s vein might have “blown”, meaning it had ruptured, and struggled to determine whether the needle had entered the vein, according to Spivey, who witnessed the execution attempt.
Despite the difficulties, the team proceeded with the injection. Pike remained alive and made snoring and choking sounds before the execution was called off.
Pike, 50, spent 10 days in hospital before returning to prison in Nashville. She has since regained the ability to walk and talk, but her long-term medical prognosis remains unclear.
Scrutiny of execution procedures
The failed execution has intensified scrutiny of Tennessee’s lethal injection procedures. Republican Governor Bill Lee suspended executions in the state pending a review.
The case has also drawn attention to the attempted execution of another death row inmate, Tony Carruthers, who survived an execution attempt in May after officials struggled to find a vein.
Lawyers representing death row prisoners say the two cases highlight serious flaws in the state’s execution protocol. They have renewed their legal challenge, arguing that the procedures risk causing severe pain and suffering.
Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer, a classmate she killed when she was 18.

Swiss watch brand Zenith could cut up to 200 jobs
Zenith, a watch brand based in Le Locle and owned by the French luxury giant LVMH, has launched a consultation process with its staff in view of a possible mass layoff.
A company spokesperson confirmed the news published in the Le Temps newspaper, stating that no further information would be provided at this stage. However, other sources within the company have spoken to the AWP news agency, mentioning that around a hundred jobs are at risk in Le Locle – out of a total of approximately 200 – and another hundred abroad, within the distribution network.
According to these sources, Zenith intends to focus more heavily on ultra-luxury watchmaking. The reorganisation is reportedly driven by the need to align production volumes with actual demand: following the post-pandemic recovery, the brand is said to have recorded losses year on year, despite the strong performance of certain collections. The difficulties encountered include the strong Swiss franc, US tariffs and international geopolitical tensions. Added to these factors are structural problems: the scale of the industrial and commercial operations is reportedly excessive in relation to current needs.

High-end boom masks Swiss watch industry polarisation
Zenith’s financial situation had fuelled rumours last January that LVMH might sell the brand – rumours which were firmly denied by the French group. The source cited by AWP has also ruled out the existence of any plans for a sale.

New horizons of economic co-op being formed between Mazandaran, Uzbekistan: Uzbek envoy
TEHRAN- According to a Khabar Online report from Mazandaran, Fariddin Nasriyev, Ambassador of the Republic of Uzbekistan to Iran, met with Mehdi Younesi Rostami, Governor of Mazandaran province, and while thanking the provincial officials for their warm hospitality, emphasized the broad capacities for economic and trade cooperation between Mazandaran and Uzbekistan.
Referring to the meeting held at the Mazandaran Chamber of Commerce, the Ambassador of the Republic of Uzbekistan to Iran stated: “A very good meeting was held with the participation of economic actors, which shows the high interest of Iranian traders in cooperating with Uzbekistan, as well as the desire of Uzbek traders to benefit from the capacities and manufactured products of Mazandaran.”
Referring to Mazandaran’s economic and production capacities, Nasriyev considered the development of interactions between the merchants of the two sides a suitable ground for increasing trade exchanges and added: “The interest of the economic actors of the two countries in joint cooperation has provided a valuable opportunity to expand trade relations and identify new areas of cooperation.”
He also expressed satisfaction over the presence of a Mazandarani in the co-presidency of the Iran-Uzbekistan Chamber of Commerce, describing this as an opportunity to strengthen economic ties and facilitate cooperation between the private sectors of the two countries.
Referring to last year’s visit of a Mazandaran delegation to Uzbekistan, the Ambassador of Uzbekistan to Iran assessed that visit as positive and constructive and said: “The trend of trade cooperation between the two sides is increasingly expanding, and there are suitable grounds for further development of these relations.”
Emphasizing the need for continued bilateral consultations, Nasriyev announced intensive planning for visits by officials in the next two to three months and stated: “In this framework, planning for a visit to Uzbekistan and inviting the Governor of Mazandaran to travel to this country is on the agenda so that the ground can be further prepared for strengthening economic and trade cooperation.”

In conclusion, the Ambassador of the Republic of Uzbekistan to Iran once again expressed gratitude for the hosting and hospitality of Mazandaran officials and expressed hope that, with continued communication among officials, chambers of commerce, and private-sector actors, economic and trade cooperation between Mazandaran and Uzbekistan would enter a broader stage.
In late September, Mehr News Agency reported that Uzbekistan’s $1.4 billion food market is open to Iranian exporters as trade between the two countries reached $305 million in the first half of 2026, and three cooperation documents were recently signed.
According to this report, Uzbekistan is becoming one of Central Asia’s growing markets, as its food imports in the first quarter of 2026 jumped by nearly 46% to $1.4 billion. Yet Iran’s share of this market remains limited, and economic actors believe that expanding Iran’s food industry exports to Tashkent requires resolving financial and transportation obstacles and gaining a more accurate understanding of the market.
In recent years, Uzbekistan has pursued its foreign trade development path more rapidly, and growth in imports, increased foreign investment, and expanded ties with regional markets have made the country one of Central Asia’s notable markets.
According to the latest statistics from Uzbekistan’s National Statistics Committee, the country’s imports in the first quarter of 2026 reached $12.2 billion. Among these, food products and live animals, with a share of about $1.4 billion, were one of the main import groups. Notably, imports in this group grew by 45.9% compared with the same period last year.
These figures show that Uzbekistan’s food market is not merely a domestic consumer market; given the country’s population of more than 37 million and its position as one of Central Asia’s trade hubs, it could become more important for regional food exporters.
Meanwhile, Iran’s commercial attaché in Uzbekistan, referring to more than $280 million in trade between the two countries in the first five months of this year, cited agricultural exports, technological cooperation, and joint investment as key pillars for expanding Iran-Uzbekistan trade.
According to IRNA, citing the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, Rahmatollah Khormali said, emphasizing the growing trend of trade cooperation between the two countries: Follow-ups by the agriculture ministries of Iran and Uzbekistan paved the way for sending a 120-member delegation headed by the Minister of Agriculture and a group of activists and experts in agriculture, aquaculture, machinery, and processing industries to Uzbekistan.
He described Uzbekistan as one of the most populous countries in Central Asia and added: Uzbekistan ranks second among Iran’s export destinations among the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) and has considerable capacity for expanding trade relations with Iran. Meanwhile, agriculture is one of the priority areas in developing trade between the two countries.
Referring to Iran-Uzbekistan trade figures, Khormali stated: In the first five months of this year, the trade volume between the two countries reached about $280 million. During this period, despite regional conditions and their impact on Iran’s trade activities, we did not see a decline in exchanges with Uzbekistan, and we hope that with continued dispatch and hosting of trade delegations and stronger ties between the two countries’ economic actors, the trade growth trend will continue in the coming months.
Iran’s commercial attaché in Uzbekistan described food security as another important area of cooperation between the two countries and said: In the Uzbek government structure, a Food Security Agency has been established with the aim of ensuring and improving food security in areas such as livestock, poultry, quarantine, and food products, which can provide a basis for developing specialized and commercial cooperation between Iran and Uzbekistan.
Citing some of Iran’s agricultural export advantages to Uzbekistan, he noted: Currently, products such as citrus fruits, apples, kiwis, pistachios, dates, dairy products, powdered milk, and fish feed are exported from Iran to Uzbekistan, and given the capacity of this country’s market, there is also room to expand and diversify Iran’s export basket.
Khormali also addressed the potential for technological cooperation and said: About 30 projects worth $770 million in various fields, including agriculture, are being implemented in Uzbekistan by Iranian companies, which indicates the considerable capacity of Iran’s private sector to enter the Uzbek market.
In conclusion, Iran’s commercial attaché in Uzbekistan considered the holding of specialized meetings and increased interaction among officials and economic actors of the two countries in various fields, especially agriculture, as paving the way for developing mutual cooperation and increasing the volume of Iran-Uzbekistan trade.

'Operation Lame': How police shootings are targeting Muslims in India
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:07:16 UTC
17:07:16 KST

Police in India’s most populous state have shot hundreds of Muslim men accused of cow smuggling in the legs in encounters that critics describe as extrajudicial justice designed to pander to India’s Hindu majority, an Associated Press investigation found.
Police in Uttar Pradesh say they shoot in self-defence and that the state’s “zero tolerance” policy on crime has helped restore law and order.
Now the tactic of shooting people just below the knee — known locally as ‘Operation Lame’ — is spreading to other states in India.
Activists, opposition leaders and local judges, however, say the violence amounts to extrajudicial punishment and intimidation that disproportionately impacts India’s large Muslim minority, and undermines the rule of law.
“This is a dangerous situation,” said Mangla Verma, a human rights lawyer based in New Delhi. “It’s become a routine police practice … Instead of investigating, police kill or injure a person and justice is done.”
The Center for the Study of Organised Hate, a Washington-based think tank, compiled records of nearly 650 cases of suspects accused of cow smuggling who have been shot and injured by Uttar Pradesh police since 2020. Its findings were shared exclusively with the AP, which independently reviewed a sample of more than 200. The overwhelming majority of cases involved Muslims, the centre found.
In case after case, bullets struck the same part of the suspect’s body — the leg, most often below the knee. This reporting is based only on incidents police themselves publicised and almost certainly represents an undercount.
Amitabh Yash, a senior Uttar Pradesh police official, told the AP that police are instructed to respond only in self-defence, and said police in his state have killed and injured far fewer suspects, per capita, than police in the United States.
Yash said there is no order to shoot suspects in the leg and added that he would investigate the consistent pattern of injuries if an appropriate complaint were lodged.
“The police must be questioned for every action they take. Every action is open to scrutiny, whether it is a death or an injury,” he said. “In the last year, there has been no reason to punish any police officer for inappropriate use of force.”
‘Operation Lame’ is now spreading to other states
The tactic of shooting to injure, known locally as “Operation Langda” — or ”Operation Lame” — has become widespread across Uttar Pradesh. It is deployed against suspects accused of cow smuggling as well as other crimes, including theft and rape. Cattle smuggling is an offence that carries particular weight in India, where cows are revered by many Hindus and cow protection has been politically charged.
India has a long history of so-called encounter killings, in which police shoot and kill a suspect often under dubious circumstances. Some activists argue that police have evolved their strategy, shooting to injure instead of kill in what are known locally as “half encounters,” to spark less public outcry.
The violence has unfolded alongside a political push for tougher policing under Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his allies in Uttar Pradesh, who have promoted a “zero tolerance” policy against criminals to instill fear and promote law and order.
Uttar Pradesh is led by Yogi Adityanath, a Hindu monk-turned-politician and a senior leader of Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party. From the time Adityanath took office as chief minister in March 2017 through October 13 of this year, 316 suspects were killed in encounters and 110 of them were Muslim, according to state police data obtained by the AP. That's a higher proportion than the state’s overall population, which is around one in five Muslim.
Over the same period, 12,890 suspects were injured, while 18 police were killed and 1,953 injured in the line of duty. Data on the religion of suspects injured by police was not available.
The zero tolerance policy "has increased fear among criminals and strengthened the feeling of security among the general public,” Uttar Pradesh police said in a May statement. “This is the reason why the state’s law and order is being appreciated at the national level.”
Activists say the practice is now spreading to nearby BJP-run states like Haryana, Bihar, Uttarakhand and the outskirts of the nation’s capital, New Delhi.
Experts question the consistent pattern in shootings
In social media posts publicised by police, officers describe similar scenes: suspects fleeing, police coming under fire and officers shooting to disable rather than kill.
But human rights advocates have long alleged that many police shootings in India occur when the suspect doesn’t pose a threat. Some question the consistent pattern of bullets delivered below the knee, arguing that it suggests the wounds were not really inflicted in self-defence.
“Such incidents make a mockery of the law. They sabotage the system,” said Sandeep Pandey, an activist and opposition political leader based in Uttar Pradesh. “It’s state-sponsored violence.”
Dr Mohd Kaleem Khan, a professor of forensic medicine at Aligarh Muslim University’s Jawaharlal Nehru Medical College in Uttar Pradesh, said it is highly unlikely a bullet could be delivered horizontally, without touching bone, through the calf muscle of a person who was fleeing or fighting, especially at a distance.
“It’s not a shot in defence,” he said. “It’s a deliberate close shot of a person.”
Judges warn that police impunity is a threat to democracy
The violence has drawn judicial scrutiny.
In January, the Allahabad High Court, the state’s highest judicial authority, issued a rare public rebuke of the growing number of police shootings in Uttar Pradesh, warning that officers cannot replace the justice system and chastising police for failing to comply with legally mandated reporting and investigation procedures.
“This Court has noticed that the practice of police encounters, particularly firing at the legs of accused persons, has seemingly become a routine feature,” one judge wrote in a ruling on a bail hearing earlier this year, calling such conduct “wholly impermissible” under the rule of law.
The Allahabad High Court suggested some officers may be motivated by career incentives or publicity, noting that police appear to be “misusing their authority in order to attract the attention of higher officers or to create an impression of public sympathy.”
In a separate case, another Allahabad High Court judge wrote in June that he had “deep constitutional concern” over what he described as a “culture of institutional impunity” in Uttar Pradesh.
Despite such public laments, judicial action in the last decade has been slow. In 2018, for example, the People’s Union for Civil Liberties, a human rights group, presented evidence of police encounter killings in Uttar Pradesh and asked the court to ensure that such incidents are investigated by an independent entity. The case is pending.
Since then, the number of police shootings — resulting in both deaths and injuries — in Uttar Pradesh has surged.
Yash, the Uttar Pradesh police official, dismissed allegations that justice has become politicised and said police are not rewarded for shooting suspects.
“There is no policy of any career advancement related to any police engagement,” he said. “Absolutely none.”
Families say the shootings leave them destitute
The AP spoke with the families of six Muslim men in Uttar Pradesh who had been shot in the leg by police. All spoke on condition of anonymity, saying they were too fearful to speak publicly. All six men were still in jail or living in hiding at the time.
One woman told the AP that her son had supported the extended family by trading buffalo, which don’t fall under cow protection laws.
“He’s been left lame. His leg has developed a large swelling,” she said. “If someone gives us something, we accept it. That’s how we’re getting by. That poor man can’t go out and work anymore. Whatever people give us, we eat.”
Another woman said her son, who worked as a dairy buffalo trader, had been shot in both knees, leaving the family to survive by taking out small loans. When she went to see him in the hospital, she said, blood was oozing from his wounds.
“He’s completely broken,” she said. “He just held our hands. The whole family cried. He cried continuously.”
The police shootings also have a religious dimension
According to data compiled by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate, nearly 93 percent of suspects injured in cow-smuggling-related encounters were Muslim. Both India’s population and its police are overwhelmingly Hindu.
The analysis reflects only the 627 cases where names or other identifying information were available.
The evidence collected on hundreds of shootings “clearly shows that the state institutions, particularly the law enforcement, are increasingly being used as the vehicles for the persecution of Muslim minority,” said Raqib Naik, the centre’s executive director. “This appears to have evolved into a bureaucratisation of persecution, where policing increasingly seems to appear to be intertwined with majoritarian politics.”
Under Modi’s leadership, India has moved away from its founding as a secular democracy and towards a Hindu-first state. In Uttar Pradesh, the chief minister, Adityanath, has positioned himself at the hard edge of this surging religious nationalism, and critics say his tough-on-crime approach amounts to a veiled attack on Muslims that panders to the hard-line Hindu vote.
“When you shoot people who are carrying cattle, you are sending a message that you are upholding a Hindu agenda,” said Pandey, the activist and opposition leader.
Police official Yash said the high proportion of Muslims among cattle smuggling suspects injured by police reflects the large number of Muslims involved in the cattle trade.
“The police itself has all castes and religions,” Yash said. “You cannot try to target one group.”
India stopped reporting the proportion of Muslims serving as police officers more than a decade ago, when they were significantly underrepresented in Uttar Pradesh at just 4.8 percent of the force, according to 2013 National Crime Records Bureau data.
For victims and their families, the consequences of the shootings can be lasting.
“They target perfectly decent people,” said a Muslim man who told the AP that his nephew was picked up by police while on the way to see his children, accused of cow smuggling and shot in the leg. “The only fear now is that they’ll pick up someone else in the name of cows — or shoot someone else.”

New famine risk haunts war-torn Sudan with El Niño-driven drought
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:07:06 UTC
17:07:06 KST

New famine risk haunts war-torn Sudan with El Niño-driven drought
NORTH KORDOFAN, Sudan, Oct 23 - Across Sudan, farmers who have struggled to harvest their crops since a civil war flared in 2023 are now battling a new enemy that could plunge the nation back into famine: the weather.
El Niño, the climate pattern threatening parts of Africa with floods, is bringing higher temperatures and drought to Sudan, where pockets of famine have already emerged during more than three years of conflict, mainly in areas under siege.
Parched conditions are hurting crops and livestock across the southern region where rain-fed agriculture produces much of Sudan's food, according to UN officials and aid experts, along with more than two dozen farmers interviewed by Reuters. One large-scale farmer expects his harvest to be a quarter of last year's.
"The risk of famine is growing in many conflict-affected areas of Sudan, with the impact of El Niño-induced drought compounding already dire conditions," the United Nations-backed global hunger monitor, the IPC, wrote in an October 12 alert.
Rainfall in July to September, the peak rainy season, was the lowest in more than three decades across the country, United States Geological Survey (USGS) data shows. In North Darfur state in the west, it was the lowest since 1984 - the same year a famine devastated Sudan and Ethiopia. In North Kordofan state in the central region, it was the lowest since 1990, while in Gedaref state in the southeast it was the lowest since 1991.
In June, the IPC said 5.1 million people in Sudan faced severe hunger. The IPC is currently updating the numbers. They had been expected to fall once harvesting started in November and December, helped by a lull in fighting in some areas. But the El Niño-driven drought is now expected to push them up.
The UN World Food Programme forecasts an additional 350,000 people will experience severe hunger by the end of 2026, rising to 1.2 million more by August 2027, the WFP head of programme for Sudan, Samuel Clendon, told Reuters in October, citing figures shared with donors but not publicised widely.
The worst-hit areas are Darfur and the Kordofan region, the WFP said.
'THE CATTLE BECAME SKINNY'
In North Kordofan state, Mariam Omar digs out weeds poking up between crops that should be close to harvest but instead are shrivelled in the dry, sandy soil. "This year is terrible," she said on her smallholding near the town of Um Ruwaba.
Mohamed Abdelrahman, a farmer with about 420 hectares in the Um Rawaba area, told Reuters many farmers displaced by war were returning to drought-stricken land. Abdelrahman, who is also a sesame trader providing finance to smallholders, estimated about 40% of land in the area would have no harvest.
In the livestock market of El Obeid, North Kordofan's capital, the ribs of cows protrude through their dusty hides.
"Usually at this time the cattle are fat and everyone is making a profit. But now, with this autumn's scarcity, the cattle became skinny," trader Sirajaldeen Abdellateef said, as he counted Sudanese pounds which have been rapidly losing value, stoking inflation and causing further hardship.
The WFP has focused on delivering food to the 5 million most needy people, but it says it cannot reach all of them. For those it can reach, it has cut rations to stretch limited resources.
As of October 17, the WFP had $276 million to fund its Sudan operation, less than half of last year's budget. It says it needs an extra $134 million to tackle hunger caused by drought.
The decline of both aid and harvests at once is a “recipe for disaster,” Carl Skau, acting executive director of the WFP, told Reuters in Cairo after a trip to Darfur, where he said he had seen the impact of drought.
'IT'S NO LONGER JUST ABOUT BULLETS'
Rations had been halved in Tawila, a sprawling Darfur camp of about 700,000 people displaced by war, according to Skau, even as aid workers said 9,000 more people had arrived between the start of September and mid-October.
Suad Ahmed, a teacher who said she had been displaced from her home multiple times through the war, came to Tawila seeking food after leaving her village east of al-Fashir, the capital of North Darfur state.
"As I was coming here on the road, so many people said: ‘If you find food and drink there, please tell us’," she said.
Adam Rojal, spokesman for the non-governmental group, the General Coordination of IDPs and Refugee Camps in Sudan, said hunger rather than war was now driving people from their homes. "It's no longer just about bullets," he said.
Gedaref state has been crucial to Sudan’s food supply during the war because it escaped the fighting. But it hasn’t escaped the drought.
"Even if we get rain going forward, I'll only have about 25% of last year's crop," said Emad Kabsoor, who runs several large farms covering 14,700 hectares, adding that searing temperatures were also scorching fields.
"We’ve never had a season like this," he said.
Temperatures in Gedaref ranged between 7 and 9 degrees above the historic average for October 20, the Reuters Climate Monitor showed.
Sudan's government has played down the threat to food supplies. Sudanese Agriculture Minister Esmat Qureshi told a news conference on October 8 in Khartoum that this year's harvest would be lower but "not significantly less than last year's."
'WE DON’T KNOW HOW IT WILL END'
When asked about the drought, the head of the RSF's humanitarian aid authority, Abdelrahman Ismail, told Reuters: "We have made efforts to coordinate and invite an early response, and we believe we can do more if the necessary resources and capacity are provided."
Humanitarian agencies have repeatedly accused government troops and rival Rapid Support Forces (RSF) of blocking or hindering aid during the conflict, which both sides deny.
The IPC declared pockets of famine in Sudan in 2024 and 2025, including in al-Fashir, where government forces and their allies, as well as up to a quarter of a million people, were under siege by the RSF for a year and a half before the city fell.
The drought means there’s little respite for a nation with a history of humanitarian crises, including the 1984 famine that killed hundreds of thousands of people across the region.
"The situation today is in most respects much, much worse because of the conflict," said famine expert Alex De Waal, adding that in the 1980s the world mobilised aid resources, while international aid budgets have now been cut back.
Back in 1984, harvests failed, livestock died and people were forced to migrate, said Sirajaldin al-Tahir, a farmer in Um Ruwaba. "But God took pity on us, and the US government brought in aid and distributed it to our village," he said.
"This year, 2026, we don’t know how it will end." REUTERS

France mounts major security operation for fresh wave of protests
PARIS, Oct 23 - France will deploy 70,000 police backed by specialist units for protests on Saturday, Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said on Friday, accusing ultra-left groups of encouraging violence and looting after unrest shocked the country last weekend.
The government is seeking to prevent a repeat of last week's demonstrations that descended into riots, looting and arson in several cities, triggering widespread criticism of authorities for not preventing the mayhem.
"We will be uncompromising with rioters, looters and all those who commit acts of violence," Nunez told reporters on Friday after meetings involving President Emmanuel Macron, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu and senior security officials.
Nunez said authorities had identified numerous online calls from hard-left groups encouraging attacks and urging activists to target public buildings.
"We are not talking about a nice, friendly demonstration," Nunez said, adding: "We are ready for tomorrow. We will be extremely vigilant, extremely firm, and we will let absolutely nothing pass."
MUSEUMS, MAJOR EVENTS SHUTTERED AS PRECAUTION
Anger over living costs and strained public services has drawn students, workers and unions onto the streets of France in recent weeks, but authorities say radical militants and bands of young looters have taken advantage of the dispute to sow chaos.
Police have authorised only a union demonstration in Paris on Saturday, rejecting requests for rallies lodged by France's main student union, UNEF, and the Yellow Vest movement, an anti-establishment force that first emerged in 2018.
Many French cities beyond Paris have also banned protests, including France's second and third largest cities, Marseille and Lyon.
UNEF said its rallies, which grew from high school protests last month against teacher shortages and shabby facilities, would go ahead regardless.
Fears of renewed turmoil prompted several of Paris' best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, to close on Saturday, while the city's normally bustling Art Basel fair will remain shut throughout the weekend.
Business groups also urged shops to stay shut after some 3,000 stores and businesses were ransacked last weekend.
Nunez said 10,000 more police would be on the streets than a week ago, while the specialist RAID and GIGN units, mounted police, helicopters, drones and anti-drone systems would be deployed across the country.
Armoured vehicles and water cannon vehicles would also be available, while curfews imposed in some sensitive areas this past week would remain in force.
FAR-RIGHT CONGRESS A POSSIBLE FLASHPOINT
Authorities are also concerned that the annual congress of Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally in Orleans this weekend could become a flashpoint, with left-wing and anti-racist groups announcing counter-demonstrations.
The upsurge of violence has boosted poll ratings for Le Pen, who is the frontrunner for next year's presidential election. She has portrayed the unrest as evidence of a collapse in state authority.
Adding to tensions, one person was killed and four injured in a shooting west of Paris on Friday in an attack that police said could be racially motivated.
Macron is due to meet student representatives later on Friday for the first time, seeking to de-escalate a crisis that has exposed deep social and political tensions.
Marylise Leon, the general secretary of the CFDT, one of the nation's largest trade unions, criticised him on Friday for refusing to grant permission to more rallies on Saturday.
"It's counterproductive because there is a lot of anger, a lot of anger and a demand to be considered and to be listened to," she told French broadcaster TF1. "It's not for the president to decide who can legitimately request to protest."
The social turbulence has intensified scrutiny of France's economic outlook and ratings agency Moody's is widely expected to cut the French credit rating on Friday, underscoring concern that the government had not reined in public spending. REUTERS

Seoul again proposes talks with North Korea on border lines amid rising tensions

Gender pay gap stubbornly remains among one-quarter of employers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:05:15 UTC
17:05:15 KST

Women are still earning an average of 5% less than men in management functions in Belgium, according to the latest research by Randstad
In some 25% of companies in Belgium, women in management functions still earn an average 5% less than men. The figure takes into account comparable functions and ages of the employees.
The latest study by HR expert Randstad compared the salaries among more than 1,000 companies. “We see the difference particularly in leadership positions,” says Wouter Beuckels of Randstad, who offers two explanations for the phenomenon.
“Only one-quarter or one-third of management positions are held by women,” he says. “This means that fewer women are also involved in making decisions about salaries or promotions. In addition, we also see that women negotiate their salaries less frequently. As a result, they are less likely to get the best deal.”
Belgium postpones EU guidelines
The pay gap is less acute in functions outside of management. “In those cases, representation is more equal, and the gender pay gap falls under that 5% margin,” says Beuckels.
He points out that large companies with more structured pay scales have far less of a gender pay gap than small and medium-sized companies.
The EU has been trying to tackle the gender pay gap in companies for some time and has drawn up guidelines requiring companies to be more transparent about salaries. “Incorporating these guidelines into Belgian law was postponed by six months last June,” notes Beuckels. “Due to the uncertain economic situation, companies may have less budget available to address the gender pay gap.”

French companies plan to invest €1.5 billion in Kazakhstan over the next three years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

French companies plan to invest €1.5 billion in Kazakhstan over the next three years
French companies plan to invest an additional €1.5 billion in Kazakhstan over the next 3 years, with projects expected in renewable energy, hydropower, urban utilities and tourism, France’s ambassador to Kazakhstan, Sylvain Guiaugue, said at a briefing at the French Embassy’s residence, Qazinform News Agency correspondent reports.
The planned investments reflect French companies’ continued interest in the Kazakh market, the ambassador said, noting that businesses also intend to expand local hiring and production.
French companies currently employ around 200,000 people in Kazakhstan. They plan to hire another 1,000 local workers over the next 3 years, according to the ambassador.
Renewable energy and infrastructure
Renewable energy is among the main areas attracting French investment. Potential projects include wind farms and hydropower facilities, as well as the modernization of existing dams.
French companies are also exploring opportunities in urban infrastructure, particularly water management and heating networks in major cities.
Tourism is another area of cooperation. French company Poma has signed a contract to supply cable car systems for a project in the Almaty region. The company is also expected to localize part of its equipment production in Kazakhstan.
The ambassador said French businesses increasingly seek local suppliers and partners. Major projects can create opportunities for Kazakh small and medium-sized enterprises to join supply chains.
Nuclear energy cooperation
France and Kazakhstan are also exploring opportunities to expand cooperation in nuclear energy, building on existing partnerships.
The ambassador cited the long-running cooperation between Kazakhstan’s Kazatomprom and France’s Orano through the joint venture KATCO, as well as nuclear fuel production in Kazakhstan using Framatome technology.
French engineering company Assystem has also been selected as an adviser to Kazakhstan’s government on nuclear power plant development.
The ambassador said contacts between the two countries were continuing as Kazakhstan plans to build at least two nuclear power plants. Potential cooperation could also include research and university training to prepare specialists for the sector.
Kazakhstan as a regional hub
The ambassador said French businesses were interested in using Kazakhstan as a base for reaching wider regional markets.
He also highlighted the importance of the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route, which he said was becoming increasingly significant for trade and connectivity between Europe and Central Asia.
The investment plans are outlined in a new study, French Business in Kazakhstan: A Lasting Impact, published by the French Embassy’s Economic Department in October 2026. It examines the economic contribution of French businesses, including their investment, employment, local production and exports.
Earlier, Qazinform reported that Kazakhstan showcased its agricultural exports at SIAL Paris 2026, held on October 17-21. The national pavilion was presented by the National Association of Oilseed Processors of Kazakhstan (NAOPK) and its member companies. Kazakhstan is among the EU’s top three suppliers of sunflower seed meal.

Iran war could worsen after US midterms
- Vali Nasr says the US-Iran war is in an “inconclusive holding pattern” and may worsen after the US midterms, as Tehran now wants more than it did in June.
- He says Trump has a three-month window to negotiate peace or strike, but any new attack could trigger wider conflict and damage the global economy.
- Nasr says US weakness in the war has hurt its security image in West Asia, while China benefits from less American influence and countries now must rethink their defence plans.
AI generated
SINGAPORE – The US and Iran war is in an “inconclusive holding pattern”, and there is no knowing which way the situation might go once the United States midterm elections are over, more so since Tehran’s demands have hardened.
That is the word from Professor Vali Nasr, one of the world’s most renowned experts on Iran and a former adviser to the US State Department.
“President Trump was forced into a memorandum of understanding which actually looked very much to be in Iran’s favour. Since then, he has been trying to claw back what the US lost in those first 40 days,” said Nasr, referring to the failed June agreement for a 60-day ceasefire.
“This can be resolved by them going into another bout of war. Or they can do what they have been doing, grinding this (out) going forward. The Iranians are now asking for more than they asked for in June.”
The 14-point agreement, reached in Islamabad, undertook to release substantial frozen funds of Iran, allowed Iran to resume oil exports, and envisaged a massive reconstruction fund for Iran. Tehran reaffirmed its commitment to never acquire or develop nuclear weapons and to allow the International Atomic Energy Agency to supervise the blending down of its uranium stockpile.
Asked whether he thought Tehran may be overplaying its hand, he responded: “They don’t think they are overplaying their hand. They think they have a winning hand, and they want to get something big out of this war.”
At the same time, he pointed out that Iran could not withstand the economic blockade indefinitely, nor continue resisting military attacks as it has. Neither is the war sustainable for the global economy with the Strait of Hormuz all but closed and Gulf economies held hostage to inconclusive hostilities.
Interviewed for The Straits Times Asian Insider podcast, Nasr noted that US President Donald Trump will either have to negotiate peace with Iran, or strike forcefully – and he has a three-month window between the midterm elections and before the US Congress convenes next January to do things his chosen way, without legislative oversight.
“My own sense is that it is not easy for the US and Iran to arrive at an agreement,” said Vasr. “So, we are inching our way to a resumption of conflict.”
The Iran-born scholar, educated in the UK and the US, is a senior academic at Johns Hopkins University's School of Advanced International Studies. He is also a visiting professor at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies.
Nasr served the Obama administration as an adviser on Iran and has been a member of the State Department’s Foreign Affairs Policy Board.
Speculation is mounting that Trump, chafing from the ignominy of the battlefield reversals that Iran’s drones and missiles have wreaked on American bases in the West Asian region, will unleash the most heinous weapons on Iran.
There is also talk that the US and Israel have agreed to escalate, particularly after the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia. On Oct 19, US War Secretary Pete Hegseth reportedly held unannounced discussions with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at an air force station in the Negev desert.
After Trump backed Netanyahu to win next week’s Israeli national polls, the Premier responded warmly about “completing the mission we had started together”. The US midterms are scheduled for Nov 3, and surveys suggest a Democratic victory is on the cards. Israelis go to the polls on Oct 27 to elect a new Parliament.
Depleted ammunition stocks notwithstanding, the US retains the firepower to inflict crippling damage on Iran. While the use of nuclear weapons has been ruled out by Trump, his options include dumping massive ordnance – “the Mother of All Bombs” – on Iranian infrastructure such as power and desalination plants.
Yet, doing so is tempered by the knowledge that it would embolden Russia and China to consider similar means themselves, in their respective domains. Besides, the inevitable Iranian retaliation would be devastating for the Middle East region.
“Iranians have been saying it very openly... that when the dust settles, we won’t be the only people going down. Others will, too, and that will have great consequences for the global economy,” Nasr said, adding that Trump is caught between governments advising caution and others egging him on to “finish the job”. He is also conscious of his legacy.
“Americans are not comfortable with the image of losing.”
As for US influence in the West Asian region, Nasr said Washington’s inability to protect Gulf states – most recently Saudi Arabia – has evaporated confidence in the American security umbrella.
“The US brought a war to their doorsteps in which the Gulf states became collateral damage. Then, the US proved incapable and unwilling to defend them... they could not (even) defend their own bases.”
A result of all this is that every country in the region will recalculate its security requirements. Indeed, it is time to think of the West Asian region as you would of Nato and Europe, with Trump “jumping over Europe to shake hands with (Russian President Vladimir) Putin, and wanting Ukraine to surrender”.
While outside powers such as China and Russia will not hasten to fill this gap until they define their interests in the region more clearly, the setback to US influence is considerable.
“Already, China has won,” said Nasr. “(The) Chinese do not need to step in and do what the Americans did – the very fact that there is less American influence is to their benefit.”
It is the same with the rest of Asia, including East and South-East Asia.
“(Trump) has left many countries around the world sort of exposed because they had built their security under assumptions of the old American security order, which is in question because of this war... Every country will have to do its own calculation about its security needs and its interests.”
Besides, the way the US fought this war also revealed fundamental shortcomings in its military, including its inability to match China in producing weapons at scale. Moreover, it is unclear what sort of America will emerge after the inevitable period of retrospection on both military and strategic fronts.
What are the global implications if the US and Israel tried one more devastating strike on Iran? Nasr said a wider conflagration could not be ruled out, with North Korean soldiers fighting alongside Russians in Ukraine, Russia supporting Iran, Pakistani troops in Saudi Arabia helping to defend the kingdom, Ukraine itself assisting some Gulf monarchies with defence technology and counter-drone expertise, and Britain saying it will move fighter jets to help protect Saudi Arabia.
“Big wars don’t stay localised,” said Nasr. “If you have more than one of them happen at the same time, inevitably they get connected.”

Exercise COPPER HORSE found that Military Working Horses may be able to support a limited range of field tasks under controlled training conditions, with further development needed on equipment, load carriage and operating endurance, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what findings were made on the feasibility of the operational use of horses during Exercise Copper Horse.
Louise Sandher-Jones, the Minister for the Armed Forces, said: “Exercise COPPER HORSE found that Military Working Horses may be able to support a limited range of field tasks under controlled training conditions. It also identified areas requiring further development, including equipment, load carriage and operating endurance before any judgement can be made on potential operational use.”
Britain’s forces keep around five hundred horses, almost all of them in ceremonial roles with the Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment in London, the King’s Troop Royal Horse Artillery at Woolwich, and the Defence Animal Training Regiment at Melton Mowbray, which trains horses and military working dogs.
A horse can carry around a fifth of its body weight, and United States special forces operated on horseback in northern Afghanistan in 2001, and the French, Italian, Austrian and Swiss armies retain mules or horses for mountain logistics.
We reported recently that the British Army has been experimenting with the use of horses for reconnaissance, patrol and security tasks in terrain where military vehicles may struggle to operate, according to imagery released by the Ministry of Defence.
Soldiers and Military Working Horses from the Household Cavalry Mounted Regiment took part in a mounted combat capability experiment on the Barossa training area at Sandhurst, exploring how mounted troops could support battlefield activity beyond the Regiment’s familiar ceremonial duties.
The training was conducted across difficult terrain and focused on environments where conventional vehicles could face restrictions, giving soldiers an opportunity to examine how horses might provide an alternative means of moving personnel during reconnaissance and security operations.

Galerie Patrick Seguin shows demountable Jean Prouvé house with Japanese tea room interior at Design Miami.Paris
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Galerie Patrick Seguin shows demountable Jean Prouvé house with Japanese tea room interior at Design Miami.Paris
Galerie Patrick Seguin in Paris has brought a 1944 house by architect Jean Prouvé to Design Miami.Paris, where it was reinterpreted as a Japanese pavilion.
The 6×6 Demountable House was designed in the 1940s to be assembled at speed and function as housing for those who had been made homeless by war.
It is currently for sale via Galerie Patrick Seguin and on show in the gardens of the Hôtel de Maisons during Design Miami.Paris.
“This house was designed at the end of the second world war to provide temporary accommodation for displaced families whilst their homes were being rebuilt,” the gallery’s founder Patrick Seguin told Dezeen.
“Its exposed structure showcases all of Prouvé’s ingenuity; he was able to respond to the urgency of post-war reconstruction with a design that could be assembled in a single day,” Seguin continued.
For Design Miami.Paris, the gallery reimagined its interior as a contemporary chashitsu – a traditional Japanese pavilion used for tea ceremonies.
“This new reading creates a dialogue between Prouvé’s architecture and Japanese aesthetics and reflects the close ties he maintained throughout his life with Japan, where he was invited to give lectures on several occasions,” Seguin said.
“Japanese architect Reiko Hayama was also one of his closest collaborators, joining his atelier in the early 1970s.”
Because it had been designed to be demountable, taking the wooden house to Paris for the show was easy, according to the gallery.
“Prouvé designed the houses to be easily assembled and dismantled; that’s the ingenuity of these structures,” Seguin said. “The 6×6 house only requires a single day to be assembled by three people.”
After the end of Design Miami.Paris, the Prouvé house “will no doubt be moved to its new owner’s home,” the gallerist concluded.
This year’s edition of Design Miami.Paris also saw Apple unveil its Designers of Tomorrow.
The Jean Prouvé house is on show at Design Miami.Paris 2026 from 21 to 25 October 2026 at L’hôtel de Maisons, 51 Rue de l’Université, 75007 Paris, France. See Dezeen Events Guide for more design events and exhibitions around the world.

TCCIMA energy committee chairman raises 6 demands to facilitate exports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:58:08 UTC
16:58:08 KST

TCCIMA energy committee chairman raises 6 demands to facilitate exports
TEHRAN- Saeed Tajik, Chairman of the Energy and Environment Committee of the Tehran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture (TCCIMA), and Chairman of the Board of Directors of Iran Quality and Standard Inspection Company, at the 30th National Export Day ceremony, raised six demands from the 14th government and emphasized the need to end the “neither war nor peace” situation and to use upcoming opportunities to develop exports.
The government’s exit from the pricing process and the exchange of export proceeds, the removal of currency contracting, and the elimination of non-tariff export barriers were among the demands he raised.
The Chairman of the Board of Iran Quality and Standard Inspection Company took the podium at the National Export Day ceremony, held at the Summit Hall, as one of the country’s selected exporters for the year 1405, and, in the presence of President Masoud Pezeshkian, addressed the need to remove export barriers.
In his remarks, Saeed Tajik described the past year as one of the hardest years the country has experienced in the last 50 years and said: “The resilience of Iranians in the conditions of crisis and the Ramadan war is one of the wonders of the world in 2026.”
Referring to the costs imposed on the country during the war, he said: “The resistance of the Iranian nation and the armed forces in this period has caused people and trade parties in different parts of the world to speak with greater respect about Iran and Iranians. Now that the world has realized Iran’s importance more than before and the country has borne heavy costs, this exceptional opportunity must be used for Iran’s return to the global economic cycle.”
He, stating that “the 14th government is at a historical juncture,” emphasized the need to use the opportunities ahead and called for an end to the neither-war-nor-peace situation.
He added: “This situation must end so that we, the economic soldiers, can demonstrate Iran’s economic authority and export capacity on the global stage. Until we return to the world economic cycle, the government’s budget deficit will not be resolved, inflation will not be curbed, the exchange rate will not be controlled, and the country’s trade balance will remain defective, disrupted, and unbalanced.”
The Chairman of the Energy and Environment Commission of the Tehran Chamber enumerated three main obstacles to the development of exports of Iranian goods and services and said: “Sanctions and restrictions on access to the international trade system; domestic policies and regulations restricting exports, referred to as ‘domestic sanctions’; and weakness in competitiveness and compliance with the requirements of target markets are among these obstacles.”
Tajik, explaining the effects of sanctions and restrictions on access to the international trade system, referred to sudden export bans, currency contracting, and government intervention in pricing the foreign currency obtained from exports and its exchange, and said: “What concept and achievement has the limit and ceiling on commercial cards for exports had other than increasing the number of rented cards?”
Tajik then stated that “the country’s export process does not have the required quality due to restrictions” and added: “The problem of acceptance of quality conformity and standard certificates for Iranian goods in destination countries still persists. Iran’s inspection, testing, and certification network must still be approved by destination countries, and this problem has caused non-tariff barriers such as standard certificates, quarantine, and similar measures to obstruct exports, despite the signing of preferential trade agreements with many countries, including the Eurasian Union, and the removal of tariffs on many goods.”
The Chairman of the Energy and Environment Committee of the Tehran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture considered another problem of the country’s exports to be the Law on Combating the Smuggling of Goods and Currency in the current and wartime conditions and stated: “In this law, the boundary between intentional smuggling, document deficiencies, or delays caused by conditions is not clear, and this situation sometimes causes economic actors to be identified as violators.”
Tajik, stating that “today, transportation restrictions, customs, and technical and quality controls of Iranian goods in target markets are more evident than ever,” noted: “If national determination is formed to support the issuance of guarantees, economic diplomacy, and international recognition of Iran’s conformity assessment system, technical and engineering services can become the main driver of the trade balance and the flag-bearer of Iran’s credibility and quality in international and regional markets.”
He referred to the testing, inspection, and certification (TIC) industry as one of the fields of technical and engineering services that plays an important role in ensuring quality, safety, health, and trust in international trade, and called for the assistance of the Minister of Industry, Mine and Trade in amending ISIC codes.
He continued by criticizing the neglect of “technical and engineering services” in support systems and proposed six demands to facilitate exports, including “suspension of the Law on Combating the Smuggling of Goods and Currency in wartime conditions” and “the government’s exit from the pricing process and the exchange of export proceeds.” Tajik also emphasized the necessity of determining commodity priorities for the allocation and exchange of exporters’ foreign currency, removing currency contracting for exporters, and eliminating the complicated bureaucracy of order registration for importers.
He listed strengthening the capacity of export management companies with the aim of improving the quality of export processes among his other demands and called for recognition of technical and engineering services companies as service producers in the International Standard Industrial Classification (ISIC). Removing non-tariff export barriers, including through concluding bilateral agreements and accepting standard certificates issued in Iran in target countries, was among the other demands of the Head of the Energy and Environment Commission of the Tehran Chamber at the ceremony.

China Focus: China's "city of the future" takes center stage at global governance talks
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:55:27 CST
16:55:27 KST

SHIJIAZHUANG, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Xiongan New Area, China's "city of the future" built on the North China Plain, is drawing wide attention with the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan) scheduled to kick off there on Friday.
The forum brings together leading figures in strategic affairs, politics, academia, business, media and youth affairs from around the world, particularly those working on issues related to the United Nations, climate change, artificial intelligence and multilateral trade.
While the attendees discuss frontier topics ranging from climate change and AI governance to multilateral trade and sustainable urban development, the host city Xiongan, located in north China's Hebei Province, itself serves as a living laboratory for global governance, with hands-on experience in urban governance, green transition and digital governance.
Located about 100 kilometers southwest of Beijing, the new city that is still taking shape has covered 222 square kilometers of developed urban area. Over 5,300 buildings have been completed, with a total floor area exceeding 62.14 million square meters.
In April 2017, China decided to establish the Xiongan New Area as part of a strategy to promote the coordinated development of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region. Serving as a hub to accommodate non-capital functions relocated from Beijing, the city was designed to be smart, green, innovative, livable, and free from "urban ills."
DIGITAL CITY
When it comes to digital governance, the Xiongan Urban Computing Center, notably, holds more than 40 billion high-quality data records. The city has built over 500 kilometers of smart roads, leveraging 5G technology for intelligent connected vehicle trials. The roads are equipped with lampposts that integrate traffic lights and various sensors.
The computing center, with its facade reminiscent of the shape of an eye, is considered the city's "brain." On a huge electronic screen, real-time data show the city's operation in nearly every respect. Which road has more traffic? Anything unusual in the underground pipes? Are the neighborhood trash cans full? In Xiongan, every building has its digital model, and every pipe is fitted with sensors.
Xiongan has been planned and built as three synchronized cities. Beyond the urban surface buildings, there is a city in the cyber cloud and another underground.
Beneath the ground run utility tunnels. Water, electricity, gas and heating pipelines are all placed inside these tunnels, with reserved lanes for logistics.
On Tuesday, China National Data Group Co., Ltd., a new state-owned enterprise (SOE) directly administered by the central government, was officially inaugurated in Xiongan.
It is positioned as a national team for data services, a leader in data infrastructure connectivity, and a strategic force for national data sci-tech innovation.
GREEN DEVELOPMENT
Above ground, Xiongan is a garden city. Residents can reach a park within a 300-meter walk, and a woodland within three kilometers.
Xiongan's urban development places the natural landscape at the heart of the city's design, laying a solid foundation for an eco-friendly future city to ensure quality of life.
Since 2019, Xiongan has embarked on a comprehensive initiative to treat rural sewage, garbage and toilet waste in the vicinity of Baiyangdian Lake, one of northern China's major wetlands.
Latest figures reveal that the city has completed 484,500 mu (roughly 32,300 hectares) of new afforestation, bringing its total green area to 744,500 mu and lifting its forest coverage rate to 35.2 percent.
According to Xiongan's planning and construction bureau, green buildings account for 100 percent of new projects, with some achieving ultra-low energy consumption.
ALLEVIATING BEIJING'S PRESSURE
After nine years of construction, Xiongan has become a key hub for the relocation of Beijing's non-capital functions.
Among these relocated projects, the headquarters of China Satellite Network Group Co., Ltd. operates steadily. Headquarters of Sinochem Holdings and China Huaneng Group Co., Ltd. have settled and begun regular operations in Xiongan. Also, China Mineral Resources Group Ltd. has seen the near completion of the main structure of its headquarters in the city.
Four universities and several hospitals from Beijing, including Beijing Jiaotong University and Peking University People's Hospital, are under construction in Xiongan.
To date, more than 400 branches of state-owned enterprises (SOEs) directly administered by the central government and over 600 high-tech firms have settled there.
"The forum held in Xiongan builds an important platform to exchange urban governance ideas and share cutting-edge insights with the world," said Li Huaxia, head of the publicity, cyberspace affairs and information bureau of Xiongan New Area.
By hosting this international forum, Xiongan is putting its capacity to the test, while demonstrating its pivotal role in the coordinated development of the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region and its unique geographic advantages.
In terms of transport, it sits close to Beijing Daxing International Airport. A direct expressway opened in 2023 connecting Xiongan and this airport.
Xiongan is just a 30-minute high-speed rail ride away from Beijing. Last month, China also opened a high-speed rail section connecting Xiongan with Shangqiu in central China's Henan Province.
Noting that the Xiongan-Shangqiu section fills a gap in Xiongan's southbound high-speed rail corridor, Liu Yanhong, deputy general manager of Xiongan high-speed railway corporation, said the line facilitates commuting and business exchanges for relocated enterprises and institutions, and supports stronger industrial cooperation along the route. ■
