Swiss former president tackles Nazi-era and colonial loot in museums
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

Swiss former president tackles Nazi-era and colonial loot in museums
A new Swiss commission, led by former president Simonetta Sommaruga, is now accepting claims for Nazi-looted art and colonial-era cultural property. It will review disputed cases and issue recommendations. Sommaruga spoke to Swissinfo about its mission and priorities.
Almost three decades after endorsing an international agreement on handling Nazi-looted art in public collections, Switzerland now has a commission to adjudicate claims. The Commission for Historically Problematic Cultural Heritage announced in September that it is ready to accept requestsExternal link from the victims of spoliation and their heirs seeking to recover stolen cultural property in Swiss museums.
Back in 1998, Switzerland, along with 43 other countries and organisations, endorsed the non-binding Washington PrinciplesExternal link. These call on governments to create national structures to facilitate the restitution of Nazi-looted art. Switzerland joins a small group of countries to have done so – Austria, Germany, France, the Netherlands and the United Kingdom all introduced commissions to evaluate claims more than two decades ago.
“In Switzerland, things sometimes take a little longer,” said Sommaruga, the president of the new commission. “But that does not mean that nothing has happened in the country over the years. Some museums have taken a very progressive approach in recent years and decades.”
Sommaruga named the Bern Museum of Fine Arts as one example. In 2014, the museum inherited the troubled collection of Cornelius Gurlitt, the son of an art dealer who had bought art in occupied France for Adolf Hitler’s planned “Führermuseum”.
The way the museum handled this tainted legacy – conducting provenance research and restituting art that had been looted from Jews or sold under duress – “set international standards,” Sommaruga said.
“In my view, the fundamental issue is that Switzerland must take responsibility as a state,” she said. “During the Second World War, as today, Switzerland was an important marketplace for art and cultural property.”
Tainted collections
The impetus for the new commission arose in part because of a number of high-profile disputes in Switzerland. In particular, the Bührle Foundation’s collection of Impressionist masterpieces, which went on display in a new extension at the Zurich Fine Arts Museum in 2021, has drawn widespread criticism and concern.
Emil Bührle, a Swiss industrialist who built his fortune by selling the anti-aircraft cannons his factories produced to Nazi Germany. He is also known to have bought paintings that were looted from Jewish owners.
Switzerland’s commission differs from its counterparts in other European countries in that it will also address claims for objects removed from former colonies. Other countries have introduced separate commissions for colonial-era acquisitions: no other national commission handles both kinds of dispute.
“Although Switzerland never had any colonies of its own, Swiss people were involved in colonial contexts in various ways, including through trade, missionary work and research,” Sommaruga said. “Parliament has created a legal framework that is unique in its kind, as well as bold and forward-looking.” The commission’s broad scope also demands a wide range of expertise: it comprises specialists in law, art history, ethics, museology and both colonial and 20th-century history.
A signature of authority
Some Swiss museums have already seized the initiative in returning objects removed from colonies. Earlier this year, the ethnographic museums of Geneva and the University of Zurich and the Rietberg Museum in Zurich agreed to return to NigeriaExternal link 18 “Benin bronzes” that were probably looted by British troops in a raid in 1897. Under the terms of the agreement with the Nigerian government, ten further objects, also with questionable provenance, will stay in the Swiss museums on loan, although their ownership has been transferred to Nigeria.
Sommaruga says such creative agreements may offer potential solutions for the commission, which can also act as a mediator in disputes.
“I think that, in the spirit of the Washington Principles, restitution need not always be the only just and fair response or solution,” she said. “Other options are possible, and the commission deliberately wants to leave open the forms that a just and fair solution might take in each individual case.”
Having twice served as president, Sommaruga is a prominent figure in Swiss public life and lends the new commission authority. She has navigated similarly sensitive unresolved historical issues in the past.
As justice minister, she commissioned the first report into child labour practices in Switzerland: tens of thousands of children were taken from their families and put to work on farms, part of a harsh foster care system that continued until as late as the 1980s. In 2013, she issued an official apology to the victims.
Look back, don’t look away
“I have always maintained that a country must confront its own history and must not look away, particularly when dealing with difficult or painful issues,” she said.
Sommaruga described the issue of human remains in Swiss collections as a “highly sensitive” one “that raises particularly difficult ethical questions.” The commission has made addressing these a priority and plans to create an inventory of remains and their places of origin.
Here too, some Swiss museums have already taken steps: the Basel Natural History Museum, for instance, returned the remains of three people of Kawésqar origins to their Brazilian descendants in September. These remains had at one time been used for race research that turned human beings into objects of study and helped legitimise racist hierarchies and colonial violence.
Another priority for the commission, Sommaruga said, is the Swiss national collectionExternal link, which encompasses around 22,000 objects assembled over more than a century and dispersed around the country’s museums and government offices.
“The commission believes that the federal government must set an example in how it deals with historically tainted cultural heritage in its own collections,” she said. “For the sake of consistency, the commission cannot make recommendations to private collections that the federal government does not also follow in managing its own collections. It therefore wants to gain a more in-depth understanding of what has been done so far. How are cases where there are grounds for suspicion handled, and what approaches to finding solutions have been pursued to date?”
Queries relating to potential claims have already reached the commission, Sommaruga said. “The big unknown,” she said, is how many claims the commission can expect to receive. “We will be in a better position to judge this in a year’s time.”

How Trump’s magnet fixation puts Swiss high-tech industry in tough spot
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

How Trump’s magnet fixation puts Swiss high-tech industry in tough spot
As China and the United States vie for control of rare-earth minerals, Switzerland faces growing risks to supplies vital for its high-tech industries.
It was in July that US President Donald Trump, in his unmistakable style, drummed home to a room full of defence investors in Pennsylvania the importance of magnetism.
“I hope you’re gonna do magnets. Somebody out there, I hope – you’re all brilliant people – magnets. Do magnets, ok? I’ll tell you how to make money. Do magnets. You’re doing a lot of great stuff. Do magnets. Because one thing we don’t have, but we’re getting close – but do magnets.”
While some media speculated that the 80-year-old president had suffered a “senior moment” and others noted his son’s interest in a related business, Trump’s verbal excursion illustrated how the US sees the arcane world of high-tech magnets – and the rare earths used to make them – as key to its battle with China for global dominance.
It’s a conflict over international supply chains with consequences for manufacturers of products from weapons to wind turbines and watches, particularly in small nations like Switzerland that rely on secure access to critical materials for their high-tech industries.
Around 12,500km east of where Trump was speaking lies the rare-earth heartland of Ganzhou in southern China. Samarium is just one of the elements scraped from the region’s mines, processed into alloys and shipped all around the world. In the Swiss town of Lupfig, in canton Aargau, Arnold Magnetic Technologies converts it into samarium-cobalt magnets used in aerospace, industrial motors and other precision technologies.
China dominates rare earths production
The company describes its trade with Chinese raw-material producers as a “mine-to-magnetExternal link” supply chain. Yet as tensions between China and the US have ratcheted up, particularly over critical minerals, so has the threat of trade tariffs and export controls.
In late 2025, Arnold Magnetic announcedExternal link that it was creating new partnerships with UK and Belgium companies to secure “reliable, Western-origin” rare-earth materials.
“The situation around rare-earth-mineral supply security is not going to go away anytime soon,” Matt Blake, chief executive officer of Arnold Magnetic, told Manufacturing Today Magazine. “China will remain an important part of the global rare-earth supply chain for the foreseeable future […] As such, we embraced a multifaceted approach to mitigate risk along that supply chain, which includes diversifying our sourcing strategies.”
Despite the name, rare earths are not scarce. Yet China dominates their production. The country spent decades building up mining, refining and processing on a huge scale. By 2024, it delivered about 60% of world rare-earth mineExternal link output and 90% of separation and refining capacity. Economies of scale make it hard for anyone else to enter the market.
That was fine as long as trade tensions were muted. But in recent years, the US, Europe and Japan have become increasingly concerned that China is exporting goods at below cost, hollowing out the wider manufacturing bases of its competitors and gaining a chokehold over supplies critical to areas such as defence and strategic infrastructure. These fears have only been heightened by China taking Russia’s side in the Ukraine war.
“Rare earths and other critical raw materials, which were once merely viewed as the commodities that power modern industry, are increasingly being used as strategic assets and geopolitical tools rather than simply being traded,” said Alessandra Hool, managing director of the ESM Foundation, set up in 1951 to carry out research into rare metals in an effort to secure essential supplies for a resource-poor Switzerland.
“While mining capacity for some critical raw materials has become somewhat more diversified in recent years, processing capacity for many of these materials remains heavily concentrated in China,” Hool said.
China restricted exports of certain minerals in 2023, including to European countries, following US limits on the sale of high-end microchips to the communist nation. China imposed further controls in subsequent years as leverage against rivals such as Japan.
This move “could have a dramatic impact on global supply chains, as many strategic sectors rely on products and components containing the controlled Chinese rare-earth elements. These sectors include energy, automotive, defence, semiconductors, aerospace, industrial motors and AI data centres,” the International Energy Agency said of the curbs.
The biggest economies have taken a variety of steps in response.
The US is building a networkExternal link of critical-mineral partnerships backed by investment and national-security policies. Japan has accumulated stockpiles of materials, invested in overseas mining projects and formed partnerships with producers such as Lynas Rare Earths in Australia. The EU’s Critical Raw Materials ActExternal link aims to meet 10% of the bloc’s needs for extraction, 40% of its processing and 25% of recycling demand domestically.
Others have imposed their own trade restrictions. OECD statistics indicateExternal link curbs on critical materials grew fivefold between 2009 and 2024, leaving around 45% of rare-earth exports facing such limits. “Importing industrialised countries increasingly perceive risks to their economic security,” the organisation said.
More
Switzerland and Indonesia sign deal on access to raw materials
Yet some of these options aren’t viable for small nations like Switzerland, with tiny local markets and economies that have benefited from years of open world trade. While the country imports less than 30 tonnes of rare-earth metalsExternal link and compoundsExternal link directly each year, lots of Swiss manufacturers rely on components made from such substances.
“The Swiss tech industry’s dependence on rare earths and other critical raw materials from China is significant,” said Martin Hizel, chair of Swissmem, the main trade body for the sector in Switzerland. “In the event of a supply-chain disruption, it is virtually impossible to find an alternative supply channel at short notice.”
“Switzerland is at risk of becoming ‘collateral damage’ in the global rivalry between the US and China,” he added. Chinese export controls are also affecting Swiss industrial firms, even though Switzerland has played no part in the international trade conflicts.
A survey of Swissmem members in April 2026 found that around a third of companies’ import goods are subject to Chinese export controls. “Of the firms affected, over half have faced delivery delays and disruptions,” Hizel said.
Alliances, recycling and substitution
Swiss companies also face indirect shocks, including rising costs and increased regulatory complexity, according to Hool at the ESM Foundation.
Switzerland lacks the market size, international influence or mineral resources to try to become more self-sufficient, she said. Nor can it simply replicate Japan’s strategy of using state-backed investment to secure overseas resources at scale.
Instead, its strongest bet may be, like Arnold Magnetic, to diversify supply as best it can.
The country has already built ties with resource-rich nations such as Indonesia, among the largest producers of minerals used in batteries and clean-energy tech. Economics Minister Guy Parmelin signed a preliminary declaration of intent to boost cooperation on raw materials and supply chains on a visit to the Southeast Asian country in 2025.
According to Hizel, a diplomatic channel is being established between Switzerland and China on the basis of their existing free trade agreement to help Swiss companies deal with any problems they face over procurement of materials.
Industrial recycling of minerals from discarded products, such as electric vehicle batteries, may also be “one of the most promising long-term opportunities for Switzerland to reduce its dependence on imported critical raw materials,” Hool said.
Scientists at Swiss federal technology institute ETH Zurich have developedExternal link technologies to extract rare-earth elements from electronic waste, launching its “REEcover” spinoff to commercialize the process. Researchers are also working on ways to use less material and replace scarce elements with alternatives or develop entirely new products that do not depend on them.
Still, such efforts are either at an early stage or tinkering at the edges of the problem.
“Partnerships cannot generally eliminate global market risks, supply disruptions or geopolitical tensions,” Hool said. “Switzerland’s response should reflect its specific position as a small and highly globalised economy.”
As long as the US, China and EU remain in conflict – and Trump maintains his fixation with magnets – that may be the best that the world’s smaller nations can hope to achieve.

Siberian linguists find specific word perception in different peoples
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:59:27 UTC
15:59:27 KST

TOMSK, October 23. /TASS/. Linguists at the Tomsk State University (TSU) found that native speakers of Russian and Khakass associate words with visual images and the position of objects in different ways, the university's press service told TASS. When perceiving a word, a person refers to its dictionary meaning, as well as to visual images, sensations of movement and sounds.
The bilingualism problem is typical for people all over the world, since about half of the world's population speaks two or more languages. There are more than 120 languages in Russia, and many native speakers of those languages are bilingual. Since 2017, specialists of the Tomsk University's Linguistic Anthropology Laboratory have been researching the linguistic diversity of Southern Siberia, and they were among the first in the world to create a psycholinguistic database using the Russian language as a basic one. Right now, the laboratory is engaged in documenting and preserving languages of Southern Siberian peoples, including the Chulymsky, Teleutsky and Shorsky languages. The research's results are published in the Rusin journal.
"Linguists at the Tomsk State University have studied the sensory experience reflection in meanings of Russian and Khakass words," the press service said. "They compared how bilinguals - native speakers of two languages - evaluate the connection of words with vision, size and position in space. They have found both common patterns and differences."
The surveyed participants rated Russian and Khakass words on a seven-point scale. It turned out that in both language groups, word connections positively correlated with vision and position in space, but among Russian native speakers these relationships were more pronounced, and the assessments were more diverse. In particular, Russian speakers had a clear pattern: the higher the object, the more strongly it is associated with vision. Among Khakass native speakers, this pattern related to the top and bottom is less pronounced, although on average they rated higher the connection of words with vision. At the same time, words for movement and physical contact evoked tactile associations in both groups.
Scientists also have found that not all differences are preserved when evaluating individual traits. For example, the groups did not demonstrate noticeable differences when estimating the size of an object. Such details help experts to understand which perception aspects are common for both languages, and which are differently reflected in the assessments. "Our results show that the sensations that arise when interacting with the world are involved in the formation of ideas related to words. Both language groups have common patterns, but the strength of individual connections varies," the laboratory's junior researcher Irina Korshunova added.
"Our approach is based on the premise that the meaning of a word is related not only to logical categories, but also to a person's visual, auditory, bodily and emotional experience. At the same time, linguistic and cultural experience can influence the structure of such connections," the project's scientific director and the laboratory's leading researcher Professor Zoya Rezanova said.
About the peoples of Russia
According to the Federal Agency for Ethnic Affairs, as of April 30, 2026, more than 190 peoples live in Russia, where 47 are classified as low-numbered indigenous peoples. On May 8, 2025, the government approved the Concept of Sustainable Development of the Indigenous Peoples of the North, Siberia and the Far East of the Russian Federation for the period up to 2036.
The low-numbered indigenous peoples are Russian peoples fewer than 50,000 people. The government approved a unified list of Low-Numbered Indigenous Peoples of the Russian Federation on March 24, 2000. The most recent updates were made on December 18, 2021, where the list contains 43 peoples, including the Abaza (41,793 people), the Veps (4,534), the Koryaks (7,485), the Mansi (12,228), the Sami (1,530), the Udege (1 325), the Khanty (31,467), the Eskimos (1,657). The smallest group at that time was the Kereks (23 people), the most numerous - the Nenets (49,646).
Changes to the list may be made by the Russian government at the suggestion of the Federal Agency for Ethnic Affairs, based on initiatives from governors of the territories where low-numbered peoples live.

Services, smart products fuel new momentum in China's consumer market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:58:23 CST
15:58:23 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China's consumer market is finding new growth momentum in services and smart products, reflecting shifting spending patterns as the country seeks to strengthen domestic demand.
Consumption remained the largest contributor to China's economic growth in the first three quarters of 2026, accounting for 46.7 percent of the expansion, up 0.7 percentage points from the first half of the year, the Ministry of Commerce said Friday.
Services consumption has emerged as a bright spot. Retail sales of services rose 5 percent year on year during the period, outpacing goods retail sales by 4 percentage points, as China's consumption structure continued to evolve.
Technology-driven products are another source of emerging demand. Sales of smart glasses on major platforms monitored by the ministry rose 110 percent year on year in value during the first nine months, while sales of exoskeleton assistive devices and embodied intelligent robots increased 46.4 percent and 22.6 percent, respectively.
Guotai Haitong Securities said in a research report that artificial intelligence (AI) glasses are moving beyond early experimentation toward mass-market adoption as the industry enters a growth phase.
Demand for green and health-related products is also expanding. Sales of organic food on major platforms monitored by the ministry rose 6.4 percent year on year during the period, while the retail penetration rate of new energy passenger vehicles reached 67 percent in September.
The emerging trends are taking shape as China steps up efforts to boost consumption and promote closer integration between technological innovation and consumer demand. The country has released new guidelines to promote the application of AI and other advanced technologies in commerce as part of efforts to expand consumer demand, upgrade traditional businesses and improve the efficiency of goods distribution.
China's AI industry has expanded rapidly, with AI-powered smartphones, intelligent connected vehicles and humanoid robots among the products seeing broader application. ■

Xiplomacy: Reading Xi's vision for global governance through metaphors
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:58:17 CST
15:58:17 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- The 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiong'an) is set to open on Friday in the Xiong'an New Area, north China's Hebei Province, bringing into world focus a pressing question: How can countries work together to address shared challenges in an interconnected world amid growing protectionism and unilateralism?
In speeches and meetings on multiple occasions, Chinese President Xi Jinping has used vivid metaphors to articulate his vision for global governance. These metaphors offer insights into his approach to building a more just, equitable and inclusive global governance system.
IN SAME BOAT
"I was looking at the vast ocean when I boarded the ship, and it struck me that we are all indeed fellow passengers in the same boat," Xi said while addressing the 2018 APEC CEO Summit hosted at a unique setting -- onboard the giant cruise Pacific Explorer in Port Moresby, Papua New Guinea.
The metaphor embodies the essence of Xi's vision of building a community with a shared future for humanity, highlighting the interconnectedness of countries and the need for solidarity and cooperation in addressing common challenges.
Today, the interconnected world is grappling with four mounting deficits: a peace deficit that exacerbates geopolitical conflicts, a development deficit that widens the North-South divide, a security deficit that erodes mutual trust, and a governance deficit that undermines the effectiveness of multilateralism.
In 2019, at the China-France Global Governance Forum held in Paris, Xi proposed a four-pronged approach to addressing the four deficits. First and foremost, he called for fairness and reasonableness to address the governance deficit.
"It is advisable to uphold a vision of global governance featuring extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefits," Xi said, calling for actively advancing the democratization of global governance rules.
As the world has found itself in a new period of turbulence and transformation, global governance has come to a new crossroads. Against this backdrop, Xi put forward the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit in September 2025 in China's coastal city of Tianjin.
"I look forward to working with all countries for a more just and equitable global governance system and advancing toward a community with a shared future for humanity," Xi said, stressing sovereign equality and genuine multilateralism.
TRAFFIC LIGHTS
"A world without rules is like a crossroads without traffic lights, where chaos and disorder are all but guaranteed," Xi said at the 2026 BRICS Summit in New Delhi, India.
This metaphor highlights the importance of rules in maintaining the international order. While having rules in place matters, how they are made and who gets to make them matter even more.
International rules must be written and upheld jointly by all countries based on the purposes and principles of the UN Charter, rather than dictated by those with the strongest muscles or the loudest voice, Xi once stressed.
He has also called for the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and other universally recognized basic norms of international relations to be observed comprehensively, fully and in their entirety.
"There should be no double standards, and the house rules of a few countries must not be imposed upon others," he said.
The GGI proposed by President Xi reflects the objective transformation of the world system and responds to the aspirations of most countries for a fairer and more representative system of global governance, said Rahmon Ulmasov, a professor at the Russian-Tajik (Slavonic) University.
MAKING THE PIE BIGGER
Xi has repeatedly used the metaphor of a pie to describe the gains of international cooperation. "We should make the pie of win-win cooperation bigger, and ensure that more development gains will be shared more fairly by people across the world," he said at the 23rd meeting of the Council of Heads of State of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization in 2023.
The pie metaphor reflects the people-centered and action-oriented vision of the GGI: making the gains of cooperation bigger while ensuring that they are shared more widely and fairly. When proposing the GGI, Xi emphasized the importance of "ensuring that the people of every nation are the actors in and beneficiaries of global governance."
The SCO, the platform where Xi proposed the GGI, provides an example. Within the grouping, China has announced the establishment of cooperation platforms in energy, green industries and the digital economy, as well as centers for scientific and technological innovation, higher education, and vocational and technical education.
The expanding scope of cooperation shows how the "pie" can be made bigger in practice: by opening up new areas of cooperation, creating more opportunities for development and ensuring that the benefits reach more people.
Beyond making the pie bigger, Xi has also called for sharing the pie fairly to ensure justice and equity. For him, the ultimate purpose of better global governance is to promote common development and improve people's well-being across the globe.
At the G20 summit held in Brazil in 2024, Xi called for building a just world of common development, saying "prosperity and stability would not be possible in a world where the rich become richer while the poor are made poorer, and countries should make global development more inclusive, beneficial to all, and more resilient."
To build such a world, Xi said, there should be more bridges of cooperation, and less "small yard, high fences," so that more and more developing countries will be better off and achieve modernization. ■

S. Korean banks' loan delinquency rate rises to 0.69 pct in August
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:58:15 CST
15:58:15 KST

SEOUL, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- South Korean banks' loan delinquency rate rose for a second consecutive month due to more new delinquent loans than bad loan settlements, financial watchdog data showed Friday.
The delinquency ratio of bank loans, overdue by at least one month, gained 0.06 percentage points from a month earlier to 0.69 percent at the end of August, after going up 0.07 percentage points in the previous month, according to the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS).
Newly generated delinquent loans reached 3.0 trillion won (2.3 billion U.S. dollars) in the cited month, larger than the settlement of non-performing loans worth 1.5 trillion won.
Excluding the settled bad loans, the delinquency rate for new bank loans stood at 0.12 percent in August, unchanged compared to the previous month.
The delinquency rate for corporate loans increased 0.08 percentage points from a month earlier to 0.86 percent at the end of August, and the ratio for household loans added 0.03 percentage points to 0.45 percent.
The financial watchdog cautioned that there remained a possibility of a gain in delinquency rate among vulnerable groups, affected by the trend of interest rate hikes and economic uncertainties both at home and abroad.
The country's central bank delivered back-to-back policy rate hikes in July and August, indicating a further monetary tightening later this year or early next year. ■

SINGAPORE, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- Singapore's core inflation eased to 2 percent year-on-year in September, from 2.2 percent in August, due to lower services and retail and other goods inflation, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) and the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry said on Friday.

Domestic price pressures are expected to remain subdued, supported by productivity gains and government subsidies for healthcare and education.
Core inflation is expected to remain slightly elevated in the coming quarters before easing more noticeably from mid-2027. ■

China earmarks 80 mln yuan for Xizang quake relief, recovery efforts
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:57:59 CST
15:57:59 KST

An aerial drone photo taken on Oct. 23, 2026 shows emergency tents at an earthquake-hit village in Maru Township of Baqen County, Nagqu City, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. Sixteen people were killed and 65 others injured after a 7.0-magnitude earthquake struck Baqen County of Nagqu City in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region at 10:33 p.m. Thursday, the city's earthquake relief headquarters said on Friday. The Ministry of Emergency Management and authorities in Xizang have mobilized resources for rescue and relief operations. (Xinhua/Purbu Tsering)
BEIJING, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- China has allocated 50 million yuan (about 7.5 million U.S. dollars) in emergency disaster relief funds and earmarked another 30 million yuan for recovery efforts following a 7.0-magnitude earthquake in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region.
The earthquake struck Baqen County of the city of Nagqu at 10:33 p.m. on Thursday, leaving 16 people dead and 54 injured.
The Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of Emergency Management jointly allocated 50 million yuan to support rescue operations and assistance to affected residents, while the National Development and Reform Commission earmarked the additional 30 million yuan from the central budget to help restore damaged infrastructure and public service facilities.
The country has also upgraded its national earthquake emergency response from Level IV to Level III, while activating a separate Level-IV national natural disaster relief response.
China's national comprehensive fire and rescue force has dispatched a total of 350 rescuers and 83 vehicles for rescue operations. The emergency management ministry has guided Xizang's emergency management department in arranging for Wing Loong drone deployment to the quake-hit area for disaster reconnaissance.
As of 6:30 a.m. on Friday, 120 rescuers and 27 vehicles had arrived in the quake-hit area, while the remaining 230 rescuers and 56 vehicles from the Xizang fire and rescue corps were en route as reinforcements, having all entered Nagqu's administrative area.
Earlier, as of 4:30 a.m. on Friday, authorities had mobilized relief supplies at the central, regional, municipal and county levels, and delivered them in batches to the affected area.
These supplies included 1,000 prefabricated housing units, 3,239 tents, 2,821 folding beds and 4,280 quilts, among other essentials. ■

====================================================================================================

China's environmental rule of law offers lessons for global biodiversity efforts, experts say
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:57:31 CST
15:57:31 KST

YEREVAN, Oct. 23 (Xinhua) -- "Nature doesn't have an advocate or a lawyer to defend its interests. And so this is very important that the law guarantees protection for the weak," Norbert Barlocher, a councilor of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, told Xinhua on Wednesday on the sidelines of the 17th meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the UN Convention on Biological Diversity (COP17).
The conference is conducting the first global review of collective progress in implementing the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF). Participants from several countries have praised China's recently enacted Ecological and Environmental Code, saying its experience in environmental rule of law offers important lessons for countries working to implement the framework.
China's code is designed "to elaborate a modern Code that gives clear guidance in the field of the environment," Barlocher said, adding that countries could "learn together from each other" through China's integrated approach to environmental governance.
Basile van Havre, co-chair of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, noted that many countries have responded to challenges involving climate change, nature and pollution by introducing successive layers of legislation, creating increasingly complex regulatory systems. "What happened in many countries is they have been piling up legislation one on top of the other," he said.
Doreen Robinson, deputy director of the Ecosystems Division at the United Nations Environment Programme, described China's Ecological and Environmental Code as forward-looking and a model from which other countries could learn.
"I think that China is very progressive in its ecological code, and I think it's got an innovative way of approaching it," Robinson said. She added that the experience "can help them adapt and transform to their own national circumstances."
Diego Ochoa, programme management adviser with the National Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans Accelerator Programme, said political will was among the most important factors in advancing biodiversity conservation, restoration and sustainable use. This required "the translation of these ideas into legislation, laws and regulatory frameworks," he said.
Strengthening regulatory frameworks is itself an important step toward implementing the KMGBF, Ochoa said, adding that China's experience "is a great step for other countries to understand how China does this kind of work."
During COP17, the English version of the think tank report "China's Innovations and Global Contributions Through the Ecological and Environmental Code" was released at the China Pavilion on Wednesday as one of the research outcomes highlighting achievements in building a Beautiful China.
The Chinese version was released on Aug. 15, 2026, by the National High-Level Think Tank of Xinhua News Agency, the day the Ecological and Environmental Code of the People's Republic of China took effect.
The report was jointly compiled by a research team from the Research Center for Xi Jinping Thought on Ecological Civilization, Xinhua Institute and the Research Center for Xi Jinping Thought on the Rule of Law. It examines the code's historical context and significance, explains its legislative innovations and distinctive Chinese characteristics, and explores its global value and contributions.
Nancy Kananu Marangu, a technical consultant at Kenya's Chemichemi Foundation, said the English version would help the international community better understand China's experience in environmental rule of law and demonstrate the code's value globally, particularly for developing countries.
Karen Ghazaryan, dean of the Faculty of Biology at Yerevan State University, said after reading the report that the code brings pollution prevention and control, ecological conservation, and green and low-carbon development under a unified framework. He described it as "the first of its kind in the world," adding, "I think this complex approach is very important not only for China but also for the whole world."
Barlocher said the fact that the code had been developed by a developing country demonstrated that countries at different stages of development could use the rule of law to establish an environmental governance framework that balances environmental protection with development. This, he said, was an important part of the code's global significance.
Robinson said the next step was to help countries identify the key elements of the code that could be adapted to their own circumstances and support them in applying those elements nationally.
Ghazaryan said he maintains ties with many Chinese scientists and hopes to apply lessons from the code to environmental governance in Armenia, including efforts to address soil degradation and water pollution.
Sergey Rybakov, director general of the Nature and People Foundation in Russia, highlighted the long-term perspective offered by China's experience.
"China is showing us where we will be in 10, 20 or 25 years. This is extremely important because when you know where you are going, it becomes much easier to get there. You understand what your goal is and what you need to achieve," he said. ■

L3Harris warns lasers will push U.S. Navy power limits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:57:15 UTC
15:57:15 KST

- L3Harris supplies power distribution systems and universal modular masts for every U.S. Navy Virginia-class submarine and is extending that work to the Columbia class.
- The company named directed energy weapons, advanced radars and new propulsion as future drivers of heavier power demands on U.S. Navy platforms.
L3Harris Technologies says it supplies the power distribution systems and universal modular masts on every Virginia-class submarine in the U.S. Navy fleet, and the company is now carrying that work into the Columbia-class ballistic missile submarine program while preparing for the heavier electrical loads expected from directed energy weapons and other new naval systems.
The company laid out its submarine power role in an editorial published Oct. 22, 2026, describing decades of work on rugged, high-density power conversion and distribution equipment for the U.S. Navy’s undersea fleet.
Near the end of the piece, in a passage Laser Wars highlighted when sharing the editorial on X, L3Harris said naval platforms are growing more electrically complex with every generation and named advanced radar systems, directed energy weapons and next-generation propulsion as the technologies that will place extraordinary demands on shipboard power infrastructure.
“The Navy trusts us with the most critical systems on its most advanced platforms, and that is not something we take lightly,” said Nino DiCosmo, president of L3Harris Maritime. “Every power system we deliver has to work the first time and every time after that, whether a submarine is on its first patrol or its fiftieth.”
Directed energy weapons, such as high-energy lasers, fire beams of energy instead of physical rounds and draw their “ammunition” directly from a ship’s electrical system, which is why they demand far more power generation, storage and distribution than conventional weapons. The U.S. Navy has already fielded lasers on surface ships, including the HELIOS system installed on the destroyer USS Preble (DDG 88) in 2022. L3Harris said it is investing in power technologies to meet those growing demands across the Navy’s most advanced platforms, without tying the directed energy reference to any specific submarine program.
On the Virginia-class attack submarines, every sensor, weapon, propulsion component and crew system draws from a single power architecture that must keep working for months at a time at every depth. L3Harris described its submarine portfolio as running from switchgear and power protection systems to advanced power conversion equipment, all designed to meet strict requirements for shock resistance, electromagnetic compatibility, heat management and long-term reliability.
The universal modular mast is the other half of the company’s Virginia-class role. The two-stage, telescoping mast raises sensors above the waterline without penetrating the pressure hull, lifting photonics imaging masts, communications antennas and electronic warfare sensors, and each Virginia-class boat carries a bank of eight. In April 2026, Naval Sea Systems Command awarded L3Harris a contract worth up to $129.9 million for universal modular mast production and engineering support for both the Virginia and Columbia classes.
The Columbia class will replace the Ohio-class ballistic missile submarines as the sea-based leg of the U.S. nuclear deterrent, and the Navy plans to build 12 of the boats. The lead submarine, the future USS District of Columbia (SSBN 826), was about 65% complete in February 2026, and shipbuilders General Dynamics Electric Boat and HII Newport News Shipbuilding are working toward a 2028 delivery ahead of a first patrol planned for 2030.
L3Harris said its power systems for the Columbia class are being built to the same standards as those already serving across the Virginia-class fleet, with the first boat on track to begin patrols after its planned 2028 delivery.

Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:55:03 UTC
15:55:03 KST

Tharoor backs Raihan Vadra, says protest photos are not political in themselves
NEW DELHI: Senior Congress leader Shashi Tharoor on Friday criticised the removal of photographs from Raihan Vadra's exhibition at Bikaner House in New Delhi, saying the move had damaged India's global reputation as a freedom-loving democracy and raised serious concerns over freedom of expression.In a post on X, Tharoor described the incident as a "disgrace at so many levels", arguing that photographs documenting protest demonstrations depicted events and did not necessarily convey political positions.
"This is a disgrace at so many levels," Thiruvananthapuram MP said, listing his objections to the decision to remove the photographs from the exhibition, "No Idea Is Final".
He said the images documented events that had already received widespread public and media attention, questioning why photographs of demonstrations should be considered political content simply because they depicted protests."The images are of events that have already been burned into the public consciousness, and many of the photos would have echoed similar images that the public has already seen in the media and online," Tharoor said, adding that "While Bikaner House is free to have a policy against political stands, photographs of a protest demonstration are a depiction of an event and not political in themselves; they would almost certainly have passed muster had the matter been brought to a court as an issue of freedom of expression.
"He further alleged that the decision had hurt India's international image."And worst of all, this censorship has driven one more nail into the coffin of India's global reputation as a freedom-loving democracy," the Congress MP said.Tharoor also pointed out that the controversy had brought significant attention to Raihan Vadra's photographic work, potentially exposing it to a much wider audience than the exhibition would otherwise have reached."Anyway, the publicity this episode has received will have reached a far larger audience, in Delhi and worldwide, than the exhibition itself might have, had it been allowed to proceed undisturbed. I thank heavy-handed officials for giving a well-deserved boost to the photographic talents and career of Raihan Vadra," Tharoor said.The row began after Raihan Vadra, son of Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, alleged that Bikaner House management had asked him to remove several photographs from his exhibition shortly before its scheduled opening. According to him, the images included photographs documenting student protests and two pictures of the Indian national flag.The Bikaner House Management Society said certain photographs did not comply with its policy and that their removal had been requested. It maintained that photographs meeting the venue's guidelines continued to be displayed.
The incident sparked a political confrontation, with Congress leaders criticising the decision as an infringement on artistic expression, while the BJP maintained that exhibitions must follow the venue's rules.Amid the controversy, Keralam chief minister VD Satheesan offered to host the exhibition in its entirety, saying the state would be proud to welcome “No Idea Is Final”, with "no exclusions, no exceptions".However, Kerala BJP president Rajeev Chandrasekhar questioned the offer, alleging preferential treatment for Raihan Vadra and asking whether ordinary young people received similar attention to their rights and work.

U.S. Army takes over retired U.S. Navy drone helicopters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:45:18 UTC
15:45:18 KST

- The U.S. Army received four retired U.S. Navy MQ-8C Fire Scout unmanned helicopters and began flight testing them as testbeds for Army sensors.
- The transfer saved the U.S. Army just over $70 million in procurement costs and took 14 months from request to first flight tests.
The U.S. Army has started flight testing four MQ-8C Fire Scout unmanned helicopters that the U.S. Navy was retiring, turning aircraft headed for long-term storage into flying testbeds for Army sensors and saving the Army just over $70 million in procurement costs.
The Army’s Redstone Test Center at Redstone Arsenal, Alabama, received the four aircraft along with two Mobile Mission Control Systems, spare engines and support equipment, and completed ground testing in August 2026. Flight tests are now underway at Dugway Proving Ground, Utah, and at Redstone Arsenal to build aircrew confidence and give maintainers hands-on experience with the system.
The Navy began divesting the MQ-8C in February 2024, with the final retirement scheduled by the end of fiscal 2026. The Navy’s Multi-Mission Tactical UAS program office, known as PMA-266, was about 60% of the way through sending aircraft, mobile control systems and support equipment to the 309th Aerospace Maintenance and Regeneration Group in Tucson, Arizona, the military’s aircraft storage and regeneration center often called the boneyard, when the Army asked about taking over some of the fleet.
That request came in November 2024, when the Redstone Test Center asked whether the Fire Scout could serve as a captive carry testbed for Army sensor packages. In captive carry testing, a sensor or payload is mounted on an aircraft and flown in realistic conditions without being released, giving engineers flight data without dedicating a new aircraft to the job. Army and Navy teams visited Point Mugu, California, in December to evaluate the MQ-8C and its control systems, and the Redstone Test Center submitted a formal request to the Navy in January 2025 for four aircraft, two control systems, spare engines and support equipment.
The Navy approved the transfer in May 2025, and all four aircraft and both control systems arrived at Redstone Arsenal by July 2025. The program office also worked with Naval Supply Systems Command to recover communications security equipment, including radios, transponders and modems, that had already been returned to common stock during the divestment, and the last of those assets reached Redstone in July 2026.
“Considering where we started—having zero experience with these systems—it’s quite remarkable what has been accomplished. We are certainly thankful for the many people across various organizations that helped us along the way,” said Chief Warrant Officer 4 Taylor Kiel, a test director and experimental test pilot with the Redstone Test Center’s Aviation Flight Test Directorate.
Beyond the $70 million in procurement savings, the Navy said the Army avoided additional costs in research and development, flight hours, data collection, contracts, asset sourcing and manpower. The program office said the full transition, from the first request to the start of flight tests, took 14 months.
“Our priority is delivering lethal and ready capabilities to the warfighters,” said Col. Leigh Irwin, PMA-266 program manager. “Repurposing these MQ-8C assets from storage to active testing is a major acquisition win for both services, demonstrating how we can supercharge existing capabilities and increase acquisition velocity to support joint operations.”
Built by Northrop Grumman on the airframe of the commercial Bell 407 helicopter, the MQ-8C was designed to fly from the Navy’s littoral combat ships and other air-capable vessels, providing surveillance and targeting support with up to 12 hours of endurance and a range of about 150 nautical miles (280 km). The Navy reached initial operational capability with the MQ-8C in June 2019 and bought 38 of the aircraft, but by 2023 it was operating only 10 of them and keeping the rest in storage.
With the Navy’s MQ-8C retirement now complete, the four aircraft at Redstone Arsenal continue flight testing at Dugway and in Alabama as the Army prepares them for sensor test work.

Two Projects in Paris Win the European Collective Housing Award
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:45:00 UTC
15:45:00 KST

As cities struggle to provide adequate and affordable housing, examining built examples of collective housing can help inform decisions about what to build and how. These projects offer opportunities to assess solutions, understand their limitations, and consider what might be applied elsewhere. In Paris, two recent examples combine apartments of different sizes with access to gardens, courtyards, and other outdoor spaces, working with structures already in place.
La Métropolitaine, by Ignacio Prego Architectures and Thibaud Babled Architectures, and a garage conversion by Atelier Téqui Architectes won the second edition of the European Collective Housing Award in the new construction and renovation categories, respectively. The winners were announced on October 8, 2026, in San Sebastián, following a selection process involving 192 entries from 36 European countries.
One builds above existing transportation infrastructure; the other adapts and expands a former garage. Alongside their architectural solutions, the jury highlighted their provision of affordable homes in sought-after urban areas.
Living Above Infrastructure
Built above existing transportation infrastructure at the boundary between Paris and its neighboring municipalities, La Métropolitaine forms a continuous frontage facing the new Palais de Justice. The complex brings together social housing, affordable student housing, and public and community facilities within a single structure.
The building's shallow depth guides the apartment layouts. Ranging from one to five bedrooms, all units extend through the building, facing the city on one side and a garden on the other. The jury recognized the ambition of bringing these uses together above existing infrastructure and highlighted the public owner's commitment to maintaining affordable rents in this location.
Turning a Garage into Housing
In the renovation category, Atelier Téqui Architectes received the award for the conversion and expansion of a garage in Paris's 11th arrondissement. The 1957 building, designed by Grand Prix de Rome winner Claude Béraud, now houses 63 apartments and a retail space.
The intervention retained much of the existing building. Floor slabs, columns, beams, and the facade's cantilevered concrete elements were preserved, while the vehicle ramps were removed. Landscaped courtyards, winter gardens, and a rooftop vegetable garden were introduced.
Above the retained structure, the vertical addition combines a steel frame, cross-laminated timber (CLT) floor slabs, and larch cladding. According to the award documentation, this addition incorporates up to 99 kg/m² of bio-based materials.
The jury highlighted the apartment layouts and efficient use of the available space, which made it possible to accommodate different housing types within the original structure. It also emphasized the spatial quality of the resulting homes.
An Award Dedicated to Collective Housing
Established in 2024, the European Collective Housing Award is organized by the Basque Architecture Institute in San Sebastián and arc en rêve centre d'architecture in Bordeaux, with support from the Basque Government. The initiative recognizes built projects for their architectural quality, social impact, and contribution to housing in Europe.
In its second edition, the number of countries represented nearly doubled, from 19 to 36, while the total number of entries rose from 170 to 192. The inaugural edition recognized La Borda in Barcelona, by Lacol, and the conversion of a wine warehouse in Basel, by Esch Sintzel Architekten.
The 2026 jury was chaired by Carme Pinós and included Jing Liu, Catherine Sabbah, David Madden, and Lucia Tozzi. The ceremony took place in the new home of the Basque Architecture Institute at Tabakalera, with opening remarks by Denis Itxaso, head of the Basque Government's Department of Housing and Urban Agenda. The event brought together the nine finalist teams, members of the award's advisory board, institutional representatives, and invited guests.
The announcement concluded the European Collective Housing Days, two days of debates, conversations, and presentations on housing. The finalist projects will be featured in a publication and a traveling exhibition scheduled to visit European museums over the next two years.
The two winning projects demonstrate ways to add housing to the existing city while providing varied apartment layouts and access to outdoor spaces. Their affordability also matters: as the jury noted, maintaining affordable homes in sought-after neighborhoods can help retain residents and support greater social diversity. The architectural decisions described here are part of that broader task of making room for people to live in the city.

U.S. drone boat runs naval intercept demo in Japan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:40:11 UTC
15:40:11 KST

- A Splash Industries Typhoon uncrewed surface vessel demonstrated naval interception at Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni, Japan, on Oct. 21, 2026, during Keen Sword 27.
- The 11-foot jet-powered boat earlier docked autonomously inside USS Essex during RIMPAC 2026 and can now launch one-way aerial drones.
A Typhoon uncrewed surface vessel built by California-based Splash Industries demonstrated naval interception during a drone demonstration at Marine Corps Air Station Iwakuni, Japan, on Oct. 21, 2026, as part of the Keen Sword 27 exercise between U.S. forces and the Japan Self-Defense Forces.
The demonstration put the small, fast drone boat through an intercept scenario on the water off Iwakuni, a joint U.S. Marine Corps and Japan Maritime Self-Defense Force air station on the Seto Inland Sea coast in Yamaguchi Prefecture.
The Typhoon is an 11-foot (3.4-meter) jet-powered boat that Splash Industries has been developing for national security missions, including cargo delivery and maritime surveillance. The company says it can sustain speeds above 50 knots (93 km/h), and its CEO, Ivan Avanesov, has said the boat reached and held speeds of more than 70 knots (130 km/h) in testing, which makes it well suited to chasing down and intercepting other small craft.
The boat has had a busy year at major U.S. Navy exercises. During Rim of the Pacific 2026 off Hawaii in July, a Typhoon autonomously approached the moving amphibious assault ship USS Essex (LHD 2) and guided itself into the ship’s flooded well deck without human intervention, which Splash Industries described as the first fully autonomous underway resupply of a U.S. Navy warship. In another RIMPAC demonstration, a Typhoon navigated rough seas to meet up with a U.S. Navy aircraft carrier more than 160 km (100 miles) offshore.
Splash Industries has also been adding strike options to the platform. In August, the company introduced the Airstrike Pack, a mission module that lets operators launch one-way aerial drones from the boat with the press of a button through the company’s Splash C2 command-and-control software, and said the module had already been tested in a force-on-force exercise. The Inglewood, California, company came out of stealth in July with a $4.2 million funding round led by Ubiquity Ventures.
Keen Sword 27 runs from Oct. 19 to Oct. 29 and brings together about 45,000 Japanese and roughly 12,000 American personnel, along with close to 300 aircraft and ships, in what is the largest edition of the biennial exercise so far. Much of the training focuses on the defense of Japan’s southwestern islands, and the program covers air and missile defense, amphibious landings, logistics and maritime operations.
The Typhoon’s appearance at Iwakuni added a drone boat to an exercise that also features U.S. Marine Corps NMESIS anti-ship missile launchers and MADIS air defense systems deployed to Yonaguni Island, with the exercise continuing through Oct. 29.

U.S. Navy buys another carrier air traffic radar from Saab
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:34:39 UTC
15:34:39 KST

- The U.S. Navy exercised a $14.3 million option for Saab to build one more AN/SPN-50 shipboard air traffic control radar.
- The radar replaces the AN/SPN-43C on Nimitz-class carriers and amphibious assault ships, with work in East Syracuse, New York, through June 2028.
The U.S. Navy is buying one more AN/SPN-50 shipboard air traffic control radar from Saab under a $14.3 million contract option, adding to a growing fleet of new radars that track and guide aircraft around aircraft carriers and amphibious assault ships.
Naval Air Systems Command at Patuxent River, Maryland, exercised the option on Saab Inc.’s existing contract, with the work to be done at the company’s facility in East Syracuse, New York, and completed by June 2028. The unit is a low-rate initial production radar, and the full $14.3 million comes from fiscal 2027 Navy procurement funds obligated at the time of award, which was made on a sole-source basis.
The AN/SPN-50(V)1 is a U.S. version of Saab’s Sea Giraffe Agile Multi Beam radar and serves as the primary air traffic control surveillance radar for both crewed and unmanned aircraft aboard Nimitz-class carriers and large-deck amphibious assault ships. Shipboard air traffic controllers use it to identify, marshal and direct aircraft within about 50 nautical miles (93 km) of the ship, handling sequencing and separation, safety alerts, traffic advisories and guidance into final approach.
The new radar replaces the AN/SPN-43C, an S-band air traffic radar that has served on U.S. Navy ships since the mid-1960s. Part of the push to retire the older system came from spectrum changes: regulators reassigned the top quarter of the SPN-43C’s frequency band to commercial fixed wireless use, which restricts the legacy radar’s operation within 50 nautical miles of the coast.
Saab first won the program in 2016 with a $38 million engineering and manufacturing development contract covering three radars over four years. Later orders included a $25 million contract in 2020 for two units destined for USS Dwight D. Eisenhower (CVN 69) and the amphibious assault ship Bougainville (LHA 8), a $47.5 million order in December 2023 for three more systems and a $41.7 million contract in October 2024 for another three.
The latest award follows a $74.6 million modification in August 2026 for five more SPN-50(V)1 radars, with work split between Syracuse and Gothenburg, Sweden. The Navy has planned to procure 25 SPN-50 radars in total, and with this option the newest low-rate production unit is scheduled for completion in June 2028.

U.S. Air Force expands StormBreaker deal to $950 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:31:57 UTC
15:31:57 KST

- The U.S. Air Force raised Raytheon’s StormBreaker life cycle support contract by $350 million, to a total ceiling of $950 million.
- Work on the GBU-53/B Small Diameter Bomb II support contract will take place in Tucson, Arizona, through Dec. 31, 2030.
The U.S. Air Force has raised the ceiling on Raytheon’s life cycle support contract for the GBU-53/B StormBreaker, also known as the Small Diameter Bomb II, by $350 million, bringing the total potential value of the deal to $950 million.
The modification lifts the contract from $600 million and extends work at Raytheon’s plant in Tucson, Arizona, through Dec. 31, 2030. The ceiling increase gives the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center at Eglin Air Force Base, Florida, room to place more orders under the contract first awarded in 2019, with funds to be obligated as individual orders are issued.
StormBreaker is a small precision-guided glide bomb designed to hit moving targets in bad weather, smoke or dust, at night and from long range. It weighs about 93 kg (204 pounds) and is about 1.75 meters (69 inches) long, with wings that pop out after release so the bomb can glide to its target.
Its key feature is a tri-mode seeker that combines millimeter-wave radar, an imaging infrared sensor and a semi-active laser receiver, backed by GPS and inertial navigation. The radar lets the bomb find and track vehicles through clouds and rain, while the infrared sensor helps it pick out a specific target. When released from high altitude, StormBreaker can reach moving targets more than 72 km (45 miles) away and fixed targets beyond 100 km (62 miles). It can also receive updated target information during flight through Link 16 and UHF data links, which allows crews to redirect the weapon after launch.
Because of its compact size, an F-15E Strike Eagle can carry up to 28 StormBreakers on seven four-round racks, and the bomb is sized to fit inside the internal weapons bays of the F-35.
The U.S. Air Force cleared StormBreaker for operational use on the F-15E in September 2020 and declared initial operational capability in September 2022. The U.S. Navy approved it for operational use on the F/A-18E/F Super Hornet in February 2026. Integration on all three F-35 variants continues, and Raytheon recently reported an F-35B launching eight StormBreakers simultaneously during a flight test in Arizona, as The Defence Blog has followed since formal F-35 testing began.
In April 2026, the U.S. Department of War awarded Raytheon a $708.9 million contract for StormBreaker production, and the weapon has a growing list of international customers, including Australia, Norway, Germany, Italy, Finland and Belgium for their F-35 fleets. The United Kingdom approved its purchase in 2026 as an interim stand-off weapon for its F-35B jets.
Work under the expanded support contract will continue in Tucson through the end of 2030, supporting a weapon now in service with both the U.S. Air Force and the U.S. Navy.

Indonesian wildfires threaten world’s oldest cave paintings in Sulawesi
While Sumatra and Borneo are the worst affected, fires have also spread to Sulawesi, where limestone caves house art as old as 67,000 years
2-MIN READ2-MIN
 Listen
The world’s oldest cave paintings on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi are under threat as heat and smoke from the country’s worst wildfires in more than a decade risk accelerating the deterioration of the more than 67,000-year-old works of art, according to researchers.
Indonesia is battling its most intense forest and land fires since 2015 as a severe El Nino drives up temperatures and reduces rainfall, leaving its forest and peatland vulnerable to fire. While the islands of Sumatra and Borneo are the worst affected by the disaster, fires have also spread on the island of Sulawesi, including in South Sulawesi where limestone caves house the world’s oldest prehistoric art.
In a cave in South Sulawesi’s Maros-Pangkep, an artwork depicting human-like figures interacting with a pig was dated by researchers from Australia’s Griffith University to be at least 51,200 years old. In a cave on Muna island, off Sulawesi, a reddish-coloured hand stencil was dated to at least 67,800 years.
Near the Maros-Pangkep cave, firefighters worked to put out fires as smoke drifted over the dramatic karst landscape that is a defining feature of the national park and Unesco Global Geopark surrounding the cave.

CHYBÍK + KRIŠTOF has opened Building the Existing City, an exhibition at Aedes Architecture Forum in Berlin that transforms the gallery into a working architecture studio. Running from October 23 to December 3, 2026, the exhibition centres on four architectural and urban design proposals for sites or urban situations in Berlin, selected through an open call. Over six weeks, visitors can follow the practice's research, discussions, and design work as the proposals develop, gaining insight into the processes through which architectural interventions are conceived in response to local conditions.
The four projects were identified through 4 Transformations for Berlin, an open call that ran from September 11 to October 11, 2026, inviting individuals, community initiatives, public institutions, property owners, and other organisations to nominate buildings, sites, or urban situations in need of transformation. The selected projects will be developed pro bono by CHYBÍK + KRIŠTOF in collaboration with the communities and organisations connected to each site, with the team preparing initial architectural and urban design studies during the exhibition. The proposals will be presented at a closing event on December 3, marking the culmination of the six-week process.
Founded in 2010 by Ondřej Chybík and Michal Krištof, CHYBÍK + KRIŠTOF works across architecture, urban design, research, and education, with offices in Prague, Brno, Bratislava, and London. Its projects span cultural, residential, educational, and civic buildings, alongside masterplans and public spaces. At Aedes, this broader portfolio is presented through four themes: PLAY, LIVE, ACTIVATE, and ADAPT, each organised around a built project and accompanied by drawings, models, videos, material studies, and research from a selection of 20 projects. Alongside the project displays, a programme of public lectures, film screenings, and workshops for school groups will extend these discussions beyond the gallery. Lectures and critique sessions for university students will also connect the exhibition to architectural education, bringing students and practitioners into conversation around the design challenges explored in the studio.
Building the Existing City builds on CHYBÍK + KRIŠTOF's work with temporary and experimental formats, including pavilions, installations, and urban activations. Its completed projects include the Jihlava Municipal Arena, the Nusle Brewery neighbourhood, and Lahofer Winery. Other exhibitions this year explore how architecture engages with existing urban environments, cultural histories, and social conditions. At the Canadian Centre for Architecture in Montreal, The fortune of the city is that it has never been perfect, on view through January 10, 2027, examines Álvaro Siza's approach to city-making through projects shaped by the historical, social, and physical conditions of their surroundings. In Shanghai, The Poetics of Survival, presented at the Power Station of Art through October 25, explores the work of Brazilian architect Lina Bo Bardi through an exhibition designed by OPEN Architecture and curated by Renato Anelli. Meanwhile, the Museum of Modern Art in New York is presenting Architects of Liberation: Modernism in Western Africa through January 2, 2027, examining modern architecture across seven West African countries in the context of political independence from the late 1950s to the early 1980s.

Tech titans, crypto moguls dominate US midterm money race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:27:44 UTC
15:27:44 KST

The 15 largest contributors in the upcoming U.S. midterm elections have donated over $1.5 billion, an AFP analysis of Federal Election Commission data shows, as the race shapes up to be the most expensive midterms to date.
The biggest donors, as of Oct. 21, have made contributions to both parties and to special interest groups, such as super political action committees (PACs) lobbying for deregulated AI and cryptocurrency.
World's richest man and Republican ally Elon Musk has donated over $365 million, including $278 million since July 1. According to campaign finance tracker OpenSecrets, this makes him the largest individual contributor in a federal election cycle since unlimited election spending was allowed in 2010.
"We're on track to have the most expensive midterm elections in U.S. history," Michael Beckel, director of money in politics reform at bipartisan advocacy organisation Issue One, told AFP.
AFP analysed contributions since Nov. 6, 2024, counting businesses and their leaders, as well as business partners and/or spouses as a single contributor where relevant, based on a New York Times methodology to track campaign finances.
Of the top 15 biggest contributors, five are in tech, particularly in the AI and cryptocurrency sectors.
These donors, who tend to favor deregulation in their industries, are "pumping massive sums of money into U.S. elections hoping to elect politicians who will advance their preferred policy positions," Beckel said.
Venture capitalists and business partners Marc Andreessen and Benjamin Horowitz have spent over $113 million so far.
They donated $50 million to the pro-AI super PAC Leading the Future and $46.8 million to Fairshake, a cryptocurrency super PAC.
They also donated $12 million to U.S. President Donald Trump's Make America Great Again (MAGA) Inc super PAC.
Cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase has donated close to $57 million in total this election cycle, including donations from its CEO and co-founder Brian Armstrong.
Ripple Labs, another crypto firm, and its co-founder Chris Larsen have donated over $68 million.
The majority of those two companies' contributions were to Fairshake.
The Winklevoss brothers Cameron and Tyler, major figures of the crypto landscape, donated to MAGA Inc and to their own pro-crypto super PAC.
Musk's donations have mostly gone to his Republican-leaning America PAC, as well as to the Republican Senate Leadership Fund super PAC (SLF).
The SLF used Musk's $158 million donations in September to support Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas.
Four anonymous nonprofit groups, known as 501C4 organisations or dark money groups, are amongst the top 15 donors this election cycle.
These nonprofits fund campaign finance but are not legally required to publicly disclose their donors.
"Dark money spending has been increasing year over year, and it is a troubling trend because voters should be able to know who is financing the ads that they see", Shanna Ports, Senior Legal Counsel at the Campaign Legal Center, told AFP.
One Nation, a Republican nonprofit group, gave almost $138 million to the SLF.
The American Action Network, another Republican dark money group, has contributed over $64 million to the Republican Congressional Leadership Fund, which is the SLF's counterpart for electing Republicans to the House.
Two Democratic nonprofit groups -- House Majority Forward and Majority Forward -- respectively contributed $95 million to the House Majority PAC and $104 million to the Senate Majority PAC.
Both focus on getting Democratic candidates elected to Congress.
Some historic donors have continued giving this election cycle.
Billionaire couple Elizabeth and Richard Uihlein donated over $135 million this election cycle to support Republicans.
George Soros, a longtime Democratic donor, has contributed at least $102 million.
The Israeli American businesswomen and conservative political donor Miriam Adelson gave close to $67 million to various Republican PACs.
Other big donors on the list are billionaire businessman Jeff Yass, who has donated $109 million so far, mostly to Republican groups, as well as hedge fund manager Paul Singer, who donated over $52 million, also to Republican groups.
Billionaire ex-mayor of New York City Michael Bloomberg has spent $52.6 million so far, including around $30 million in contributions made after September 1.
His team told the New York Times he will spend $80 million in September and October.

Europe records over 50,000 heat-related deaths this summer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
06:26:02 UTC
15:26:02 KST

Europe records over 50,000 heat-related deaths this summer
According to a new study, over 50,000 people died as a result of scorching heatwaves that gripped Europe this summer, Qazinform News Agency cites WAM reports.
Researchers modelled heat-related deaths for different age groups in 854 European cities during repeated heat waves in June, July and August and found that 50,391 people died from warmer temperatures, and of those, 32,619 died because of the extra heat caused by the burning of coal, oil and gas, according to a study in an upcoming issue of Nature Health.
That’s 71 percent higher than the previous deadliest summer, which was 29,480 in 2022, according to the same researchers, who produced a study earlier this month tracking yearly summer heat-related deaths in those European cities.
This summer’s death figures are underestimates because they don’t count a deadly heat wave in May, and they only look at deaths in those 854 cities, which are about 40 percent of Europe’s population, the study authors said.
As written before, the impact varied considerably across Europe, with southern and southeastern parts of the continent recording the highest estimated heat-related death rates relative to population.
Croatia had the highest average rate, with an estimated 327 heat-related deaths per million residents over the study period. Malta followed with 226 deaths per million, and Romania with 223.
Among European capitals, Zagreb, Bucharest and Rome had the highest average annual heat-related death rates during the period studied.
The researchers also found that the proportion of heat-related deaths attributable to climate change increased over time in all 30 countries included in the analysis, although the scale of the impact differed by location.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett issued the order during a hearing in Miami on Thursday after lawyers for the British broadcaster accused Trump of delaying his deposition. The president had canceled a previously agreed October 16 appearance, citing matters of national importance. The BBC's attorney, Charles Tobin, argued that Trump had instead attended a political campaign event in Georgia that day.
The judge ruled that Trump must appear for questioning by December 11 or risk sanctions, including possible dismissal of his lawsuit, unless the court extends the discovery period. The current deadline for exchanging evidence is December 18. The BBC's lawyers have maintained that obtaining Trump's testimony before that date is essential to preparing their defense.
According to court filings, the broadcaster first requested deposition dates in July and repeatedly sought confirmation from Trump's legal team. After the October appearance was canceled, the BBC was informed that the president would not be available before the discovery deadline and could instead testify in January 2027. Trump's lawyers have cited his presidential responsibilities in explaining the scheduling difficulties.
The hearing also addressed a dispute over access to financial information. Lett authorized the BBC to obtain records showing the number of membership applications at Trump's Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida between January 2020 and January 2026, along with membership and initiation fees. The broadcaster argues that such information could help establish whether the documentary affected Trump's reputation and financial interests. Trump's lawyers disputed the relevance of the records, arguing that the president does not personally manage the club and that its membership does not directly reflect his reputation.
Trump filed the lawsuit in Florida in December 2025, accusing the BBC of defamation and violations of the state's laws against deceptive and unfair trade practices. He is seeking at least $10 billion in damages over a documentary that included edited footage of his January 6, 2021, speech, delivered shortly before his supporters stormed the U.S. Capitol.
The documentary, titled "Trump: A Second Chance," aired as part of the BBC's Panorama program shortly before the 2024 U.S. presidential election. Trump alleges that the broadcaster combined separate portions of his speech in a way that falsely suggested he had directly encouraged the violence at the Capitol.
The BBC has acknowledged that the editing created a misleading impression and apologized to Trump, although it maintains that the broadcast did not constitute defamation. The controversy also led to the resignations of the broadcaster's director-general and its senior news executive.
