US judge blocks federal operations seeking to identify non-citizen voters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
21:52:52 UTC
06:52:52 KST

US judge blocks federal operations seeking to identify non-citizen voters
Homeland Security targets nine states in a push to identify voting fraud, a move critics denounce as tantamount to voter intimidation.
A United States federal judge has ordered the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to halt operations aimed at finding non-citizen voters in nine states ahead of the midterm elections.
The ruling by US District Court Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin said the investigations likely violate a provision of the Voting Rights Act that prohibits voter intimidation. She further said the DHS may have relied on flawed data in its investigations.
That leads to “an objectively reasonable fear of law enforcement entanglements that intimidates citizens from urging or aiding others in exercising their right to vote”, she wrote.
The order applies to federal efforts targeting California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wisconsin.
The DHS has publicised what it has described as a push to identify individuals who have committed voter fraud, with some local offices posting photos of agents knocking on the doors of suspects.
The operations come as the administration of US President Donald Trump has sought to highlight instances of voter fraud ahead of the November 3 midterm vote.
While there are recorded instances of fraud in every election cycle, such isolated cases remain exceedingly rare.
There has been no evidence to indicate that non-citizen voters have influenced the outcome of any election at any level in the country.
In a statement following Thursday’s ruling, the DHS maintained that its investigations were aimed at “removing aliens who vote and dilute the votes of US citizens”.
“We have no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be US citizens,” it said.
In their lawsuit challenging the DHS’s efforts, the California Nurses Association and National Nurses United, along with the Voto Latino Foundation, San Francisco and Santa Clara County, said that some US citizens felt they were wrongly identified and questioned as part of the investigations.
A lawyer representing the groups said it was “clear from the start that DHS built its lists on bad data, never checked how often it was wrong, and recklessly sent agents to people’s homes weeks before an election”.
Benjamin Farley, the supervisory counsel for democracy defense at the National Immigration Law Center, said the ruling sent a strong message about voter intimidation ahead of the midterm vote.
“Yesterday’s decision is a clear rebuke of the government’s efforts to scare voters away from the polls this November and a reminder that all US citizens – regardless of color, place of birth, or the nationality of their family members – have the right to participate in American elections free of intimidation,” he said.
“No armed federal agent is going to stop us from casting our vote.”

German student representatives and opposition parties call for mass protests on Oct. 31
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
21:52:13 UTC
06:52:13 KST

Oliver Towfigh Nia
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
A German student organization and opposition party The Left voiced support Thursday for protests planned for late October calling for increased funding and investment in education and better conditions at schools, according to press reports.
The Federal Student Conference supports the protests planned for Oct. 31 in many German cities, Isabelle Seltenreich, a spokesperson for the organization, told the daily Rheinische Post newspaper.
She added that students have both the right and every reason to take to the streets to advocate for improvements to the education system.
The youth and student movements GenZ regelt’ (Gen Z Takes Charge) and GenZ steht auf (Gen Z Stands Up) have launched online campaigns to mobilize support for the protests.
They also advocate for greater climate protection, measures to address the rising cost of living and opposition to mandatory military service, with the initiative explicitly rejecting the use of violence.
Seltenreich said the Federal Student Conference shares many of the demands that have also emerged during protests in France and Italy.
"These include, among other things, better facilities and infrastructure in schools, a sufficient number of teachers, smaller class sizes, improved learning conditions, and an education system that offers equal opportunities to all young people, regardless of their social background," she said.
With regard to France and Italy, she warned that such protests could be exploited by various political groups.
Seltenreich’s support for the protest movement was partially echoed by Ines Schwerdtner, the co-chairwoman of the opposition party The Left.
In a video briefing with the Socialist Democratic Student Association (SDS), she said that what is working in France—connecting various movements—must now also be achieved in Germany.
Schwerdtner assured the activists of the SDS—an organization currently under surveillance by the domestic intelligence agency in the southern states of Bavaria and Baden-Wuerttemberg—by saying: "I will stand in your defense—no matter who attacks you, whether it be the police or the media."
In France, students have been protesting since the end of September, calling for better school facilities, more teachers, and improved learning conditions. Similar protests have since spread to Italy. In both countries, these demonstrations have also involved acts of violence.
Separately, Jochen Kopelke, the federal chairman of the German Police Union (Gewerkschaft der Polizei), said he believed that the German police are better prepared to handle violent protests than their French counterparts.
"I believe the quality and professionalism of the German police are of a different caliber," Kopelke told newspapers belonging to the Mediengruppe Bayern.
He noted that the "guardrails"—the operational frameworks—in Germany are more modern and place a much greater emphasis on communication.
"We employ different tactics and use different equipment," he noted.
Baden-Wuerttemberg Interior Minister Manuel Hagel told the daily BILD newspaper that there are concrete indications that the protests are set to spread to his state.
"We will do everything in our power to prevent this 'protest tourism' from reaching our state," he said.
Hagel added that there are now "specific calls to bring the violent protests from France over to us in Baden-Wuerttemberg."
He was backed up by his Bavarian counterpart Joachim Herrmann, who also announced a zero-tolerance strategy.
“In Germany, we must do everything in our power to ensure that riots like those in France are prevented from the outset. We certainly protect the right to freedom of assembly—there is no question about that. But we will deploy a strong police presence to ensure that no violent confrontations, acts of arson, or similar incidents occur—the kind we witnessed in France,” Hermann told BILD.

RAF Chinooks and A400M to fight UK wildfires from the sky
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
22:38:52 BST
06:38:52 KST

The Royal Air Force will equip its Chinook helicopters and A400M Atlas transport aircraft to fight fires, giving Britain an aerial firefighting capability permanently based in the United Kingdom for the first time, according to the government.
Wes Streeting, the Defence Secretary, said: “As the threat of wildfires in the UK grows, defence will step up to provide greater support to our emergency services and protect military training areas across the country.
“This will see the RAF’s Chinook helicopters and A400M aircraft equipped with new specialist firefighting equipment to enable them to tackle wildfires from the skies for the first time.”
Ministers had ruled out precisely this six weeks ago, when Louise Sandher-Jones, a defence minister, answered a question from Neil Duncan-Jordan, the Labour member for Poole, who had asked whether the A400M fleet could be adapted to carry water. Her answer, published on 9 September, said that “responsibility for responding to wildfires in the UK rests with the relevant civil authorities and emergency services” and that “the Department is aware of the Airbus A400M aerial firefighting system currently under development and testing.” It concluded: “Consequently, the Department has no plans to adapt the RAF A400M Atlas fleet for aerial firefighting purposes.” That position was reported here in September.
Pressure on the question had built through the summer, when a wildfire that broke out near Glenmore in the Cairngorms on 15 July burned across roughly thirty square kilometres of heather, woodland and conservation land, and the UK government offered military helicopters for heavy lifting alongside support from stand-by battalions. The Scottish government declined. Neil Gray, the Justice Secretary, said the requirement on the ground was for waterbombing helicopters, that every commercial waterbombing aircraft in the country was already committed, and that the military did not hold that capability. Royal Air Force Chinooks of 1310 Flight had dropped around four hundred and fifty tonnes of water on a Cypriot wildfire in July 2025, flying from Akrotiri with Bambi buckets, which this publication set out at the time.
The Prime Minister said: “I stood in Stourbridge and watched families lose everything. I will never forget it. Our firefighters were heroes that day, but heroes shouldn’t have to fight with one hand tied behind their backs.
“Crews will now have the kit they need to stay safe and military aircraft will stand ready to help tackle wildfires from the sky. We cannot put people through another summer like this one.”
Firefighters in England will be given additional specialist wildfire teams and lightweight personal protective equipment designed for wildfires, backed by up to £45 million. The kit crews currently wear is built primarily for fires in buildings and is not meant to be worn for long stretches, and the replacement is intended to be lighter and more breathable so it can be used for longer periods.
Angela Rayner, the Communities Secretary, said: “The wildfires we’ve faced this year have been unrelenting, leaving a devastating impact on communities, homes and our precious countryside.
“We’ve heard loud and clear from communities, experts and emergency services that more needs to be done. That’s why we’re taking immediate action now, while working across government and the sector to build a stronger, more resilient national response to wildfires for the future.”
On prevention, the government will put £25 million into restoring dried-out peatlands in England so that they hold more water and act as natural firebreaks, and will give farmers financial support to fireproof their land by digging ponds and clearing burnable material in high-risk areas. The new Peatland Restoration Grant Scheme will be run by Natural England and is expected to operate from April 2027 to April 2029. Tougher local restrictions and bans on particular products are also being examined as a way of stopping fires being started when the risk is high.
Dame Angela Eagle, the Environment Secretary, said: “The wildfires that tore through our countryside this summer showed the urgent need to adapt to our changing climate.
“Nature is our greatest ally in preventing wildfires starting in the first place, with healthy landscapes keeping more moisture in the ground to stop fires spreading.
“That’s why we are stepping in and investing £25 million to restore peatlands as well as backing farmers to deliver natural fire safety measures on their land.”
A Wildfires AI Unit will be created inside the National Situation Centre in COBR, drawing together universities, technology firms and government departments to spot and fight fires faster. The government will work with the Met Office on better wildfire forecasts and risk assessment, develop England’s first Wildfire Action Plan covering prevention, preparedness, response and recovery, and work more closely with the devolved governments on shared expertise. An interministerial meeting between the UK and devolved governments will be convened to coordinate the response across all four nations.
Louise Haigh, the First Secretary of State, said: “The UK has world-leading expertise in the application of new technologies to track and tackle wildfires. By bringing together the work of the National Situation Centre, leading academic institutions and our international partners, we are building a centre of excellence at the heart of government that will share best practice and strengthen our national preparedness.”
Katie White, the Minister for Climate Transition, said: “Anyone who thinks climate change is a problem for our children and grandchildren, rather than here and now, should spend a shift with a firefighter. This summer, crews battled devastating wildfires in extreme heat, risking their lives to protect the places we love. The threat is already here, staring us in the face.
“We can’t stop every wildfire, flood or storm, but we can make sure Britain is ready. This summit is about better equipping our brave emergency services, protecting our people, and building a stronger country, whatever the weather.”
Civil fire and rescue services across all four nations will continue to request firefighting support through the Military Aid to the Civil Authorities process. The Ministry of Defence is the second largest landowner in the United Kingdom, and the government said the department requires an aerial firefighting capability of its own to adapt to the increased risk of wildfires facing the country.
The package was announced ahead of a summit at which the Prime Minister met fire chiefs, local leaders and experts. Airbus, Google and VodafoneThree attended, setting out how satellite monitoring, early warning, connectivity and aerial capability can help communities prepare for and respond to fires. Kata Escott, managing director of Airbus Defence and Space UK and head of UK public affairs, said: “Today’s Wildfire Summit is an important step toward strengthening wildfire preparedness and prevention in the UK. With our life saving capabilities, we are supporting the UK effort in the air, in the digital domain, and with our early warning assets in space.”
This summer was the United Kingdom’s hottest on record, and the Met Office has found that climate change made the extreme heat around one hundred and thirty times more likely. The government held the first meeting of its Climate and Nature Security Taskforce last month, which will establish the most significant climate and nature security risks facing the country and shape the government’s approach to them.

Starobelsk massacre survivors recount lingering terror to RT (VIDEO)
The survivors of the deadly Ukrainian drone attack on the Starobelsk college in May have spoken to RT about the emotional scars left behind by the tragedy that killed 21 students in their sleep.
Multiple waves of kamikaze UAVs struck the dormitory of the Starobelsk Professional College, located in Russia’s Lugansk People’s Republic (LPR), on May 22. The building partially collapsed as a result of the strikes, killing 21 people and injuring 42 others, mostly teenage girls studying to become teachers. The Ukrainian military subsequently targeted first responders with additional drones, according to investigators.
Twenty students who survived the attack on the dormitory that fateful night came to Moscow on Wednesday at the invitation of Russia’s Commissioner for Human Rights Yana Lantratova.
Lantratova and the students discussed their professional aspirations, with the official noting that some of them have already become volunteers in various projects. She also said that the human rights commission’s doors are open to survivors wishing to undertake an internship there. The official gifted a bus to the college as well as tablet computers to its students.
Speaking to RT, one of the survivors recounted how she took cover in the basement on the night of the attack and “ended up getting buried under the debris.” Acting on “autopilot,” she extricated herself from the rubble and ran for her life. The student said that in the wake of the tragic incident, she “started to be afraid of everything, even the slightest rustle.”
“Especially during the first week, it was absolutely terrifying. I was afraid of every single loud noise,” the survivor told RT.
Another student shared a similar experience of lingering trauma, saying that following the attack, “any loud noise, even just something falling was terrifying. My heart would immediately start pounding violently.”
Lantratova said the attack had been funded with Western taxpayers’ money and accused Kiev’s backers of glossing over the atrocity perpetrated by the Ukrainian military. Kiev has denied responsibility for the incident, with various officials providing conflicting accounts of the massacre.
President Vladimir Putin vowed “inevitable punishment” for the Starobelsk massacre, and several days later, Russia launched one of its largest retaliatory drone and missile strikes, targeting Ukrainian military command facilities, air bases, and defense industry enterprises.

====================================================================================================

Awkward questions linger as creaky Australia receives South African hiding
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
21:29:37 UTC
06:29:37 KST

That Australia slowly folded and lost the Gqeberha Test by an innings and 31 runs late on day five was hardly surprising in light of its batting calamities of 24 hours earlier. That Kagiso Rabada and Marco Jansen ran through the tail to finish things off even less so.
But it remains startling to consider the reversal of fortunes this quite disastrous loss represented for Australia. On day two, they were 1-0 up in the series, had South Africa on the ropes at 5-97, on a greenish pitch, and fancied a rout of their own.
Instead, in a game that lost 145 overs to rain and associated delays, the annihilation took place in reverse and a series some considered Australia's stepping stone to more difficult engagements ahead is now set for an enticing decider. For Australia, the task ahead is now daunting on multiple levels — not just to find form and the right combination of players to defeat an ascendant and cohesive opponent, but how to do so in Cape Town, with all the extra heat that will entail.
First the few positives. Travis Head, whose role as opener will continue to be endlessly scrutinised, laboured unselfishly for five hours to make 121. Nightwatchman Scott Boland, who was Australia's best all-round performer of the game, absorbed 187 deliveries for his rearguard 40.
The negatives? Australia's next-best batsman was Mother Nature, who wiped out the first session of play and briefly raised hopes that Australia would force a draw. It didn't, for neither did Boland's patient hand inspire his better credentialed batting partners to hang around and save the day.
It is pointless to analyse the tail. Most culpable this time was Steve Smith, who in his short and strange stay at the crease was given a reprieve by Proteas keeper Ryan Rickelton but failed to make South Africa pay, falling soon after to an objectionably unserious dismissal in a game that was, from Australia's perspective, a little too full of them.
Australia was 5-219 at the time of this pivot point, not entirely written off. Rabada had just taken the second new ball. Boland, batting steadily, had just driven him to the long-off boundary with a beautifully straight bat. Smith? Convention be damned. Rabada sent down a length ball on a fourth-stump line. Smith, for reasons known only to him, decided he should launch over the fence at deep mid-wicket. Instead he skied it and Matthew Breetzke juggled a catch. Therein lay the death of the contest.
Much has been made of Marnus Labuschagne's battle against his cricketing mortality, but Smith is now a fairly pressing problem too. For a long time, he has been Australia's Mr Dependable — not simply a better batsmen than younger alternatives, but an undroppable ornament, encouraged to play how he likes, to bat where he wants and indulge his obsessions however he sees fit.
Yet that greatness is suddenly fading fast, the numbers dwindling, Smith's insularity intensifying into less pardonable distractions. It is hard to shake the feeling that he and Labuschagne's overall effect on Australia's flaky batting group is a net negative on a psychological level as much as a statistical one.
A subtle but remarkable insight into this dynamic — ignored at the time — was glimpsed during the Bangladesh series in August, when Cameron Green used a post-match interview to explain the genesis of his own breakthrough first Test century on home soil.
"I was able to go back to Shield cricket … kind of a good little reminder about how I want to go about it," Green told ABC Sport at the time. "I think when you're playing in a pretty good Australian Test team, you bat behind some pretty good players in front of you and I think I probably got caught up in how they go about it. So, I think the beautiful thing about going back to state cricket is to remind myself how I want to go about it."
In other words, Australia's most gifted player of the generation to come was admitting that in order to get himself firing as a middle-order batsmen in this Test side, first he had to get himself far away from the influence of his teammates.
Green, of course, will be pushing his case for selection in Cape Town after injury ruled him out of the first two Tests. Should he be declared fit, the Beau Webster dilemma need not be as emotive as Australian coach Andrew McDonald made it in his press conference on day four.
But it is puzzling to consider the reasoning for even selecting Webster in this match, in which he was never likely to bowl many of his seamers in an attack featuring four frontline quicks, was not asked for his off-spin, nor deemed top-six material with the bat.
McDonald was right to say the issue is not as straightforward as armchair selectors would have it. Like Mitch Marsh before him, Webster is clearly a much-loved team man. Over the English summer just gone, Warwickshire teammate Sam Hain spoke with genuine emotion of the mutual respect and pride Webster had created from the minute he arrived. Warwickshire duly won the championship trophy. But Webster's numbers told a less compelling story: 403 runs at 33, 12 wickets at 40. At Test level, same goes.
The most sensible scenario at the top of the order is that Nic Maddinson, a walking wicket against Rabada, will drop out and Matt Renshaw slide up. Cooper Connolly, who at ODI level recently justified the hype around him, must surely be in line to enter a team crying out for fresh blood.
Looking beyond this result and this series, one wonders whether Australian cricket can find a clarity of purpose and be as ruthless as it needs to be to avoid toppling over a cliff when Smith, Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon are finally gone.
On that note, here is a quote to consider, from Australia's chairman of selectors: "Part of our charter is obviously to provide for the future," he said. "We are very aware that some of these blokes are getting on in age, and that's why it's very, very important for them to continue to perform."
Unfortunately, that was not George Bailey referring to this current Australian team, average age 34, which in Durban was the oldest XI since the 1920s and the first in Test history to not feature a single player under the age of 30.
No, it was Trevor Hohns, late in 2000, referring to arguably Australia's greatest combination ever. Its average age? Erm, 30.
Time, perhaps, for a new charter.

Efforts headed by the US to pursue talks stalled in February with the outbreak of the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.

Japan to reduce subsidies for eco-friendly vehicles next year
The Japanese government will cut its subsidies for the purchase of eco-friendly vehicles, including electric and fuel-cell vehicles, to 60-80 pct of their current levels next year, the industry ministry said Wednesday, JIJI Press reported.
The reduced subsidies will apply to cars registered from Jan. 1.
The ministry is expected to temporarily stop accepting subsidy applications as early as December, instead of next February as previously projected, because of strong sales of such vehicles. The cut in the subsidies is designed to keep the program in place within the current budget.
The maximum amount of subsidies for EVs will be reduced to 750,000 yen from the current 1.25 million yen. The upper limit will be lowered from 550,000 yen to 440,000 yen for electric minivehicles, from 800,000 yen to 480,000 yen for plug-in hybrid vehicles, and from 1.45 million yen to 870,000 yen for fuel-cell vehicles.
The maximum amount of additional subsidies, determined by evaluating automakers' efforts to reduce environmental impacts, including using steel sheets that reduce carbon emissions during manufacturing, will also be cut to 30,000 yen from 50,000 yen. For electric minivehicles, the ceiling will be reduced to 18,000 yen from 30,000 yen.

Powerful earthquake in Tibet kills at least 16 people
Authorities warn they expect death toll from magnitude 7 quake that hit remote part of Tibet to rise.
A magnitude 7 earthquake has killed at least 16 people in China’s Tibet Autonomous Region.
Search and rescue efforts were continuing on Friday after the quake, whose epicentre was in a remote region of northern Tibet, struck at 10:33pm (14:33 GMT) on Thursday.
A level-II earthquake disaster emergency response was activated in the area, the Xinhua news agency said. Electricity and communication lines were reported to be down.
Officials in Nagqu, a sparsely populated, high-altitude city, said up to 65 people have been injured, according to the Reuters news agency, although other reports suggested a slightly lower figure.
It was the strongest quake to hit China since January 2024. Officials reported the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds.
Videos released by state media showed people leaving their homes and seeking shelter outside or in their cars parked on the street.
The United States Geological Survey said the earthquake’s epicentre was in a mountainous area about 190km (118 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu and 390km (242 miles) northeast of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa.
Beijing announced it has deployed 1,600 rescue personnel, said Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu, reporting from Beijing, but reaching the area, which sits at an altitude of about 4,800 metres (15,748ft), is difficult with many roads blocked or affected by rockfalls.
“Snow is forecast over the next few days and hours,” she added, noting that the region “is no stranger to earthquakes”.
Authorities suggested the sparse population in the area may have contributed to the relatively low death toll counted so far. However, Yu noted, casualty numbers are expected to rise in the coming hours.

Venezuelans call for elections in first national protest in nearly two years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
21:21:39 UTC
06:21:39 KST

Venezuelans call for elections in first national protest in nearly two years
CARACAS/MARACAY, Venezuela - Thousands of Venezuelans took to the streets on Oct 22 in the first nationwide opposition protest in nearly two years, as demonstrators demanded free elections and other political changes with a notably thin presence of security forces.
The United States has been working closely with the interim government led by acting President Delcy Rodriguez since US forces captured President Nicolas Maduro in January. Both US President Donald Trump and Rodriguez, Maduro’s former deputy, have said there will be elections, but have not set a date either for a legislative vote or a national contest for president.
Opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize winner Maria Corina Machado, who has been outside the country for nearly a year after living in hiding following a contested 2024 election, has said elections must take place by July 2027.
Her Vente Venezuela movement organised the protest, which took place in the capital Caracas, as well as cities including Valencia, Maracay, San Cristobal and Maracaibo.
“Seeing this makes me happy because I know change is possible,” said 18-year-old cosmetology student Leosmary Hernandez, as she gathered with hundreds of others in northern Maracay. 
“I’ve been through so many hardships, so many problems because of the dollar, and difficulties studying. I have high hopes for my country and for our next leader, president, Maria Corina.”
“I went out to protest before, when things were much tougher, and I’m even less afraid today because I want my voice to be heard,” she added as music boomed around protesters waving Venezuelan flags.
Venezuela’s socialist movement, in power since 1999 under late President Hugo Chavez and then Maduro, has in the past deployed security forces against protesters decrying political repression, dizzying inflation, poor public services and other problems in the economically battered country, including after the 2024 presidential election.
Security forces had minimal presence at protest sites on Oct 22, and in many smaller cities demonstrators dispersed before dark.
The ruling Socialist Party called for its supporters to march from Caracas’ Plaza Venezuela, the same place the opposition planned to gather two hours later, to a location near the presidential palace to commemorate breast cancer awareness month.
Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, known for his close ties to the security services, was pictured on state television attending the march, while the opposition supporters moved their protest to a nearby location.
Negotiations continue
US-backed talks between a faction of the opposition and the interim government, aimed at remaking the top court and the electoral council with an eye toward ensuring fairness at eventual elections, held their latest session this month, but changes could take significant time. The negotiations do not include Machado’s political movement, though she has said she will not stand in the way of their progress.
Machado’s proxy roundly won the 2024 election according to vote tallies released by the opposition. But the government, which never released full counts, backed Maduro, as did the country’s legal and electoral institutions.
“We want presidential elections now. We want an electoral timetable to be announced now. We are not going to wait until 2028,” said Maria Debora Marin, 57, who runs a clothing store in central Valencia, referring to rumours elections may only take place the year after next. “What we want is to move forward and finally get out of this nightmare.”
Amid the arrests of some of her closest collaborators, Machado went into hiding. Her last public appearance in Venezuela was at protests to mark Maduro’s third inauguration in January 2025, where she was briefly detained.
Machado has for years sought US support, aligning with hawks in the Trump team who argued that Maduro - through links to drug gangs - represented a direct threat to US national security.
Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, are facing drug and torture charges in the US. They have pleaded not guilty.
But Trump has repeatedly praised Rodriguez’s management and her willingness to welcome US investors, saying last month it is too soon to consider elections.
Machado’s desire to return home, especially after devastating twin earthquakes in June, has caused friction in Washington, with US officials asking her to delay her trip, Reuters has reported.
“We’re in limbo,” said recent graduate Rayeska Puesme, 18, as she attended the protest in Caracas, adding she had considered leaving because of a lack of opportunities. “The United States removed one big problem, which was Maduro, but the rest are still there.”
“I feel in my heart that things are going to change, but I don’t see when.”
Demonstrators were also calling for the release of prisoners they say are held for political reasons.
Legal rights group Foro Penal, which represents opposition figures and others who have been detained, often on charges like treason, says there are still more than 320 political prisoners in Venezuela, despite releases that took place under an amnesty law backed by the legislature earlier this year.
The government has repeatedly denied holding political prisoners and says the amnesty is generous. REUTERS

Trump ordered to sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit

Trump ordered to sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit
Judge says Trump must sit for questioning from a BBC lawyer by December 11 or face possible dismissal of lawsuit.
A federal judge in the United States has ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition as part of his $10bn defamation lawsuit against the British broadcaster BBC.
On Thursday, US Magistrate Judge Enjolique Lett ruled that Trump would be required to answer questions under oath in a session with the BBC‘s lawyers.
The deposition is scheduled to take place no later than December 11, or Trump could face sanctions, including the possible dismissal of the lawsuit.
Trump had previously been scheduled to sit for deposition on October 16 but had cancelled due to a “matter of national importance”.
Charles Tobin, a lawyer for the BBC, said that the president was in fact campaigning in the state of Georgia on that day.
“He was participating in party politics and prioritised that over sitting for the deposition,” Tobin said.
The BBC lawsuit is one of several he has launched against news outlets over coverage he dislikes or casts as unfair.
Trump is currently enmeshed in another $10bn defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal that he refiled in May after it was previously dismissed. Another defamation case seeks $15bn in damages from The New York Times and Penguin Random House, a book publisher.
That streak of litigation has alarmed press freedom advocates who say that the president frequently uses government pressure and legal threats to shape coverage in his favour.
His case against the BBC centres on a documentary it aired, titled Trump: A Second Chance.
The documentary features clips of a speech Trump made on January 6, 2021, the day that Trump supporters later attacked the US Capitol.
Trump has said that a clip from his speech was misleadingly edited to suggest he encouraged attendees to storm the Capitol, the seat of the US Congress. Legislators inside had been in the process of certifying Trump’s 2020 election defeat at the time of the riot.
The British broadcaster has acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together different segments of Trump’s remarks on January 6.
The head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned, and the outlet issued an apology. But the network has denied Trump’s defamation claims.
Trump has maintained that he never told his supporters to commit violence in a bid to prevent the peaceful transition of power.
Trump, however, has long pushed the false claim that his loss in the 2020 race was due to election-rigging.
On January 6, 2021, Trump had gathered his supporters on the Ellipse outside the White House to reiterate his unsubstantiated assertions.
During his speech, he encouraged them to “fight like hell” and refused to concede to what he falsely portrayed as an election stolen through “fraud”.
Trump and his allies oversaw a multifaceted effort to stay in power despite his loss, one that included the alleged recruitment of “false electors” to cast fraudulent Electoral College votes on his behalf.
He later faced federal charges of attempting to overturn the 2020 election, which were dropped upon his re-election in 2024.
Separately, a state-level case in Georgia accused Trump of engaging in a criminal conspiracy to subvert the 2020 election. The case was dismissed in November 2025 after a replacement prosecutor took over following the disqualification of Fani Willis, who brought the charges against Trump.
A congressional probe into the events around January 6 concluded that the president had been reluctant to call on his supporters to stand down after they stormed the Capitol.

US Democratic senator probes Ukraine's loss of Starshield service
WASHINGTON, Oct 22 - Democratic US Senator Richard Blumenthal on Thursday said he had opened an inquiry into Ukraine's loss of critical access to the Pentagon's Starshield satellite communications service and the resulting degrading of Kyiv's ability to defend itself against Russian attacks.
"In the late evening of October 13, Ukrainian forces lost critical access to Starshield, the military-grade counterpart to SpaceX’s Starlink network, after their access to speeds at which equipment could stay connected to the network was capped," Blumenthal wrote in a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
"The episode raises urgent questions about who possesses the technical and legal authority to alter these capabilities" and whether the Pentagon has "sufficient alternatives" if SpaceX-provided services become unavailable, Blumenthal wrote.
Blumenthal is the senior Democrat on the Senate's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations. He is seeking information on whether the change in service was directed by the White House, the Department of Defense or SpaceX.
Republicans control the Senate, so Democrats lack subpoena power. Blumenthal can only request information and briefings from officials within and outside the government.
He said the move put Ukrainian forces and civilians at risk and raised concerns "about who controls critical capabilities the US government has spent billions of dollars to procure."
WEAKENED UKRAINE DEFENSES
The Pentagon is the biggest customer of Starshield, which is the military-grade version of the Starlink service.
A Pentagon spokesperson said: "As with all congressional correspondence, the Department will respond directly to the authors."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy on October 14 said Elon Musk's SpaceX had restricted Starlink services, weakening Ukraine's air defenses.
The controversy came as the Trump administration was pressuring Kyiv to halt its attacks on Russian energy infrastructure and encouraging Russia to return to negotiations over ending its war in Ukraine.
Blumenthal told Hegseth the Senate panel will look into government interactions with and reliance on SpaceX technology. He set deadlines of November 5 for responses to questions embedded in the letter to Hegseth, and November 12 for a briefing by SpaceX officials with knowledge of the Starshield restriction.
Besides this latest inquiry, Blumenthal has been trying to investigate a series of actions related to the Trump administration, including contracts negotiated for building a White House ballroom at an estimated cost of $400 million and Trump-linked crypto firms.
If Democrats win control of the Senate in November 3 midterm elections, he likely would become chairman of the investigations panel. REUTERS

From Jan 1, WhatsApp, Telegram won’t work without SIM cards, govt issues guidelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
21:06:01 UTC
06:06:01 KST

The move is to curb cross-border cyber frauds using Indian numbers
NEW DELHI: India has made SIM binding mandatory from Jan 1, 2027, and the move will mean that messaging apps like WhatsApp and Telegram will not work without a SIM card in the smartphone. The department of telecom has issued guidelines requiring messaging platforms to integrate the accounts with live SIMs used for registration by Dec 31, 2026. If the SIM is removed, replaced or deactivated, the app’s functionality will stop until a valid SIM is reinserted.The move is to curb cross-border cyber frauds, phishing, digital arrest scams using Indian mobile numbers and enhance telecom cyber security. Apple has updated iOS with a software patch to help detect when an iPhone is operating without a physical SIM card to abide with the rules. It is learnt Signal has not yet responded to govt notices.From Jan 1, messaging services to be used will have to ensure a registered SIM card is installed in a device. This is likely to impact users of WhatsApp or Telegram over Wi-Fi without registered SIMs. And also those who use more than one device or frequently change their SIM cards.
Last Nov, DoT had issued the rules after finding “that some app-based communication services utilising Indian mobile numbers for identification of its customers allows users to consume their services without availability of the underlying subscriber identity module (SIM) within the device in which app-based communication services is running. This feature is being misused to commit cyber-frauds especially from outside the country,” a statement read.
To curb this menace, many govt agencies had been asking for SIM binding to be made mandatory. Subsequently, DoT issued directions to major app-based communication services, under the Telecom Cyber Security (TCS) Rules, 2024. These include WhatsApp, Telegram, Snapchat, Arattai, Sharechat, Jiochat and Signal.
Now, app-based communication providers will have to ensure that their service is “continuously linked to the SIM card (associated with mobile number used for identification of customers/users or for provisioning or delivery of services) installed in the device, making it impossible to use the app without that specific, active SIM.” And also ensure that “web service instance of the mobile app, if provided, shall be logged out periodically (not later than six hours) and allowing the facility to the user to re-link the device using QR code.”

The ministry has proposed waiving fees for specified DL services, including changes to address, name and contact number, if applicants avail themselves of these services through online Aadhaar authentication.
Govt plans colour-coded DLs for Indians, foreigners
At present, if an applicant cannot produce any of the 12 listed documents, the licencing authority “may accept an affidavit sworn before an executive magistrate, judicial magistrate or notary public as proof of age and address”.
Anil Chhikara, an expert in motor vehicle licencing, said, “The use of simple affidavits is being phased out after miscreants used them to register false addresses and dates of birth. Applicants must now provide verifiable documents.”Under the draft, the ministry has listed separate sets of documents for proof of address, age and identity. Address proofs include Aadhaar card, Electoral Photo Identity Card, e-ration card, electricity or gas bills for the preceding three months, and proof of legal presence for foreign nationals. Acceptable age proofs include passports, school board mark sheets, birth certificates and identity cards issued by govt departments. Aadhaar, passports, e-ration cards and PAN have been listed as acceptable identity proofs.The proposed changes aim to curb the submission of false documents, tighten assessment requirements and make licence-related services more accessible. They also seek to streamline online DL services and set timelines for processing applications to change licence particulars.
Under the proposal, the safe-driving tutorial would have to last at least 30 minutes, while the higher qualifying score of 75% is intended to make the assessment more stringent. Licencing authorities would have to approve or reject online applications to change DL particulars, including name and address, within 15 days, giving reasons for rejection.An application for a change of address that remains undecided for 30 days would be deemed approved. The draft also proposes a consolidated application form for services such as DL renewal, issuance of duplicate licences, addition of a vehicle class and changes to personal particulars. Specified applicant details would be retrieved electronically from the Sarathi portal wherever available.

Why measles outbreak in Pennsylvania poses risks beyond US borders
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
21:02:30 UTC
06:02:30 KST

Why a measles outbreak in Pennsylvania poses risks beyond US borders
The United States is facing its largest outbreak of measles since the virus was declared eliminated in 2000.
More than two decades after measles was declared eliminated in the United States, the country is experiencing its deadliest resurgence of the virus since 2000, with the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) announcing the third measles death of the year this week.
Matt Ferrari, director of Pennsylvania State University’s Center for Infectious Disease Dynamics, said the US was so successful at wiping out measles that it had “the luxury to forget” it was a serious problem.
“It’s been a long time, and for many of us in the United States, and in fact, throughout the Western Hemisphere, we have been able to forget how nasty measles is,” Ferrari told Al Jazeera.
Pennsylvania has been hit especially hard in the most recent outbreak. In September, the state sought emergency support from the CDC to control the spread, even as state and federal health officials quarrelled over the measles-associated death tally — differing over how deaths should be classified. State officials have recorded more than 1,200 cases and over 240 hospitalisations in 42 counties so far this year.
This spike in cases has raised concerns in neighbouring US states. On October 5, New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state disaster emergency in response to rising cases in rural areas, expanding the number of health professionals authorised to vaccinate and test people for measles.
“No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease,” Hochul said.
But experts warn that the risks extend far beyond US state borders. The US resurgence comes as measles cases increase globally, particularly in communities that are vaccine-sceptical or where there are gaps in healthcare access.
Vaccination coverage among US kindergartners has decreased from 95.2 percent during the 2019-2020 school year to 92.4 percent in the 2025-2026 school year. Experts warn that declining vaccination rates in one geographic location can leave people thousands of miles away vulnerable, making measles prevention a shared global responsibility.
Building trust in vaccine-sceptical communities
Pennsylvania reported in August that two unvaccinated people died of measles in Lancaster County, which is located in the South Central part of the state. Lancaster is considered the centre of Pennsylvania Dutch Country and home to the nation’s oldest Amish and Mennonite communities, both of which have under-vaccinated populations.
In Pennsylvania, public health officials have worked with community leaders to share information and expand access to vaccination. Joshua Good, principal of Ephrata Mennonite School in Lancaster County, where two students contracted measles earlier this year, worked with state officials to organise a pop-up vaccination clinic at the school.
He said officials also provided communication materials that the school adapted for its community and helped identify at-risk families.
While Good said the response was productive, he told state officials that the Mennonite community still holds a lot of vaccine scepticism.
“I said, look, if we do this, keep in mind, our community by and large…made that decision not because they don’t have access to the vaccines. They made the decision based on their own best judgement,” he told Al Jazeera.
Good, who is vaccinated and vaccinated his children, sees himself as an advocate within the community. If families have questions about measles shots, he will answer them as best he can.
“I have honest conversations with people, try to engage in respectful, charitable ways,” he said. “I’ll try to understand what their hesitancies are. That said, I respect their concerns.”
Although multiple community members received the measles vaccine at the Ephrata clinic, vaccination rates remain below the threshold for herd immunity.
Public health officials advocate for investing in robust community outreach before outbreaks happen.
“You can’t just show up in a community in an emergency– an emergency in which they might feel like you’re there to kind of blame them or shame them,” Jennifer Nuzzo, director of the Pandemic Center at the Brown University School of Public Health, told Al Jazeera. “You need to know them so that they see public health as a resource rather than law enforcement.”
She said low vaccination coverage and distrust of the government allow measles to spread even when vaccines are available. But that shouldn’t stop governments from building rapport with vaccine-sceptical communities.
“I worry that by framing it around their demographics, it lets governments off the hook in terms of what they’re supposed to be doing, which is stopping the spread of this dangerous disease,” Nuzzo said.
Experts explain that declining vaccination rates put not only these communities but also immunocompromised people at greater risk for disease. Herd immunity in the wider population formerly helped shield those most vulnerable to infection.
“Those are communities that have been at risk for years,” Ferrari said. “But higher rates of vaccination in the communities surrounding them offered a barrier.”
A shared global risk
The continental Americas was the first World Health Organization (WHO) region to eliminate endemic measles transmission in 2016. Maintaining that status requires high and consistent vaccination coverage. The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) says coverage across the region remains below the target for both doses of the measles vaccine, contributing to noticeable consequences.
PAHO holds an annual RVC Measles Elimination Status Conference where an independent technical body of international experts monitors and reviews whether countries in the Americas have successfully eliminated measles, rubella, and congenital rubella syndrome. A country can lose its “elimination status” when the same measles virus genotype has circulated continuously for at least 12 months.
Last year, Canada became the first country in the continental Americas to lose its status after an outbreak that began in 2024. Some have warned that the US may be on track to lose its status this year.
But Dr Daniel Salas, executive manager of the Special Program for Comprehensive Immunisation at PAHO, told Al Jazeera that it’s not just the US that will be under review.
“We have Mexico, we have Bolivia that is going to be closely assessed because they could potentially lose status as well,” he said.
US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr has repeatedly defended the US response to measles.
“We’re doing a better job than any country in the world at controlling the measles outbreak,” Kennedy said at an August 26 event in Florida. He cited higher case numbers in Mexico, Canada and Britain.
But Nuzzo said the repeated outbreaks across the US point to a country struggling to contain transmission.
“We have not seen it this bad,” she said. “It’s like this perpetual game of Whac-A-Mole. As long as there are vulnerable communities, as long as we don’t have strategies for early detection and rapid response and containment, measles will just keep on happening over and over and over again.”
Dr Salas told Al Jazeera that action within the first three days after a suspected case is critical, and health authorities should begin investigating and taking response measures without waiting for laboratory confirmation. Delays of a week or more can allow the highly contagious virus, marked by fever, coughing, and a whole-body rash, to spread further.
Experts warn that outbreaks cannot be treated as isolated local events. Scientific journals have found evidence that the virus strain in Canada’s latest measles outbreak was genetically linked to cases reported in US Mennonite communities. This was the same outbreak that resulted in Canada losing its measles elimination status.
“The spread of measles in the United States imperils other countries,” said Nuzzo. “It’s easy to kind of point to other countries and say that they’re the problem, but the reality is we’re all dependent on each other, and it’s very hard to protect ourselves when measles is spreading elsewhere.”

El Niño rains batter Latin America from Mexico to Chile
CIUDAD DEL ESTE, Paraguay, Oct 22 - An intensifying El Niño-linked storm season this week brought flooding to Paraguay, killed two farm workers in Argentina's cattle belt and damaged coastal communities in Peru and Mexico.
Part of a luxury condominium complex on Mexico’s Pacific coast in the tourist town of San Pancho in Nayarit State collapsed on Wednesday after pounding surf ate away the sand beneath it, exposing its foundation and leaving the structure tilted dramatically toward the sea.
In Paraguay, two dozen families took refuge late on Wednesday at a church near Paraguay's border with Brazil after their homes flooded and more residents anxiously watched the swelling Parana, South America's second-largest river, as rains battered the region.
UN officials warned this week that the El Niño weather pattern could drive a record increase in Pacific Ocean temperatures as it moves around the globe like a "wrecking ball," triggering floods in some regions and droughts in others.
In Paraguay, the rising Parana River, a key commercial waterway, has affected about 4,200 families, according to the country's national emergency agency.
A 58-year-old woman died after her home collapsed in the rains.
At the church now doubling as a shelter, in Paraguay's Ciudad del Este, dozens of residents pitched tents on a soccer field while others organized communal kitchens with support from the church and local businesses.
In San Rafael, a riverside town, Antonina Sánchez, 65, recounted how she had to flee.
"I was surprised because the water came very quickly. My house, my entire kitchen collapsed; it's caving in," she said.
The World Meteorological Organization has predicted temperatures in the central Pacific will rise about 3.8 degrees Celsius above average between November and January, peaking around December, causing one of the most turbulent storm seasons on record.
RAIN, HAIL, MUD AND EROSION
Elsewhere in Latin America this week, two farm workers died near Bella Vista in Argentina's Corrientes province while moving cattle away from flooded areas near the Parana, local media reported.
Hundreds of residents have been evacuated across the province, though above-average rainfall in parts of the Pampas agricultural belt could benefit crops.
In Chile's capital Santiago, a flooded stream triggered a mudslide on October 8 onto city streets, and days later, a storm blanketed roads with hail and flooded streets.
In Peru, authorities on Thursday announced financial aid and tax relief for businesses affected by extreme weather battering the country's Pacific coast. The government plans to allocate 18 billion soles ($5.22 billion) in 2027 towards mitigating the economic impact. REUTERS

At least 16 people killed by powerful 7.0 magnitude earthquake in Tibet, officials say
More than a dozen people were killed and hundreds of homes destroyed when a magnitude 7.0 earthquake hit China's Tibet region on Thursday evening local time, according to local officials.
The United States Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10:33 p.m. local time, with its epicenter 119 miles east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet.
At least 16 people were killed and 54 people were injured in the earthquake, Chinese state media said.
Search and rescue efforts continued following the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials. Among the injured, 11 people were in serious condition and the other 35 sustained minor injuries, the media office said.
More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units, around 3,000 tents and folding beds, as well as flashlights and winter clothing arrived in the region.
It was the biggest earthquake in the region in the last five years, China's national broadcaster CCTV said.
Nagqu is more than 186 miles north of Tibet's capital, Lhasa.
The USGS put the earthquake's depth at 11 miles. Xinhua, citing the China Earthquake Networks Center, put the depth at 6.2 miles.
The earthquake comes less than two months after a border region of Nepal and Tibet was struck by devastating flash flooding that left hundreds of people dead and destroyed several communities. Authorities said the flooding was caused by the collapse of a glacier.

'Bad actors producing fabricated data' — Fake pollsters hit US midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
21:00:51 UTC
06:00:51 KST

A self-described US polling firm whose data was tracked by political campaigns and mainstream media has admitted that its polls were fabricated, in the second such scandal to stir controversy ahead of the midterm elections.
The case involving the firm Wedgewood Polls threatens to erode trust in independent pollsters in an already hyperpolarised political climate, particularly as political pundits voice concern that fast-evolving AI tools are making it easier to fabricate results.
The case came to light earlier this week after polling aggregator FiftyPlusOne contacted Wedgewood as part of an investigation into the firm's surveys.
Wedgewood responded with a statement on X admitting that "most" of its data had been made up.
It said the firm had been experimenting on how easy it could be for "an entirely fabricated polling firm to gain traction" and "be taken seriously."
It turns out that Wedgewood, whose X account has since been taken down, was indeed taken seriously.
Michigan Senate candidate Mallory McMorrow said after the group's "poll" in late June showed her support in the single digits, she said "donations dried up," volunteers were "devastated," and the media "hounded" her "with calls to drop out."
"It killed us," McMorrow wrote on X.
The bogus data, which covered high-profile races across several states, were also highlighted by major polling aggregators and news outlets, including The New York Times.
In an editors' note, The Times said its poll tracker database included 15 surveys released by Wedgewood between June and October, all of which have now been removed.
'Undermines trust'
Brendan Carr, chairman of the Federal Communications Commission, said there has been "a significant surge in entirely fake polls and suppression polls" designed to interfere with the electoral process.
He urged the media not to amplify such hoaxes and engage in "news distortions."
In August, another phony group called Median Strategies admitted to fabricating poll results, saying it was "created as a short term social experiment," according to the Los Angeles Times.
On Thursday, in a blog titled "more pollster funny business," FiftyPlusOne said it will no longer collect polling data by another firm called SoCal Strategies, after an investigation that cast doubt on its authenticity.
The firm could not be reached for comment. SoCal Strategies's website, X account, and Substack page appeared to have been taken offline.
The revelations comes amid warnings that AI-powered tools were enabling the fakery.
"It's getting easier to conduct low-quality polls — or fake them altogether," FiftyPlusOne said.
Sophisticated AI tools were also making it difficult to identify phony pollsters and made-up data, the American Association for Public Opinion Research said in a statement.
"We are once again experiencing bad actors producing and distributing fabricated data and organisational information that undermines trust in public opinion and election polling," said the association's president, Mary Losch.
"It is important that we don't conflate fraudulent activity like this with legitimate election polling."

Judge limits election-related immigration stops amid broader legal war ahead of midterms
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
21:00:40 UTC

Judge limits election-related immigration stops amid broader legal war ahead of midterms
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- An array of election-related lawsuits between the Trump administration and California officials, groups and individuals are being litigated.
- Trump administration officials say they are working to ensure noncitizens don’t illegally dilute the legitimate votes of U.S. citizens.
- State officials and election experts say the administration is putting forward baseless legal arguments to stir up confusion.
A sweeping campaign by federal immigration agents to identify voter fraud by noncitizens through door knocks, street stops and other field interviews in California and eight other states must be reined in ahead of the Nov. 3 election, after a federal judge in Northern California ruled it has intimidated U.S. citizens and interfered with the work of voting rights groups.
Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguin said in a ruling Wednesday that limiting the Department of Homeland Security’s surging operations in those states — which she wrote “sweep in U.S. citizens for investigation” — does not prevent the Trump administration from “exercising their authority to investigate voter fraud by lawful means.”
A Homeland Security spokesperson said the agency is “laser focused on identifying, prosecuting, and removing aliens who vote,” and has “no plans to question or investigate people we believe to be U.S. citizens.”
The ruling was the latest to come out of an unprecedented legal war playing out between the Trump administration and California in recent days, in which an array of election cases are working their way through the federal courts at breakneck speed.
There is, for example, the lawsuit the U.S. Justice Department filed against California and state and local elections officials last week, demanding that they set aside any ballots from a list of 20,000 individuals identified by immigration officials as “likely noncitizens.”
A California immigrant and a Nevada group, joined by top Democrats, sue over federal election probes
The lawsuit accuses Trump and his administration of using “shoddily compiled lists of supposed noncitizens” and “coercive threats” against state officials to assert federal control over the midterms.
There are also two cases out of Washington, D.C., in which a coalition of Democratic leaders, immigrant rights groups, voting rights experts and naturalized citizens in California are challenging the Trump administration’s use of Homeland Security data to target voters.
The litigation is playing out amid an intense political debate about election security at the national level — driven in part by President Trump, a longtime election denier — and a sweeping campaign by his administration to root out and parade examples of alleged voter fraud in the final days before the election.
White House, Homeland Security and Justice Department officials have all defended the administration’s efforts as necessary to ensure that noncitizens are not illegally diluting the votes of U.S. citizens. First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli, the lead federal prosecutor in Los Angeles, has claimed to have “overwhelming evidence” that tens of thousands of noncitizens are doing so in California.
‘That is not normal’
Democratic leaders and prominent elections experts, meanwhile, have cast the administration’s claims as baseless and intentionally exaggerated to stoke uncertainty about election security and ultimately challenge midterm results the president doesn’t like, and the Justice Department’s legal arguments as fundamentally flawed and wildly out of line with long-established department policy to stay out of elections in the lead up to voting.
“That is not normal. We have literally never experienced that in American history. Not once,” said David Becker, executive director of the nonpartisan Center for Election Innovation & Research and a former Justice Department elections attorney. “The fact that the administration appears poised for the first time to act as an adversary to the states and counties who have [the] undisputed constitutional authority to run elections? That is unusual.”
At the same time, Becker and other experts stressed that those efforts to date have failed, and state and local elections have largely proceeded in recent weeks without incident, with millions of Americans having already cast their ballots.
“California voters need to know that they’re in good hands, that we have leaders at the state and local levels who are protecting our ballots and are ensuring that these attempts by the federal government to root out supposed noncitizen voting are not going to prevent Californians from casting our ballots,” said Kim Alexander, president of the California Voter Foundation. “Part of the strategy here is to distract people and scare people and raise fears, and the important thing is to continue to stay focused on ... making a plan to vote.”
Status of cases
Federal courts have already rejected multiple Trump executive orders seeking to enforce nationwide voter ID and citizenship requirements. The Supreme Court blocked an administration plan for the U.S. Postal Service to vet mail ballots. The Justice Department has compiled a stunning record of losses in its 30 lawsuits demanding state voter rolls — with 26 of those cases, including the one in California, so far dismissed.
And election experts said they expect the Trump administration to rack up more losses in coming days — including in the Justice Department’s case challenging California officials’ refusal to segregate the ballots of some 20,000 voters based on the administration’s unsubstantiated claims they are noncitizens.
That case was taken up — and scheduled for a Tuesday hearing — by Judge David O. Carter, an appointee of President Clinton who in January rejected the administration’s demand for California’s voter rolls, calling it a clear federal overreach that would have a “chilling effect” on voters and threaten American democracy.
California has called for the case to be dismissed outright, on the grounds that the administration has zero authority to make such demands, and that the demands are unlawful. The Trump administration had asked Carter to immediately rule in the matter — then, when he didn’t immediately respond, filed notice late Thursday that it was appealing the matter straight to the U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals, arguing that Carter’s “silence is a constructive denial” of its emergency request, given its “critical and exigent nature.”
Several green card holders arrested in a Trump administration crackdown on alleged California voter fraud appeared in court Monday, with some saying they had no recollection of ever registering to cast ballots.
In D.C. federal court, Judge James E. Boasberg set an Oct. 30 hearing in a case in which UCLA Voting Rights Project attorneys, the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights, or CHIRLA, and a California voter named Pedro Trujillo are challenging the administration’s use of unproven federal databases to allege California voters aren’t citizens.
Carl Bergquist, an attorney for CHIRLA, said he looked forward to bringing a host of recent Trump administration actions to the court’s attention — including the administration’s lawsuit against California, the charging this week of 28 legal permanent residents in California with election-related crimes, and Trump’s threats to arrest California elections officials who don’t comply with his administration’s demands.
“The events of the last few days, from threats to state and local officials, increased general immigration operations, the random knocking on doors by federal agents and the recent arrests are causing a chill in the community,” Bergquist said. “People, including naturalized citizens, are making their plans to vote and the Federal Government is doing its utmost to quash their attempts to exercise this fundamental right that they have lawfully acquired.”
The argument that naturalized citizens are being intimidated also features prominently in a second lawsuit filed in D.C. federal court Tuesday, in which top Democrats in Congress joined Nevada party officials and a California immigrant named Erick Jose Jimenez to challenge the Trump administration’s unprecedented voter fraud probes.
That lawsuit, also assigned to Boasberg, says Jimenez, a naturalized citizen since 2006, fears being “unlawfully targeted for voting and disenfranchised (or worse).”
Justin Levitt, a Loyola Law School professor who studies elections and was a senior policy advisor on democracy and voting rights in the Biden White House, said there is “so much noise” around the election right now, in part because the administration has been making wild legal arguments about its authority over elections.
But he said “none of the federal government’s attempts to assert power that they do not have are working,” and voting “for 99.999% of the public” will remain “wonderfully normal.”

Calley Means, one of the key figures in the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement, said on Thursday that he was stepping down from his role as a senior health adviser in the Trump Administration.
In a post on X, Means said that he was resigning “with tremendous respect” for President Donald Trump and Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
“They laid out a vision of combatting the entrenched, dark forces in DC that profit from Americans getting sick,” Means said. “More policy and cultural change has happened around these goals in the past 2 years than any time in history—and I know this movement is just getting started.”
News outlets including the New York Times and POLITICO, citing anonymous sources with knowledge of the situation, have reported that Means was becoming increasingly frustrated because he felt that there was little movement on issues central to the MAHA agenda—for instance, on the issue of defining and regulating ultraprocessed foods.
Means, who was pivotal in coordinating an alliance between Kennedy and Trump during the 2024 election cycle, has championed the Administration's food-policy agenda, including efforts to persuade manufacturers to stop using artificial food dyes in their products and to restrict the purchase of soda with Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) benefits in some states.
In his social media post, Means heralded those actions, as well as his efforts to reform dietary guidelines and his push for research into psychedelic medications.
“It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration,” Means said.
Means is the latest figure in the Trump Administration, and specifically in the Department of Health and Human Services, to resign or be ousted from their role over the past year. In May, Dr. Marty Makary stepped down as the head of the Food and Drug Administration amid pressure from within and outside of the Trump Administration. Last year, the White House fired Susan Monarez as director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
In April, Trump withdrew his nomination of MAHA leader Dr. Casey Means—Calley Means’ sister—for the position of U.S. Surgeon General after the nomination failed to garner enough support in the Senate.

Centre flags data gap, regulatory hurdles in curbing hospital mark-ups
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:58:17 UTC
05:58:17 KST

The Union govt has told the SC in its affidavit that margins on hospital consumables can range from 100% to 1,000% or more.
NEW DELHI: Amid SC’s scrutiny of hospitals charging patients steep mark-ups on medicines and consumables, govt officials have flagged gaps in data and regulatory hurdles in extending price controls to hospital supplies, saying the Centre first needs to establish the extent of margins before considering intervention.The Union govt has told the SC in its affidavit that margins on hospital consumables can range from 100% to 1,000% or more, highlighting concerns over the high mark-ups patients often face on supplies used during treatment. However, a senior official told TOI that the govt does not have the data needed to assess margins across hospital supplies and determine whether wider controls are warranted.“We first need to get the data and then examine whether there is a margin and a need to control it,” another senior official said, explaining that the purchase price of medicines and consumables would need to be compared with what hospitals charge patients before deciding on any intervention.Centre fixes ceiling prices for scheduled medicines and has limited annual price increases for non-scheduled drugs up to 10%. It has decided to cap trade margins on certain anti-cancer medicines at 30% of MRP. Extending similar controls to other medicines and hospital consumables, officials said, would require analysis and consultation.A health ministry official, however, raised doubts about how far the govt could regulate hospital billing, saying hospitals, with health being a state subject and governed by the Clinical Establishments Act or other laws enacted by state govts..
The Centre’s role, the official said, is largely confined to drug-price regulation through the National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority.
Regulating individual components of hospital bills would be difficult, the official said, pointing out that hospitals charge package rates without providing detailed itemised bills. Restricting charges on consumables could lead profitconscious hospitals to raise other fees, including surgeons’ charges, the official argued.
The official also disputed the blanket use of the term “overcharging” when hospitals bill patients at the MRP, saying there is no general legal requirement to offer discounts below the printed price. They cited delayed reimbursements from insurance firms and govt health schemes as financial pressures on hospitals that would need to be factored in while deciding any broader intervention.

Don’t blindly follow foreign custody order: Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:51:51 UTC
05:51:51 KST

As cases of estranged NRI couples fighting for child custody increasingly result in cross-border litigation, with one spouse getting a favourable order from a foreign court while the other moves an Indian court, Supreme Court has said courts here must make an independent assessment of what is good for the child and the ruling of the foreign court should not be automatically followed, though it must be accorded proper consideration.A bench of Justices J B Pardiwala and K V Viswanathan said cases already dealt with by foreign courts were coming before it time and again and their adjudication was not easy as they involved deeply emotional and sensitive issues. It added that the welfare of the child “must be understood in the widest sense, not by money or physical comfort alone”.“This position rests on two foundations. The first is that once the court is seized of the matter, it exercises its parens patriae jurisdiction. That jurisdiction obliges it to consider and assess the matter for itself, through the lens of the child’s welfare. The second is that the decision in such cases turns not on the legal rights of the parties but on the welfare of the child. The same emphasis on welfare over legal entitlement runs through our statutes on custody and guardianship. They make clear that a person otherwise entitled to custody or guardianship need not be granted it if that would not be for the welfare of the child.
There is thus no ambiguity in the fact that an order of a foreign court must yield to the welfare of the child,” the bench said.“Put differently, a court in this country, when exercising its jurisdiction, cannot blindly follow the order of a foreign court and act merely as an executing court,” the apex court bench said.SC said a parent’s disobedience of a foreign court order did not, by itself, require the Indian court to give automatic effect to that order and also that the paramountcy of the child’s welfare did not mean that the order of the foreign court had to be disregarded. “In deciding what the welfare of the child requires, the court must form its own independent judgement. In doing so, however, it must give proper weight to the order of the foreign court,” the bench said.SC passed the order while directing that a seven-year-old girl, a US citizen, who was brought to India by her mother in breach of a California custody order, return to US.
A California court had in 2022 granted the couple joint custody of the child and specifically barred her removal from California without written consent or a court order. In violation of the ruling, the mother left for India with the child after two weeks, leading to the father starting legal proceedings against her in India.SC allowed the petition of the father, who approached the court through advocate Prabhjit Jauhar, against a Karnataka HC order dismissing his plea. After hearing both sides, it said the welfare of the child lay in her continuing to reside in US.
