How Meta struck a deal to keep Mark Zuckerberg in California despite looming billionaire tax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:44:41 UTC
05:44:41 KST

How Meta struck a deal to keep Mark Zuckerberg in California despite looming billionaire tax
- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- Meta created a new class of nonvoting stock after Mark Zuckerberg threatened to leave California over a proposed one-time 5% tax on billionaires’ assets.
- The deal lets Zuckerberg sell or transfer shares without losing his voting majority, preserving his control of Meta even if the measure passes.
- Proposition 40 could raise $100 billion for healthcare, supporters say, and Zuckerberg’s potential tax bill could reach roughly $12 billion.
Meta’s Chief Executive Mark Zuckerberg has wielded enormous power over the social media empire he built more than two decades ago, leading the California juggernaut through major scandals, scrutiny and technological shifts.
But the 42-year-old tech mogul considered leaving the state because he feared that a ballot measure to impose a one-time 5% tax on the assets of California billionaires could reduce the amount of control he has over Meta, a recent regulatory filing shows. Meta’s board struck a deal so he would stay in California. Meta is the parent company of Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp.
The filing highlights how one of the world’s wealthiest people, whose net worth totals more than $200 billion, is bracing for the possibility that California voters pass Proposition 40, a wealth tax proposal that would primarily be used to fund healthcare.
Although supporters say the fear that billionaires will flee the state are overblown, the ultrawealthy have made moves to potentially avoid paying the tax or are funding campaigns to defeat it.
Prop 40, which would tax the assets of California billionaires to mostly fund healthcare, has divided Democratic politicians, labor unions and other groups.
Zuckerberg’s influence over Meta is partly tied to how the company structures its stock. Zuckerberg holds roughly 60% of voting power over Meta even though he only owns about 13% of the company’s total shares.
Meta has a dual-class share structure, dividing the stock into Class A shares with one vote each and Class B shares with 10 votes each. Zuckerberg holds a large amount of Class B stock, which gives him majority control over company decisions.
If the wealth tax proposal passes, Zuckerberg is worried that it could reduce his voting power, according to the filing. The tech executive makes an annual salary of $1, so most of his wealth is linked to his stake in Meta. If he had to sell his Class B shares to pay the tax, that would reduce his voting majority in the company, according to the filing.
In September, he told Meta’s board that he planned to list his Palo Alto home for sale, pressuring board members to find a solution.
On Wednesday, Meta announced a new class of stock with no voting rights called Class C that would take effect in January. As part of the deal, Zuckerberg could sell or transfer up to 20% of Class C stock so his voting majority doesn’t decrease even if he has to pay the tax.
“Mr. Zuckerberg’s continued leadership role in our Company, and his continuing presence at the Company’s headquarters in California, is critical at this current inflection point for the Company and the tech industry in order to continue to provide value-maximization for all shareholders,” the filing said.
Since the company’s public debut, its share price has risen more than 1,700%, outperforming the S&P 500.
In Meta’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday, Chief Financial Officer Susan Li said creating a new class of nonvoting stock benefits the company in various ways, including “capital raising, employee compensation, acquisitions, other general corporate purposes.”
“We believe this share class will maintain our founder-led structure. It will expand our funding tools and give us flexibility to invest behind the unprecedented momentum we’re seeing across every part of our business driven by AI,” she said.
Meta has roughly 66,700 workers globally. Its sprawling headquarters is in Menlo Park.
Some billionaires such as Anduril co-founder Palmer Luckey, Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen and Google co-founder Sergey Brin have opposed the wealth tax proposal. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, on the other hand, has said he doesn’t mind paying more taxes.
The Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West is backing the wealth tax proposal and says it applies to roughly 200 billionaires who have resided in California as of January 1, 2026, and could raise $100 billion.
More than $300 million has been contributed to fight the billionaire tax, including two propositions that could block it if they gather more votes. Although stock prices fluctuate, Zuckerberg could face a tax liability of roughly $12 billion based on his net worth.
In 2015, Zuckerberg and his wife, Dr. Priscilla Chan, pledged to give away 99% of his Facebook shares over their lifetimes when they celebrated the birth of their first daughter.
The couple created the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, a philanthropic organization whose efforts include curing, managing and preventing all diseases. Although Zuckerberg lives in Palo Alto, he also owns real estate elsewhere, including in Hawaii, Washington, D.C. and Ireland.
Times data journalist Gabrielle LaMarr LeMee contributed to this report.

Ahmad Tibi outlines plan to oust Netanyahu after elections if neither bloc forms majority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:40:06 UTC
05:40:06 KST

Joint List faction chairman MK Ahmad Tibi presented a two-stage plan on Sunday evening to prevent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from remaining in power after the upcoming elections, proposing to support an alternative government from outside the coalition in exchange for commitments addressing the needs of Arab society.
In a statement to the media, Tibi outlined what he described as practical steps to remove the Netanyahu government and prevent the prime minister from continuing in office as head of a caretaker government if neither political bloc secures a majority.
The plan would allow the Joint List to provide a parliamentary safety net for an alternative government without joining the coalition or abandoning its political positions. Tibi also pledged to seek the removal of Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana during the first days of the next Knesset.
"I am a doctor," Tibi began with an analogy. "If you come to my clinic and I tell you that your illness is serious, that I cannot treat it, and only explain it to you very well, what would you do? It is the same in politics. It is not enough to talk and explain. We are not a news agency. We must offer solutions to change reality."
Tibi addressed the refusal of several opposition leaders, including Avigdor Liberman, Gadi Eisenkot, and Naftali Bennett, to include Arab parties in a governing coalition, arguing that their positions strengthened the Joint List's strategy of supporting a government from outside.
Liberman recently ruled out supporting a minority government, including one formed as a temporary arrangement, while insisting that any future coalition consist exclusively of Zionist parties.
Referring to recent polls, Tibi claimed that Netanyahu's right-wing bloc would win 54 seats, while the opposition would secure 51 to 52 seats, leaving neither with the 61 seats needed for a Knesset majority.
"This change is strategic and strengthens the Joint List's position as a decisive force in the elections," he said.
Tibi says Netanyahu's strategy is to prevent opposition from forming government
Tibi argued that Netanyahu understood he would be unable to form another government and would therefore seek to prevent the opposition from establishing one, allowing him to remain caretaker prime minister.
"Month after month, he will remain in his seat, Ben-Gvir will remain a minister, and Smotrich will remain a minister. We are capable of preventing this. We will not allow Netanyahu to be caretaker prime minister."
"The first step is to bring down this government, and the second step is to clear the way for an alternative, less bad government that will have to listen to our demands," Tibi said.
The proposal comes amid polling that has left both major political blocs short of a majority, potentially placing Arab parties in a position to influence the formation of the next government.
Tibi demands action on crime, home demolitions, Arab communities
Tibi said the Joint List would demand concrete commitments on issues affecting Arab citizens in exchange for parliamentary support.
Among his demands were a comprehensive plan to combat crime and violence in Arab society, a halt to home demolitions, particularly in the Negev, and the repeal of the Kaminitz Law, which strengthened enforcement against illegal construction.
He also called for action on eviction orders affecting communities in the Triangle region, including Tayibe, Tira, and Qalansawe, alongside the approval of master plans for Arab localities.
Tibi highlighted employment difficulties among Arab professionals, citing approximately 8,000 unemployed teachers and 4,000 doctors who, according to him, were either unemployed or unable to secure medical residencies.
Crime in Arab communities has become a central issue in the election campaign. The Israel Police announced a major crackdown in February, reporting the seizure of approximately 200 illegal weapons and the arrest of more than 200 suspects as part of an operation targeting criminal organizations.
Alongside these civilian demands, Tibi emphasized that the Joint List would continue advocating for a political horizon for the Palestinian people, even if it supported a government whose political positions it opposed.
"We know that the next government will not be a peace government, and we will not agree with its basic political guidelines. But we are choosing between the bad and the worse. We will find common ground that serves our society and the issues important to it, without giving up our fundamental principles."
He stressed that providing a parliamentary safety net would not obligate the Joint List to support every policy advanced by an alternative government.
According to Tibi, the party would not be required to vote in favor of settlements, accept the Nation-State Law, or remain silent over what he described as "genocide and expulsion," visits to the al-Aqsa Mosque compound, the Citizenship Law, or cuts to Arab local authorities' budgets.
Joint List plans to remove Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana
Tibi's most immediate proposal concerned Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, whom he pledged to remove before a new government is formed.
"This time, we will not wait for a new government to be formed before we begin making changes," he declared.
Repeating a commitment made at the Joint List's recent campaign launch in Tel Aviv, Tibi said the party would cooperate with the opposition to replace Ohana.
"In the first days of the next Knesset, we will remove Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, who has turned the Knesset into a Kahanist and racist arena against all of us. The Joint List will vote with the opposition's candidate, and there will be a majority to remove him."
Tibi said the Joint List would also seek to use the proposed parliamentary majority to advance legislation benefiting Arab society, including a law preventing an individual facing criminal charges from forming a government, a measure aimed at Netanyahu.
He added that the party would demand representation on the Knesset Finance Committee before a new coalition is established.
The revived Joint List brings together Hadash, Ta'al, and Balad, following negotiations aimed at consolidating Arab political representation ahead of the elections.
"Anyone who wants a safety net from us must first guarantee a safety net for you, for our society," Tibi concluded.
"In the 1990s, there was a blocking bloc. Today, the Joint List is offering a safety net in exchange for commitments. Anyone who wants our votes knows the way. A vote for the Joint List is the vote that will decide the elections."

From preseason disaster to title contender: How Barak Bachar turned Maccabi Haifa around
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:40:01 UTC
05:40:01 KST

Back in July, Maccabi Haifa’s preseason looked like a warning sign of another difficult campaign ahead. A Toto Cup derby against city rival Hapoel Haifa exposed shortcomings in almost every facet of the Greens’ game. In attack, defense and transition, Barak Bachar’s team appeared a step behind its opponents, with the two sides looking worlds apart.
The criticism came quickly. Fans and media questioned Bachar’s approach and wondered whether his revamped squad would look much like the disappointing team that had struggled the previous season. A 3-2 derby defeat was followed by an even more damaging 3-0 thrashing at the hands of Ironi Kiryat Shmona, sending alarm bells ringing throughout the club.
A 1-0 loss to Hapoel Jerusalem in a Toto Cup placement match brought the preseason campaign to a close, leaving little reason for optimism. When the league season began, Haifa hardly offered an immediate response, scraping past newly promoted Hapoel Ramat Gan before suffering a heavy defeat to Maccabi Tel Aviv.
Yet the picture has changed dramatically in the weeks since.
The Greens have put together a run of victories that has transformed the mood around the club, highlighted by an impressive 4-2 win over Hapoel Jerusalem and a comeback 2-1 triumph over newly promoted Maccabi Petah Tikva at the Moshava Stadium last week. The results have propelled Haifa into the thick of the championship race, with the team sitting second in the table, just one point behind Maccabi Tel Aviv.
Hapoel Beersheba awaits in a couple of weeks, offering Bachar’s men another significant test, but the early-season concerns have given way to renewed belief. Whatever the outcome of that showdown, one thing is already clear: This is a very different Maccabi Haifa from the side that looked so disjointed just a few months ago.
So, what changed?
Patience and performance
The answer lies partly in patience. With numerous new arrivals, including several foreign players, Haifa needed time to develop chemistry, establish an identity, and turn a collection of talented individuals into a cohesive unit. The early results suggested that process would be more difficult than anticipated, but the pieces are gradually falling into place.
“Winning is always enjoyable,” Bachar said. “When the performance is good, it’s even better. We brought some of the pressure on ourselves with our poor results. We knew things could change if we worked quietly and ignored the pressure around us. We did that gradually, and now we’re looking better.
“We’re still not drawing conclusions, just as we didn’t after the Toto Cup, because we’ve played only six matches.”
While Bachar has been careful not to get carried away, several of his attacking players have given the Greens plenty of reason for optimism. Three, in particular, have helped transform the team’s fortunes.
Bruninho made an immediate impression upon arriving in Haifa, bringing creativity, technical ability and an eye for goal to the attacking midfield. The Brazilian has quickly become a central figure in the Greens’ offensive play, contributing directly to the majority of their goals through his own finishing and his ability to create opportunities for teammates.
His three goals and five assists tell only part of the story. Bruninho has also played a role in several scoring moves that do not appear on the stat sheet, giving Haifa a creative presence capable of unlocking defenses and connecting its attacking pieces.
The arrival of Portuguese winger Pedro Brazao in September has added another dimension. In just four appearances, Brazao has recorded two goals and two assists, providing the kind of pace, flair and individual quality that can change a match in an instant.
His recent performance against Hapoel Jerusalem offered a glimpse of his potential. Brazao weaved past defenders, rounded the goalkeeper and calmly finished with the outside of his foot, producing a spectacular solo effort that could contend for goal of the season.
It was the sort of moment Haifa had been missing during its difficult opening weeks: an individual act of brilliance that not only settled a game but also demonstrated the attacking talent at Bachar’s disposal.
Then there is Andrija Novakovich, whose contribution has given the Greens a focal point they have lacked in recent seasons.
The 30-year-old American international of Serbian descent has scored four goals and provided an assist over the past five matches, all of which he has started. Standing 1.92 meters tall, the Wisconsin native offers a physical presence that makes him a threat in the air while also possessing the finishing ability and awareness to bring teammates into play.
Novakovich is more than a traditional target man. His movement, hold-up play, and ability to link the midfield with the attack have helped Haifa become a more balanced and unpredictable offensive side. Rather than relying exclusively on individual moments from its creative players, the team now has a striker capable of bringing those talents together.
His performances have also silenced some of the early doubters who questioned whether he could make a meaningful impact after his most recent spell in Italy. With his confidence growing and his place in the starting lineup increasingly secure, Novakovich is on course to surpass several personal bests this season.
Bachar has been particularly impressed by the striker’s contribution to the team as a whole.
“The first thing we saw when we brought him in was that he’s a team player who connects the play,” the coach explained. “Beyond his goal against Jerusalem, he set up the move for Bruninho, who assisted on Brazao’s marker, and he was also involved in the third goal. Beyond the goals, he brings a great deal of presence and contributes to the team’s collective play.”
Together, Bruninho, Brazao and Novakovich have helped elevate Haifa’s attack in a remarkably short period. Their complementary qualities give Bachar a creative playmaker, a winger capable of beating defenders one-on-one and a striker who can finish chances while involving others. The combination has made the Greens considerably more dangerous and much harder to contain.
There is, however, still work to be done at the other end of the pitch.
While the attack has begun to click, Haifa’s defense remains a work in progress. Tsunami and Nigel Lonwijk are still adjusting to their new surroundings, with the former left out of the starting lineup against Hapoel Jerusalem. Jelle Bataille has also struggled to reach his best level, leaving questions about the stability of the back line.
Those concerns help explain why Haifa moved aggressively to secure the signature of Eli Dasa. In a late transfer move, the Greens landed the Israel national team captain after beating out Hapoel Beersheba, which had come close to completing a deal for the right-back.
Dasa brings experience and quality, but his value extends beyond what he can offer on the field. As a seasoned international, he is accustomed to performing under pressure and understands the demands of competing at the highest level. His leadership and professionalism could prove particularly important in a squad containing several players still learning to play together.
For Bachar, Dasa represents both a defensive reinforcement and a trusted lieutenant who can help establish standards throughout the dressing room.
“He has the complete package in terms of leadership and an exceptional personality,” Bachar said. “We’ve seen that with the national team and abroad. He’s a professional at the highest level. From a physical standpoint, the national team saw that he was good enough even without being part of a club. For us, he’s a terrific addition.”
If Dasa can help bring greater organization and consistency to the defense, Haifa could become an even more formidable opponent. The attacking quality is increasingly evident, but championship challenges are rarely sustained on goals alone. Bachar will need his side to find the same cohesion at the back that it has begun to display going forward.
For now, though, the broader message is unmistakable: Writing off Maccabi Haifa after its preseason struggles would have been premature.
The Greens have rediscovered their confidence, their new attacking players are beginning to deliver, and the team is showing signs of developing into the kind of cohesive unit expected of a club with championship ambitions. The results have followed, turning an atmosphere of uncertainty into one of genuine excitement.
Bachar, however, remains determined to keep expectations in check. He knows that a strong run of form is only the beginning of a long campaign, and that there is still plenty of room for improvement.
“Ultimately, the results speak for themselves. When the team plays good, high-quality football, it means the recruitment has been good,” he said.
'Our aim is first place'
“I feel we have a good team that is aiming high, and we’re in the middle of a process. Talking about the championship is still a long way off. We have a journey ahead of us, and we’re only at the beginning. As we strengthen the team and improve, we won’t be afraid to talk about the highest ambitions.
“Our aim is first place. That’s our goal.”
Those are ambitious words from a coach whose team looked anything but a title contender in July. But the recent performances suggest that Haifa may finally be finding the right formula. The attack has gained a new dimension, the squad is developing greater chemistry, and Dasa’s arrival offers hope of greater stability in defense.
There will inevitably be more challenges ahead, beginning with a demanding stretch of league fixtures, and the Greens must prove they can sustain their progress over an entire season. Their defensive vulnerabilities have not disappeared, and six matches are too few to draw definitive conclusions about the championship race.
Still, the transformation has been striking. A preseason that left supporters questioning the direction of the club has given way to a team playing with confidence, purpose and growing belief in its own ability.
Maccabi Haifa is not ready to declare itself champion just yet. But after a difficult start, the Greens are once again looking like a team capable of challenging for the biggest prize in Israeli soccer.

Rogue AI agents infiltrating US bank accounts – Axios
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

05:39:36 KST

Rogue AI agents infiltrating US bank accounts – Axios
Major US banks have detected outside artificial intelligence agents operating inside customer accounts, with some appearing to attempt actions beyond users’ instructions, Axios reported on Thursday.
AI agents are designed to complete tasks on users’ behalf, potentially making purchases, paying bills or moving money. Customers often give them permission and login credentials, but this can violate banks’ rules requiring account holders to log in themselves.
Lenders including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Morgan Stanley and Wells Fargo are racing to contain the risks, according to Axios, citing people familiar with the matter. Some have tracked agents contacting call centers or apparently acting independently of customer instructions.
Bank executives described the situation as “horrifying,” according to the outlet. One said lenders struggle to distinguish between authorized assistants and agents that have gone rogue.
JPMorgan, Bank of America, and Citi have now started restricting outside agents’ access, while Morgan Stanley has reportedly begun blocking them from its platforms. Chase has also urged customers not to share usernames and passwords with AI agents.
Banks generally allow, or are developing, limited access that lets outside tools view balances and other account information without moving money. However, they are now also preparing emergency plans to protect accounts and restore customers’ access if something goes wrong, Axios reported.
The banks have also expressed fear of losing profitable deposits. The Financial Times reported last week that AI assistants could move customers’ cash to banks offering better rates, forcing lenders to pay more interest to keep those customers.
The concerns come amid a string of reports of AI agents acting beyond their instructions and accessing outside systems without permission. The Wall Street Journal reported last month that OpenAI shelved its planned GPT-6.1 Astra model after testing revealed more deceptive behavior than its predecessors. The system sometimes failed to disclose its actions to human operators and attempted to use potentially unsafe external tools.
Earlier incidents included OpenAI agents escaping their testing environment and accessing servers belonging to Hugging Face, an online repository for AI models and datasets.
Financial regulators have warned that autonomous systems could also destabilize markets. Bank of England Deputy Governor Sarah Breeden warned in June that agents reacting alike to the same signals could buy or sell simultaneously, making market swings more severe.
She urged regulators to consider emergency “kill switches” that could halt trading if faulty AI systems triggered a market meltdown.

Maternal mortality in Kyrgyzstan decreases by 34.4% in 9M2026
According to preliminary data for the first nine months of 2026, 23 cases of maternal mortality, occurring during pregnancy, childbirth, or the postpartum period, were recorded in Kyrgyzstan, Kabar reports.
The Healthcare Ministry stated that the maternal mortality rate stood at 22.1 per 100,000 live births, a 34.4% decrease compared to the same period last year.
"Despite this positive trend, every instance of maternal death requires a thorough analysis of its causes and circumstances to determine the necessary measures to prevent similar occurrences in the future," the ministry emphasized.
Ensuring access to family planning services is a key priority. The state has allocated funds for the procurement of modern contraceptive methods, totaling 12.5 million soms, including provisions for women from socially vulnerable groups. Furthermore, the availability of certain contraceptives at subsidized prices has been expanded under the mandatory health insurance system.
Special attention is being given to supporting women during pregnancy and the postpartum period.
Additionally, the ministry is improving the organization of reproductive healthcare, revising record-keeping and reporting documentation to account for medical and social risk factors, and intensifying public outreach regarding family planning and the prevention of pregnancy-related complications. "Preserving the life and health of a mother requires a comprehensive approach, which includes preparation for pregnancy, seeking timely medical care, high-quality monitoring during pregnancy, and appropriate medical support following childbirth," the statement reads.
The agency emphasizes that reducing maternal mortality remains one of the most critical objectives for the healthcare system. Achieving sustainable results requires the continued improvement of medical care, the timely identification of risks, and greater awareness among women regarding how to maintain their reproductive health.
Earlier, the President said maternal mortality decreased by 35% over the past three years, while infant mortality dropped by 24%, reaching the lowest levels since independence.

tune X3 headphones by préssec take design cues from vintage studio equipment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:35:10 UTC
05:35:10 KST

tune X3 headphones by préssec take design cues from vintage studio equipment
brushed aluminum, exposed hardware, and tactile audio adjustments give this concept the character of old-school audio tech.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
tune x3 brings back tactile dials and switches
Préssec imagines a return to the tactile controls of traditional audio equipment with its Tune X3 headphones. The concept places a series of knurled dials and switches directly onto the earcups, including a dedicated control marked for bass and treble. Volume and active noise cancellation receive their own physical controls as well. These adjustments, often handled through a companion app, become part of the brushed aluminum headphones themselves and allow listeners to reach up and change the sound by feel.
The bass and treble adjustment is perhaps the most interesting detail. Borrowing from the familiar controls of stereo receivers and mixing consoles, the design brings the experience of tuning audio directly to the listener’s ears. Each dial has a ridged edge that suggests a satisfying resistance beneath the fingertips, while the different shapes help distinguish one function from another. The arrangement gives the headphones an unusually hands-on character to recall a time when interacting with music involved turning a few knobs.
brushed aluminum and orange fabric echo vintage equipment
The headphones themselves take on the appearance of old studio hardware, with brushed aluminum housings and vivid orange textile padding across the ear cushions and headband. The team at Préssec Design leaves the construction details visible, from the small fasteners along the metal body to the cylindrical fittings that connect the earcups to the headband. There is something appealingly mechanical about the whole arrangement, which could sit comfortably alongside a reel-to-reel tape recorder or an old stereo amplifier.
The contrast between the materials is especially effective. Soft orange cushions sit against hard metallic surfaces, while the slender connecting hardware gives the relatively substantial earcups a lighter profile. Even the controls contribute to the composition, their textured surfaces interrupting the smooth circular housings. The design suggests the precision of professional audio equipment, with enough color and softness to give it a playful edge.
préssec explores a family of imaginary electronics
Tune X3 belongs to a fictional product family developed by Préssec, which also includes the CINE X3 camera concept. The two objects share a visual language through their metallic finishes and exposed hardware, adapted to the proportions of each device. The studio used Vizcom as part of the design process, exploring how an established set of visual references could inform other products within the same imagined collection.
For now, Tune X3 remains a concept, with its technical specifications and production plans still to be established. Questions about weight, comfort and acoustic performance are left open. Even so, its interface offers an interesting proposition for personal audio design. The controls are visible and easily understood, giving listeners a more immediate relationship with the equipment. One can almost imagine reaching for the bass dial halfway through a favorite record.

Batteries lower evening peak prices
Continued from previous post
Violette Mouchaileh, AEMO's executive general manager of policy and executive affairs, said it was a milestone.
"Batteries continue to shift record amounts of renewable energy into the higher-demand evening period, when households and businesses typically need more power," Mouchaileh said.
"Increased battery charging and discharging contributed to significantly lower evening peak prices, with batteries setting prices in almost half of dispatch intervals, up from 18 per cent a year ago."
AEMO said the east gas market was relatively subdued during the third quarter, with prices averaging $10.77 a gigajoule, up slightly from the same time last year.
Demand was marginally lower, as declining demand from gas-fired generators was offset by an increase in exports from Queensland producers.
On the other side of the Nullarbor, demand went up by 1.6 per cent amid lower temperatures and greater heating needs.
Gas-fired plants surged 27 per cent year-on-year to meet those needs on the back of lower wind output and coal plant outages.
Prices, meanwhile, soared to uncomfortable levels in the west, where they were 30 per cent higher at an average of $117 a megawatt hour, a new record.
Once other system costs were taken into account, they averaged a painful $175 a megawatt-hour.
Power prices continue to drop as batteries flex their muscles
The latest troubles to hit Snowy 2.0 come amid profound changes in the national grid.
In its latest snapshot of the national electricity system, the Australian Energy Market Operator noted that demand for power was surging even while wholesale spot prices were easing.
So-called underlying demand, which includes the consumption households meet themselves through rooftop solar, jumped 1.3 per cent to an average of more than 25,000 megawatts in the three months to September 30 compared with the previous corresponding period.
According to AEMO, Victoria accounted for most of the growth, which was driven by the switch to electrification, high industrial demand, and the rise of power-hungry data centres.
As well as this, the market operator noted renewable energy was meeting an ever-greater share of the market.
Generation from renewable sources increased from 41.8 per cent to 44.3 per cent of demand during the quarter, which included winter months typically associated with relatively low output from wind farms and solar panels.
Leading the way was the unstoppable growth of rooftop solar, which surged 13 per cent to an average of 3,200 megawatts, followed by rises in grid-scale solar and hydropower output.
And, in a major shift, AEMO noted that batteries for the first time eclipsed the contribution of gas-fired power plants during peak hours in the evening.
Grid-scale batteries, the agency said, met 8 per cent of total generation during those hours compared with 5 per cent of gas plants as the amount of storage installed tripled over the course of the year.
Nickel prices lift on speculation of additional cutbacks in Indonesian MHP output: analyst
Three‑month London Metal Exchange (LME) nickel futures increased 2.9% to reach $US16,234/tonne in intra‑day trading on October 21 in response to news that some of Indonesia's largest Chinese-backed producers had met to discuss potentially cutting output, according to the Commonwealth Bank research team.
Producers including Tsingshan Holdings, GEM Co., Lygend Resources and Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt are understood to have debated cutting output of mixed hydroxide precipitate (MHP) from their respective HPAL (high pressure acid leach) operations by up to 50% from existing levels.
Prior to this meeting, Indonesian MHP production was already forecast to fall by around 15% from 2025 to range between 390‑400 kilotonne(kt) Ni‑in‑MHP.
Indonesian policy has been a big driver, says Vivek Dhar, head of commodities and sustainability research team at CBA.
A rise in raw material costs, predominantly for limonite ore and sulphur (for conversion into sulphuric acid), has been another factor, he says in a note.
During the third quarter, the El Nino weather pattern has contributed to additional production cuts and has been another area of focus for markets, Mr Dhar adds.
"This week's meeting of Indonesia's Chinese-backed producers highlights that there is still concern amongst them that MHP output needs to be further curtailed.
"This may mean that the additional 400 kt per annum HPAL capacity slated for commissioning by the end of the year will be delayed and potentially support firmer nickel prices."

SK Hynix puts US IPO of chip unit Solidigm on hold
SK Hynix has put on hold a planned US listing for its Solidigm chip unit due to market volatility — a move that also comes after South Korean authorities raised concerns that the deal could undermine shareholder interests.
A listing of Solidigm, a former Intel business that specialises in NAND flash memory and solid-state drives, had been under consideration to help fund a new US factory and meet surging demand for chips in AI data centres.
It could also have funded share cancellations and buybacks, SK Hynix said in a statement.
People familiar with the now-suspended IPO plans said the share sale could have raised $US15 billion ($21.4 billion) and valued the unit at $US150 billion.
The South Korean chip giant, which became dual-listed with a debut on the Nasdaq in July, said it planned to continue to explore ways to fund Solidigm's expansion and enhance shareholder value, including reviewing the timing, scale and financing of future investments.
"This decision does not reflect any change in Solidigm's growth prospects or investment needs," it said.
It was not immediately clear how the decision would be received by the Trump administration, which has put pressure on foreign chipmakers to build new facilities in the US and which has been holding discussions with SK Hynix.
According to people familiar with the matter, SK Hynix has sought to use the prospect of a potential factory in the US as a bargaining chip.
South Korean authorities said they were discussing semiconductor investments in the US with Washington as part of broader bilateral talks.
However, they are not part of negotiations about a $US350-billion investment commitment South Korea made to the US last year in exchange for lower US tariffs.
Reporting with Reuters

Corporate cop to appeal court decision on Rex directors
Corporate watchdog ASIC is seeking leave to appeal the decision of the Supreme Court of NSW that former Rex Airlines non-executive directors John Sharp AM, Siddharth Khotkar and Lincoln Pan did not contravene their directors' duties in relation to a profit forecast made by Rex on February 28 2023.
Former executive chair Lim Kim Hai was fined $800,000 and banned from running an Australian company for four years after he admitted to misleading the market and breaching his directors' duties.
But the court did not find that three former Rex directors, John Sharp AM, Lincoln Pan and Siddharth Khotkar, breached their directors' duties.
ASIC is appealing the court's decision regarding the non-executive directors because it is concerned that there were errors in the primary judge's findings.
ASIC is not appealing the court's decision in relation to Rex.
The leave to appeal will be determined by the court on a date to be decided.

David Chau's chart of the day: AI spending boom and interest rate worries
Hello there! Every afternoon, I'll give you a sneak peek at what I'll be discussing on my 7pm News finance report.
Tonight we'll be looking at the huge amounts being spent on data centres and AI infrastructure.
I thought it would be a good time for that as the AI-centric stock indices, the Nasdaq 100 (-2.9%) , Nikkei (-0.9%) and KOSPI (-1.1%) have fallen quite sharply today.
And in the past month, the Nasdaq and Nikkei have fallen by around 5%, while South Korea's KOSPI has plummeted by 22.5%!
Investors are feeling increasingly nervous about the spending splurge from the major "hyperscalers" Microsoft, Oracle, Amazon, Meta (Facebook) and Alphabet (Google) — which are expected to have poured $US804 billion on artificial intelligence this year.
And by next year, their capital expenditure on AI would have surpassed $US1 trillion!
Much of this is being financed by debt, given they don't have trillions of dollars in cash just lying around doing nothing.
And in a rising interest rate environment, that debt is getting more expensive.
In fact, markets are betting the US Federal Reserve will lift rates three more times by December 2027, according to the latest Bloomberg data.
These successive rate rises will make this rampant AI-driven borrowing a lot more expensive — and investors more impatient about when they'll finally see a return on investment from all this spending (which eats into profits).
Key Event
Chinese are still largest source of Australian residential real estate investment
The latest Foreign Investment Review Board report from the Australian Treasury is out today and it once again shows the most foreign investment came from China in 2025-26.
Approved foreign investment in residential real estate totalled $4.7 billion in 2025-26. That's down 4 per cent from $4.9 billion the year before, and down from $6.6 billion in 2023-24.
The number of approvals fell to 2,979, from 3,922 last year and 5,581 two years ago.
As the chart below shows, the Chinese accounted for the most residential investment both by number and value: $900 million across 785 approvals.
That is almost double the next largest source, Taiwan ($500 million), followed by Vietnam ($300 million), Indonesia ($200 million) and India ($200 million).
Even so, investment from China is down from $1.4 billion last year and $2.6 billion in 2023-24.
Juwai IQI co-founder and group managing director Daniel Ho said Australian taxes on foreigners had become more "prohibitive" to foreign buyers, so many now wait to obtain permanent residency before purchasing.
"Investment by those who don't have residency or citizenship has hit a multi-year low," Mr Ho said.
"Most now wait until they hold permanent residency, which removes the FIRB process, the foreign buyer fees, and the FIRB application fees."
With the ban on buying established homes now extended to June 2029, he said new housing is the only door left open to foreign buyers.
"These buyers help developers reach their presale targets and get projects built," he said.
Education is also one of the top drivers of foreign purchases.
"There were 192,225 Chinese students in Australia in October 2025, accounting for 23 per cent of the total of 833,041," he noted.
"China is the largest source country of foreign students, accounting for 23 per cent of all international students and 31 per cent of international university students.
"In the most recent financial year, 2024-25, 165,193 people became Australian citizens. That included more than 5,000 Chinese."
Among new permanent migrants arriving through skill-based or family-based visas, there were more applicants from China than from any other country but India.
"Chinese accounted for 20,405 places out of the total of 185,001," he said.

Things to watch next week
Two big events are coming next week.
Wednesday’s September CPI report and the US Federal Reserve policy meeting outcome on Thursday morning (Australian time), says David Bassanese, chief economist at Betashares.
On CPI, the market expected the quarterly gain in trimmed mean inflation to be 1.0%, which would meet Hauser's definition of a "materially worse" outcome than the Bank’s 0.8% forecast in August, Mr Bassanese said.
"To my mind, that should be enough to cement the case for a November interest rate hike, even though the Bank arguably already delivered a pre-emptive rate hike in September in response to 'materialising' upside inflation risks."
Offshore, attention turns almost immediately to the Federal Reserve.
"Although the market expects the Fed to remain on hold (93% probability), Fed chair Warsh is on record not wanting to offer market guidance and so there’s every chance the Fed could surprise," Mr Bassanese noted.
"The case to raise rates is already in place — given the recent higher-than-expected US CPI report and signs of a tightening labour market.
"A Fed rate hike just ahead of the mid-term elections would be further affirmation of the Fed's political independence, which might be an attractive proposition for both Warsh and the still nervous bond market.
"A further inflation reality check comes later in the week, with the September core personal consumption deflators expected to gain 0.3% in the month, taking annual underlying inflation to 3.1% from 3.0%."

Further on AUD and NZD
The Antipodean currencies are often sold as proxies for risk, though in this case the main losses were against the safe-haven yen and Swiss franc, with the greenback also taking a hit.
That left the Aussie flat at 70.16 US cents, having eased just 0.1% overnight and it was still 1% higher for the week. Resistance lies around 70.40 US cents with support at 68.95 US cents.
In contrast, it lost 0.9% on the yen overnight and fell 0.6% against the Swiss franc.
The kiwi dollar stood at 56.83 US cents, having slipped 0.4% overnight and away from a one-month top of 57.09 US cents. Support comes in at the recent low of 55.66 US cents.
The currency got a boost on Thursday when strong readings on core inflation at home reinforced expectations the Reserve Bank of New Zealand will hike rates next week.
Markets imply a 95% chance that rates will rise a quarter point to 3.0%, and see a peak of 3.75% next year.
Analysts at Citi changed their call from a "hold" to a "hike" for next week, citing elevated oil prices and a weak kiwi as some reasons for a tightening.
"We expect guidance to echo September, leaving the door open to further hikes," said Citi economist Josh Williamson.
"However, we see 3% as the peak given a fragile recovery, 5.6% unemployment, and slowing GDP, with binary upside risk from offshore tightening or unresolved Middle East tensions."
Analysts at Westpac also shifted to a hike next week, though they see rates rising all the way to 4.0% by September next year.
"Forward guidance will likely leave open the option to raise rates further at the December meeting without presenting it as a sure thing," said Kelly Eckhold, chief NZ economist at Westpac.
"We think a more measured tightening approach is appropriate from here as raising rates at every meeting until something 'breaks' could be a risky strategy if downside growth concerns crystallise."

Zip tumbles 30pc after fraud incident dents first-quarter customer growth
Zip Co said on Friday that an external fraud incident in the US during its fiscal first quarter temporarily weighed on transaction volumes and new customer growth, sending its shares to their lowest level since April 2025.
Shares of the Buy Now, Pay Later firm plunged as much as 30.3% to $1.44 as of 12:04 AEDT.
Analysts at Citi said the incident "raises concerns on Zip's onboarding controls".
UBS analysts said a key miss was a sharper-than-expected rise in the net bad debts ratio, which came in at 1.97% against their estimate of 1.8%, partly because the fraud event temporarily slowed growth in total transaction value (TTV) in July and August.
Zip said it identified and contained an external fraud incident in which coordinated actors opened new accounts using legitimate credentials to execute unpaid transactions.
The incident affected TTV and new customer growth in July and August, and resulted in $10.1 million of cash operating expenses.
Net bad debts were 1.93% of TTV in the quarter ended September 30, with some impact from TTV being temporarily moderated by measures taken to contain the fraud.
Despite the incident, TTV rose 18% to $4.6 billion in the quarter, while cash earnings before tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBTDA) increased 3.4% to $65 million.

Rio Tinto to invest $2.7b in Kangwinan bauxite project
Rio Tinto has said it will invest $US1.9 billion ($2.7 billion) to develop the Kangwinan bauxite project on the Western Cape York Peninsula in Queensland.
The mining giant said the project would establish a new bauxite production centre 15 kilometres south-east of its Amrun mine, 40km south of the town of Weipa.
Early works at Kangwinan began in 2025.
"It will add 20 million tonnes of annual bauxite production capacity in Weipa, leveraging some existing infrastructure, with first output targeted in 2029 and full production expected by 2032," the miner said.
"The project will replace production from the Andoom mine near Weipa as it reaches the end of its life this decade, while increasing Weipa Operations' annual capacity to about 44 million tonnes, from current production of around 38 million tonnes per year.
"It will also help compensate for the planned end of production at the Gove mine in the Northern Territory in 2029."
Ore will be transported from Kangwinan on a 15km conveyor to expanded stockyard facilities and the existing Amrun wharf, which will be expanded to accommodate larger capesize vessels.
Rio Tinto said it expected construction to ramp up in 2027, supporting more than 1,300 construction jobs.
"Longer term, the project will help sustain Rio Tinto's residentially based workforce of around 1,5000 people in the Western Cape," the company added.
Shares in Rio Tinto fell 2.2% to $147.05 per share in midday AEDT.

Key Event
The Business will be discontinued at the end of 2026
Passing on some news from ABC News Director Simon Robinson that has just been announced to staff, which is that The Business will not return to your screens in 2027.
"Business is a crucial reporting round and we're committed to finding ways for the team to do more of the original and impactful journalism it's known for," Mr Robinson writes, announcing the decision.
"To enable us to focus our resources on delivering that we've made the difficult decision to discontinue The Business TV program at the end of its current season."
He continues, saying:
"We believe the time and resources invested in this 15-minute program would be better deployed producing even more distinctive and impactful business journalism across all our platforms — the website and app, News Channel, our podcasts and our YouTube channels, as well as in our broadcast radio and TV programs.
"We're working on a range of ideas, which we'll further develop in the new year. Among them, we'll be launching a visualised format for the ABC Business Daily podcast and are looking into producing a daily afternoon wrap of the latest markets news."
The last episode of The Business will air on Thursday, December 10.
Australia Post boss Paul Graham to retire
Australia Post CEO Paul Graham has announced he will retire at the end of this financial year, after more than five years in the top job.
Graham has overseen major changes at the government-owned postal service, as it adapts to declining demand for traditional letters and the growth of online shopping.
Australia Post chair Siobhan McKenna thanked him for leading reforms aimed at modernising the business and improving its long-term financial sustainability.
"Paul has led Australia Post with purpose, determination and energy through a period of significant challenge for our business," she said.
Graham said he was proud of what the organisation had achieved, including remaining in public ownership without requiring government funding.
Australia Post's board has begun searching for his replacement, with both internal and external candidates to be considered.

Key Event
Gold is at a two-month low
Gold has fallen to its lowest level in more than two months, dropping 2.4% to about $US4,041 an ounce.
The sell-off comes as oil prices surge to a five-month high.
One of the main reasons, I would say, is because higher oil prices are fuelling inflation fears, raising expectations that US interest rates could stay higher for longer.
While gold is traditionally seen as a hedge against inflation, higher interest rates make it less attractive because, unlike bonds, gold doesn't pay interest.
Oil at a five-month high
Lots of headlines about this morning on the Middle East conflict, including fresh Houthi attacks in Saudi Arabia.
Saudi Aramco has told staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran on the Gulf near Bahrain, Reuters reports, as fighting between the world's largest crude exporter and Yemen's Houthis intensified.
Separately, there was a report in The New York Times, citing unnamed US officials, that US and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for renewed strikes on Iran after next month's midterm elections.
That led Brent crude to jump 4% to about $US113, and a 2% rise for WTI as well.
Interestingly, the Wall Street Journal reported two days ago that more oil is now being shipped out of the Persian Gulf than before the Iran war, thanks in part to what is being dubbed the "Hormuz Shuttle".
But more oil doesn't necessarily mean cheaper oil, as Rabobank's global energy strategist Joe DeLaura explains:
"The 'Hormuz Shuttle' is boosting crude flows through transfers near Oman, but rising insurance costs, tanker inefficiencies and attacks mean markets remain far from normal. Persian Gulf–China freight rates have reached $1.4m daily, adding roughly $13.5/bbl and particularly burdening Asian refiners. Brent and Shanghai physical oil consequently command $10–25 premiums over futures. Higher volumes therefore do not guarantee cheaper delivered energy: the cost of delivery is getting so expensive that it threatens the recovery."

Another major bank cuts jobs
British banking giant Barclays plans to cut about 5,000 jobs, or 5% of its workforce, this year as it turns to artificial intelligence and other technology to reduce costs.
The bank's CFO, Anna Cross, said about 1,000 positions had already been cut, with the remaining 4,000 to go by the end of December.
About 60% of the cuts will affect support roles, including developers, as technology helps staff become more productive.
The announcement follows a major restructure at ANZ here in Australia, which announced plans last year to cut 3,500 jobs and reduce its contractor workforce by about 1,000 to simplify operations and improve efficiency.

Hospitals ‘overcharging’ is a malpractice: Govt to Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:32:55 UTC
05:32:55 KST

Hosps charge up to 700% premium on cancer drugs (Generative image)
NEW DELHI: Govt has admitted before Supreme Court the “malpractice” of hospitals charging patients high MRPs for medicines and consumables, and said it was conscious of the problem, examining it and devising appropriate interventions in consultation with all stakeholders.In an affidavit filed in SC on the issue of capping prices of all medicines and medical consumables, chemicals and fertilisers ministry said that patients have a very low bargaining position with respect to hospitals, resulting in various malpractices. The affidavit noted the irony of India being home to companies making cheap drugs but patients here having to pay way above the manufacturing price, as well as patients being subjected to overcharging by hospitals.“The Indian drug market is fairly competitive, with a large number of pharmaceutical companies in every drug segment, resulting in one of the lowest prices in the world. Ordinarily, where there is substantial competition, there is no need to regulate prices. However, by their very nature, health treatment and pharmaceutical products involve information and bargaining asymmetries between patients on the one hand, and retail pharmacies, hospital pharmacies, hospitals providing treatment and doctors on the other,” the affidavit said.
Hospitals charge up to 700% premium on cancer drugs
The govt affidavit said a patient has a “very low bargaining position vis-a-vis the hospital, and the patient’s knowledge of drugs, their substitutes and their prices is also very limited”. These bargaining and information asymmetries result in various malpractices in the system despite strong competition among manufacturers, leading to the need for regulation, it said.Enumerating the steps taken by it to control the pricing of drugs, govt said ceiling prices for 935 scheduled formulations and retail prices of 3,881 new drugs have been fixed. Govt filed the affidavit on a plea filed by Dr Sanjay Kulshrestha, who referred to a Niti Aayog report and a 2020 statement of the then health minister Harsh Vardhan that expenditure on health pushed an estimated six crore families below the poverty line each year.
The affidavit said hospitals buy medicines from manufacturers who provide highest trade margin and then sell those medicines to patients at MRP, with margins ranging from 170% to 700% or more in the case of anti-cancer drugs.“That another area of concern in the sector is the supply of consumables in hospitals, where margins of 100% to 1000% or more are prevalent, along with a tendency of hospitals to purchase consumables that have a high MRP and margin, with a low price to the distributor/hospital. Ordinarily, hospital supplies are included in the package cost for treatment of major diseases/procedures under govt schemes/insurance, and govt/insurance agencies negotiate and fix the lowest rate for such packages. However, for patients making direct payment to the hospital, hospital supplies are billed separately at MRP,” it said.

ExclusiveEU mulls sanctions reprieve for Chinese fabric-maker accused of aiding Russia
Beijing offers to remove restrictions on a German supplier to chipmaking giant ASML in exchange for the EU delisting Chinese firm Yusha
Diplomats from the EU’s 27 member states were pressured this week to lift sanctions on Yusha Group, a Chinese textiles manufacturer accused of selling sensitive European technology to Russian buyers.
In exchange, Beijing has pledged that the company will refrain from shipping banned items to Russian military-linked buyers. It will also remove German company Sindlhauser Materials from its own export controls list, according to multiple sources familiar with the affair.
The unusual quid pro quo – the product of high-wire negotiations at the top level of EU and Chinese politics – is designed to protect the supply chain of Europe’s most valuable technology company, Dutch-based ASML, of which Sindlhauser is a reported supplier.

England stunned as Sri Lanka chases 430 after Brook's record ODI knock
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:27:02 UTC
05:27:02 KST

Sri Lanka has chased down a total of 430 in a one day international against England after Harry Brook scored a blistering double-century off just 114 deliveries.
Brook's 202 is now the highest individual ODI score for an Englishman and is also the fastest double century of all time.
Pavan Rathnayake scored 130 in Sri Lanka's runchase before Janith Liyanage sealed the win with a six off the penultimate delivery of the match.
Sri Lanka has chased down 430 in a thrilling one-day clash against England despite Harry Brook scoring the fastest double-century in ODI history.
Brook's double-century helped England post a mammoth score of 4-429 before Sri Lanka chased down the target with two wickets and one ball to spare.
Sri Lanka's chase is the second-highest of all time in ODI cricket, trailing only South Africa's chase of 435 against Australia in 2006.
Loading Twitter content
The 27-year-old captain rewrote the record books by racing to his double hundred in 114 balls, surpassing the previous mark of 117 deliveries set by India's Shubman Gill.
Brook's double-century was the fastest of all time and he also eclipsed England's highest individual ODI score of 182, previously held by Ben Stokes.
He made 202 from 116 deliveries, peppering the Sri Lanka attack with 21 fours and 10 sixes before departing to warm applause from the crowd.
The defeat leaves England bottom of the standings after losing both their matches, with Brook saying they need to win their next two games to reach the final in Lahore.
"Unfortunately, it [the record] doesn't matter now. I thought we were going to be in a good position but, unfortunately, it doesn't even count," Brook said after the game.
"Heartbreaking. I think you've hit the nail on the head there. It's very disappointing that we haven't been able to defend 430, but that's life, that's cricket," he added.
"You don't see many teams chase down 430 and hats off to Sri Lanka. They've played exceptionally well. We couldn't execute our skills enough with the ball and, again, they've just played an absolute blinder there.
"We'll have a good chat about it now and over the next couple of days. We've got a good opportunity in the next couple of games to really try and get to that final in Lahore."
Pavan Rathnayake top-scored for Sri Lanka with 130 from 106 deliveries, while opener Avishka Fernando and Dasun Shanaka both fell three runs short of centuries.
Needing six runs from the final two deliveries, Sri Lanka sealed victory when Janith Liyanage launched Josh Tongue over long-off for six, leaving Brook's record-breaking innings all in vain.
Tongue was England's most successful bowler with 3-79.
England lost by 87 runs at the same venue in Rawalpindi on Tuesday to Pakistan, who lead the table with two wins from two.

President Donald Trump on Thursday defended a controversial ad by the campaign of Vivek Ramaswamy featuring the estranged mother of Amy Acton, his Democratic opponent in the Ohio gubernatorial race, calling Acton a liar.
Trump's defense of the ad came after widespread bipartisan backlash to it, which focused on the fact that Acton's stepfather, Cledith Arthur, was charged with raping her when she was a child and was married to Acton's mother, Donna Arthur.
In the ad, Donna Arthur says Acton has "lied her entire life."
"Don't vote for people who lie," Arthur says in the ad. "Don't let her become your governor. If you think she'll make your life better, you're fooling yourself. It will only get worse."
Acton has said she has not seen Arthur since she was 12 years old. Cledith Arthur fled after his arrest and remained a fugitive until his death in Pennsylvania in 2004.
Trump, in a Truth Social post on Thursday, said, "Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse."
"The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad,' " Trump said. "Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor."
Trump also criticized Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine for calling for the ad to be taken down, even as DeWine continued to support his fellow Republican Ramaswamy's candidacy to succeed him.
"The ad, on its face, is deeply, deeply troubling," DeWine said in a press conference earlier Thursday.
Trump said DeWine "probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing."
"I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up, and let everyone listen to the mother of a defective, dishonest, and incapable Candidate, explain how the daughter is a DISASTER who, uncontrollably, lies, cheats, and steals!" Trump said.
Trump later told reporters that he had "no idea" about Acton's allegation of being raped by her mother's husband, and questioned when Acton had made that claim.
Trump's comments came a day after his vice president, JD Vance, during a visit to Cincinnati and said it was "not really my concern" whether the ad was appropriate.
But Vance also said, "I'm a little bit disgusted when I see Republicans across the country who are whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America."
"The media and the Democrats in the state of Ohio are obsessed because guess what? Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar," Vance said. "Whatever you think about any of the TV advertisements, focus on the substance and focus on the facts."
Ramaswamy's campaign has spent nearly $95,000 to air the ad so far, according to AdImpact, with more than 100 airings concentrated in Cleveland, Columbus, and Cincinnati — three of Ohio's biggest media markets.
Ramaswamy's campaign has said it committed $4 million to air the ad.
Acton on Thursday said of the ad, "It was a horrible and hideous thing to do. A sad thing. And I feel like it was an exploitative thing to do."
"My mother is not well," Acton said.
Her brother, Philip Stearns, told The New York Times in a statement earlier this week that he and Acton were removed from their mother's custody after their stepfather was arrested.
"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core — a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."
Former Ohio Sen. Rob Portman, a Republican, told Politico on Thursday that the ad should be taken down.
"The increasing incivility in the political arena should concern us all," Portman said, according to Politico's Jonathan Martin. "This ad is an unfortunate example of that broader trend. It crosses the line. I hope the ad will be taken down and the final days of the campaign will focus on policy differences."

Thousands gather at final student-led rally ahead of Serbia election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:21:12 UTC
05:21:12 KST

Thousands gather at final student-led rally ahead of Serbia election
The student movement aims to end Vucic’s 14 years of rule at Sunday’s vote, as he holds a rival rally across town.
Tens of thousands of supporters of Serbia’s student-led opposition movement have gathered in central Belgrade for their final rally ahead of a parliamentary election in which they hope to oust veteran leader Aleksandar Vucic’s party.
The crowds filled the capital on Thursday, as Vucic held a rival rally at a sports hall across town.
Waving “students are winning” flags and blowing whistles, the marchers converged on Slavija Square, the site of some of the movement’s biggest protests.
Sunday’s vote is seen as a chance to end Vucic’s longtime rule.
“Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible,” said Marija Nedeljkovic Radic, 47, who said young people had given her hope of “a normal country“.
The vote follows nearly two years of student-led protests triggered by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at a newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad that killed 16 people.
The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, is seeking to unseat Vucic’s right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which has been in power for more than 14 years.
It is running 250 candidates for the 250-seat parliament, many of them academics or political outsiders, on a platform centred on fighting corruption.
“We are putting an end to 14 years of humiliation, chaos and betrayal, and to decades of putting personal and party interests above yours,” university professor Jugoslav Gasic, one of the candidates on the Student List, told the crowd in Belgrade, who chanted “Victory, victory!”
“You deserve better, and we know how to deliver it. Students are winning!”
The railway disaster, widely blamed on corruption, triggered some of Serbia’s largest demonstrations since the fall of Slobodan Milosevic in 2000, and demands for transparency grew into calls for an early election.
Over the week, students marched for days across the country, including rural areas that are Vucic’s strongholds.
Vucic, who resigned the presidency in September to run for prime minister, called the snap election last month. He has accused the movement of being a foreign-funded coup attempt.
“Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!” he told supporters on Thursday.
Serbia lacks reliable independent polling. But political scientist Dusan Vucicevic told the AFP news agency he expected the students to win more than 40 percent of the vote, far more than any opposition list since the SNS took power in 2012.
The Associated Press news agency reported that polls suggested a close race between the two sides, raising fears of incidents if both claim victory.
Twenty-four Serbian civil society groups warned this week that conditions for “free and fair elections” were lacking, and a monitoring group cited more than 100 violent incidents during the campaign.
On Wednesday, prosecutors questioned six people arrested on suspicion of plotting “violence, riots and attacks” on election day.

Why has the Libya-Turkiye maritime deal stirred controversy?
Some countries in the region say it infringes on their rights.

Its rival administration, the internationally recognised Government of National Unity, signed the deal seven years ago.

They say Libya and Turkiye are ignoring their sovereign rights.

Batteries lower evening peak prices
Continued from previous post
Violette Mouchaileh, AEMO's executive general manager of policy and executive affairs, said it was a milestone.
"Batteries continue to shift record amounts of renewable energy into the higher-demand evening period, when households and businesses typically need more power," Mouchaileh said.
"Increased battery charging and discharging contributed to significantly lower evening peak prices, with batteries setting prices in almost half of dispatch intervals, up from 18 per cent a year ago."
AEMO said the east gas market was relatively subdued during the third quarter, with prices averaging $10.77 a gigajoule, up slightly from the same time last year.
Demand was marginally lower, as declining demand from gas-fired generators was offset by an increase in exports from Queensland producers.
On the other side of the Nullarbor, demand went up by 1.6 per cent amid lower temperatures and greater heating needs.
Gas-fired plants surged 27 per cent year-on-year to meet those needs on the back of lower wind output and coal plant outages.
Prices, meanwhile, soared to uncomfortable levels in the west, where they were 30 per cent higher at an average of $117 a megawatt hour, a new record.
Once other system costs were taken into account, they averaged a painful $175 a megawatt-hour.
Power prices continue to drop as batteries flex their muscles
The latest troubles to hit Snowy 2.0 come amid profound changes in the national grid.
In its latest snapshot of the national electricity system, the Australian Energy Market Operator noted that demand for power was surging even while wholesale spot prices were easing.
So-called underlying demand, which includes the consumption households meet themselves through rooftop solar, jumped 1.3 per cent to an average of more than 25,000 megawatts in the three months to September 30 compared with the previous corresponding period.
According to AEMO, Victoria accounted for most of the growth, which was driven by the switch to electrification, high industrial demand, and the rise of power-hungry data centres.
As well as this, the market operator noted renewable energy was meeting an ever-greater share of the market.
Generation from renewable sources increased from 41.8 per cent to 44.3 per cent of demand during the quarter, which included winter months typically associated with relatively low output from wind farms and solar panels.
Leading the way was the unstoppable growth of rooftop solar, which surged 13 per cent to an average of 3,200 megawatts, followed by rises in grid-scale solar and hydropower output.
And, in a major shift, AEMO noted that batteries for the first time eclipsed the contribution of gas-fired power plants during peak hours in the evening.
Grid-scale batteries, the agency said, met 8 per cent of total generation during those hours compared with 5 per cent of gas plants as the amount of storage installed tripled over the course of the year.

The Google Home Speaker Has Been Secretly Eating My Wi-Fi Data
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
20:05:51 UTC
05:05:51 KST

If you had to estimate how much data your smart speaker was using over the course of a couple of weeks, would you guess 3 terabytes? That's what one Google Home Speaker user discovered when he checked his home Wi-Fi's usage, according to Reddit posts reported on by 9to5Google. The Google Gemini–powered smart speakers have apparently been downloading huge amounts of data to the device over the past two weeks, which could put a serious damper on your Wi-Fi network.
While it isn't happening to everyone, after checking my own home internet usage, I found out that I have been experiencing the same issue. My Google Home Speaker has used 487 GB of data in the past 10 days, using almost as much as the entire rest of my home between August and September.
Google confirmed this bug has only affected some devices and that it has rolled out a solution. A spokesperson from Google told WIRED: “A server misconfiguration caused some Google Home Speakers to repeatedly download a software update. This issue has now been resolved.”
Looking into this issue made me go beyond just Google's usage, though. My husband and I started reviewing the data usage for all of the individual devices that our router could identify and found some surprising numbers. The weirdest highlight was that Amazon was listed as using 22 GB in the past week with only the Ring smoke detector set up in my house, which was similar to the use of one of the smartphones in my house. There's also a mysterious device just labeled “WATCH” that used about 21 GB in the past week, but no one in my home has a smart watch that's been on in the last year. A mystery for me to solve another day.
If you've noticed your home Wi-Fi bandwidth isn't what it used to be, it could be because one of your smart home devices (or possibly something else entirely). Here's how to check your router or Wi-Fi provider for which device could be at fault.
How to Check Your Device Usage
You have a couple of options for checking how much data a smart home device has been using. Some routers provide detailed information about where all your data is going, for starters. I have an Eero mesh system for my house, but we don't pay for its subscription fee to access detailed information—so it's fairly limited. The free version of the app lists all the connected devices in my home, but it doesn't tell me how much data each uses.
There are a lot of routers that have subscription fees and paywalls that can hide this information and other features you might want. But our favorite subscription-free mesh Wi-Fi system comes from Asus, which also makes our favorite regular Wi-Fi router, and you can track and analyze traffic for free with an Asus router. Here's how:
- Open the web interface (go to http://www.asusrouter.com/ in your browser) and log in.
- Click on the Traffic Analyzer tab and make sure it's turned on (data is refreshed every hour).
- You can see the top five clients using data listed on the Statistic tab.
- You can also see live traffic in the Asus Router app on your phone.
Folks with a TP-Link router or mesh can also review traffic. Here's how:
- Open the Deco or Tether app.
- Tap on the Network tab and select Traffic Usage.
- What you see will depend on the model you have, but with some routers you can toggle on In-depth Statistics for more detailed information.
Netgear only tracks overall traffic under Traffic Meter, you can't break it down by device. For other manufacturers it's worth poking around in the web interface. (It usually gives you access to more data than the mobile app.) If you're looking to get more information without hitting a paywall, explore both our router and mesh Wi-Fi guides for recommendations.
But there's another way. I used our internet provider's app to check exact usage data. Mine is the AT&T app, but most internet providers should have an app or login you can use to check your data activity. My data appears right at the front of the app underneath my current usage. It's more limited than the info you'd get from a dedicated router's app if you did subscribe; I'm only able to view detailed data by today, the past seven days, my current AT&T billing period, or over the past three billing periods. And the app only lists a handful of high-volume devices versus every device connected to the internet in my home.
But even that limited information revealed which devices were gobbling up the most data in the recent days and weeks, which is how we discovered the issue with both the Google Home Speaker and the Ring smoke detector.
Why Should You Check?
It's not a huge issue for me that my Google Home Speaker has been guzzling my data. I have a large Wi-Fi plan (a must as a smart home tester), and it was patched quickly. On the other hand, I have unplugged it for the time being to make sure I don't hit the 2 terabyte cap we have per billing period. But if you're on a plan where massive downloads like this can cost you, or your signal is getting clogged up by mysterious devices, it might be time to check your data usage to find out which device is at fault. You never know when you'll find a 3-terabyte bug slowing your whole network.

Epstein, Iran and ‘drain the swamp’: Have Republicans shifted before vote?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
