WHO warns ‘more complex’ Ebola outbreak now present in 3 African countries
Health officials are investigating where Nigeria’s first patient, confirmed this week, was infected.
The World Health Organization (WHO) says the Ebola outbreak that emerged in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) is growing more “complex”, with cases now present in countries in East and West Africa.
This comes as health authorities investigate where Nigeria’s first case, which was confirmed this week, originated, raising questions about whether the patient crossed paths with Kenya’s first patient at a Ugandan airport.
“We are facing a more complex outbreak landscape,” Mohamed Janabi, regional director for WHO in Africa, told an online media briefing on Thursday.
Nigeria reported its first case of the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola on Tuesday, becoming the fourth African country and the most populous yet to be affected by an outbreak that was announced in DRC in mid-May and has since killed more than 4,000 people there.
Kenya, DRC and Nigeria all have active or recent cases of the Bundibugyo strain, while Uganda had cases earlier in the year but has since been declared Ebola-free.
The Nigeria patient is the Ugandan-born wife of a Swiss diplomat based in Abuja. Authorities in Uganda said she had travelled to eastern DRC before transiting through Uganda. But the WHO and Africa’s top health agency said on Thursday they had not received confirmed information that the woman travelled to the DRC.
A Swiss government statement to the Reuters news agency also said the patient is believed to have contracted the disease while travelling in Uganda.
Wessam Mankoula, the head of Emergency Preparedness and Response at the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC), said on Thursday that both the first Nigerian case and the first Kenyan case had left Entebbe on October 3, and that a possible encounter between them was under investigation.
Ugandan authorities rejected the suggestion that she was infected in the country. Government spokesman Alan Kasujja told the AFP news agency that it was “preposterous” to link Uganda to the case simply because she had holidayed there.
However, Mankoula said there was no validated information that she had been to DRC, and Jean Kaseya, the Africa CDC director general, said the same. Pavel Ursu, the WHO representative in Nigeria, said the information given to the organisation included no travel outside Uganda.
Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response manager, said on Thursday the source of her infection was still unknown as health authorities were working to piece together her travel history.
Investigators were looking at which Abuja health facilities she visited between the onset of symptoms and her hospitalisation 48 hours later, he added.
An increase in numbers
Kenya’s Ministry of Health confirmed its first case earlier this month and had reported eight more since. Patrick Amoth, the Health Ministry’s director-general, said officials had traced all 135 contacts of the first case.
Nigeria is now tracing 44 contacts, and Mankoula said more had since been identified but did not give a new number.
The current outbreak is the deadliest in DRC’s history, according to the country’s health authorities. It has killed more than 4,000 people out of more than 9,000 confirmed cases since May.
Neighbouring Uganda recorded 20 confirmed cases, including 15 imported from the DRC, and two deaths, before it was declared Ebola-free in August.
The Africa CDC has warned of an “extremely serious threat”, with the fatality rate in DRC approaching 50 percent.

Quick hits: Bavuma hides from Smith implosion as Boland outgrits batters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:30:31 UTC
04:30:31 KST

Temba Bavuma turns his back as Steve Smith throws his wicket away, while nightwatchman Scott Boland shows the batters how it's done as the Aussies go down in Gqeberha.
Here are the quick hits from the final day of the second Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Head passes 100 but can't go on
Travis Head began day five needing 13 runs for a gritty, fighting century.
And after a two-hour rain delay, the punchy southpaw reached three figures with relative ease, bringing up the milestone with two leg-side boundaries against South African destroyer Marco Jansen in the sixth over of the day.
His celebrations were understandably muted given the state of the game, with his helmet staying in place as he raised his bat and a grin not even threatening to peek through his grill.
It was just Head's second overseas ton after his effort in the 2023 World Test Championship final at the Oval against India, and first against a team on its home patch.
But Head was unable to set up for the long haul his team so craved, with the Australian departing just after the first drinks break, chopping on while attempting a cut shot that was never there.
Head was out for 121 and Australia was 5-209.
2. Boland shows batters how it's done
By now, Australian cricket fans should know better than to doubt Scott Boland.
But even the most optimistic of those watching back home surely wouldn't have expected the nightwatchman to outlast both Head and Steve Smith, take his innings deep into the day and soak up a staggering 166 deliveries.
There were a couple of streaky moments, sure, but Boland made his luck more than he rode it, defending with the kind of authority and simplicity his more celebrated batting teammates were so desperately lacking throughout the Test.
He even played a few memorable shots, including an immaculate straight drive back past South Africa spearhead Kagiso Rabada.
But finally, in the second over after tea, Boland's marathon vigil was over, with Wiaan Mulder producing a jagging peach to have the brave nightwatchman bowled through the gate for a new Test best of 40.
3. Bavuma can't watch as Smith throws it away
It was the moment — and didn't Temba Bavuma know it.
The South Africa captain just couldn't watch as Steve Smith top-edged a Kagiso Rabada bouncer high into the blue Gqeberha sky, turning his back completely as Matthew Breetzke raced back and settled under the ball.
It was a rash, ugly shot from Smith, and certainly not one befitting of a man tasked with saving a Test match.
But for a moment, it looked like he was going to get away with it.
Having just-about settled underneath the ball, Breetzke juggled once and then twice before securing the wicket that was destined to end the Australian resistance.
Smith, perhaps still struggling with his neck issue from day four, was out for 3 and Australia was 6-255.
4. Mulder does damage after tea
With four wickets still in reserve, Australia reached tea still with a sniff of pulling off one of the great escapes.
But in removing Australia's best two batters, the Proteas had already done the hard part, and there would have been no panic as they readied themselves for the game's final stanza.
And in the opening exchanges of what was being sold as a marathon, 44-over evening session, all-rounder Mulder struck not once, but twice.
First, he ended Boland with that divine off-cutter; then he produced something similarly inspired to send the newly-arrived Pat Cummins packing for 4.
At 8-262, it was all beginning to unravel.
There was only one thing that could save the Aussies now ...
5. South Africa beats descending gloom
All of a sudden, things were beginning to darken in Gqeberha.
With ominous clouds gathering on the outskirts of the oval and ground staff poised to pounce at the boundary rope, the South Africans were in a race with the elements.
Two wickets were needed.
Well aware of the descending gloom, Bavuma threw the ball to his premier spearhead.
And Rabada delivered in the first over of his spell, bowling Mitchell Starc with the tailender attempting an ugly and wholly unnecessary slog.
But with the skies continuing to intimidate, we were treated to surely one of the most farcical drinks breaks in Test history.
Those five lost minutes, however, were not enough to save the Australians.
The heavens never did open, and number 11 Josh Hazlewood was promptly caught behind the wicket, confirming a chastening innings and 31-run defeat for Australia and a richly deserved series-levelling triumph for the South Africans.

Monet’s Iris fetches €50 million at Paris auction

Monet’s Iris fetches €50 million at Paris auction
- Claude Monet’s “Iris” sold for €50 million in Paris, the highest auction price ever for art in France. It had been kept in the Schlumberger family home and was known only from a black-and-white photo.
- The painting was bought by Jeanne Schlumberger and was made in Monet’s later years. Sotheby’s said the sale marked the centenary of Monet’s death, with Paris exhibitions honouring him.
- Three Paul Cezanne works were withdrawn before the auction after a deal to return them to Aix-en-Provence. Christie’s also sold 26 works for €41.6 million, including Monet, Renoir and Picasso pieces.
AI generated
PARIS - Iris, a monumental painting by Impressionist Claude Monet, sold for €50 million (S$70 million) including buyer fees in Paris on Oct 22, becoming the most expensive artwork ever sold at auction in France.
The 1.60m high and 1.8m wide work had never left the billionaire Schlumberger family’s mansion in Paris and was known only through a black-and-white photograph.
It was acquired by Jeanne Schlumberger (1889–1983), according to Thomas Bompard, co-head of the Modern and Contemporary Art Department at Sotheby’s France.
Iris had been estimated at between €22 million and €30 million, “the highest valuation ever given to a painting offered at auction in France,” Sotheby’s noted when presenting the sale.
It was painted by Monet in his twilight years.
Alongside Iris, three other canvases by Monet were included in the sale, among them “Saule Pleureur” (Weeping Willow), valued at €9 million to €12 million.
The sale comes in the year marking the centenary of Monet’s death on Dec 5, 1926, which is being commemorated by two Paris exhibitions – Monet, Painting Time and Stories Of Landscapes, From Monet To Hockney.
Three paintings by Paul Cezanne classified as “national treasures” were withdrawn from the sale a few hours before the auction began “with a view to their return to the artist’s hometown, Aix-en-Provence,” Sotheby’s said.
It followed an agreement between the current owners and the city of Aix-en-Provence, which, with the support of the French culture ministry, is considering acquiring these works.
Another Paris auction by Christie’s on Oct 22 saw 26 works being sold, including two Monet paintings – “Bord des falaises a Pourville”, which went for €12.7 million and “Trois pots de tulipes”, which sold for €3.1 million.
A work by Pierre-Auguste Renoir, “Jeunes filles au bord de la mer,” fetched €5.8 million, while “Nature morte au gruyere” by Pablo Picasso sold for €3 million.
The total amount of Christie’s sale was €41.6 million, buyers fees included. AFP

Omar recalled waking around 6 a.m. to Homeland Security investigators banging on her door with a warrant. They searched for four or five hours and seized 17 items, including phones, notebooks, a Somali language children's book and a vintage camera that her husband had received as a gift, she said.
The Justice Department has shared few details about the case other than saying it was a criminal investigation.

Congressional Democrats also questioned the timing. The Justice Department has historically avoided overt investigative actions involving candidates in the immediate run-up to an election.

Multipolarity and peace take centre stage at 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:23:30 UTC
04:23:30 KST

The emergence of a multipolar world, Europe’s future role and approaches to ending the war in Ukraine have dominated the opening day of the 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum in Istanbul.
Political, business and academic figures from more than 30 countries gathered at Ciragan Palace on Thursday to discuss how to navigate the changing global order without fuelling further conflict.
Discussions repeatedly returned to the need for dialogue and a new balance of power among the US, Russia, Europe and other global and regional powers.
Türkiye prioritises stability amid global uncertainty
In his opening remarks, Turkish Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said conflicts, supply chain disruptions and rising commodity prices were putting mounting pressure on the global economy.
Türkiye’s response centres on maintaining macro-financial stability and strengthening its resilience to external shocks, he said.
Ankara would maintain a data-dependent, restrictive monetary policy, rebuild fiscal buffers and accelerate its green transformation to reduce reliance on imported primary energy, Simsek added.
He also highlighted Türkiye’s diplomatic role amid growing geopolitical tensions, saying the country benefits from “stability, peace and prosperity” in surrounding regions and continues to invest in mediation and dialogue.
US faces era of 'permanent rivalry'
Speaking at a special session of the forum, Thomas Graham, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and former senior US official on Russia policy, argued that Europe would have to play a central role, while describing the changing international system as an unprecedented challenge for Washington.
"For the first time in history, the United States faces a multipolar order from which it cannot withdraw," Graham said.
The US could no longer dominate the international system as it had during earlier periods, he said, arguing that Washington instead had to adapt to an era of "permanent rivalry" with other major powers.
That would require avoiding direct conflict, particularly given the destructive capacity of modern weapons, while maintaining enough cooperation to address transnational challenges.
Graham said the objective should be to establish regional equilibria in Europe, the Middle East and East Asia that could ultimately underpin a broader Eurasian balance.
He rejected the idea that Washington, Moscow and Beijing could determine the future of the rest of the world among themselves, saying Europe remained a critical part of any such arrangement.
Türkiye's role in emerging multipolar order
Necmeddin Bilal Erdogan, chairman of the Ilim Yayma Foundation, placed Türkiye's growing regional role within the same shift toward a more multipolar international system.
Erdogan said regional actors should be encouraged to take greater responsibility for their own security and future, arguing that those living in a particular region ultimately bear the greatest consequences of instability there.
Türkiye, he said, had sought to play such a role through efforts concerning Syria, Iraq and the Caucasus and its ability to maintain dialogue with competing sides.
Erdogan called for dialogue channels to remain open despite conflicts and political disagreements, saying prejudices and double standards in international affairs were eroding trust between countries.
He argued that both Türkiye and Russia were part of the broader European space and that losing sight of such historical and geographic realities amid current conflicts would make prospects for peace more difficult.
He also linked the debate over international security to wider questions about technological and economic development, questioning the purpose of advances in areas such as artificial intelligence if they failed to contribute to peace, human welfare and greater equality.
'Without Europe there can be no peace'
Romano Prodi, former president of the European Commission and former Italian prime minister, recalled a dramatically different atmosphere in Russia-Europe relations two decades ago, saying cooperation between the two sides had once appeared capable of reaching much further.
The war in Ukraine had since made the divide extremely difficult to overcome, he said, while a succession of conflicts from Ukraine to Sudan, Gaza and Iran had created an increasingly dangerous international environment.
"It is time to change," Prodi said, arguing that Europe had been marginalised amid contacts between Russia and the US, partly because of its own internal divisions and weaknesses.
But excluding the continent from a future settlement would be a mistake, he said.
"Without Europe there can be no peace," Prodi said, stressing the bloc's economic weight, technological capabilities and experience in overcoming historical conflicts.
Referring to discussions about a potential understanding among major powers, Prodi used the analogy of a "little Yalta," suggesting that the world could be moving toward negotiations in which major powers establish new rules for managing relations.
He cautioned, however, that a potential US-Russia energy understanding alone could not resolve broader international problems and that any durable arrangement would also require Europe's participation.
Approaches to ending Ukraine war
The discussions also focused on possible paths toward ending the war in Ukraine.
Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's special representative for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries and CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, said Moscow was seeking a permanent end to hostilities and a stable European security architecture rather than temporary ceasefires.
"It's not about temporary ceasefires. It's not about temporary solutions," Dmitriev said, arguing that an interim arrangement could eventually lead to renewed hostilities.
He said recent US-Russia discussions had been positive in this regard and praised efforts by the Trump administration to balance the interests of Russia, Ukraine and Europe in search of a lasting settlement.
Graham said permanent peace could not realistically emerge from a single agreement but would have to develop through a longer process.
"To demand permanent peace as a condition for a ceasefire actually is a call for continued warfare," he said.
He said negotiations could first establish principles and parameters for a future settlement, followed by a ceasefire that would allow detailed talks to continue in a less volatile environment.
Such an outcome would require concessions from both Russia and Ukraine and active European participation, he added.
Dmitriev urges renewed Russia-Europe economic ties
Beyond the Ukraine negotiations, Dmitriev argued that economic ties could eventually help rebuild relations between Russia and Europe.
He said there was "no question" that Russia wanted to and would cooperate with Europe, while criticising European efforts to increase defence spending and rejecting claims that Moscow posed a threat to the continent.
Dmitriev also urged European business leaders to press policymakers more forcefully over restrictions on access to the Russian market and the economic consequences of reduced Russian energy supplies.
In separate remarks during the discussion, he argued that the resumption of broader Russian energy supplies to Europe was ultimately "economically inevitable."
He also said Russia-US economic cooperation could expand beyond energy, pointing to potential collaboration in areas including fertilizers.

Trump's Pentagon breaks world? Just historic globe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:12:00 UTC
04:12:00 KST

Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth asked aides to retrieve a globe linked to legendary World War II General Dwight Eisenhower, only for them to break it, a report said Thursday.
The large orb fell while being carried by untrained staff, resulting in the loss of a large chunk of the world near Antarctica, The Washington Post said.
The Post reported that historic items are typically moved around the Pentagon premises by trained curators. However, Hegseth's office had dispatched its own team.
Photographs published by the Post showed the hole in the Antarctica area and an accompanying plaque identifying it as one of two nearly identical, historic "Eisenhower Globes" in the Pentagon's possession.
The Army acknowledged the damage in a statement to the Post. Army spokesperson Christopher Surridge said the globe was damaged during an "attempted move" on Feb. 3. Aside from the hole, "the spherical portion of the globe was detached from the metal mounting that allows it to rotate," Surridge was quoted.
After the report, a Defense Department official provided the Post with a brief, unattributed statement acknowledging the mishap.
"Accidents happen," it said. "We are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired."
President Donald Trump's secretary of defense has focused on promoting a muscular image for the U.S. military, starting by attempting to restore the Department of War name, which was dropped in 1947 for the Department of Defense.
Hegseth, who rose as far as major during an Army National Guard career before becoming a Fox News host, regularly does televised exercise routines with troops. He has ordered mandatory testosterone screening for male military staff over 30.
He is currently overseeing the eight-month war against Iran, which Trump has promised repeatedly to bring to a rapid conclusion.
Eisenhower led the U.S. war effort against Nazi Germany, commanding the D-Day landings that launched the phase of conflict leading to Adolf Hitler's defeat.
A five-star general, he was then elected president in 1952, taking the helm of the White House as the Cold War gathered pace. He was often photographed posing alongside elaborate globes.

UN says settler attacks, Israeli restrictions block Palestinians from olive harvest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:11:59 UTC
04:11:59 KST

Rabia Iclal Turan
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The UN said Thursday that recurrent attacks and Israeli access restrictions are preventing Palestinians in the occupied West Bank from safely harvesting their olive crops.
Spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told a media briefing that Acting Special Coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov traveled to Jenin with diplomats from 13 member states to learn about challenges linked to the olive harvest and the prolonged displacement of Palestinian communities.
“In the village of Arraba, they heard from farmers growing olives about recurrent settler attacks, which, combined with Israeli access restrictions, are undermining food security,” said Dujarric. “Our humanitarian partners briefed the delegation on efforts to protect olive pickers, including by accompanying them to the groves and providing legal aid to challenge Israeli-imposed access restrictions.”
Dujarric said that Alakbarov indicated that “the harvest season should be a time of celebration, with up to 100,000 Palestinian households depending on olives for their livelihoods, but many Palestinians are being prevented from gathering their crops safely.”
“He said that crimes committed against them must stop, and the perpetrators must be held to account by the Israeli authorities,” said Dujarric.
“At a clinic in the city of Qabatiya, diplomats met with Palestinians who, since early 2025, have been prevented from returning to Jenin Camp by the Israeli authorities, where many of their homes have been destroyed,” he said.
Alakbarov “stressed that more funding is needed so that humanitarian organizations can help the displaced Palestinians and urged Israeli authorities to enable their safe and dignified return,” said Dujarric.
The visit came days after Israeli occupiers attacked a delegation that included European diplomats and Catholic Church officials near the town of Taybeh, east of Ramallah, according to the Palestinian Foreign Ministry.
Israeli Army Radio reported that seven masked attackers surrounded a diplomatic car and smashed a window of a Belgian consular vehicle, and that Israeli troops and police did not arrive for three hours.
The Israeli military described the attack as a “serious violent incident,” but said the delegation had not coordinated the visit in advance, and that no troops were present at the scene.
Occupier attacks have intensified since the olive harvest began earlier this month, with the Palestinian Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission reporting 40 attacks and violations against farmers, farmland and olive crops in a single day last weekend.

MOSCOW, October 22. /TASS/. Russians and Ukrainians are not merely close, they are genetically one people, Russian President Vladimir Putin told Vesti journalist Pavel Zarubin.
"These are a people very close to us," Putin said. "No matter how you look at it, recent genetic studies show that they are one people, Russians and Ukrainians."
At the same time, he expressed respect for the fact that a political division of the broader Russian nation had occurred historically.
"Someone has a different opinion, fine," he admitted. "Alright, we agree, this is how the history of Russia shaped out, and such are the realities of today. But everything is negotiable.".

21 years on, double life term for Jammu terror attack that killed baby, 2 others
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:02:53 UTC
04:02:53 KST

The court ordered that the fines be paid to those injured in the July 2005 terror attack
JAMMU: A Jammu court has imposed two life sentences and fines of Rs 2 lakh on Mohammed Sharief, a terrorist who gunned down three members of a family, including a six-month-old infant, in Ramban district’s Gool area over 21 years ago.In his order on Wednesday, principal sessions judge Ramban Ajay Kumar Gupta rejected defence arguments that the attack had taken place more than two decades ago when Sharief was young, his long incarceration and possibility of rehabilitation.Besides the life sentences, the court imposed two separate terms of 10 years on Sharief under various sections pertaining to murder and arms act offences. “All sentences shall run concurrently, while the period already spent in custody shall be set off in accordance with law,” the judge said.The court ordered that the fines be paid to those injured in the July 2005 terror attack and directed J&K State Legal Services Authority to provide compensation to heirs of the deceased and the survivors.Judge Gupta rejected defence arguments about the testimony of two injured eyewitnesses, saying they were reliable and corroborated by medical and other evidence. Defective investigations or delay in recording statements could not automatically result in acquittal when credible evidence otherwise established the accused’s guilt beyond reasonable doubt, the judge said.
Public prosecutor Wajid Ahmed pressed for maximum punishment under law, contending that the murder of three innocent family members, including the baby, and the use of an AK-47 rifle warranted a stringent sentence.The court considered aggravating and mitigating circumstances and held that although the crime was extremely grave, the case did not warrant the death penalty under the rarest of rare principle.

Indonesia records over 333,000 acute respiratory infection cases as fires rage in several regions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:00:02 UTC
04:00:02 KST

Saadet Gokce
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
Indonesia has recorded 333,470 cases of acute respiratory infections (ARIs) linked to forest and land fires in several regions, the Health Ministry said Thursday.
The ministry's director of environmental health, Then Suyanti, said that daily cases remained high, with 4,522 new cases reported, according to state-run news agency Antara.
She said the latest Air Pollutant Index showed that air quality in several areas had reached hazardous levels, particularly in six provinces prioritized for fire management: Riau, Jambi, South Sumatra, West Kalimantan, South Kalimantan and Central Kalimantan.
Suyanti said exposure to wildfire smoke, which contains fine particulate matter such as PM2.5, carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide and other organic compounds, can cause health problems. including ARIs, asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, eye and skin irritation and other systemic health effects.
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto said Thursday that if foreign-backed companies are responsible for recurring forest and land fires, those businesses could lose their operating permits, and revoked concessions could be reassigned to younger Indonesians.
"Regarding forest fires, there are indications that many foreign companies bear responsibility. They have held concessions for over a decade, yet some have committed violations three, four, or even a dozen times --some as many as 19 times," Prabowo said, adding that their permits should be revoked if they commit two violations.
Separately, thousands of students and others demonstrated in Samarinda, the capital of East Kalimantan, demanding the government declare forest and land fires a national disaster, according to iNews.
Indonesia is experiencing an unusually prolonged dry season, with El Nino contributing to conditions favorable for wildfires.

EU Sanctions Envoy Pushes for Action Against Rusal’s Irish Alumina Refinery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:56:00 UTC
03:56:00 KST

Material produced in a major metals refinery in Ireland is “undoubtedly” going into Russia’s weapons supply chain, the European Union’s Sanctions Envoy David O’Sullivan said on Thursday, adding that “there is a very real issue to be addressed.”
The comments, made at the Institute for International and European Affairs (IIEA) in Dublin, come seven months after OCCRP and partners published an investigation showing that the Aughinish Alumina refinery in western Ireland was indirectly supplying Russian weapons producers.
As much as half of the alumina from the Aughinish refinery was shipped to smelters owned by its parent company, United Company Rusal, and used to produce aluminum. The metal was then sold to a trading company supplying dozens of EU-sanctioned Russian weapons manufacturers, OCCRP’s investigation showed.
Weapons made by these firms have leveled entire city blocks in Mariupol, struck a children’s hospital in Kyiv, and blown open an apartment building in western Ukraine, according to EU sanctions listings, Ukraine’s military intelligence, and the London-based Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
Aughinish Alumina's sales to Russia — which have increased since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — are entirely legal under EU trade rules. That is because although EU exports of finished aluminum are banned, shipments of the intermediate material alumina are not, partly as a result of lobbying years ago by Ireland, where Aughinish Alumina is an important employer.
OCCRP’s investigation sparked controversy in Ireland and internationally, and led to growing pressure to sanction EU alumina exports. The Irish government launched its own investigation, which reached an ambivalent conclusion, saying that a lack of data made it “difficult to ascertain where Russia is sourcing its tools and weapons from.” It shared its findings with the EU Commission in July.
O’Sullivan was less cautious in his assessment.
“The alumina goes to smelters in Russia, who produce stuff which undoubtedly goes at least in part to the military-industrial complex,” he said. “I've read the government report. I personally, I think there's no doubt the investigative journalists got it right.”
O’Sullivan did not say whether the EU would eventually ban alumina exports to Russia.
“I think there is a very real issue to be addressed. We just have to find the best way of doing it, which doesn't have unhelpful collateral consequences,” he said, noting that Aughinish Alumina also supplied smelters in Europe.
In July, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a visit to Dublin that “Every ton of raw material that ends in Russia is used against us. I do hope whatever we are doing now, we are cutting every possibility, every sphere for Russia to build up, to militarize itself.”
Aughinish Alumina has said that its material is not used to make weapons, and that almost all the alumina it sends to Russian smelters is solely used to produce aluminum for onward export out of Russia.
OCCRP’s original investigation was published in partnership with iStories, the Irish Times, KibOrg, De Tijd, The Guardian, and Delfi.

Space Force Picks Six Companies for Commercial Reserve Fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:52:34 UTC
03:52:34 KST

The Space Force has selected six commercial space domain awareness companies to support military operations with both steady-state and surge capacity, as part of the service’s new Commercial Augmentation Space Reserve.
Officials have been working since 2022 to establish a fleet of commercial satellites and other assets to provide capabilities like satellite imagery, space domain awareness, and communications during peacetime that can be surged on demand. The concept is not unlike the Air Force’s Civil Reserve Air Fleet, which leases aircraft capacity from commercial airliners for use during a conflict.
Last year, the Space Force announced it would pilot the CASR program with four unnamed companies who specialize in identifying and tracking objects in space—also called space domain awareness. The service awarded them 90-day contracts worth a combined $1.1 million, and in the ensuing months conducted a series of wargames and training events to better understand how to integrate their capabilities and services into its operations.
These new contracts announced Oct. 22 are meant to operationalize that capability and create a pool of CASR companies specifically focused on SDA. Those firms include:
- Anduril
- Intrack
- Slingshot
- LeoLabs
- EOS, an Australian firm
- Northstar, a Canadian firm
Space Force officials explained to reporters Oct. 21 at AFCEA’s annual Space Industry Days conference that the six companies initially tapped for CASR are firms that operators already trust today and would turn to should something happen on orbit that requires more visibility or object tracking capabilities. According to Lt. Col. Brandon Galindo, all of the companies in this initial cohort currently work with the Joint Commercial Operations Cell, a Space Force hub that integrates commercial space data and services and shares it with joint international partners.
“What we heard from the operational community is that … if something were to happen on orbit, debris or some breakup scenario, these are the companies on the commercial side that we would really depend upon,” Galindo said.
That said, the initial cohort of space domain awareness companies isn’t meant to be static. Col. Tim Trimailo, director of the Commercial Space Office said other companies will have a chance to onboard in the future.
“This is not a chalk line that we’ve snapped that says you can never get into CASR for the space domain awareness mission,” he said during. “It’s a living program. So, we’re always looking for new entrants, new opportunities, new companies that have proven themselves and that are trusted partners to be part of CASR.”
While these are operational contracts, Trimailo said the initial dollar values—which he didn’t disclose—are fairly low. As the Space Force gets a handle on how much demand there is for the capabilities from operators within combatant commands, it will look at options to adjust funding.
Galindo echoed that sentiment, describing the program’s work to establish the reserve as an iterative process that will include regular updates within each mission area as well as opportunities to add new mission areas under the CASR umbrella. He also noted that contract terms and strategies will vary by company and by mission.
“It’s not cookie cutter,” he said. “Each mission area is so unique, the companies within a mission area are unique. And we love that, because then we can assemble the best companies that offer something unique and we can put them together.”
The Commercial Space Office has started to look at what its next CASR mission will be and is considering commercial satellite communications, launch, and telemetry, tracking, and command—which would leverage the Space Force’s existing Joint Antenna Marketplace—as potential options.

The Ukraine conflict has clearly demonstrated that Russia cannot be defeated on the battlefield, the president argued, adding that the idea of inflicting a “strategic defeat” on the country was “simply not realistic.” Putin expressed hope that those still entertaining such a scenario would “come to recognize the realities of modern life.” 
“They will hopefully realize that it is better to live in harmony with Russia – a path that truly serves the interests of their own peoples. If you look at the political processes currently underway in Europe, it becomes evident that the European peoples have no desire to go to war with Russia,” the president stated.
In fact, Russia does not want to fight Ukraine either, Putin said, pointing at the shared past and the longstanding ties between Russians and Ukrainians. Still, Kiev itself chose war in 2014, when it opted to fight the people of then-Ukrainian Donbass, who had rejected the Maidan coup, the president said, adding that Ukraine has also rejected Moscow’s repeated attempts to mediate that conflict.
“If the current Ukrainian leadership wishes to fight, then let them fight. But why do they expect everyone else to foot the bill and supply them with weapons? I suppose they have their arguments – likely rooted in past promises of help. But it seems that the ‘help’ was intended to last until the very last Ukrainian,” Putin said.
The Russian president also touched upon the territorial issues between Moscow and Kiev, pointing out that the loss of formerly Ukrainian regions should not be treated as such, since they were never Ukrainian in the first place.
“It is not their territory, it is a part of historic Russia,” he stressed, adding that local residents voted to secede from Ukraine and reunify with Russia.
Russia remains ready to resolve the Ukraine conflict through diplomacy, Putin said, reiterating Moscow’s willingness to resume trilateral talks with Washington and Kiev.
“The purpose of these negotiations will be to discuss how to ensure the security of both Ukraine and Russia following the conclusion of peace agreements, specifically, definitive, long-term agreements, rather than a mere temporary cessation of hostilities,” the president said, adding that the discussions should involve a wider all-European security architecture.
Moscow announced it was ready to resume the trilateral talks following Putin’s meeting with US special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday. Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov subsequently said the next round could take place in Abu Dhabi around mid-November.

He stressed that the architecture of international settlements has undergone fundamental changes over the past four years. By 2025, complex functional systems for foreign trade settlements had emerged.
"In 2025-2026, businesses moved toward widespread adoption of all available foreign trade settlement arrangements. According to aggregated industry data, the monthly volume of cross-border payments by Russian businesses stabilized at the equivalent of $12-14 bln in 2024-2025," Murychev said.
He noted that amid changing conditions for foreign economic activity, businesses need a systemic solution rather than temporary adjustments. "At the RSPP level, we have identified the following priorities. First, creating our own payment infrastructure under the control of a Russian bank. Second, developing infrastructure controlled by major importers and exporters. Third, developing barter arrangements, with mandatory simplification of accounting and taxation at the legislative level," Murychev said.
He also identified other priorities, including developing insurance for foreign trade transactions, increasing the settlement capacity of Russian banks’ foreign branches, and establishing a legislative framework for the use of digital financial assets in foreign economic activity.

A Norwegian auction house canceled the sale of a valuable parchment fragment from a Torah scroll, following intervention by Israel’s Foreign Ministry.
On Sunday, Valkyrie Historical Auctions listed on its auction itinerary a “Very Old Piece of Jewish Torah Roll Plundered by German SS Soldiers During Shoah.”
In the item description, the auction house wrote that the fragment was sent to a relative as a souvenir. This piece is handwritten in calfskin and shows signs of damage, probably from a fire. The fragment is said to have been used by an SS soldier as wrapping paper to mail a package to an address in Germany. The soldier’s field unit and the address to which he sent the package are still partially legible in the handwriting. The estimated sale price was listed as $1,500-$2,000.
Valkyrie Historical Auctions is a web-based platform auctioneer offering authentic historical items to collectors and museums worldwide. It specializes in historical artifacts from World War II and Holocaust-related material.
One thousand two hundred and fifty items were for sale in Sunday’s auction, ranging from postcards to private notebooks and photo albums.
Foreign Ministry outraged by sale
The news that the item was for sale sparked outrage from Israel’s Foreign Ministry, which called the sale “a Nazi celebration in Oslo.”
“It is a parchment sheet from a Torah scroll that was desecrated, looted, and defaced by the SS and was even used as wrapping paper by SS soldiers. At the same time, the Norwegian government is expected to cancel its financial support for visits by Norwegian students to extermination camps. Auctions of sacred texts looted by the Nazis: ‘In.’ Visits to extermination camps: ‘Out,’” the ministry said, calling on the Norwegian government to put “an immediate stop to this moral obscenity.”
Recently, in its national budget proposal, the Norwegian government suggested ceasing funding for school trips to World War II concentration camps.
However, following the end of the auction, the item was listed as sold for $8,500, with an additional 25% buyer’s premium payable to the auction house, bringing the total to $10,625
A spokesperson for Valkyrie Historical Auctions told Norwegian media outlet Verdinytt that the Torah parchment had been withdrawn from sale just 10 minutes before the auction was due to begin, due to the Israeli Foreign Ministry’s strong reaction.
Regarding why it was listed as “sold,” the spokesperson said that the auction house had no practical way of removing the item from the auction on such short notice before it began, and had instead placed its own bid that was so high that nobody would outbid it.
Scroll set to be donated to nonprofit in California
Allegedly, the scroll will be donated to RUTH – Remember Us The Holocaust, a nonprofit organization in San Diego, California.
“We are currently working with some organizations in the United States that display Holocaust-related artifacts in public spaces and preserve them for educational purposes. We believe that such an institution is a far more appropriate place for this piece than a private sale,” a spokesperson for the Foreign Ministry told Verdinytt.
On Elpeleg, a Norwegian-Israeli activist, told The Jerusalem Post that he hopes the same approach will be taken with all other personal belongings that once belonged to Jewish victims of the Holocaust.
“These items should be returned to their rightful owners or their descendants. Where that is not possible, they should be donated to the Jewish Museum in Oslo,” he said.
Elpeleg also said it is important that museums around the world dedicated to Holocaust education be given priority when purchasing historical artefacts from World War II, so that these objects can be used to educate future generations, preserve historical memory, and honor the victims of the Holocaust.
The Jerusalem Post reached out to the auction house for comment.

High Court blocks Likud-backed digital voter tracking at polling stations ahead of elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:48:45 UTC
03:48:45 KST

Ahead of the elections, the High Court of Justice ruled Thursday that party representatives serving on polling-station committees or as observers cannot digitally count voters who have cast ballots and relay those totals in real time to the parties they represent.
The 2-1 decision follows a September ruling barring those representatives from reporting which identifiable voters had voted. The latest dispute concerned whether they could instead send numerical totals without identifying anyone.
Justices Khaled Kabub and Ruth Ronnen comprised the majority, with Justice David Mintz dissenting. The court issued its operative decision on Thursday and said its reasons would follow.
The ruling came on a petition by the Israel Democracy Guard organization challenging permission granted by Dean Livne, acting director-general of the Central Elections Committee, the body responsible for administering Knesset elections.
In an October 14 clarification issued following a request from Likud attorney Ilan Bombach, Livne said polling-station committee members and party observers could use digital tools to count voters and send numerical information to their parties, provided they did not identify the voters.
High Court restricts voter tracking by political parties
Parties generally use turnout information to direct their efforts to get supporters to the polls. Earlier reporting systems, including applications such as Elector, enabled campaigns to compare information from polling stations with their own databases and contact likely supporters who had not yet voted.
The legal dispute began with restrictions imposed in August by Supreme Court Deputy President Noam Sohlberg, chairman of the Central Elections Committee (CEC). After Likud challenged his decision, the issue went before the full committee, which voted in September to allow the reporting practice to continue under restrictions.
On September 17, the High Court unanimously overturned that permission. It held that party representatives at polling stations perform public functions and lack legal authority to pass identifiable voter information to their parties for campaign purposes. The court also found that the practice infringed voters’ privacy.
The new petition argued that removing voters’ names did not resolve the separate question of whether officials working inside polling stations could collect information for party headquarters.
The organization maintained that its role was to administer and oversee voting, and that a legitimate interest in encouraging turnout did not authorize it to transmit information obtained in that role.
The state and Likud defended Livne’s clarification, arguing that numerical reporting was different from identifying individual voters and could help parties encourage participation.
They maintained that the clarification did not change the existing legal position and had been issued with Sohlberg’s approval.
The dispute also concerned who should provide turnout figures. Under an arrangement previously established by Sohlberg, the CEC was to publish turnout data for each ordinary polling station at least four times during Election Day.
That official reporting mechanism differs from the continuous updates Livne’s clarification would have allowed party representatives to send directly to their headquarters.

People power in the suburbs exposes the fragility of the AI boom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:47:44 UTC
03:47:44 KST

analysis
NEXTDC slump and Firmus float flop signal investor doubts over AI boom
A small data centre operator with three sites being briefly valued at $44 billion, more than Woolworths.
A neighbourhood dispute over power poles that wipes $3 billion off a listed company's value in a single day.
And trillion-dollar global infrastructure build-out getting a wake-up call from the suburbs.
The fragility of the AI boom has been on full display in recent weeks.
An industry that has ignored the concept of "social licence" is colliding with people committed to their communities. And investors are feeling the financial consequences.
Australia ringing the alarm on AI valuations
It's a long way from West Footscray to Wall Street.
But as information has come to move in milliseconds, the titans behind trillion-dollar deals in our AI-boom economy may have spent time looking up "WeFo" on Google Maps, reading about plans for Tasmanian data centres, and wondering: is this where it started to unravel?
Let's step back.
Shares in data centre operator NEXTDC fell 42 per cent in a single day after the company revealed that delays in getting power to a proposed expansion of its massive complex in inner-west Melbourne meant its future earnings would be cut by a third.
Those delays were due to an act of civil disobedience.
When power company Jemena's crews dug holes in Sanderson Street, Yarraville, a suburb next to West Footscray, residents who had warily watched the approach of industrial-scale power poles took action, leaving cars and bins in the street to block the workers' access.
Unable to get equipment in position, the Jemena crews filled in the holes they had prepared, left and have not been back.
That quiet act of suburban defiance not only stopped infrastructure meant to provide the juice for the next stage of NEXTDC's West Footscray data centre, it resulted in the company's very bad day on the stock exchange on Wednesday.
Firmus hit a similar hurdle.
The AI data centre company wanted to list on the stock exchange with an initial public offering (IPO) that would have valued it at about $44 billion.
It would have been one of the five biggest floats in the world this year, the biggest in Australia since Telstra went from being government-owned to listed on the markets.
But it fell apart. For one reason, and then a lot of them.
The key reason was that large investors didn't think the company was worth what it thought it was. They refused to buy it at $11 a share, which would have made it one of Australia's 20 largest firms, more valuable than toll road operator Transurban and supermarket giant Coles.
But the others are important, too: growing community opposition to power and water-hungry data centres and the transmission lines needed to feed them; fears about the job-killing nature of artificial intelligence; the collision of election cycles in the US and Australia with voter unhappiness about economic instability and uncertainty.
AI not dead, but hitting resistance
The idea of social licence is that it's the ongoing acceptance and approval of an organisation's activities by people affected by them and society at large.
Whaling has lost its social licence. Very few countries now kill whales.
AI and data centre companies, spawned from the "move fast, break things" ethos of the tech sector, rapidly evolved from medium-sized warehouses in industrial areas to massive facilities closer to homes.
They became the physical manifestation of people's fears about AI. At the end of their street.
Standing outside NEXTDC's massive facility, the behemoth is undeniably dystopian. Devoid of any visible staff, the entirely black box rises vastly above the single-story brick and weatherboard houses on the other side of the street.
Protests in Europe and the US tuned leaders to the bad vibes coming from constituents. They didn't see the benefits of facilities that drove up power bills, drained precious water resources, and seemed to be in the business of making masses of people unemployed. The number of jobs in data centres, post-construction, is minimal.
But don't expect the sector to go away. As analysts at Morningstar detail, NEXTDC's assets, "both current and planned, are still in great demand". In addition, community concerns over the centres may increase costs and force new ones further away from built-up areas:
"However, this will affect all developers, will likely be factored into new contracts, and will likely make existing data centres even more valuable."
A single-street power pole dispute that costs $3 billion
There's a reason NEXTDC's difficulties are getting attention. It exposes the fragility of the AI boom, already unfolding on a scale the world has rarely seen.
Filip Tortevski, senior analyst at Wealth Within, calls it the "first serious warning shot" as investors weigh if this is an isolated incident or the beginning of something much bigger.
"What's concerning isn't simply the $140 million in revenue affected by electricity delays," they write.
Loading...
"It's the potential chain reaction nobody was pricing in. NEXTDC has acknowledged that delayed customer billing could affect its ability to draw on $6.7 billion in available debt facilities. It has also warned that the delays could affect property valuations, with the financial impact still unknown.
"Think about that. A delay in connecting electricity can potentially affect revenue, financing flexibility and asset values simultaneously."
UniSuper's chief investment officer John Pearce helps manage $175 billion in assets.
Before the Firmus float was pulled, he wished the company well and explained why the fund wouldn't invest a cent in it.
"It all comes down to valuation. We think that Firmus indeed has a compelling story. It just doesn't have a compelling valuation. At the current valuation, it's priced to perfection. So much has to go right to justify the valuation."
Priced to perfection. The amount the company is valued at requires every single plan to run perfectly, in every element.
Many of our large AI and data centre companies appear to rest on the same belief.
This is a world of storms and natural disasters. Of electricity pole installation. Of technologies from labs we hadn't heard of three months ago. Of changes in government. Of residents who don't feel heard. Of shipping delays. Of construction challenges.
Our world is a lot of things. Perfect it is not.

This implant burns up excess blood sugar with electricity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:43:34 UTC
03:43:34 KST

A new wireless implant could burn up excess sugar in the blood, letting people with type 2 diabetes live healthier lives without having to completely rely on medication.
Traditional drugs used for diabetes such as insulin, metformin and glucagonlike peptide 1 (GLP-1) agonists all treat the condition by effectively forcing the body to keep glucose levels under control—but these treatments are prone to side effects and many involve taking a fixed quantity of medication regularly despite blood sugar changing with mood, sleep and meals. Automated insulin pumps can adjust dosing to a patient’s blood sugar in real time, but they still deliver drugs that can linger in the body.
“We wanted to have a completely new principle,” says Martin Fussenegger, the study’s senior author and a bioengineer at the Swiss Federal Institute of Technology Zurich. For a new study in mice, published in Science, he and his team abandoned drugs altogether by developing a below-the-skin implant that chemically eliminates glucose from the blood on its own rather than triggering the body’s own mechanisms in order to do so.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The device, called ECHO, which stands for electrocatalytic closed-loop health optimization, looks like a little flat rectangular chip, roughly the size of a USB stick. It contains a graphite wafer that carries an electric current, embedded with branching structures of gold nanoflakes that are studded with even smaller spheres of platinum. These structures work as a catalyst—a substance that speeds up a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process. The implant is operated and powered wirelessly, and when voltage is applied, the surface oxidizes glucose into an easily processed metabolite called gluconate. The mouse subjects’ bodies burned roughly a fifth of the resulting gluconate for energy, and the rest was flushed out through the kidneys.
Blood carries important molecules similar to glucose such as fructose, galactose and lactose, but the implant successfully targeted glucose specifically. Fussenegger admits the researchers don’t yet know why it is so successful, although that likely relates to the particular combination of gold and platinum. “We have no functional or structural explanation for that. We did not design for it,” Fussenegger says. “The specificity is, I would say, a lucky strike.”
In diabetic mice with obesity, the implant brought blood glucose levels under control within an hour when turned on, and repeated treatment held it there for six weeks. The mice also showed reduced triglycerides—a type of fat associated with disease risk—and lower body weight.
The team also tested the implant while connected via a smartphone to a commercial continuous glucose monitor, which relayed blood sugar readings that allowed the smartphone to turn the implant on and off as needed. For two weeks, this closed-loop system ran with no human involvement.
Many glucose-focused implants under development rely on capsules containing engineered cells that secrete therapeutic proteins—these tend not to last because they get sealed off by scar tissue in the body. But for ECHO, the mice’s tissue showed no signs of inflammation around the implant, no scarring and no leached metal. Implants removed after six weeks still worked, and some remained active even after three months under the skin, according to the study.
“Six weeks of operational stability is already well beyond the current technology,” says Luisa Torsi, a chemist at the University of Bari Aldo Moro in Italy, who was not involved in the study. “The crucial next steps are to establish long-term tissue compatibility, sustained catalytic activity and safe, effective glucose removal at the scale required for human treatment.”
A mouse has roughly two milliliters of blood, whereas humans typically hold five liters—ECHO would need to scale up to function at that level. Fussenegger is confident about that task, however. As part of the study, the team circulated sugary fluid through a five-liter flask—a stand-in for human blood volume—and the implant cleared it just as efficiently.
Because the device is small and sits just under the skin, Fussenegger expects the implantation procedure in humans would require a minor incision rather than complex surgery. “If it’s possible to do this maybe every three months or up to a year, and then ‘I can forget my diabetes,’ I think people would be happy,” he says.

Attorney-general urged to step in as court data breach concerns grow
In short:
The Coalition and the Greens are calling on the Attorney-General to set up an independent audit after several court data breaches.
New emails reveal Federal Court CEO Sia Lagos was notified of a 2014 breach.
What's next?
The Federal Court said it was reviewing a report into the latest data breach. The Office of the Australian Information Commissioner is also looking into the issue.
An integrity crisis in Australia's court system has deepened, prompting calls from the Coalition and the Greens for the Attorney-General to step in and set up an independent audit.
Revelations that highly sensitive court data was accessed in India on at least two occasions has sparked national security fears.
Now, internal court emails have revealed the Federal Court CEO was notified in 2016 of the first data breach — an incident for which no action was taken.
However, a spokesperson for the Federal Court said its CEO, Sia Lagos, had no recollection of having been notified of the data breach by the then-deputy principal registrar.
Security concerns were first raised in 2014 by former Auscript national manager, Paul Cutbush, who made Public Interest Disclosures (PID) to both the family court and the Federal Court as well as the Australian Federal Police (AFP) about the offshoring of sensitive data.
In an email from then-Deputy Principal Registrar of the Federal Court John Mathieson to Mr Cutbush in 2016 he stated:
"I have notified Ms Sia Lagos, who is Acting Chief Executive Officer and Principal Registrar of the Federal Court, in Mr Soden's absence, as I am required to do so, of the decisions and determinations I have made under the [Public Interest Disclosure] Act."
A spokesperson for the Federal Court of Australia said it was "not accepted that there has been a failure to act" in either the data breach earlier this year or the historical incident.
"Ms Lagos did not have any recollection of a procedural notification she had received almost 10 years earlier concerning the Family Court of Australia and matters pre-dating the present administrative entity," the spokesperson said.
"Beyond that single notification, Ms Lagos had no involvement in the management of this matter."
Neither the Federal Court, nor the family court acted on the disclosures made to them by Mr Cutbush in 2014. The family court responded two years after the disclosures were made, classifying the breach as "minor and inconsequential" in emails seen by the ABC.
The family court has denied any current executives had knowledge of the first breach despite Mr Cutbush's disclosures.
Last week, Mr Cutbush said the most recent data breach was a "slap in the face" after his concerns were ignored in 2014.
Auscript was responsible for court transcription services in 2014 before VIQ Solutions took over around 2020.
A second data breach occurred earlier this year when VIQ was managing transcription services and the company was shutdown shortly after.
Cases heard in the Federal Court include critical human rights matters, industrial relations cases, taxation law and matters involving multi-million-dollar corporations while the Federal Circuit and Family Court hears migration cases, and matters involving child sexual abuse, domestic violence and property settlements.
It is unclear how many files were accessed in India during either of the offshoring incidents.
'Warning signs ignored by court leadership': Greens
A spokesperson for Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said the courts were "responsible for their own operation and management" — a position ridiculed by the Opposition.
Shadow Attorney-General Michaelia Cash said the latest developments strengthened the need for a full independent audit coordinated by the Attorney-General.
"I again call on the Attorney-General to take control of this matter and organise a whole-of-government response," she said.
"We need to know what has occurred and how widespread this issue is. It is not good enough for the Attorney-General to keep her head in the sand."
Greens Leader Senator David Shoebridge took aim at the court's leadership.
"It's almost impossible to believe that we are now facing another round of obfuscation from the Federal Court," he said.
"These data breach issues date back to 2014 and it appears that at least some senior staff members of the court have known this.
"This requires a prompt and public explanation from the court.
"Family court transcripts hold some of the most private and painful moments in people's lives, and twice now that material has gone offshore while the warning signs were ignored by the leadership of the court.
"The Attorney-General keeps saying the responsibility is solely with the court, but the fact is the listed entity is under her administrative authority so she also has a clear role here.
"The Attorney-General should order a forensic audit across every agency in her portfolio that used Auscript and VIQ transcription services to provide people with real certainty about what on earth happened with their sensitive court data."
The Federal Court said it was currently reviewing a report by CyberCX into the latest data breach.
A privacy complaint has also been passed on to the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) regarding the offshoring of Australian citizen's data.
The Federal Court said it had provided information to the OAIC and the family court said it would "fully cooperate" with the OAIC or any other government inquiry.

The Trauma Recovery Centre's head of programs and founder of Doctors Against Violence Towards Women, Karen Williams, told SBS News that Australian women are "rightly" feeling unsafe.
"The reality is that it isn't actually safe for women. You don't want to gaslight people into thinking they shouldn't feel unsafe," she said.
"These things are happening on a significant level. It's not a one-off, occasional thing ... These are not small risks; they're real.
"We are powerless against it really ... There is a level of fear that women just live with and regard as normal."
She said the news of Haines' attack could exacerbate that fear for many women.
"Community is meant to be a place where you feel safe... but events like what's happened with Dr Haines make people think our community itself is not safe," she said.
"Dr Haines is someone who should have the resources and protections, and even she isn't safe from violence."
While media reporting of violence against women can be triggering and retraumatising for some, Williams said it's "the only sort of information or education women are getting on the risks they're exposed to".
"Everything we ever hear about is only through the media," she said. "They have a very important role in explaining to people that these risks do exist because they do."
No 'real deterrent' for violence against women
Williams believes reducing violence against women requires a "huge systems change" that begins with having "deterrents to harming women".
"There isn't a real deterrent. You can hurt women and get away with it ... and [perpetrators] know they can get away with it," she said.
She said that, until there is a "deterrent", people would "keep harming women".
For those experiencing distress, Williams recommends focusing on basic needs: physical exercise, eating well and creativity.
"We know from research that having physical capabilities does actually help, so getting out there and exercising and moving ... training your body to feel like you have some control over your body, feeling autonomous and empowered," she said.
"Music and creativity are also really important things for a person trying to regulate their nervous system."
Marie has started gardening, alongside seeking professional support and counselling, grounding techniques and leaning on her support network.
"I want to be able to present, and I want to be able to enjoy my life again because I don't feel like I've had any capacity to do so."
If you or someone you know is impacted by family and domestic violence or sexual assault, call 1800RESPECT on 1800 737 732, text 0458 737 732, or visit 1800RESPECT.org.au. In an emergency, call 000.
The Men’s Referral Service, operated by No to Violence, can be contacted on 1300 766 491.

====================================================================================================

A $3 billion downgrade could send a ripple through a surging Australian industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:40:36 UTC
03:40:36 KST

When energy provider Jemena announced on Wednesday that it had paused the installation of new 22-metre-tall concrete power poles needed for a nearby data centre, it triggered a chain reaction.
One of the country's biggest data centre operators, NEXTDC — which was forced to delay a planned expansion of its M3 data centre in West Footscray, Melbourne — quickly saw its market valuation drop by around $3 billion.
The plunge was equivalent to about 42 per cent of the company's value, which could send fears through a surging sector still reeling from the failed float of one of its other biggest players.
Luke Laretive, CEO of Seneca Financial Solutions, said fear of "a significant downgrade" to NEXTDC's future earnings and a "contagion-type vibe" had spooked the share market.
"Are [data centre operators] going to be in a position now where ... despite having insatiable demand, they're unable to actually build these facilities in locations that have access to power, water, a community that's happy to have them nearby and are still close enough to the businesses and the people that want to use them?" the investment adviser told SBS' On The Money.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Some of the community around NEXTDC's West Footscray facility seemingly aren't happy to have it nearby. Local residents have previously expressed fears about the amount of diesel stored on the site and raised concerns about noise pollution.
The installation of the power poles required to meet the facility's significant electricity needs has also sparked community anger, with some residents of a nearby suburb using their cars and bins to block equipment deployed for the electricity network upgrade in September.
"Has NEXTDC lost its social licence to operate here, or have data centre providers more generally lost their social licence to operate?" Laretive asked.
Data centres and social licence
Less than two weeks earlier, data centre operator Firmus Technologies withdrew its application for public listing on the Australian Stock Exchange — a move that had been touted as the biggest since Telstra's 1997 float.
Firmus Technologies operates a data centre in Melbourne and is currently building another in Tasmania, with plans for at least two more — despite facing some community backlash.
A month before cancelling its public listing, Firmus announced several-year sponsorship deals with the Tasmania Devils AFL teams, Cricket Tasmania, and Tasmania JackJumpers and Jewels basketball teams, raising concerns of 'sportswashing'.
Olivia Shen, director of strategic technologies at the University of Sydney's United States Studies Centre (USSC), thinks the social licence for data centres could be in the process of being lost across Australia.
"The build-out has been incredibly fast and incredibly rapid," she said.
"And I think at the local level, communities are just feeling quite blindsided by all this development, and especially where it's happening on very large scale in areas where they're not used to this kind of development."
This sentiment conflicts with government messaging that, according to Shen, is more focused on a "narrative that these data centres are incredibly important public facilities for AI development".
That narrative may not be cutting through, with the USSC's 2025 annual poll finding that 67 per cent of Australians "want to prioritise the regulation of AI even at the cost of innovation".
"These Australians are basically saying that even if it slows innovation, we want to progress at a bit of a slower pace rather than having these technologies being shoved down our throats and being told that they're actually good for us," she said.
However, Shen said people should be careful in making broad generalisations about the entire industry.
"Not all data centres are the same, not all of the technologies they use are the same from one operator to another, and the impact on the community really, really depends on the local conditions of that community," she said.
A data centre reliant on a polluting energy plant planning to build next to rural farmland used for cattle production will have a different impact to one hoping to build in a quiet suburb in the city.
Laretive, meanwhile, suggested data centre operators "learn from the likes of the BHP's and the Rio [Tinto]'s of the world" for community engagement.
"They are a real participant in the community, and they're not just there kind of soaking up resources," he said, referencing jobs created by mining companies.
Fears history is repeating itself
The Western Downs Digital Park is a $32 billion proposed data centre in Queensland. AI giant Anthropic signed a lease for the first of four planned buildings, but the site has not yet received approval.
Luke Munn, an Australian Research Council future fellow with the University of Queensland, and Joanna Horton, a postdoctoral research fellow, are studying the proposed site.
"I think what we've seen in the last couple of years is a kind of increasing recognition from the public that there's an infrastructure and a material footprint around the AI boom," Munn said.
Horton said the community have been "really pushing back against the proposed development".
A petition to stop the project already has 23,496 signatures — the most support for any active e-petition on the Queensland parliament website.
"It has been a hotspot for gas extraction, which has been a really big 'boom and bust' industry for the region," she said.
It's left residents concerned about history repeating, with new jobs being created only to disappear before too long. Another concern is natural resource extraction and water use, which critics have said could have a significant impact on the drought-prone region.
Horton said locals are also taking action, with the Environmental Defenders Office, a non-profit community legal centre, reporting a 250 per cent increase in inquiries related to data centres since January of this year.
"I think that shows that all over Australia really are seeing data centres as a) something that they're not sure about that they have very real concerns about, and then b) something that they actually want to take action and push back on," she said.
Munn added that some companies now saw potential community opposition as a more important factor than geography or energy supply when choosing potential sites for data centres.
Is the data centre bubble starting to pop?
Shen doesn't think challenges faced by companies like Firmus are necessarily a sign that Australia's data centre boom is over, but she sees it as a warning that not every data centre company will see its investment pay off.
"There are firms jumping on this data centre bandwagon that are probably not going to be the best firms," she said.
"This is complex physical and digital infrastructure, and I don't think every single investor in a data centre is necessarily going to make their money back."
She says it could be a good thing if it encourages "more level-headedness with people investing in the right places".
Laretive said the NEXTDC case likely doesn't say too much about the demand for AI, but he still urges caution for investors.
"We need to be careful about evaluations and the amount of the future that we price into today's numbers and today's market capitalisation."
