====================================================================================================

Promised a better life, New Zealand voters are asking what went wrong
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:37:41 UTC
03:37:41 KST

Māori and Pacific communities weigh what it takes to stay before New Zealand election
Families living in campervans, workers spending their house deposits and communities watching loved ones leave for Australia.
As New Zealand heads to the polls, voters are asking what happened to the promise of a better life.
For generations, New Zealand has offered a simple promise: work hard, look after your whānau, your family and build a future here.
But for many, that promise is getting harder to keep.
About 350,000 people, including non-New Zealand citizens, are estimated to have left New Zealand over the past three years, with almost half of them moving to Australia.
For those who stay, frustration over the rising cost of living is spilling onto the streets. In August, hundreds of people marched on parliament in protest at soaring bills from Tiaki Wai, the Wellington region's water provider. The average annual bill is now almost $NZ2,390 ($2,000).
Ahead of the November 7 election, Māori and Pacific communities, which are among those hardest hit by unemployment and homelessness, are asking whether politicians can give them a reason to stay.
Katherine Taniwha's family knows how to build a home.
She is a rigger. Her husband David is a crane driver. Their son Eli builds houses.
Now all three live in a campervan while Katherine, 62, undergoes treatment for blood cancer. She says she takes her chemotherapy tablets at night to sleep through the side effects.
David has had to cut back his working hours so he can take his wife to appointments and weekly tests.
As their savings dwindled, Katherine says they sought housing assistance but were told David's campervan counted as their home.
"They said, 'You don't qualify. David has an RV. That's your home,'" Katherine says.
The family has lived in the campervan for more than two years. David says he has sometimes had to borrow money just to get to work and put food on the table.
"We don't really have that much to stretch out anymore," he says. "I almost have to beg for some money at work just to help me get to work or help put a little bit extra on the table for my wife and son."
For Katherine, it's a situation she has come to accept.
"This must be how it is now," she says.*
Their story is not unique.
At the 2023 census, about 112,500 people were severely housing deprived across New Zealand, a figure some housing organisations say has only grown, with Māori and Pacific people disproportionately affected.
"By almost every measure, things have gone backwards quite significantly in the past three years," Paul Gilberd, from Community Housing Aotearoa, says.
Katherine wants politicians to see that reality for themselves.
"Get your hands dirty. Don't say you're doing your best, 'cause your best isn't enough apparently," she says.
The promises and the politics
Loading...
New Zealand is home to about 5.4 million people. Unlike Australia, voting is not compulsory, although enrolling is.
At the last election in 2023, about 2.9 million voted, just over 78 per cent of those enrolled.
Prime Minister Christopher Luxon is seeking another term for his National-led coalition with ACT and New Zealand First.
Labour, now led by Chris Hipkins after he succeeded Jacinda Ardern in 2023, hopes to return to government, potentially with support from the Greens and Te Pāti Māori.
But New Zealand's electoral system works differently from Australia's.
Voters get two votes: one for their local MP and another for a political party. The party vote largely determines how many seats each party wins, making coalition negotiations central to who governs.
One of the system's most distinctive features is its seven Māori electorates: voters of Māori descent can choose to enrol in these electorates, where they elect their own local MPs, or join the general electoral roll. Both groups also cast a party vote.
About two-thirds of New Zealand's Pacific population lives in Auckland, many in the south, making it a key electoral battleground and a familiar stop on the campaign trail, despite traditionally being a Labour stronghold.
At Johnnie Timu's Brown Pride gym, there's frustration with politicians who turn up during elections but struggle to connect with the people they're trying to reach.
"They always come out in community, but they make a big racket out of it," Johnnie says.
He wants politicians to build trust beyond election season.
Finding work remains a pressing concern.
Unemployment reached 5.6 per cent in the June quarter, with unemployment among people with a Pacific background double that at 11.6 per cent.
For Haora Hema, who lives down in Wellington, the economic downturn has come at a high personal cost.
He spent five years as a principal adviser helping the public service work with Māori and the Crown, before his team was disbanded last year.
His partner, who has a PhD and worked on a programme supporting Pacific leaders, also lost her job, leading the couple to start spending their house deposit just to get by.
"The reality is the job market is smashed," he says.
They pulled their children out of sport and swimming, and slept beside a single heater during winter to save on electricity.
The family wonders if they'll ever own a home.
Beyond financial issues, Haora says he is also worried about how Māori issues have become a source of political division.
"My wish is that people understand that Te Tiriti and Māori stuff is not about division: it's about how we exist here in a harmonious way," he says.
Te Tiriti o Waitangi, or the Treaty of Waitangi, is New Zealand’s founding agreement between Māori chiefs and the British Crown, signed in 1840. Its place in modern New Zealand remains a source of political debate.
National minister Paul Goldsmith says the previous Labour government's spending and public service expansion were unsustainable.
"It's not fair to make future generations pay for uncontrolled spending today," he says.
He points to forecasts of stronger growth and jobs. Haora is still waiting for that recovery.
"What is the vision for our country?" Haora says.
A reason to stay, a reason to leave
Loading...
In Waihi, a gold-mining town a couple of hours' drive from Auckland, mining offers some a reason to stay.
Chloe Witika, a young Māori woman who spent some time growing up in Australia, returned to New Zealand to be near her parents.
She works as a purchasing officer at the local mine.
She says Māori workers are a rare sight in the industry, but sees mining as a source of opportunity and hope, despite economic trade-offs.
"The pay is so low in New Zealand," she says, when asked about life in comparison to Australia.
"However, my mind has changed: home is everything for me, and to be able to work in a mining industry in New Zealand with my family is all I ever wanted."
When it comes to politics, she says she's still undecided on how to vote.
The government sees mining and infrastructure projects as a way to boost the economy, introducing controversial fast-track laws to speed up approvals for priority developments.
But the changes, which allow some projects to follow a streamlined approval process, have sparked opposition from communities, including around Waihi.
Neville Williams, a spokesman for a Māori collective opposing the mining development, says the approval process left too little room for their concerns.
"That's just some of the duality and the conflict that our people suffer from when confronted with a taniwha like gold mining — it divides, and it separates," he says.
For Chloe and Neville, both Māori, the debate exposes different views about what a future at home should look like.
Despite differences of sentiment or feeling though, Neville urges communities to vote.
"I want [Maori communities] to have hope, and to use their vote," he says.
But across the country, the question of staying or leaving is increasingly familiar, as more New Zealanders watch family, friends and colleagues make the move to Australia.
Back at the gym, Johnnie says several people he knows have moved to Australia this year, seeking secure work and better opportunities for their children.
For families like Johnnie's, New Zealand was once the destination. His own family's journey began in Samoa.
"They done all they could in Samoa and moved to New Zealand," he says.
"Now most of the families here have felt like they've done all they could in New Zealand, now move to Australia."
It's a move he admits he's considered himself, for his children's future. But despite the uncertainty, he remains optimistic.
"Regardless who's in power, we're gonna figure it out — we're gonna learn to survive."
A home worth coming back to
At South Auckland's 275 Markets, Savele "Fitz" Refiti sees neighbours helping each other through hard times.
"Coming together, we can stretch our dollar," he says.
"The village mentality has always worked for us."
But helping each other only goes so far.
Whoever forms the next government faces bigger questions about jobs, housing and whether families can afford to stay together.
For a country that has long promised opportunity and a better life, the challenge is not just stopping people from leaving, but giving them something to stay for.
Labour finance spokeswoman Barbara Edmonds knows that pull personally: her daughter plans to move to Australia after graduating.
"My job, as both a mother and as finance spokesperson, is to ensure that children like my girl will want to come back home," she says.
It's a dilemma facing families across New Zealand: how to build a future for the next generation, without losing them to somewhere else.
But for Katherine and David, the future is a more immediate concern, as the family fights for housing while receiving cancer treatment.
As voters prepare to decide who will lead their country, David hopes the next government will see the people struggling to get by.
"Open your eyes. See who needs help," he says.

Raiding super to pay medical bills leaves trail of 'financial damage'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:35:08 UTC
03:35:08 KST

Australians raid $1.4b from superannuation for medical costs as regulators warn of 'predatory' tactics
In short:
Australians withdrew $1.46 billion from their superannuation on compassionate grounds in 2025-26, with the vast majority used for medical costs.
There was a 13-fold increase in the amount withdrawn for dental treatment.
Regulators are cracking down on predatory practitioners who inappropriately help people access their superannuation.
Australians withdrew a record $1.46 billion from their superannuation last financial year on compassionate grounds, prompting regulators to sound the alarm over "predatory" sales tactics being used by health practitioners.
The amount of money taken from retirement nest eggs for compassionate reasons like medical treatment has skyrocketed in recent years, up about 220 per cent since 2018-19.
Consumers Health Forum (CHF) CEO Elizabeth Deveny said it reflected a health care system that had become increasingly unaffordable.
"When people are hit with a health bill on top of the cost-of-living crisis, it's understandable people reach for the only tools available to them," she said.
"Increasing numbers of Australians are having to choose between living in pain now or being poor in retirement."
Under the Australian Tax Office (ATO) early release rules, Australians can apply to withdraw money from their retirement funds on compassionate grounds, such as medical or funeral expenses.
Australians withdrew about $1.46 billion from their superannuation on compassionate grounds in 2025-26, with the vast majority of that — about $1.42 billion — used for medical costs including dental work.
Super Members Council CEO Misha Schubert said compassionate release provisions were an important safety net, but were designed to be used only in extremely rare circumstances.
"We're deeply concerned to see the scale of the financial damage that's being done often to very vulnerable Australians," she said.
Almost 65,000 applications for compassionate release of super were approved in 2025-26, which the ATO said was a 5 per cent decrease from the previous year.
ATO Deputy Commissioner Ben Kelly said while that drop was promising, some businesses were still trying to exploit the system.
"Our message to individuals and medical practitioners is clear, compassionate release of super should only be considered as a last resort," he said.
Total compassionate release of super applications
Source: ATO
'Concerning trend' from health practitioners
For the early withdrawal of super to be approved on medical grounds, two medical practitioners need to verify it is necessary to alleviate pain or mental illness, or to treat a life-threatening illness or injury.
The ATO has been working with the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency (AHPRA) to crack down on a "concerning trend" of health practitioners, like dentists, encouraging people to withdraw their superannuation inappropriately for services, such as cosmetic dental procedures.
"We are concerned by predatory sales tactics that use social media and internet advertising to attract patients for high-cost treatments they do not need or cannot afford," AHPRA CEO Justin Untersteiner said.
Over the past year, the ATO has ramped up compliance and fined practitioners a total of $1.5 million for making misleading statements so patients could secure early superannuation access.
One practitioner was fined around $30,000 for writing a medical report that relied on false clinical information, including an incorrect classification of the patient's condition.
A GP found to have engaged in professional misconduct while helping a patient access almost $20,000 of her superannuation for cosmetic liposuction was one of two health practitioners referred to tribunals by regulators, amid almost 100 related complaints between 2019 and April this year.
Ms Schubert said consumers needed stronger protections, calling for a ban on any advertising that promotes access to early super withdrawals.
"We're calling for this to be a real moment for the parliament and lawmakers to step in to protect vulnerable Australians to make sure that they have that strong nest egg of their retirement savings secured for them in retirement," she said.
What type of treatments was money withdrawn for?
Dental was again the most popular reason for someone to withdraw their superannuation on medical grounds, with $892 million taken out in 2025-26.
That is a 13-fold increase since 2018-19, when about $66 million was approved for release.
Public health researchers and the peak industry body have told the ABC the dramatic increase in early superannuation withdrawals for dental treatment pointed to "historical neglect" of the public system.
Dr Deveny said some providers were exploiting those gaps in care.
"It's completely understandable if you're living in constant dental pain, that you'll do whatever it takes to fix it… I think we need to be careful not to blame people for doing that," she said.
Early super withdrawals for IVF have more than doubled in the past eight years, from $36.2 million in 2018-19 to $76.4 million last financial year.
Ms Schubert said Australians needed to understand the long-term impact of raiding their nest eggs, saying withdrawing $20,000 of superannuation could ultimately cost someone $93,000 by retirement because they lose the compound interest they could have earned.
Financial Services Minister and Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino said the government would continue to monitor the issue, including whether further measures were needed to protect patients.
"Australians should not be pressured into accessing their superannuation for unnecessary medical or dental procedures."

Type 45 extension not part of the plan, committee told
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
19:29:05 BST
03:29:05 KST

The Ministry of Defence does not want to extend the life of the Type 45 destroyers and would rather spend the money on new technology, with £1.5 billion set aside in this Parliament to initiate hybrid Navy projects, according to evidence given to the Defence Committee.
Air Marshal Tim Jones, Deputy Chief of the Defence Staff for Force Development, was giving evidence alongside Wes Streeting, the Secretary of State for Defence.
Jesse Norman, the Conservative member for Hereford and South Herefordshire, asked about the timing of the Type 45 replacement. Jones said: “As you know, the Type 45s are due to start going out of service from 2035. At the moment, we have started investment in a hybrid Navy alternative for that. You probably heard the First Sea Lord talking quite passionately about his vision for a hybrid Navy. The early investment that we are doing is to get those projects up and running so that, by the time the Type 45 starts going out of service, we have a hybrid replacement for that capability coming into service.”
Asked whether the current ships would have their lives extended, Jones said: “We don’t want to extend the Type 45. Rather than extending older platforms that cost a lot of money to run, we would rather spend the money focusing on new technology. That is what the First Sea Lord wants, and that is what we are aiming to do.”
Pressed on whether a capability gap could open before the hybrid Navy is established, Jones said: “We have almost 10 years to get the Type 45 replacement up and running. We are in a world where we are seeing innovation moving quickly and the market being disrupted by start-ups and new tech companies.”
Norman asked for reassurance that adequate capability would cover the gap and more by the time the class is retired, and Jones said: “We will.” Asked whether the replacement would be comparable or better, he said: “It should be better, because new technology will come online, and the aim is to do that in a more effective way. As to when the transition happens in detail, that is what we are working through at the moment. We do not want to extend Type 45. It is clearly an option, but it is not part of our plan.”
Luke Pollard, the Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, told Andrew Bowie, the Conservative member for West Aberdeenshire and Kincardine, in a written answer in July that detailed planning for the transition between Type 45 and the hybrid Navy maritime air defence capability would be done with industry, “which will determine whether a Type 45 extension is implemented”, and that “a final decision is not expected until 2027-28.”
Answering James Cartlidge, the Conservative member for South Suffolk, in August, Pollard said the Defence Investment Plan contains “a specific funding line within this parliament to conduct a study” covering “whether a life extension will be required”, and that this “will be assessed in 2027-28”, as this publication reported at the time. Jones did not mention the study to the committee, and Norman was pressing on exactly the transition it exists to examine.
On funding, Jones said: “We have £1.5 billion in this Parliament set aside for initiating hybrid Navy projects, and that project team is standing up now.” He described it as a start, and said it is by no means the limit of investment.
He told the committee that the Royal Navy is “already almost on contract for an uncrewed surface vessel; the competition is in the final stages, and the results of that will be announced soon. That vessel will be in the water next year, so we are getting on with it.”
The Royal Navy operates six Type 45 destroyers, which provide the fleet’s area air defence through the Sea Viper system. The Defence Committee reported this week that it is not persuaded the Hybrid Navy allocation will be sufficient to develop, procure and integrate its five planned classes, which include a crewed Common Combat Vessel to replace the Type 45.
Streeting told the committee that innovation always involves risk and that politically “we need to be more comfortable than we sometimes are with carrying risk.” He described the First Sea Lord’s hybrid Navy concept as “genuinely world-leading” and said counterparts are actively tracking it.

Louvre, Orsay, Picasso museums to close Saturday ahead of nationwide protests

Necva Tastan Sevinc
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in Paris will remain closed on Saturday due to new planned demonstrations, the French government said Thursday.
The Culture Ministry also urged all institutions under its supervision to take measures to ensure “the safety of visitors,” “the protection of staff” and “the preservation of works.”
The closures come as authorities tighten security ahead of new nationwide protests.
Jean-Didier Berger, France’s minister delegate to the Interior Ministry, told broadcaster BFMTV that authorities were maintaining a “maximum level of vigilance,” with security force deployments set to be 20% higher than during demonstrations on Oct. 17.
He said leave had been canceled and personnel recalled. Sentinelle military forces and specialist police units, including the GIGN and RAID, would also be deployed.
President Emmanuel Macron said demonstrations not organized by trade unions would be banned in the coming days, particularly on the weekend, “wherever possible.” Prefects would examine requests submitted by unions.
Authorities have banned demonstrations across Lyon and in central Toulon for Saturday, while shopkeepers have been urged to secure premises and remove objects that could be used to cause damage.
Yellow Vest demonstrators and students rallied nationwide last weekend over living costs and fuel prices. Violence and damage to businesses and public buildings prompted localized curfews.
Unions have also called a nationwide strike and protest day for Nov. 5.

EU will ‘inevitably’ restore economic ties with Russia – Putin aide (VIDEOS)
European countries will inevitably resume economic cooperation with Russia, following Washington’s lead, Russian presidential aide Kirill Dmitriev has predicted. Politicians who continue to blame Moscow for their domestic problems rather than address them risk losing power, he warned.
Dmitriev, who also heads Russia’s sovereign wealth fund, made the remarks on Thursday at the 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum in Istanbul.
The Russian official hailed Trump’s readiness to restore dialogue with Russia and reverse a “very dangerous situation where top nuclear powers don’t communicate.”
He said the recent Russia-US diesel deal could lay the groundwork for broader cooperation between Moscow and Washington, potentially paving the way for further agreements on energy and fertilizers. Under the deal, Russia has agreed to release more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel to US and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and additional supplies thereafter.
Commenting on Europe’s problems, including high energy costs and mass migration, Dmitriev accused European politicians of “using Russia as a boogeyman” to distract from more fundamental issues, warning that they have come to believe their own narratives and are unwilling to correct their mistakes.
However, Dmitriev argued that attitudes within the EU were beginning to shift, with more voices calling for renewed dialogue with Moscow. “Cooperation with Russia economically will be inevitable,” he said, adding that “as soon as we do more deals with the US, European companies” will want a piece of the action, too.
Dmitriev suggested that European politicians who stubbornly refuse to change course, such as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, would be replaced by “new forces” that are more realistic and pragmatic. He also predicted that the Nord Stream 1 and Nord Stream 2 gas pipelines, three of whose four strings were damaged by underwater explosions in September 2022, would “inevitably” resume operation “at some point in the future” for economic reasons.
“Once people start paying double, triple their bills of energy in Europe, the resumption of energy supplies from Russia is absolutely inevitable and politicians who refuse that will lose in any way possible,” Dmitriev argued.
“Once people are rational, once people stop reading fake stories in the media, once they stop sort of living in this matrix of fake narratives…, they’ll understand that only through dialogue, through cooperation, through working together, we can go forward successfully.”
Dmitriev also argued that many of today’s “great leaders,” including Russian President Vladimir Putin, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, prioritize national sovereignty over what he described as the “failed policy of globalism.”

Hegseth’s staff damaged Eisenhower’s World War II-era globe during Pentagon move: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:19:21 UTC
03:19:21 KST

Diyar Guldogan
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s staff damaged a historic globe associated with Gen. Dwight D. Eisenhower during an attempt to move the artifact to Hegseth’s Pentagon office, according to a report published Thursday by The Washington Post.
Photographs obtained by the newspaper show a gash several inches wide near Antarctica on the globe, which reportedly fell onto its base during the relocation attempt on Feb. 3.
It is one of two 30-inch floor globes housed at the Pentagon that are said to have been used by Eisenhower during World War II. The artifacts have been maintained by successive generations of army leaders, according to people familiar with the history and a plaque dating them to the 1930s, the Post reported.
Hegseth’s interest in the globe’s historical significance prompted his staff to request that one of the artifacts be moved to his office, according to the newspaper. But rather than using the Pentagon’s customary process for relocating historical items under the supervision of trained curators, Hegseth’s staff sent its own team to handle the move, the Post reported, citing those familiar with the incident.
The team lost control of the globe, causing it to crash onto its base and puncture its fragile outer shell, according to the report.
The army acknowledged the damage in a statement to the Post. Army spokesman Christopher Surridge said the globe was damaged during an “attempted move” on Feb. 3. Aside from the hole, “the spherical portion of the globe was detached from the metal mounting that allows it to rotate,” Surridge was quoted.
The army’s office responsible for the artifact had expected to consult specialists at the US Army Center of Military History about safely transporting the globe and documenting its relocation, according to two people familiar with the matter.
But those experts had been furloughed during a partial government shutdown stemming from a congressional dispute about aspects of the Trump administration’s immigration policy. With the specialists unavailable, Hegseth’s staff decided to move the globe themselves, the Post reported.
After the Post published its report, a Defense Department official provided the newspaper with a brief, unattributed statement acknowledging the mishap.
“Accidents happen,” it said. “We are grateful no one was harmed, and the globe is being repaired.”

Ex-prosecutor’s killing puts Guatemala’s crime-politics nexus back in focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:16:41 UTC
03:16:41 KST

Ex-prosecutor’s killing puts Guatemala’s crime-politics nexus back in focus
GUATEMALA CITY, Oct 22 - Former Guatemalan anti-corruption prosecutor Juan Francisco Solorzano Foppa was one of the country's most high profile voices denouncing alleged links between politicians and business leaders and the country's increasingly powerful organized crime groups.
Over the weekend, he was shot dead on a soccer field, a killing that former officials and diplomats consulted by Reuters said has heightened concerns over organized crime's influence in the Central American nation.
The killing of an outspoken former prosecutor who had publicly challenged powerful interests shocked the country and revived debate over criminal networks’ penetration of state institutions.
"This is a threat against human rights defenders. This is a threat against activists for democracy," said Frank La Rue, a human rights advocate, who attended the wake for Solorzano Foppa on Monday, which featured portraits of the slain lawyer with his family.
For many Guatemalans, it recalled the 1998 assassination of Bishop Juan Jose Gerardi, beaten to death two days after presenting a report documenting atrocities from the country’s civil war, and stirred fears that violence could again be used against prominent critics of powerful interests.
Experts said criminal networks have strengthened their influence in recent years as anti-corruption efforts and institutions tasked with combating impunity have weakened, issues likely to loom over the June 2027 election as Guatemala chooses President Bernardo Arevalo’s successor.
Authorities have not established a motive for Solorzano Foppa's killing. But officials and diplomats said the case has fueled concerns about criminal groups’ ability to intimidate or silence critical voices.
More than 100 former prosecutors, judges, journalists and human rights defenders have left Guatemala in recent years, according to some international human rights organizations, after denouncing corruption or alleged links between state structures and criminal networks.
This week, following Solorzano Foppa's killing, a high-profile lawyer who also railed against political corruption said he has received death threats. On Wednesday, Arevalo denounced the threats against the lawyer, Edgar Ortiz.
"Guatemala cannot return to being a country where defending democracy can cost one peace, freedom, or their life," Arevalo wrote on social media.
'RED LINE CROSSED'
Corruption has been a major institutional challenge in Guatemala for decades. From 2007 to 2019, the UN-backed International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG) helped investigate corruption and organized crime networks within the state, including cases that led to the resignation and subsequent prosecution of then-President Otto Perez Molina and his former vice president, Roxana Baldetti.
Since CICIG's departure in 2019, human rights groups, prosecutors and international observers have denounced setbacks in the fight against corruption. President Arevalo, who took office in 2024 promising to tackle the problem, has acknowledged difficulties advancing reforms and dismantling structures accused of corruption.
In videos posted on Facebook, TikTok and Instagram, and seen by Reuters, Solorzano Foppa alleged links between Barrio 18 leader Aldo "El Lobo" Ochoa, who is serving combined prison sentences of more than 1,600 years, and people close to the leadership of the National Unity of Hope (UNE) party, headed by former first lady Sandra Torres. Reuters could not independently verify the allegations.
UNE told Reuters in a statement that "those allegations were never proven and should not be presented as established facts."
Solorzano Foppa, a former head of Guatemala's SAT tax administration agency, also alleged ties between criminal networks, political figures and sectors of the judicial system, though the accusations did not result in judicial proceedings.
Officials have not identified who ordered the killing. The Organization of American States and the United Nations have called for a thorough investigation.
The Public Prosecutor's Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. On Sunday, following the murder, it said in a statement that "in order to guarantee due process, it will not disclose additional details about the evidence gathered or the specific lines of investigation."
A former government official, who was not authorized to speak publicly, said insiders had turned to Solorzano Foppa with information they felt unable to expose themselves, making him an outlet for allegations from within the state. His killers "left no trace," the former official said, complicating the investigation.
Guatemala's criminal networks range from gangs and drug traffickers to structures involving former officials and members of the security forces. Analysts say some have retained influence over state institutions, while armed groups like Barrio 18 and Mara Salvatrucha (MS-13) remain involved in extortion and territorial control.
They include the so-called CIACS, or Illegal Clandestine Security Apparatuses, networks linked to former security structures that experts say retain political and economic influence. Guatemala is also a major drug-trafficking corridor to the United States, with groups associated with Mexico's Sinaloa Cartel and Jalisco New Generation Cartel operating through local criminal networks.
"Many of us fear that a red line has been crossed," said Stephen McFarland, former US ambassador to Guatemala from 2008 to 2011. "A return to political assassination as a way of settling scores and protecting the ambitions and money of certain people." REUTERS

Egypt calls for Yemen talks as parliament weighs military support to Saudi Arabia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22

Egypt calls for Yemen talks as parliament weighs military support to Saudi Arabia
Oct 22 - Egypt advocates exploring "every opportunity" to resolve the Yemen conflict diplomatically, its foreign minister said, ahead of a parliamentary vote next week on authorising the armed forces to support Saudi Arabia against the Iran-aligned Houthis.
Any direct involvement of the Egyptian military, one of the region's largest, would raise the stakes in the conflict between the kingdom and the Houthis, an increasingly destabilising front in the spreading US-Israeli war on Iran.
President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi called on Saturday for an urgent parliamentary session to authorise military involvement supporting the kingdom. After a closed session on Sunday, lawmakers postponed the vote until October 26 to allow more deliberation.
Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty and intelligence chief Hassan Rashad travelled to Riyadh on Wednesday to deliver a letter to Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman from Sisi, who said Egypt's support would be limited to defending Saudi territory and borders rather than attacking Yemen.
What kind of support Egypt will ultimately provide remains unclear.
EGYPT HAS LIMITED ROLE IN SAUDI-LED YEMEN COALITION
Abdelatty said on Thursday that Egypt underlined the need to "explore every opportunity for the possibility of reaching political solutions" ensuring a full Houthi withdrawal from territory seized during the group's advance in September near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a critical chokepoint at the Red Sea's mouth and gateway to Egypt's Suez Canal.
"So that we can move on the political path that we always emphasize, and also side by side in support of the defensive path for the kingdom," Abdelatty told a press conference.
Clashes between the Houthis and the Saudi-led coalition backing Yemen's internationally recognized government have intensified since the group's push towards Bab el-Mandeb on the Red Sea further strained global oil supplies. The militia has since attacked Saudi airports and oil facilities.
Saudi Arabia, the world's top oil exporter, is a vital strategic and economic partner for Egypt, providing billions in aid, central bank deposits and energy supplies under Sisi.
The war in Yemen, which has caused a humanitarian crisis, started in 2014 when the Houthis drove the internationally recognised government out of the northern capital, drawing Saudi-led military intervention.
Egypt joined the Saudi-led coalition in March 2015 mainly as a naval partner, sending warships to secure Red Sea shipping lanes while pledging air support. It also deployed around 800 ground troops but played only a limited combat role.
A US-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted attacks.
While Cairo has voiced support for Riyadh since the resumption of hostilities, it has avoided direct combat. It did not join the Mecca mutual defense pact linking Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey, though it says membership remains under consideration.
The Saudi crown prince sought military assistance from the United States, but President Donald Trump did not agree to the US striking Houthis, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters in September. Washington told Riyadh that it would help with intelligence sharing and targeting, they added.
Yahya Ali al-Rai, speaker of the Houthi-run House of Representatives, warned on Saturday against Egyptian involvement, urging parliament to reject the proposal. "Should Egypt slide down this path, it would pose a grave threat to its own national security and internal stability," he said. REUTERS

New norms to limit fuel leaks, protect EV batteries in rear-end crashes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:06:07 UTC
03:06:07 KST

In a notification, road transport ministry has also made the automotive standard, AIS-192, mandatory. (File photo)
NEW DELHI: Govt has tightened norms for protection of fuel systems and electric power drive systems, with all new vehicles manufactured from April 2029 onwards required to comply with the new standards, a move that will prevent fire in rear-end collisions.In a notification, road transport ministry has also made the automotive standard, AIS-192, mandatory for Event Data Recorder (EDR) from Oct 2029 if it is installed in any car. The EDR feature is not mandatory for all cars, and it remains an optional feature. EDR records crash details, which help establish what happened immediately before and during a collision. It is similar in purpose to an aircraft’s flight-data recorder or black box.In the case of standards for fire safety, the revised automotive industry standards (AIS)-101 specify that after a rear-impact crash test, liquid-fuel systems must not develop more than slight leakage and continuous leakage must not exceed 30 grams per minute. The key safety requirements include the fuel system not allowing a fire to be sustained following the impact. In the case of electric vehicles, the battery and its securing mechanism must remain in position during and after the impact test.
This standard lays down requirements for protecting occupants from electrical hazards, including the high-voltage circuit being automatically disconnected after a collision.
The ministry has notified revised vehicle safety standards, including updated frontal and side-impact crash protection requirements, with implementation for new models scheduled from Oct 2027 and for all models from Oct 2028.It has also revised requirements for protecting pedestrians and other vulnerable road users. The updated standard will apply to new models from Oct 2028.

Rwandan, Chinese academics urge strong research collaboration to tackle environmental challenges
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:01:06 CST
03:01:06 KST

KIGALI, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Academicians, researchers and officials have called for strong research collaboration, increased investment in scientific research and the application of homegrown knowledge to address environmental challenges and promote sustainable development in Rwanda and across Africa.
The call was made on Thursday, during the International Conference on Environment, Energy and Development held in Kigali, the capital of Rwanda, under the theme, "Resilient Earth: Water, Ecosystems, Energy and Sustainable Development."
The conference was co-organized by the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography (XIEG) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, the University of Lay Adventists of Kigali (UNILAK) and the Sino-Africa Joint Research Center (SAJOREC) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences.
Olivier Habimana, head of the department of Digitalization and Research at the Rwanda's Higher Education Council, said Rwanda needs locally generated scientific knowledge to achieve its development ambitions, particularly in water management, environmental protection, renewable energy and climate resilience.
"That ambition cannot be achieved through borrowed knowledge alone. Instead, it requires homegrown science," Habimana said, urging universities and research institutions to strengthen collaboration with government agencies, industries and local communities.
He noted that research must go beyond academic publications to inform policy decisions, generate practical solutions and benefit communities. He also highlighted the need to increase investment in research and development and strengthen links between academia and industry.
At the conference, Jean Ngamije, vice chancellor of UNILAK, urged researchers to pursue evidence-based solutions and expand scientific cooperation among Rwanda, China and other African countries.
"I call upon our researchers to pursue scientific evidence and strengthen collaboration," Ngamije said, emphasizing the importance of turning research findings into practical interventions that improve people's lives.
According to Duan Weili, deputy director of XIEG, the ICEED series has been successfully held in Kigali six times since its inception in 2013. Over the past decade, this conference has grown from a regional academic platform into an important space for dialogue, bringing together peers from China, Africa, and beyond.
"East Africa is facing multiple pressures from water security, ecosystem degradation, and climate-induced disaster risks," Duan said, noting that this year's conference is highly relevant and timely.
Speaking at the event, Wang Shengwei, deputy director of SAJOREC, called for stronger cooperation in student training, academic exchanges and capacity-building to advance biodiversity conservation and ecosystem restoration.
Wang said the partnership had supported the training of more than 10 Rwandan postgraduate students and contributed to research on Rwanda's plant diversity.
At the conference, UNILAK, XIEG and SAJOREC renewed their tripartite partnership for 2027-2031, with plans to strengthen joint research, scholarships, staff exchanges and scientific cooperation.
The conference brought together researchers, policymakers, academics and development partners to share knowledge and explore solutions to climate change, water insecurity, biodiversity loss and other environmental challenges. ■

"They threaten not one party but the right of every citizen to choose his or her leaders," he added.
Deng urged the CTSAMVM to step up monitoring and patrols in potential flashpoints, such as Jonglei State, that remain vulnerable to pre-election violence.
He also stressed the importance of accelerating verification and reporting on violations to establish facts before rumors and disinformation spread.
Deng highlighted the need for close coordination between the CTSAMVM, the National Elections Commission, the United Nations Mission in South Sudan, and local security agencies to establish a unified security framework for the general elections set for Dec. 22.
Two peacekeepers serving with the UN mission were killed, and seven other people wounded, three of them peacekeepers, when their patrol was ambushed near Pajut in Jonglei State in late August.
Earlier this month, 71 people were reported killed in communal violence in Lakes State.
Hailu Endashaw Atomsa, chairperson of the CTSAMVM, said that the security situation across South Sudan remains mixed. While some regions are experiencing relative calm, others continue to face localized armed clashes, road ambushes, and intercommunal violence.
Atomsa said that clashes between the Sudan People's Liberation Movement/Army-in-Opposition and the South Sudan People's Defence Forces in Mugwo Payam in Central Equatoria State have displaced civilians.
He said the ongoing fighting in Panyume has restricted civilian movement and humanitarian access, aggravating severe food shortages in the area.
Atomsa added that ambushes along the Mundri-Juba Highway, a vital route linking to Western Equatoria State, have heightened overall insecurity and severely restricted movement of civilians and commercial vehicles.
Atomsa called on the warring parties to reaffirm their commitment to the permanent ceasefire and maintain full compliance with Chapter II of the 2018 Revitalized Peace Agreement.
He emphasized the urgent need for all groups to strictly adhere to transitional security arrangements and refrain from offensive, provocative, or retaliatory actions. ■

Feature: When a Ghanaian college student meets with Chinese traditional face-changing art
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
02:00:34 CST
03:00:34 KST

Austin Elikem Afiawo, a final-year Chinese language and linguistics student at the University of Ghana, speaks during an interview with Xinhua in Accra, Ghana, on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Seth/Xinhua)
by Justice Lee Adoboe
ACCRA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Amid the sweeping green oasis that rises gently over the Legon Hill in the northern part of Accra, Ghana's capital, lies the 11.4-square-kilometer University of Ghana, the country's premier higher-education institution.
As a typical ivory tower, the university is made up of different schools, departments, and institutes, including the Confucius Institute. Here, many young Ghanaians come to study the Chinese language and culture.
Among the current crop of students is 20-year-old Austin Elikem Afiawo, a final-year Chinese language and linguistics student at the university, who loves to spend time at the Confucius Institute working on his Chinese language and cultural studies.
For young Afiawo, his academic journey, including structured classroom work and writing test papers, is also interspersed with cultural activities such as Chinese dance, stage performances, music, and drawing, among others.
One specific Chinese art form that the Ghanaian student has taken keen interest in and has been mastering is "Bian Lian," the traditional Chinese Sichuan Opera's face-changing performance.
Afiawo, then a first-year student, attended a cultural performance at the Confucius Institute. But this turned out to be a moment that would transform him from being part of the audience to a key cast member in cultural performances at the institute.
"I watched one gentleman, Jesse Twumasi-Ankrah, on stage in a blue costume just changing faces. I was really shocked and got interested in it. So, I decided to approach him after the program and ask him how he did it," he told Xinhua in a recent interview.
Twumasi-Ankrah, then a senior student, began teaching Afiawo the basics of the face-changing performance, and Afiawo gradually started perfecting the art. Later, other teachers of the Confucius Institute at the University of Ghana (CIUG) also joined in to train him.
Being new to the stage craft, the young student found the performance initially difficult to learn and cope with. But gradually, he mastered the art and has established himself as a face-changing art performer in Ghana.
"The first difficulty is that, while people think the performance is just about changing faces, the real challenge is the costume. Putting on the costume is a very difficult part of the performance," he said.
According to him, "The costume with several masks is very heavy. It puts a lot of stress on you. So those are some difficulties we face."
"I remember my very first performance, which was here at the Confucius Institute. I was very nervous, being the first time I stood in front of a large audience to perform, and one mistake can destroy the entire performance," he said.
To manage his stage fright, Afiawo avoided eye contact by looking above the audience's heads and pretending he was alone in the auditorium, which helped him enjoy his act.
Afiawo has since mastered the art and is able to perform during events organized by the three Confucius Institutes in the West African country and other events organized by Chinese organizations in the country.
Chinese Director of the CIUG Liu Baijun spoke highly about Afiawo's enthusiasm. "He's very active in CIUG activities. He always comes to the Confucius Institute and learns some Chinese culture."
"Face-changing is a tradition in China. Maybe it's quite strange for some of the foreigners, but for Austin, he likes it very much," Liu said. "He practices face-changing in his spare time, and his skill has improved a lot."
One of the values Afiawo has learned through performing the face-changing art is endurance, as the heavy costume he puts on to perform on stage causes him to sweat a lot in Ghana's warm, humid tropical weather. Furthermore, the need to pile up different masks in the costume, which he keeps changing on stage to portray different looks, requires enduring discipline.
"But after every performance, we realize that no matter the struggle we go through, we can actually pull through," added the Ghanaian student.
Afiawo expressed gratitude to the CIUG for the enormous support he continues to receive from them, both for his academic work and training in stage performance.
Liu noted that more and more Ghanaians are eager to learn the Chinese language and culture in recent years. The CIUG will introduce more Chinese culture, not only traditional but also the latest Chinese technology, to the Ghanaian people. ■

RIO DE JANEIRO, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Brazil's presidential runoff, scheduled for Sunday, Oct. 25, will pit incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva against Flavio Bolsonaro in a closely fought contest that could shape the country's policy direction over the next four years and influence Latin America's political balance.
Lula, of the Workers' Party, is seeking to overcome a first-round deficit against Bolsonaro, the Liberal Party candidate and son of former President Jair Bolsonaro.
Bolsonaro won 47.03 percent of valid votes in the first round, against Lula's 45.16 percent. Neither secured more than 50 percent of valid votes, the threshold required to win outright.
A Quaest poll released on Wednesday put Bolsonaro at 45 percent and Lula at 44 percent, with the gap within the poll's two-percentage-point margin of error. The survey interviewed 2,154 people between Oct. 17 and 20.
Both campaigns are courting supporters of eliminated candidates and voters who stayed home in the first round, when abstention reached 21.08 percent.
Lula has stepped up his digital campaigning, drawing on younger politicians and influential online supporters. Since Oct. 7, he has posted selfie-style videos urging supporters to take their campaign onto the streets and speak directly to voters.
Bolsonaro has consolidated support among conservative politicians and business leaders while seeking a more moderate public image, emphasizing policy proposals and steering clear of controversies that could alienate undecided voters.
At their televised debate on Sunday, Lula pledged to sustain economic growth, strengthen public security and defend Brazil's sovereignty in international affairs. He also proposed a public security ministry to coordinate federal, state and municipal action.
Bolsonaro emphasized tougher measures against organized crime, including classifying criminal factions as narco-terrorist organizations and expanding prison capacity. He also pledged to reduce public debt, support debt restructuring for businesses and individuals, and improve public healthcare by bringing in specialists and adopting advanced technology.
The contest has also moved into the courts. Bolsonaro's campaign filed a case on Tuesday seeking to disqualify Lula's ticket, and Lula's coalition filed a similar request against Bolsonaro's ticket on Wednesday. The allegations remain subject to judicial examination.
The congressional results will also shape the next government's room to maneuver. The Liberal Party won 121 of the Chamber of Deputies' 513 seats, compared with 88 for the Workers' Party-led federation.
The Liberal Party is set to hold 28 of the Senate's 81 seats starting in 2027, making it the largest party bloc, although it will still fall short of an outright majority. Whichever candidate wins the presidency, building support across party lines will be important to advancing his legislative agenda.
Beyond these domestic challenges, the outcome could influence Latin America's wider political direction.
Zhou Zhiwei, a researcher at the Institute of Latin American Studies of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, said Brazil's election offers an important window into the region's changing political landscape.
Conservative forces have gained momentum across Latin America over the past year or two and demonstrated their strength in Brazil's first-round contests, he said.
A rightward turn in Brazil could further weaken the Latin American left, while Lula's re-election would give it a significant boost, Zhou said.
For both candidates, the immediate challenge is to turn support into votes. Their ability to reach beyond committed followers and bring voters to the polls could prove decisive. ■

====================================================================================================

Older adults with depression tend to have smaller volumes of a specific part of the hippocampus brain region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:00:23 UTC
03:00:23 KST

An analysis of more than 2,000 cognitively healthy older adults found that those with depression tended to have a smaller volume in one part of the hippocampus, a brain region central to memory and one of the first affected by Alzheimer’s disease. The association did not appear to be explained by amyloid and tau, two proteins linked to Alzheimer’s disease. The paper was published in Translational Psychiatry.
Alzheimer’s disease is the most common form of dementia in older adults. It gradually disrupts memory, thinking, behavior, and everyday functioning. The disease is accompanied by characteristic changes in the brain, including abnormal clumps of amyloid protein, called plaques, and twisted strands of tau protein, called tangles, along with the loss of nerve cells.
Research suggests that depression may also play a role in the risk of Alzheimer’s disease. People who experience depression during their lifetime appear to have a higher risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease later on. One possible connection between the two conditions involves the hippocampus, which is central to memory and is among the first areas affected by Alzheimer’s disease.
Depression has likewise been associated with changes in the structure of the hippocampus, although previous studies have produced inconsistent findings. Part of the difficulty may be that the hippocampus is not a single uniform structure but consists of several smaller regions (called hippocampal subfields) that can be affected differently by depression and Alzheimer’s disease. Antidepressant medications may also play a role, as some evidence suggests that they could protect against hippocampal shrinkage, while other findings raise questions about their effects in older adults.
Study author Danielle Luu of the Stevens Neuroimaging and Informatics Institute at the University of Southern California and colleagues set out to examine how depression and antidepressant use relate to the volume of hippocampal subfields in older adults without cognitive problems. They also wanted to know whether Alzheimer’s-related factors, including amyloid and tau buildup and the APOE4 gene variant, which raises Alzheimer’s risk, play a role in these relationships.
The researchers considered two possibilities for antidepressants. The medications might be linked to larger subfield volumes by relieving depressive symptoms. Alternatively, they might be linked to smaller volumes, either because of unknown harmful effects on the brain or because doctors are more likely to prescribe them to people with more severe depression.
The researchers analyzed data from the Health and Aging Brain Study-Health Disparities, which recruited Hispanic, Black, and white older adults through the University of North Texas in Fort Worth. The analysis included 2,009 cognitively unimpaired adults between 50 and 90 years of age, with an average age of about 65.
Of these participants, 630 were classified as having depression, either because they scored 10 or higher on the Geriatric Depression Scale or because they reported having been diagnosed with depression by a health care provider. The remaining 1,379 participants were classified as not depressed.
Participants underwent high-resolution MRI scans of the hippocampus and reported whether they used antidepressant medications. The researchers used the scans to calculate volumes of three hippocampal subfields: the CA1, the subiculum, and a composite region that included the CA2, CA3, and the dentate gyrus (CA23DG). Subsets of participants also underwent PET scans measuring amyloid (684 people) and tau (386 people) in the brain.
Participants with depression tended to have a smaller CA23DG, but depression was not associated with the volume of the CA1 or the subiculum. The association was small and held after the researchers accounted for body mass index and physical activity, as well as tau levels and APOE4 status. When amyloid was added to the analysis, the association was no longer statistically significant, but its size was similar, which the authors attribute to the smaller number of participants with amyloid scans.
The severity of current depressive symptoms and the age at which depression began were not associated with the volume of any subfield. In exploratory analyses, the link between depression and smaller subfields appeared stronger in men than in women, but the authors interpret this cautiously because the formal test of a sex difference was not statistically significant.
Among participants with depression, those who used antidepressant medications tended to have smaller CA1 and CA23DG volumes than those who did not. These associations weakened to borderline levels after the researchers accounted for body mass index and physical activity. When antidepressant use and depression were included in the same analysis, the link between depression itself and a smaller CA23DG faded, while antidepressant use remained associated with a smaller CA23DG.
The authors suggest that the medication findings may reflect what is known as indication bias, meaning that people with more severe depression may be more likely to be prescribed medication in the first place. Antidepressant users reported fewer current depressive symptoms than non-users, suggesting the medications were relieving symptoms, but the researchers did not have information on how severe participants’ depression was before treatment or how long they had taken medication.
“It is important to study AD [Alzheimer’s disease] in the context of mental health, since rates of depression rise with age. Moreover, it is crucial to investigate how depression and antidepressant medication use affect the hippocampus, a region of the brain that is heavily impacted by AD. Understanding the relationship between depression and the development of AD is important for exploring preventative measures against brain atrophy and dementia,” study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of the neural underpinnings of depression in older adults. However, it should be noted that the design of this study does not allow any causal inferences to be derived from the results. Depression diagnoses and medication use were self-reported rather than drawn from medical records, and the analyses involving amyloid and tau were based on smaller subsets of participants.
The researchers did not compare different types or doses of antidepressants. They note that the possibility that the medications themselves affect hippocampal structure should be tested in randomized controlled trials.
The paper, “Depression and hippocampal subfield volume in older adults,” was authored by Danielle Luu, Alicia M. Twisselmann, Victoria R. Tennant, Brandon J. Hall, Arjun Mahajan, Audrey Kim, Jamie Terner, Marylan L. Davison, Koral Wheeler, Christopher R. K. Ching, James Hall, Matthew T. Borzage, Leigh Johnson, Arthur W. Toga, Sid E. O’Bryant, Kristine Yaffe, and Meredith N. Braskie for the HABS-HD Study Team.

A New Ice Age Was Beginning. Then Humans Started Burning Fossil Fuels
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
18:00:00 UTC
03:00:00 KST

Burning fossil fuels may have stopped the Earth from entering another ice age, a new study suggests. The research, published Thursday in the journal Science, uses samples of ancient vegetation and rock records to analyze the growth—and sudden retreat—of an ice cap that is the last vestige of an ice sheet that once covered much of North America.
The findings shows the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers parts of Canada’s Baffin Island, started growing a few thousand years ago before rapidly reversing course beginning in the 1960s as carbon pollution ramped up.
“A question that’s in the popular consciousness is, have we caused enough global warming to stop the next ice age from happening?” says Andrew Wickert, an associate professor of environmental science at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, who was not involved in the research. The new research shows that “even as we were just starting to ramp up emissions, we’ve already done enough damage to cause the major North American ice sheet to already start retreating. That’s significant.”
The planet regularly goes through phases where ice extends down from the high latitudes—what we colloquially call "ice ages"—due to natural shifts in the Earth's rotation and orbit, known as Milankovitch Cycles. Those are followed by interglacial periods where ice retreats toward the poles.
The last ice age ended 12,000 years ago. At its peak, what's known as the Laurentide Ice Sheet covered all of Canada and extended as far south as New York and the Midwest. It retreated to form the Barnes Ice Cap, which covers an area the size of Delaware on Baffin Island.
Unlike glaciers, which can move, the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to the bedrock, preserving the vegetal record of what grew around it under the ice. That quirk allowed the scientists leading the new study to glean information about how much it has grown—and shrank.
To determine when it first reached its modern size, they used an exposure dating technique to calculate roughly how long rocks several meters from the glacier’s edge had been exposed to the sky. Using measurements of Beryllium-10, an element that forms on the surface of exposed rock, the authors calculated that the ice sheet first reached the size it is today around 3,600 years ago.
Next, they wanted to see how much the ice cap had regrown from that point. To do this, they turned to the humble denizens of the tundra in front of the glacier: mosses and lichen.
“After the ice cap retreated, mosses eventually colonized this newly exposed land,” says Nicolás Young, a paleoclimatologist at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory at Columbia University and lead author of the new paper. “These mosses are living there, and things are normal—then, eventually, the ice cap starts to re-expand. The ice covers the moss, and kills it.” The traces of the dead moss are preserved in newly reexposed land, allowing Young and his team to piece together a timeline of how the ice has moved across the landscape.
Thanks to these records, Young and his coauthors estimate that the glacier started growing again around 2,000 years ago. This may have signaled the start of another glaciation period.
But starting in the 1960s, the ice cap has done something that wouldn’t correspond with another ice age: It started getting smaller again. The team used historic aerial photos that showed that the ice has reversed course, retreating significantly back from its new margins. The Barnes Ice Cap’s edges have retreated an average of 4 meters per year since the 1980s. That coincides with a period of rapidly increasing carbon emissions, which has caused ice to go into retreat worldwide. The ice cap offers a particularly stark example, though, given the growth prior to the 1960s.
“Modern retreat of this glacier has reversed 2,000 years of net expansion—that’s a pretty decent chunk of time,” Young says.
Meredith Kelly, a professor of earth sciences at Dartmouth, says the data gathered in the study is “awesome” and that the study shows a “clear pattern of what the ice cap was doing.” However, Kelly says that she would like to see a comparison of some of the data to other sites around the world to more fully grasp how, exactly, the Earth was moving into its glaciation period before the effects of human-caused warming kicked in. While we have a broad understanding of what kicks off periods where ice can grow, the exact mechanisms are still something that require more research.
The evidence presented in this paper, Young says, could also validate a decades-old hypothesis that has long been held up by climate deniers as “evidence” climate change is a hoax. In the early 1970s, scientists gathered for a meeting at Brown University to discuss hypotheses of when the next ice age might happen. (Young says that two of his coauthors on this paper were at that meeting.) The scientists concluded that a glaciation period was so imminent that they sent a warning letter to President Richard Nixon.
“I think this study actually helps show that scientists were right about a pending glaciation,” Young says. “
Media coverage of the meeting, as well as a colder period of weather in the 1970s, have long been pitched by climate deniers as “proof” that global warming isn’t actually happening. It very much is, though, and the new research actually adds to the evidence.

The new roles will concentrate on local and state advocacy, K-12 and higher education, and interfaith and intergroup partnerships, joining existing teams to counter hate manifesting across civic life.
JFNA is carrying out this hiring effort through its Frontline initiative. Backed by more than 25 funders, the $35 million initiative distributes targeted grants to 120 local federations while providing professional training, shared tools, resources, and expert guidance.
Highlighting the urgency of the initiative, JFNA reported that antisemitic incidents have surged following the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks on Israel, with physical assaults reaching record highs last year and Jews targeted in 64 percent of religiously motivated hate crimes. Furthermore, polling cited by the organization indicates that 65 percent of Jews in the US believe the country has a significant amount of antisemitism, compared to 45 percent in 2020.
Rising US antisemitism prompts Jewish Federations to expand advocacy network
JFNA stated these personnel will function as a community defense line in municipal meetings, healthcare environments, school boards, and educational curricula.
Detailing the broader aims of the program, Shira Hutt, Executive Vice President of JFNA, said, “Federations have been deeply engaged in the work of community relations and civic engagement for decades. Today, we require new strategies and increased resources to address the dramatic rise of antisemitism that is permeating every facet of civic life. Federations are on the ‘frontlines’ of this work every day.”
Hutt added: “Frontline is a game-changing initiative that will equip Federations with the talent, support, and resources they need to confront the increasingly complex and growing challenges they face, whether in government, in educational institutions, in media, or our other civic spaces.”
Beyond personnel additions, the Frontline program funds several targeted engagement projects. These include year-round training sessions, the Project Halo messaging hub for data-driven strategic guidance regarding security and Israel advocacy, and the Student to Student high school initiative.
The Student to Student program operates in 50 communities to foster connections with non-Jewish teens and has reached more than 60,000 students over the past three years, with nearly half of those engagements occurring in the preceding year. Additional investments back the One Mitzvah A Day mobilization platform, which has grown to reach a daily distribution list of 25,000 individuals.
Julie Platt, Chair of Frontline and immediate past Board Chair of JFNA, said, “In the aftermath of October 7, our community was very disappointed to see that many people we thought were our allies stayed silent. We learned the hard lesson that our civic engagement efforts must be more focused, more targeted, and more outcomes-based, and that is exactly what Frontline is designed to do.”
She added, “Only through deep, sustained, and strategic engagement can we ensure that antisemitism is neither tolerated nor normalized, and that our communities remain safe.”
The Frontline effort mirrors the operational model established by LiveSecure, a $130 million security initiative launched in response to the 2018 Tree of Life synagogue shooting in Pittsburgh. In 2018, fewer than 20 communities maintained professionally managed security programs that met necessary standards; since then, LiveSecure has expanded that national infrastructure to more than 140 communities within four years—a systemic scale-up that JFNA now aims to replicate across its advocacy and civic relations networks.

What happens when ideology becomes more important than the people? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:56:52 UTC
02:56:52 KST

A Jewish town is attacked. Agitators have just entered. Suddenly, three SUVs pull in. They have Palestinian license plates. Keffiyehs around their necks. One man holds a selfie stick. A Jewish resident tells them to stop. Asks them the purpose of their visit. Requests they turn around.
What is the appropriate response when the driver hesitates?
That happened to me this week. Except I was in the car. It wasn’t a Jewish town. It was Arab. We weren’t wearing keffiyehs, but our drivers wore kippot. Israeli flags hung from our rear-view mirrors. When the Arab resident politely asked us to turn around, we answered with questions.
Except I didn’t know. I assumed we’d only go to Area C. I wasn’t in the car that spoke to the Arab resident. I didn’t hear what he said. I only saw frantic gesticulations. I felt only fear, dread, and confusion.
This week I was invited on a tour to Area C in the West Bank. I was told we’d see the mansions the Palestinian Authority was building and that we’d have an experienced field coordinator who had IDF approval.
Suddenly, I found myself entering an Arab village in a convoy of three cars. A resident asked us to turn around. I never heard the conversation. When a crowd surrounded us, I assumed he intended harm.
When we finally escaped under threat of attack, our story went viral instantly. A Knesset candidate was the victim of aggression! This must prove settler violence is a hoax!
Even my first video reflected that same assumption. I, too, had already begun interpreting what happened through a narrative I thought I understood.
I never heard the Arab resident ask us to leave.
It was only in the coming hours when the adrenaline subsided. When everyone began to post videos of the incident. That I began to piece together what actually happened.
And what happened?
I was a victim of a terror attack. A mob encircled me. Boulders were thrown at my car. It missed my car’s window by centimeters. I thought I was going to die. I’ve woken up in middle of the night screaming. But I garnered no sympathy.
Both sides asked, “Why were you there?” And they are correct. Why was I there?
Imagine agreeing to a trip based on the itinerary you were given, only to find yourself somewhere you hadn’t understood you would be going. To be met with violence, fear, and terror. And when you share your experience, you’re told you should have expected it.
Nobody sympathizes with you. You can barely sympathize with yourself.
Caught between competing narratives
The right says you deserved it for calling it the West Bank. The left says you deserved it for agreeing to go. The world says it should have been worse because you’re a Jew. But you’re only there because your friend told you it was an opportunity to learn.
And suddenly, you’ve never been more confused.
Because what if three SUVs entered a Jewish village with Palestinian license plates?
Everyone tells influencers that they have a responsibility. You must document. You must show. And when we’re pressured to do just that, we’re told we risked our lives for attention.
But who actually benefits from the attention we bring?
What happens when the narrative becomes more important than those who experienced it?
Thirty-one years ago, Yitzhak Rabin was assassinated by a Jew who opposed the peace process he championed. Rabin was also one of the architects of the Oslo Accords. A contributor to the current reality in the West Bank. The confusion between Area A, Area B, and Area C. A division he thought would finally bring peace.
But people were afraid. Afraid for the Jewish future. Afraid of what this division of land would bring.
An area of land so misunderstood that I agreed to go on an educational trip to hear a new perspective. The trip was described as an opportunity to see the “Palestinian Authority’s efforts to… advance a de facto state in Area C.”
A scary reality. A reality that deserves to be shown. A reality influencers are pressured to portray – the truth.
But what is the truth?
Does the truth change based on the ideology of the people delivering it?
How far will an ideology go to deliver its message?
And what happens when you didn’t consent to be the messenger?
Thirty-one years later, is the legacy of the Jewish state still stained by those that can’t separate an ideology from the person delivering it?
The writer is an accidental hasbara content creator. Originally from New York, she graduated from Columbia with a degree in biomedical engineering before making aliyah and enlisting in the IDF after October 7. She now hopes to follow in the footsteps of her great-grandfather, Ben-Gurion’s private doctor, and practice medicine in the hospitals he helped create.

Paraguay's central bank under pressure over politically connected lender
ASUNCION, Oct 22 - Paraguay's central bank and its president face mounting calls to resign as scrutiny intensifies over how they supervised a fast-growing digital bank with political ties.
Senators from the ruling party and the opposition have urged President Santiago Peña to remove the central bank's top leadership, despite it being credited with helping Paraguay secure investment-grade status.
The case is testing the reputation that has helped Paraguay become one of South America's emerging destinations for foreign capital, much of it from neighboring Brazil.
In recent weeks, authorities have repeatedly tried to calm financial markets after it emerged that ueno bank faced regulatory scrutiny of its business and an administrative investigation. The bank uses lower case in company statements.
In written statements to Reuters, Paraguay's central bank defended its governance structure, saying regulatory and supervisory processes operate independently and in accordance with established legal procedures.
Ueno said it would continue to "fully cooperate" with the central bank and maintained that the preliminary administrative proceeding did not constitute a finding of wrongdoing.
Ueno has scaled rapidly from a niche local fintech player to a mid-tier bank, in line with digital platforms like Monzo and Nubank. It says it has 3 million customers and manages roughly $800 million to $850 million in public funds.
Details of the preliminary probe appeared in a central bank report sent to the Senate this month. The report aimed to dispel doubts about loans issued by ueno to related companies, but it ended up fueling more questions from lawmakers, the banking association and other business groups.
"The replacement of the Central Bank authorities must take place," ruling-party Senator Gustavo Leite said in an interview with Reuters. "The people at the Central Bank have lost credibility."
Opposition Senator Rafael Filizzola said the financial system was "suffering" and filed another request for information on ueno, which experienced a major selloff of its global bonds. Fitch Ratings changed the outlook on the company's securities from stable to negative last week.
Paraguay's Banking Association, which represents 14 private lenders including Brazil's Itau, published a statement on October 18 reiterating that the central bank's response to the senate was "incomplete."
POLITICAL TIES
The case is politically sensitive. Paraguay's central bank president, Carlos Carvallo, previously worked at ueno and served as its president until August 2023, the company confirmed in a statement to Reuters. Peña, a former economist, was a business partner of the group that owned the bank until March 2025. Ueno said Peña never had a relationship with the bank itself as a shareholder or investor.
Much of the pressure for answers has come from lawmakers of the ruling Colorado Party, amid an internal dispute over the party's presidential nomination for the 2028 general elections.
In a written response to Reuters, the central bank said there was no conflict of interest, saying Carvallo had "recused himself" from all decisions related to ueno bank.
Paraguay’s presidency did not respond to a request for comment.
In remarks to local media in early October, Peña described the situation as an "overflow" of a technical matter that was taken into the political arena and had done "tremendous damage to the image of the entire country."
The ueno case has put a spotlight on stability in Paraguay's grain-exporting economy that won investment-grade credit ratings from Moody's in 2024 and S&P Global last year.
The IMF expects growth of 4.5% this year, almost double the regional average. REUTERS

'Post' sees letter requesting West Bank trip coordination despite IDF denial - exclusive
Unknown

2026-10-22
