02:56:26 KST

The incident on Wednesday in which the IDF detained a US congressional nominee and around 90 foreign volunteers, including senior members of Rabbis for Human Rights (RHR), as they attempted to assist Palestinians in harvesting olives in the West Bank, was a highly complex situation, IDF sources told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.
Given extensive recent reports of Jewish extremists harassing Palestinians and preventing them from completing their harvests, the activists sought to assist in the olive harvest.
Claims from both sides involved were subjected to careful examination. One issue that remains unclear is the status of communications between the sides before the incident.
RHR initially said that they had sent letters requesting to coordinate their visit with the IDF Chief’s office and with the IDF Central Commander, to the IDF head of COGAT, to the Samaria Brigade Commander, and to the Etzion Brigade Commander, but had received no response.
Letter requesting to coordinate visit seen by 'Post'
The IDF and the Foreign Ministry initially said that RHR had failed to coordinate its visit to the West Bank area and that the area was a prohibited zone.
However, on Thursday evening, the Post received a copy of the letter sent by Rabbis for Human Rights to the IDF. The letter is undated, but the organization said that it was sent to the IDF on August 25, nearly two months in advance of the visit.
At press time, the military had not clarified whether or not it had received the letter.
Earlier on Thursday, IDF sources had expressed that they were unaware of such a letter.
Further, they indicated that the IDF receives many letters and sometimes may not see or respond to all of them on time.
If the RHR had indeed sent such a letter to the IDF, and the military simply had not read it in time due to being overwhelmed with paperwork, this would neutralize one of the main justifications for its detention of the activists seeking to assist the Palestinian olive harvesters.
Yet there is another complex series of arguments regarding the incident.
RHR said that the village they visited was in a Palestinian area and, as such, did not require coordination with the IDF.
Faced with this claim, the IDF sources explained to the Post that 90% of the area where the olives were harvested was open and did not require coordination with the military, but 10% did require such coordination.
Regarding the visit, IDF sources argued that a large part of the problem – which had prevented a slower and more careful assessment of the situation – was the very large number of foreign visitors and the fact that they had come within some 50 meters of a Jewish village known to have provocative and aggressive members.
In other words, when the IDF arrived in the area, some two hours after the olive harvesting had begun, they were seriously concerned that even if the RHR group was peaceful, the extremists from the nearby Jewish village would attack them, given the size of their group.
Of course, RHR and the Palestinian harvesters could respond that it was the IDF’s job to protect them and allow them to do their harvesting; not to forcefully evacuate them – let alone detain them – to avoid provoking extremists into breaking the law.
IDF sources did not have a satisfactory answer to that question, saying that the soldiers on the ground had not known that US Congressional candidate Brad Lander (D-NY) was present or understood much about the group when they arrived.
Rather, IDF sources said that since a series of provocative incidents involving Palestinians, Jews, and foreign visitors have taken place and since there was no registered coordination, the military assumed that the visitors were provocateurs who had to be detained and removed from their proximity to potential Jewish extremists, in the interests of avoiding a potentially large-scale and deadly incident – in light of recent occurrences.
Later, when the IDF officials realized who Lander was, they immediately released him. Further, they said, they released almost all the detainees within a matter of hours.
While the military’s narrative of the incident was not particularly favorable, IDF sources said that the broader olive harvesting situation was very favorable.
They said that a huge area of Palestinian West Bank olive harvesting had been properly coordinated with the IDF in the last week and a half.
The IDF said that over 100 olive harvest trips had been coordinated with the IDF without any problems. The military added that 22,500 tons of olives were harvested, and 5,600 tons of olive oil were packaged, worth around NIS 225 million.
The Foreign Ministry said that one quarter of the entire area had already been harvested.
However, the letter from RHR to the IDF noted data indicating that there had been a 63% increase in Jewish crimes against Palestinians during the first half of the year. The military had not allowed harvesting in the specific area in question.
Lander was specifically released with a warning, he recalled in a statement.
“I’ve been released from IDF custody with a ‘warning,’ apparently because of my public profile (I told them I wasn’t even a congress member yet, just a nominee),” he wrote. “But several dozen rabbis and participants harvesting olives with me are still in detention. For harvesting olives. They should all be released immediately,” he said, adding that “Palestinians face far worse consequences every day.”
Rabbis for Human Rights activists detained in West Bank
RHR said that the volunteers had worked in the village of Nahalin near Bethlehem, accompanying Palestinian farmers to groves during the olive harvest.
RHR leadership said that their work in the West Bank was peaceful, and that it was the organization’s policy to comply with IDF orders.
“We came to accompany farmers to land they had been unable to access for three years, and after two hours of peaceful olive harvesting, large numbers of troops arrived and closed off the area. No one could have known about this order in advance.
“Instead of protecting people working their land, the army is keeping them away from it and detaining those who came to accompany them for identification,” acting HRH Executive Director Anton Goodman said.
“The fact that Israeli and American rabbis are compelled to stand alongside Palestinian farmers to help them harvest their olives and protect them from settler violence is a damning indictment of the Israeli government. The fact that these same rabbis are detained by security forces, rather than the authorities protecting the farmers and taking action against those perpetrating the violence, is nothing short of a disgrace,” Yizhar Hess, vice chairman of the World Zionist Organization, said.
Meanwhile, the IDF and the Foreign Ministry view the entire incident as planned and designed to be more of a public relations incident than focused on helping with the olive harvest, which they say is generally proceeding well, despite some increased Jewish extremist violence.
Corinne Baum contributed to this report.

Turkish parliament passes law on liquidation of certain investment funds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:53:02 UTC
02:53:02 KST

Adem Balta, Gazi Nogay and Gokhan Ergocun
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The Turkish parliament passed legislation Thursday establishing procedures for the liquidation of certain investment funds and the recovery of assets unlawfully removed from their portfolios.
The law applies to funds ordered liquidated by the Capital Markets Board of Türkiye (CMB) on Sept. 17, whose liquidation had not been completed by the law's publication date.
Under the legislation, liquidation will be carried out by designated institutions under the supervision of the CMB, with proceeds added to the funds' liquidation assets after necessary expenses are deducted.
The law allows interim payments of up to one million Turkish liras ($20,150) to eligible investors in funds designated by the CMB, subject to their net investment amounts and other conditions.
Investors whose net investment amounts are below one million liras may receive payments up to those amounts, while payments to those with higher balances will be capped at one million liras.
Individuals and institutions found by the CMB to have engaged in specified market abuse, insider trading or market manipulation involving the affected funds will be barred from receiving payments from their liquidation assets or recovery accounts.
The legislation makes portfolio management companies that established or managed the funds primarily responsible for losses, with other parties held liable under specified conditions if the losses cannot be recovered from those companies.
The Savings Deposit Insurance Fund (SDIF) will be authorized to pursue the recovery of losses from responsible parties identified by the SPK and may be appointed as trustee over certain assets.
Assets seized or confiscated in connection with the affected funds may be returned to the funds or transferred to recovery accounts under the procedures set out in the law.
Recovered funds will be distributed to investors through designated liquidation institutions or, where liquidation has been completed, through the Investor Compensation Center (ICC) in proportion to their fund holdings.

Our digital lives increasingly depend on data centers. How do we secure them?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:49:58 UTC
02:49:58 KST

When Alexander Olshansky received a call in September telling him that the data center hosting his company's infrastructure in Kyiv had been destroyed by a Russian attack, he made a beeline for the scene.
“As I was driving up to the data center, I saw a column of black smoke, a block cordoned off by the police and fire trucks,” recalls Olshansky, president of the Ukrainian domain registration and Web hosting provider MiroHost. The data center was damaged, but Olshansky’s employees had been sheltering elsewhere when the attack happened.
Despite the facility’s destruction on September 23, just around one in 20 of MiroHost’s customers were affected. The company had reserved enough computing capacity in Poland, the Czech Republic and Slovakia to back up its Ukrainian infrastructure in the event of an attack.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Other data centers haven’t fared as well. In October Ukrainian drones struck three data centers operated by the Russian technology giant Yandex, disrupting services and damaging artificial intelligence infrastructure. Earlier this year Iranian drones damaged Amazon Web Services facilities in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain, causing Web outages across the region.
What is inarguable is that, like them or not, data centers are increasingly important parts of our lives, and as such, they’re increasingly seen as fair targets in war. How they are secured is a matter of national—and even international—importance.
“I would say 2026 is going to be the first year of drone strikes taking out data centers being a thing,” says Doug Madory, head of international Internet analysis at the cybersecurity company Infoblox. “I just don’t think that anybody had anticipated this as a risk to interrupt service.”
Because of their vital role in the economy, data centers are designed with multiple layers of security. These include restricted access to the site, constant surveillance and backup power systems. In the event of fire, suppression equipment keeps flames at bay. But those defenses are mostly focused on stopping bad actors from getting inside or on keeping services running when equipment fails—not on withstanding attacks from the air.
“Most data center security standards in the industry focus on physical access restrictions,” says Connor Martin, an international affairs fellow in national security at the Council on Foreign Relations. But protecting facilities against drone or missile strikes is a different challenge—and one the sector must start focusing on. Data centers can seem like sitting ducks from the air because they’re massive, cavernous buildings containing enormously expensive equipment in often remote areas. They “can’t pick up and move,” Martin says.
Still, some protection is possible without going as far as installing missile defenses at key data center locations. Peter Judge, senior research analyst at the Uptime Institute, says operators can build shields around vulnerable equipment such as generators and air-handling units and use overhead netting or screens to hinder aerial surveillance. Yet more sophisticated systems might combine radar, cameras and radio sensors to identify approaching drones or aircraft.
But if a craft is spotted, what can actually be done is trickier. Aviation laws typically prevent jamming drone signals—scrambling their radio signals—or bringing them down without authorization. Some newer drones don’t transmit radio control signals at all.
For his part, Olshansky isn’t convinced physical protection is viable in a war zone anyway. “No fire suppression system is designed for a direct hit by a bomb, missile or drone,” he says.
Truly protecting such a facility could mean burying it deep underground, which isn’t feasible. Instead, the industry’s best approach may be in redundancy—distributing services across multiple facilities so that when one is destroyed, another can take over. It works, as MiroHost showed, but it also costs more: Olshansky says his company effectively doubled its available computing capacity to prepare for an attack.
Madory points out that cloud providers already offer ways to distribute workloads across different geographic regions. The problem is that many customers don’t bother because of the additional cost and technical complexity. “In theory, you could be resilient, but in practice, a lot of stuff is not,” he says.
The recent attacks could change where companies choose to build their data centers, Martin says. The Gulf states have invested heavily in attracting those kinds of instalments, but their proximity to regional conflicts could make future projects harder to justify. Larger countries such as the U.S. and China, meanwhile, have more opportunities to build facilities far from potential conflict zones. But even then, there are no guarantees. As Olshansky says, “It is always better to have two copies of something than just one, even if it is highly protected.”

Millions in cheese revenue lost as protest hits Italy’s buffalo mozzarella output

A truckers’ protest in southern Italy has halted the production of the famed buffalo mozzarella, causing an estimated loss of €3 million (US$3.37 million) in just 24 hours as the milk cannot reach dairies in the Naples region and the finished cheese cannot reach customers, an official said.
The week-long strike by truck drivers over the high cost of diesel driven up by the Iran war has also blocked deliveries of other basic goods to supermarkets and left fuel pumps empty in much of southern Italy.
The government approved new tax breaks for truckers on Thursday, but it was too early to tell whether they were enough to end the protest.
The disruption is particularly damaging to buffalo mozzarella because the production of the protected cheese depends on a tightly timed supply chain.

19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum multipolarity, Europe and peace in focus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:42:33 UTC
02:42:33 KST

The emergence of a multipolar world, the future role of Europe and different approaches to ending the war in Ukraine dominated the first day of the 19th Verona Eurasian Economic Forum in Istanbul on Thursday, as political figures and experts debated how to manage the changing global order without triggering further conflict.
The discussions at Istanbul's Ciragan Palace brought together political, business and academic figures from more than 30 countries, with debates repeatedly returning to the need for dialogue and a new balance of power among the US, Russia, Europe and other major and regional powers.
Türkiye responds to global uncertainty with stability, investment push
In his opening remarks, Turkish Treasury and Finance Minister Mehmet Simsek said the world was going through a period marked by volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity, pointing to conflicts, disruptions in global supply chains, rising commodity prices and mounting pressure on the global economy.
Simsek said Türkiye's response was centered on maintaining macro-financial stability while strengthening its resilience to external shocks.
He said Ankara would continue with a data-dependent restrictive monetary policy, rebuild fiscal buffers and accelerate the country's green transformation to reduce its dependence on imported primary energy.
He also stressed Türkiye's diplomatic role amid growing geopolitical tensions, saying the country benefits from "stability, peace and prosperity" in its surrounding regions and therefore continues to invest in mediation and dialogue.
US faces era of 'permanent rivalry'
Speaking at a special session of the forum, Thomas Graham, a fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and former senior US official on Russia policy, argued that Europe would have to play a central role, while describing the changing international system as an unprecedented challenge for Washington.
"For the first time in history, the United States faces a multipolar order from which it cannot withdraw," Graham said.
The US could no longer dominate the international system as it had during earlier periods, he said, arguing that Washington instead had to adapt to an era of "permanent rivalry" with other major powers.
That would require avoiding direct conflict, particularly given the destructive capacity of modern weapons, while maintaining enough cooperation to address transnational challenges.
Graham said the objective should be to establish regional equilibria in Europe, the Middle East and East Asia that could ultimately underpin a broader Eurasian balance.
He rejected the idea that Washington, Moscow and Beijing could determine the future of the rest of the world among themselves, saying Europe remained a critical part of any such arrangement.
Türkiye's role in emerging multipolar order
Necmeddin Bilal Erdogan, chairman of the Ilim Yayma Foundation, placed Türkiye's growing regional role within the same shift toward a more multipolar international system.
Erdogan said regional actors should be encouraged to take greater responsibility for their own security and future, arguing that those living in a particular region ultimately bear the greatest consequences of instability there.
Türkiye, he said, had sought to play such a role through efforts concerning Syria, Iraq and the Caucasus and its ability to maintain dialogue with competing sides.
Erdogan called for dialogue channels to remain open despite conflicts and political disagreements, saying prejudices and double standards in international affairs were eroding trust between countries.
He argued that both Türkiye and Russia were part of the broader European space and that losing sight of such historical and geographic realities amid current conflicts would make prospects for peace more difficult.
He also linked the debate over international security to wider questions about technological and economic development, questioning the purpose of advances in areas such as artificial intelligence if they failed to contribute to peace, human welfare and greater equality.
'Without Europe there can be no peace'
Romano Prodi, former president of the European Commission and former Italian prime minister, recalled a dramatically different atmosphere in Russia-Europe relations two decades ago, saying cooperation between the two sides had once appeared capable of reaching much further.
The war in Ukraine had since made the divide extremely difficult to overcome, he said, while a succession of conflicts from Ukraine to Sudan, Gaza and Iran had created an increasingly dangerous international environment.
"It is time to change," Prodi said, arguing that Europe had been marginalized amid contacts between Russia and the US, partly because of its own internal divisions and weaknesses.
But excluding the continent from a future settlement would be a mistake, he said.
"Without Europe there can be no peace," Prodi said, stressing the bloc's economic weight, technological capabilities and experience in overcoming historical conflicts.
Referring to discussions about a potential understanding among major powers, Prodi used the analogy of a "little Yalta," suggesting that the world could be moving toward negotiations in which major powers establish new rules for managing relations.
He cautioned, however, that a potential US-Russia energy understanding alone could not resolve broader international problems and that any durable arrangement would also require Europe's participation.
Approaches to ending Ukraine war
The discussions also focused on possible paths toward ending the war in Ukraine.
Kirill Dmitriev, Russian President Vladimir Putin's special representative for investment and economic cooperation with foreign countries and CEO of the Russian Direct Investment Fund, said Moscow was seeking a permanent end to hostilities and a stable European security architecture rather than temporary ceasefires.
"It's not about temporary ceasefires. It's not about temporary solutions," Dmitriev said, arguing that an interim arrangement could eventually lead to renewed hostilities.
He said recent US-Russia discussions had been positive in this regard and praised efforts by the Trump administration to balance the interests of Russia, Ukraine and Europe in search of a lasting settlement.
Graham said permanent peace could not realistically emerge from a single agreement but would have to develop through a longer process.
"To demand permanent peace as a condition for a ceasefire actually is a call for continued warfare," he said.
He said negotiations could first establish principles and parameters for a future settlement, followed by a ceasefire that would allow detailed talks to continue in a less volatile environment.
Such an outcome would require concessions from both Russia and Ukraine and active European participation, he added.
Dmitriev urges renewed Russia-Europe economic ties
Beyond the Ukraine negotiations, Dmitriev argued that economic ties could eventually help rebuild relations between Russia and Europe.
He said there was "no question" that Russia wanted to and would cooperate with Europe, while criticizing European efforts to increase defense spending and rejecting claims that Moscow posed a threat to the continent.
Dmitriev also urged European business leaders to press policymakers more forcefully over restrictions on access to the Russian market and the economic consequences of reduced Russian energy supplies.
In separate remarks during the discussion, he argued that the resumption of broader Russian energy supplies to Europe was ultimately "economically inevitable."
He also said Russia-US economic cooperation could expand beyond energy, pointing to potential collaboration in areas including fertilizers.

Romania to speed up development of Black Sea capabilities after cargo ship attacks
BUCHAREST, Oct 22 - Romania will accelerate its development of surveillance capabilities and equipment to counter mines and drones in the Black Sea after a series of drone attacks on commercial ships off its coast, its top defence council said on Thursday.
At least seven cargo ships have been hit near the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria in the past two weeks, with some 30 sailors reported dead or missing. Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots shot down two of the latest generation of Russian drones over Romanian territorial waters on Saturday.
NATO said on Tuesday it will send more maritime patrol aircraft, radar systems and drones to the Black Sea.
• Romania's top defence council said latest ship attacks are direct consequences of Russia's aggression beyond Ukraine's borders.
• Threats to freedom of navigation and critical energy projects in the Black Sea pose a security crisis for Romania.
• The current risks require concrete measures to protect human lives, maintain free access to national ports, and ensure the security of energy facilities in the Exclusive Economic Zone.
• The top defence council said it will accelerate the development of capabilities for maritime surveillance, countering naval mines and intervening against drones illegally breaching national airspace and waters.
• Authorities will practice to improve the efficiency of their operational response.
• Romania will seek to improve cooperation with fellow NATO members Bulgaria and Turkey with whom it shares the Black Sea.
• "The Council members also analyzed ways to intensify coordination within NATO. This includes strengthening the deterrence and defense posture on the Eastern Flank and identifying new measures to respond to threats in the Black Sea region." REUTERS

‘Longer we wait, worse it gets’: Struggle of Gaza’s breast cancer patients
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:40:24 UTC
02:40:24 KST

‘Longer we wait, worse it gets’: Struggle of Gaza’s breast cancer patients
Breast cancer patients in Gaza face delayed diagnoses, medicine shortages and limited access to scans and treatment, leaving many fearing their condition is worsening.
Deir el-Balah, Gaza Strip – Hiba Musbah has already been through seven rounds of chemotherapy for the breast cancer that is plaguing her body. Next week will be the eighth.
But the 36-year-old mother of three, from eastern Deir el-Balah, says her condition has continued to deteriorate as she waits to travel outside Gaza for further treatment.
“I can no longer take care of my children as I used to. My son is the one who helps me,” she told Al Jazeera. Her husband Motaz, who has a heart condition, has had to take on more responsibility as her health has worsened, caring for their three children – Mohammed, 13, Jaber, 10, and Ahmad, eight.
Musbah first noticed lumps around her right breast in January 2024, a few months after the beginning of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza. At the time, she initially ignored them because she was displaced and the war was intensifying. Her mother eventually insisted that she seek medical attention.
Doctors confirmed it was cancer, but despite needing urgent surgery, it took two months for Musbah to be operated on, with the delay caused by Israeli military attacks around the Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis, where she was being treated.
“The situation was difficult, with the bombardment and the tanks,” she said. “I delayed the operation because of the war. The last time, I nearly died from tank fire, so I postponed the operation.”
Her chemotherapy was initially also delayed for seven months because medicines were unavailable at Nasser Hospital.
Musbah’s experience reflects the reality facing hundreds of women with breast cancer in Gaza, where Israel’s war and blockade have severely weakened the health system’s ability to diagnose and treat the disease.
Shortages of medicines and medical equipment, broken diagnostic machines, the absence of radiotherapy and difficulties leaving the Gaza Strip for specialised care have turned the fight against cancer into another struggle amid Gaza’s deepening health and humanitarian crisis.
Surgery, chemotherapy and the cost of waiting
The lack of access to diagnostic equipment is now another source of anxiety for Musbah. She explains that she needs a new computerised tomography (CT) scan to assess how her condition has progressed, but has been unable to obtain one because the equipment is unavailable at public hospitals.
A private hospital has a scanner, she said, but the examination costs about 150 shekels ($48), which she cannot afford. The waiting time for an appointment can also exceed three months.
“I am now suffering from pain in my back and leg, and I have not had a scan for three months because the equipment is unavailable,” she said. “My doctor told me he was concerned that the disease might have spread through my body, but I still do not know.”
Musbah now struggles to walk and move one of her arms, and experiences pain in her shoulder, legs and eyes, as well as damage to her hair and nails during treatment.
“If I had received treatment early, things would not have reached this point. My condition has become much more difficult because my treatment was delayed,” she said. “Cancer patients also need good food, fruit, meat, fresh produce, but we cannot afford everything we need.”
According to Musbah, she has been waiting for around two years to leave Gaza for treatment after receiving a medical referral. But Israel, which controls all entry and exit from Gaza, has yet to give her security approval to travel.
“I want to travel, receive treatment and get better,” Musbah said. “I want to regain my health and return to the way I was before.”
Growing crisis
According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, the Gaza Strip recorded about 360 new breast cancer cases annually before the war, compared with 250 in 2024 and around 260 in 2025.
The ministry has warned that these figures may not reflect the true number of cases because screening and early-diagnosis services have largely collapsed, potentially leaving hundreds of patients undiagnosed.
In a statement on October 1, the ministry said repeated breakdowns of mammography machines and shortages of laboratory supplies had severely restricted early detection in Gaza. Chemotherapy, hormonal and targeted therapies were also unavailable or critically scarce, while radiotherapy was completely unavailable.
The ministry said surgery for advanced tumours had also been halted because of a lack of specialised medical capabilities.
The shortage of diagnostic equipment adds another obstacle for women who suspect they may have cancer.
Dr Iman al-Haj Ahmad, an obstetrician and gynaecologist at Hikmat al-Jamei Health Centre in Deir el-Balah, understands these barriers both as a doctor helping women seek diagnosis and as a breast cancer patient herself, having been diagnosed in May 2025.
“I had to search until I found a place where I could get a mammogram,” al-Haj Ahmad said. “I kept thinking about ordinary women who don’t have the medical knowledge or connections that I have. If it was this difficult for me, how much harder must it be for them?”
Before the war, women could seek an initial examination at a primary healthcare centre and be referred to hospitals for mammography, ultrasound scans, and further tests.
Now, al-Haj Ahmad said, imaging services are limited, some cancer specialists have left Gaza, and tests needed to confirm a diagnosis are not always available through public health services. Some patients have to pay privately.
Al-Haj Ahmad waited about a month for surgery, eventually undergoing the operation at Nasser Hospital with a visiting Jordanian medical team while the hospital was operating under dangerous conditions.
Chemotherapy and severe food shortages later took a heavy toll on al-Haj Ahmad’s health. She said she lost about 20kg (44lb), her immune system weakened significantly, and doctors had to pause chemotherapy temporarily.
Al-Haj Ahmad is now receiving hormonal treatment while waiting to travel abroad for radiotherapy. Her referral for treatment abroad had been pending since September 2025.
Despite her own illness, she continues to examine women and refer suspected cases to the surgery department at Al-Aqsa Hospital. She also encourages women with a family history of breast cancer to be especially attentive to changes in their breasts.
“Early detection is especially important in Gaza because treatment options are so limited,” she said.
Pink October
It has been a year since the “ceasefire” began in Gaza, although Israeli attacks continue, bringing the death toll from the war up to more than 74,400 Palestinians.
October is the global Breast Cancer Awareness Month – also known as Pink October. Health workers in Gaza are participating in the international initiative, with staff at Hekr al-Jameh Health Centre in Deir el-Balah trying to reach women through healthcare visits and targeted awareness sessions.
It’s part of a Pink October campaign they’ve called “pink blooms from among the rubble”, which teaches women about breast cancer, demonstrates breast self-examination, and offers psychological support to those affected by the disease.
Sabreen al-Buhaisi, who supervises Hekr al-Jameh’s primary healthcare services, said the centre had screened between 700 and 800 women during the campaign. Seven or eight cases were referred to hospital surgical departments for further assessment.
But identifying women who may have cancer is only the first step. Al-Buhaisi said free mammography was available at a limited number of hospitals, where women face long waits for appointments. Private screening is too expensive for many families.
“The financial cost is very high for women. Our people cannot afford these expenses,” she said.
Still, al-Buhaisi urged women to continue examining their breasts despite the difficult circumstances the vast majority live in.
“Even displacement and living in the camps should not stop you from examining yourself,” she said. “Take five minutes of your time. It can make a big difference in your treatment journey.”
Amid these hardships, Musbah continues her fight against time.
She says she has repeatedly followed up on the travel arrangements, but remains unable to leave, with no clear explanation for the delay.
The evacuation process is coordinated between the World Health Organization and Gaza’s Ministry of Health, but they have to then submit patients’ files to Israel for security screening and approval.
“I have been waiting for two years,” Musbah said. “And I still haven’t travelled.”

Türkiye, Canada seal strategic partnership to advance economic, defence ties
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:36:25 UTC
02:36:25 KST

Türkiye and Canada have launched a strategic partnership aimed at strengthening bilateral cooperation in trade, investment, energy, defence, security, and technological development.
The announcement followed a meeting between Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney on Thursday at the Presidential Complex in Ankara, where Erdogan welcomed Carney with an official ceremony.
The leaders held bilateral talks, followed by discussions between their delegations and a joint news conference.
'Canada-Türkiye partnership is essential'
In a joint statement on the partnership, the leaders said: "In an increasingly complex global security environment, rising geopolitical uncertainties, and evolving humanitarian challenges, a strong and resilient Canada-Türkiye partnership is essential, providing a foundation to mitigate shared threats and capitalise on new opportunities.”
Building on 83 years of diplomatic relations, the partnership aims to expand political dialogue, boost economic growth and trade, advance technological development, and strengthen shared security objectives, it said.
Both countries are NATO allies and reaffirmed their commitment to human rights, individual liberties, democracy, and the rule of law.
The leaders also launched a three-year action plan built around four pillars: trade, investment, and innovation; energy and climate cooperation; defence and security; and government-to-government dialogue and people-to-people ties.
Trade, investment, and innovation
Under the first pillar, Canada and Türkiye agreed to work toward successfully concluding a bilateral free trade agreement and expanding trade and investment in priority sectors, including energy supply, defence production, aerospace, and artificial intelligence.
They also committed to ratifying the Canada-Türkiye Air Transport Agreement, strengthening cooperation between trade and export agencies, including on projects in third countries, and promoting collaboration between their innovation ecosystems.
Energy and climate cooperation
The two countries pledged to advance cooperation across the energy sector, including liquefied natural gas, civil nuclear energy, renewable energy, clean technologies, and the resilience of critical energy infrastructure.
The plan also calls for encouraging investment, facilitating dialogue among nuclear sector stakeholders, strengthening sustainable mining and critical minerals supply chains, and expanding cooperation on climate resilience and environmental protection.
The leaders welcomed a joint statement on energy cooperation agreed upon by their respective energy and natural resources ministers.
Canada also welcomed Türkiye's role as host and president of next month’s COP31 UN Climate Change Conference in the southern city of Antalya, starting on November 9.
Ottawa expressed its readiness to work closely with Türkiye's presidency to ensure a successful conference.
Defence and security
The leaders pledged to deepen bilateral and multilateral defence cooperation, including through NATO, building on a recently signed statement of intent on defence cooperation.
They agreed to strengthen efforts to support peace and security in the Euro-Atlantic region and beyond, including in Ukraine, the South Caucasus, and the Middle East, particularly Gaza.
The statement also welcomed the conclusion of a memorandum of understanding on defence sector partnerships between Global Affairs Canada and Türkiye’s Defence Industries Secretariat.
The agreement is intended to facilitate expanded defence industry partnerships and advance discussions on further cooperation in areas of mutual interest.
The leaders also emphasised the importance of initiating a dialogue on strengthening mutual legal assistance in criminal matters and extradition.
Political dialogue and people-to-people ties
Under the fourth pillar, the countries agreed to establish an annual Canada-Türkiye Strategic Dialogue while continuing annual meetings of the joint economic and trade committee, as well as political-military and counterterrorism consultations.
They also pledged to strengthen cooperation on consular matters and migration, explore measures to facilitate travel and mobility, and promote cultural exchanges and engagement with their respective diasporas.
The two leaders agreed that their foreign ministers would oversee implementation of a three-year action plan with the goal of deepening bilateral relations, promoting international security, and building prosperous green economies.
Carney expressed appreciation for the Turkish government's warm hospitality during his visit, described in the joint statement as the first visit by a head of government between the two countries.
Türkiye also welcomed an invitation for Erdogan to visit Canada at a mutually agreeable time.

Foreign national beaten to death by a mob in South Africa

Foreign national beaten to death by a mob in South Africa
Police say a 50-person mob in Durban killed a man amid a wave of anti-migrant marches.
A mob has beaten a foreign national to death during a protest in the South African port city of Durban, amid a wave of anti-immigrant tension.
Police said the group approached the man as he stood by the side of a road in Durban’s central business district.
The victim was allegedly assaulted by a group of about 50 people and was declared dead at the scene, a police statement said.
Police did not reveal the nationality of the man or details of the march.
They said the victim was in his 30s or early 40s, and they were still trying to identify suspects in the attack.
Anti-migrant marches
Durban has been at the epicentre of months of protests against foreign nationals, with looting and violence erupting after an anti-migrant march in the city two weeks ago.
Demonstrations calling for government action against African migrants who entered the country illegally began in June, with some escalating into violence.
Nigeria, Mozambique, Malawi and other countries have said some of their citizens have been killed in xenophobic attacks in South Africa.
South African authorities disputed some of those claims, saying that some deaths were linked to criminal activity.
Tens of thousands of migrants have left South Africa in recent months in one of the largest mass exoduses in years to avoid the violence.
The government also said that many were deported for not having the required papers to be in the country.
South Africa is Africa’s largest economy and migrants have moved to the country for opportunities. But communities in South Africa say there are not enough jobs and public services are overburdened.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa has denounced anti-migrant violence but acknowledged that weak border control systems allowed undocumented migrants to travel to and stay in the country.
Government figures show there are about 2.4 million foreign nationals living among South Africa’s population of 62 million.

Thousands of student movement supporters rally as Serbia heads to poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:31:00 UTC
02:31:00 KST

Tens of thousands of supporters of Serbia's opposition student movement gathered in central Belgrade on Thursday, as the country's longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic rallied across town at the dueling final events ahead of pivotal parliamentary elections.
The Student List, a leaderless movement of student-backed candidates, is seeking to end more than 14 years of rule by Vucic's right-wing populist Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) when the country votes on Sunday.
It is the biggest threat Vucic has faced to his hold on power, and civil society groups have warned the election campaign has been marred by intimidation, arrests, attacks, misuse of public resources and a distorted media environment.
"I came to support the Student List because young people finally gave me hope that it is possible to live in a normal country," 47-year-old Marija Nedeljkovic Radic told Agence France-Presse (AFP) as she arrived for the students' rally.
"Really, for the first time in my life, I believe that it is possible."
The vote comes after nearly two years of student-led protests sparked by the 2024 collapse of a canopy at the newly renovated Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.
The tragedy, widely blamed on corruption, triggered some of Serbia's largest protests since the fall of Slobodan Milosevic, accused architect of genocide in the Balkans, in 2000.
The anti-corruption movement, led by university students, snowballed from demands for a transparent investigation into the tragedy into calls for an early election.
Waving "Students are winning" flags, chanting and blowing whistles, students marched through Belgrade before converging on Slavija Square, the site of some of their biggest protests.
By early evening, thousands had arrived, and crowds were still growing.
Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for over a decade, serving as either prime minister or president.
Amid mounting pressure, he announced the snap vote last month, setting up his biggest electoral challenge since his party took power in 2012.
Vucic, who addressed supporters at a sports hall in the capital on Thursday, has regularly accused the student movement of being a foreign-funded coup attempt.
"Let us never forget how they tried to bring down our state. Let us always protect and defend it," said the 56-year-old, who resigned to run for prime minister.
"Let us go out and defeat them! Defeat them decisively!" he said before white ticker tape and balloons showered the crowd.
Many of the 250 candidates of the Student List running for the 250-seat parliament are drawn from academia or are deliberate political outsiders.
The movement has a broad platform, but at its core is a pledge to fight corruption.
Serbia lacks reliable independent polling, and surveys have produced widely differing results.
Political scientist Dusan Vucicevic from Belgrade University told AFP it was difficult to predict an outcome but expected students to win more than 40% of the vote, a result significantly larger than any opposition list since SNS came to power.
Days before the vote, Serbian civil society groups warned that conditions for "free and fair elections" were lacking.
"This assessment is not based on isolated incidents, opposition claims or political disagreement with the government," a joint statement by 24 organizations said.
"It is supported by documented findings from independent Serbian organizations working in different fields."
On Wednesday, Belgrade prosecutors questioned six people arrested on suspicion of plotting "violence, riots and attacks" on election day.
Reports of threats and intimidation targeting student demonstrators have grown in recent months, but their rallies have remained largely peaceful since they began.
"I've been following this fight since the very beginning," 35-year-old student rally attendee Igor said.
"Today is the last rally, and it's important that we all come here to send a message of love and peace and that we see each other on the 25th at the polling stations."

An artist's answer to finding a place for uncomfortable feelings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:30:00 UTC
02:30:00 KST

The first time Clare James arranged funeral flowers was for her friend's 10-year-old son Harper, who was killed, along with his father, when a tree fell on their car in 2019.
Impelled by the urge to give the children in the room something to look at beyond their friend's coffin, she created a wild and twisting semi-circle of branches, flowers, moss, pebbles and fungi. Woven into the installation were Harper's toys, and guests were invited to light a candle and place it among the pebbles when they arrived.
"So, that was the first one. I just did that because I was worried about how the kids would get through such a funeral," Clare says.
That same year, Clare, an artist based in Victoria's Yarra Valley, created a similar installation in her backyard. Using flowers recycled from a wedding — floristry has been her long-time side hustle — she built a flowery alcove, an altar upon which to lay the grief that doesn't find a home at a funeral.
"For relationships broken, parents that had to leave, pets who died, bodies that no longer work, regrets that haunt, wilderness lost, rivers poisoned, animals slaughtered and the endless amount of grief out there which need a place to be acknowledged," she said at the time.
Growing up with anxiety disorder, Clare says her thoughts get caught in a loop and "things that have upset me or worried me in the world I've not found it easy to let go of". For once, until the flowers wilted and the candles melted, this altar gave her thoughts a place to rest.
The Place for Lost Feelings
In 2022, she built a similar installation for the public. With her sister, artist Kate James, she created The Place for Lost Feelings in an old hall in Healesville. "While we were building it, we got the giggles a few times going, 'Do you think anyone will come?'" Clare says.
But she had a hunch that she wasn't the only one searching for this place, or this experience, outside of organised religion. A church is a place she says she wouldn't feel safe or comfortable.
The two sisters weren't quite ready for what happened next.
"People came from so far and wide and people came with extraordinary grief," Clare says. They came to mourn, to remember and forget, to confront death.
One man in his 50s, diagnosed with terminal cancer, arrived with his wife and his two best friends. When it was their turn to enter the space, the man lay down in front of the installation and they sat with him, Clare says. Later, he told her "it was the first time he actually accepted his mortality".
In the comments book, someone wrote: "It's not like we were hungry for this; we were starving." Clare says it struck her as a "profound thing to say and feel about this little pop-up flower thing".
Clare's installations reflect a high-end floristry movement that has emerged over the past two decades. A slave to the vase no more, bold installations of traditional cut flowers, branches, grasses and edible plants scrunch and twist up walls, creep along ceilings, and hang in defiance of gravity. They scream with life, and they're not cheap. They appear at well-heeled weddings, events and restaurants.
For Clare, giving everyone the chance to experience such a luscious installation at a free event is part of the appeal. Fresh flowers and candles are "there for the most important celebrations in our life", she says. And there's something about their fragility, their ephemerality, which make them the perfect medium for these artworks.
Tomorrow, Clare will open the doors on the second iteration of The Place for Lost Feelings in Healesville. For two days, people will have the opportunity to spend five minutes alone in the space and light a candle. As they exit, two trauma response workers will be available to check in with people.
A new understanding of grief
The event was meant to occur in March, but as Clare was preparing it, her husband Mark suffered a massive stroke. Since then, grief has gained new meaning for her.
There is a "new, profound grief that I feel, and that Mark feels, for everything that he has lost", she says. "The things that we together have lost is huge, and the level of his brain injuries is just so life changing." There is also gratitude that things could have been worse.
"I said to my sister the other day, 'Oh my God, I need The Place for Lost Feelings,'" she says. "I'll go in there and sob for myself and for Mark."
At the same time, she doesn't understand what it's all for: "It doesn't bring back your child, it doesn't make your body better, I don't understand, yet, what it is that makes it feel alright."
After we speak on the phone, Clare texts me photos of the flowers she was looking at in her garden while we talked. There are Granny's Bonnets in different shades of purple, an orange tree bursting with blossom, and a delicate flower, the colour of mango, turning its face to the sun. Brief glimpses of beauty that will return to the soil.
The Place for Lost Feelings, supported by the Margaret Lawrence Bequest and Yarra Ranges Council, is a free event open from 3pm - 6:30pm for people without bookings at The Healesville Living And Learning Centre on October 24 and 25.

Guterres also dismissed concerns about institutional damage to the UN from violations of international law, declaring that the real crisis is the suffering of ordinary civilians whose survival is threatened by war-induced inflation and violence.
"The problem is not for the United Nations. The problem is for the people that is suffering dramatically everywhere," he said.

Tuesday Labs debuts "droid butler" Voxel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:24:56 UTC
02:24:56 KST

Tuesday Labs debuts “droid butler” Voxel
New York technology company Tuesday Labs has debuted its first semi-autonomous robot Voxel Series-1, designed to help with household chores and to avoid the appearance of an “uncanny valley” humanoid robot.
Voxel Series-1 (Voxel) performs tasks such as watering plants and sweeping crumbs, which it currently achieves with a combination of autonomous intelligence and teleoperation.
The robot is counter-height and covered in a colourful matte plastic shell with primarily “cuboid” body parts, LED eyes and 1-DOF grippers for hands. Tuesday Labs founder Rosalind Shinkle told Dezeen that initial designs were informed by home objects such as lamps, chairs and briefcases.
Working with former Pixar character designer Alonso Martinez, Shinkle said the finalised Voxel is a combination of “exceptional capability and charming character”.
“We deliberately didn’t build a humanoid,” Shinkle said. “We wanted to stay far from the uncanny valley, and far from robots that fill a human-shaped space in the home.”
“Instead, we made Voxel relatively small and cuboid, to signal his role in your life: a droid butler, not a human butler.”
“We know we don’t want him to feel almost-human, and we know we don’t want him to feel like a toaster,” she continued. “A believable character needs every element sitting at roughly the same point on that human–toaster spectrum.”
Shinkle said five key principles drove the design of Voxel, including easy integration into the home, a maximalist appearance, simplicity, luxury and playfulness.
Part of the strategy was also “affordance matching”, or that, when Voxel is perceived by a human, its capabilities can be inherently understood.
“When someone looks at a robot, they should be able to roughly predict what he’s capable of,” Shinkle said. “If you correctly match perceived and actual affordance, you can avoid that constant feeling of disappointment when a humanoid robot isn’t quite as good at doing things as a human.”
Voxel’s plastic shell and finishes are meant to keep it relatively lightweight, but Shinkle said the external design should also communicate its quality.
Like another home robot that is currently in production, Neo by 1X Technologies, Voxel’s initial customers are “early adopters” who opt in to help informally train the robot’s autonomous software at home.
“We’re starting with a limited number of robots for early adopters who are excited to experience and help shape this technology,” she said.
“Voxel’s estimated price is $20,000, so he will be a luxury product. But our ambition is much bigger – as the technology improves and production scales, we want to make household robots accessible to far more people.”
Shinkle said her own distaste for household chores was part of what drove Voxel.
“Robots will soon be a part of our homes,” she said. “I set out to build the robot that I would actually want to live with.”
“Also, I hate cleaning my apartment, and I’d much rather spend my time building something that solves that problem once and for all.”
Voxel is powered by a rechargeable battery and will charge in an at-home docking station as part of “his normal routine”.
Tuesday Labs is based in New York City and was founded in 2025 by Shinkle, who previously worked as an engineer at Boston Dynamics. The studio is focused on creating “robots that feel natural and delightful to live with”.
The combination of advanced technology and autonomous intelligence has made the creation of robots more possible than ever at this point in history.
This has allowed the field to diversify, and technology companies and studios have released a varity of different types of robots in recent years, including all the cute robots from CES 2025 and five that were displayed at Carlo Ratti’s architecture biennale.
Other recent home robots that debuted include Neo by 1X Technologies and CLOiD by LG.

Why Russia wants peace between Iran and the Gulf
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:23:21 UTC
02:23:21 KST

Why Russia wants peace between Iran and the Gulf
On October 18, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov visited Manama, where he attended the ninth ministerial meeting of the Russia-Gulf Cooperation Council strategic dialogue and held separate talks with the foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. The following day, he traveled to Tehran to meet with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and President Masoud Pezeshkian.
In Manama, discussions centered on de-escalation in the Persian Gulf, maritime security, and Russian proposals for a collective security framework, while bilateral meetings provided an opportunity to clarify individual countries’ positions. Lavrov and his Kuwaiti counterpart stressed the need to reduce tensions quickly and agreed that a political and diplomatic settlement is the only viable way forward. In Tehran, regional affairs featured alongside Russian-Iranian cooperation, with Moscow reaffirming its commitment to economic and investment agreements despite the deteriorating security environment.
Diplomacy between the Gulf’s two shores
The trip aimed to prevent a new divide between Iran and the Arab monarchies from becoming entrenched, as the consequences of the US-Israeli aggression against Iran are affecting the security of the entire region. Yet rebuilding trust also requires acknowledging that the Gulf states have their own grievances against Tehran over strikes on their territory and threats to maritime routes.
During the Manama talks, Arab representatives explicitly said they hope Moscow would use its relationship with Iran to convey their concerns. Discussions also covered Yemen, maintaining the ceasefire in Gaza, humanitarian access, and the resilience of energy and food supply chains – the various and interconnected sources of instability plaguing the Middle East.
In Tehran, Lavrov reaffirmed Moscow’s support for restoring security and shipping conditions to what they were before the US-Israeli military operation began. Iran, which sees the attack as the primary cause of the current crisis, likewise stated its commitment to resolving disputes through diplomacy. Agreement on broad principles, however, does not yet amount to agreement on the specific obligations that the parties must accept.
Russia could mediate efforts to de-escalate tensions and mitigate the deterioration in relations between Tehran and the Gulf monarchies, since it maintains close ties with Iran while developing political, economic, and energy cooperation with the Arab states. These relationships allow Moscow to relay messages, identify the scope for compromise, and facilitate direct dialogue, which can easily give way to competing ultimatums during a crisis.
However, this two-way access does not mean Moscow can dictate what its partners actually decide, and its closeness to Tehran may raise questions among Arab participants. The effectiveness of Russian mediation will ultimately depend on whether the parties themselves are willing to negotiate, acknowledge one another’s concerns, and take practical steps to address them.
Inclusive security as an alternative to permanent crisis
In Manama, Lavrov once again presented Russia’s updated concept of collective security in the Persian Gulf as a potential contribution to a lasting settlement. The proposal continues a longstanding initiative rather than a document developed solely for this visit. As early as June, he reported that updated proposals had been circulated to regional capitals and that Moscow was receiving initial responses.
The approach rests on the premise that the Arab monarchies and Iran must take part in a shared framework, because attempts to secure one group of states by isolating another reproduce the causes of confrontation. Confidence-building measures and regular contact are intended to reduce uncertainty gradually, while the Gulf countries and their immediate neighbors should have the decisive voice in shaping the regional order.
An earlier Russian concept circulated at the United Nations in 2019 already envisaged a gradual normalization of conditions, respect for sovereignty, the peaceful settlement of disputes, and the development of collective security mechanisms. The current proposals can be assumed to carry over the same spirit, even if specific provisions have changed or been updated.
Moscow has argued that the region needs an inclusive security system of its own, free from external military intervention and imposed political arrangements. This does not rule out international assistance, however, as Russian diplomacy allows for support from outside actors, including members of the UN Security Council, provided that it serves the interests of regional states.
The practical value of this model will depend on whether broad principles can be translated into agreed procedures for preventing incidents, protecting civilian infrastructure, and keeping maritime routes open. These arrangements could provide the first steps towards a more stable order, whereas an attempt to resolve every political disagreement at once could obstruct even limited measures to ease tensions.
Why expensive oil does not make war good for Russia
Western media and expert debates, including those focused on Middle Eastern politics, frequently portray Russia as a beneficiary of the war, arguing that disruptions to Gulf supplies drive up energy prices and create opportunities for Russian exporters.
A short-term price benefit is certainly possible, but to assume that war gives Russia a strategic advantage is analytically unsound, because the country’s national interests are not limited to a single source of export revenue. Additional income from commodity sales says little about the cost of damaged partnerships, postponed investment, and worsening conditions for long-term projects.
The Middle East matters to Russia as a political and economic partner, and stable relations depend on predictable institutions, transport routes, and financial transactions. A prolonged war raises shipping and insurance costs, complicates infrastructure agreements, and forces partners to divert resources from development toward immediate security needs.
This is evident in Russia’s cooperation with Iran, where its projects require a stable operating environment. In Tehran, Lavrov spoke of Russian specialists gradually returning to the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, as well as prospects for cooperation in hydrocarbon production and transportation. A protracted war creates additional risks for these activities, and higher oil prices cannot remove them.
Moreover, a sustained energy shock can weaken the global economy, while the resulting decline in demand limits exporters’ initial gains. Even if some consequences of a Middle East war can benefit Russian suppliers in the short term, claims that Moscow wants endless war in the region are superficial at best. Russia’s strategic interest lies in the region’s long-term stability, which would allow it to preserve partnerships, markets, and opportunities for economic engagement.
Regional autonomy in a changing world order
The transformation of the world order and the erosion of Western hegemony give Middle Eastern states greater scope to pursue independent policies, but a redistribution of international influence does not in itself resolve regional disputes. If dependence on external guarantees is merely supplemented by new competing patrons, while mechanisms for direct dialogue remain weak, the Middle East will continue to serve as an arena where local conflicts intersect with rivalry among major powers.
Regional autonomy requires that neighboring states agree on rules for coexistence, even when their foreign policy priorities and perceptions of threats differ substantially. A durable system will require mutual respect for sovereignty, a rejection of imposed military solutions, and recognition that lasting security cannot be built on another state’s permanent vulnerability.
Russia can support this process by providing diplomatic channels and helping identify a workable sequence of agreements, but only the countries of the region can build a peaceful future. External mediation delivers results when it supports an existing willingness to compromise, while even substantive initiatives can remain on paper if that willingness is absent.
Lavrov’s visits to Manama and Tehran highlighted an opportunity to connect urgent de-escalation with discussions about a more durable regional order. Seizing this opportunity will take time and difficult political decisions, because the parties will need to constrain their own use of force, rebuild damaged trust, and accept reciprocal obligations. Moscow can mediate this process, but its outcome will depend on the desire and readiness of the Gulf states and Iran to reach an agreement.

Türkiye's Central Bank lowers policy rate to 36% after 5 consecutive holds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

02:22:59 KST

Türkiye's Central Bank lowers policy rate to 36% after 5 consecutive holds
Türkiye's central bank cut its benchmark policy rate by 100 basis points to 36%, in accordance with market expectations, after holding rates steady for five consecutive meetings, Anadolu Agency reports.
The bank's Monetary Policy Committee, headed by Governor Fatih Karahan, lowered the one-week repo auction rate from 37%.
It also reduced the overnight lending rate from 40% to 39% and the overnight borrowing rate from 35.5% to 34.5%.
According to the committee, despite monthly fluctuations, recent inflation figures and leading indicators confirm a slowdown in the underlying inflation trend.
Economic activity data and the limited pass-through of supply shocks to domestic prices suggest that domestic demand remains weak, it added.
However, elevated energy prices stemming from ongoing geopolitical tensions continue to pose an upside risk to the inflation outlook.
The committee said it is closely monitoring how geopolitical developments influence inflation through costs, economic activity, and expectations.
“The tight monetary policy stance, which will be maintained until price stability is achieved, will strengthen the disinflation process through demand, exchange rate, and expectation channels,” it said.
Future rate decisions will take into account realized and expected inflation, as well as its underlying trend, to maintain the tightness needed to support the projected disinflation path in line with interim targets.
The size and timing of policy steps will be determined prudently on a meeting-by-meeting basis, with a focus on the inflation outlook.
“In case of a significant and persistent deterioration in the inflation outlook, monetary policy stance will be tightened,” the committee said, reiterating its attention to upside inflation risks.
Additional macroprudential measures will support monetary transmission if unexpected developments emerge in credit and deposit markets, while liquidity management tools will continue to be used effectively.
Earlier, it was reported that Türkiye expects 4.2% economic growth in 2027.

Palantir’s Thiel laments Iran war – Politico
Billionaire tech investor and Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel has expressed regret over the US war against Iran, warning that it could ultimately lead to International Criminal Court warrants for the Trump administration and have broader implications for the US, Politico reported on Thursday.
The outlet cited a transcript of a lecture given by Thiel earlier this month, part of the series of private events held in Nashville.
Thiel, a staunch backer of US President Donald Trump, has expressed doubts over the Iran war, which was launched by the US and Israel earlier this year, suggesting that it has exposed America’s weaknesses.
“I’m skeptical of [the war], I think we should not have done it. There were a lot of mistakes that were made,” Thiel said, as quoted by Politico.
Maybe we don’t have the hard power. Maybe we’re going to lose the soft power war.
While reiterating his support for Trump, he warned that the war could backfire for the administration and lead to legal troubles with the International Criminal Court (ICC). 
The Trump administration has had a hostile relationship with the ICC, particularly over the decision to issue arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza.
The US, which does not recognize the ICC’s jurisdiction, has enacted sanctions against the court’s top officials, describing it as a “corrupt and fatally politicized supranational court that has maliciously abused its authority and exceeded its mandate.”
“I have come to suspect that the threat of an ICC arrest warrant is the sword of Damocles hanging over the Trump administration as it tries to persecute this war in Iran,” Thiel said.
He also claimed that George W. Bush-era neocon figures such as Donald Rumsfeld and Dick Cheney have been colluding with the ICC against Trump. “I read the Cheney family’s Trump derangement syndrome as an attempt to buy favor with the [ICC] and avoid prosecution. Probably too late,” he said.
Palantir has been heavily involved in the hostilities, as its products have been used by the US military. The use of AI products was reportedly linked to one of the worst mass-casualty events of the war – the strike on a school in Minab on the first day of the conflict, which killed at least 156 civilians, predominantly schoolchildren. According to media reports, the facility was targeted based on outdated data used by Palantir’s analysis and surveillance software.

====================================================================================================

China Focus: Yangtze River governance shows progress, offers insights for regional cooperation
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:08:05 CST
02:08:05 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Along the Yangtze River in Yichang, central China's Hubei Province, steel frames that once supported sand-and-gravel conveyors now hold swings, while a former industrial building has been transformed into an art gallery.
The structures stand in Lighthouse Square, a riverside public space created on the site of a former port, where phosphate ore, sand and gravel were once loaded and unloaded.
Chen Yuanyuan, a local resident who now volunteers to patrol the riverbank, recalls when dust was so thick that residents kept their windows closed. Today, the restored waterfront has become a popular spot for daily walks and environmental education.
Since 2018, Yichang's riverbank restoration project has removed 15 docks, relocated 35 enterprises and 113 households, restored vegetation across 87 hectares and rehabilitated eight kilometers of Yangtze River shoreline.
Along the Yangtze River, shoreline restoration is accompanied by broader efforts to improve water quality, control pollution and restore aquatic habitats across the basin.
FROM LOCAL RESTORATION TO BASIN-WIDE GOVERNANCE
China's efforts to protect the Yangtze River have improved water quality and supported the recovery of native species, although restoring a healthy river ecosystem will require a substantially longer period of time.
The Ministry of Ecology and Environment rated the Yangtze River basin's water quality as excellent in the first quarter of 2026. Across the wider Yangtze River Economic Belt, the proportion of monitored sections meeting Grade I to III water quality standards has risen from 67 percent in 2015 to 96.5 percent.
Habitat restoration has helped create conditions for the recovery of endangered species. In April 2025, researchers recorded natural spawning and successful hatching of Yangtze sturgeon in a restored spawning ground in the Chishui River, a tributary of the upper Yangtze River.
Researchers released 20 adult sturgeon into a restored habitat of about 8,000 square meters, where a natural spawning ground had been created. The species had not reproduced naturally since the early 2000s and was declared extinct in the wild by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2022. The recent successful spawning and hatching mark an important step toward rebuilding a wild population.
In 2018, the southwestern Chinese provinces of Yunnan, Guizhou and Sichuan established a water environment compensation fund for the Chishui River basin, creating the first cross-provincial ecological compensation mechanism in the Yangtze River Economic Belt.
The three provinces jointly contributed 200 million yuan (about 30 million U.S. dollars) under the initial agreement, with compensation allocations linked to water quality at designated monitoring sections. A second-round agreement signed in 2023 increased annual funding to 300 million yuan for the 2021-2025 period.
In the Yunnan section of the Chishui River, water quality at the exit monitoring section had remained at Grade II for five consecutive years as of the end of 2024, while the number of recorded fish species in the section had risen from 36 in early 2020 to 43.
At the basin level, the Yangtze River Protection Law, which took effect in March 2021, provides a legal framework for ecological conservation, pollution control and resource management. Under the river chief system, officials at different levels are responsible for waterway protection, with mechanisms in place to clarify responsibilities across administrative boundaries and coordinate action among upstream and downstream areas.
According to Li Xiaokai, senior water resources management specialist at the World Bank, China's approach to Yangtze River governance features integrated management of the basin as an ecological and economic system, coordination across government levels and sectors, and the integration of ecological protection with economic development.
The World Bank-supported Yangtze River Protection and Ecological Restoration Programs, which cover three provinces in the middle reaches of the river basin, place institutional development at their core, recognizing that sustainable outcomes depend as much on governance systems as on infrastructure investments, said Li.
LESSONS FOR REGIONAL COOPERATION
Despite differences in geography and development contexts, China and many countries across the Asia-Pacific face similar challenges in river governance and ecological protection, Li said. One major challenge is institutional fragmentation.
River basins rarely conform to political boundaries, and responsibilities for water resources, environmental protection, agriculture, energy, transport and land management are often divided among multiple agencies. Decisions made in one sector or jurisdiction can therefore have unintended consequences elsewhere in the basin, said Li.
In the Lancang-Mekong basin, China has provided year-round hydrological information from two upstream stations to the Mekong River Commission (MRC) since November 2020, supporting river monitoring and upstream-downstream coordination on flood and drought risks. The country has proposed further cooperation on urgent notifications, wider data sharing across the basin, and joint work on flood forecasting and drought response to strengthen upstream-downstream coordination in addressing flood and drought risks.
Sun Jingrui, an associate professor at Yunnan University, said the Yangtze River governance experience shows that fish recovery depends on a governance system capable of sustaining the costs of conservation, rather than on fishing restrictions alone.
Fish protection must be treated as both an ecological issue and a matter of food systems and livelihoods, Sun said. Measures to reduce fishing need to be accompanied by alternative sources of income and food, vocational training and social security for affected communities.
This is particularly important in the Lancang-Mekong basin, where fish resources are closely linked to food security and community culture, especially in downstream countries. Differences in countries' enforcement capacity, development priorities and dependence on fisheries mean that a uniform, long-term fishing ban across the entire basin would be difficult to implement, Sun said.
Fish recovery also requires restoring river connectivity and protecting the habitats needed for fish to complete their life cycles. A paper co-authored by Sun found more than 10,000 small river barriers in the lower Mekong, disrupting connectivity along fish migration routes.
Sun suggested introducing seasonal or area-specific fishing restrictions during key migration and breeding periods, prohibiting destructive fishing methods, improving fish passage around barriers and adjusting dam and sluice operations where feasible. Protecting key habitats, including spawning grounds, deep pools and floodplain nursery areas, is another priority, Sun said.
"Truly sustainable conservation must give affected people the means to make the transition with dignity," said Sun. ■

HARARE, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Regional leaders on Thursday called for stronger integration and increased intra-African trade to boost economic growth at the 25th Common Market for Eastern and Southern Africa (COMESA) Heads of State and Government Summit held in Mount Hampden on the outskirts of Zimbabwe's capital, Harare.
Held under the theme of "One Market, One Future: Advancing Inclusive Industrialization, Investment and Regional Integration in COMESA," the summit brought together regional leaders and senior government officials across its 21 member states to discuss trade, investment, industrialization and economic integration.
In his acceptance speech upon taking over as COMESA chairperson, Zimbabwean President Emmerson Mnangagwa urged the 21-member regional bloc to harness its resources and investment potential to accelerate modernization and industrialization.
"Our common market must enable enterprises to produce at scale, facilitate cross-border movement of factors of production and reach new customers. The future we envision requires every member state to contribute to, and benefit from, our collective progress," said Mnangagwa.
He called for measures to address persistent non-tariff barriers, infrastructure gaps and policy misalignments, urging member states to simplify border procedures, embrace digital trade systems and adopt innovative financing models for long-term infrastructure development.
Mnangagwa underscored the importance of climate change mitigation, environmental sustainability and regional cooperation in strengthening food security, while calling for greater local processing of natural resources to promote sustainable economic development.
"The message to the region is that the natural endowments of Africa must industrialize our economies, create jobs and broad-based empowerment which improves the quality of life for our peoples," said Mnangagwa.
Outgoing COMESA chairperson, Kenyan President William Ruto, said regional integration is essential for the bloc's member states to navigate growing global fragmentation.
"The global order is shifting. Geopolitical tensions are rising. Protectionism is returning. Supply chains are breaking. Competition for critical and strategic resources is intensifying," Ruto said.
In this regard, he urged African countries to increase intra-African trade, build resilient regional value chains, reduce reliance on exporting raw materials and focus on adding value to their resources, adding that COMESA could strengthen Africa's position in global trade by negotiating as a unified market.
On regional stability, he said COMESA should strengthen its capacity to prevent conflict, stressing that peace, security and good governance were essential for achieving prosperity. "Because there is no prosperity without peace, no peace without security and no security without good governance, we continue to strengthen our capacity to prevent conflict," he said.
COMESA is a regional economic community working to promote regional integration through trade, investment and infrastructure development. ■

IOM warns Somalia floods could displace 874,000 people
