Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:07:53 CST
02:07:53 KST

MOGADISHU, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Imminent flooding could displace nearly 874,000 people in Somalia over the next three months, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) warned Thursday.
Heavy rainfall and rising rivers now threaten communities already struggling with drought and repeated displacement, the UN migration agency said in a statement, urging international support for preparedness and early action.
"There is still time to reduce the impact, but that window is closing. We urgently need funding to help people protect their homes and livelihoods, reach safer ground where necessary, and avoid another cycle of displacement," said Manuel Marques Pereira, chief of mission for IOM in Somalia.
New projections by IOM and the Danish Refugee Council estimate that 874,319 people could be displaced between October and December, with flooding driving 92 percent of that displacement.
The warning comes as Somalia enters its rainy season, which is forecast to bring above-normal rainfall driven by strengthening El Nino conditions.
According to IOM, signs of flooding are already emerging across the country.
The Jubba River at Dollow is approaching flood levels, while the Shabelle River at Jowhar is rising toward the top of its banks.
Heavy rainfall in Baidoa has already damaged homes, forcing families to flee several neighborhoods.
Despite the mounting crisis, IOM said it has secured just 14.4 percent of the 16.62 million dollars needed to respond to the impending El Nino floods.
The severe funding shortfall jeopardizes critical relief efforts aimed at supporting over 517,000 vulnerable people across flood-prone areas of Somalia, it said.
IOM said rising floodwaters threaten to wipe out crops, devastate livelihoods, contaminate water supplies, and cut off access to healthcare and essential services, further deepening crisis levels in communities already battered by successive climate shocks.
According to IOM, while it is working with Somali authorities and local partners to strengthen early warning systems, map evacuation routes, and prepare emergency aid, acute funding shortages are bottlenecking critical response efforts.
"Without immediate resources, plans to build safe relocation sites and deliver emergency shelter, clean water, sanitation, and healthcare remain severely constrained," IOM said.
IOM called for urgent international support to scale up early action before rising floodwaters displace hundreds of thousands more families. ■

"Today, conflicts are not only intensifying. They are expanding," Guterres told reporters. "In climate, we know El Nino as a disturbance in one part of the planet that disrupts weather patterns and upends lives thousands of kilometers away. We are now witnessing an El Nino of war."
Conflicts are fueling one another, with consequences spreading farther and faster, he warned.
Guterres said attacks against civilians and civilian objects are prohibited under international law and must stop. But the effects of war extend beyond battle zones, disrupting energy markets, shipping lanes, supply chains and financial systems.
He warned that these shocks were hitting an already deeply unequal world, where some people could absorb higher prices while others had to choose between food and heating, and where poorer countries faced difficult choices between servicing debt and investing in health and education.
Guterres called for an end to fighting, including in the Middle East, and urged respect for international law, civilian protection and freedom of navigation, while giving diplomacy room to succeed.
Speaking ahead of a planned visit to Egypt on Friday, Guterres reiterated his call for peace.
"We need to stop the widening of war, protect civilians and create the political space for diplomacy and peace," he said. "People everywhere want security. They want dignity. They want governments and international institutions to deliver." ■

Roundup: Ebola spread raises regional alarm in Africa, urging coordination
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
01:07:17 CST
02:07:17 KST

KINSHASA, Oct. 22 (Xinhua) -- Africa is facing "a more complex outbreak landscape" as Ebola spreads across borders and persistent surveillance gaps cast doubt on whether recent signs of a slowdown can be sustained.
Despite a temporary decline in transmission in some affected areas, gaps in contact tracing and delays in diagnosis have heightened concerns that undetected infections could fuel further spread, elevating the ongoing Ebola outbreak to a regional public health threat.
As the outbreak widens, the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) are calling for stronger regional coordination to contain transmission and prevent further cross-border spread.
CROSS-BORDER SPREAD RAISES ALARM
Africa CDC data shows five countries, the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria and France, have reported Ebola cases linked to the current outbreak since May.
"Ebola does not wait. It follows movement, exploits gaps, and tests the strength of our health systems," WHO Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Yakub Janabi said Thursday during an online press briefing.
"Today, the test is no longer confined to one place... We are facing a more complex outbreak landscape," Janabi said, calling for stronger regional vigilance and collective action.
The DRC remains the epicenter, accounting for 9,704 confirmed cases, including 4,687 deaths as of Tuesday, with a case fatality rate of 48.3 percent, according to a situation report released Wednesday by the DRC health authorities. The outbreak has affected eight of the country's 26 provinces and 66 health zones.
Beyond the DRC, Kenya has confirmed nine cases, including one death, while Nigeria reported its first imported case on Tuesday.
All eight secondary cases in Kenya had been detected among previously identified contacts who were already under quarantine, suggesting that the known transmission chains remained traceable, said Wessam Mankoula, head of the Continental Incident Management Support Team for the Ebola response at Africa CDC, at an online press briefing Thursday.
Kenya has identified 135 contacts, with 118 currently in quarantine, Mankoula said.
In Nigeria, the confirmed patient, a woman who arrived from Uganda on Oct. 3, developed symptoms four days later but was not diagnosed with Ebola until Oct. 20.
The WHO's latest regional situation report released Tuesday showed that the prolonged interval between symptom onset and confirmation raises concerns about possible undetected exposures and secondary transmission, requiring urgent retrospective investigation and intensified surveillance.
Mankoula said the source of the patient's infection remained unknown, with Nigerian and Ugandan authorities conducting joint investigations into her travel and exposure history.
On Tuesday evening, following Nigeria's confirmation of its first Ebola case, Africa CDC Director-General Jean Kaseya warned that the outbreak had become the most geographically widespread Ebola epidemic on record, with infections reported across Central, Eastern and Western Africa.
FRAGILE SLOWDOWN MASKS PERSISTENT TRANSMISSION
Despite recent signs of easing transmission in some affected areas in the DRC, health authorities warned that the outbreak remained far from under control.
The WHO's latest regional report showed that Ebola infections in the DRC have rebounded after a brief decline.
"The most recent seven-day moving average indicates a modest upward trend, suggesting renewed intensification of transmission," the WHO Regional Office for Africa said in the report, highlighting the outbreak's "widening international dimension and the growing complexity."
Beyond the fluctuating case numbers, health authorities identified persistent weaknesses in early detection, contact tracing and access to treatment as major obstacles to controlling the outbreak.
Africa CDC data showed only about 12 percent of confirmed cases in the DRC have been identified among previously known contacts, meaning that nearly nine in ten infections are being detected outside established contact-tracing networks.
"This means there are ongoing chains of transmission that we are not detecting," Mankoula warned.
Africa CDC announced Wednesday that it would convene an extraordinary virtual meeting of African health ministers on Oct. 28 to coordinate efforts against the escalating outbreak.
The epidemic was declared in the DRC on May 15 and designated a public health emergency of international concern by the WHO two days later. The Africa CDC subsequently declared it a public health emergency of continental security.
The current Ebola outbreak has become the largest and deadliest ever recorded in the DRC and the second-largest Ebola outbreak globally, after the 2014-2016 West Africa epidemic. ■

'The future of Hungarian Jewry’: Budapest opens synagogue run entirely by teens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:02:08 UTC
02:02:08 KST

In a Budapest synagogue that has stood for more than 150 years, the next generation is now taking the lead. The Hungarian capital’s Jewish community has reopened the historic Wagon Drivers’ Synagogue as a space exclusively for teenagers, in what may be the world’s first teen-run synagogue.
Established in 1870, the building served as the central synagogue for the Orthodox community following the Communist era, until its closure in 2014. It has now reopened after extensive refurbishment and is designated exclusively for teens up to the age of 18.
The officer holders, board leaders, and event organizers are all local teens. The “oldest” regular worshiper at the sanctuary is youth community emissary Rabbi Tzami Bassman, an American-born and extremely jovial rabbi and Chabad emissary in his early 30s.
It will be operated moving forward by the C-Teen youth organization, with full funding and logistical support from the Association of Hungarian Jewish Communities (EMIH).
The Jerusalem Post visited the synagogue on Monday in Budapest. The inside of the building is beautifully decorated and still smells of fresh paint.
Rabbi Bassman took time out from helping a 12-year-old boy with his bar-mitzvah preparation to speak with the Post.
Opening ceremony drew 200 teens
At the opening ceremony, just before Rosh Hashanah, there were 200 teens present, he said.
“It was really, really incredible. We had a teen blow the shofar, a teen carrying the Torah, and teens cutting the ribbon. It was special and moving.”
During the ceremony, President of the Budapest Orthodox Rabbinate Rabbi Baruch Oberlander highlighted that it is critical for young people to be active leaders and decision-makers, not merely passive participants in communal life.
“These young people represent the future of Hungarian Jewry,” he said. “It is deeply moving to see that they are not satisfied merely learning and participating, but are eager to assume active responsibility for shaping Jewish life.”
Just two weeks after the opening, Bassman said there was a minyan of teens for Kol Nidrei. They also constructed a sukkah in the courtyard.
Now, every Thursday night, the synagogue hosts a learning program comprising 70 to 80 teens, Bassman said. It also includes Hebrew, Hungarian, and Russian classes, the latter because many members of the Budapest community are those who fled Ukraine during the war.
On Friday nights, Bassman said, they can expect between 30 and 50 teens.
The demographic is wide, he added, although the teens are “primarily not religious.”
“Some teens are familiar with davening [“praying”] and things like that, but primarily these are teens that come from non-religious families.” Many do not attend one of the Jewish schools in the city.
Several of the teens and their parents learned about the synagogue from social media – where Bassman and his wife are active – or met Bassman on one of his Chabad-mobile visits to the local stores.
Eventually, he said, there will be a kitchen and a lounge area with couches and games.
Bassman is most looking forward to growing Friday night Shabbats, which have only just started.
“I’m looking forward to growing them and making them really, really special,” he told the Post. “We’re really just at the beginning, and we have lots of ideas, lots of plans. With God’s help, it will be amazing.”

====================================================================================================

The West Bank must not hold Israel’s European security ties hostage - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:01:47 UTC
02:01:47 KST

Israel supplies the postcodes the EU uses to deny settlement goods preferential tariffs.
Under a 2004 technical arrangement, Israeli origin certificates identify production sites, distinguishing settlement goods from exports made in Israel without either side conceding sovereignty.
Israel has not annexed the West Bank as a whole. The Supreme Court holds that territory under military administration lies outside the state, with commanders deriving authority from the law of belligerent occupation, not sovereignty.
Pre-1967 local law and military orders govern; even settlement councils derive authority from orders incorporating Israeli municipal law.
Israeli legislation does not apply automatically: the Knesset renewed regulations in 2023 that apply specified laws to Israeli residents personally, not territorially.
The Central Bureau of Statistics counts West Bank Israelis in the national population but classifies Judea and Samaria separately from Israel’s six districts.
Under Oslo, Israel transferred defined civil and policing powers in Areas A and B to the Palestinian Authority, retained specified security responsibilities, and reserved borders and settlements for final-status negotiations.
The International Court of Justice, the UN’s principal court, identified duties in its 2024 advisory opinion to distinguish dealings with Israel from those involving the West Bank, east Jerusalem, and Gaza and withhold assistance sustaining what it deemed an unlawful Israeli presence there.
It imposed no blanket ban on defense procurement from sovereign Israel. Tariff preferences, settlement-import bans, and defense-supplier exclusions require distinct legal bases.
Ireland instructed its defense ministry not to buy Israeli military equipment; its tender rules allow it to reject Israeli and other third-country bids on defense and security grounds.
Germany’s Israeli Arrow 3 achieved initial operational capability, enabling ballistic-missile interception beyond the atmosphere. These are national choices, not an EU arms embargo.
Europe was Israel’s largest regional defense market in 2025, accounting for 36% of a record $19.2 billion in signed export agreements. Those contracts sustain research, industrial capacity, and the IDF’s force buildup.
Europe needs Israeli defense capabilities; Israel needs European technology, components, and industrial capacity.
By October 2026, British and Canadian arms manufacturers had asked Israeli firms to identify production sites, raw materials, and subcontractors beyond the Green Line, the pre-1967 armistice line.
A settlement-made component does not determine the origin or legality of a system assembled in sovereign Israel, but can trigger contractual or regulatory scrutiny. Prime contractors, financiers, and insurers may exclude suppliers rather than verify compliance.
A seal costing a few hundred dollars can jeopardize a multimillion-dollar defense contract; replacing it in a missile, aircraft, or communications system may require months of requalification, disrupting Israeli production and delaying deliveries to European forces.
Under the US military-aid agreement, spending American assistance on Israeli production is being phased out by 2028, steering orders towards US plants and risking Israeli jobs and wartime industrial capacity. That is a strategic mistake.
Settlement-origin exposure calls for the reverse: move production into sovereign Israel or qualify alternative suppliers without sacrificing domestic capacity.
Israel’s security is the objective; a supplier’s location is a means. If relocation preserves military capability, expertise, wartime capacity, IDF supply, and operational freedom, it is a supply-chain decision.
Restrictions on equipment that may be used in Gaza are different: export controls govern supply; the laws of war govern use. Israel must obey those laws, but cannot submit its lawful defense to foreign approval or sacrifice essential capabilities for a contract.
Keeping production in the West Bank, despite a viable alternative, is a political choice the government may make, but must own its cost, not disguise it as military necessity.
Defending Israel's sovereignty
Beyond procurement, Israel’s 2021 Horizon Europe research agreement excludes territories brought under Israeli administration after June 5, 1967, without prejudicing its position on their status.
The EU’s 2011 data-adequacy decision, retained after its 2024 review, permits certain civilian personal-data transfers but recognizes only Israel as defined under international law.
Both exclude east Jerusalem and the Golan Heights, where Israel has applied its law. The adequacy decision does not authorize operational police-data exchanges.
Europol, the EU’s law-enforcement agency, has a 2018 arrangement with Israel permitting strategic exchanges and liaison, not routine transfers of suspects’ personal data or investigative records.
A draft initialed in September 2022 covered terrorism, organized crime, and cybercrime, but excluded use of European information in territories brought under Israeli control in 1967, subject to exceptions for imminent threats to life and criminal investigations.
The Council Legal Service, the EU Council’s legal advisers, objected to those exceptions under EU and international law, citing Palestinian self-determination and policing powers transferred under Oslo.
Israeli intelligence protects Europe against threats unrelated to Israel or Jewish communities. In 2018, an Israeli diplomat confirmed that the Mossad, Israel’s foreign intelligence agency, helped Denmark thwart an Iranian plot to assassinate a dissident.
Israeli reports also credited the agency with helping French, Belgian, and German authorities foil a bombing at an Iranian opposition rally near Paris, and linked its warning to Danish raids against suspected jihadist cells in 2019.
In November 2025, Austrian investigators seized five handguns and 10 magazines from storage in Vienna, allegedly intended for attacks on Jewish and Israeli institutions.
The following month, Italian authorities uncovered an alleged €7 million Hamas-financing scheme involving charities.
Israeli intelligence aided the Italian investigation, which was coordinated with Dutch authorities through Eurojust, the EU agency supporting cross-border prosecutions.
These operations relied on national, case-specific channels, not routine EU-Israel data transfers. Eurojust agreements permit systematic exchanges of case information and evidence, as well as the appointment of liaison prosecutors.
A warning can cross a border. A prosecution needs a lawful chain of evidence.
The European Commission proposed talks in 2020 subject to territorial exclusion; the Council authorized them in 2021. By September 2026, the EU had signed agreements with Armenia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Lebanon, but not Israel.
National channels may warn of imminent threats from the West Bank; a Europol agreement cannot automatically authorize using EU-origin personal data there. Any lawful emergency procedure must be agreed beforehand.
The EU and Israel should conclude separate Europol and Eurojust agreements, backed by one Israeli law binding every recipient of European personal data, including security agencies and onward recipients, to agreed territorial, purpose, retention, and onward-transfer restrictions under independent oversight.
Both must comply with EU and international law, including fundamental-rights and data-protection safeguards. Exceptions require mutual consent and prior authorization where applicable; emergency procedures, if lawful, need independent oversight and auditing.
Israeli law alone cannot resolve EU legal objections. Israel retains its final-status positions and lawful powers over independently obtained intelligence.
To distinguish the West Bank from sovereign Israel is to defend Israel’s sovereignty, not condemn it.
Secure, negotiated borders are an Israeli strategic interest: they establish jurisdiction, delimit security responsibilities, and anchor enduring partnerships.
The writer is founder & principal of Line of State, an international strategic practice for strategic affairs, government relations, and public power. He previously served as vice president of external relations at Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI) and as chief of staff to its chairman.

02:01:32 KST

Attorney-General Gali Baharav-Miara has urged the High Court of Justice to consider further orders restricting financial benefits for those who fail to meet their military recruitment obligations, saying the state is far from using all its powers to enforce the draft.
In an update on Wednesday, the state reported that 110,330 people had either been formally classified as draft evaders or issued orders requiring them to enlist despite not completing preliminary recruitment procedures. The figures were current as of September 8, with military officials estimating that roughly four-fifths were haredi (ultra-Orthodox).
The filing points to delays in decisions on municipal property-tax discounts, public transport concessions, and other subsidies. It argues that further court intervention is needed because ministers have not exercised powers already available to them, while the army urgently needs more personnel.
The update forms part of proceedings over draft enforcement among haredi men. In November 2025, the court ordered the government to formulate an effective, equal, and proportionate enforcement policy within 45 days, including economic measures alongside criminal enforcement.
According to the latest filing, the government still has not adopted that policy, despite this year’s January 4 deadline.
The state asks the court to consider additional instructions allowing ministries to make benefits conditional on compliance with IDF recruitment requirements through administrative decisions, without new primary legislation.
AG targets tax, transport, and education benefits for draft evaders
It singles out property-tax and public transport discounts, saying the professional assessments have been completed, but the necessary ministerial decisions remain outstanding.
It also identifies Education Ministry subsidies for after-school and holiday programs, along with state-assisted housing loans, among the measures.
The filing describes these as incentives to encourage enlistment, rather than criminal penalties. It says any conditions must apply equally to people called up across the population, while leaving eligibility unaffected for groups not currently called for military service.
Implementation remains disputed in some areas. The Education Ministry’s director-general has sought to postpone changes to the Nitzanim after-school and holiday programs until the next school year, saying the proposed timetable is unworkable for programs involving hundreds of local authorities and hundreds of thousands of children.
The filing also describes shortcomings in cooperation between the IDF and Israel Police.
According to the update, no planned enforcement operations took place between July 1 and October 12, although limited individual arrests and enforcement at border crossings continued.
IDF, police dispute delays arrest operations targeting draft evaders
Police postponed coordinated arrest operations planned for late May and mid-October. A dispute arose over police demands for substantial additional military personnel: The army argued that maintaining public order was a police responsibility, while police said the requested soldiers were needed to carry out arrests, not control disturbances.
Police also reported that 192 people liable for conscription who were stopped during chance encounters were released with instructions to report to military police. Police said military personnel generally had not arrived within the agreed collection period.
Military police said they were unfamiliar with those cases and had not received the requested list by the time the update was submitted. Police said they would provide it after internal approval.
The state nevertheless reported an increase in haredi enlistment: approximately 4,298 recruits in the recruitment year running from July 2025 through June 2026, up from 2,811 the previous year.
It attributed the increase to expanded service options and stronger enforcement, including economic measures, but noted that recruitment remained far below military needs – in numbers, pace, and the proportion assigned to combat roles.
The state also asked the court to set a further reporting deadline focused on military and police enforcement. Its submission seeks additional judicial instructions; it does not by itself impose the proposed benefit restrictions.

CAM study reveals extensive bot network amplifying anti-Israel, antisemitic content
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:01:21 UTC
02:01:21 KST

Nearly one-in-four unique accounts that follow or amplify posts by the prominent anti-Israel profile @Wallface exhibit strong bot-like signals, according to a study released by the Antisemitism Research Center (ARC) of the Combat Antisemitism Movement (CAM) on Wednesday.
The study, titled “Bots, Fake Profiles, and Inauthentic Accounts Amplifying @Wallface on X,” was conducted between October 19 and October 20, and examined 10,709 unique X/Twitter accounts interacting with the profile.
The account @Wallface has roughly 51,000 followers on X; the account bio says: “Research and data analysis” and shares content critical of Israel.
The research forms part of CAM’s Bots Accountability Project, an initiative that documents and reports bots, fake profiles, and inauthentic accounts while tracking platform responses.
To evaluate the accounts, ARC used CAM’s detection model, known as X model v1.4.0, which assigns every account a score from 0 to 100 based on signal weights grounded in research from the Digital Forensic Research Lab, Indiana University’s Observatory on Social Media, and Cresci studies.
Twenty-five percent of accounts show signs of being bots
The methodology evaluates signals including account age, posting rates and activity bursts, follower ratios, handle patterns, default avatars, and profile completeness, while ensuring that post content and ideology are not used as inputs.
The report applies a conservative cutoff score of 75 or higher, meaning that each step up removes accounts that still look automated, ensuring the figures understate rather than overstate the presence of inauthentic profiles.
Out of the 10,709 unique accounts analyzed in the sample, CAM’s model identified 2,597 accounts, or 24.3%, as showing strong signals of being bots, fake profiles, or inauthentic accounts.
The breakdown across specific user groups showed that 27.2% of the newest followers sampled, 23.7% of reposters, 13.9% of commenters, and 8% of quoters met the threshold for bot-like activity.
The study found that the proportion of flagged accounts among amplifiers grew as the profile’s posting frequency accelerated over the months. Among accounts amplifying posts published in July, 15.9% showed automated signals, climbing to 19.1% in August, reaching 23.2% in September, and settling at 22.2% in October, during which time the account’s daily output jumped significantly.
The analysis highlighted that certain individual posts attracted exceptionally high concentrations of automated engagement.
Heavy volume of automated accounts
An October 16 post asserting that Israel maintains a paper trail for its social media operations was amplified by 86 accounts, of which 31.4% were flagged as inauthentic. Similarly, an October 19 post in which @Wallface complained about being targeted by a coordinated bot-reporting campaign faced a heavy volume of automated accounts, with nearly a third of its 68 amplifying profiles showing clear signs of inauthenticity.
Further investigation into the flagged profiles revealed significant overlap with previous research. Out of the thousands of automated profiles detected, 428 had previously surfaced in past CAM investigations, with the vast majority receiving similar inauthentic ratings.
The most prominent overlaps occurred with accounts previously identified around figures such as Roger Waters, where 237 shared profiles appeared, and Jake Shields, with 162 overlapping accounts, alongside smaller overlaps linked to networks surrounding Ana Kasparian, Abdul El-Sayed, Rabbi Jeffx, and Mario Nawfal.
Among the specific examples highlighted in the data, a profile named @Rajdhani108306 achieved a near-maximum bot score of 99.9 out of 100 after generating roughly 171,000 posts since its creation in June, translating to an average output of more than 1,200 posts every single day.
CAM noted that the results “raise concerns about how bot-like amplification can distort perceptions of online influence and public support. The recurrence of flagged accounts across multiple audiences suggests the problem extends beyond any single X account.”

hayden clay williams reinterprets everyday objects as sparkling stained glass sculptures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:00:55 UTC
02:00:55 KST

hayden clay williams reinterprets everyday objects as sparkling stained glass sculptures
the artist brings 'suburban surrealism' to familiar throwaway objects by rebuilding their shapes in jewel-toned glass and soldered seams.
prefer designboom on google
[FEATURED]
stained glass takes on unexpected forms
An ordinary egg carton becomes something unexpectedly precious in the hands of artist Hayden Clay Williams. Its familiar folded shape is reconstructed from fragments of jewel-toned stained glass, with turquoise, amber, and soft pink panels joined by silver-colored seams. Sunlight passes through the delicate structure, scattering patches of color across the surface below. The humble carton, designed to protect fragile eggs, has become an object that needs protecting itself.
Williams brings the same playful approach to a traffic cone and a folding wet floor sign, recreating familiar objects in a material usually associated with decorative windows and Tiffany lamps. Their recognizable silhouettes remain intact, though their surfaces have taken on an entirely different character. There is something playful about a roadside safety object made from breakable glass, especially when the finished sculpture looks somewhat convincing from a distance.
hayden williams reconstructs familiar objects in glass
The artist’s Egg Carton (Six Wells) is perhaps the most intricate of the works. Angular pieces of colored glass form a shallow container with six recessed compartments, while the soldered joints trace its ridges and folds. Viewed from above, the carton becomes a composition of overlapping colors and geometric patterns. In direct sunlight, those individual pieces dissolve into soft, irregular reflections.
His stained glass traffic cone is just as recognizable. The small sculpture follows the tapering profile of the familiar orange marker, complete with a broad square base and narrow opening at the top. Its surface is divided into amber and copper-colored sections, interrupted by small diamond-shaped details. Placed beside a conventional traffic cone, the contrast is particularly amusing. The two objects share the same basic geometry, though one is built to endure the street while the other belongs somewhere considerably safer.
A wet floor sign offers another variation on the idea. Williams recreates the familiar folding A-frame in golden glass, with a small warning symbol assembled from translucent pieces at its center. The figure appears to be slipping, just as it would on the original plastic sign. Here, however, the warning takes on a second meaning. The sign itself is vulnerable to the very accident it illustrates.
from digital experiments to physical sculpture
Williams has spent years exploring surreal suburban environments through digital imagery. He often inserts strange details into otherwise familiar suburban scenes. His earlier work includes World Underwater, a series of digitally rendered landscapes in which rising floodwaters transform residential neighborhoods (see designboom’s larger coverage here). More recently, his interest in familiar objects and altered materials has taken shape through stained glass, and has brought ideas previously explored on screen into physical space.
The transition introduces its own practical challenges. Williams spent around three weeks constructing the wet floor sign, using lead-free solder to join its individual glass pieces and zinc framing for structural support. Its hinge is functional, allowing the two panels to rotate through a limited angle. These details preserve something of the original object’s construction, even as the material changes its purpose entirely.

All four Point class roll-on roll-off vessels are scheduled for an extensive refit under the Strategic Sealift Interim contract, with Eddystone and Hartland Point dry docking this year and Hurst Point and Anvil Point following in 2027, according to an answer given in Parliament.
Ben Obese-Jecty, the Conservative member for Huntingdon, asked the Secretary of State for Defence what the planned schedule is for the refit of the Point class vessels Hurst Point, Hartland Point and Anvil Point under the Strategic Sealift Interim contract.

“Hurst Point is scheduled to dry dock in Q3 2027.
“Hartland Point dry docked this year, 2026 – in Q3.
“Anvil Point is scheduled to dry dock in Q2 2027.
“Eddystone dry docked this year, 2026 – in Q2.”
The Point class are the ships that move the British Army, carrying vehicles, containers and ammunition by sea on the scale a deployed brigade needs. Six were built in Germany and Britain in the early 2000s under a private finance initiative with Foreland Shipping, four of which remain in the arrangement, and they have carried British equipment to Iraq, Afghanistan, Estonia and the Gulf as well as the stores sent to Poland for onward movement into Ukraine.
The Strategic Sealift Interim contract bridges the gap to a longer term arrangement, and the Defence Investment Plan committed to a sealift capability beyond the current ships. Keeping four hulls working through to the end of the decade requires the refits now being scheduled.

A nanoparticle revealed the tiny impact of a single gas atom
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
17:00:00 UTC
02:00:00 KST

It’s one of gentlest caresses imaginable: the touch of a single atom of gas. Now, scientists have measured its impact.
A levitating nanoparticle jiggled when hit by individual gas atoms or molecules in a nearly empty vacuum chamber, scientists report in the October 23 Physical Review Letters.
The force exerted by a gas is usually the result of many atoms or molecules bouncing around all at once: Think of the air inside a balloon keeping it inflated. But even an individual atom can exert a tiny force. To detect that force, researchers used a laser to levitate a glass sphere, just 100 nanometers across and weighing about a quadrillionth of a gram, inside a vacuum chamber. Then, the researchers added small amounts of a heavy gas, either krypton, xenon or sulfur hexafluoride. The first two are gases made up of atoms, while the third consists of molecules.
The nanosphere was about 10 million times as massive as an individual gas particle, making the impact extremely difficult to detect. But, by monitoring the laser light that reflected from the sphere, the researchers could measure its tiny movements when hit by a gas particle. The resulting impulses were as small as a billionth of a Newton acting for one ten-trillionth of a second. And the rate of the collisions grew as the researchers introduced more gas into the chamber, increasing the pressure within.
That suggests a possible application for the technique. “This could enable a very good way to sense pressure,” says physicist Yu-Han Tseng of Yale University, especially at very low pressures — such as in space or in vacuum chambers. The system could also distinguish between the different types of gases Tseng and colleagues studied, as each one interacted differently with the nanoparticle.
A device like this could help reveal the composition of particles in space, and even on other worlds, Tseng says. “You can imagine putting it on another planet and [using] that to study the environment there.”

Astronomers unlock a mystery hidden in van Gogh’s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:55:29 UTC
01:55:29 KST

Researchers say they’ve identified the constellation depicted in Vincent van Gogh’s famous painting The Starry Night—and that the discovery changes what historians have assumed about the timing of the artwork’s creation.
The painting, now in the permanent collection of the Museum of Modern Art in New York City, is said to date back to mid-June 1889, when van Gogh was in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in France. But astronomers seeking to use the painting’s stars to pin down the exact time and place it was created have reached conflicting conclusions.
In a paper published on October 22 in Scientific Reports, researchers identified the stars in The Starry Night as those of the V-shaped Hyades cluster within the Taurus constellation, as observed on July 22, 1889.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“To my eyes, the star cluster in The Starry Night was the Hyades in Taurus. But earlier studies explained it as Aries,” says space researcher Elijah Jeong-hyun Kim, who is first author of the paper. “At that moment, I was sure this painting was worth studying.”
To find the constellation in The Starry Night, the researchers used a software program called Procrustes, which looked for patterns based on the shape formed by the relative positions of a group of stars rather than likely artistic embellishments such as size or color. This “shape analysis” technique matched five stars in the painting with five stars in the Hyades cluster, which had the strongest statistical fit out of any of the alternative constellations tested, including Aries, which had previously been proposed to be the constellation in the center of the painting. The researchers also tested this method on a van Gogh painting with a known constellation in it, the Big Dipper in Starry Night over the Rhône, and found its match had a comparably strong result to that of The Starry Night and Hyades.
To bolster their case, Kim and his colleagues looked to evidence from van Gogh’s letters at the time he was working on The Starry Night to show that perhaps he had painted it in several sessions, with the stars being observed from late July. Although van Gogh mentioned “a new study” of the starry sky in a June 18, 1889, letter, the researchers say that doesn’t mean he had finished the painting. Van Gogh’s letters also make no mention of Aries, despite his regular references to observing Venus, which was close to that constellation in the sky. “The stars of Aries are relatively faint, hardly enough to inspire a painter” at dawn, Kim says, which was when van Gogh often watched the stars.
Another argument against a mid-June date for The Starry Night is the lunar cycle—at that time, the moon would have been in a waning gibbous phase, with its sunlit side appearing as a lopsided oval. Yet the painting shows a waning crescent moon, as it would have been in a late-July sky. Kim also visited Saint-Rémy-de-Provence in June and July 2019 to fully capture van Gogh’s field of view from the precise location where he painted The Starry Night. Kim’s observations there, he says, further confirm the match with the Hyades cluster.
“During this time, van Gogh’s view of the sky was quite restricted” from his window at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole mental asylum, says James Beattie, a Hubble fellow at NASA. “If the identification holds, we can look up today and recognize the same stars van Gogh saw.”
Despite the study’s thoroughness, of course, for a painting as iconic as The Starry Night, there will always be competing versions of an origin story.
“The calculated position of brilliant Venus, in relation to the V shape of the Hyades asterism, does not match the painting,” says Don Olson, a self-proclaimed “celestial sleuth” for astronomical artwork and a professor emeritus of physics and astronomy at Texas State University. The researchers’ conclusions “require strong evidence to overcome Vincent van Gogh’s plain statement that ‘at last I have... a new study of a starry sky’ ... on June 18, 1889.”
Although there are still mysteries to resolve, Kim says the burden of proof has now reversed to proving the painting could not have been made in late July.
“The Starry Night spoke to an astronomer like me,” Kim says. “I listened to its voice.”

The inside story behind OpenAI’s million-dollar math proof
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:55:04 UTC
01:55:04 KST

Room 109 of New York University’s Warren Weaver Hall wasn’t ready for what hit it.
A half hour ahead of a special seminar scheduled for 3:30 P.M., attendees hoping to snag a seat already packed the hallway outside. When the doors opened, they all surged in, some climbing over rows of chairs to secure a good spot. Soon every inch of floor and both aisles were filled, with late-arriving onlookers trailing out the entrances. “Surely this is the most people this hall has ever seen,” I heard one bystander say. “This is no ordinary seminar. This is a rock concert,” said another.
The headliner was N.Y.U. mathematician Tristan Buckmaster. It was his first public lecture since September 8, the day OpenAI claimed to have solved one of math’s “million-dollar problems”—right after Buckmaster publicly called the company out for seeming to steal his work.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
While Buckmaster set up, I peeked at the open laptops in the row ahead of me. Each showed a chat window with a large language model (LLM), either Anthropic’s Claude Code or OpenAI’s ChatGPT Codex. The prompters were asking their LLM to help construct a mathematical proof, or rewrite part of a manuscript in progress. In other words, they were doing math in 2026.
“I hope you stay with me,” Buckmaster began. “I have been so busy these last few weeks that I literally wrote this talk last night.”
The public discord surrounding the biggest math breakthrough in decades capped off a summer of disruption that has left humanity’s oldest academic discipline forever changed. Ever since the momentous OpenAI announcement, the events behind it have appeared as messy and confusing as the proof itself. But now, as the community races to reverse-engineer the LLM’s opaque logic, a few things are becoming clear.
OpenAI’s internal model indeed found the right answer. And it did so by following a different path than anyone—including the company’s top mathematicians—initially realized.
Clearest of all, though, is that we’re entering a troubling new era. Inscrutable models are making scientific history while cloaked in proprietary secrets. Humans, with their foibles and petty jockeying, are barely keeping up. Consequently, that history has never been harder to write down.
The North Star
Buckmaster’s tale starts a year ago, with an e-mail from someone he’d never met: mathematician and Anthropic employee Levent Alpöge.
“I fear a world in which corporations are the only ones with claim to the deepest pure math work,” Alpöge wrote. “It seems to me there will be only one Millennium Problem solved in the foreseeable future,” he continued, proposing that he and Buckmaster could work together to solve it.
That problem—one of Clay Mathematics Institute’s seven “Millennium Prize Problems”—is known simply as “Navier-Stokes.” The nickname refers to the Navier-Stokes equations, which dictate how fluids swirl and flow. Mathematicians had long suspected that the equations don’t always work. That sometimes, they would predict that a fluid does the impossible—that its flow, at points, “blows up,” reaching an infinite and entirely nonsensical velocity.
Find such a flaw—using a mathematical proof—and the Clay Institute would owe you a cool $1 million. Alpöge wasn’t the only one in Silicon Valley who thought that goal was within reach.
“At that time, you have to understand that the Navier-Stokes equation became this tech bro obsession,” Buckmaster told N.Y.U. audience. Most of those tech bros didn’t even understand the equations, he said, but they’d heard mathematicians point to them as a place artificial intelligence might help. As Buckmaster put it, solving Navier-Stokes was becoming “the yardstick to say, ‘We’re better than that other AI company.’”
In fact, Buckmaster had collaborated with Google’s DeepMind team in their own pursuit of this goal—Navier-Stokes, he tells me, has always been the “North Star” of his research. So he accepted Alpöge’s overture.
They focused on a potential loophole in the Clay Institute’s posing of the problem, which said a mathematician could “stir” the fluid with a finely-tuned force. A few years ago, the Spanish mathematicians Diego Córdoba and Luis Martínez-Zoroa realized that phrasing might allow an exploit. The Spaniards sketched out a specific program—to contrive an ultraprecise, unrealistic force that pokes and prods each point in the fluid just so, massaging it into blowing up.
Alpöge and Buckmaster started by instructing their LLMs—a mix of Anthropic and OpenAI models—to carry out Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa’s program. They first managed to blow up simpler sets of equations describing idealized fluids—easier proxies for Navier-Stokes. Buckmaster told me their collaboration was “purely personal,” without official involvement from Anthropic—although, he acknowledged in his lecture, during their work Alpöge did have access to Anthropic’s computing resources and unreleased versions of Claude.
Alpöge’s math output has been the subject of some consternation. In the last several months, he’s prodded Claude into resolving several famous open problems, often announcing them in cryptic, playful posts on social media. He’s left mathematicians unsure to what extent these explosive results represent his employer and has built a strange reputation somewhere between folk hero and Internet troll. Downplaying his affiliation, Alpöge has characterized his work with Buckmaster as “mostly me and Claude having a good time YOLO-ing random stuff in the corner.”
Contrast his approach with that of OpenAI, whose assault on mathematics has been overwhelming and deliberate. The company has strategically poached much of the field’s top young talent, arming them with lavish resources to bag the biggest mathematical game they can. They unveil their papers alongside carefully-worded press releases, substituting the impersonal, monolithic byline “OpenAI” for the traditional list of human contributors. They’ve become notorious for disregarding academic norms, and their lead scientist Sébastien Bubeck has now had to apologize repeatedly after these aggressive rollouts sparked furious backlash.
In August, after several months of slow progress, Alpöge and Buckmaster’s prompting suddenly took off. On the 15th, Alpöge informed Buckmaster that Claude had blown up the Euler equations—equivalent to Navier-Stokes without friction, a simplification seen as a crucial step toward solving the full problem. “He didn’t quite believe it himself,” Buckmaster recalled during his public talk. Looking at the document the AIs had spit out explaining their proof, Buckmaster didn’t believe it, either.
“This was the most horrible mathematics I’ve ever seen in my life,” he said to laughter as he flashed a slide showing some of the proof’s impenetrable wall of garbled text and numbers.
“Although they’re English words, it’s not English,” Buckmaster went on. “But all the different LLM models understand this complete gibberish.” As unbelievable as it seems, when LLMs team up on a math problem, they begin communicating in their own “weird slop dialect,” as one mathematician put it to me.
And on August 22 Buckmaster and Alpöge prompted their LLMs to code the whole thing in Lean—a programming language that breaks a math proof into tiny steps and confirms that each follows from those before it. “This complete and utter nonsense was Lean-verified,” Buckmaster said, meaning it was correct.
But he and Alpöge didn’t want to post a result they didn’t understand. So the pair began a sprint to rewrite the proof for human consumption, relying heavily on OpenAI’s ChatGPT Codex.
The Blowup
Here the timelines get fuzzy. The following was gleaned from public statements plus supporting documentation provided by Buckmaster. Alpöge and Bubeck both declined on-the-record interviews, but Bubeck corroborated the basic facts and direct quotes.
On August 28 OpenAI happened to begin training a new internal model that proved to be far better at math than any predecessor. Then, on August 31, Alpöge tweeted “Augustus Mirabilis”—Latin for “miraculous August.” Alarmed, Bubeck and his team at OpenAI took this and other rumors to mean Anthropic “had solved at least one Millennium Problem.” By Tuesday, September 1, they had launched a rushed counterattack, sending a squadron of copies of their new model at each open Millennium Problem, plus a few others—including the Euler equations for fluids.
The following day, Wednesday, Buckmaster and Alpöge learned through back channels about OpenAI’s frenzied efforts. Buckmaster attempted a détente on Thursday morning, e-mailing a mathematician on the company’s math team. He informed them that his collaboration with Alpöge was the subject of the rumors and clarified that their work was not an official Anthropic effort—that he’d been using OpenAI models as well, in fact. The mathematician’s response was encouraging—offering computing resources and asking for more details because “it would be useful to avoid competing here.”
But that night, a squad of 100 agents that OpenAI had set upon the Euler equations leapfrogged Bubeck and Alpöge. The agents figured out a way to remove the weird force that was the centerpiece of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa’s approach—that is, OpenAI’s agents managed to make the fluid blow up on its own, without stirring it at all, producing their own Euler proof.
Stunned, the team decided to redirect all its resources at Navier-Stokes. The researchers assembled a swarm of 10,000 intercommunicating agents and fed it the new Euler proof as a starting point.
On Saturday, after consuming a reported $15 million in computing resources, the 10,000-agent swarm solved Navier-Stokes. It had to reintroduce a force to do so—reopening the loophole it had managed to close for Euler.
On Sunday, Buckmaster and Bubeck finally spoke. Bubeck claimed that OpenAI’s new model had solved the Clay problem in a single go, without any input beyond the official problem statement. He then backpedaled, revealing some details of the company’s weeklong agent extravaganza. Seeing Bubeck’s story change mid-telling, Buckmaster lost confidence that OpenAI was acting in good faith. He became suspicious that the company’s internal model had somehow accessed the work he had done with their public Codex model.
From there, the conversation couldn’t be salvaged. “You are not going to be able to convince me that you did not get the key ideas from a leak,” Buckmaster told Bubeck. Bubeck offered Buckmaster lead authorship on OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes paper—but demanded that Alpöge’s name be removed because of his affiliation with OpenAI’s competitor. When Buckmaster threatened to go to the press, Bubeck asked, “Why would you risk your career?” After Buckmaster’s defiant reply, Bubeck rejoined, “if you don’t want me to be nice, then I don’t have to be nice.”
At that point, there was nothing more to say. By Tuesday morning, each team had posted their proof, along with their side of the story.
A Maze of Math
In the Sunday phone call with Buckmaster, and their blog post and press conference on Tuesday, OpenAI’s math team said that their solution to Navier-Stokes followed the same mathematical path as Buckmaster and Alpöge’s.
But it turned out they were wrong. The models had carved out their own way.
The swarm’s proof does exploit the same loophole before—it constructs a strange, perfectly calibrated force to coax the fluid into blowing up. But the way it constructs this force is distinct from the Spanish program and thus distinct from Buckmaster and Alpöge’s Euler proof.
Buckmaster himself acknowledges that OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof introduced new ideas. But he still believes OpenAI somehow relied on his progress. The company’s Euler proof, he said in his lecture, clearly uses the Spanish program. “That was our result,” he said plainly.
As he sees it, his work with Alpöge on the Spanish program blazed a trail to get to a specific destination—using a force to blow up the Euler equations. And he believes OpenAI’s agents followed that same trail. From there, Buckmaster thinks, the agents continued in two forking directions.
The left fork cleverly removed the force after doing all that work to construct it. OpenAI’s 100-agent squad found a way to encode that complicated stir into the fluid’s initial state, rather than applying it externally. Buckmaster says this fork only goes a tiny distance further, mathematically, than their own preexisting proof.
Mathematicians are still comparing the two Euler proofs, but at least one expert agrees with Buckmaster’s take. “As far as I can tell, OpenAI’s proof basically follows the framework of our program,” says Fan Zheng, a collaborator of Córdoba and Martínez-Zoroa at the Institute of Mathematical Sciences in Spain. “But OpenAI is able to overcome a couple of technical difficulties to remove the force.”
The right fork, according to Buckmaster, led to Navier-Stokes. He views it as an extension of the same path that added some more significant new ideas—still a fork, but a longer one. (He also says that he and Alpöge used similar ideas in an alternate AI-generated Euler proof that they never made public but that they did feed into Codex.) Other experts studying OpenAI’s Navier-Stokes proof, however, feel that the company’s swarm instead carved an entirely new path that bears only cursory similarities to the trail Buckmaster and Alpöge’s AIs had previously blazed.
OpenAI emphatically denies the allegations. “No user inputs, including anything from Dr. Buckmaster’s Codex and ChatGPT usage, after July 3, 2026, could have influenced the model or the math results it produced in any way,” a spokesperson wrote in a statement to Scientific American.
This narrative, still murky more than a month after the fact, warns of a new normal that has already arrived. LLMs are proving math results far faster than humans can make sense of them. OpenAI announced one of the most important proofs in history without anyone on staff understanding even the broad strokes of the math it contained. Bubeck himself said on X that OpenAI “collectively had no research-level expertise in fluid dynamics.”
In Buckmaster’s first e-mail to OpenAI back on September 3, he explained why he and Alpöge were taking the time to rewrite their Euler proof before posting it. “I feel strongly that the first thing anyone reads should be a mathematical argument they can follow and argue with,” he said. The company disagrees—as punctuated a few weeks later, when it dropped hundreds more nigh-impenetrable math results on the community, many without Lean verification.
In the Q&A after Buckmaster’s talk, he declined the audience’s requests to predict the future. He only knows that September 8 marks the day after which math would never be the same, and that mathematicians need to decide how to respond. But his own feelings on that question, he said, still change day to day.
Asked what should happen next, his reply received the loudest applause of the day—a clear signal of the audience’s pent-up feeling.
“What we should do right now,” he blurted out, “is get the AI companies to stop acting like children.”

Three Ukrainian children, their mother and two young people brought back from occupation

Three Ukrainian children, their mother and two young people brought back from occupation
Another five children and young people have been successfully brought back from temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine.
Source: Bring Kids Back UA, a Ukrainian government-led effort to bring Ukrainian children home from temporarily Russian-occupied territories
Details: Under occupation, the children were forced to accept Russian passports and sing the Russian national anthem at school, Bring Kids Back UA reported.
When the full-scale invasion began, brothers Ihor, Andrii and Dmytro (names changed) and their mother were living in their hometown, which was soon occupied by Russian forces. From then on the family lived under constant pressure and restrictions from the occupation authorities.
Andrii attended a kindergarten under occupation, while Dmytro was in the sixth grade at a local school. Their mother said the children were forced to sing the Russian national anthem there, and the curriculum contained Russian propaganda.
The family also faced forced "passportisation", with the occupation authorities demanding that the parents obtain Russian documents.
Experts from the Ukrainian Child Rights Network, working with The Humanity Funds, helped get the family out safely.
The boys and their mother are now in Ukrainian-controlled territory. They will be helped through the adaptation and reintegration processes and will return to the Ukrainian education system.
Two young people, Albina and Viacheslav, were brought back with the assistance of a team from Helping to Leave.
Albina lived in the temporarily occupied part of Zaporizhzhia Oblast and decided to leave for Ukrainian-controlled territory on her own. She planned her route herself and got as far as the Mokrany-Domanove checkpoint between Belarus and Ukraine, but she could not cross the border because she did not have a Ukrainian passport.
It was then that she contacted Helping to Leave. Volunteers advised her on the documents she needed and helped coordinate her onward route.
In Minsk, Albina obtained a certificate enabling her to return to Ukraine and was able to continue her journey. She is now with relatives in Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Viacheslav found out about Helping to Leave from a friend whom the team had previously helped leave the occupation. After he reached out, volunteers helped him plan his route and supported him during his departure.
On the way, Viacheslav also helped a friend by taking two of her cats with him. Upon arrival in Ukraine, Viacheslav was met by a team from Helping to Leave who helped him find temporary accommodation.
He is currently obtaining new documents and planning his future in Ukraine. The cats have been reunited with their owner too.
Background: Previously, we reported on how 23 children and teenagers who had endured constant pressure, threats and fear were brought back from occupation to Ukrainian-controlled territory.

Powerful magnitude 7.0 earthquake strikes China's Tibet region
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:46:45 UTC
01:46:45 KST

A powerful magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck southwestern China's Tibet region late Thursday, the China Earthquake Networks Center (CENC) reported, with the tremor recorded at 10:33 p.m. local time (2:33 p.m. GMT).
Local authorities have found at least two people injured in a village near the epicentre, with some houses in villages closest to the epicenter showing cracks, the state broadcaster said. The quake is the strongest to hit China since January 2024.
The epicenter was in a sparsely populated, high-altitude county in Nagqu, northern Tibet, at a depth of 10 km (6.2 miles). The average elevation within 5 km of the epicenter is about 4,864 meters (15,960 feet), CENC data showed.
Videos released by local officially run media showed people leaving their homes and seeking shelter outside or in their cars parked on the street. One resident reported being awakened by the strong quake and heard the house squeaking in the tremor.
The quake was clearly felt in the local area, CENC said. The epicenter was around 400 km from the Tibetan capital of Lhasa.
Local fire and rescue teams have mobilized and are heading to the affected region, state media said.
A string of smaller tremors of around magnitude 3 and 4 have been recorded in surrounding regions following the magnitude 7 quake, CENC data showed.
In 2010, a magnitude 7.1 tremor struck Yushu in neighboring Qinghai province, killing at least 2,698 people and leaving nearly 300 people missing.

Doncic also won this fight decisively on the scoreboard when the Los Angeles Lakers blew out Lendeborg and the Warriors 127-105, with Doncic scoring 28 points in just three quarters.
Photo: AFP
Yet Lendeborg somehow was not finished talking: He called out the six-time All-Star as a complainer and a free-throw merchant during his post-game news conference.
“I lost all respect [for Doncic], man,” Lendeborg said. “That was awful... A lot of flopping, a lot of foul-baiting, a lot of praying to the ref, man. Interesting first game for me, for sure.”
The Warriors’ 24-year-old rookie first-round pick said he sparred with Doncic on the court because of the Slovenian superstar’s constant complaining to the officials — admittedly a common feature of most games in Doncic’s nine-year career.
Photo: AP
Lendeborg, who won an NCAA title with Michigan last season, said he enjoyed watching highlights of Doncic’s electric scoring performances in the past — but he has a more jaded perspective on Doncic’s skills now.
“Me getting frustrated, it’s not about the foul being called,” Lendeborg said. “It’s about him complaining the entire game, and then you get the foul call, and congratulations, bro. And then you talk to me like you did something great? Bro, come on. That’s just weak, you know? It kind of threw me off for a little while, because like I said, I had so much respect for him. Gone, man. Gone.”
Lendeborg and Doncic exchanged insults for much of the second quarter, with Lendeborg being whistled for a technical foul after saying something so loud and profane it caught the officials’ attention.
“I was telling him he sucks,” Lendeborg said with a smile. “‘You can’t score on me.’ I said it the whole game. I said a couple of cuss words, obviously. That’s why I got the technical and all that, but I was letting him know, because he was laughing and talking, all this because of that one foul call.”
Doncic mostly laughed off Lendeborg’s provocations, but the Lakers star obviously thrives amid confrontation. He was whistled for 16 technical fouls last season, earning a one-game suspension for exceeding the single-season limit.
“He was talking crazy, but I wasn’t trying to talk back this season,” Doncic said of Lendeborg. “Not trying to get techs. For the first time, that was not a double tech, because I didn’t say nothing, so I’m working on it. As you see, I think it worked great.”
Doncic got the ultimate victory at the final buzzer — but his halftime win was incredibly sweet as well.
“I knew that was going in before I got it in my hands,” Doncic said with a grin. “I work on those.”
He got the ball near the scorer’s table and let it fly with nearly three seconds left on the clock. When it banked through and set off pandemonium in the Lakers’ downtown arena, Doncic gleefully pointed at the fuming Lendeborg, who was not impressed.
“His only bucket on me was a banker from half court,” Lendeborg said. “I know it’s a team sport. He had 28 on us as a team. Me, I took my matchup personally. Tried not to get called on the fouls. Tried my best. I was thinking about playing him with my hands behind my back to see if that worked. Probably would have still got a foul call. But interesting.”

Rom-com or  sib-com?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:35 UTC
01:44:35 KST

It is a truth universally acknowledged, as somebody once wrote, that a Jane Austen novel is a precursor to the modern rom-com.
And so we find ourselves, in a new adaptation of Sense and Sensibility starring Daisy Edgar-Jones, rooting for one thing: a kiss. A simple kiss, to break through the miscues and misunderstandings and finally release all that romantic tension.
Of course, we get it. Elinor locks lips with her Edward, out there in the grassy Devon fields, just as Bridget Jones did with Mark Darcy, in the snowy London streets. It’s a lovely kiss, and worth the wait.
Photo: AP
But then … we get something better: A hug, between sisters, even more joyful. And that’s what we remember as the credits roll.
Sisters. They’re not exactly “doing it for themselves” in this new version directed by Georgia Oakley — we’re still in 18th-century England, after all, and young women need to find husbands.
But Oakley, seeking a 21st-century approach to the Austen classic, finds a way to subtly shift the weight from romantic chemistry to the more profound chemistry between no-nonsense Elinor (Edgar-Jones, in the “sense” role) and turbulent Marianne (Esme Creed-Miles, in the “sensibility” role.) And this alone — well, and two killer dance scenes — seems reason enough to revisit the story, three decades since Ang Lee’s (李安) 1995 version won Emma Thompson a screenplay Oscar.
Oakley also brings a welcome naturalistic feel to a script by Diana Reid, with a strong sense of nature itself but also the reality of economic hardship — or what stands for economic hardship in an Austen novel. When Elinor and her mother (Caitriona Balfe) and sisters are relegated to a small cottage upon their father’s death, they’re hardly starving — they still have a servant, after all. But they share clothes, their hair is unkempt, they perform country chores. Their dresses are even stained.
We begin with some bad news. Marianne is lying in the grass, with the caterpillars, waiting for the day’s letters. Soon, the Dashwoods are in tears. Their father has left his wealth to a son from a previous marriage, meaning John Dashwood and his insufferable wife Fanny (Stacy Martin, amusing) will be moving into their sprawling country estate.
Mom and sisters soon decamp to a much smaller cottage — only one servant — in Devon, thanks to the help of Mrs. Jennings, “mother of your mother’s cousin’s cousin’s wife,” as she announces herself (a delightful Fiona Shaw).
But not before Elinor has fallen in love with Edward Ferrars (George MacKay), Fanny’s handsome and upstanding brother, during a family visit.
It seems these two are perfect for each other, both honorable and sensible but also just a little sexy underneath — Edgar-Jones and MacKay are well-matched here.
Complications arise, though — duh, this is an Austen novel! Ferrars is, well, otherwise engaged, literally. Elinor learns this on a trip to London, from the fiancee herself. It will take the rest of the movie for this to be ironed out. Meanwhile, Marianne is going through her own romantic journey.
There’s no need to count the times Marianne is tasked with explaining here that she’s the passionate one, more in touch with her turbulent emotions, and expects the same from a partner. A few too many, anyway.
But Creed-Miles, whose mother, Samantha Morton, is having a scene-stealing moment herself in The Odyssey, gives an exhilarating turn as the sister who, yes, seems to wear it all on her sleeve, making it totally believable when she screams into the rain or laughs with delirium. Or falls head-over-heels with Willoughby, a handsome rake (deliciously played by Frank Dillane) who swoops in to save her when she turns her ankle on a beach.
These two, also, seem perfect for each other — especially when dancing. Kudos to choreographer Holly Blakey, who makes the most of two social dance scenes: the exuberant “hop” in the countryside (what fun the actors seem to be having), and the more refined but still creative London ball.
But Willoughby, as Austen’s readers know, will prove an even more elusive catch than Ferrars. Meanwhile, waiting in the wings is a man of few words — and initially, few feelings, or so thinks Marianne — the steadfast Colonel Brandon (Herbert Nordrum).
Will he find a way to her heart? It’s hardly a spoiler to reveal the end of a novel published centuries ago, but more importantly, we know how all rom-coms end — with the “rom” part working out, somehow.
We’re happy for the sisters, of course. They landed a couple of nice guys.
But most of all? We’re happy they have each other.

France’s unrest lays bare the ‘slow agony’ of Macron’s final months in office
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:34 UTC
01:44:34 KST

France’s worst bout of civil unrest in years has plunged French President Emmanuel Macron’s final months in office deeper into turmoil, exposing the powerlessness of a leader struggling to contain social anger with little money to spend, scant political capital and an increasingly fragile grip on public order.
The rioting that swept across France on Saturday last week, leaving a trail of looted shops, torched buildings and defaced public institutions, presents Macron with perhaps the most explosive challenge of his twilight presidency: A country demanding more from a state that can no longer afford to give much.
Macron came to power almost a decade ago promising to upend France’s sclerotic political class, turbocharge economic reforms and restore authority through a more assertive presidency.
Instead, with just six months left in office, he finds himself effectively a lame-duck head of state presiding over a country mired in political paralysis, facing acute financial pressures and grappling with unrest that has exposed the limits of state authority.
Unlike during the yellow vest uprising of 2018 to 2019, when Macron sought to defuse public anger with billions of euros in concessions, France’s strained public finances and fractured parliament leave him with precious few levers to pull.
Even former allies are openly scathing, tracing the country’s current impasse to Macron’s decision to call a snap parliamentary election in 2024 that weakened his authority.
“The end of this term is a slow agony,” said Loic Kervran, a former lawmaker from Macron’s camp. “The president paralyzed the country with his absurd decision to dissolve parliament in 2024. Arguably the worst decision in the history of the Fifth Republic.”
The turmoil might benefit far-right National Rally leader Marine Le Pen, who is already the frontrunner in next year’s presidential race and stands to gain from the anger over declining living standards and the fears over law and order unleashed by the weekend’s violence.
“Le Pen no longer needs to spend any money to campaign,” said Jean-Baptiste Moreau, another former Macron lawmaker. “It’s not just a clear path ahead of her — it’s a six-lane highway.”
Le Pen delivered her own message to the nation in a video statement on Sunday, portraying Macron’s administration as a crumbling power and casting herself as the figure capable of restoring order.
When Macron later addressed the country, he offered little concrete action, stopping short of declaring a state of emergency. As he spoke, looting was continuing for a second consecutive night, including in affluent Paris districts, prompting Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu to announce local curfews on Monday.
Opponents and one-time allies alike were underwhelmed. His former prime minister, Edouard Philippe, preparing his own presidential run, was unsparing in his criticism.
“Mr President, I listened to you last night,” Philippe said on X. “I would have preferred, like millions of French people, decisions and initiatives to restore order.”
“Our country needs to be commanded,” he added.
However, even Philippe is struggling to shake off his past association with Macron, and most recent polls show far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Melenchon edging ahead of him in the race to qualify for the second-round runoff vote. That outcome would all but guarantee a Le Pen victory, the opinion polls show.
Macron’s office on Monday announced that he had refused his interior minister’s resignation and ordered a review into apparent failures in intelligence gathering and police preparedness — deepening the impression of a government struggling to regain control.
Investors also took fright. Market analysts say the violence adds another layer of political risk at a time when France is already under scrutiny over its swelling debt burden and struggle to reduce one of the euro zone’s largest budget deficits.
The president finds himself trapped between bond markets demanding spending restraint and protesters demanding the opposite.
Despite calls from opponents to remain in France, Macron arrived in Kuwait on Monday on a Gulf tour he says would help secure fuel supplies and ease some of the economic pressures that have helped swell the ranks of the protesters.
The trip carries risks, reinforcing perceptions of a president disconnected from the public mood. Images of Macron attending a Celine Dion concert with his wife Brigitte on Friday last week, hours before the unrest erupted, prompted ridicule on social media and became an easy symbol for critics seeking to portray him as detached from events.
In a sign of the depth of disenchantment in parts of his political camp, some former allies have begun openly discussing whether he should leave office before the end of his term. Moreau, who spoke to Macron on Sunday, said he urged him to prepare an orderly early departure to break the political deadlock and avoid another six months of drift.
“He doesn’t want to give up, that’s not his character. But that’s what he should do for the country,” he said.

Micron announces a new profit-sharing program
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
16:44:33 UTC
01:44:33 KST

Micron Memory Taiwan Co (台灣美光) yesterday unveiled a new profit-sharing program and structural wage hikes as part of its efforts to build a predictable and transparent compensation framework in response to feedback from unions.
The memorychip maker, a subsidiary of US-based Micron Technology Inc, announced the major compensation structural overhaul during an online news conference following a milestone agreement with the union representing more than 10,000 workers at its Taichung facility.
Under the new framework, quarterly profit-sharing bonuses would supplement payments under the Incentive Pay Plan (IPP), the company said.
Photo: Lisa Wang, Taipei Times
The IPP formula has also been substantially enhanced, it said.
“Profit-sharing mechanisms are common among Asian companies, but they are rarely seen among American technology firms,” Micron Memory Taiwan chairman Donghui Lu (盧東暉) told the news conference. “This approach offers transparency and, to a certain degree, predictability.”
The new mechanism is to take effect in fiscal 2027 and apply to eligible employees in Micron Technology’s global workforce.
Quarterly net income minus forecast capital expenditure for the following quarter would be the basis for calculating profit-sharing bonuses, the company said.
The payout will be distributed equally between stock — subject to one-year vesting — and cash, it said.
Following its annual wage adjustments, Micron Memory Taiwan is to implement another structural payroll increase in an extensive way to avoid salary inversion.
Previously, Micron Memory Taiwan’s wage hikes primarily targeted entry-level personnel and newcomers.
The company hopes to implement the adjustments by Lunar New Year next year, it said.
Micron Memory Taiwan also plans to increase shift differential pay from December. The monthly allowance for day shifts would triple to NT$4,500 (US$138.43), while the allowance for evening shifts would increase to 15 percent of their regular pay, and night shift workers would receive a 20 percent shift differential, it said.
After the adjustments, the conditional top-end compensation for an entry-level engineer would be nearly NT$4 million in fiscal 2027, up from NT$1.45 million in fiscal 2025, while the amount for mid-to-senior-tier engineers is projected at NT$6 million, up from more than NT$2 million, the Taichung union said.
The projections include stock awards and employer retirement contributions.
Micron Memory Taiwan said it would increase its employer pension contribution rate to 10 percent of workers’ regular pay from 8 percent to retain talent.
Representatives of the company’s Taoyuan union yesterday held a one-day strike over accusations that company management had failed to disclose its profit-sharing ratio.
The Taoyuan union is demanding that the allocation be set at 15 percent of Micron Technology’s global operating profit.
