PHP security crisis prompts websites worldwide to push updates for critical vulnerabilities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:58:11 UTC
00:58:11 KST

Mert Davut and Emir Yildirim
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The widely used PHP programming language was found to have two critical security vulnerabilities affecting digital infrastructure worldwide, prompting organizations across the globe to implement updates.
The “PHP2Shell” vulnerability stems from errors in code and memory management, which allow remote code execution on compromised systems without entering a username or password.
The US Federal Bureau of Investigation and the National Security Agency both warned the public about these newly discovered vulnerabilities.
Websites providing citizenship services were taken down in the Netherlands, while similar measures for prefectural websites came to the fore in France.
Countries including Denmark, Norway, Finland, Japan and South Korea issued cyber crisis alerts and implemented immediate updates.
Türkiye’s Cybersecurity Directorate instructed public institutions and private organizations to migrate their PHP infrastructure to secure versions, while nationwide security scans and technical monitoring are underway.
Probes into Türkiye’s e-Government Portal yielded no issues compromising the security of the digital services offered, authorities said.
These security vulnerabilities pose a theoretical risk to websites that contain sensitive information, and the mere existence of these security flaws does not necessarily mean personal data has been compromised.
Everyday users of the internet and online applications are urged to stay vigilant and practice basic digital security measures, while businesses and institutions are urged to determine which internal systems use PHP and identify which version is active, experts said.
An official security patch has already been released, but it is up to organizations to identify affected systems and update their PHP installations to a secure version.
Experts also advised blocking all international web traffic to domestic systems and enterprise applications that do not need global access and allowing traffic only from trusted and authorized IP addresses.

U.S. Army to test robot supply vehicles in Hawaii
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:54:30 UTC
00:54:30 KST

- The U.S. Army selected nine finalists for an autonomous sustainment competition focused on resupplying troops across contested Pacific island chains.
- Finalists will demonstrate their ground and air delivery systems to soldiers at the Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center in Hawaii Nov. 4–15, 2026.
The U.S. Army has selected nine companies as finalists in a competition to find autonomous ground and air vehicles that can resupply troops spread across Pacific islands, and their systems will go before soldiers in Hawaii next month.
The competition, called G-TEAD USARPAC ACE 27-01: Autonomous Sustainment, is run by the Army’s Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate with U.S. Army Pacific and the Army FUZE xTech program. The finalists will take part in a live Soldier exercise scheduled for Nov. 4–15, 2026, at the Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center in Hawaii, the U.S. Army’s main combat training center for the Pacific.
Eight of the nine finalists are competing with ground delivery systems, and one with an air delivery drone, according to the competition page. The ground entries are Ark Robotics’ M4 unmanned ground vehicle, BlueSky Innovations’ Jekyll US, Cyborg Autonomy’s modular tracked robot, Dataspeed’s TWEEDLE attritable wheeled dolly, Hypercraft’s Razorback, which also provides tactical power, Raptor Defense Company’s PIT VIPER personal combat vehicle, Stridar’s Siderunner Pro and Swarmbotics AI’s FIREANT, designed for the last tactical mile of resupply. Phenix Solutions is the sole air finalist with its Ultra 2XL heavy-lift drone.
The Army framed the problem around the vulnerability of traditional supply lines in a Pacific conflict. Resupply between islands currently depends on high-value crewed ships and aircraft that would face serious risk in contested waters, while moving supplies on land puts a heavy physical load on soldiers. The service wants unmanned air, ground and surface systems that can carry different payloads over a range of distances, managed by software that routes supplies automatically and lets small teams control groups of vehicles.
The competition was open to three capability areas: attritable air delivery systems, attritable autonomous surface vessels able to carry one to four standard shipping containers, and autonomous ground delivery systems. Attritable means cheap enough to be lost in combat without major impact. The finalist list includes ground and air entries.
Entries had to meet demanding baseline requirements. Systems needed to be mature enough for testing in a realistic environment, be fieldable within 180 days of a contract award, work with the Army’s command and logistics networks, and keep operating when GPS and communications are jammed or degraded. They also had to show safe behavior around soldiers, including obstacle avoidance and emergency stops, and alert operators when a sensor or software fault occurs.
Each finalist receives $25,000, and those whose systems are successfully integrated into the November exercise will receive another $25,000. After the exercise, the Army plans to select up to five winners for an additional $150,000 each, with winners scheduled to be announced on Nov. 15.
The competition offers up to $1.5 million in cash prizes in total. From Nov. 30, 2026, through March 31, 2027, selected participants can submit proposals for follow-on prototype agreements worth up to $2 million, giving the Army a path to put the best-performing systems into units’ hands.

Ben-Gvir arms more West Bank settlers ahead of Israeli elections
Far-right Israeli National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir has approved the expansion of gun licence across 11 additional illegal settlements and outposts in the occupied West Bank, despite warnings from Israeli security officials of a potential wave of settler attacks against Palestinians following next week's elections.
The decision, reported by Israel's Channel 14 on Thursday, comes as the Israeli military, Shin Bet security service and police face mounting criticism over their failure to contain settler violence, with security officials warning that extremist groups could attempt to seize more Palestinian land if Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu loses power.
Ben-Gvir's move will allow residents of 11 more settlements and outposts in the northern occupied West Bank to apply for firearms licences, provided they meet the criteria set by Israel's National Security Ministry.
"We are continuing the arming revolution and expanding this reform to include the new settlements we have established in the northern West Bank," Ben-Gvir was quoted as saying by Channel 14.
The extremist minister pledged to continue expanding the programme, which his ministry claims is intended to strengthen security within settlements and enable residents to respond to attacks.
The expansion comes amid a campaign of settler violence against Palestinians, including assaults on farmers, land seizures and attacks aimed at forcing residents from their homes.
Yossi Dagan, head of the Northern West Bank Settlements Council, welcomed the decision, arguing that settlers who had served in Israeli combat units or military reserves needed weapons to defend their families and settlements.
He described the northern occupied West Bank as a "strategic defensive line" for Israel.
Fears of settler violence after Israeli elections
The expansion comes just days before Israel's 27 October parliamentary elections, with Israeli security officials warning that extremist settlers could launch a coordinated campaign of attacks against Palestinians if Netanyahu's governing bloc loses power.
According to Haaretz, which cited sources familiar with military assessments, far-right activists could seek to establish new illegal outposts, seize Palestinian land and attack residents in an attempt to prevent a future government from dismantling illegal settlements.
The concern is that extremist settlers may refuse to accept a change in government and instead attempt to impose new realities on the ground before any incoming administration can act.
The growing availability of firearms among settlers could further complicate efforts to evacuate illegal outposts, potentially increasing the risk of armed resistance to any future government seeking to remove them.
Israeli military officials are reportedly reinforcing troop deployments in the West Bank and seeking additional Border Police personnel in areas where violent settler groups operate.
Yet sources familiar with the security assessments have acknowledged that the army, Shin Bet and police are struggling to contain attacks, particularly when settlers strike several locations simultaneously.
"Anyone who tells you there is control is lying. The army, Shin Bet and police have lost control of the area," a security source familiar with the situation told Haaretz.
"They are running from one location to another chasing rioters. The problem is that no real effort is being made to regain control."
The remarks reflect growing frustration within Israel's own security establishment over the authorities' failure to stop settler terrorism, despite knowing where violent groups operate and the identities of prominent perpetrators.
Military officials have reportedly questioned why no effective preventive plan has been developed, rather than relying on forces to respond after attacks have already taken place.
Israeli security chiefs meet but take no action
Israeli military chief Eyal Zamir convened a meeting on Tuesday with senior security officials to discuss the escalating attacks and the risk of further violence surrounding the elections.
Despite the warnings, the meeting ended without significant new decisions, according to sources familiar with the discussions.
Officials within the military's Central Command reportedly criticised the absence of representatives from Netanyahu's office, Defence Minister Israel Katz and the National Security Council, arguing that the situation required direct political intervention.
One source described the meeting as little more than an exercise in recording a security assessment, with no meaningful steps agreed to prevent further attacks.
The failure to act comes as Katz has discontinued the use of administrative detention against Israeli settlers, removing a measure previously available to security forces dealing with extremist violence.
Instead, the military, Shin Bet and legal authorities are reportedly preparing exclusion orders that would bar individuals involved in incitement or attacks from entering the West Bank.
Security officials have acknowledged, however, that such orders would do little to prevent other settlers from establishing illegal outposts, seizing Palestinian farmland or carrying out attacks.
Ben-Gvir's drive to arm settlers
Ben-Gvir has made expanding access to firearms a central policy since becoming national security minister in early 2023, easing licensing requirements and widening the categories of Israelis eligible to carry weapons.
The programme accelerated following the start of Israel's genocidal war on Gaza in October 2023, alongside an intensification of Israeli military raids and settler attacks across the occupied West Bank.
On 21 January 2026, Ben-Gvir approved the addition of 18 settlements in the occupied territory to the list of locations whose residents could apply for firearms licences.
According to Israeli newspaper Israel Hayom, more than 200 cities, towns and other localities had been included in the expanded eligibility programme during 2026.
Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank are illegal under international law, which prohibits an occupying power from transferring its civilian population into occupied territory.

FIFA is launching its tender offer Thursday for the 2030 U.S. media rights with an option for potential partners to also buy rights for the 2034 World Cup. FIFA wants bids in by Nov. 19.
YouTube, Netflix, Amazon and Disney are all interested, CNBC reported in July. Rights could sell for between $1.5 billion and $2 billion, some media executives predicted at the time. FIFA hasn't sold U.S. men's World Cup TV rights since 2011.
Fox paid $425 million for the 2026 World Cup, which broke U.S. ratings records. Matches averaged 13.5 million viewers — up 166% from 2022.
The 2030 World Cup will take place in Spain, Portugal and Morocco.
FIFA would prefer to sell the English and the Spanish-language rights packaged together to one media partner – a departure from previous deals. For this past World Cup, NBCUniversal's Telemundo owned the Spanish rights while Fox owned the English rights. That led to some tension between the broadcasters and FIFA, as Peacock carried the Spanish-language rights for a less expensive price than Fox One, which streamed the games with English announcers.
FIFA Chief Business Officer Romy Gai said it's too early to gauge what price is realistic for the 2030 World Cup. FIFA is willing to listen to offers where just one media company buys the entire package or a joint offering – potentially between a streamer and a traditional broadcaster.
"We want to be flexible," said Gai in an interview. "We expect a big number of participants, both from the linear side and from the streamer side, but we want to listen to what is relevant for them, and then we can build up the best case together."
While the 2026 World Cup took place in the U.S., Canada and Mexico — allowing matches to be played during U.S. afternoons and nights — the 2030 World Cup will have a significant time difference. The 2034 World Cup will be played in Saudi Arabia. Riyadh is seven hours ahead of New York.
The time zones may make it difficult for games to be played during U.S. primetime hours. That will play a role in how much media companies are willing to spend on both tournaments, but Gai doesn't expect the time zone challenges to play too much of a role in the bidding.
"I'm sure that we will have every day matches that will be available in the right time zone for the U.S.," Gai said. "We expect it to have an impact [on the bidding], but not as big as you think."
If a streaming service wins the rights, FIFA will ensure that a certain number of matches are available for free, either by forcing the streamer to sublicense certain rights or by putting some games on a free version of the service, if such a thing exists.
Netflix has already acquired the 2030 World Cup rights in Spain. That deal allows a free-to-air broadcaster to show at least one game each day.
After Nov. 19, when bids are due, a contingent from FIFA will come to the U.S. around Thanksgiving and begin speaking with media companies in person, Gai said. At that point, FIFA could narrow down the field and ask for one more final bid – or it could just choose a winner.
FIFA intends to select its next media partner before the end of the year, said Gai.

UK plans tougher penalties for damage to undersea cables, pipelines
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:48:47 UTC
00:48:47 KST

Aysu Bicer
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The UK government has proposed tougher prison sentences and unlimited fines for those who intentionally damage critical undersea infrastructure, citing growing security threats, including suspicious Russian activity in British waters.
A White Paper published on Thursday outlines plans to modernize legislation dating back 140 years to strengthen the protection of undersea telecommunications cables, energy pipelines and electricity interconnectors.
Under the proposals, those who intentionally damage critical undersea energy and telecommunications infrastructure could face prison sentences of up to 14 years, alongside tougher financial penalties.
The plans would also introduce new security and resilience requirements for subsea telecommunications companies, obliging them to identify and manage risks to their networks.
The government would gain additional powers to direct telecommunications providers to take protective measures against threats such as sabotage and espionage. The proposals also include safeguards for fiber-optic sensing technology, which can detect activity at sea but may pose national security risks if sensitive data is compromised.
“Undersea cables are the hidden backbone of modern Britain, carrying the data we rely on every day to message friends and family, do our banking, and run our businesses,” Telecoms Minister Ian Murray said in a statement.
He added: “We intend to modernise those laws with tougher penalties, stronger requirements on industry and new powers to protect our national security, making sure the UK’s critical infrastructure is fit for the threats of today and tomorrow.”
According to the government, undersea fibre-optic cables carry around 99% of the UK’s international data, while subsea pipelines provide 74% of its gas supply. Electricity cables also support energy imports from Europe and connections to offshore wind farms.
Energy Minister Michael Shanks also said the legislation would strengthen deterrence and help prevent, detect and respond to threats against the country’s energy supply.
The publication of the White Paper marks the start of a 12-week public consultation seeking views from industry, experts and the public.

CEC impeachment: Speaker Om Birla says fresh motion against Gyanesh Kumar will be examined as per rules

Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said if the opposition brings any fresh impeachment motion against the country's top poll officer, it will be examined according to rules and procedures.
Lok Sabha Speaker Om Birla on Thursday said any fresh motion seeking the impeachment of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar would be examined in accordance with parliamentary rules and procedures, as opposition protests demanding the poll panel chief’s removal intensified over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.The opposition has made two attempts to remove Kumar, with notices in the first attempt rejected by both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. Notices submitted in the second attempt are still pending in the Upper House.
“If any fresh notice comes, we will see and examine it accordingly under rules and procedures,” Birla told a press conference, responding to a question on the possibility of another impeachment motion against the CEC.Protests against Kumar have intensified over the past fortnight, with opposition parties demanding his resignation over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls. The agitation gathered momentum after The Indian Express reported that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had recorded objections at least 14 times over the past 10 months to decisions and orders related to the SIR, alleging that these were issued without their knowledge or recommendation.
Under the Constitution, the CEC can be removed only through a parliamentary process similar to that prescribed for the removal of a Supreme Court judge. The Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023, also provides for the CEC or an Election Commissioner to resign by submitting a written resignation to the President.The removal process is governed by constitutional provisions and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968. Once a removal motion is admitted in either House of Parliament, the Speaker or the Rajya Sabha Chairman constitutes a three-member committee to investigate the charges. The panel comprises the Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge, a chief justice of a high court and a distinguished jurist.
If the committee finds the charges unsubstantiated, no further action is taken. If it finds the allegations proved, the motion is taken up for consideration in Parliament. Removal requires each House to pass an address supported by a majority of its total membership and a two-thirds majority of members present and voting, in the same session.The opposition’s attempts to remove Kumar have brought the Election Commission’s handling of the SIR under renewed scrutiny, with the possibility of another motion now hinging on the formal parliamentary process and the admissibility of any fresh notice.

Japanese troops test-fire air defense missiles at New Mexico range
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:47:27 UTC
00:47:27 KST

- Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force has been conducting live-fire air defense training since July 2026 at Shizunai, Rokkasho and other ranges in Japan.
- At McGregor Range in New Mexico, its Type 03 medium-range missile units are firing alongside Japan Air Self-Defense Force Patriot units.
Japan’s Ground Self-Defense Force has been carrying out live-fire air defense training since July 2026 at ranges in northern Japan and in the United States, where its medium-range missile units are firing alongside Japan Air Self-Defense Force Patriot batteries at McGregor Range in New Mexico.
The Ground Self-Defense Force, Japan’s army, said on X that units at home are firing at the Shizunai range in Hokkaido, the Rokkasho range in Aomori Prefecture and other sites. The training covers the force’s layered short-range air defense weapons: the Type 81 short-range surface-to-air missile, the Type 93 close-range surface-to-air missile and the Type 87 self-propelled anti-aircraft gun.
Those systems cover the lowest and closest layers of Japan’s ground-based air defense.
The Type 93 mounts short-range missiles on a light utility vehicle, while the tracked Type 87 carries twin 35 mm cannons to engage aircraft, helicopters and other low-flying targets at close range.
In New Mexico, the Ground Self-Defense Force is firing the Type 03 medium-range surface-to-air missile, known in Japan as Chu-SAM, in coordination with Air Self-Defense Force Patriot units. Built by Mitsubishi Electric, the Type 03 replaced the U.S.-designed HAWK missiles Japan had used since 1965 and has a range of about 50 km (31 miles), with the system designed to hit aircraft, air-to-surface missiles and cruise missiles directly.
The Type 03 has a long history at the New Mexico range. Japanese forces fired it in a live training exercise for the first time at McGregor Range in late 2006, after six earlier test launches at nearby White Sands Missile Range.
McGregor Range, part of the Fort Bliss training complex, offers the open airspace and distances needed for live missile firings that are difficult to arrange in Japan. The Air Self-Defense Force has held annual Patriot live-fire training there since 1963, and recent iterations have included combined live firing with Ground Self-Defense Force anti-aircraft units, bilateral firing with U.S. Army Patriot units and, in 2025, counter-drone training.
Pairing the two services lets Japan’s army and air force practice defending against air threats as a single network, with the medium-range Type 03 and the longer-range Patriot covering different layers of the airspace.
The Ground Self-Defense Force said it will continue firing training at home and abroad to further strengthen its air defense capabilities.

France hands out swift verdicts in fast-track justice after riots

- Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said 2,500 were arrested and 917 prosecuted, calling the response a sign of “great firmness”.
- Lawyers say the process is rushed and harsh, with one calling it “state repression” and warning judges face pressure for tougher penalties.
AI generated
PARIS – French courts have swiftly handed out verdicts, including orders to serve jail time, in fast-track justice for defendants accused over the rioting that erupted on the sidelines of protests at the weekend.
The government says the accelerated legal processes are needed to restore order after some of the worst urban violence in recent years on Oct 17.
But courts are also overwhelmed, while some lawyers say the scale of the hearings reeks of state repression.
Mathilde B, a student, 19, and 20-year-old Francois D, who said he wants to be a mountain guide, had come to Paris on Oct 17 from Auxerre, a city south-east of the capital.
But police found a knuckleduster and flick knife in the young man’s bag and discovered the pair had discussed “guerrilla warfare” and “beating up riot police” on social media.
Mathilde B received a five-month suspended prison sentence; but Francois D was sent to jail immediately as part of an eight-month sentence, with two months to be served in custody.
Tristan Lawless, a lawyer at the bar in Melun south of Paris, said he was defending a client for whom prosecutors had demanded a five-month sentence with immediate custody.
He said the trial was taking place “on the basis of a 50-page case file that, in my view, was put together in haste, with reports that are often vague and lacking detail”, and alleged his client had been beaten in custody.
‘Pressure on judges’
Speaking on Oct 21 in the southern city of Marseille, which saw some of the worst violence, Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin said that out of some 2,500 people arrested nationwide at the weekend, 917 were being prosecuted, a number he hailed as a “truly impressive figure”.
“The holding cells are full,” he said, referring to the units where people are held ahead of trial, adding this was proof of “our great firmness”.
One of the most longstanding and hyperactive members of the government, Darmanin, a former interior minister, is taking a high profile as Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu’s Cabinet seeks to show it is in control.
Once seen as having presidential ambitions himself, he is a leading supporter of former centre-right premier Edouard Philippe, who is seen as one of the few candidates capable of defeating far-right front runner Marine Le Pen in 2027 elections.
“We’re here to firmly oppose what we see as an attempt by Gerald Darmanin to make the justice system more punitive,” said Paris lawyer Romain Ruiz, a member of the “Colere noire” (Black anger) collective, which is highly critical of the judicial system.
He accused Darmanin of “putting pressure on judges in pursuit of harsher penalties” and “publicly celebrating the imprisonment of young people”.
“We will never accept that the justice system should become an arm of repression.”
‘Perhaps unprecedented’
Manuel, a 21-year-old cook from central France with no prior criminal record, said he had come to Paris “on a whim” to celebrate his birthday with a friend.
But police who stopped him on Oct 17 close to the starting point of a demonstration found several glass bottles, some rags, and a lighter – what the prosecutor described as “the perfect kit” for a Molotov cocktail. He was sentenced to two months in prison and another six suspended.
Souleymane, a 19-year-old from Ivory Coast without valid residency in France, was arrested in northern Paris while allegedly trying to steal a scooter after storming a corner shop. Convicted three times previously, he was sentenced to eight months in prison and taken into custody.
Julien M, 27, a video artist from south-east France, is accused of hurling a traffic cone which just missed a policeman. He vowed that the protest would be his last and the court set him free under judicial control until a trial at the end of November.
In comments on Oct 20 in the northern city of Lille, also badly hit by rioting, Darmanin said 150 people had already been sent to prison, a colossal figure in a country where short sentences are often served outside of prison with electronic tags.
“People with no previous criminal record are being sent to prison. This is extremely unusual, perhaps even unprecedented, for offences involving damage to property,” he added. AFP

The Defense Innovation Unit, which runs the program with the Test Resource Management Center, said orders are now in the works following Gauntlet II, a month-long flyoff held in August 2026 at Fort Carson, Colorado. Perennial Autonomy took the top spot in the Deep Strike mission area with 80.1 points, while Neros led the Close Quarters Battle category with 88.1 points, according to the program’s published leaderboard.
“Congratulations to all the winners. Now, it’s time to deliver,” the Defense Innovation Unit wrote in announcing the results.
The orders are split evenly between the two mission areas, with 30,000 drones in each, and scale with each company’s ranking. In Deep Strike, Hyperscale placed second and is in line for 7,000 drones, followed by Neros with 6,000, Skycutter with 5,000 and Swarm Defense Technologies with 4,000. In Close Quarters Battle, ORQA US placed second with 7,000, followed by XTEND with 6,000, Vector with 5,000 and ModalAI with 4,000. Neros is the only company to place in both categories, bringing its combined allocation to 14,000 drones, and final quantities will be set when contracts are awarded.
Gauntlet II tested the drones on a find-fix-finish mission, meaning locating a target, confirming it and striking it. Deep Strike lanes required drones to hit targets from 15 km (9.3 miles) away, while Close Quarters Battle lanes tested performance in confined spaces such as buildings, with part of the testing repeated at night. Additional lanes evaluated controlled strikes and electronic warfare performance, with the drones flown against counter-drone systems designed to jam or defeat them.
Companies were scored on more than flight results. The final rankings combined Gauntlet II performance with evaluations from military operators who flew the systems and an assessment of each company’s ability to produce drones at scale and secure its supply chain.
The second round raised the bar considerably on range. Gauntlet I, held at Fort Benning, Georgia, in February and March 2026, sent 25 companies through testing that included strikes at about 10 km (6.2 miles), and the Defense Innovation Unit said only 24% of drones in that round reached 10 km. That first round produced orders for about 30,000 one-way attack drones worth roughly $150 million, with London-based Skycutter topping the leaderboard and Neros in second place.
The program grew out of Secretary of War Pete Hegseth’s July 2025 memo on military drone dominance, which called for every U.S. Army squad to be armed with small one-way attack drones by the end of fiscal 2026. The Department of War plans to spend about $1.1 billion across four phases of the program, which is designed to build a U.S.-based industrial base for low-cost expendable drones. Officials said in testimony earlier this year that Phase II would exclude systems using motors or batteries from so-called covered countries, a requirement aimed at Chinese components.
Several of the Gauntlet II winners have already shared details of their orders. Vector said it received orders for up to 5,000 drone systems along with its high-voltage electronic safe and arm device, which lets operators arm drones with different munitions, and XTEND said it delivered 120 STRIKER systems for testing, as The Defence Blog reported when the Close Quarters Battle scores were released.
Officials plan to follow Gauntlet II with Gauntlet 2.5, focused on bomber drones that drop munitions, and Gauntlet 3 is scheduled to begin about six months after Gauntlet II.

ChatGPT adds PIN and Face ID chat locks
According to the company’s official guidance, locked conversations disappear from regular chat history, pinned chats and standard conversation searches.
“This can help keep sensitive conversations out of view when you share your screen or use a shared device,” OpenAI said.
Users can access protected conversations through Projects > Locked chats by entering a four-digit account PIN. Supported mobile devices also offer Face ID, Touch ID or device unlock.
To protect an existing conversation, users select “Lock chat” from its options menu and create or enter their PIN.
The feature is rolling out across Free, Go, Plus, Pro, Business, Enterprise and Edu plans, although some conversation types are ineligible.
Locking a conversation does not add end-to-end encryption or change data retention and model-training settings.
OpenAI also cautions that resetting a forgotten PIN permanently deletes locked conversations and content protected solely by that PIN. Changing a known PIN preserves them.

Oct 22 - Greece and Egypt are discussing extending their Exclusive Economic Zone eastwards towards Cyprus after eastern Libya's parliament ratified a disputed maritime agreement with Turkey earlier this week, Greece's foreign minister said.
Greece, Egypt and Cyprus have long opposed the Turkey-Libya maritime accord, arguing that it infringes on their own maritime claims in the eastern Mediterranean.

Hundreds of Ethiopians flee into Kenya after border town fighting
ISIOLO, Kenya, Oct 22 - Hundreds of Ethiopians have fled into Kenya following fighting in the border town of Moyale, Kenya Red Cross and local government officials said on Thursday.
Fighting broke out on Wednesday and gunfire could still be heard a day after in parts of the town on the Ethiopian side of the border, residents said. The settlement straddles the frontier and also extends into Kenyan territory.
It was not immediately clear what had started the fighting in parts of the town in the south of Ethiopia's Oromiya region. Officials there were not immediately reachable for comment.
"We have hundreds of people from Ethiopia, mainly children and women," the commissioner from Kenya's Marsabit county, Stanley Kamande, told Reuters.

"No camp is ready to host those displaced but we shall most definitely work on it," Red Cross official Ibrae John said.
The fighting broke out hundreds of miles away, on the other side of Ethiopia, from a conflict in the northern Tigray region between government forces and a rebel alliance led by the Tigray People's Liberation Front. REUTERS

Hendel: Reservists/Economic Party may not the biggest, but it will be most important - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:35:06 UTC
00:35:06 KST

The Reservists or the New Economic Party will be the most important party in the election even if it is not the largest, its leader Yoaz Hendel told The Jerusalem Post on Thursday.
“We may not be the biggest party, but we will be the most important, because we are in nobody’s pocket,” Hendel said.
The party, he explained, will only join a coalition of Zionist parties, and isn’t ruling any of them out based on whether they are or are not current Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
“If a government comprising Gadi Eisenkot, Netanyahu, and [Naftali] Bennett were formed tomorrow morning, I would be part of it,” he added. “I’m not in the ‘anyone but Bibi’ camp.”
Hendel distinguished between his opposition to Netanyahu’s leadership and his willingness to join a government that includes him. His coalition decisions, he argued, would depend on its partners and policies rather than the prime minister’s presence alone.
“I make no secret of wanting to persuade everyone not to vote for Bibi. I make no secret of believing he bears responsibility for October 7,” he said. “But Netanyahu is not the central issue in my outlook.”
Reservists-Economic chair says his party will decide coalition for 2026 election
His refusal to sit with the haredi (Ultra-Orthodox) parties would also exclude a partnership with Likud if Netanyahu insisted on bringing them into the coalition.
“I won’t sit with the haredi parties. If Likud can’t part ways with them, I won’t sit with Likud,” Hendel said.
Hendel presented his party’s position outside the two rival blocs as the source of its potential influence, arguing that neither camp could form a government without it.
“Without the Reservists/Economic Party, there is a zero percent chance that either bloc will form a government. Zero, not even one percent,” he said.
That prediction underpins his argument for supporting a smaller party: Rather than strengthening an existing bloc, he wants voters to give his party the leverage to demand a different coalition.
“Every vote for our party influences Israel’s future. Every vote for the blocs keeps us stuck,” he said.
Hendel described a constituency spanning voters on the right who support settlement but oppose draft evasion, and voters in the center and on the left who reject cooperation with Arab parties that have not recognized Hamas as a terrorist organization.
“We want to hold the deciding vote,” he said.
Asked whether pressure on parties hovering around the electoral threshold could persuade him to withdraw, Hendel rejected the premise that other political leaders should determine how his supporters vote.
“That’s a quarter of a million Israelis who have the right to choose what they want to do,” he said. “Nobody can tell them what they should do.”
He criticized both Winter’s alignment with Netanyahu and the haredi parties and what he characterized as Eisenkot, Bennett, and Avigdor Liberman’s membership in an opposing bloc dependent on Arab parties.
“The moment you say you will only go with Netanyahu and the haredi parties, you are in the ‘only Bibi’ bloc. That means you won’t address conscription,” he said of Winter.
“There is no chance of recruiting soldiers when you’re with Goldknopf and Goldknopf is your partner.”
Hendel said he had repeatedly urged Winter to break that partnership, describing his own party as Winter’s “natural political home.”
Asked what would make parties such as Ra’am or Shas acceptable partners, Hendel said his objection was not to Arab or haredi citizens.
“I have nothing against haredim or Arabs,” he said. “I hope that one day there will be a haredi party of people who enlist and serve, and that one day there will be an Arab party of people who serve and see themselves as part of Israel.”
He linked that position to demands for core curriculum studies, the teaching of Zionism, and Israeli flags in publicly funded classrooms. Families rejecting that framework should fund their children’s education themselves, he argued.
“Every Israeli citizen will do something for the country, and anyone who doesn’t will receive nothing.”
Hendel backs Zelekha on economic demands
Hendel’s coalition conditions also extend to the economic agenda of his political partner, Yaron Zelekha of the New Economic Party.
“Both issues weigh heavily on reservists,” he said. “It isn’t only conscription. The cost of living hurts them badly, too.”
He also cautioned that easing the burden on existing reservists would take time. Training an infantry soldier takes approximately eight months, he said, while reducing annual reserve service to 30 days under current conditions remained a “pipe dream.”
Asked what he would change about his earlier conduct in politics, Hendel acknowledged making “plenty of mistakes,” pointing to the cycle of elections and dissolving Knessets, arguing that remaining in politics could not be an end in itself.
“Politics brought us to October 7, and politics has to get us out of it,” he said.
Hendel said his experience commanding reservists taught him that leadership depends on persuasion rather than simply issuing orders - an approach he said also shaped his partnership with Zelekha.
“Ultimately, what matters isn’t your rank but your level of commitment,” he said. “The same applies to politics.”

US House committee investigation exposes antisemitism, political indoctrination in public schools
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:34:26 UTC
00:34:26 KST

A congressional investigation released on Wednesday has detailed widespread antisemitism and political activism within American K-12 public schools and major teachers' unions following the October 7, 2023 attacks against Israel.
The majority staff report, called “Antisemitism in K-12 Schools” and published by the House Committee on Education and the Workforce, stated that antisemitic incidents in US schools increased by 135 percent in 2023, prompting congressional inquiries into several major school districts and labor organizations.
Committee Chairman Tim Walberg said, “Parents send their children to school to learn reading, writing, and math—not to be taught to hate Israel or embrace radical political causes. Yet that’s exactly the kind of material our investigation uncovered. Jewish students deserve to feel safe in their classrooms, and parents deserve to know what their children are being taught. Schools that receive taxpayer dollars must be held accountable when they fail to protect students from antisemitism.”
Investigations opened into California, Pennsylvania, Virginia schools
Under Chairman Walberg’s leadership, the committee opened investigations into Berkeley Unified School District (BUSD) in California, the School District of Philadelphia (SDP) in Pennsylvania, and Fairfax County Public Schools in Virginia.
The committee selected school districts of varying size and geographic location after receiving numerous reports of antisemitic incidents. The committee noted that its inquiry into Fairfax County remains ongoing.
As part of the wider inquiry, the committee conducted a transcribed interview with Philadelphia Superintendent Dr. Tony Watlington on September 18, 2026, and also investigated the nation’s largest teachers union, the National Education Association (NEA), over allegations of antisemitism.
The committee released documents obtained through its investigations into Berkeley, Philadelphia, and the NEA while continuing its inquiry into Fairfax County.
Focusing on the SDP, the report examined the ninth-largest school district in the US, which comprises 330 schools. The district entered into a federal civil rights resolution agreement with the US Department of Education in December 2024 to address the handling of antisemitic harassment following a sharp rise in incidents after October 7, 2023. According to the congressional report, the investigation found that district curricula promoted ideology justifying violent resistance and legitimized radical groups that incite antisemitism.
Curriculum writers portrayed all resistance as righteous
For example, investigators detailed that a world history curriculum unit covering resistance movements directed students to honor a movement of their choice, listing the Gaza Great March of Return as an option, and opened by teaching that the fight to decolonize in India was not always peaceful.
The report noted that teachers were told to examine the works of Frantz Fanon, whose writings argue that decolonization is inherently violent and who is frequently cited by anti-Israel activists to justify the October 7 attacks.
The congressional report stated that the Philadelphia district’s materials also relied on resources from the Racial Justice Organizing Committee, noting that leaders of the group declared that all resistance is righteous and that there are no two sides to ‘apartheid, occupation, and genocide’.
In lessons using these materials, the report found that Philadelphia students were asked to color-code aspects of their identities as dominant or oppressed. These lessons categorized males, white people, and Christians as dominant, and black people, LGBTQ people, immigrants, and non-Christians as oppressed.
Furthermore, investigators outlined that district curricula introduce far-left activism and terms like “intersectionality,” “ally,” and “social justice” as early as the third grade. The report added that curricula recommended children’s books introducing pronouns such as “ey/em” and “ze/zir”.
According to the report, investigators established that district employees responsible for writing curricula fomented antisemitism online and among colleagues. This included the director of social studies curriculum, Ismael Jimenez, who the report noted had repeatedly rationalized violence against Jews.
The report stated that other curriculum writers maintained that all resistance is righteous. Additionally, investigators documented that the district has repeatedly partnered with the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) Philadelphia. The report highlighted that a representative previously suggested that curricular materials be reviewed for bias by qualified Muslim educators, and that Superintendent Watlington’s transition team included the group’s former executive director.
During his September 2026 interview with the committee, Superintendent Watlington stated that the social studies curriculum complied with district policies and did not indoctrinate students. He added that the district would standardize its curriculum by using national experts and that the social studies curriculum director was undergoing termination proceedings.
In Berkeley Unified School District, consisting of 20 schools in California, investigators examined extensive antisemitism complaints lodged by parents and students since October 7, 2023. These complaints occurred alongside the district’s adoption of liberated ethnic studies.
The report found that BUSD collaborated with the Liberated Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum Consortium, paying over $111,000 for curriculum writing and consulting since August 2023. According to the congressional findings, this collaboration resulted in lessons littered with antisemitic resources and activist ideology.
Berkeley’s ninth-grade Arab American Studies unit featured an ancestor acknowledgment of Helen Thomas. The report stated that the unit defended her remarks, which told Jewish people to leave the Middle East and go home to Poland and Germany, by framing the controversial statements as constructive activism, asserting that she was engaged in what is termed “good trouble” and that her comments had been taken out of context.
The congressional report noted that BUSD’s ethnic studies units cover topics like the seven pillars of colonization, including killing cultures and exploiting land, and feature specific lessons arguing that Asian people have been weaponized as pawns to serve a white supremacist agenda.
Leadership rationalized Hamas attacks
Berkeley elementary and high school teachers also collaborated on teaching guides that featured the alphabet book P is for Palestine. The book includes selections such as ‘I is for Intifada’. The guides recommended organizations such as the Middle East Children’s Alliance (MECA) and the Arab Resource and Organizing Center (AROC).
Berkeley high school teachers approved an Israel and Palestine lesson set that the report stated whitewashed terrorism and portrayed the phrase "from the river to the sea" as a call for freedom and peace. The committee noted that teachers warned colleagues that the curriculum could not be shared directly with families.
Furthermore, investigators documented that district staff and students raised money through bake sales and bracelet sales for MECA. The report highlighted that the Network Contagion Research Institute (NCRI) identified this organization as having fiscal and personnel ties to the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine (PFLP), a US-designated foreign terrorist organization.
At the NEA, representing more than three million educators and administrators, investigators found that antisemitism surged following October 7, 2023. This surge culminated in a 2025 delegate vote to ban Anti-Defamation League (ADL) materials.
According to internal NEA documents cited in the report, the union was already not working with the ADL because of the watchdog’s efforts to combat contemporary antisemitism. Internal memos criticized the ADL for denigrating the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement.
The report also detailed that the NEA’s Center for Racial and Social Justice (CRSJ) advised against implementing a resolution by the union’s Jewish Affairs Caucus (JAC) to combat antisemitism because it utilized the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA) definition.
Union staff wrote in a briefing document that the definition had been used by racist and nationalist actors as cover. Additionally, internal documents showed union leaders were advised to avoid action language regarding historical events in the Middle East because history is hotly contested.
Leadership was also explicitly advised that keffiyehs should be allowed at association gatherings as a sign of support for Palestine. The report confirmed that the union pledged thousands of dollars to Rethinking Schools and the Zinn Education Project.
According to the committee, these organizations published statements after October 7 rationalizing Hamas terrorist attacks by pointing to US and Israeli colonialism.
The committee concluded stating that political activism has increasingly displaced educational neutrality across American public education. This has created an environment where antisemitism is minimized, excused, and permitted to flourish.
The committee stated that “public schools should educate students, not enlist them in political causes.” The report added that “parents should be able to trust that schools will educate their children without subjecting them to radical ideology.”
The report stressed that “Jewish students are entitled to the same protection from discrimination and harassment as every other student, regardless of whether hostility toward them is expressed in overt antisemitic terms or cloaked in political rhetoric.”
The committee vowed that it “will continue to use its oversight authority to examine these issues, consider appropriate legislation, and hold federally funded institutions accountable for compliance with federal civil rights law.”

Lockheed lines up deal for 850 U.S. F-35s over 10 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:32:33 UTC
00:32:33 KST

- The U.S. Department of War and Lockheed Martin agreed on a framework for 850 U.S. F-35s over 10 years, covering Lots 21 through 30.
- The deal keeps production at 156 aircraft a year and moves to a formal contract once Congress grants multiyear authority and funding.
The U.S. Department of War and Lockheed Martin have agreed on a framework for a 10-year F-35 production and sustainment deal that covers 850 aircraft for the United States, along with spare parts, modification kits and international orders across production Lots 21 through 30.
The framework keeps F-35 production at 156 aircraft a year and folds three things that have traditionally been bought separately into one long-term plan: new jets with their initial spares, a decade of modification kits, and fleet sustainment. The next step runs through Congress: once multiyear authority and the associated funding are granted, the F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will finalize contract terms, pricing and delivery schedules in a formal contract award.
“This multiyear framework strengthens the way we can plan and invest in the F-35 enterprise,” said Lockheed Martin Chairman, President and CEO Jim Taiclet. “With the greater certainty that comes from the U.S. government’s transformative approach to F-35 production and sustainment, we can make the upfront investments needed to expand capacity, improve efficiency, and build a more resilient supply chain. That’s good for the taxpayer, good for our suppliers and, most importantly, good for the United States and its allies.”
The 850 U.S. aircraft over 10 years work out to an average of 85 jets a year for the U.S. Air Force, U.S. Navy and U.S. Marine Corps, with the remainder of the 156-a-year production rate going to international partners and foreign customers. The United States plans to buy a total of 2,456 F-35s across its three services.
Until now, the F-35 has been bought in lot-by-lot contracts that often took years to negotiate. The most recent deal, covering Lots 18 and 19, was finalized on Sept. 29, 2025, after a handshake agreement the previous December, and covers 296 aircraft worth about $24.3 billion. Long-lead funding for parts for Lot 20 and Lot 21 aircraft has already been awarded, and Lot 21 is now the first lot included in the new framework.
A multiyear arrangement lets Lockheed Martin and its suppliers commit to larger, longer orders for raw materials and parts. The company says that approach will produce volume discounts, lower unit prices and savings for taxpayers estimated in the billions of dollars over the life of the program, while giving the government more predictable costs.
Readiness is a central part of the plan. The framework links aircraft production with purchases of spare and modification parts and adds integrated analytics that tie budget decisions to readiness results and give real-time visibility into parts inventories. Lockheed Martin says replacing the annual contracting cycle with long-term supplier contracts will cut turnaround times for parts and repairs and raise mission capable rates, the share of the fleet ready to fly its assigned missions.
“Our new multiyear framework gives suppliers stability to plan for the future and invest with confidence, improving readiness across the F-35 fleet,” said OJ Sanchez, president of Lockheed Martin Aeronautics.
The company estimates the program will support 317,000 U.S. jobs and generate about $79 billion in annual economic activity over the next decade. International customers would share in the benefits through economies of scale across the global fleet and its shared sustainment network.
More than 1,375 F-35s are now in service around the world, operating from 42 bases, including in 13 countries that fly the jet from home soil, and the fleet has passed 1 million flight hours. Lockheed Martin delivered a record 191 F-35s in 2025.
The F-35 Joint Program Office and Lockheed Martin will move to a formal contract award for Lots 21 through 30 once Congress grants multiyear authority and the associated appropriations, which the companies expect in the coming months.

Save $150 on the Apple Mac Mini M4, but There’s a Catch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:30:31 UTC
00:30:31 KST

Apple’s Mac Mini M4 has become a popular mini-yet-mighty desktop computer for running local agentic AI 24/7—so much so that it’s been out of stock for months. But with the introduction of the new Mac Mini M6, the older M4 is no longer as scarce (there was no M5 Mac Mini), and the base model (256-GB hard drive, 16-GB unified memory) is on sale for $649—$150 off MSRP and $250 cheaper than the M6.
It’s a good deal for a computer that is plenty powerful for most people, and some M4 Mac Mini configurations can even handle AI tasks. But—and it’s a big but—shoppers should be aware that the M4’s original base price was $599 when it launched in 2024. However, with Apple raising prices on hardware across the board this year, driven by chip and memory shortages, the M4 ended up costing $799. In comparison, the new M6 starts at $899.
Depending on how you look at it, it’s either a discount or a hard pill to swallow, knowing that it used to be much cheaper. If you’ve been eyeing a new Mac Mini and don’t need the better performance of the M6, you’re unlikely to get a lower price than this M4.
Older but Still Capable
The M4 Mac Mini may no longer be Apple’s most powerful tiny computer—that title now belongs to the M6 and M5 Pro models—but the M4 is still an incredibly strong and efficient processor. When it was discovered that it could easily run agentic AI locally, people gobbled up the Mac Mini as the affordable computing option.
Of course, for intensive tasks like AI or video editing, you really need more than 16 GB of memory; those who bought it for AI purposes loaded it up with 32 GB of RAM. For most users, however, this base-specs machine is more than capable. While the M6 system on a chip is extra powerful due to having more CPU and GPU cores, Neural Accelerators, and higher memory bandwidth, the M4 Mac Mini isn’t lagging far behind. For things like web browsing and general productivity, you won’t see much of a difference in performance.
If you need the performance, we recommend the newer M6. But for most people, the M4 Mac Mini is more than sufficient for everyday computing, and you're unlikely to find a better deal than this one.

The situation across the occupied West Bank has deteriorated beyond control as escalating attacks seek to drive Palestinian communities from their land, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned on Thursday, Anadolu reports.
“In the occupied West Bank, Palestinians continue to suffer daily attacks by Israeli settlers. The clear goal is to drive communities off their land,” Guterres told reporters.
He said the situation in the occupied territories is “simply out of control” as occupiers also target journalists and diplomats.
On Gaza, the UN chief pointed out that essential humanitarian assistance remains “severely restricted” ahead of winter, compounding obstacles facing the Security Council-backed roadmap to resolve the conflict.
Guterres stressed that the World Food Program “urgently” requires $450 million to feed populations across Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months, noting that the sum equals approximately 90 minutes of global military expenditures. He appealed to international donors to step up while urging an end to the occupation to achieve a viable two-state solution.
‘El Nino of war’ and economic strain
Guterres compared modern conflicts to the climate phenomenon El Nino, and cautioned that cascading hostilities are reverberating through international energy markets, shipping corridors, and financial systems.
READ: Israel uses occupier violence to ‘ethnically cleanse’ Palestinians from West Bank: Amnesty
He linked widespread street protests over inflation, food, and fuel directly to the fallout of expanding global wars. “War does not create all these inequalities, but it feeds and exploits them,” Guterres said, emphasizing that while street violence is unacceptable, authorities cannot allow disorder to obscure the legitimate cost-of-living grievances of peaceful protesters.
Regional diplomacy, Sudan, and Yemen
Turning to Yemen, Guterres described continued Houthi attacks against civilian targets in Saudi Arabia as “totally unacceptable,” urging restraint amid mounting displacement in Yemen.
Guterres said he will travel to Egypt to advance regional de-escalation, underscoring Egypt’s essential diplomatic role as a mediator in the war between the US and Iran, alongside its neighboring stakes in the wars in Sudan and Libya.
He also demanded that neighboring and distant nations halt weapons supplies to factions in Sudan that are “killing civilians in an absolutely devastating way.”
Disregard for international law
Guterres dismissed concerns about institutional damage to the UN from violations of international law, declaring that the real crisis is the suffering of ordinary civilians whose survival is threatened by war-induced inflation and violence.
“The problem is not for the United Nations. The problem is for the people that is suffering dramatically everywhere,” he said.

The provision in the 2027 social security financing bill would have reduced employer contribution relief for companies paying profit-sharing or employee share ownership bonuses.

Rejection of the entire revenue section would prevent lawmakers from proceeding to examine the bill’s spending provisions, according to the report.

Turkish army gets more Tayfun ballistic missiles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:24:21 UTC
00:24:21 KST

- Türkiye delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to its Land Forces Command, following earlier deliveries in May and June 2026.
- The Tayfun Block 2 has a range of more than 500 km and a reported accuracy of under 10 meters.
Türkiye’s Ministry of National Defence has delivered a new batch of Roketsan Tayfun Block 2 ballistic missiles to the Turkish Land Forces Command, adding to a missile force that began entering service only five months ago.
The delivery was reported on Oct. 22, 2026, and in line with previous handovers, the ministry kept the number of missiles classified. The new batch is at least the third known delivery this year: the ministry announced on May 20, 2026, that Tayfun Block 2 missiles had been accepted into the Land Forces inventory for the first time, and a second batch followed on June 25.
Tayfun, Turkish for “typhoon,” is the longest-range ballistic missile Türkiye has developed on its own. Roketsan, the state-owned missile maker, describes the Block 2 as having a range of more than 500 km (310 miles) and designed to strike high-value targets deep behind enemy lines, including air defense systems, command and control centers, aircraft hangars and other critical military facilities.
The missile is about 6.5 meters (21.3 feet) long and 610 mm (24 inches) in diameter, with a launch weight of 2,300 kg (5,070 pounds). It is fired from a wheeled transporter-erector-launcher, a truck that carries, raises and launches the missile and holds two rounds, which allows crews to move quickly between firing positions.
Roketsan says the Tayfun Block 2 lands within 10 meters (33 feet) of its target, measured as circular error probable, the radius within which half of the missiles fired are expected to land. It uses coordinate-based guidance, meaning it flies to a fixed point programmed before launch, and the company says it is highly resistant to GPS jamming and can operate day or night in poor weather. The missile carries a pre-formed fragmentation warhead, which breaks into a pattern of fragments on detonation.
Türkiye first test-fired Tayfun in October 2022 from Rize-Artvin Airport on the Black Sea coast, when the missile flew 561 km (349 miles) in 456 seconds before striking a target area off Sinop. That distance was roughly twice the 280 km (174-mile) range of Roketsan’s earlier Bora missile, previously the longest-range ballistic missile in Turkish service. Further test firings followed in May 2023 and in later years as the program moved toward serial production.
Roketsan has continued to expand the family alongside the Block 2 deliveries. In July 2025, the company unveiled the much larger Tayfun Block 4 at the IDEF defense fair in Istanbul, a missile about 10 meters (33 feet) long and weighing roughly 7,200 kg (15,900 pounds), which Roketsan presents as a hypersonic ballistic missile system. In July 2026, Roketsan released footage of a Tayfun Block 3 striking an unmanned boat at sea, which the company said was the first time a Tayfun had been used against a naval target and the first use of a seeker on the missile.
With three batches delivered since May, the Tayfun Block 2 is now steadily building up inside the Turkish Land Forces, while the Block 3 and Block 4 versions continue through development and testing at Roketsan.

Livestock virus claims first human victim in France
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:22:57 UTC
00:22:57 KST

Livestock virus claims first human victim in France
The world’s first documented human infection with the Shamonda virus has been reported in France, where a hospitalized patient later died, according to the health authorities.
The insect-borne disease, which has circulated among livestock for decades, was previously believed to be incapable of infecting humans.
In a joint statement on Thursday, the French Health and Agriculture Ministries confirmed that the patient, who had a severely weakened immune system, died in early October after being hospitalized in Lyon.
“Until now, the Shamonda virus was considered non-transmissible to humans,” the ministries said, according to AFP. They described the infection as the first confirmed detection of the pathogen in a person.
The patient developed severe neurological complications that the authorities believe were linked to the infection. However, investigators have still not established conclusively whether the virus was responsible for the death.
Officials suspect that the patient contracted the virus through the bite of an infected midge in eastern France, where the pathogen has recently been detected in cattle. The circumstances of the infection remain under investigation.
Despite the unprecedented case, the French authorities said there is currently no indication of a wider threat to public health. They stressed that the patient was severely immunocompromised and that no other human infections have been identified.
The Shamonda virus belongs to the orthobunyavirus group and was first identified in Nigeria in the 1960s. It is transmitted by tiny biting insects known as Culicoides midges and has been detected in livestock in Africa and Asia.
The virus has recently emerged among European cattle, triggering concern among the veterinary authorities. In France, infections have been reported across dozens of departments, with affected animals suffering fever, diarrhea, weakness, and falling milk production, according to the French agricultural authorities.
Other viruses that have crossed from animals to humans include HIV, Ebola, and bird flu. The Covid-19 pandemic was caused by a virus widely believed to have originated in bats.
The European Center for Disease Prevention and Control has confirmed the unprecedented human case and is working with the French authorities to assess its implications.
Health officials are continuing epidemiological and laboratory investigations to determine how the patient became infected and whether other cases may have gone undetected.

Türkiye aims to strengthen energy, climate diplomacy through next month's COP31 UN Climage Change Conference
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
15:22:52 UTC
00:22:52 KST

Gulsen Cagatay and Halis Sunnetci
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
As Türkiye prepares to host next month's 31st UN Climate Change Conference (COP31 or COP31 Türkiye), it aims to strengthen its role in energy and climate diplomacy, help turn global climate targets into concrete action and harness its renewable energy potential through international partnerships.
COP31, scheduled for Nov. 9-20 in Antalya, will provide an opportunity to highlight Türkiye's diplomatic capabilities, position in the energy transition and climate policies on the international stage.
Türkiye will hold the COP31 Presidency and lead the Action Agenda, while Australia will serve as President of Negotiations.
Türkiye's approach to the summit focuses on turning existing climate commitments into achievable and measurable outcomes through dialogue, consensus and action.
Priority areas include electrification, the clean energy transition, green industrialization, the circular economy, climate-resilient cities and climate finance.
The COP31 Presidency has announced initiatives aimed at increasing electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035, reducing energy intensity in buildings by at least 25% and cutting the rate of growth in global waste generation by half.
Turning climate commitments into bankable and investment-ready projects is also a central part of the agenda.
 
Renewable energy potential supports cooperation
Türkiye's solar and wind energy potential provides a foundation for partnerships that could emerge from COP31.
Expanding renewable energy capacity, strengthening electricity grids and accelerating electrification are among the country's energy transition priorities.
Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar has announced that Türkiye aims to increase its installed renewable energy capacity to 120 gigawatts by 2035, with work underway on more ambitious targets for 2040.
COP31 is therefore expected to offer opportunities to advance Türkiye's clean energy investments through international financing, technology transfer and partnerships.
 
Geographic location enables regional energy cooperation
Situated at the crossroads of Europe, the Middle East and Asia, Türkiye is strategically positioned to connect energy sources with consumer markets, creating opportunities for cooperation in climate diplomacy.
Its location along international trade and energy routes allows the country to develop regional partnerships in electricity interconnections, renewable energy investment, energy efficiency and low-carbon industry.
Making better use of this potential to meet climate targets will require increasing the share of renewables in the energy system, upgrading electricity grids and accelerating the transformation of energy infrastructure.
 
International partnerships, green industry gain prominence
Global Energy Association President Murat Dilek told Anadolu that expanding Türkiye's manufacturing capacity for renewable energy equipment, particularly wind turbines and solar panels, offers significant opportunities for green industrialization and for strengthening the country's role in energy and climate diplomacy.
Increasing domestic manufacturing capacity would support renewable energy investment, while Türkiye's strategic position connecting Europe, the Middle East and Asia could help the country play a greater role in regional supply chains, Dilek said.
He added that these developments would improve Türkiye's competitiveness in the global clean energy market.
"Türkiye's diplomatic success in this process will be measured not only by the establishment of dialogue between countries, but also by the transformation of the targets set out in Antalya into concrete partnerships and viable projects," Dilek said.
"To turn this potential into lasting gains, Türkiye needs to implement its national climate targets, accelerate clean energy investments and facilitate access to climate finance," he said, adding: "By boosting domestic manufacturing and technological capabilities, reducing environmental impacts and strengthening international partnerships, Türkiye can demonstrate its potential not only as a diplomatic actor in the COP31 process, but also as a manufacturing and technology hub contributing to the global green transition."
