Situation in occupied West Bank 'simply out of control,' UN chief says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-22
13:58:49 UTC
22:58:49 KST

Yasin Gungor
22 October 2026•Update: 22 October 2026
The situation across the occupied West Bank has deteriorated beyond control as escalating attacks seek to drive Palestinian communities from their land, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres warned on Thursday.
"In the occupied West Bank, Palestinians continue to suffer daily attacks by Israeli settlers. The clear goal is to drive communities off their land," Guterres told reporters.
He said the situation in the occupied territories is "simply out of control" as occupiers also target journalists and diplomats.
On Gaza, the UN chief pointed out that essential humanitarian assistance remains "severely restricted" ahead of winter, compounding obstacles facing the Security Council-backed roadmap to resolve the conflict.
Guterres stressed that the World Food Program "urgently" requires $450 million to feed populations across Gaza and the West Bank over the next six months, noting that the sum equals approximately 90 minutes of global military expenditures. He appealed to international donors to step up while urging an end to the occupation to achieve a viable two-state solution.
'El Nino of war' and economic strain
Guterres compared modern conflicts to the climate phenomenon El Nino, and cautioned that cascading hostilities are reverberating through international energy markets, shipping corridors, and financial systems.
He linked widespread street protests over inflation, food, and fuel directly to the fallout of expanding global wars. "War does not create all these inequalities, but it feeds and exploits them," Guterres said, emphasizing that while street violence is unacceptable, authorities cannot allow disorder to obscure the legitimate cost-of-living grievances of peaceful protesters.
Regional diplomacy, Sudan, and Yemen
Turning to Yemen, Guterres described continued Houthi attacks against civilian targets in Saudi Arabia as "totally unacceptable," urging restraint amid mounting displacement in Yemen.
Guterres said he will travel to Egypt to advance regional de-escalation, underscoring Egypt's essential diplomatic role as a mediator in the war between the US and Iran, alongside its neighboring stakes in the wars in Sudan and Libya.
He also demanded that neighboring and distant nations halt weapons supplies to factions in Sudan that are "killing civilians in an absolutely devastating way."
Separetely, Guterres's spokesman Stephane Dujarric told reporters that he is visiting at the invitation of Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and is expected to arrive in Cairo early Saturday.
Over the weekend and on Monday, Guterres will meet senior Egyptian officials, including Sisi and Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty, as well as Arab League Secretary-General Nabil Fahmy, Dujarric said.
“Egypt has been actively engaged in these efforts, working with regional and international partners,” he said, adding that the talks will also cover the situation in Sudan and Gaza.
Disregard for international law
Guterres dismissed concerns about institutional damage to the UN from violations of international law, declaring that the real crisis is the suffering of ordinary civilians whose survival is threatened by war-induced inflation and violence.
"The problem is not for the United Nations. The problem is for the people that is suffering dramatically everywhere," he said.

Iran slams IAEA for silence towards attacks on its sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:50:39 UTC
22:50:39 KST

The statement criticized the IAEA for applying double standards and discriminatory approaches, emphasizing that the Statute is a binding legal document and must not be used as a political instrument to serve the interests of certain powerful states.
Iran also condemned the unacceptable silence of the Agency’s governing bodies regarding the military attacks by the US and the Zionist regime on its peaceful nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026. Furthermore, it highlighted the IAEA's failure to address the lack of comprehensive safeguards on the Zionist regime’s nuclear activities.
The Islamic Republic also called for the full, balanced, and non-discriminatory implementation of the IAEA Statute for all member states, particularly regarding technical cooperation and access to peaceful nuclear energy.
The full text of statement by the Iranian permanent mission in Vienna is as follows:
Permanent Mission of the Islamic Republic of Iran  
  
to the United Nations and other International Organizations in Vienna 
 
PRESS RELEASE  
   
On the Anniversary of the Approval of the IAEA Statute   
   
23 October 2026  
   
Seventy years after the adoption of the Statute of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) 
 
on 23 October 1956, a fundamental assessment is required as to the level and extent of the 
 
adherence to the principles and objectives of the Agency’s founding document. 
This anniversary must therefore be more than an occasion for commemoration; it must serve as 
 
a moment of critical reflection, institutional accountability and a renewed commitment to the full, 
 
impartial and non-discriminatory implementation of the Statute. 
The Statute: A Binding Mandate, Not a Political Instrument
The continued relevance of the IAEA Statute lies in the objective it establishes and the principles 
 
it enshrines. It implementation over the past seven decades has produced achievements in 
 
important areas. However, the failure to implement it fully, consistently, effectively and without 
 
discrimination, under all circumstances and with respect to all Member States, has caused the 
 
Agency to drift away from its core objective and priorities, undermine the principles governing its 
 
conduct, compromise its professionalism, and tarnish its authority and credibility. 
The undeniable fact is that the Statute is the Agency’s constitution, not a document to be invoked 
 
selectively or interpreted according to the interests of powerful States or a group of States. 
Beyond Safeguards: Upholding the IAEA’s Full Statutory Mandate
Article II establishes the Agency’s fundamental objective: to accelerate and enlarge the 
 
contribution of atomic energy to peace, health and prosperity throughout the world. Article III.A.1 
 
requires the Agency to encourage and assist research, development and the practical application 
 
of atomic energy for peaceful purposes. Article III.B.3 further requires the Agency to allocate its 
 
resources efficiently to achieve the greatest possible general benefit, with due regard to the special 
 
needs of developing countries. 
While safeguards are part of the IAEA’s mandate, the Agency is not merely a “watchdog” 
 
organization, as some Member States, in contravention of the Statute, seek to portray it. Such a 
 
narrow and politically motivated characterization distorts the Agency’s mandate and shifts its 
 
priorities away from its broader statutory objective that is the promotion of peaceful nuclear 
 
applications and international scientific and technical cooperation. Verification must not eclipse 
 
peaceful nuclear cooperation, development and the legitimate rights of Member States. An Agency 
 
that concentrates on scrutiny while failing to advance its key statutory responsibilities cannot claim to be fulfilling its mandate in a balanced manner.
Sovereign Equality Cannot Coexist with Double Standards
Article IV.C expressly establishes that the Agency is based on the sovereign equality of all its 
 
members and requires them to fulfil their statutory obligations in good faith. Article III.C prohibits 
 
the Agency from making assistance subject to any political, economic, military or other conditions 
 
incompatible with the Statute. Article III.B.1 requires the Agency to conduct its activities in 
 
accordance with the purposes and principles of the United Nations, while Article III.D requires 
 
due observance of the sovereign rights of States. 
These provisions are neither optional nor subordinate to geopolitical calculations. Sovereign 
 
equality requires that every State be treated fairly and without discrimination under the legal 
 
instruments applicable to it, free from double standards, selective interpretation and politically 
 
motivated action. 
A clear example is the continuing disparity between the scrutiny applied to Iran and the absence 
 
of comprehensive safeguards covering all nuclear activities of the Israeli regime, which remains 
 
outside the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons. This disparity raises 
 
fundamental questions about the credibility and consistency of the international nuclear non-
 
proliferation norms. A credible, comprehensive and non-discriminatory approach to nuclear 
 
verification throughout the Middle East is a legitimate demand and a longstanding objective of 
 
regional countries that are parties to the NPT. Regional security cannot be built on selective 
 
scrutiny and unequal expectations. 
Peaceful Nuclear Cooperation: A Right, Not a Political Privilege
Peaceful nuclear cooperation must not be subject to political pressure. Article III.C of the Statute 
 
is clear: assistance must not be subjected to conditions incompatible with the Agency’s legal 
 
mandate. Political pressure and geopolitical rivalries must not obstruct legitimate scientific 
 
cooperation or turn access to peaceful nuclear technology into a privilege reserved for selected 
 
countries. The Agency is expected to defend the integrity of its technical cooperation mandate 
 
and ensure that its programs serve the development needs of all Member States fairly and without 
 
discrimination. 
Attacks on Nuclear Facilities and Unacceptable Institutional Silence
Attacks on safeguarded nuclear facilities demand strong and unequivocal condemnation. The 
 
military attacks by the U.S. and the Israeli regime against Iranian nuclear facilities in 2025 and 2026 constituted serious and material breaches of peremptory norm of international law on the 
 
prohibition of aggression.  They presented a grave challenge to nuclear safety, nuclear security, 
 
peaceful uses of nuclear energy, the credibility of the IAEA and its safeguards system.  
The Agency’s General Conference and Board of governors has repeatedly adopted resolutions 
 
expressly stating that armed attacks on, or threats against, nuclear facilities devoted to peaceful 
 
purposes violate the principles of the UN Charter, international law and the Agency’s Statute. 
 
Nevertheless, the Agency’s governing bodies and Secretariat failed to issue even a simple statement to condemn clear acts of aggression against Iran’s nuclear facilities – unprecedented in the Agency’s history. This failure represents a serious institutional shortcoming and raises troubling questions about the consistent application of the principles the Agency is mandated to uphold. 
The Agency cannot credibly defend the integrity of safeguards while treating attacks against 
 
facilities subject to those safeguards as a secondary concern. The Agency must therefore 
 
unequivocally reaffirm that attacks against peaceful nuclear installations are unlawful and 
 
unacceptable and must not be tolerated under any pretext.
Safeguarding the IAEA’s Independence, Integrity and Confidentiality Principle
Independence, confidentiality and professional integrity must be protected. Article VII.F of the 
 
Statute prohibits the Director General and Agency staff from seeking or receiving instructions 
 
from external sources. It also requires the protection of confidential information acquired in the 
 
course of their official duties and obliges Member States to respect the international character of 
 
their responsibilities and refrain from seeking to influence them improperly. 
These are concrete institutional safeguards, not ceremonial principles. Reports, assessments and 
 
decisions must be based on verifiable evidence, sound technical analysis and applicable legal 
 
obligations—not political demands, unsupported allegations or selective approaches. Any breach 
 
of confidentiality or attempt to instrumentalise safeguards information undermines cooperation, 
 
erodes trust and may compromise the safety and security of nuclear activities. The Agency must 
 
address credible concerns, protect sensitive information and ensure accountability. 
Restoring the IAEA’s Credibility: From Selective Implementation to Full Compliance
Cooperation must be matched by institutional responsibility. Iran recognises the importance of 
 
credible safeguards and professional verification and remains committed to engagement within 
 
the framework of its applicable legal obligations and its inherent and sovereign rights and interests. 
However, cooperation requires good faith, mutual respect, professional integrity and the 
 
consistent implementation of agreed legal commitments.  
On this anniversary, Iran calls upon Agency, particularly the Board of Governors and the Director 
 
General to end double standards, resist politicisation, protect confidential information, condemn 
 
attacks against peaceful nuclear facilities, and restore the full and balanced implementation of the 
 
Agency’s statutory mandate. Iran also calls for an effective and non-discriminatory technical 
 
cooperation policy that enables all Member States, particularly developing countries, to benefit 
 
from nuclear science and technology. 
The Agency’s credibility cannot rest solely on its authority to inspect. It depends equally on its 
 
adherence to the law, its impartiality, its independence and its willingness to uphold the legitimate 
 
rights of all its members. 
The Statute must be implemented as a whole, equally and in good faith—not selectively, not 
 
conditionally and not according to political convenience. The Agency owes this obligation to every 
 
Member State. On the seventieth anniversary of the Statute’s adoption, the Agency is expected to 
 
honour letter, spirit, object and purpose of the Statute through concrete action, not merely words, 
 
and to uphold its principles without political selectivity, discrimination or exception. 
MNA
Seventy years after the adoption of its Statute, the IAEA’s credibility rests on upholding its Statute 
 
in full, serving all Member States equally, and demonstrating that international law and statutory 
 
principles cannot be sacrificed to political convenience.

Melania Trump helps secure "temporary ceasefire" between Russia and Ukraine in city of Oleshky
First lady Melania Trump's office on Friday said she — not President Trump or another top official — has secured a temporary ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine for the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky for humanitarian reasons.
In an unusual announcement for a first lady's office, it said both nations agreed to temporarily halt all military action in the southern Ukrainian city "to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway." The localized ceasefire will begin Thursday, Oct. 29.
Russia and Ukraine have not commented on the first lady's announcement.
The first lady's office says she worked "directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire."
"The situation in Oleshky is dire," the first lady said in a statement. "Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water. The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible."
The first lady's office said she "initiated discussions with both nations and aligned the parties on the agreement's objectives, technical procedures, timing, processes, and terms, in her formal role as Exclusive Intermediary."
"Non-military, civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require," the first lady said. "Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine."
The first lady added that she's secured an American media organization to document both Russian and Ukrainian teams. Newsmax, a conservative outlet, said it would be going.
White House communications director Steven Cheung called the announcement "amazing news."
"This is a major, positive step towards peace," Cheung said on X. "History will remember her tireless work to help those in need."
Melania Trump has worked to reunite 34 children so far with their families, after Russia forcibly removed children.
Although he said he would bring about an end to Russia's war with Ukraine on his first day back in office, peace has remained elusive for Mr. Trump. The president has grown increasingly frustrated with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in recent days, saying Ukraine should have a new leader and dismissing concerns about Russia's continued slaughter of Ukrainians.
"Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine," Mr. Trump told reporters earlier this week. "They haven't been doing much."
U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff faced backlash for calling Russian President Vladimir Putin a "humanitarian" upon the release of American Stephen Hubbard.

Iranian men to go on trial next year over alleged plot to target UK Jewish community

Gunman in Paris suburb kills 1, wounds 4 in possible terrorist act, wanted "to cause a bloodbath," officials say
A gunman firing from his car killed one person and wounded four in the Paris suburb of Trappes on Friday, authorities said, and prosecutors investigating the case as a potential terrorist act. Officials say at least two of the victims were from immigrant backgrounds.
The man, who was arrested shortly after, was "firing at random, wanting to cause a bloodbath" as he drove through Trappes and neighbouring La Verriere, Trappes mayor Ali Rabeh told broadcaster BFMTV.
A 12-year-old girl was "seriously wounded" after being shot eight times, but is in stable condition, the mayor of La Verriere, Nicolas Dainville, told the Agence France-Press news agency.
The alleged shooter — a 39-year-old man, according to a source familiar with the case — was arrested in the nearby town of Coignieres.
Rabeh, who said the man was firing in a "relatively random" manner, noted that the person killed was "of African origin" and one of the wounded, "in critical condition, is of north African origin."
Prosecutors said they were investigating whether the acts targeted the "real or supposed race, ethnicity, nationality or religion" of the victims. They said they have opened an investigation for "murder in connection with a terrorist enterprise."
The mayor added that he did not want to say anything "definitive" about the motive yet but called it a "miracle" that there were not more casualties.
Bursts of gunfire and "loud bangs"
A police source told AFP that the gunman had fired in bursts from his vehicle around 10:30 a.m. local time.
Samy, a resident of Trappes, about 13 miles west of Paris, told AFP he saw a body on the ground from his window.
His mother, he said, saw a grey Renault Clio car speeding by and heard "loud bangs."
Writing on X, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said the case was "very serious" and that "all resources of the security forces and the judiciary are fully mobilised."
President Emmanuel Macron said "the nation is standing with" the victims of this "terrible ordeal."
Trappes previously experienced tensions after a teacher there reported receiving threats after writing that the state did not do enough to protect another teacher, Samuel Paty. Paty was beheaded by a radical Islamist in 2020 in another Paris suburb after he showed his class caricatures of the Prophet Mohammed.
France on edge after street violence and protests
The shooting came with France on edge following riots that erupted amid mass protests over the cost of living, which saw some of the worst street violence in recent years. Demonstrators, including students, labor union members and activists from France's "Yellow Vest" movement, are expected to take to the streets again Saturday.
French police have promised a larger presence to maintain order after a week of overnight curfews across the country. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said authorities would deploy some 70,000 law enforcement officers and gendarmes. Elite police units will help secure public buildings, he said. Other resources, including helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons, will also be deployed.
Nuñez said at a news conference that officials will be "absolutely uncompromising" with those involved in violence, looting or vandalism. Police will have a "very firm approach to making arrests, and there will be legal consequences," he said.
Major Paris museums, including the Louvre, will be closed. Art Basel Paris has canceled its weekend program due to safety concerns, the Associated Press reported.

Gunmen kill at least 7 in attack on Jordan church, authorities say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:39:27 UTC
22:39:27 KST

Gunmen kill at least 6 in attack on Jordan church, authorities say
Gunmen carried out a deadly attack on a church in southern Jordan on Friday, authorities said. The public security directorate initially said at least seven people were killed but later lowered the death toll to six.
Two assailants stormed the compound of a Greek Orthodox church in the village of Hammoud in Karak governorate before opening fire, the directorate said in a statement. Karak, home to a significant Christian community in the Muslim-majority kingdom, is 110 miles south of the capital, Amman.
The gunmen got out of a vehicle and opened fire during a funeral procession, the directorate added, saying a manhunt was underway for the perpetrators.
Minister of Government Communications Mohammed Al-Momani said security forces were investigating the attack.
An eyewitness told the kingdom's state broadcaster, Al-Mamlaka, that a vehicle arrived carrying the gunmen, who fired continuously for five minutes before fleeing the scene.
Between 150 and 200 people were in and around the church at the time, the witness said, adding most of the victims were aged between 50 and 70.
In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed the gunmen after a long standoff.

France unrest sparks travel jitters for Southeast Asian tourists
Safety alerts and riots lead to itinerary changes at a time when tourism from the region to France is experiencing an uneven recovery
3-MIN READ3-MIN
1
 Listen
Fatimah Zainal had already paid for her flights and accommodation when videos of the unrest in France made her jittery about the Paris leg of her European holiday.
“The videos definitely made me panic,” said Fatimah, who plans to visit the French capital solo from October 31 to November 3 after travelling through Belgium.
The press officer for an international organisation said the Malaysian government’s travel advisory gave her second thoughts, and changing her flight would cost up to an additional 1,200 ringgit (US$293).
Friends living in Paris encouraged her not to cancel, but she has told her travel agency she may need to change her plans if conditions do not improve.

‘Opportunistic’: experts weigh Manila’s minilateral agenda ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
14:00:14 UTC
23:00:14 KST

Advertisement
‘Opportunistic’: experts weigh Manila’s minilateral agenda ahead of Trump-Xi meeting
Philippine push for US-linked security ties alongside Asean chair duties triggers debate on regional unity and flexibility towards China
5-MIN READ5-MIN
 Listen
The Philippines’ dual push for stronger “minilateral” defence links and a more robust Asean security role is dividing analysts, with one calling the move “opportunistic”.
Some experts view Manila’s advocacy for the “Squad” alliance as a strategic opportunity to deepen core security partnerships while chairing the Association of Southeast Asian Nations. Others question how much actual weight is carried by this informal defence grouping – comprising the United States, the Philippines, Japan and Australia – which aims to counter China’s influence in the region.
They also caution that a flurry of US-led small-group diplomacy could undermine Asean’s centrality in a coming summit and leave Manila with less strategic leeway ahead of next month’s Trump-Xi talks.
In an exclusive interview with the South China Morning Post, Philippine ambassador to the US Jose Manuel Romualdez indicated that the Squad could meet on the sidelines of next month’s Asean summit in Manila.

Italy first in Europe to establish national plan against fentanyl says Meloni
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:45:19 CEST
22:45:19 KST

Italy is the first country in Europe
to establish a national plan against fentanyl, Premier Giorgia
Meloni said Friday.
                                    
"Prevention also means knowing how to act before a danger
escalates," she told a high-level international meeting on
addiction prevention and recovery—hosted by Italy and France,
co-founders of the European Coalition Against Drugs (ECAD)—held
at the San Patrignano rehabilitation community near Rimini.
                                    
"That is why I want to highlight that we were the first in
Europe to establish a national plan to combat the misuse of
fentanyl and synthetic opioids.
                                    
"We have trained personnel, made antidotes available, and
today," the Prime Minister added, "we are also strengthening
controls over the storage of these substances—particularly in
hospitals and healthcare facilities—to ensure they do not end up
in illegal channels, where they could turn thousands of people
into 'zombies'."

The Embassy in Lisbon presents the new version of the “L’Italia a Tavola” website
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
15:43:59 CEST
22:43:59 KST

The Italian Embassy in Lisbon presents the new version of “L’Italia a Tavola,” the website dedicated to discovering Italian cuisine in Portugal. Launched as part of “Italian Cuisine Week Around the World,” the project aims to promote Italian culinary traditions and businesses in the food and wine sector operating in the country.
                                    
Now in its third edition, the initiative has been revamped with a new design and a dedicated website, designed to make navigation simpler and more intuitive. Users can explore participating businesses by geographic area—including the North, Central Region, Greater Lisbon, the Algarve, and the Islands—or by category, with sections dedicated to restaurants, pizzerias, gelaterias, and retailers.
                                    
The platform is open to new participants and is continuously updated, with the goal of raising the profile of Italian businesses and strengthening the network of operators who promote Italian culinary culture in Portugal.

OPEC Fund approves record $250M loan for Istanbul North Rail Crossing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:51:23 UTC
22:51:23 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
23 October 2026•Update: 23 October 2026
The OPEC Fund for International Development has approved a $250 million loan for the Istanbul North Rail Crossing project, marking the largest single financing commitment in the institution’s history.
According to a fund statement, the loan is part of a broader approved package of up to $500 million to build a new railway bypassing the Istanbul metropolitan area.
The 127-kilometer (79-mile) double-track, electrified line will run between Cayirova on the Asian side and Catalca on the European side, crossing the Bosphorus via the Yavuz Sultan Selim Bridge.
Carrying both passengers and cargo, the link addresses a critical bottleneck in Asia-Europe rail traffic. Currently, freight trains only use the Marmaray tunnel during limited nighttime hours, restricting annual capacity to 3 million tons.
The new line will expand this to 50 million tons, cutting freight journey times between Cayirova and Catalca from 13 hours to 3.6 hours.
It will also link Istanbul Airport and Sabiha Gokcen Airport to the national rail network, reducing inter-airport transit time from two hours to 65 minutes.
Strengthening global trade corridors
The railway provides an integral missing link for three international rail-served trade corridors crossing Istanbul: the Trans-Caspian Middle Corridor linking China and Central Asia with Europe; the Iraq Development Road connecting Asia and the EU via the Middle East and Türkiye; and the Türkiye-EU corridor, which accounts for a third of Türkiye’s international trade.
Shifting freight from road to lower-carbon electrified rail will ease congestion and strengthen Türkiye’s position as a logistics hub linking Europe, Asia, and the Middle East.
The $8.3 billion project is backed by the Turkish government and a World Bank-led consortium including the Asian Development Bank (ADB), Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank (AIIB), Islamic Development Bank (IsDB), European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), and European Investment Bank (EIB).
"Türkiye has been an important partner of the OPEC Fund for nearly five decades," said OPEC Fund President Abdulhamid Alkhalifa, noting the record financing supports infrastructure that boosts connectivity and sustainable growth.
Since 1979, the OPEC Fund has approved nearly $850 million for Turkish projects across transport, agriculture, health, and energy.

Everyone walks in major drugs trial due to excessive delays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-23
13:44:45 UTC
22:44:45 KST

More than 30 defendants, including one of the Netherland’s most notorious career criminals, are free today following a court ruling that the case has dragged on far too long for a country governed by the rule of law
A Hasselt court has dropped charges against some 30 suspects in a criminal drugs manufacturing trial due to undue delay in the proceedings. It has been 10 years since the start of an investigation into a soap manufacturer in Lommel for the production and trafficking of MDMA, amphetamine and cocaine as well as the transportation of narcotics.
Among the suspects was John H, a drugs kingpin and one of the Netherlands’ most notorious criminals. Other charges in the case related to firearms offences and leadership of criminal organisations.
The court has identified several periods of unexplained inactivity, amounting to almost five years
“The active investigation by the federal police was completed in 2018,” announced the court. “The court subsequently identified several periods of unexplained inactivity, amounting to almost five years in total.”
The court said it could find no explanation for the delays in either the complexity of the case or the conduct of the defendants. The court ruled that there had been a “serious breach of the right to trial within a reasonable time”.
Such delays are not uncommon in the justice system, and often result in a reduced sentence. But this time the prosecution was declared inadmissible, allowed the defendants to walk away free. It’s an extremely rare decision and one that the public prosecutor’s office does not take lightly. It is appealing.
The court also took some of the defendants’ circumstances into account. Nine of them are now over 65, some have serious health problems, and others appear to have rebuilt their lives since the offences, without any further convictions. Almost all the defendants had also already spent time in pre-trial detention.
“The judgment does not constitute an assessment of the seriousness of the offences with which the defendants are charged,” said a court spokesperson, “although this was also taken into account when weighing up the interests at stake. It is a ruling on what a state governed by the rule of law owes defendants – proceedings within a reasonable time and a genuine opportunity to defend themselves.”
